This commentary was composed by synthesizing various interpretations. Originally, there were no topical outlines (*ke*). Now, if I were to add them, they would seem to contradict the original commentaries;
yet if I were to omit them, they would fail to elucidate the structural divisions of the sūtra’s prose. Therefore, I have employed...
Writing in small characters alongside the main text is called a "side-section" (pángkē), much like the marginal notes used by people today.

If one does not find such fine detail tedious, it is perfectly fine to enjoy its nuances from the side. If, however, one considers it overly cumbersome, one may simply read the main scripture and omit this section;
the choice between inclusion and exclusion should follow what is appropriate for the occasion, as it is merely a provisional expedient suited to the moment.
Now, since this commentary has already divided the sūtra according to its topical sections (*pārśva-krama*), the sūtra itself ought to follow the order of those sections.

However, the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) already possesses established chapter and section divisions; furthermore, as the commentary follows the sūtra, the placement of the subject matter (*karma*) must adhere to fixed conventions and cannot be further subdivided.

Therefore, there are instances where the sūtra text that should logically appear earlier is instead placed later, and where the topical section that should logically appear later is instead placed earlier.
It is placed before you; readers may understand it according to their own insight.
In this commentary on the sutra text, where a single character is written in a large and lofty script, it is intended to honor the golden mouth of the Buddha.

The *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Meaning) transcribes one character of the sūtra in large script; that the present sub-commentary (*shū*) and the commentary (*jiě*) are written side by side in small script is intended to honor the ancients.
The intention is that those who read this sūtra may find the sūtra itself so clear that the commentary can be omitted;
and if the commentary is clear, the sub-commentary may likewise be omitted. To employ it when appropriate and to set it aside when not—this is to remain non-adapted yet never non-conforming.
It is acceptable.
Within this *Huìjiě* (Collected Explanations), there is not a lack of praise or criticism.

The reason I have not dared to arbitrarily add or subtract anything is that I reflect upon how, during the initial drafting stages, Master Tianru had already eliminated more than half [of the errors] when he compiled his *Huìjiě*. If I were now to further...
To omit these would seem to leave later students entirely ignorant of where the ancients applied their minds.
Even within the commentaries and exegeses of former masters, there are still points not yet fully incorporated; yet, they truly illuminate the meaning of the sutras.
I have now extracted them once more and used small characters for them, fearing that I might dilute or diminish their significance.
This is the "milk flavor" of the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Meaning). As for the mention of "Master So-and-so," one should know that this is not an act of plagiarism;
occasionally, passages from his own commentary are interspersed with those of others so that the literary meaning remains continuous.
Regarding the discernment of right and wrong, it is difficult to arbitrarily apply the "yellowing and whitening" (i.e., revision) of one’s own personal opinions.
Only when there are temporal circumstances that may cause mutual obstruction, or when principles and practices are in conflict, should one clarify and rectify what is erroneous.
Beyond this, one should simply leave matters as they are.
That this commentary selects only the ancient masters and omits the contemporary ones is not intended to say that the ancients were right and the moderns were wrong.
This is because the writings of each master constitute a distinct school of thought;
if all were included, the volumes would become excessively numerous, yet if too few were taken, it might give rise to resentment among people. For these reasons, I have desisted.

This commentary also contains passages where it engages in debate with the present master; thus, it serves as a firm citadel for our own school and a deep, warm moat for its comprehensive interpretation.
As for the single bend of the great river of our own house or the tiny flaw in the beautiful jade of another school—how can these withstand public scrutiny?
How can they uphold our family tradition? Furthermore, this does not hinder the "Yang" of those who might raise such objections.
Autumn. Like blowing upon a hair to find a flaw, or pushing aside the sun to seize the shade—how could the brilliant three-foot sword yield to such pretenses?
Preface to the *Combined Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, by the Lion Grove śramaṇa Weize.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the life-blood of the wisdom of all Buddhas, the thorough path for sentient beings, the grand mainstay of the Dharma-net, and the essential gateway of the Chan school.
Since the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, his dispensation throughout the five periods has been nothing other than for the sake of this one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa*).
To seek that which universally encompasses the capacities of those to be transformed, directly points to the essence of the mind, and proclaims the truth—this is it.

In its ultimate nature (*paramārtha*), it distinguishes and establishes true reality through perfect penetration, enabling one to transform objects and transcend the stage of no-more-learning with a mere snap of the fingers;
thus, nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama*. To explain its name:

"the ultimate solidity of all phenomena" refers to that which thoroughly reaches the source of dharmas—unmoving and indestructible—and constitutes the secret cause of the Tathāgata and the myriad [practices] of the Bodhisattvas.
There is no practice that does not take its beginning from this and find its ultimate consummation in this alone. Examining what it elucidates:
it expounds the perfect principle to clarify true nature and opens up the perfect practice to demonstrate true cultivation. As for this nature, both essence and function are manifested together;
as for this cultivation, cause and fruit are realized in unison. This is the explanation of the doctrine that traces the origin and examines the end. It is truly because...
Those who practice the path may turn their backs on the truth and head toward delusion, failing to achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Some may cherish the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and consider minor attainments sufficient; others may fail to eliminate the outflows of desire while accumulating learning, thereby turning it into a fault.

Thus, Ānanda, taking his extensive learning and improper attachments as conditions, the Great Teaching was precipitously brought forth. And the World-Honored One first addressed him, saying: "All sentient beings..."
The continuous succession of birth and death arises entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.
By employing various false thoughts—because these thoughts are not true—there is cyclic transmigration. Furthermore, it is said:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the single gate through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend to reach wondrous adornment."

The Path. Is this not the fundamental principle for practicing this single Dharma? From this, one breaks through the攀缘 (pān-yuán, objective attachments) of the seven locations and distinguishes the two kinds of roots.
Because seeing reveals the mind, and because the mind reveals seeing—though mind and seeing manifest each other, the primary manifestation lies in the mind.
It is like using the metaphor of a blind man staring into darkness to show that seeing is not the eye; it is like bending one's fingers to test the flight of light to verify seeing.
Unmoving, he contemplates that the river is unchanging, comparable to the hand hanging down without omission. He discerns through the "eight returns" and selects among all things;
it neither expands nor contracts, and there is neither right nor wrong. This causes one to realize that the pure, perfect true mind is falsely manifested as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing.
Having realized that these are false manifestations, one may still doubt their intermingling; therefore, he further refutes the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Through causes and conditions, it is shown that what is perceived as seeing is not actually seeing. By combining individual karmic actions with the commonality of shared experience (*sabhāgatā*), it points out that seeing arises from delusion.

Furthermore, by using one person as an example for many people, and one country as an example for all countries, it generally reveals that the objective world (*bhājana-loka*) and the physical bodies of sentient beings (*indriya-śarīra*) are collectively nothing but a single delusion.
Proceeding from the shallow to the deep, and from the narrow to the broad, although various methods are employed to reveal this delusion, [the ultimate truth remains...]

To manifest that it is solely the True [Suchness], he further cites the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), and extensively the seven great elements, fusing them into the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

This causes one to realize that things and self share the same root and that right and wrong are of one substance; that they are delusive and lack intrinsic nature, and that the entire body is itself the True.
Thus, the phenomena of the support and the supported within the ten realms are merely manifestations arising in accordance with karma. Having realized this...

Since the deluded wandering has already been set in motion, he further answers the challenge regarding the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, profoundly investigating the causes of their arising.
He uses the analogy of empty space, which does not obstruct the manifestation of all forms, to reveal that the wondrous, true, awakened clarity perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.
The one and the many correspond to each other; the small and the large contain one another. Being both essence and function, they are neither conventional nor ultimate.
As for transcending identity and non-identity, as well as being and non-being—then the wondrous nature of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) transcends all names and words.

Furthermore, he cites the analogy of a madman running while looking in a mirror to show that delusion has no cause. He concludes by rebuking mere erudition and exhorting the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*), speaking in general terms.
These are all matters of perfect principle. Although understanding may be perfect, it cannot be realized without practice; therefore, he further clarifies the two definitive meanings.
First, he examines the initial arousal of the bodhicitta in the causal stage, wherein the subduing and severing of ignorance is the essential requirement for cultivation.

Second, he examines the root of afflictions, intending to select the faculty of perfect capacity as the basis for initiating practice. Thereupon, he determines the relative superiority and inferiority of the six faculties.
He caused [practitioners] to enter deeply through a single gate; he struck a bell to verify the permanence [of the auditory faculty], and tied a cloth to demonstrate the formation of knots.
He set forth the Dharma-gates realized by the twenty-five sages and commanded that the faculty of hearing be selected as the expedient means for beginners.
Furthermore, he taught the rules for collecting the mind, the establishment of the *dōjō*, and finally, the fourfold precepts and the *dhāraṇī* of the Light on the Crown. Generally speaking...

All these constitute the practice of perfection (*pūrṇa-caryā*). Even up to the point where one achieves the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi through the three progressive advancements, although this discusses the stages of realization (*sākṣāt-kriyā-bhūmi*), it does not exhaust the causal practices.

From the observance of precepts and karma down to the cultivation of mental states regarding the seven destinies, and from the prevention of meditative concentration against the demons of the five aggregates and false views—all are matters of the gate of practice. One must ultimately aim for their complete fulfillment.
Enlightenment returns to non-attainment; only then can it be called the ultimate, steadfast realization.

Thus, based on the principle of ultimate steadfastness, one establishes the practice of ultimate steadfastness; by cultivating the practice of ultimate steadfastness, one realizes the principle of ultimate steadfastness.
Such is, in general, the essential teaching of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. It is therefore known that:
The three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle are all designated as *Śūraṅgama*. No definitive exposition (*nītārtha*) surpasses this.

Those who have categorized the sutra take the principle and practice together as the primary teaching (*mūla-siddhānta*), and divide the primary teaching into five sections: first, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); second, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);

third, the realization of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*); fourth, the conclusion of the sutra; and fifth, the auxiliary path (*upāya-mārga*). This means that after the path of seeing, one cultivates the path of cultivation, and after the path of cultivation...
That this is the standard sequence for realizing the fruit is indeed so;

yet, when examining the cultivation and realization of those of superior faculties, we find that after the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is revealed, it is said that one attains the *dharmakāya* without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Furthermore, prior to entering the jeweled hall, it is said that doubts are eliminated and the mind awakens to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). How could such cases be restricted by the common rule? How magnificent is the Teaching!
Now, those who wish to give rise to the truth, return to the source, clarify the mind, and perceive their nature should apply themselves with all their heart to this.

Yet, there is no teaching in this scripture that is not included, and no capacity for understanding that is not encompassed. Sometimes the words appear partial while the meaning is complete; sometimes the names are identical while the essence differs.
Those of dull and inferior capacity may fail to comprehend it; thus, those who propagate the sutra reflect upon how to bring about such understanding and proceed to provide commentaries.
From the Tang through the Song dynasties, there have been some ten or more such commentators.
Initially, I encountered the expositions of Master Changshui Xuan, Master Gushan Yuan, Master Letan Yue, and Master Wenling Huan; furthermore, I perused the works of Master Wuxing Yue.
The masters gathered together, including Xingfu Ku, Zizhong Yun, Zhenji Jie, and Xiali Min; the intentions of these various masters were for the most part in complete agreement.
Only because their perspectives followed individual strengths did minor differences arise, which caused practitioners to weep at the fork in the road, unable to distinguish the true guide.
Thus, the calamity of failing to reach the goal does not lie with them.

It all depends on this. Now, I have compiled the essential commentaries of various schools to clarify the general course. Where interpretations differ from what is accepted by the public, I have abridged them;
where they differ yet are mutually compatible, I have preserved both; and where they challenge one another, I have examined their authoritative sources and adopted the most accurate.
In instances where there are omissions, obscurities, or contradictions, I have further appended my own observations.
As a supplementary note: because diverse streams, when united, all return to the sea, this work is called the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation).
Alas! The Way is fundamentally wordless, yet it is not revealed without words; thus the Buddha had no choice but to speak.
If words fail to reach the Way and the Way cannot thereby be clarified, then the words of the various masters could not help but be employed as well. Since words have become numerous and divergent...
As one moves further away from the Way, how could those who provide commentaries and expositions allow themselves to remain stagnant?

Once the expositions have been understood, it is hoped that readers will, through these commentaries, come to know the words of others, and through the words of others, come to know the words of the Buddha.
When the words of the Buddha are known, that which is ultimate and firm is attained. These are what are called practice, principle, teaching, and...
To speak of "Chan" as the realization of the Way and "wisdom-life" (hui-ming) is already superfluous talk; how much more so regarding what are called "understanding" and "realization.
On the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the second year of the Zhizheng era, the year Renwu (1362), the śramaṇa Weize of Luling composed this at Shizi Lin within the city of Gusu.
In the past, when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai heard that this sutra existed in the Western Regions, he gazed westward day and night, vowing to see it, yet he did not live to do so.
Toward the end of the Chang’an era during the reign of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāmitra first brought the Sanskrit manuscript from the South Sea to Guangzhou.
It was there that he met with the Chancellor Fang Rong, who was serving as the Superintendent of the Southern Examination.
He was invited to the Zhizhi Monastery to translate it, where he served as the scribe (*bishou*).

On the thirtieth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Shenlong era (the year of Yisi) during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, the scripture was completed; a copy was transcribed and submitted to the throne.
As the court was beset by many troubles, there was no leisure for its promulgation. At that time, Chan Master Shouxu entered the inner palace chapel and saw the manuscript that had been submitted.
It was transcribed and brought back to Dumen Temple in Jingzhou. At that time, Dharma Master Huizhen visited Dumen Temple and obtained it;

he began the transmission. In the tenth year of the Tianbao era, Dharma Master Weiqu at Xingfu Temple in the Western Capital further obtained a manuscript of the oral transcription from the former Chancellor Fang Rong’s residence, whereupon he first composed a commentary (*shu*) to expand upon it.
This was transmitted down through the ages. Following this, masters such as Changshui, Gushan, and Wuxing successively elucidated it, so that the commentaries became increasingly detailed.
Nevertheless, students were sometimes hindered by this abundance of detail and unable to explore them all thoroughly.
Now, with the emergence of the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary) by Chan Master Tiantú Rénzhī of Shizilin, one need not wait to explore them all extensively for the many [teachings] to be revealed.
The beauty [of this work] is fully present; without the need for laborious investigation, all doubts are naturally dispelled.
As for the convenience of recitation and study, nothing is more convenient than this. I, a fool, have associated with the Master for a long time.

From the time he began to compile and synthesize the various schools, weighing their merits and demerits, until the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) was completed—spanning three years—all of this was witnessed by my own eyes. Thus, I am also somewhat familiar with it.
There have been those who have rendered great service to this scripture.
Now, having raised funds to carve it into woodblocks for circulation, I have further recorded the years and months in which the scripture arrived. Recorded by the śramaṇa Keli of Linchuan.
List of Names of Various Masters of Teaching and Chan Cited in the *Huìjiě* (Wholeness Commentary) (Dates unknown; recorded here provisionally based on what has been heard):

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa,
and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume One (also known as:
The Scripture of the Great Maṇḍala of Nālandā in Central India, Extracted and Circulated Separately from the Abhiṣeka Section).
The Combined Explanation by the Śramaṇa Weizé of Shizi Lin and the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Tiantai on the *Yuantong Shu* [Commentary]. [Explanation] Wēn-líng says:
"The fruit-body of the Tathāgata is such that its essence is inherently so; why should it depend upon secret causes? This refers to the path and function of the Bodhisattva."
Its function is non-action; what could constitute the myriad practices? There is no cause and no practice, no cultivation and no realization, and neither enlightenment nor non-enlightenment.
Names and characteristics, whether great or small, are all not established; this is the true Śūraṅgama, the ultimate and adamantine state.

It is simply because the Tathāgata is hidden within the *ālayavijñāna* (the store-consciousness) of sentient beings that he is not revealed except through the secret cause. [The bodhi of] sentient beings...
Sentient beings have sunk into the seven realms of existence; there is nothing among the myriad practices they do not cultivate.
Thus, the Buddha-King reveals to them the Great Dharma so that they may not be deluded by minor paths and may silently attain the essence that transcends all boundaries.

He employs the metaphor of the *uṣṇīṣa* (Buddha’s crown) so that they do not stagnate in the perception of forms, yet his subtlety reaches the ultimate state of the Unsurpassed. He points directly to the secret cause of the Tathāgata.
It clarifies that the fundamental wondrous mind is the primary cause upon which all Buddhas of the three periods rely;

it elucidates the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, enabling one to awaken to the ultimate Dharma and know that all sages rely upon this to realize the fruit, even unto the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices of a Bodhisattva.
Thus, there is not a single phenomenal phenomenon that does not ultimately reach the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

It is firm and indestructible; therefore, it is named *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
A "sūtra" (*jing*) is merely the text that expresses [the meaning]. To express is like a trap for catching fish.
Knowing that the sutra is a fish-trap, those who follow it and interpret it are all merely using the trap; it is not the fish itself.
Students must be careful not to mistake the trap for the fish, and only then can the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* be truly attained. Tianru’s Supplemental Commentary states:
In Sanskrit, *śūraṅgama* is the general name for the Great Samādhi. This is translated as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.
An ancient master said: "Before one has cultivated this samādhi, all phenomena appear distinct and are bound by those very dharmas.
When this samādhi is attained, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, form, and space—all phenomena—[become thus]."
Abiding in quiescence is precisely the eternally abiding nature of mind; therefore, it is called "ultimately firm and solid. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in its own place;
the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. National Teacher Shao said: "There is no dharma outside the mind;
the green mountains filling one's eyes are also this very meaning. This concludes the brief explanation of the title of the sūtra. As for the translation and the transcription of the oral dictation:

Regarding the provenance [of this text] and such matters as its structural divisions and topical outlines, since there are already clear explanations by various masters, I shall not cite them at length here.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This sutra is titled according to both person and dharma; it concerns the eternally abiding true mind known and perceived by the Buddha.

Its essence is the Buddha’s ability to know, see, and perceive with perfect clarity the Buddha-nature; its thesis is the revelation of the true knowledge and vision of the Buddha-dharma realm by shattering the deluded knowledge and vision of the nine dharma realms;
and its pedagogical characteristic is the "melted butter" (sarpis) of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Regarding the first [part], "naming by way of person and dharma": "person" refers to the person of fruition and the person of cause, such as the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva;
"dharma" refers to the dharma of fruition and the dharma of cause, such as the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the secret cause, and the myriad practices.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, which is the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, encompasses both cause and fruit in its entirety. This is what is indicated at the outset by the title of this sutra.
Regarding the term *Dàfóding* (Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa), there are many divergent interpretations. Some explain it solely from the perspective of the dharmas:
for instance, Master Yihai states that "Great" refers to the Dharmakāya, "Buddha" to Prajñā, and "Uṣṇīṣa" to Vimukti.

While such an explanation may be logically sound, it does not satisfy common sense, as it involves breaking the phrasing by assigning meanings to individual characters. Others explain it solely through metaphorical interpretation.
As Master Wenling said, he used the metaphor of the Buddha’s crown to prevent one from becoming stuck in the perception of forms.
Although such an explanation may be called skillful, it does not accord with the scriptural text, for the scripture does not state, "It is just like the Buddha’s crown.
Furthermore, there are those who explain it solely through the dharma of the crown, as various masters such as Juefan do when they claim this scripture is supreme.

Because it concerns the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Crown, [the previous interpretation] may be considered skillful, yet it ultimately remains somewhat forced. Now, I shall provide a direct explanation based on the facts;
by using these facts to encompass the underlying principle, we can still subsume the partial views of various schools.

For "Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata" fundamentally refers to the manifested Buddha appearing within the crown of the World-Honored One’s head. At that time, Ānanda was undergoing the defilement of the evil [spirit], and although his mind—
Though one may possess clear understanding, if one’s power is not autonomous, one will encounter bondage because of attachment to signs regarding the meaning. As the subsequent text says:
"Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts. When the Tathāgata provides rescue, the transformed Buddha within his crown recites the mantra;
because the meaning is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one is able to attain liberation. As the subsequent text says: "Why must you wait for me?"

"This is the Buddha-peak Divine Mantra that brings you liberation. Ānanda, seeing the Buddha, prostrated himself in worship and wept with grief as he entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the primary expedient means of the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* by which they attained Bodhi.

This was truly an instance of cherishing the excellence of the fruit in order to give rise to a longing for it, and seeking the cause through the realization of the result. Thus, this is what Ānanda took as his fundamental principle.

This is liberation. As for the wondrous medicine that addresses illness and the excellent ferry that rescues from suffering, nothing is more honored than the Transformation Buddha within the crown of the head.
When the Tathāgata attained Bodhi, was this not precisely what is titled the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata"?
Therefore, the Tathāgata is liberation among the three virtues. What is called the "Great Buddha" is the subtle and wondrous wisdom of Śākyamuni’s recompense-body.

This refers to the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Since "Buddha" carries the meaning of "awakening," it corresponds to *prajñā* among the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The specific mention of "Great" (*mahat*) signifies that this is the fruition (*vipāka*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because one is able to attain the Dharma-body, one is called a "Great Buddha" when referring to a Buddha, a "Great Bodhisattva" when referring to a Bodhisattva, and a "Great Person" (*mahāpuruṣa*) when referring to an ordinary person;
from the very beginning, there has been no distinction between them. For this reason, the title is established at the outset.
To speak of it as "Great" is to reveal the very foundation of Ānanda’s liberation. Why is this?

Because liberation is realized through *prajñā*, and *prajñā* is perfected by means of the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, for those who aspire to liberation, there is nothing more fundamental than cultivating *prajñā*;
for those who cultivate *prajñā*, there is nothing more fundamental than awakening to the *dharmakāya*. Thus, prior to this sūtra—
Throughout these three fascicles, there is nothing that does not clarify the matter of the dharmakāya inherently possessed by sentient beings.
When it says, "If your dharmakāya were thus to ultimately undergo extinction, who then would cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas? the intent is perfectly clear.

Therefore, when Ānanda describes his realization, he specifically states, "I have attained the dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*"; is this not a demonstration of the very foundation of liberation?

From the fourth fascicle to the sixth, there is nothing that does not clarify matters pertaining to *prajñā* (wisdom). From the seventh fascicle to the tenth, there is nothing that does not clarify matters pertaining to *vimukti* (liberation).
This is because *prajñā* belongs to the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), while *vimukti* belongs to the realm of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Nevertheless, the mutual identity of these three dharmas is also reflected and explained throughout; for instance, the second fascicle states: "In *śamatha*, [one perceives] the subtle..."
Even with secret contemplation and observation, the mind has not yet been fully realized. The fifth fascicle states: "The perfect luminosity of emptiness constitutes the liberation of dharmas.
Once dharmas have been liberated, both are empty and do not arise. Is this speaking of the Dharmakāya encompassing Prajñā, and Prajñā encompassing Vimukti?
As for discussing the essential points of practice, these three dharmas must necessarily coexist, as it is said: "Seeing the seeing."
At that time, what is seen is not true seeing; even seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. The first instance of the character "seeing" (jiàn) refers to *prajñā*;
the second instance of the character "seeing" refers to the *dharmakāya*; and "even seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it" refers to liberation (*vimukti*).
It is further said: "If one extracts a single root according to its nature and detaches it from its clinging so that it recedes inwardly, then all dark appearances can never again cause obscuration."
To pull out even a single root is *prajñā*. To suppress it within is the *dharmakāya*. It can never again be obscured;
this is *vimukti*. Furthermore, it is said: "Entering the stream and losing the object. Entering is *prajñā*. The stream is the *dharmakāya*. Losing the object is *vimukti*.
Therefore, this great character constitutes the central theme of the entire sutra. What it says is: "The hundred-thousandfold clear and pure great ocean;

the seeing-nature that is all-encompassing and pervades the lands of the ten directions; the unmoving, all-encompassing, wondrous True Suchness-nature; pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the Dharma-realm;
each and every one knowing for themselves that their own mind pervades the ten directions. All of these are expounded from this great character.
It emerges. Indeed, that which this sutra venerates is the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*). Is it not as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"I shall place all my children within the secret treasury, and before long, I too shall enter therein myself"?
Therefore, the Great Buddha’s finger points to the Lord of the Sutra; he touches the invisible crown-mark (*anavalokitamūrdha*) of Śākyamuni. Within the crown of the Tathāgata...
This is the manifested Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*). "Great" refers to the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*), "Pinnacle" (*śikhin*) refers to Prajñā, and "Tathāgata" refers to Liberation;
thus, the Tathāgata is the most supreme liberation within liberation. If explained in this manner, the meaning of the "Ocean of Meanings" is established.
If one does not stagnate in the perception of signs but instead honors the Pinnacle-dharma alone, then the teachings of the two masters are also fully realized. This is indeed so.
To have both the phrasing and the meaning coincide without resorting to metaphors may indeed be called a source of great joy in the exposition of a title.

As for the term "mysterious cause" (mi-yin), it refers to Ānanda’s regret over his mere erudition and his weariness with bondage; looking up toward liberation, he requested the method for cultivation.
Although this belongs to the realm of cultivation, this very cultivation is itself the nature (*xing*). To manifest the nature so as to perfect cultivation—this is precisely what is meant. Therefore:
The first two fascicles of the sutra define its nature by means of the eye; the Bodhisattva Pumen elucidates its cultivation by means of the ear.
To speak specifically of "esoteric" (mi) is merely to do so in contrast to delusion. From the perspective of awakening, the entire esoteric is manifest.
Just as the ten meanings of seeing one's nature are majestically and uniquely revealed—what else could this be but the wondrous nature of the Dharmakāya? Now, let us borrow a metaphor.
The word "releasing" (*śe*) makes the meaning easy to manifest, being as subtle and dense as the honey within a flower. The flavor of honey is exceedingly sweet, yet it is hidden within the blossom;
people see only the flower and overlook the honey, whereas only the clever bee follows the flower to sip it. This honey is called *amṛta* (ambrosia);
when humans obtain and consume it, it heals their ailments and prolongs their lives. It is like the trees that grow and produce [honey] in the garden of Śakra-devendra.

The nectar of immortality (*amṛta*): when the various devas partake of it together, they all attain deathlessness and long life. It is the same with the six faculties of sensory reception of sentient beings:
the physical forms of the coarse faculties are manifest like flowers, while the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness is like the nectar of immortality.
One who can awaken to this immediately attains non-arising (*anutpāda*). As the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* says:
"Compassion is the stem, wisdom is the leaf, samādhi is the filament, and liberation is the blossom; the Bodhisattva bee-king feeds upon the nectar—I now pay homage to the Buddha-lotus.
This also serves to realize this very meaning. Regarding "cultivation and realization," speaking in general terms, it is not [the case that] at the time of cultivation...
Realization is not contingent upon cultivation; rather, seeking it further, one finds that the present secret cause is entirely Buddha-nature.

To realize this is called cultivation, for there is no cultivation other than this. Thus, at the very moment of cultivation there is realization, and at the very moment of realization there is cultivation.

As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings have already realized perfect enlightenment"—this is what that means. Furthermore, "realization" refers to the realization of verification.

Clarification: This is because the principle of unarisen permanence can be verified through the very phenomena of the six sense-faculties of experience belonging to sentient beings—whether they remain unmoving or do not undergo transition—and thus serves as proof.
If one follows Master Wenling’s interpretation, there are two points where his explanation of cultivation and realization contradicts the title [of the sutra]:
first, the Tathāgata originally took the *Śūraṅgama* (Heroic March) as the primary focus of cultivation and realization; [second, Master Wenling]... [text fragment].

Ling [Huiyuan] thus took non-cultivation and non-realization as the true Śūraṅgama; however, the intent of the Sūtra is fundamentally that the very state of cultivation and realization being without cultivation or realization constitutes the Śūraṅgama.
This is like how names and categories of cause and effect must correspond with certainty. It is like the nature of delusion having no substance and thus nothing upon which it can rely.
When one wishes to restore the truth, the moment the "true" is sought, it is already not the true suchness-nature.
These are all its intended meanings. Wēnlíng, however, maintains that having cultivation and realization constitutes a non-genuine Śūraṅgama;
since this does not accord with the perfect principle, it is not adopted here. The Sūtra reveals this meaning as the Mahāyāna among Mahāyānas and the Sudden-Perfect among the Sudden-Perfects.
Because it proclaims the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the supreme meanings, it is called "definitive" (nītārtha).

Regarding the statement that "the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas" are the secret cause of the Tathāgata: although it is said above that these are the secret cause of the Tathāgata, one must know that they are in fact the secret cause of sentient beings.
For when one is deluded, one is a sentient being; when one realizes them, one is a Tathāgata—there is no Tathāgata apart from this.

By analogy, if one is currently deluded regarding this, one is a sentient being; if one cultivates them, one is a Bodhisattva—there is no Bodhisattva apart from this. This is the aforementioned secret cause.
This is the true essence of the myriad practices, while the myriad practices themselves are the auxiliary functions of the secret cause.

Essence and function mutually possess one another, and the primary and auxiliary aspects are fully integrated. Indeed, this secret cause is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; by invoking it, the whole is encompassed, leaving no need for separate cultivation.
Even if one were to cultivate separately, one would never depart from this samādhi. This is what is meant by the unmoving state of quiescent realization manifesting in all things.
Regarding the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), the Sūtra states that there is samādhi which fulfills the ten thousand practices; how could one possibly rely on separate cultivation?
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* exists in two different translations: one translates it as "the vigorous discernment of characteristics," whereby its meaning belongs to practice (*caryā*);
the other translates it as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena," whereby its meaning belongs to principle (*tattva*). Both of these are expressed through verbal designations.

When explained and analyzed, its meaning pertains to the teaching (*śāsana*). As the ancient masters maintained—that the teaching, practice, and principle are all designated as *Śūraṅgama*—this is indeed trustworthy and verifiable.

Seeking [the meaning] through this, one finds that the single title serves as the general designation for the entire work, while the specific explanations of teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit are none other than the ultimate and adamantine. Furthermore, this...
If one investigates the ultimate purport of these nineteen characters in the title of the sutra, they are not without their secondary and primary meanings;

in essence, they are all established as "secret causes. This means: revealing cultivation through nature, revealing cause through fruit, revealing practice through teaching, revealing the Dharma through the person, and revealing the primary through the auxiliary.
Regarding "revealing cultivation through nature": "Great" refers to the Dharmakāya, and "Buddha" refers to Prajñā. "Crown" (mūrdhan) [refers to the stage of]...
This is liberation itself. These three natures are used to manifest the three cultivations: the Dharma-body is *dhyāna*, Prajñā is *śamatha*, and liberation is *samādhi*.
That cultivation arises entirely from nature and that cultivation is entirely within nature is the secret cause of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa.
To manifest the cause by means of the fruit: the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is *dhyāna*, and the Saṃbhogakāya Tathāgata is...
The Tathāgata of the Body of Essential Nature (Svabhāvakāya) is precisely the Tathāgata of the Ocean of the Fruit Transcending the Cause and the Source of the Cause Penetrating the Fruit;
this is the secret cause of the Tathāgata. To manifest practice through the teaching: it is not that the teachings of definitive meaning do not expound the principle of definitive meaning.

Without the principle of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the practice of definitive meaning cannot arise. Teaching, practice, and principle—these three are all designated as the *Śūraṅgama* (Heroic March), the definitive and secret cause.
To manifest the Dharma through the person is to show that this secret cause is what is cultivated by the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle].
That is to say, "I have also realized it from within this; it is not only the secret cause of Avalokiteśvara and the other Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, as for "to assist in manifesting the correct": if one can correctly cultivate the secret cause, one will be able to fulfill the myriad practices;

these myriad practices are themselves the secret cause. The *Śūraṅgama* (Heroic March) is precisely a praise of this secret cause as the ultimate Great Samādhi, which is collectively termed the "Secret Cause of Śūraṅgama.
Therefore, these nineteen characters serve to mutually illuminate the secondary and the primary, and to interrelate the guest and the host.
Yan: "Examining [the title] separately, the general purport of this single sutra is thus fully exhausted; hence it is called 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa,' and so forth.
The above constitutes the specific title of the sutra, while [the following] is its general designation. The Sanskrit term *sūtra* is here translated as "Sutra of Accordance" (*qijing*).

This means that above it accords with the principle of the Buddha, and below it accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Furthermore, it instructs on the Dharma and instructs on the eternal; it penetrates and encompasses.
"Eternal" refers to the path that guides all Buddhas, while "Dharma" refers to the model of virtue for the myriad spirits.

"Encompassing" means to gather these profound meanings, and "penetrating" means to uphold the principles without loss. Because they were proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, they are called *sūtras*. Master Juefan cited this.
The *Shuowen* says: "In weaving, there is the warp (*jing*) and the weft (*wei*). The warp remains constant while the weft varies.
Now, the warp serves merely as the warp, and it is the weft that completes it; thus, what the warp cannot express must be clarified by the person who employs it.
Therefore, Confucius valued the spiritual resonance (*shen*), for its manifestation depends upon the individual.
Regarding the second point—that the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision takes the eternally abiding true mind as its essence—there are four general meanings.

First, it serves as the foundational premise of the sutra; at the very outset of the text, it states that all sentient beings fail to attain liberation precisely because they do not know this eternally abiding true mind.
Second, it is the central theme of the sutra, as demonstrated by such passages as the examination of the unshakable nature of seeing through the "fingering of light."
The vision of the river does not shift from childhood to old age; thus, up to the fourth fascicle, it clarifies that the eternally abiding true mind is such.
Third, verifying the truths through wisdom: its essence is the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom, the dharma that exhausts all things to the ultimate.
Since it says, "I unite with the Tathāgatagarbha through non-extinction and non-arising," that which is able to exhaust [all things] is eternally abiding; therefore, that which is exhausted...

How could this not be permanent? Fourth, one examines the essence by means of the thesis: since the essence is that to which the thesis returns, if the thesis is permanent, the essence should likewise be permanent.

As the Sūtra says: "If, during the causal stage, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for cultivation, yet seeks a fruit that is neither born nor extinguished, such a thing is impossible.
Since the thesis of cause and effect must be permanent, [the essence must also be so].

As for abiding: how could the essence to which one returns not be permanent? Furthermore, since the causes for the manifestation of practice according to the capacity of the practitioner must fully possess the three meanings of perfection, roundness, and constancy, it is all the more necessary to take the permanently abiding true mind as the essence.
Regarding the third point—that the Buddha’s ability to know, see, and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature constitutes the central thesis:
adopting this as the thesis not only ensures a comprehensive inclusion of all phenomena, but its textual meaning is also manifestly clear. As stated at the very beginning of the sutra:
"They do not know the eternally abiding true mind. This indicates that by speaking of "not knowing," one reveals "knowing. At the outset of the inquiry into the mind, it is said to be "mind alone."
"Where is he now? The disciple requested, "Please cause my wondrous, luminous mind to awaken and open my eye of the Way.
The Tathāgata granted, "You shall obtain the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature of pure, luminous mind; you shall attain the eye of purity. In the fourth fascicle, it says:
"Using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Regarding the request to enter the jeweled house, it says: "Obtaining the *dhāraṇī*, one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
[The Buddha] saw [this]. The Tathāgata replied: "Those who cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
The five-fascicle version states: "To establish knowledge within knowledge and vision is the root of ignorance; that knowledge and vision are without seeing—this is *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, "knowledge and vision" is a brief mention that encompasses all six sense faculties. Therefore, it is said that the root of the fetters of birth and death, and the wondrous permanence of peace and bliss, are both these six [faculties].
The faculties are not separate from other things; however, the faculties must encounter their objects, and upon such encounter, consciousness necessarily arises.
Thus, the Sūtra states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attain Bodhi by practicing within each of the eighteen realms. This clearly explains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Regarding the statement that his inclusion of phenomena is exhaustive and complete: since his knowledge and vision are already complete, [it extends to] the six faculties, beginning with the ear.
The faculties (*indriya*) are contained therein. Since it is said that "knowing-seeing is non-seeing," this is itself *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, these six faculties must all take the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi as their basis before the knowledge-and-vision of Buddhahood can be realized.
When the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to select the faculty of hearing, it was because although there are many gateways to the Path, how could a beginner enter them all? Therefore, he [instructed him].
One need only enter deeply through a single gate; once one has entered one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once.
However, there must necessarily be a vital point regarding the gate one enters. If one attains that vital point, it will differ from those with incomplete faculties by a factor of many eons.
Among the sentient beings of this region, only the faculty of hearing is most acute; therefore, Mañjuśrī selected this in accordance with their capacities.

The "Perfect Penetration of the Auditory Faculty" (*śrotra-indriya-pariśuddhi*) is the essential gateway for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it does not mean that perfect penetration refers solely to the auditory faculty.
This is analogous to the *Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Mohe Zhiguan), where one who begins practice must first cultivate the internal mind.

Therefore, among the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], one sets aside the bases and elements; furthermore, within the five aggregates, one excludes the first four and specifically takes up the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

It serves as the object of contemplation. It is like setting aside the *zhang* to focus on the *chi*, or setting aside the *chi* to focus on the *cun*; it is like cutting down a tree by reaching its root, or treating an ailment by finding the correct acupuncture point.
Thousands of branches and hundreds of ailments will naturally wither away; they are largely the same, differing only in minor details.

As for the phrase "clearly seeing the Buddha-nature," this refers to the eternally abiding true mind (*nitya-citta*) explained in the sutra, which is like the "ten meanings of seeing the nature" regarding the faculty of hearing.
These three dharmas are all the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings. Within the sense-gates, they are not at all unclear;
one sees them with perfect clarity and hears them with perfect clarity. To be able to realize this is to be a Buddha; it is to know and see with perfect clarity.
Regarding the Buddha-nature, there is no separate Buddha-knowledge or Buddha-vision that can be manifested.

The fourth [section], which functions as the power to shatter the deluded knowledge and views of the nine realms and reveal the true knowledge and views of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm, demonstrates that the power of this sutra’s shattering and revealing is supreme.
Its shattering of delusion reaches the ultimate point of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), while its revelation of truth aligns directly with Wondrous Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi).

Furthermore, it should be understood that this does not mean there are separate states of Equal or Wondrous Enlightenment to be shattered or revealed; rather, it points directly to sentient beings themselves.
In the midst of daily seeing and hearing, when not a single speck of dust remains established, it is called the ultimate penetration of delusion at the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
When the nature of seeing is clearly manifest, it is called the revelation of the True, directly equaling Wondrous Enlightenment.

This is because when sentient beings attain Buddhahood, they simply exhaust the emotional consciousness upon this present seeing and hearing, and simply reveal the Buddha-nature within this very seeing and hearing.
As it is said, "When seeing the seeing, that seeing is not seeing. This single act of seeing the seeing is precisely the seeing of the Buddha-nature;
it is the power that shatters ignorance—is this not a magnificent function? However, this is still spoken of in terms of the power and function of the *zong* (the ultimate principle).
If one applies this power, its efficacy must be made manifest; the Buddha taught that the function of this sutra is exceedingly great.

It can shatter such doubts and delusions of sentient beings, it can reveal such buddha-nature within sentient beings, and it can cause sentient beings to awaken to buddha-nature, practice accordingly, destroy the false, and manifest the true to the ultimate degree—thus, both its principle and its function are vast.
Regarding the fifth category, the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) teaching, which takes "fresh butter" as its pedagogical characteristic: this sutra is said to belong to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class.

While the Vaipulya encompasses all four teachings, this sutra speaks exclusively of Buddha-nature. It states that if the deluded mind ceases, that cessation itself is bodhi. Therefore, in terms of doctrinal classification, it is judged as Perfect and Sudden;
in terms of the flavor of the Dharma (wei), it is classified as fresh butter. This has already been explained previously in the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
What has been stated here will not be debated again. Regarding the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation), it says:

"As for the lineages of those involved in the translation and transcription, as well as matters such as the classification of sections (*fēnmén kējù*), since various masters have already provided clear textual evidence, I shall not cite them at length here.

From this, we know that Master Tiānrú did not disregard the discourse on sectional classification and the like. Now, following the ancient masters, I shall provide a complete explanation of the translation.
The translation pen-receiver’s account of the provenance and the structural analysis (*ko-p'an*) of the sutra state:
"Also known as the *Nālandā Mahāvihāra Sūtra* from Central India, excerpted and circulated separately from the *Abhiṣeka Section*.
[Commentary] Changshui says: This is a specific title. Regarding the Indian month name, it is fully called *Indraka*, which in this [language] means...
The Land of the Moon. This great kingdom stands among the small kingdoms like the moon among the stars; it corresponds to the region of the Five Indias.
It is the name of the capital city of a single realm, yet within that single realm there are many distinct countries.
The most honored and greatest is called Magadha, which here means "Great Body" (*mahā-deha*) because it encompasses all; it is also called "Non-Harming" (*Ahiṃsā*).
"Yi" (義) is a translation of the meaning. "Nālandā" is translated here as "Giver Without Weariness" (*apratikṣiptadāna*); it is the name of a dragon.

The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that there is a pond in the country of Āmra, and within that pond dwells a dragon named "Giver Without Weariness. Because the monastery is near that pond, it was designated by this name.
A "Great Place of Practice" (*mahā-maṇḍala*) is a site where śramaṇas cultivate their minds and practice the Way. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...

The six subsequent emperors continued its restoration. From afar, the azure heavens were uplifted as monasteries and groves were established throughout the capital, with a single main gate built for all.
Ten thousand monks resided there, and the administration became increasingly rigorous. No famous monastery in India preceded this one; therefore, it was named "Great" (Mahā).
As for the *Abhiṣeka* section, that [tantra] consists of five families (*kula*), and this is one of them, with Vairocana as the presiding lord. Thus, its family affiliation has been designated.
This can be verified and relied upon. Do not claim that because it was translated recently, it is suspected of not being an authentic teaching.
It is the twenty-third day, the *xinchou* day, of the fifth month in the year of *yisi* (the Year of the Dragon), the first year of the Shénlóng era of the Great Táng.
[Commentary] Changshui says: In the third year of Chang’an, Empress Wu retired from power and Zhongzong succeeded to the throne. This year was changed to the first year of Shénlóng.
As for "the dragon gathering," the dragon star is also called the Year Star (Sanskrit: *āṣāḍhā*); it completes one circuit in a year.

This is a compilation. "Yisi" (乙巳) refers to the sequence of the days following the new moon. "Shuoso" (朔穌) means the new moon; it is the resurrection of the moon after its waning. "Suosheng" (穌生) means the rebirth of life.
Translated at the Zhizhi Daochang in Guangzhou by the Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra from Central India.
[Commentary] Changshui says: In India, it is also called *Gāndhāra*, *Kandhu*, *Śendu*, *Indu*, and so forth.
*Śramaṇa* means "diligent" and "resting," a term for one who cultivates what is wholesome and extinguishes what is unwholesome. *Pāramitā* here means "reaching the other shore."
The translator, possessing talent and wisdom, is proficient in the languages of the four quarters; this is called the "Learning of the Elephant-Necked Interpreters" (xiàngxū).
Each of the four quarters has its own specific name for this office, but here we take the term used for those who preside over language in the north.
[Saṃgha] of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī; Mīgha Śākya, Translator of Terms. [Commentary] Changshui says:
The name of the kingdom is not clearly known. "Mīgha Śākya" means "Able to Subdue. Because he translated from Sanskrit into Chinese, he is called a "Translator of Terms" (yìyǔ).
There should be a separate record for the verification of the meanings therein. The rest is as in the section on Translation.
Recited throughout the year.
Transcribed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, Former Minister of Correct Admonition, Concurrent Vice President of the Secretariat and Chancellery,
Fang Rong of Qinghe.
[Commentary] Changshui said: "Even though one serves as a government official, if one has received the Mahāyāna precepts, the Sūtra states:
'When desiring to assume the position of a king, or even when the various officials assume their positions, they should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

All ghosts and spirits will then protect the person of the king and the persons of the officials. One relies upon the teacher and elders with the same reverence accorded to a father and elder brother."
Because of their service, they are called *dizi* (disciples). A *zhengjian* (right admonisher) is equivalent to today’s *jianyi* (adviser).
Because they recommend the worthy and promote those of great ability, they are called *dafu* (great officers). The names of the two provinces, Zhongshu and Menxia, are used here.

To harmonize and clarify matters of state administration is called *pingzhangshi*. *Bishou* (literally "pen-receiver") is also written as *bishou*; it means to record the text according to this method.

He took the Sanskrit manuscript he had been entrusted with and transcribed it, refining the phrasing and polishing the style so that it accorded with human sentiment while remaining faithful to the correct principles.

At first, when Kumārajīva cut his own arm to provide ink for the scriptures, the blood soaked the paper; Kumārajīva’s wife then cleared it with water, only then could he proceed with the transcription.
Tiantai says: Following the standard method of scriptural classification, this is divided into three parts.

First, the Introduction, beginning with "Thus have I heard" and ending with "returning to the presence of the Buddha. Second, the Main Body, beginning with "Ānanda saw the Buddha" and ending with "no longer longing for the triple world.
All that follows belongs to the third part, the Dissemination.

[Opening Preface, Part One: General Introduction, Section Six; First, Indicating the Essence of the Dharma] Thus. [Second, Revealing the One Who Heard] I heard. [Third, Clarifying the Response of the Capacity] At one time. [Fourth, Naming the Teacher] The Buddha. [Fifth, Describing the Abode] At the Jeta Grove Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī.

[Sixth, Citing Those Who Heard Together, Section Three; First, Śrāvakas, Subsection Five; First, Clarifying the Class] Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. [Second, Indicating the Number] One thousand two hundred and fifty persons.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha. This compiler merely established these words based on the Buddha to certify that there was a transmission of the Dharma;
it does not necessarily require the words of another. The discourse of "at one time" is likewise established based on the Buddha.
Because it is used generically across various sūtras, it does not point to a specific location. Guishan said:
Śrāvastī, also called Śāvatthī, is newly translated as "Abundant Virtue" (Fēngdé), because the kingdom abounds in four virtues: first, wealth; second, objects of desire;
third, extensive learning; and fourth, liberation. Jeta is fully called Jetavana; *Jeta* correctly refers to the name of the Crown Prince "Victorious in Battle" (Zhànshèng).
Furthermore, at the time of his birth, his father, the King, was victorious in battle against foreign nations and consequently established an auspicious title for him.
It was there that Sudatta purchased a grove and constructed a vihāra to offer to the Buddha; "Huan" (桓) refers to the forest. The term "bhikṣu" contains three meanings.
"The mendicant who destroys evil and terrifies Māra. Changshui said: "As for the one thousand two hundred and fifty people:
first, he converted the five men beginning with Cunda; next, he converted the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their one thousand disciples;
next, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with their one hundred disciples; and finally, he converted the householder Yaśas and his fifty followers."

Regarding the humans: because the sutra cites a large total number, five people have been subtracted from it. This assembly had previously served non-Buddhist paths for many kalpas, practicing with great austerity, yet they achieved nothing.
Upon encountering the Buddha, they immediately attained the supreme fruits. Thus, moved by the Buddha’s grace, they constantly followed him in his transformations to serve as his constant retinue.
Tianru’s Supplemental Notes states that the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) does not categorize them by the human class.
The sequence is arranged according to chronological order. Regarding the commentaries of various masters, there is mutual selection and rejection;
however, the selected interpretations are inserted in accordance with the sequential order of the sutra text. Interpretations that are identical are not redundantly included.
The priority lies solely in ensuring a single, coherent flow that appears as if issuing from the mouth of a single person.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "It is not necessary to rely on other explanations" refers to the various doctrines established since antiquity for the interpretation of the scriptures, such as the "six accomplishments" (*ṣaḍ-vidha-sampad*) and the "fourfold division or combination of Ānanda.
These were all formulated by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla and are the principles revered by Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna.
While the general introduction (*sāmānya-nidāna*) conveys a universal meaning, its underlying intent lies in the specific [context]. This is like a ring...
The Master’s exegesis of the sutra largely follows the essential and the concise; therefore, his words are as such.

While it is permissible to encompass the extensive through the concise, it is utterly unacceptable to reject the extensive on account of the concise. Students ought to preserve both perspectives so as not to contradict the sacred scriptures.
Now, following the interpretation of Changshui, I shall extend and clarify its meaning. If one proceeds in this manner...
"I have heard" (*yathā mayā śrutam*) is a phrase used to refer to the Dharma. "Such Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"At the time of the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*), the assembly collectively requested, saying: 'Just as you have heard it, so should you speak it.'"
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma granted his permission, saying: "It shall be spoken thus, just as I have heard it.

To depart from such an explanation is to fail in the accomplishment of faith. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that by which one enters, and wisdom is that by which one crosses over.
One who has faith says, "This matter is thus"; one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus."
Master Sengzhao also said that these are words of faith and compliance. When there is faith, the principle of what is spoken is compliant;

when there is compliance, the way between teacher and disciple is perfected. Therefore, among the myriad practices, faith is primary; thus it is called "Thus" (Evam). Furthermore, to accord with the principle and accord with the capacity [of the listener] is called "Thus";
to be forever free from faults and transgressions is called "Is" (Satyam). Because one speaks according to the principle and believes according to the principle, it is so named.
It is said: "Thus. If we refer to this present sutra, it is called "Thus" because the essence and nature of the Tathāgatagarbha-citta are immovable;
it is called "is" because it is the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*). Furthermore, all phenomena are fundamentally without arising or ceasing, for they are all the Tathāgatagarbha;
thus they are named "Thus. Because it is free from all marks yet is identical with all phenomena, it is termed "is. There are further meanings, but they would be too numerous to elaborate upon.
This is not discussed. "I who hear" refers to the accomplishment of hearing. "I" here refers to Ānanda himself, designating the conventional entity composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
However, the Buddha has taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*). Now, when the term "self" is used, there are four kinds of self:
