"One can know it. (2. Examining the nature of that knowing by means of vision: "I shall now show you my hand, which is as soft as *tūla* cotton.

When your eyes see it, does your mind discern it? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. (3. Challenging the nature of that knowing by questioning its location: The Buddha told Ānanda, "If this knowing is the same as the hand, why is it located outside?"
○ (Breaking the Third Knot): Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognitive awareness dwells outside the body—is impossible.
[Commentary] Wénlǐng says: From "The body and mind are external to one another" below, he refutes the notion that it is external. From "I shall now show you" below...
This proves it is not external. *Tūla* is translated here as "fine fragrance. Its cotton is colored like frost, and the Buddha’s hands are as soft as it.

[2. Refuting the Hidden Root] [3. First, the Shifted Calculation] [4. First, Acknowledging and Refuting the Shifted Calculation] Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, according to what the Buddha has said, because one does not see within, [consciousness] does not reside inside the body.”
Because body and mind know one another and are not separate, they do not exist outside the body;

as I now contemplate, I know they reside in one place. (II. Explaining the reason through a detailed exposition [divided into two parts]: First, the Buddha questions him regarding their location. The Buddha said: "Where is that location now? (II. Explaining the meaning and establishing an analogy [divided into two parts]: First, the formal exposition and establishment. Ānanda said:

"This cognizing mind neither knows the interior yet is able to see the exterior. As I contemplate it, it must be hidden within the faculties, like someone taking a crystal bowl and placing it over [the eyes]."
Although his two eyes are covered by objects, they are not obstructed; as soon as he sees, his faculty of perception immediately discerns.
(This is the second reversal of the previous objection: "However, my conscious mind that is capable of knowing does not see within because it resides in the faculties;
yet it clearly gazes outward without obstruction because it is hidden within the faculties."

[Commentary] Changshui says: "Lapis lazuli" is a metaphor for the sense organ (*indriya*), and "the eye" is a metaphor for the mind (*citta*). The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is pure in its form;
it does not obstruct the mind, just as a lapis lazuli bowl does not obstruct the eye. As one object is illuminated, the mind knows it in accordance with the faculty.

[II. Refuting [the opponent's position] by following the example (divided into two parts: first, establishing the example and determining the point; second, refuting the attachment by following the example). The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As you have stated, that which is hidden within the root of the eye is like lapis lazuli.

That person should see mountains and rivers through the eyes when covered by lapis lazuli, yet they do not see the lapis lazuli itself. "World-Honored One, it is not so. If that person were to cover their eyes with lapis lazuli, they would indeed see the lapis lazuli.
[II. Refuting the attachment by following the example (divided into two parts: first, restating the attachment). The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If your mind were the same as the lapis lazuli..."

Regarding "conjunction": (2. Refutation by Example) When you see mountains and rivers, why do you not see your own eyes? If you were to see your eyes, the eye would become identical to its object, and the principle of "following" [the object] could not be established.
If you cannot see it, how can you say that this cognizing mind is latent within the sense organ, like being enclosed in lapis lazuli?
(3. Conclusion of the Refutation) Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognition and awareness is hidden within the sense organ—is untenable.
"It is as impossible as seeing through lapis lazuli. [Commentary:

Zhenji said, "This rebuke points out that Ānanda has committed the error of inconsistency between the dharma and the metaphor. In the metaphor, one sees the lapis lazuli, but in the dharma, one does not see the faculty.
Even if we grant that the faculty is seen, the faculty is itself an object. If it is an object, one cannot say..."
"Following. As the preceding text states: "Because those faculties follow what is seen, they immediately engage in discrimination. Wēnlíng says:
"When both fact and principle are contradicted, it is not a case of the faculties remaining latent.

(3. Refuting the Internal and External [Faculties]. Part 1: Shifting the Argument. Sub-part 1: Stating the Adherence. Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I now further reflect that this body of sentient beings..."
The solid organs and hollow viscera reside within, while the apertures and cavities dwell without; where there are internal organs, there is darkness, and where there are apertures, there is light.

Now, when I face the Buddha with my eyes open and see light, it is called seeing the external; when I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called seeing the internal. (2. Request for Judgment) What is the meaning of this?
[Commentary] Wuxing said: First, he calculated that the mind is within the body; the Buddha refuted this by pointing out that one cannot see the internal organs.

Next, he calculated it to be outside the body; this again invited the difficulty of the body and mind being separated. Furthermore, he calculated that it is hidden within the sense organs; this moreover contradicts the analogy of the glass eye-socket.
Now, he establishes [the mind as being both] inside and outside in an attempt to avoid the three aforementioned errors. Why is this? It is truly because...

Where there is concealment, there is darkness; therefore, when one perceives darkness, it is designated as "internal. Why must one necessarily perceive internal objects? Where there is an aperture, there is light;
therefore, when one perceives light, it is designated as "external. How could one further demand that the external be unrelated?
If "internal" and "external" are thus established, they naturally reveal that this mind does not abide in a single location, nor is it distinct from the hidden sense-organ.
Nevertheless, although it is said that one sees what is external, the substance of the mind that performs this grasping actually remains within.

This is because seeing light with the eyes open is not the same as a lamp being outside a room. Lektan said: The *Baibutong* states that the five viscera (*pañca-dhātu*) are the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys, and spleen;
the six hollow organs (*ṣaḍ-koṣṭha*) are the palaces and offices of these five viscera. The stomach is the office of the spleen.
The bladder is the palace of the kidneys; the triple burner is the palace of the life-force; the gallbladder is the palace of the liver;
the large and small intestines are the palaces of the heart and the lungs. Wénlǐng says: Furthermore, since the heart is within, it perceives darkness;
thus, by seeing [the internal], one perceives the viscera. Below, he summarizes this in three sections to analyze it.

[2. Refuting [the claim] by examining each point (initially refuting it based on external views; first, clarifying that the eye facing non-internal objects is not internal; first, clarifying that what is in front is not internal)] The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye or does it not face the eye?

If it faces the eye, the darkness is in front of the eyes; how can it be considered internal? [Next, revealing the fault in its being established as internal] "If it were established as internal, then when you are in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, this darkness within the room would all be your own internal viscera. [Second, clarifying that it does not face [the eye] and is therefore not the seeing] "If..."
"If it is not so, how can it constitute a view? [Commentary] Wēnlíng says:
"You should immediately question him; if he agrees, you should challenge him with a refutation; if he does not agree, you should conclude [the argument]."

II. Refutation by Internal Correlation (Divided into two; first, restating the opponent's position). If [the self] is established through internal correlation apart from external seeing: II. Sequential Refutation (Divided into two; first, the direct refutation; divided into two; first, the analogical objection). If one sees darkness with eyes closed, this is called "seeing within the body";
yet when one opens the eyes and sees light, why does one not see one's own face? II. Conclusion and Rebuttal. If one does not see one's own face, then internal correlation is not established.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The realm before one's eyes is called 'external seeing,' while the realm within the body is called 'internal facing.

Previously, it was argued that because the eye faces outward, it cannot constitute an internal [perception]. Now, even if one were to set aside external seeing to achieve internal facing, this would mean the eye itself is capable of looking back.
Furthermore, if the eye can look back at the body when closed, it should likewise be able to look back at its own face when open."
If it were not so, the meaning would not be established.

(2. Refutation by hypothetical concession; Part 3: First, if seeing the face, the mind should be in space. If seeing the face were established, then this cognizing mind and the eye-organ would be in empty space;

how could they be said to be within? (2. If they were in space, then self and other would be confused; Part 1: Being in space is not your own fault. If [the mind] were in empty space, it would not be your own substance. (Next: Your seeing is the same as the Tathāgata’s fault. It would follow that the Tathāgata’s seeing of your face now—[would also be yours].

This is your body. (3. If [the eye] were in space, then the eye would not be the perception of the body; Part Two: First, directly refuting that the perception of the eye is the perception of the body. Your eye already knows that the body is conjoined with it, yet it is not the perception of the body. (2. Shifting the argument, one calculates that there must be two distinct perceptions.
If you insist that the perceptions of the body and the eye should each have their own cognition, then this single body of yours should become two Buddhas.
(3. Concluding the refutation. Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing within" is impossible.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To explain and clarify this through successive stages is because there is no principle of 'turning back to observe' [the self].
Since your eye already possesses cognition, the body must not be that which is conscious. Furthermore, since it exists within empty space, it cannot be your own substance.

If you insist that both possess cognition, then two distinct entities would result. Wǔxīng says: "Therefore, one should know that what follows below does not state that seeing brightness is external."
This is an abbreviation. Furthermore, seeing the external as established [proves] the internal; now, following the correct calculation, the conclusion is reached.
[Commentary] The Supplement states: Next, the two external positions are refuted. First, the concession (*anujñā*). The Sūtra says:

"If seeing the face were established," which is a concession to your position regarding the meaning of seeing the face. Fearing that others might argue: "Even if it is not explicitly the case that one sees the face, since the mind-consciousness..."
Since the eye faculty has already confronted the face within itself, this constitutes the meaning of "confronting externally" (i.e., seeing the face).
Therefore, for the time being, we shall concede this position. How do we know this is so? According to the refutation that follows, it says:
"This cognizing mind and the eye faculty are located in empty space. The implication is that if one were to maintain such a position, it would necessarily be the mind [that sees].

It is plausible that the eye is in space. If it were attached to the face and facing outward, it would not be possible. Next, there are three further refutations. First, regarding the refutation based on the premise that the eye is in space:
if one wishes to establish the position that the face faces outward, this must presuppose that the eye is in space;
only then can this position be permitted. Since such a principle does not exist, the seeing of the face cannot be established. Therefore, it is said: "This is what is known."

This refers to the mind and its like. As for the statement, "How can it be established as being internal?"—although Ānanda reckons that the substance of the mind, which pervades both the internal and external, actually resides within because of the clarity of the aperture and because one sees through the internal and external, the mind also possesses the sense of being outside.
Now, since the eye and mind are in the void, the previous claim that they reside within also falls away. Second, this is an analysis based on the mind.
The eyes are taken away by another. If you calculate that they reside in space, they are no longer your own and are entirely the same as the substance of another.
Thus, the Tathāgata seeing your face right now is the very eyes of your own body; hence it is said, "If they were in empty space," and so forth.
Third, regarding the impossibility of two cognitions within a single body, [it is argued] that if the mind-eyes were separate from the body... [the body would be joined with them].
It is not a matter of conscious awareness. If the body and the eye were each to have its own conscious awareness, there would have to be two minds;
by the time one attains Buddhahood, there would necessarily be two Buddhas. This point is made merely to refute the attachment of an ordinary deluded person who cannot become two Buddhas;
it is not intended as a mistaken interpretation that a single Buddha on the stage of fruition within enlightenment universally responds to beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

[4. Refuting the Conjunction of the Mind with Objects] (Part 1: The Initial Argument; Part 2: The Initial Adherence to Scripture) Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now reflect upon this very essence of reflection, it is truly my own mind-nature that exists wherever it conjoins with an object.
[2. Refuting the Four Previous Arguments] "Nor does it exist in any of the three locations: the internal, the external, or in between."
[Commentary] Gushan said: "When the mind arises, phenomena arise; the objective realm originates from the mind. When phenomena arise, the mind arises;
the mind shifts in accordance with the realm. Wunling said: "Because the mind and phenomena arise together, the contemplation that follows the realm is precisely the substance of the mind;
the point where the mind and phenomena unite is precisely where the mind resides."

○ (2. Refutation by Pursuit; Part 1: Restating the Position) The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various kinds of mind arise, and that wherever they meet, the mind exists accordingly.
○ (2. Refutation by Analogy; Part 1: Directly Clarifying the Lack of Substance) This mind has no substance, and thus there is nothing with which it can meet.

If it were possible for something without substance to meet [with others], then the nineteenth sense-field would meet with the seven objects; this principle is not so. If it did have substance, then as you [have described]...
If you prick your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within, or does it enter from without?
If it emerged from within, you should see what is inside your body; if it came from without, you should first see your face.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Because one takes the very substance of thought as the mind, it is merely a floating ideation; therefore, it is difficult to determine whether its substance exists or not.
If it were without substance, it would be empty of name alone—how could it then accord with and combine [with objects]?
It would be like the nineteenth element or the seventh sense-object, which are merely empty names. If it does have a substance, where should it be located? Let it be touched upon the body.
And it is verified that the substance [of seeing] actually has no location.

"Tí" (挃) means "to touch. (2. Thoroughly refuting the existence of a substance. Part 1: Refuting by means of internal and external movement and entry. Part 1: The rescue. Ānanda said: "Seeing is the function of the eye; it is not the case that the mind knows through the eye. For seeing to be something other than the eye is illogical. (2. The refutation. The Buddha said:

"If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, those who are already dead still have their eyes remaining; [if the eye were the seer, they] should [still be able to see]."
"If one sees objects in all cases, how can it be called death? [Commentary] Wēnlíng says:
This is Ānanda’s resolution of the preceding difficulty. He means that the mind is merely capable of knowing and cannot be said to "see";

he simply fails to realize that the capacity to see resides within the mind itself, and that it is not merely the eyes that fail to see. The passage beginning with the Buddha’s words introduces the gateway.
The analogy is that while the capacity to see resides in the mind, when one is dead, it is clear that the eyes alone cannot see.

(2. Refuting both the "one" and the "many" through the distinction between pervasiveness and limitation; first, the proposition. Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that perceives and knows, if it must have a substance, does it have a single substance or multiple substances?
Is it now located within your body, and is it pervasive throughout the body or not pervasive? (2. The refutation. If it were a single substance...
Thus, when you prick one limb with your hand, the other four limbs should feel it; if all were to feel it, there would be no specific location for the prick.
If the prick occurs at a specific location, then your single body cannot be established as such. If there were multiple bodies, you would become many people—then which body would be "you"?
If it pervades the entire body, it is the same as the previously mentioned case of being pricked; if it does not pervade the body, then when you touch your head...
Furthermore, when the foot is touched, the head perceives it; if the foot were to respond with consciousness, then the head would have to be without cognition. But this is not the case for you.
(Third refutation concluded) Therefore, one should know that wherever there is contact, the mind must likewise be present; it is impossible for it to be otherwise.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: One should know that the true mind is neither one nor many, and neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
Since these four attributes do not apply, it cannot be said that the mind exists wherever it encounters an object.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the refutation based on the limitation of the essence of "one" and "many," the first two phrases of the initial determination mention the mind but not the body;
therefore, it simply says, "Furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is aware and capable of cognition. The next two phrases speak of the body and mind together;
therefore, it says, "Now, within your body, is it pervasive throughout the entire body or not pervasive? Next, regarding the middle refutation:
All four propositions are refuted by means of the mutual dependence of the part (the body) and the whole (the support).
Although there are four propositions, they constitute only three meanings, because the meaning of refuting through "identity" and "pervasion" is the same.

○ (5. Refuting the Middle [Position]; Part 1: The Initial Argument; Part 2: 1. Narrating the Scriptural Passage that Gives Rise to the Adherence) Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha and Mañjuśrī and other Dharma-Princes discuss the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) when they spoke:
'World-Honored One, you also said that the mind is neither within nor without.

As I reflect upon this, I see nothing within, and without, there is no mutual cognition. ○ (2. Reversing the Previous Objection) Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established. This is because the characteristics of the body and mind...
Knowing is not in the external, for [external things] do not know one another;
nor is it within, for there is no seeing therein. It must therefore be in between. [Commentary: Wēnlíng says: If it were within, one would not see the internal organs;

if it were without, the body parts would not know one another. Since these two positions are untenable, it must reside between the sense organ and its object. Chángshuǐ says: They do not know one another externally...
The commentary notes that "knowing" (*zhī*) should perhaps be "together" (*hé*), and "fear" (*kǒng*) should likely be "mutual" (*xiāng*), as these characters may be errors.

[2. Refuting the Middle (Two Parts): First, Refuting by Way of Body and Location (Two Parts): First, Establishing the Ground] The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'the middle,' the middle must not be confused; it cannot be without a location. Now, when you investigate this middle, where does it reside?

Does it reside in a place, or does it reside in the body? [2. Refuting by Investigation (Two Parts): First, Refuting its Residing in the Body] "If it resides in the body, it would be at the periphery, not in the middle."
Within the center, there is sameness. (2. Refuting the location of the center) If [the center] exists as a location, is it something indicated or is it not indicated?
If it were unindicated, it would be the same as non-indication; thus, there would be no fixed center. Why is this so? It is like a person using a marker to designate a center:
when looking from the east, it is south; when viewed from the west, it becomes north. Since the substance of the marker is thus confused, the mind should likewise become disordered.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: This section briefly establishes the middle position by examining the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) respectively. "The body" refers to the faculty, while "the location" refers to the object.
Regarding the passage "If it is in the body," etc., this means that the body has two meanings: the center and the periphery. If it were on the periphery, it could not be the center;
if it were at the center, then—as in the previous case of being "inside"—it should perceive what is internal. Regarding the passage "If it is in the location," etc., it is likewise...

The *Madhyamaka-vibhāga* states that there is no fixed [middle]. "To manifest" means to indicate an object in order to make it clearly evident. If things are in a state of confusion, there is nothing from which a middle can be grasped.

[2. Refutation by way of the sense-faculties and their objects; Part One: The Objection] Ānanda said: "The 'middle' I speak of is not these two kinds [of extremes], as the World-Honored One has stated that the eye and visible forms serve as conditions."
When visual consciousness arises, the eye possesses discrimination while the object of form lacks consciousness;

when consciousness arises between them, it is then said that the mind exists therein. (2. Refuting the two [positions]; first, establishing the premise. The Buddha said: "If your mind were located between the sense organ and the object, would this essence of the mind encompass both, or would it not encompass both?

(2.1. Refuting the two; first, refuting the position that it encompasses both. "If it encompassed both, the substance of the object and the essence of consciousness would be intermingled and confused. The object would not be the essence of knowing, and the two would stand as adversaries."

What is meant by "middle"? (2. Refuting the claim that it encompasses both: If it were to encompass both, it would not be established; since it is neither knowing nor not-knowing, it lacks any intrinsic nature—what, then, could serve as its characteristic?
(3. Concluding the refutation: Therefore, one should know that for it to exist in the middle is impossible.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "If one combines both," refers to the subsequent refutation that combining both cannot constitute the Middle Way. "Objects" (*wu*) refer to the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects (*viṣaya*);

"substance" (*ti*) refers to the substance of the mind. "Objects are not the substance of cognition" means that if objects were not of the same substance as cognition, then the sense bases/objects and the mind would stand as two separate entities, leaving no middle position.
"Combining both is not established" refers to the subsequent refutation of not combining both.
This constitutes the Middle Way. If it does not encompass both faculties (*indriya*), it is not "knowing"; if it does not encompass both objects (*viṣaya*), it is not "not-knowing.
Since both meanings are not the Middle, how can they be definitive? Tianru’s *Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes) states:

"When Master Huan explains that 'objects are not knowing by nature,' he says that while the faculties and objects lack cognition, the substance of the mind possesses cognition. Furthermore, when he explains 'neither knowing nor not-knowing,' he again [relies on] the faculties..."

To claim that there is "knowing" seems somewhat inconsistent with this. Now, one should instead attribute "knowing" to the substance of the mind (*citta*), while not attributing it to the sense organs (*indriya*) or their objects (*viṣaya*).
This is because if it did not encompass both, it would be neither mind nor organ or object; thus, it would lack any essential nature (*svabhāva*). What characteristic could it have in the interim?
That external things are not the substance of knowing is incorrect, for there are those among the ancients who take "substance-knowing" to be the sense organs. This is wrong.
This is because the Buddha spoke explicitly of this essence of mind.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the character *tǐ* (essence), Wēnlíng’s interpretation is incorrect at first but correct in the end; Tiānrú, however, conversely takes what is correct to be incorrect.
He fails to realize that there is inherently the "essence of the essence of mind" and the "essence of the essence of the root. The Buddha spoke of this...

The essence of mind follows the perspective of the refuter in accordance with one's own intention; the essence of the sense-faculties follows the perspective of the refuted in accordance with the other's intention.
Since Ānanda maintains that the eye possesses discrimination, [the Buddha] refutes him by proceeding according to that very tenet.
One must recognize the general direction of such timely speech.
○ (Sixth: Refuting the Attachment to Non-attachment; Part One: The Initial Deviant Calculation; Part Two: The Initial Adherence to Scripture and the Arising of Attachment) Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, in the past I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of Dharma.
He constantly spoke of the nature of the mind of awakening and cognition, saying that it is neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location at all, being entirely non-existent."
"It is renowned as 'mind. [Question: "Then do I not have that which is renowned as 'mind'? [Commentary] Lektan said:
"Since it is neither internal, external, nor in between, one knows that the mind has nothing to which it clings.

However, he did not realize that the Buddha’s intent was to shatter the delusion of having no substance, thereby causing one to recognize the original reality. As it is said: "When sought throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found."
Because the mind does not exist, delusion is fundamentally non-existent. Since there is no locus for the deluded mind, this is itself bodhi; birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal.
Failing to understand this meaning, one erroneously cites the Buddha's words and falsely establishes "non-attachment."

[2. Refuting [the opponent’s position] point by point (ārambha-pratiṣedha). Part 1: Restating the thesis and establishing the premise. The Buddha said to Ānanda: “You say that the nature of the mind which perceives and discriminates has no location whatsoever.
Yet, the empty space of the world, water, land, flying creatures, and all such material objects are called ‘everything. If you do not cling to them, does this ‘everything’ exist or does it not exist?

[2. Refuting both existence and non-existence. Part 1: The direct refutation. 1. If it does not exist, its essence is lost. If it does not exist, it would be the same as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns; how then could there be non-clinging? [2. If it exists, it contradicts the name. If it exists, yet you do not cling to it—this is not possible.
"It may be called non-existent.
[Commentary] Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state: "The text of the seven inquiries all serves to refute that deluded mind so that it has no place of dependence.
Ānanda previously said that 'wherever there is a point of contact, the mind exists accordingly'; the Buddha now challenges him regarding the substance of that mind."
Whether it exists or does not exist, whether it is one or many, and whether it is pervasive or non-pervasive— although this seems to refute the mind that follows after existence,
since it causes one to touch the body to verify [the sensation], the intent lies in refuting [the notion] that follows wherever contact occurs.
Now, "mind" is designated as that which is named for non-attachment to all things.

When the Buddha then challenges whether the various phenomena of the world—such as empty space, water, land, and flying creatures—are existent or non-existent, he is likewise refuting them by way of their respective bases.
Wénlǐng says: "Whether they are existent or non-existent, you are asked about your mind; it is not those objects themselves that are unattached."
Is the elephant existent, or is it empty and non-existent? If it were empty and non-existent, it would be like a tortoise’s hair;
how could one be attached to it, yet you say one is not attached? If there is something to which one is not attached, then it must be a real entity; therefore, it cannot be called "non-existent.
These [points] all restate the objections, after which the refutation is concluded.
○ (Double Rebuttal) If there is no characteristic, then there is nothing that is not non-existent; if characteristics exist, then they are present. How can there be non-attachment?
○ (Third, Refuting the Conclusion) Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for the awakened mind to perceive anything as being characterized by non-attachment.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "If things truly lacked characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they would be identical to a tortoise’s hair. If things are not non-existent, they must inherently possess characteristics.
To know that characteristics exist is to know that the mind has a locus; how, then, can this be called 'non-attachment'? Wǔxīng says: "Characteristics do not exist of themselves;
they exist because the mind is present. The mind does not cease of itself; it ceases because characteristics are exhausted. This is so.
To claim that there is non-attachment while [the object] possesses characteristics is logically untenable. Gushan said: "Taken together, these seven inversions seem to refute the four natures.

When it is within and the faculty is hidden, seeing the internal seems to be the nature of self; when it is external, it seems to be the nature of other; in between, it seems to be the nature of both;
and following the union without attachment, it seems to be the nature of no cause. Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: 'All phenomena are...'"
"Neither self-arisen, nor arisen from another, nor co-arisen, nor without cause; therefore, it is said to be non-arising.

Thus one knows that the Tathāgata, through seven successive refutations, leaves not even a moment’s illusory mind with any place of escape. Once the thieves of delusion are eliminated, the True King is revealed;
herein the principle of non-arising is seen. Those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom have already merged [with it] in secret.
[The Master] said, "I have already awakened [to this]. I have merely explained it more extensively for the sake of those of middling and inferior capacities.
Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state: "The false and floating mind arises in dependence upon sensory objects; fundamentally it has no substantial reality and no fixed location.

The sevenfold refutations in the preceding text were intended to demolish its false locus in order to reveal the Truth. However, because Ānanda had not yet awakened to this, he again requested instruction in the following text."
The World-Honored One then again emitted light and manifested his countenance to reveal two kinds of roots.

Next, he raised his fist to test their vision and interrogated them closely regarding their minds. He led them to recognize and investigate the capacity for discernment, and then rebuked them, saying:
"Even down to making them minutely examine how [the mind] lacks substance apart from sensory objects," whereby he first began to shatter their deluded mind and its lack of reality.
This is the essence.
[Commentary] Tiāoxī says: "If the four natures have not yet been demolished, this awakening mind is the mundane and not the truth.

Once the attachment to natures has been demolished, it is then called 'mundane truth' (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Mundane truth is false and provisional, as its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) still persist. Only when these characteristics are demolished..."
It is called the True Truth (*satyadharma*) and is also termed the Ultimate Truth (*paramārthasatya*). Thus, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai said:

"The Worldly Truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) refutes substantiality, while the True Truth refutes the provisional. When the provisional is refuted, it is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); when substantiality is refuted, it is the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Speaking from this perspective, the sevenfold repetition in the scriptural text contains the meaning of these two types of emptiness. Changshui remarked: "Although that which is conceptualized by ordinary sentiments..."
There are ten thousand differences, yet the bases upon which they depend do not exceed these seven. To investigate the essence of delusion, one must first destroy its basis.
It is like this: when a city falls, the rebels perish; when a nest collapses, the eggs are destroyed. Although there are seven points of inquiry, they actually constitute five.
Because the fifth and seventh [moments] have no distinct location, they accord with non-attachment; they resemble the destruction of the support, yet the primary intention resides in the object.
When seeing the internal, it is likewise destroyed as being internal; when accords with the external, it is likewise destroyed as being non-attached.
Tiantai said: "In the preceding passage, the Tathāgata first demonstrated two kinds of mind—the eternally abiding mind and the deluded conceptualizing mind—intending for Ānanda to grasp the former.
However, Ānanda was unable to look back and contemplate the meaning of the 'eternally abiding true mind';
instead, he took that which is non-abiding as his abiding and ultimately fell into the latter."
Answer: It is said that the mind resides within, or without, or hidden in the sense organs, up to the point of non-attachment. One does not realize that these seven states all have fixed abodes.
Since the mind is established by dwelling in such places, how could this be what is called the "ever-abiding true mind"?

However, the deluded mind has no inherent substance; it manifests its substance according to where it dwells. Initially, when it resides within, its attachments are extremely narrow; subsequently, when it is outside, there is a shift.
Third, the "hidden root" is narrow; fourth, the "internal and external" is broad; fifth, "conforming to union" and sixth, "the intermediate" are pervasive according to their respective objects;
seventh, "non-attachment" is merely not being attached to the preceding six, and thus its essence is also broad.
All of these do nothing more than take that which dwells within the square inch of the physical body and moves to and fro therein as the mind.
This is precisely the root of birth and death, the very foundation of saṃsāra. Is it not for this reason that it says:

"By employing various false imaginings, because these imaginings are not true, there is cyclic wandering"? Furthermore, of the seven types of self-conception, the first four are based on one's own calculations, while the latter three cite the scriptures.
Although there are four types of calculation, the primary intent lies solely within the internal [self]. However, the first...
The second [position] regarding the external does not exceed the point that, when calculations are exhausted, one merely flees in haste; it is not the fundamental intent.

The "hidden roots" and "darkness of views" and so forth are merely sufficient to provide a resolution for those who hold to the internal. The latter three citations from the sūtras are skillful analytical distinctions that further employ the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) as their basis.
Therefore, throughout the combinations and the intermediate stages, all are explained in terms of the faculties and objects. Thus, there is none [that is not so].
To say that "all things" are likewise so is precisely this point; it further encompasses both the internal and external to exhaustively encompass the entirety of one's lifelong study.
The Mañjuśrī Chapter of the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Only by eternally severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way. It asks: "What is ignorance?

It is the deluded recognition of the four great elements as the characteristics of one's own body, and the shadows of conditions from the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind. Up to this point...

The "Universal Eye" chapter instructs one to rely upon the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*. First, by examining the body in terms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one realizes that the body lacks the characteristic of a body.

Next, by investigating the mind in terms of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), one realizes that the mind lacks the characteristic of a mind. Now, this sutra first examines the mind through the seven locations (*sapta-sthāna*) and finds it has no locus;
subsequently, it refutes the mind through three meanings to show it has no substance. This is identical to the second meaning in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).
All of these are instances of *śamatha*. Thus, one should know that the general purport of the two sutras is in agreement.
Although the attachments of those present at the time were broken then, the obstructions of the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) of today still persist like ice.
However, among the seven points of inquiry, the most stubborn and difficult to attack lies in the beginning and the end; for it has long been held by the world as being within [the self].

Maintaining this without attachment is the fundamental principle for beginners in Buddhist study; by doing so, one will naturally attain thorough understanding of the preceding scriptural passages as they are read.
Otherwise, there is a great danger of falling into the fault of slandering the Dharma.
I have already encountered such individuals. Now, let us attempt to clarify this through a series of questions and answers; herein lies no small measure of *śamatha*.
Zhu said: [The opponent] asks: "It is universally acknowledged that the mind resides within; both Confucians and Buddhists revere this as their common principle. Why do you say it is not so?
It might be acceptable to say it does not reside exclusively within, but to state definitively that it is *not* within is a grave contradiction of the maxims of the former masters.
As Master Cheng [Zhao] said: 'When extended, it fills the six directions; when withdrawn, it retreats and hides in the profound.'"

When it pervades the six directions of the universe, it reveals that this mind is omnipresent, reaching everywhere. When it is hidden within the secret, it reveals that this mind is clearly manifest within.
Furthermore, the *Dharmadhātu-gāthā* states: "If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, the *tathatā* within the body likewise pervades the outside.
Since it says that *tathatā* is within the body, it is also evident that it pervades the outside; thus, this mind is within.

Yet it is able to pervade the exterior; how much more so when we verify through experience that the discrimination of my current body and mind possesses reality, while those external objects lack such distinct differentiation.
When I do not perceive the interior, it is comparable to a lamp:

its radiance certainly illuminates the ten directions thoroughly, yet the fact that the wick is burning does not prevent it from being consumed within; one cannot claim the lamp is not bright simply because the wick is burning.
Yet it lacks the function of dispelling darkness. In this way, both phenomenon and principle are mutually non-contradictory, and both the analogy and the dharma are free from fault.
Furthermore, although the Buddhas and Patriarchs are said to have attained the Way, is there anything that is not internal in essence yet external in function?

Is there anything where the root is one while the branches are manifold? Without arising from meditative stillness, they manifest all manner of dignified deportments; with a single release of the radiance of the mind, the six [senses]...
The gateway is open and through. That the mind resides within is thus made even clearer. He replied: "You seek only the branches while forgetting the root.
You know the one, yet you do not yet know the two. Why is this? There is the true mind and there is the deluded mind;
there is that which brings delusion along with it while manifesting the truth, and there is that which is purely true and without delusion; there is that which follows from the truth..."

Yet one should respond with what is illusory. What is meant by "true mind"? It is precisely that which is called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*) in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*).
The treatise states: "The meaning of 'enlightenment' refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought.

This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. The single characteristic of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body. Relying upon this dharma...

The body is said to be named "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*). This is also what this sutra refers to when it says: "The nature of enlightenment is wondrously luminous; original enlightenment is luminously wondrous;
it is pure and self-sovereign, pervading the entire dharma-realm," and so forth. Such a true mind has no distinction between the sentient and insentient worlds, nor any division of inner and outer.
How could it be a deluded mind? As the sutra states: "The nature of enlightenment is necessarily luminous; it is through delusion that [it becomes otherwise]."
Based on the clarity of awareness, one establishes the "object" (*ālambana*); once the object has been falsely established, your false "subject" (*grāhaka*) arises.

Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed. Thus, the sentient world and the physical vessel-world are established, and the distinction between internal and external arises.

In a single thought-moment, the conscious mind seizes upon red and white forms; these various mixed delusions and perceptions constitute the body. Aggregating conditions, it stirs within and rushes outward, turbid and chaotic.
They take the characteristics [of the body] to be the nature of the mind; this refers to the passage: "One is deluded and takes the mind to be within the physical body, becoming decisively confused.

How can one bring forth the truth while still carrying delusion? It is because the Buddhas and Patriarchs established their teachings mostly by relying on delusion to break through delusion, and by relying on inversion to give rise to awakening.
As it is said: "The True Suchness within the body pervades the outside as well"—this is the simultaneous loosening of all bonds.

These words are insufficient to designate as the ultimate teaching. If one says that the nature of delusion has no substance and nothing upon which it depends—like flowers in the sky that originally do not exist—and that this seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi;
this is like pointing to a bubble and saying it is the ocean, using delusion to illustrate the Truth. How could this be considered the state of absolute purity?
Non-delusion. This is precisely the nature of the Dharma-body realized by the Tathāgata; his mind pervades the Dharma-realm, and his body envelops empty space.
This body is the mind, and this mind is the body. As the mind extends everywhere, so too does this body extend everywhere.

There is no distinction between body and land, no division between the insentient environment and its inhabitants, no birth or extinction, no coming or going, and no internal or external, light or darkness. [End of] Scroll.
When expanded, it is that which even the *śaṅkha* (conch) cannot fathom; it is that which the vital energy of commands (*ādeśa-vāyu*) cannot constrain.
As for the body of actual retribution and adornment (*vipāka-saṃbhoga-kāya*), it accords with reality in its reception of retribution, being free from all obstacles.

Although its manifested lands and bodies are not truly material vessels, they are perfectly detached from the four propositions and completely eliminate the hundred negations. Only these two kinds of bodies are in accord with the true mind and its original source.
Jue Qi: This present scripture first refutes the consciousnesses of the seven locations, causing the mind and intention to turn back from delusion to return to the truth;
by following the branches to return to the root, one realizes this Dharmakāya, the ultimate primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

As for the Nirmāṇakāya of the Tathāgata, although it responds to and appears as the myriad things, its having a body is nothing other than arising as function based upon the essence; it is through function that it is simultaneously the essence.
Since the essence of the Dharma-body and Reward-body transcends the realm of emotional and intellectual measures, how could the function of the Response-body be compared to that of ordinary beings?
Although it possesses the six sense organs, these do not exceed their role as provisional supports for the manifestation of clarity; thus, darkness cannot obscure them.

Therefore, the metaphor of the burning wick may illustrate the delusory, but it cannot illustrate the Real; the function of radiance may be likened to the Buddha, but it cannot be likened to [the ordinary].
To falsely assume that the mind clings to being within cannot even illuminate the internal, much less the external.
Based on this, it may be said that the deluded, false mind resides within; yet it may also be said that the true mind pervades all that is within.
If delusion resides within, then that [delusion] acts as the subject and the self as the object; because its power of self-illumination is feeble, it cannot perceive the internal.
That which pervades all within is the self that masters the guest; it illuminates everything without exception.

Yet, delusion has no inherent nature, and its entire substance is the Truth itself. However, man, from a single point of confusion, takes this as his mind and is certain that it resides within his physical body.
That [delusion] is in fact the entirely true mind—how could it ever be subject to your confusion? Therefore, for those who have long remained in a state of stagnation and extension...
Thus, the long night is not darkened; those who have mastered the power of meditative concentration remain unclouded until dawn.

How much more so for one who realizes that the five aggregates are all empty and returns to the state of non-attainment? Their clarity is like the bright sun traversing the sky, illuminating no depth of darkness;
their stillness is like a clear pool reflecting objects, wherein every image is contained. This can be compared to various vessels, whether internal or external, large or small.
How could one possibly confine it within the dimensions of that vast void? Or, another might ask:

"It may well be that the six realms—internal, external, and so forth—are indeed places relied upon by the deluded and floating mind, and that while ordinary beings cling to them as real views, the Tathāgata rightly refutes them."

If one were to further state that "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) can also serve as a term for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it represents the gradual stage of dissociation from fetters (*visaṃyoga*).
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. This "non-abiding" (*asthāna*) is precisely non-attachment.
The Arhat of the fourth fruit is called a "Great Śramaṇa without attachment," precisely because he has attained the great fruit by means of a mind free from attachment.
Why does the Buddha also refute this? The answer is: if one seeks meaning based on names, not one in ten thousand can be found;
if one establishes names based on meaning, not one in ten thousand can go astray. This is because the term "Vajra" refers to non-abiding:

since the Bodhisattva has first realized that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and that his own mind is signless, subject and object are as one and all dualistic oppositions have ceased. That which remains unexhausted is...

It is simply because your thoughts have not yet been emptied. A Buddha wishes for a bodhisattva who practices profound *prajñā* to forget their emotions while meeting the Way, and to realize the principle while practicing *dāna*.
Therefore, it is said: "One should not dwell on form when giving; one should not dwell on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas when giving;
one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. It is like a live mechanism: if even one part is missing, it will immediately turn.
What is called "entering into principle" is termed "abiding. One abides within the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the dharma of non-abiding.
The four types of *śrāmaṇeras* who are free from attachment have also deeply realized this. It is fitting that Subhūti has long entered into non-abiding.
When the Buddha instructs him to "give rise to the mind while remaining in non-abiding," it is intended to further advance his skill. As for the Venerable Ānanda—
This person, displaying a mind of attachment identical to that of ordinary beings, possesses both a subjective body upon which they rely and an objective locus upon which they depend.
As soon as they are questioned by the Buddha, they employ every means to evade him;
yet when pressed to the point where no escape remains, they falsely cite the Buddha’s words to establish their own non-attachment—how could this be what is truly meant by "non-attachment"?

The Buddha now provisionally addresses this by examining whether that which is capable of being refuted has been refuted or not; thus he asks: "If you are not attached, does this non-attachment exist or does it not?
Generally speaking, the terms "attachment" and "non-attachment" depend upon objects.

If there were truly no objects, then non-attachment would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—originally nonexistent. How then could one speak of "not being attached"? If, on the other hand, there is an object present...
It has long been attached, yet it cannot be called unattached. This passage refutes the underlying intention in two senses.

First, it incidentally refutes the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of that which is the primary tenet; thus, the subsequent explanation establishes: "If there are no marks, then there is nothing. Second, it directly refutes the failure of the primary tenet to be established;
thus, the explanation establishes: "It is not non-existent; since the marks exist, they are present—how could they be non-existent?"

[This is] an attachment. However, regarding this preliminary stage of the path of *śamatha*, whether there is an object or not, whether there is attachment or non-attachment, whether there is an essence or no essence—none of these are anything other than delusions, and all are rejected.
This is because one has not yet reached the state where this mind is non-referential and without essence, and because one has not yet truly seen the Path (*darśanamārga*).
One must know that this sutra [proceeds] by means of the true seeing of the Path.

This serves as its foundation. If one truly perceives the Way, then within the samādhi in which one abides—just as the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas do—one sees that both the seeing and its conditions, as well as the characteristics of what is conceived, are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and these conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. How could they...?
If there were both "is" and "is not," then where would the two characters for "non-attachment" (*wu-zhuo*) be placed?

(3. Refuting the illusory mind as having no substance by means of the two kinds of roots, thereby revealing the true mind; Part One: Repenting of Faults) At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata, having received the Buddha’s compassion..."

Although you have now left the household life, you still rely on pride and affection; thus, despite your great learning, you have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) and cannot subdue the *śāpīra* spell.
Consequently, you were turned by it and fell into a house of debauchery, likely because you did not know the true destination of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
(2. Requesting the Dharma) We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so as to cause all...
After the icchantika Huimili (隳彌戾車) had spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground;
the great assembly likewise leaned forward in eager anticipation, thirsting for and awaiting his instructions.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because of the preceding inquiry and exhortation, one comes to realize the nature of delusion and falsehood; thus, one reproaches oneself, requests instruction, and seeks to reach the goal.
The "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*). The limit of reality is the true mind’s ultimate reality. The path of *śamatha* is that by which one reaches this limit of reality.
Changshui says: "Icchantikas" refers to those who deny [the existence of] all things; it means to destroy and ruin. "Mlecchas" refers to those with evil views.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The repentance for the offense committed at the opportune moment involves seven successive layers of remorse. The fault of drowning in the house of lust arises from being unable to subdue the depraved;
the fault of being unable to subdue the depraved arises from the presence of outflows (*āsrava*); the fault of outflows arises from excessive learning;
the fault of excessive learning arises from relying on the Buddha’s compassion and pride; the fault of relying on the Buddha’s compassion and pride arises from being the Buddha’s youngest disciple.
Cousin: These six are merely the lesser ones; as for the greatest, it must be because they do not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one were to know that destination, one would have long since realized entry [into it]; all else is not worth relying upon. What can the *sābīra* spell do to me?
Since the household of the true limit takes *śamatha* as the means of reaching it, I request the World-Honored One [to explain].
Please explain for me what it means to cause those icchantikas to destroy their mleccha-nature. This is because the root of nihilism lies in evil views;
the root of evil views lies in delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*); and the root of delusive conceptualization lies in not knowing that the essence of the deluded mind is empty.
Therefore, to penetrate this emptiness of essence is precisely to attain the path of *śamatha*, which causes those icchantikas to destroy their mleccha-nature.
[End of section]. (2.
Manifesting Auspicious Omens to Reveal the Teaching; Part 1: Manifesting Auspicious Omens to Symbolize the Dharma) At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face.

Those lights shone brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns, and the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways. Thus, the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions were simultaneously opened.
The Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power, causing all worlds to merge into a single realm;
all the great bodhisattvas residing within those worlds remained in their respective lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Because he is about to reveal the fundamental luminosity, he first manifests this auspicious sign.
To say that 'various lights are emitted from the face' means that the lights from the mouth, eyes, ears, nose, and the space between the eyebrows are all emitted simultaneously.

This demonstrates that this fundamental luminosity manifests through every sense faculty without exception. Because it manifests everywhere, they shine forth together and illuminate in unison, like hundreds of thousands [of suns]."

The "Day" signifies that the entire Buddha-world is, in itself, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The "sixfold earthquake" symbolizes the shattering of the ignorance of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) that gives rise to the delusory objects of attachment.
"The lands of as many atoms as there are suddenly open and appear" means that fundamental luminosity shines through clearly, such that delusory dust does not obstruct it.
"The worlds of the ten directions merge into a single realm" means that the sphere of wisdom manifests perfectly, while the measures of emotional cognition do not.

It is an obstruction. As for the statement that the Bodhisattvas and the assembly all reside in their own lands: the mind-measure is fundamentally pervasive, and the mind-hearing is fundamentally cavernous.
To comprehend this auspicious radiance is to attain the primordially pure essence of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state:
"The six kinds of shaking" refer to moving, surging, trembling, rising, roaring, and striking; they cause things to sway and remain unsettled.

It is said: "Moving" (*iṅgana*) refers to [the earth] shaking. "Leaping up" (*udgata*) refers to its ridges and mounds becoming unevenly elevated. "Quaking" (*prakaṃpana*) refers to making a low, rumbling sound.
"Rising up" (*samudgata*) refers to ascending from below. "Roaring" (*nirghoṣa*) refers to emitting a crashing resonance. "Striking" (*abhinirghāta*) refers to clashing against and startling objects.

Furthermore, each of these has three degrees: simple movement is called "moving"; movement throughout the four continents is called "universal moving"; and movement throughout the entire great trichiliocosm is called "equal universal moving. The remaining five [types of earthquakes] are likewise.
[Commentary] Tiantai says:
This scripture’s emission of light and manifestation of auspicious signs is most numerous; this [incident] is at its head and serves as the general omen.
It is because, being about to reveal the path of *śamatha*, [the Buddha] first employs a semblance of form. This semblance of form is sudden. Above.
For those of sharp faculties and keen wisdom, the Way exists through direct perception; for those of middling and inferior capacities, realization comes only through oral instruction.
Now, this scripture employs both form and sound, applying both the sudden and the gradual methods. There is no dharma that it does not harmonize, and no capacity that it does not encompass.

First, regarding the similarity of form, there are three sections. The first six lines concern the auspicious signs of the six sense organs, which serve as the basis for the subsequent revelation of the Truth.

The vision serves as the foundation for what follows. Next, the auspicious signs regarding all phenomena serve as the foundation for the manifestation of the Tathāgatagarbha through the aggregates, bases, elements, and the seven great elements.
Furthermore, the auspicious sign of hearing from afar serves as the foundation for the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
This indicates that when the original clarity is revealed, all visions are true visions and all phenomena are Buddha-dharma; there is no need for further contrivance.
Each and every one of these manifested omens fully reveals the great purport of the *Śūraṅgama*;

more than half the meaning has already been considered. (2. Direct Instruction, Part Two: First, the Marking and Explanation of the Two Kinds of Roots; Second, First, Pointing Out Delusion and General Reproach. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed various inverted karmic seeds that naturally cluster like the *akṣa* berries. Even those practitioners who cultivate themselves cannot achieve unexcelled Bodhi, let alone others..."

The attainment of the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, as well as becoming non-Buddhist deities, Māras, and their retinues, all arise from practicing erroneously due to ignorance of the two kinds of roots—like boiling sand in the hope of producing fine food;

even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed. (2. Setting forth the inquiry and showing the distinctions: Ānanda, what are these two? First, the root of birth and death from time immemorial.

Thus, you who now, along with all sentient beings, take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind that clings to objects) as your own nature, and the two—the beginningless essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, the fundamentally pure body—[are distinct].
This very essence of consciousness (*shì-jīng*), which is originally luminous, is capable of producing all conditions, yet it is that which is lost amidst those conditions.
Because all sentient beings have lost this original luminosity, although they act throughout the day, they do not realize it themselves.
They enter erroneously into the various realms of existence.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: That sentient beings accumulate karmic seeds and practitioners fail to achieve the correct fruit is entirely due to not knowing the two roots and practicing in a confused manner;
therefore, one must exercise decisive discernment. "Karmic seeds" refers to inverted, deluded afflictions.

Furthermore, just as a single branch of the akṣa fruit produces three seeds that must necessarily grow together, so too the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—must necessarily coalesce. The "攀緣心" (攀緣心;

*pān-yuán-xīn*,攀緣心) refers to what was previously identified as the false recognition of the seven locations. The "清淨體" (清淨體; *qīng-jìng-tǐ*,清淨體) refers to that which is now being definitively discerned.
That which is untainted by afflictions is called *bodhi*; that which does not involve birth-and-death is called *nirvāṇa*. Not...

Because it is untainted by defilement, it is called the Primordially Pure Essence (*āśraya*). Its nature is the *ālayavijñāna* (the essence of consciousness), which is the fundamental awakening of primordial luminosity.
The root-body, the vessel-world, and all conditioned phenomena arise in dependence upon this. Yet, human beings mistake conditions for reality and lose the truth;
thus it is said that "that which is lost due to conditions. Because of this loss, ignorance and non-awakening lead to wrongful existence.

Entering the various realms of existence. To speak of "original substance" (*yuántǐ*) as "originally luminous" (*yuánmíng*), and to speak of it as "fundamental luminosity" (*běnmíng*): that which emerges from its own source is called "original" (*yuán*);
that which points directly to the actual substance itself is called "fundamental" (*běn*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The two kinds of fundamental [nature] are shown so that those who encounter the teaching may know what to adopt and what to reject.

There is one who does not understand and thus completely reverses everything; for does he not take what should be abandoned and instead take what should be grasped, while abandoning what should be grasped?
Those who practice now are all thus inverted. This is a great affliction for those who study the Buddha-way;
therefore, the Tathāgata spoke to them concerning this: "The mind that conditions takes as its object that which it should grasp."
Taking objects as conditions: ordinary beings grasp at the six sense-objects; non-Buddhists and celestial Māras grasp at false views and barren emptiness;
those of the Two Vehicles grasp at partial emptiness; and Bodhisattvas grasp at the provisional nature of dependent origination.

In discussing these in turn, there are indeed differences of superiority and inferiority, and entry into the Way must be distinguished as inverted or correct. As previously stated, they separately achieve the state of a Śrāvaka.
The Pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and the celestial Māras are all rooted in this. The primordial pure essence (prakṛti-viśuddha-svabhāva) is itself the fundamental transformation;

its textual expression is merely a variation. "Essential consciousness" (vijñāna-śukra) refers to the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). "Primordial luminosity" (prakṛti-prakāśa) refers to the ninth consciousness (amala-vijñāna).

"All conditions" specifically points to the discriminative consciousness of phenomena (nirvikalpa-kalpa-vijñāna); this is what was referred to in the preceding passage as taking the攀緣心 (clinging and seeking mind) as one's own nature. To state it briefly:
When these sights and sounds reach the mind, the essence of both the true and the false becomes intermingled, like gold and sand that have not yet been distinguished.
Whether one can discern and separate them depends on the person. In the following text, seeing that "seeing is not seeing" serves as an analogy for hearing that "hearing is not hearing";
thus, it constitutes Bodhi and Nirvana. If, however, one discriminates based on sensory objects, it constitutes affliction and birth-and-death.
Thus, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are fully present within the boundaries of daily life, in the midst of seeing and hearing; how can one not know to exercise discernment?

The "pusher" is what I shall take as the mind.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Where the golden fist is raised, one must directly recognize fundamental luminosity; yet if the marks of sensory dust are not eliminated, one will continue to mistake the thief for one's own son.

Having first manifested various lights from his face through a resemblance of form, he next, through a resemblance of sound, further demonstrated the two kinds of fundamental sources.
Thereupon, [the Buddha] raised his fist to definitively examine the essence of Ānanda’s mind, as Master Wēnlíng said:

"Where the golden fist is raised, one must directly recognize fundamental luminosity. However, because Ānanda had not yet eliminated the signs of external objects, he continued to mistake the thief for his son;

[III. Revealing that it is merely delusion (divided into two parts; first, refuting what is not so)] The Buddha said: "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind. [II. Asking in astonishment] Ānanda was startled;

Clarifying that the Arising of Good and Evil is Due to the Mind] Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha. Because my heart loves the Buddha, I have now left the household life.
Why is it that my mind alone offers sustenance to the Tathāgata, even as I travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to serve all Buddhas and virtuous teachers?”
Consciousness gives rise to great courage and vigor; all practices of the most difficult dharmas are performed using this mind.

Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it is still because of this mind. (2. Revealing that the absence of mind is identical to earth and wood: If this manifesting consciousness were not the mind, I would then be without mind, identical to earth and wood;
apart from this awareness, there would be nothing else at all. (3. Concluding with the mutual alarm and doubt of self and others: Why does the Tathāgata speak thus?

"This is not the mind; I am truly terrified, and there is not one among this great assembly who does not harbor doubt. (2. Requesting Instruction) I pray that you will, out of great compassion, reveal and instruct those of us who have not yet awakened."
[Commentary] Wuxing said: Ānanda distinguishes between the awareness that perceives objects and the insentient nature of earth and wood, designating the former as his "self.
This is precisely the characteristic of the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*). Suddenly hearing this reprimand, he therefore raises the objection regarding the insentient.
Yet he does not realize that true self is no-self, and that spiritual cognition is non-cognition; how could the wondrously pure and luminous mind not be present everywhere? This—
Since this teaching was initiated through great transformative power (*mahopāya*), how could it be considered the literal truth of Ānanda?

(2) The Revelation (in two parts; first, the narrator’s account of the intent): At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), touched the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying:

(2) The Tathāgata’s Correct Revelation (in two parts; first, the demonstration of the true and the false; first, clarifying the true essence through the false; first, the direct clarification of the true essence): The Tathāgata has always taught that all dharmas...

All that is produced is but a manifestation of the mind; all causes and effects, worlds, and even the finest atoms, take their substance from the mind. (2. Raising the False to Contrast with the True. Part One: Raising the False Phenomena.
Ānanda, if one were to examine the root source of everything existing within all worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots—they would all possess a substantial nature;
even empty space has its name and appearance. (Part Two: Comparing with the True Substance. How much more so for that which is pure, wondrously pure!
[The text] clarifies that while all minds are the nature of mind, they themselves have no substance.

[Commentary: Wénlǐng says: Because they are terrified by the claim that there is "no-mind," [the Buddha] cites what is commonly taught to lead sentient beings, demonstrating the existence of the true mind so that they may know where to apply themselves.
As for "the mind entering the patience of the non-arising of dharmas," it causes one to realize the reality.

Phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) do not arise or perish; they are the mind itself. Since the three realms are but mind and the myriad dharmas are but consciousness, it is said that "the arising of all dharmas is but the manifestation of the mind.
"All causes and effects" refers to the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*) of the ten realms.

"The atoms of the world" refers to the secondary retribution (*bhājana-loka*) of the ten realms. Since there is nothing whose substance is not formed by the mind, how can one say that there is no mind?
They are of the same substance as earth and wood. That which is inherently undefiled is called "pure"; that which is defiled yet remains undefiled is called "wondrously pure."孤山 (Gushan) says:
"That all phenomena arise and are manifested solely by the mind means that because the mind is fundamentally endowed [with all things], it can create in accordance with conditions;
therefore, the created phenomena are entirely capable of creating the creating mind. Since the environment and its inhabitants are already one mind, this one mind is truly non-existent."
Subject and object: For example, it is because water possesses the nature of waves that it can produce waves;

since the produced waves are entirely the producing water, when one contemplates the produced, one sees only what is inherently present. This is the natural state (*dharmatā*) of the true mind of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*):

all phenomena are inherently complete within it, yet these phenomena are by their very nature originally unarisen. Therefore, although they are inherently present, they do not exist as [separate] entities.
It is neither mixed nor separate, and though it pervades each and every thing, it has no location.
That which is the nature of all minds is precisely the eternally abiding true mind, which serves as the fundamental nature of the deluded minds of the nine realms.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The Dharma of Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma*) is spoken of in terms of the nature that is without distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas.
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) is spoken of in terms of the stages and positions (*bhūmi*). "Entry" (*praveśa*) is spoken of in terms of cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*).
From the first fascicle to the fourth fascicle of the Sūtra, the elucidation of the eternally abiding true mind all pertains to the meaning of the Dharma of Non-arising. *Śamatha* and so forth are...
Regarding the method of cultivation and entry: the following clarifies the path to Bodhi, which is the stage of realization.
First, one awakens to this Dharma and perceives that not a single phenomenon can arise, nor does one perceive that a single phenomenon can cease.

One understands that all phenomena and events are ultimately and entirely firm and solid. Relying upon this to practice, one clearly illuminates this truth and, reaching the ultimate limit, realizes the final consummation.
This is the correct lineage of this very sutra. ○ (2.

Showing that the deluded mind has no substance; Part 1: Clarifying that it has no substance apart from objects. If you stubbornly cling to the nature of discernment, awareness, and observation as you understand it, and insist that this must be the mind, then this mind should exist as a complete, independent nature, separate from all objects such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, as well as from all activities.
○ (Part 2: Revealing that the arising of thought is entirely dependent on objects. As you...
Now, to receive and listen to my Dharma is to have discrimination based on sound;

even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of discrimination regarding the dust of dharmas.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: This is based on the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) to demonstrate the absence of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). "Discriminating between vitarka and vicāra" refers to the mind that performs investigation.
This mind, being devoid of sense-objects, lacks inherent nature and should not be grasped as real. When sensory cognition ceases, the mental faculty becomes profound and tranquil;
yet even that which is profound and tranquil is still a mere reflection of the dharma-objects (*dharmaviṣaya*) and likewise lacks self-nature.

The True Limit (bhūtakoṭi) says: "The activities of the various objects—namely, the six sense-objects such as form and so forth—all possess the functional activity of drawing the mind toward them as conditions.
