This refers to what follows below: "The mountains, rivers, and great earth suddenly arise without cause; the person named Yan-rada-ta (Hanuman) runs madly without cause.
"Not moving the eyes, staring until they become fatigued" refers to falsely conceiving of luminosity as a conscious awakening.

"Then seeing wild flowers appearing separately within empty space" means that because of this perceived luminosity, an objective realm is established; once that objective realm is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. Is this not the same?

Among the differences, the blazing [of the flames] constitutes the difference and so forth. As for what is called "distinct vision": when the eyes are strained by flowers, one sees them as clear and bright, yet when the eyes are healthy, they are not seen;
this serves as a metaphor for sentient beings, who perceive the existence of Buddhas where there is actually none.

○ (2. Refuting Attachment by Employing a Simile; Part 1: Showing that the Characteristics of the Aggregates Are Unarisen; Sub-part 1: The Direct Demonstration) Ānanda, these various delusory flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes. ○ (Sub-part 2:
Refutation by Contradiction) In this way, Ānanda, if they came from space, having come from space, they would have to return to space. If there were coming and going, they would not be empty space.
If space were not empty, it could not accommodate the arising and ceasing of these flower-forms, just as your own body, Ānanda, cannot accommodate you yourself.
If it emerges from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, it must also enter back through the eyes; since this nature of the flower emerges from the eyes, there ought to be seeing [of it].
If there is seeing, then as it departs into the empty space of the flower, upon its return it should see the eyes.

If there is no seeing, then as it obscures the empty space upon its departure, it should likewise obscure the eyes upon its return. Furthermore, when you see the flower, your eyes should be free of obstruction; why then is there only clear sky?

He is titled "The Eye of Pure Clarity. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says: If there were coming and going, there would be a substantial entity; therefore, it is not empty space. Since it is not empty, it is substantial;
thus, like Ānanda’s body, there is nowhere else for it to be contained. This argues that the wild flowers do not arise dependent upon empty space.

If the flower emerged from the eye, one would have attained the nature of the eye and thus possess the faculty of vision. Now, when you turn [your gaze], you neither see the eye nor does the eye become obscured;
therefore, the flower did not emerge from the eye. Furthermore, if the flower emerged from the eye, then while the flower was in space, the eye should no longer be obscured.
Why then do you still see the flower with your eye obscured? You must see the empty sky without [obscuration].
The Flower Garland School calls this the "Pure and Bright Eye. This argument refutes the claim that the delusory flowers do not arise from the eyes.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Next, in the refutation of [the view that the flowers] do not arise from the eyes, he first establishes their fundamental tenet based on two meanings.

The first two phrases definitely establish the presence of entering and exiting; the latter two phrases definitely establish that the nature of the flower has visibility. Next, the middle two sections are refuted.

First, the refutation is based on the presence of visibility regarding the entering and exiting of the nature of the flower; thus it says: "If there were visibility, then when [the flower] went away, since the flower was empty, upon its return it should have been seen by the eye.
Second, the refutation is based on the absence of visibility regarding the nature of the flower. This has two parts; first, based on the absence of...

When you see it turning, the cataract on the eye is shattered. Therefore it is said: "If there were no seer, then when [the cataract] emerged, it would have obscured the sky; when it turned back, it should have obscured the eye.
Second, regarding the absence of seeing, this directly refutes the emergence of non-obscuration. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, when you see flowers, your eyes should be free of cataracts.
The statement, "Why is the clear sky called 'clear and bright' while the eyes are called 'obscured'? follows from this to refute [the opponent's position]. This is because there is none.
The cataract-obscured eye is the clear and bright eye. The clear and bright eye should perceive the clear and bright sky.
Now, those who see flowers [in the sky] are instead called "clear and bright-eyed. Furthermore, why must one necessarily see a cloudless sky to be designated as having a clear and bright eye?
○ (2. Concluding that [the aggregates] are false and transcending conceptualization): Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is false;

fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor of spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*). [Commentary: Wēnlíng says: "Since one has realized that illusory flowers have no cause, one should know that the aggregate of form is false;

fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature—it is precisely the wondrous *tathatā* nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. The other four [aggregates] follow this example. Zīzhōng says: "If..."
Knowing that the characteristics of flowers are themselves emptiness, one reveals that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: That which is neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous does not go beyond the four modes of being (*catur-koṭi*).

The text states that emergence from the eye is "self-arising," while emergence from space is "other-arising. The combination of these two factors constitutes their arising together; thus, these three modes of being are all identical as causes.
If dependent origination does not belong to causes and conditions, then one reckons it as spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, within the text, by performing only two investigations, both sets of four [alternatives] are subsumed. In the Tiantai *Lotus Samādhi*, the mind is investigated according to the four propositions:
because the mind is taken as the cause, the mind is investigated as belonging to self-arising; because the mind is not taken as the cause, the mind is investigated as belonging to ignorance.

If one holds that it arises from both self and other, because it is both caused by the mind and not caused by the mind, then the mind immediately infers that the ignorance which deviates from the *dharmatā* belongs to the co-arising of self and other.
If one holds that it is neither caused by the mind nor not caused by the mind, then the mind immediately infers that the ignorance which deviates from the *dharmatā* belongs to arising without cause.
In the present text, "clear and bright eyes" serves as a metaphor for the *dharmatā*.
A clear sky is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*). Although there are no floating flowers in the clear sky, once they appear before the eyes, the duality of subject and object is established.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The primordial clarity shines and produces the objective field; once the objective field is established, the nature of the illuminating clarity is forgotten.
Does not this act of staring with wide-open eyes serve as the cause for the floating flowers? Could they possibly arise without it?
“Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose entire body is in harmony, such that they momentarily forget their very existence and feel neither discomfort nor comfort.
For no apparent reason, this person rubs his two palms together in the air, and within those hands, various sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat falsely arise.
You should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this.”
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To let the emotions touch the objects and to take those objects into the mind is called 'feeling' (vedanā).

To be at ease and well-adjusted, with the nature being neither contrary nor compliant, is a metaphor for the fundamental nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) originally being devoid of all feelings. The two hands rubbing empty space and producing sensations of roughness or smoothness is a metaphor for how false contact gives rise to various feelings.
Forgetting one's existence is as described in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng): 'suddenly forgetting my body.'"
This speaks of the ultimate state of harmonious adjustment. [Part Two: Refuting Attachment by Employing Similes (2):

First, the simile showing that the characteristics of the aggregates are unborn (2): First, the direct demonstration. Ānanda, these illusory sensations do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm. [Second, the refutation by way of reductio ad absurdum.
In this way, Ānanda, if they came from space, since they can touch the palm, why do they not touch the body? It would be illogical for space to select [a specific spot] to touch.

If it were to emerge from the palm, it would not depend upon contact; furthermore, since it emerges from the palm, if there were contact, the palm should perceive it, and when separated, the sensation should enter the arm, wrist, marrow, and bones.

There should likewise be awareness of its path as it enters. Surely there must be a conscious mind that knows its emergence and entry, such that there is a distinct entity within the body that comes and goes.
Why wait for contact to know it? This is what is called "contact. (2. Concluding the Falsity and Dispelling Calculations) Therefore, one should...
One knows that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false, fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The essence of emptiness is eternally pervasive and should not involve selection. A palm should emerge from itself and should not depend on anything else.
Furthermore, if it were to emerge from the palm, then wherever there is emergence, there must be entry. Yet when it emerges while the palms are joined, although the palms possess cognition..."
When one enters [the state of concentration] while detached from it, even the arms are not perceived. Since there is no fixed reality, it is entirely a mere illusion.
[Tiantai’s Commentary: The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally devoid of all sensations. That they now exist is because they arise from what was originally non-existent.
Just as the phenomenon of touch must depend upon an object to arise, a body alone cannot constitute touch by itself.
Now, by rubbing two hands together in the void, one falsely perceives roughness and smoothness within a single entity; how could this have any basis?
This is like the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm; both subject and object are thus, and all dualistic oppositions are utterly severed.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have given rise to forced awakening, suddenly producing false notions of self and person, and the division between faculties and objects.
Within the nature of the *ālaya*, they undergo illusory loss and gain.

The Tathāgata, wishing to clarify that one receives without receiving and receives while not receiving, so as to return to true reception, now employs this analogy to examine and detach from emotional attachments. [This nature] does not come from emptiness, nor...
It is clear that it does not belong to another, for it does not emerge from the palm; it is clear that it does not arise from itself.

Since it cannot be found through the analysis of separation, it likewise cannot be found through the analysis of conjunction. Being neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously, the contemplation of samādhi is thereby revealed.

○ (Third: Establishing a Simile to Clarify the Aggregate of Perception) Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who, upon speaking of sour plums, has water flow from his mouth; or one who, thinking of treading upon a precipice, has his feet turn numb and sour.
You should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise so.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The thought of a non-existent object produces a mental image;
this refers to the thought of a cliff while tasting plums, whereby saliva flows and the mouth becomes sore. All such thoughts are like this."

○ (2. Refuting Attachment by Employing Similes; Part 1: The Simile Showing that the Characteristics of the Aggregates are Unborn; Part 1: Direct Demonstration) Ānanda, as I have just said, this sourness does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth. ○ (3. Refutation by Contradiction) In this way, Ānanda, if it arose from the plum, the plum should speak of it itself;
why wait for someone else to say so? If it entered through the mouth, the mouth should hear it itself; why must one wait for the ears?
If it were heard solely by the ears, why would this sourness not emerge from within the ears? It is like imagining oneself standing on a precipice.

This is similar to what was previously explained. (2. Concluding that it is false and transcending conceptualization: Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: When people talk of plums and their mouths water, yet the plums cannot speak, those who calculate that [the moisture] comes from the plums are deluded.
When one hears of plums with the ears and the mind conceives them, yet the mouth cannot hear them, those who calculate that [the sensation] enters through the mouth are deluded.
If one hears of plum blossoms yet there is no water in the mouth, then both the conceptualization and the verbal explanation are false. The supplementary note says:
"Saliva flows at the mention of plums" refers to when saliva emerges from one's own mouth because of hearing another person speak of plums;
"the feet ache from thinking of Mount Siya" refers to when one thinks of it oneself. Zhenji said: "That which is similar to speaking should be called 'thinking thus' regarding treading [upon it]."

It does not come from the precipice, nor does it enter through the soles of the feet. If it were to come from the precipice, the precipice would have to merge with itself; why wait for the thought of another?

If it were to enter through the feet, the feet would have to merge with themselves; why wait for the thought of the mind? If it were merely the thought of the mind, why would there be a sensation of aching bitterness felt in the soles of the feet?
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The five sense organs and the six sense objects are both termed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When the organs and objects come into contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises. As residual objects fall away, perception (*saṃjñā*) is produced; this is precisely what it originates from.
Now, when one speaks of a "sour plum," one perceives its acidity and saliva flows; when one thinks of treading on a precipice, one perceives its danger and the feet ache. This is perception.
How could it be that the subsequent experience is not its own cause? It is simply because one has no cause for forming such a thought that one imagines this emptiness.

Now, taking the entry through the mouth as the self and the production of the plum as the other, when one investigates and pursues them through successive stages, neither cause nor condition can be found.
Since even causes and conditions do not exist, how can there be anything "spontaneous"? Free from both extremes, the true and eternal is revealed in its solitary clarity.

○ (4. Establishing a Simile to Clarify the Dharma: First Part) Ānanda, it is like a torrential stream where waves succeed one another, such that the preceding limit and the succeeding limit do not overstep each other.
You should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is likewise.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The wondrous clarity [of the mind] undergoes false movement, shifting and migrating according to objects. From moment to moment it changes and passes away; ever-new, it never stops.

Therefore, it is called the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), and is likened to a torrential stream. Because each thought arises and perishes such that what follows does not reach what precedes, it is said that they do not overlap."

○ (2. Refuting Attachment by Employing Similes; Part 1: The Simile Showing that the Characteristics of the Aggregates Are Unborn; Subsection 1: Direct Demonstration) Ānanda, this nature of the current does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water;

it is neither the nature of water, nor is it separate from space and water. ○ (Subsection 2: Refutation by Contradiction) In this way, Ānanda, if it were to arise because of space, then the inexhaustible space of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow, and the worlds would naturally all be submerged.
If it were to exist because of water, then this torrential current...

The nature [of water] should not possess the characteristics of water; yet now it must be present. If it were identical to the substance of water, then when it is clear and still, it would not be the essence of water.
If it were separate from space and water, then space would not exist externally, nor would there be external flowing water. (2. Concluding that it is illusory and free from conceptualization:
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This is an exegesis of the text. It explains that the nature of the flow does not depend on the water; it is neither identical to nor separate from it, thereby clarifying that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has no substantial reality.
"Having the characteristic of existing" means that the flow should have a distinct essence and characteristic apart from the water.

Space is not something external to which water flows within it. There is no flow apart from the water; the flow ultimately depends upon the water. Thus, it is not separate from space and water. Zizhong said:

"If [the flow] exists because of the water" means that if one were to claim there is a distinct nature of flow (pravāha-svabhāva) existing because of that water, then since cause and effect would be of different natures, the nature of the torrential flow should not be the water itself. That which possesses the water is the water itself. What is possessed...
This is a flow. If the two characteristics were distinct, both would have to be present simultaneously.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The first three aggregates (skandhas) all take their analogies from the body; thus, those metaphors are direct.

Now, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) takes its analogy from empty water; thus, that metaphor seems indirect. It is said: it is not indirect. This is because they are related through a succession of transformations.

This is to extensively fulfill the aspirations of those who are ready for the teaching. For the five sense organs and six sense objects are so vast in their scope that they encompass the entire Dharma-realm;
how could they exist outside of space and water? Therefore, the latter four aggregates all pervade form.

Just as the nails grow, the hair lengthens, the tendons turn, and the veins throb—shifting and changing in dense succession yet remaining entirely without awareness—the fruit ripens, the flowers fall, the tree ages, and the vine withers.

Moment by moment, they shift and pass away without being visible or knowable; thus, even in a torrential stream, there is no aspect that is not the shifting flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Now, taking water and the nature of water as the self and the cause, and taking space as the other and the condition.
These two phenomena combine to form the conditions for co-arising. By setting aside space and water, one regards them as causeless and spontaneous;

yet through successive investigation and inquiry, one reveals the nature of the hidden treasury (tathāgatagarbha). Furthermore, the waves are used as a metaphor for the delusory, while the moisture is used as a metaphor for the True.

The waves and water depend upon space and pervade it in accordance with space, yet they do not abide within space. Within this, there inherently exists that which, while undergoing flux, [is nevertheless constant].
That which does not migrate or flow resides therein.

(5.1.2.1 Establishing a Simile to Reveal the Dharma) Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar, plugs its two openings, fills it with empty space, and carries it a thousand li away to present as a gift to another country.
You should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exactly like this.

[Commentary]: Jueli says that the *piṅgā* is a bird with a beautiful voice, and the shape of the vase is modeled after it. Gushan says that the vase symbolizes deluded karma (*karma*), while the emptiness symbolizes deluded consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Karma drags the consciousness along as the vase carries the empty space. The discarding of one body and receiving another is likened to traveling far away;
the present *skandhas* (aggregates) are like one's own country, while the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the future *skandhas* are like other countries.

○ (2. Refuting Attachments by Employing Similes; Part 1: The Simile Showing that the Characteristics of the Aggregates Are Unborn; Sub-part 1: Direct Demonstration) Ānanda, in this way, empty space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter here. ○ (Sub-part 2:

Refutation by Contradiction) In this way, Ānanda, if it came from that direction, then since the space was already contained within the original bottle when it was removed, there should be a deficiency of empty space on the spot where the original bottle stood.

If it entered here, then upon opening the hole and overturning the bottle, one should see the space coming out. ○ (Part 2: Concluding that It Is False and Free from Conceptualization) Therefore, you should know that the aggregates of consciousness are empty.
Delusion is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Empty space does not come from that direction to enter this direction.
If a bottle were to contain space and move it from that place to this, why would one not see the space decrease in that place, or see the space emerge in this place? (Wenling).
It is said that the true awakening of the nature of emptiness pervades the entire Dharma-realm. When there is a single delusion, it becomes consciousness; thus, it is like the space within a jar.

That the inner and outer spaces are one is a metaphor for the identity of the nature and consciousness. The blocking of both holes is a metaphor for the false differentiation of sameness and difference.
That space has no coming or going and cannot be carried or offered is a metaphor for the fact that the nature is without birth or extinction, and is likewise without giving up or receiving. Now...
To speak of "carrying offerings" is a metaphor for the nature of delusion, which is consciousness falsely following along with the flow of transmigration.

The myriad phenomena of body and mind are none other than the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. On the Path, one loathes discrimination; in Principle, one forgets conceptualization.
All verbal expressions are but frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); every intention or thought involves delusion and inversion. The Great Awakened One is about to bestow awakening.

Therefore, at the beginning of this fascicle, I have provisionally clarified the distinction between the correct and the inverted, analyzed the "shadow-condition" (yuan-ying), and selected the "essence of seeing" (jian-jing) to demonstrate the true measure.
First, I have addressed their deluded emotional calculations to sweep away the dust and cataracts from the eye of the mind and wash the filth and turbidity from the lungs and intestines.
Once the mind and its objects are cleared and both truth and falsehood are forgotten, one may then merge and enter the state of the Tathāgata.
[The text] concludes: "Thus one comes to know that the faculties, objects, bases, and elements—every phenomenon—is none other than the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the general purport of the second and third fascicles.
[Commentary: Tiantai says: "The ten directions of empty space" is a metaphor for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). "The *piṅgala* bird and the vase" [refer to] blocking both [nostrils].

The "hole" is a metaphor for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). Filling it with air and carrying it a thousand li to provide sustenance for another country is a metaphor for the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Now, the nature of consciousness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true consciousness; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Yet, through its own obscuration, it becomes stubborn emptiness; furthermore, by binding darkness together, it forms the basis for form, and through deluded thought, it coagulates into solidity.

Taking the aggregate of form as a body, they recognize one another in their nature, yet oppose one another in their functions. How is this different from taking a *piṅgala* jar, plugging both its holes?
Yet people, once deluded, take this as their mind and are firmly convinced it resides within the physical body.
How is this different from filling a jar with empty space, carrying it a thousand li on a long journey to offer it to another country? The jar has gone away, but the space remains.
The metaphor of coming and going being empty of entry or exit illustrates that while the body possesses the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), consciousness is without arising or ceasing.

Through this, one can understand that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is falsely existent, while the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is fundamentally empty; there is only the single consciousness, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Although the ancient sages used hemp to represent the perfected nature, a rope for the dependent nature, and a snake for the imagined nature—metaphors that are indeed apt—they are not as effective as [the following].

The analogy of space is applied directly to the body. If one explains the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) according to the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, then one takes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as the thesis, and "neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous" as the reason.
Using the emptiness of a vase as a metaphor for the absence of coming, going, entering, or exiting— this principle applies by analogy to the four aggregates (*skandhas*).

(II. Refuting the Illusory Nature of the Six Entrances. 2. First, General Inquiry. Furthermore, Ānanda, how is it that the six entrances are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
[Commentary] Changshui says: The Sanskrit term *praveśa* is translated here as "entry" (*ru*) or "abode" (*chu*). It refers to the place where objects enter;

it is also the place where consciousness arises. Although both the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are places where consciousness arises, since we are now analyzing and refuting them individually by way of the six faculties, we designate only the faculties as "entries."

○ (2. Specific Explanation of the Six [Sense Bases]. First, the Eye Base. 1. Initial Establishment. 1. Initial Metaphor: Arising of Delusion Based on Reality. Ānanda, that very act of the eyes staring fixedly until they become fatigued—both the eyes and the fatigue—are, in themselves, the appearance of delusion arising from enlightenment through fixed staring.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: In the previous section on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it was likened to how the eye-gazing becomes strained, causing one to perceive illusory flowers and other such signs within empty space.
Therein, the eye is used as a metaphor for the True, the strain for the delusive, and the flowers for form.
Now, referring back to that previous analogy, it says "that very eye-gazing and so forth. This includes both the eye and the strain, which are taken up here below.
The sense faculties mentioned in the preceding passage as the "similes" (dṛṣṭānta) now serve as the "dharmas illustrated" (dārṣṭāntika) within this context.

This is because those "fatigued eyes" are precisely the false and illusory characteristics of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*). One should know that from the eye-base up to the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*), all are like flowers in the sky.
Therefore, the passages concerning the six bases all state: "These are likewise the characteristics of fatigue produced by staring at Bodhi. Question: Why not speak directly [of the dharmas]?
In analyzing the nature of seeing by examining the sense organs and their objects, why must one point to the previously mentioned matter of the weary eyes? Answer:

Since the sense organs and objects are universally deluded, awakening must proceed from the essential. Therefore, by pointing to the false phenomena easily understood by ordinary people, one uses them to open up Ānanda’s unclarified attachments.
The subsequent examples—plugging the ears to hear sound and using the nose to perceive touch—are treated in the same manner.

This is so. [The Commentary] states: Master Wuxing further says that one should know that in the preceding passage, the metaphor of "empty flowers" universally represents the forms of the five sense organs across the nine realms;
whereas here, the "empty flowers" represent only the characteristics of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within the nine realms. The former is broad and this is narrow; they must not be conflated.
The same. Tiantai says: Previously, the *rūpa-skandha* (form-aggregate) was explained by means of analogies;

thus, the "pure eye" was used as a metaphor for the true wisdom inherently possessed, while the "wild flowers" were a metaphor for the deluded forms of the nine realms. Now, in explaining the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), we abandon the analogy to follow the actual phenomenon (*dharma*).

Furthermore, because we wish to borrow an analogy to illustrate this phenomenon, it is said: "that very pupil of the eye," and so forth. Moreover, there is a fear that people might cling to the previous "pure eye."
Because it is real, [the text] refutes it by stating that both are equally "symptoms produced by staring.

As for the mention of *bodhi* and so forth, this is also spoken in reflection of the second fundamental consciousness—the original clarity of the essence—which is capable of producing all conditions and is what remains when those conditions are discarded.
Now, regarding these symptoms of staring, there is the root and the branch; the root refers to the beginningless past, while the branch refers to the present moment.
Therefore, know that if one can perceive the seeing as it was previously described, then throughout the entire day it will not differ from Bodhi.

If it were otherwise, it would be nothing more than a mere exhaustion of appearances. This principle applies to all six sense faculties; there is no exception to this. If one remains at a lower level of existence, these words do not apply.
Is it not profound that those who pursue the superficial fail to grasp this? Thus, the subsequent passage also merely says: "It shall cause you to attain stillness."
Quiescence, peace, bliss, subtlety, and constancy—these six are nothing other than the six sense faculties themselves.

(2. Explaining that they have no substance apart from their objects. Because of the two kinds of delusory objects, light and darkness, the faculty of seeing arises within them; it draws in these objective images and is called the "nature of seeing. Yet this seeing has absolutely no substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.
(2. Refuting [the notion of a self-nature]. First, explaining that the aspect of entering has no arising. First, the direct demonstration. Thus, Ānanda, you should know:
This seeing does not come from light, nor does it come from darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. (2. Refutation by Contradiction) Why is this?

If it came from light, it would cease when darkness follows, and thus one should not see darkness. If it came from darkness, it would cease when light follows, and thus there would be no seeing of light.
If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness. Thus, this essence of seeing fundamentally lacks self-nature. If, regarding...

When empty space emerges and gazes forward, it perceives the objects of the dust; when returning, it sees the sense organs. Furthermore, when empty space observes itself, what concern is that for your sense entrances? (2.

Concluding that delusion is itself truth) Therefore, you should know that the eye entrance is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because visual perception arises due to objects (*viṣaya*) and because the sense organ (*indriya*) draws in those objects, it is called the "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

However, since it has no substantiality apart from the objects, one can know it to be empty and false. It continues, saying: "It does not come from light or darkness, nor does it issue from the sense organ," and so forth.

Since it has no point of origin, it is neither produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor is it spontaneous (*svabhāva*). It is fundamentally the wondrous *tathatā*-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. — Tianru.

The supplementary note states: According to Master Huan’s classification of the scripture, there are three sections. First, from "That is his pupils" downward, it explains how delusion arises based on the truth.

Second, from "Caused by light and darkness" downward, it demonstrates that delusion has no reality. Third, from "Therefore one should know" downward, it shows that when delusion is extinguished, it is immediately the truth.
This means that because delusion lacks self-nature, its entire substance is the truth. The remaining five cases follow this pattern.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the statement that "sucking in these sensory objects is called seeing the nature," this word "suck" (吸) has the same meaning as a magnet attracting a needle.
Because the magnet is fundamentally the "mother" of iron, it is called the "Compassionate Mother Stone" (慈母石).

It is simply because their elemental constituents are identical and their innate natures are not different that the magnet alone attracts the needle and does not attract other things. This is the sixth point in the present text.

The sense organs are likewise so. It is simply because their elemental constituents are identical that the eye alone absorbs form and binds form as its root, yet it cannot absorb sound and the other objects.
If the six organs were to function interchangeably, then organ and object would be one, and illumination and function would be quiescent;
what, then, could be said of "absorbing"? It is due to the two kinds of delusory objects—light and darkness—that the faculty of seeing arises.
The one situated in the middle refers to what is stated in the following passage: "Cognition arises from the sensory objects.

To absorb these objective images and call this "seeing-nature" is because the sense-faculties possess characteristics. This seeing, when separated from those two objects—light and darkness—is ultimately without substance;

thus, the characteristic and the seeing lack inherent nature, being like two reeds leaning against each other. However, while the following passage addresses the refutation of the objects as well, here it deals with them alone.
The refutation of the sense organs is merely a different point. In the refutation of [the claim that] they do not arise from emptiness, one should have said:
"If they emerged from emptiness, you ought to see the sense organs. Now, however, it says: "Previously, when gazing at external objects, upon returning [to the senses], one ought to see the organs.

One must understand that by refuting the external and refuting emptiness, one in turn establishes the refutation of the internal—the sense organs. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "Furthermore, if emptiness observes itself, what concern is that with your sense-faculties? Indeed, this is empty.
Reality is the opposite of falsehood, and falsehood is the counterpart of truth. Generally speaking, what is true is real, while what is false is empty;

it may also be said that what is real is true, and what is empty is false. That the sense-base of the eye is empty and false—like flowers appearing to a person with cataracts—and that one calculates its arising as being due to causes and conditions or occurring spontaneously, is incorrect. The nature of the storehouse (ālaya) is truly real...
Just as the pure eyes in a cloudless sky remain unmoving and all-pervading, so too does the wondrous nature of True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) manifest.

In this single truth and single reality, how could the wild flowers [of delusion] pose any obstruction? In this single void and single falsehood, the cloudless sky is by its very nature vast and open.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* examines non-arising through the four modes of existence (catuṣkoṭi), stating: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both, nor without cause."

Because there is no such thing as causelessness, it is said that there is no arising. Now, although the text concerning the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) addresses only the refutation of arising from conditions, from nature, or from both, thereby revealing the wondrous true *tathatā* nature of the fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*, in reality, all four modes of arising are fully present therein.

For instance, when it says "it does not come from light or darkness," this means it is not born of another; when it says "it does not emerge from the sense organs," this means it is not self-born. If [it were to arise] from the sense organs...
If arising from both [self and other] were impossible, it would not be arising from both; if it did not arise from emptiness, it would not be arising without cause.

If one takes self, other, and both as causes and conditions, while taking arising without cause as "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), then although one speaks of two combinations, they actually constitute four.
Is this not the same as the meaning established by the investigation in the Sūtras and Śāstras? Or, as asked in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, why does it refute these four?

By nature, this only accomplishes the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Now, since it is categorized as "samādhi," this refers to emerging into the provisional (*niṣkrānta-prajñapti*);

why, then, is it also traced back to non-arising (*anutpāda*)? Answer: Within the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there are two different modes of cultivation: that of the initial mind and that of the subsequent mind.

For a Bodhisattva of the subsequent mind who cultivates the contemplation of the provisional, it is truly appropriate to emerge from emptiness into the provisional, to know the illness and recognize the medicine, and to administer the medicine according to the illness.

This enables them to practice accordingly. Now, this treatise discusses the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) cultivated by the beginner. Cessation through realizing the reality (*tattva*) is simply the convergence of differences back into unity.
Cessation through skillful means (*upāya*) is simply proceeding from unity through diversity.
It is precisely because it employs skillful means to investigate each of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) one by one, causing the mind to... [proceed].
To abide in that which is the place of abiding—meaning that when movement and stillness are always one within the mind, one is then able to see Prajñā—is precisely this.
To explain this by means of the Samādhi of Perfect Enlightenment is like fitting two halves of a tally together.

○ (2. The Ear-entrance, Part 1: Establishing the Analogy; Sub-part 1: Delusion Arising Based on Reality) Ānanda, it is like a person who blocks his ears tightly with two fingers. Because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head.
Both the ear and the strain are, in fact, manifestations of fatigue produced by the *bodhi* [enlightened nature] itself staring fixedly.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "For example" (*pí-rú*) is used here to establish a hypothetical situation in order to instruct and lead one to awakening; thus it is called "for example.
It does not carry the sense of a formal analogy. The same applies to the subsequent passages.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The sense-base of the eye has analogies that can be borrowed, so an analogy is borrowed to clarify it.

For the other five [sense-bases], there are no analogies to borrow, so analogies are established to reveal them. None of these fail to use the near to illustrate the distant, or rely on the false to manifest the true.
For example, although the ear is fundamentally without sound, if one suddenly blocks both ears with the fingers, they become fatigued and produce sound; this illustrates the True.

Originally non-existent, delusion takes false causes as its cause; through the clarity of awakening, it establishes objects, thereby becoming delusion. One must know the affairs of today and believe in the person of the original source.
Once one knows that delusion has no cause, what need is there to wait for [proof of] its unreality?

When it is said that both the ears and the fatigue are equally the "fatigue-phase" produced by staring into the state of Bodhi, this does not mean that the production of sound specifically within the head constitutes fatigue. That is to say:
To have "hearing" because of this is also a manifestation of conditioned effort. If one can discard both sound and hearing, this is the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. (2.

Clarifying that there is no substance apart from sensory objects) Because of the two kinds of delusory objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective phenomena, which is called "listening."

In its nature, this hearing is devoid of the two objects of motion and stillness; it ultimately has no substance. (2. Refuting the Two: First, clarifying that the characteristics of entry are unborn; 2.1.

Direct demonstration) Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from motion or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. (2.2. Refutation by contrapositive) Why is this?

If it came from stillness, it would cease as soon as motion occurs, and thus it should not hear motion. If it came from motion, it would cease as soon as stillness occurs, and thus it should not [hear] stillness.
If awakening and stillness were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no movement or stillness. Thus, the essence of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature.
If it emerged from space and possessed the nature of hearing, it would not be empty space; yet if space itself hears, what concern is that for your auditory faculty? (2.
Concluding that the delusory is itself the real) Therefore, you should know that the auditory faculty is illusory; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "The ear hearing movement and stillness is like the eye seeing light and darkness.

What is taught in various sutras is that there is hearing in response to sound, and there is seeing conditioned by light. In the present text, the definitive meaning is that stillness is also called hearing, and darkness is also called seeing.
The nose perceives openness and obstruction; the mind knows arising and ceasing—the analogy is likewise so.

(3. The Nose-Entrance, Part 2: Initial Establishment, Part 1: The Metaphor of Arising Delusion Based on Reality) Ānanda, it is like a person who pinches their nose tightly; after pinching for a long time, it becomes fatigued, and within the nose they perceive a sensation of cold.
Because of this sensation, they distinguish between openness and obstruction, emptiness and solidity. This extends even to all fragrant and foul odors.

The nose and fatigue are both delusive manifestations arising from the glare of Bodhi. (2. Explaining that it has no substance apart from objects) Because of the two kinds of delusive objects—openness and obstruction—the faculty of hearing arises within and draws in these objective images;
this is called the nature of smelling and hearing. This hearing is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects, openness and obstruction.

(2. Refuting [the source of] the two [faculties]. First, explaining that the characteristics of entry have no birth. First, the direct demonstration: You should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor does it arise from space.

[Sound] arises. (Second refutation: Why? If it comes from the open space, then when there is obstruction, hearing should cease; how then could one know the obstruction? If the open space exists because of the obstruction, then there would be no hearing;
how then could it manifest the perception of fragrance, stench, and so forth? If it were produced from the sense organ itself, there would necessarily be neither openness nor obstruction.
Thus, the faculty of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature. If it emerged from empty space, then this hearing should naturally turn back and smell you yourself.

The nose is empty; its capacity for smelling exists inherently—what concern is this for your "entrance"? (2. Concluding that delusion is itself reality) Therefore, you should know that the nose-entrance is illusory;
it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Accumulation" refers to the gathering of breath. Cold exists because of accumulation; without accumulation, it fundamentally does not exist.

The delusions of the nose entering [the air] are all like this. Wŭxīng says: A "trigger" (*jī*) is the bolt of a crossbow. Because the sense-faculties (*mūla*) have the meaning of "discharging," the analogy is drawn from them.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: The nose functions by means of smelling fragrances, and its gateway consists of being open and obstructed, or empty and solid.
When it is open and empty, one smells; when it is obstructed and solid, one does not smell. Whether there is smelling or no smelling is simply due to the nose-faculty being open or obstructed;
it is not that your nature of smelling momentarily ceases to exist therein. Furthermore, the function of the nose is entirely dependent upon the breath.

Therefore, when [the breath] goes out it takes up fragrance, and when it comes in it smells fragrance; furthermore, the inhalation and exhalation must rely upon the physical, superficial nose as their support.
For this reason, because the sutra text wishes to clarify the function of taking up and smelling fragrance, it first states:
"For example, suppose there is a person who suddenly pinches his nose," and so forth. Now, "pinching" (畜) means to contract or to inhale. As for exhaling...

"That which is hot becomes cold when inhaled" is a common saying in medical treatises. Now, by means of this, the basis for the primary function of smelling—the sense-object upon which it depends—is revealed;
yet Jiaguang claims that the tactile sensation of cold is fundamentally an object perceived by the body-faculty (*kāyāyatana*).
This is because of the effort expended in maintaining the nose; there is no distinct fragrance or stench, but only the sensation of coldness.

This is merely borrowed as an analogy to show that all fragrant and foul odors are equally illusory. Furthermore, this indicates a lack of clarity regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

"Ānanda, it is like a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking them repeatedly until they grow weary, if that person is ill, they will perceive a bitter taste, whereas a healthy person will experience a slight sweetness.
Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, it is revealed that when the tongue-faculty is at rest, its nature of neutrality is ever-present.
Thus, both the tongue and the weariness are but manifestations of the *bodhi* (enlightened mind) appearing as a symptom of fatigue due to fixed gazing."

(2. Explaining that there is no substance apart from objects) Because of the two kinds of delusive objects—sweet, bitter, and bland—a cognition arises within. This cognition absorbs the images of these objects and is called the nature of knowing taste.

This nature of knowing taste has absolutely no substance apart from those three objects: sweet, bitter, and bland. (2. Refuting [the sense-faculties]; first, explaining that the mode of entry is unborn;

first, the direct demonstration) Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this cognition which tastes bitterness and blandness does not come from the sweet or the bitter, nor does it exist because of the bland, nor does it arise from the faculty.

It does not arise from emptiness. (Second reversal of the refutation. Why is this? If sweetness and bitterness come, then one knows that the blandness has ceased; how then could one know the blandness?
If sweetness were to emerge from the blandness, then one would know the blandness has vanished; how then could one know the sweetness and bitterness?

As for these two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness, if they were to arise from the tongue, then there would necessarily be no external objects of sweetness, blandness, or bitterness; thus one would know that the root of taste has no self-nature. If [taste] were in emptiness...

The empty space that emerges is its own inherent flavor; it is not known by your mouth, nor does the space know itself—what concern is this for your faculty of taste? (2. Concluding that delusion is itself reality) Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is false and illusory;
fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] The Supplement states: From "the self-taste of empty space" to "what concern does this have for your tongue," these four phrases appear to be overlapping.
One should know that the first two phrases clarify the object-field of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*), while the latter two phrases clarify the sense-base of the tongue (*jihvā-āyatana*).
Tiantai says: Although the text on the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) speaks of destroying the sense organs (*indriya*), it actually does so by way of the sense objects (*viṣaya*).

This is because, apart from those six objects, they ultimately have no substance. For example, the eye depends on light and darkness; the ear, on movement and stillness; the nose, on openness and obstruction; the tongue, on sweetness and blandness;
the body, on separation and contact; and the mind, on arising and ceasing. It is simply that the six superficial, floating functions exist.
It is the same. For example, the eye has opening and closing, the tongue has movement and stillness, and the mind has opening and closing, whereas the other three [faculties] do not.

Now, regarding the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*), it is said to be manifested through sweet and bitter; this refers to the fact that when the tongue-root is unmoving, its nature of neutrality (*madhura*) is ever-present.
This is precisely what is meant by the statement that it is "due to the two objects of sweet, bitter, and neutral," which correctly indicates the movement of the tongue-root.
When [the mind] is still, it encounters its respective objects (*viṣaya*). If it were to move, it would experience all five flavors; how could it be restricted solely to sweet and bitter?

This is explained by means of a hypothetical case to clarify the nature of affliction (*kleśa*): that which is bitter is affliction, whereas that which is not is sweetness. This is stated in reference to that which remains unmoving.
If one were to extend this reasoning to other objects, such as form (*rūpa*), they are no less than ten thousandfold in their diversity. What about sound (*śabda*)...?
It is not merely a matter of thousands of differences; even the dharmas that give rise to them exceed the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River.
When the sutra speaks of "two," it refers to these in their general sense.
○ (The Five Bodies; Part Two: Establishing the Initial [State]; Part One: The Metaphor for How Delusion Arises Based on Reality) Ānanda, it is like a person who touches a warm hand with a cold hand.

If the power of the cold is greater, the warm hand becomes cold; if the efficacy of the warmth prevails, the cold hand becomes warm. In this way, through the touch of these joined sensations, the knowledge of separation is manifested.
When these forces interact and form a cause, they result from the contact of weariness. Both the body and its weariness are equally the Bodhi of the staring [eyes].

The manifestation of the sign of fatigue. (2. Clarifying that there is no essence apart from objects) Based on the two kinds of false objects—separation and conjunction—the faculty of awareness arises in the interim and draws in these objective images;

this is called the nature of cognitive awareness. This essence of cognitive awareness has absolutely no substance apart from those two objects of separation and conjunction, or of opposition and compliance.

○ (2. Refuting the Two [Theories]; Part 1: Clarifying that the Nature of Perception is Non-arising; Sub-part 1: Direct Demonstration) "Ānanda, you should know that this perception does not come from conjunction or separation, nor does it exist through opposition or compliance;

it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it born from space. ○ (Sub-part 2: Refutation by Contradiction) "Why is this? If it came when there was conjunction, it would have already ceased upon separation;

how then could one perceive separation? The two characteristics of opposition and compliance are likewise so. If it emerged from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no conjunction, separation, opposition, or compliance—these four."

If you examine your body, you will find that its faculty of cognition has no inherent nature of its own; it must emerge from space and space itself possesses self-awareness—what concern is this for your sense-faculties?

(2. Concluding that the delusory is identical to the Real) Therefore, you should know that the body and the sense-faculties are empty and false; they are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: “The body enters into the primary sense-object of touch. Yet touch has no self-nature;

it is like two hands, one cold and one hot, coming into contact with each other—neither has a fixed nature. From this we know it is illusory. The hand does not touch itself, but because of their conjunction, touch is perceived;

thus it is called ‘the touch perceived through conjunction. Conjunction does not conjoin itself, but because of separation, conjunction is known; thus it is said to be ‘manifested through separation.’”
"Knowing. As for 'entering heat to become cold' and so forth, it means that by entering heat from cold, one causes the cold to become heat;
this too is merely the sensation of exertion.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "By combining this with the sensation of awareness to manifest 'separation and knowing,' it clarifies that both separation and combination are present."
"Awareness" refers to hearing both movement and stillness, and seeing both light and darkness.

Wuxing says this is not "coming from separation or combination," which refutes co-arising because even "separation" implies a correspondence with an object. It is not "due to opposition or compliance," which refutes other-arising.
It does not "emerge from the sense organ," which refutes self-arising. Furthermore, it is not "born from space," which immediately refutes non-arising.
It arises from causes. ○ (Sixth: The Six Sense-Bases;

Part Two: Initial Establishment; Part One: Clarifying that Delusion Arises Based on Reality) Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep, and upon waking from deep slumber, perceives objects and thus recollects them;

losing this recollection is what we call "forgetting. This process of inversion, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, as well as the inhalation and practice [of consciousness] returning to the center, do not exceed one another; they are called the [six sense-bases].
The faculty of mental cognition (manas-vijñāna) involves both the mind and weariness; these are both manifestations of the fatigue arising from the glare of Bodhi.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: When awake, one perceives objects and thus remembers them; when asleep, one loses this memory and it becomes forgetfulness.
Furthermore, dreaming while asleep and forgetting while awake are both manifestations of losing the memory of perceived objects. From remembering arises forgetting.
Because [the mind] ceases when these are absent, the subsequent passage states that it is "due to the two kinds of delusory objects, arising and ceasing.
To oppose the false to the true is itself an inversion. These two delusory objects further constitute the four subtle characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

In inhaling and practicing this sign, the mind returns to the mental faculty (*manas*). Because the four signs are momentary and do not intermingle before or after one another, they are said to be "not mutually transgressing.
[The *Shu* (Commentary) states: It explains that the mental faculty is the seventh consciousness; in Sanskrit, it is called *kliṣṭa-manas*.
This is called the *kliṣṭa-manas* (defiled mind). That which constantly and deliberatively cogitates is termed "mind" (*manas*).
According to the teachings of the Abhidharma-kośa school, it merely takes the internal aspect of the eighth consciousness as its object, reckoning it as an internal self.

If one follows the Hīnayāna, it is taught that all phenomena are established solely from the six consciousnesses, and the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are not mentioned. Nevertheless, the mind is of many types; according to the Abhidharma-kośa school...
The seven consciousnesses are said to be the root of the mind; these are invisible phenomena, unlike the superior reality (paramārtha) of material forms which are visible.
As for the "flesh-heart," its shape is like a lotus flower with seven petals, which constitutes the physical sense-organ (āśraya-indriya).
However, this present sutra does not distinguish between what is material and what is non-material; all are but the wearisome manifestations of ignorance within the nature of bodhi.
They are all identical to flowers in the sky, having no substance that can be apprehended, for they are precisely the storehouse-nature (ālaya-dhātu).

Tiantai said: "Although that which is subverted by the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) properly resides in the ultimate truth (paramārtha), the basis of that ultimate truth nevertheless lies within the superficial realm (tuccha-rūpa).
It is like when one does not move the eyes but stares fixedly until fatigue arises; because the faculty of hearing is fatigued, sounds are produced within the head."
If one forcefully holds the nose, holding it for a long time results in exhaustion. If one licks the lips with the tongue, licking them until they are numb results in exhaustion.
When these conditions reach their limit, exhaustion arises from such contact. When exhausted, one falls asleep; when fully rested, one awakens—all of which are instances of this principle.
Therefore, the six peripheral sense organs all belong to the body organ (*kāyendriya*). As stated below: "The two states of waking and sleeping correspond to the opening and closing of the body."
Thus, one knows that when weary, one sleeps; when sleep is deep, one awakens—this is the physical substrate (*bu-chen*) upon which the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) relies.
To grasp sensory objects and thus recollect them, or to lose such recollection and thus forget them, is the function of the faculty of mind.

To experience awakening, to experience sleep, to perceive, and to lose [perception]—this is the true substance of the faculty of mind. When it recollects, it gives rise [to thought]; when it loses [recollection], it...
Cessation is awakening, while birth is sleep; that which lies between these two is called "abiding," and what precedes and follows it is called "change.
These constitute the inverted notions of birth, abiding, change, and cessation. The characteristics of the mental faculty (*manas*) are nothing other than this.

As for the term "inverted," its meaning is identical to that of the second fascicle, where the beginning is treated as the end and the end is treated as the beginning. Indeed, such is the nature of birth and the others.
The four marks arise based on recollection and forgetfulness; recollection and forgetfulness, in turn, arise following waking and sleeping.
These two states of waking and sleeping are themselves the opening and closing of the body; what connection do they have with the mind? Thus, where does the substance of the mind reside?
The mind is fundamentally without mind, and delusion is likewise without delusion. That people recognize delusion within awakening is the nature of perversion.
It exists. If one can investigate each point as detailed in the following text, one will find that causes and conditions are naturally and utterly unobtainable.
Thus, the path wherein awakening within delusion occurs—wherein both delusion and awakening are forgotten—is attained.

(2. Explaining that there is no substance apart from objects) Because it arises in dependence upon the two kinds of delusory objects—birth and death—it gathers consciousness within and draws in internal objects;

its seeing and hearing flow against the current until the flow reaches a place where it cannot go, which is termed the "nature of awareness. This nature of awareness is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects of waking and sleeping, birth and death.

[Commentary] Gushan says: Of the four characteristics previously mentioned, only two are cited here. This is because "abiding" is subsumed under "arising," and "difference" is gathered within "cessation.

Furthermore, that which is remembered is taken as arising, and that which is forgotten is taken as cessation. "Internal objects" refers to mental objects (*dharmas*). As for "reversing the flow of seeing and hearing":
because of memory, one is able to retroactively perceive the five sensory objects that have already fallen away; thus, by apprehending these objects, they are remembered.
Furthermore, regarding "the flow not reaching the ground": because of forgetfulness, it forms a condition upon that which the thought cannot reach; thus, the loss of memory constitutes forgetfulness.
Another interpretation holds that while the five faculties, such as the eye, only take present objects as their conditions, only the mental faculty (manas) can take the past as its object;
this is what is meant by the flow entering a ground not reached by the five faculties. Although both interpretations are valid, the former meaning [is preferred].
This is correct.
[Commentary] Xunwen says: That which has fallen away from the five sensory objects is called "non-informative matter" (*avijñapti-rūpa*) in the *Abhidharma*;
it is also termed "invisible and non-obstructive matter."

[2. Refuting the Two [Origins] (Part 1: Clarifying that the Nature of the Perceiving Faculty is Unborn)] [2.1 Direct Demonstration] Ānanda, you should know this: such a faculty of perception does not come from waking or sleeping; it does not arise through birth or extinction;

it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it produced from space. [2.2 Refutation by Contradiction] Why is this? If it came from waking, it would perish as soon as one sleeps; what then would there be to sleep?
If it must exist when arising and yet perish, it would be equivalent to non-existence—what would there be for anyone to undergo extinction? If it were to come from extinction...
That which arises must immediately perish; who knows its arising? If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two states of waking and sleeping would correspond to the body’s opening and closing.
Apart from these two forms, this conscious knower is like a flower in the sky—ultimately devoid of self-nature.

If it were born from space, it would simply be the knowing of space; what concern would it have with your faculties? (2. Concluding that delusion is itself reality: Therefore, you should know that the faculty of mind is illusory and fundamentally non-existent.
"Causes and conditions are not of spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Zizhong said: *Liezi* states, "When one awakens, the form opens; when one sleeps, the form joins. "Joins" means to unite.
These two states of awakening and sleep are simply the opening and closing of the physical form. Your nature of awareness, however, has no such distinction.
Because it is the essence [of delusion], it is said to be identical to a flower in the sky. Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state: "With what would one sleep? Who would undergo extinction?
The characters "to undergo" (shòu) should be "to know" (zhī). Awakening and sleep should mutually negate each other; however, the text is merely abbreviated.

[Commentary] It is said that "perfuming hearing" refutes co-arising by showing it does not come from either waking or sleeping; it refutes other-arising by showing it does not exist through birth or extinction;
it refutes self-arising by showing it does not emerge from the sense organs; and it refutes causeless arising by showing it arises from emptiness.
Tiantai’s *Supplementary Commentary* states: "What will be made to sleep? Who will undergo extinction? [The text] contains two characters, "shòu" (to receive), which should be "zhī" (to know).
I say that if the characters were changed, the meaning would instead become obscure; moreover, since one has already entered sleep, there is no further cognition.
It is better to leave the characters as they are, for their meaning is consistent. This is because it says: "Since one follows along with awakening and extinction, what then..."
Is man one who sleeps? Since he follows along with arising and ceasing, who is it that undergoes cessation?

That the two characteristics of waking and sleeping open and close according to the body refers to the "flesh-heart" (the physical heart). For the six sensory objects of the floating dust and the ultimate reality merge and return to it, all belonging to the faculty of the body.
As the subsequent text says, "The mind is like seeing within a dark room," precisely because of this.
The floating dust and the flesh-ball are like a dark chamber; its three hairs and seven apertures resemble windows and doors, serving as the locus for the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
When they open, the ultimate reality awakens; when they close, the ultimate reality sleeps. Thus it is said that the two phases of waking and sleeping correspond to the body’s opening and closing.
That being so, apart from waking and sleeping there is no cognition, and apart from opening and closing there is no waking and sleeping; [yet] apart from the body...
Furthermore, no opening or closing can be apprehended. The opening and closing of the body are merely superficial phenomena; what connection do they have with the mind?
Thus, since the faculty of perception exists only because of the sense organ, it has no inherent essence of its own. Is this not identical to a flower in the sky, which ultimately lacks any nature?

○ (The third section: Refuting the twelve bases; Part 2: Initial general inquiry) Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?

[Commentary] Gushan says: In the preceding section on the six *āyatanas*, although the analysis was conducted by contrasting the objects (*viṣaya*) with the faculties (*indriya*), the primary intent lay in the faculties themselves.
Now, in the twelve *āyatanas*, although the faculties and objects are mutually analyzed, the primary refutation lies in the objects.

In the subsequent eighteen *dhātus*, although the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are all three mutually examined and refuted, the primary intent lies solely in the six consciousnesses. Wuxing says:
In the initial section on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the Dharma is illustrated through metaphors to shatter clinging attachments.
Next, in the section on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), provisional phenomena are pointed out to reveal their false characteristics.

Now, from the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) up to the seven elements (*sapta-dhātu*), the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is demonstrated within the very objects currently seen and heard, as well as those directly perceived nearby. Thus, the scriptural text proceeds from the remote to the immediate.
"Abandoning the provisional to approach the real"—the intent behind this skillful means of revelation can now be clearly distinguished.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: I venture to suggest that when the Buddha taught the three categories (the six sense bases, twelve entrances, and eighteen elements), he took consciousness as the primary subject.

For instance, regarding the "six sense organs," is it not the case that the organs themselves, in their fundamental nature, can produce the six derivative consciousnesses? Regarding the "twelve bases," is it not likewise so?
If one asks whether there are twelve bases upon which consciousness relies, the answer is no; it is the eighteen *dhātus* that serve as the causal bases for consciousness.
Therefore, among the great afflictions of human birth and death, none precedes consciousness. When consciousness exists, all phenomena exist;
when consciousness is empty, all phenomena are empty. This is why Tiantai takes the six consciousnesses as the object [of contemplation].
To observe the object and break through it—this alone is the essential point. As it is said: "It is like felling a tree by reaching its root, or treating an illness by hitting the vital point;
then a thousand branches and a hundred ailments will naturally wither away. This may be called truly grasping the core of the teaching.
[2. Specific Refutation of the Six Sense Bases (Initial Section: Eye and Form)] "Ānanda, you should observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think?

Do these forms arise first and are then seen by the eye, or does the eye arise first and then perceive the characteristics of form? [2.1. Refuting the Assertion that the Eye Produces the Characteristics of Form] "Ānanda, if it were the case that the faculty of the eye produces the characteristics of form, then when looking at empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to vanish.
If it were to vanish, then everything would be revealed as utterly devoid of the characteristics of form."

Since there is no one to clarify the substance of emptiness, emptiness itself is likewise thus. (2. Refuting that form gives rise to visual perception: If, moreover, the sensory object of form gave rise to visual perception, then when observing empty space—which is not form—visual perception would immediately vanish;

once it has vanished, it would be utterly non-existent, and who then could clarify the distinction between emptiness and form? (3. Realizing that the delusive is itself the true: Therefore, you should know that both seeing and the emptiness of form have no location;
thus, form and seeing are both locations of falsehood, fundamentally not produced by causes and conditions.
"Not of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "If the eye could produce form, then the eye would be the nature of form.
However, when seeing space, since there are no characteristics of form, the nature of form should dissolve. Once the nature of form within the eye has dissolved, it reveals a single..."
All things are entirely devoid of the characteristics of form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the two dharmas of form and emptiness manifest through mutual opposition.

Since the characteristics of form do not exist, by what means could emptiness be manifested? Therefore it is said: "Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? Thus, to calculate that the eye arises in the locus of form is an error.
That emptiness is likewise so is because, by analogy with form, emptiness also has no fixed location. If, moreover, there were the dust of form...
The "lower" refers to the notion that form can produce vision; however, when one contemplates emptiness, vision has nothing from which to arise, and thus it is said to be "dissolved.
When it is dissolved—that is, when there is no vision—who then clarifies the relationship between emptiness and form? Therefore, to calculate that form produces the locus of the eye is an error.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? This statement by Wenling is incorrect. One should instead follow the commentary in the Tongjiang Collection, which says:

"Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? This is a reprimand for his error. If one were to say that when form is dissolved and the faculties are extinguished, who would clarify the substance of the seeing of emptiness? This interpretation is correct.

○ (2. The Sense Base of Sound; Part 3: First, citing an instance to raise the inquiry) "Ānanda, listen further to this: within the Jeta Grove, when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck and the assembly gathers, and the bell is tolled.
The sounds of the bell and drum follow one another in succession. What do you think? Do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?

○ (2. Refuting the opponent's position; Part 2: First, refuting that the sound comes to the ear) "Ānanda, if this sound were to come to the ear, it would be like my going to Śrāvastī to beg for food."
If the city of Rājagṛha were in the Jeta Grove, then this sound would necessarily come to Ānanda’s ears;

yet Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it simultaneously, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas within who, upon hearing the bell, all come together to the place of the meal.
(2. Refuting the Ear’s Traveling to the Place of the Sound) Furthermore, if your ear were to travel to the location of that sound, it would be like my returning to dwell in the Jeta Grove.
In the Śrāvastī city within the Jeta Grove, there is no "self" that exists. When you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is being struck.
When the sounds of bells ring out simultaneously, would you not hear them all together? How much more so for the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within that space?
If there were no coming and going, there would likewise be no hearing. (3. Realizing the False as the True) Therefore, you should know that listening and sound—
Since both have no location, it is understood that the two locations of sound and the ear are false; they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Just as when I enter a city, the Jeta Grove is no longer 'I,' so too when sound comes to the side of the ear, there is no sound in other places.
Yet since a thousand people all hear it, the location of the sound has no reality. Furthermore, regarding "if your ear... [and so forth].
This means that just as when I return to the city of Lin, my ears are no longer in that place; if the ears go to the location of the sound, they would not exist elsewhere.
Yet, since sounds of all kinds are heard, the location of the ears must lack substantial reality. Gu Shan said:
"If there is no coming or going—meaning that the sound does not come to the ear and the ear does not go to the sound—the principle of hearing cannot be established."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: All the texts rely on what ordinary beings commonly perceive and hear as their basis in order to refute delusion;
therefore, it is impossible to use the True Mind as a counter-objection.

If one applies this principle, then according to what is revealed in the following passage—where drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions and heard at once in all ten locations—this is...
To employ "perfect reality" (yuan zhenshi) as a term would block the gateway to human awakening; it is what is called "a phrase that strikes one right over the head.

One must understand that within the four categories (sike), the Buddha has two intentions. First, to infer non-arising (wusheng) in order to establish perfect understanding—this is the primary intention.
Second, to employ the investigation of the four propositions (siju) in order to establish perfect practice—this is because nature (xing) and cultivation (xiu) reflect and interpenetrate one another.

This is precisely the meaning of the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment* (Dacheng yuanjue jing), which teaches the cultivation of the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*) to transform illusory beings.
(3. The Nose and Fragrance; Part 3: First, citing a phenomenon to pose a question. Ānanda, you now smell this sandalwood in the incense burner.
If one were to burn only a single *zhu* of this fragrance, the scent would be perceived simultaneously throughout the forty *li* of Śrāvastī. What do you think? Does this fragrance arise...?
Does the sandalwood incense arise from your nose, or does it arise from space? (2. Restating the position to refute it—first, refuting that it arises from the nose:

Ānanda, if this fragrance were to arise from your nose, then as something produced by the nose, it would have to issue forth from the nose. Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?
