○ (2. Rebuking Delusion to Induce Awakening) Ānanda, your mind is muddled and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should contemplate whether empty space comes out or goes in, or whether it neither comes nor goes.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "If one awakens to the fact that the nature of empty space is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally has no entering or exiting, then one awakens to the fact that the nature of the four great elements is truly perfect and harmonious, and fundamentally has no arising or ceasing."

[II. Explaining the Principle of Innate Endowment] "You do not know at all that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of awakening is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awakening. [III. Explaining the Substance and Function of Nature (in two parts: first, explaining immutability as being like spontaneity rather than non-spontaneity)] "Pure and fundamentally so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

[Second, explaining adaptation to conditions as being like dependent origination rather than non-dependent origination (in three parts: first, explaining the capacity to respond)] "It responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know.

[Second, citing examples to verify this] "Ānanda, just as when one well is dug, empty space arises within that one well, so it is with the empty space of the ten directions. It fills the ten directions completely; how could there be..."

Location. (Third, explaining what can be induced: Manifesting in accordance with karma. (Second, refuting deluded sentiments as being without foundation: That which is known in the world as having ignorance as its cause and condition, or as being of a spontaneous nature, is entirely the conceptualization and calculation of the discerning mind;
it consists only of verbal expressions and possesses no real meaning whatsoever.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Emptiness" (kōng) and "awakening" (jué) are different designations for essence and function. Because essence and function are non-dual, they are mentioned in mutual dependence.
[Sub-commentary] Tiāntái says: The nature of emptiness has no form; it is manifested through form. "Through" (yīn) means "in dependence upon" (dài). Of the myriad phenomena of the world...
Things depend upon one another to form their shapes; emptiness depends upon form. This serves as the root source of all mutual dependencies.

When it is said that for every foot of earth dug out, there is a foot of empty space, both of these meanings are simultaneously revealed. Previously, the "greatness of earth" was clarified in relation to space;
now, the "greatness of space" is defined in relation to form. By this principle, each of the other three great elements [should be understood] accordingly.
One may infer that each lacks the other by waiting for its counterpart. Yet, since it is said that color is manifested through causes, there must be a cause.
When one investigates further, finding that neither earth nor the act of digging can serve as the cause, what cause could there be? Furthermore, why was there no obstruction before the earth was dug?
To say there is no cause is also untenable. It is neither produced by conjunction nor by combination, and it does not arise from itself.
[The text] emerges. When one is free from the four natures and completely dispels the hundred negations, then that nature of empty space is perfectly pervasive.
One must know that space and earth originally have no different cause; likewise, the other three great elements also have no different cause.
Therefore, if one can realize emptiness, one can realize form, and one can realize the other three great elements. Thus it is said: "If this empty space... and so forth.

This means that by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the four [elements] are equalized and returned to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Next, in order to censure delusion and cause awakening, it is said:
"Your mind is clouded and confused; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha," and so forth.

For while from the perspective of the characteristics of the five great elements, one is empty and the four are substantial, making them unequal, from the perspective of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), they are all equally and identically the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is truly and perfectly interfused. Only after establishing the equality [of the four teachings] does he demonstrate the principle of the inherent nature (xingju).
For phenomena (xiang) are derivative, while nature (xing) is fundamental. Since the perfect interfusion of phenomena originally derives from the inherent nature, it is said:

"You do not know at all... (and so forth). The manner of this dialectical refutation differs from the previous one; previously, he wished to equalize the four [teachings] through emptiness, and thus he addressed them individually.

This is empty sophistry. This [passage] seeks to demonstrate that because the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are equally empty, it is contrasted with the "awakened" (*jue*) to establish the argument;

its ultimate aim is to return to the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*), and its progression follows a specific order. Wēn-líng was not clear about this and therefore explained it in terms of essence and function (*tǐyòng*).
Jiāo-guāng was likewise not clear about this and claimed that compared to the preceding [text], the phrasing has been altered and the meaning inverted. Such is the error of Master Huán.
The Master Jue’s error lay in his conceptualization; Master Jian’s error lay in his artificiality. Nevertheless, there is also emptiness that accords with pure conditions:

in terms of the primary retribution, it is the true emptiness of precious enlightenment; in terms of the resultant environment, it is the wondrous land of tranquil light. [There is also emptiness] that accords with defiled conditions.

In terms of the primary retribution (*vipāka*), it is like filling a *pinga* jar to provide sustenance for other lands; in terms of the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), it is the dark obscurity that constitutes the vast expanse of the universe.
One who awakens to the Way by relying on this is the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. He said:
"This great supernatural power arises from my contemplation that the four great elements have no basis, and that they are born and perish through deluded thought. Space has no..."
The two Buddha-lands were originally identical, and upon their simultaneous realization and attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it was truly as the saying goes:
"When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions all vanish away."

○ (6. The Six Faculties, Part 2, Section 1: Brief Demonstration) Ānanda, you perceive that this faculty of seeing has no inherent knowledge; it exists because of form and space. ○ (2. Detailed Demonstration, Part 1: Refuting Falsity by Citing Examples, Section 1:
Citing Examples) As you now stand here in the Jeta Grove, it is bright in the morning and dark in the evening; even if it were midnight, it would be light under a full moon and dark under a new moon.

Thus, brightness and darkness are analyzed by means of seeing. ○ (2. Refutation through Inquiry, Part 1: Establishing Propositions and General Inquiry) Is this seeing joined with brightness and darkness, or is it identical to the great void of empty space?
The essence is neither a single entity, nor identical, nor non-identical, nor different, nor non-different.
[Commentary] Xielǐ says: This question consists of four propositions: first, identity; second, difference; third, both identical and different; fourth, neither identical nor different.
However, in the scriptural text, these are divided such that two instances of "identity" and two instances of "difference" each constitute a single proposition.

○ (2. Citing the four specific points to refute them) Ānanda, if this seeing were fundamentally one entity with light, darkness, and empty space, then the two entities of light and darkness would mutually negate each other;
when it is dark, there would be no light, and when it is light, there would be no darkness. If it were identical with darkness, then seeing would cease when light appears;
if it were identical with light, then seeing should perish when darkness appears. If it perishes, how could it see light or see darkness?
Light and darkness are seen as distinct, yet there is neither birth nor extinction; how can they be one?

If this essence of seeing and darkness, and light, are not of one substance, then when you separate it from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or characteristic would the source of seeing have?

Separated from light, separated from darkness, and separated from empty space, this source of seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare—light, darkness, and empty space being three [distinct things].

Since the objects are both distinct, from what basis can "seeing" be established? How could seeing light and seeing darkness be mutually opposed? Why might they be the same? Apart from these three, there is nothing; how then could they be different?

Since the division of space and the division of seeing are fundamentally without boundaries, how could they not be the same? Since the nature of seeing darkness and seeing light does not undergo change, how could they not be different? (3.
Exhortation to Observe and Summary Rebuke) You should further examine minutely, examine in detail, examine with precision, and observe with clarity.
Brightness follows the sun; darkness accompanies the dark moon. They pass through and belong to empty space, or they become congested and return to the great earth.

Thus, from what source does this essence of seeing arise? Seeing is aware, while emptiness is inert; they are neither a blend nor a union. Therefore, it cannot be that the essence of seeing arises from nowhere of its own accord.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: From "Ānanda" downward, he distinguishes that they are not of one substance. From "if this essence of vision" downward, he distinguishes that they are not of different substances.
From "light and darkness oppose each other" downward, he distinguishes that they are neither identical nor non-identical, and neither different nor non-different.
"You should further issue an order to examine in detail whether this nature is truly perfect and interfused, without involving any delusions.

(2. Revealing the Truth Based on Principle; Part 1: Clarifying that the Awakened Nature is Perfectly Interfused; Section 4: First, showing that the sense organs are equal to the five elements. "If the natures of seeing, hearing, and knowing are perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unshakable, you should know that boundless, unmoving space, along with the shaking earth, water, fire, and wind, are all equally called the six great elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and interfused; they are all the Tathāgata."

In the Treasury [of the Tathāgata], there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing. (2. Revealing the Reality of the Six Faculties) Ānanda, your nature is mired in saṃsāra because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.
You should examine this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: are they subject to arising or ceasing? Are they identical or different?
Are they neither subject to arising nor ceasing, nor neither identical nor different?

[Commentary] Gu Shan says: Regarding "seeing, hearing, knowing," previously, when refuting the six faculties in detail, the seeing of the eye was extensively analyzed while the other faculties were treated briefly.

Now, by analogy, it is shown that their natures are all pervasive. "Hearing" refers to the ear faculty; "perceiving" (*jue*) refers to the nose, tongue, and body faculties; and "knowing" refers to the mind faculty.
The term "perceiving" was not mentioned [in the previous section] as a matter of brevity. Wen Ling says: "To arise" and "to cease."

The "etcetera" refers to arising and ceasing, sameness and difference—all of which are caused by delusive objects. That which neither arises nor differs is not separate from delusive conceptualization;
to be free from these various delusions is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha.

○ (The Principle of the Innate Endowment of the Three Clarities) You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing is the clarity of awareness, and the clarity of awareness is the essence of seeing. ○ (Fourth: Clarifying the Nature and its Function; Part One: Clarifying Unchanging Nature as Appearing Spontaneous, Yet Not Spontaneous) It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

○ (Part Two: Clarifying Following Conditions as Appearing Dependent, Yet Not Dependent; Sub-part One: Clarifying the Capacity to Respond) It responds according to the minds of sentient beings, corresponding to the measure of what they know. ○ (Sub-part Two: Citing Facts as Verification) For example, when this single faculty of sight perceives, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm;
so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the awareness of touch—all these wondrous virtues are luminous and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.

The perfection of the ten voids—how could it have a specific location? (3. Explaining what can be induced) It manifests in accordance with karma. (2. Refuting deluded sentiments as being without foundation) That the world lacks knowledge and takes delusion as its causes and conditions, or that things possess a nature of spontaneity—all these are merely calculations and discriminations of the conscious mind; they are nothing but words and lack any real meaning.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The seeing of nature" and so forth are also mentioned by way of the mutual dependence of essence and function.
Although having seeing and having awareness is a fault of the clarity of awareness, the essence is actually the seeing of nature, and the function is actually the essence of awareness.

This is an example for the other faculties as well. "Tasting and touching" refers to the tongue faculty; because one only becomes aware [of taste] when it meets with flavor, it is also called "touching. Thus, one is aware of touch.
"To perceive" refers to the faculty of the mind within the body. [Commentary] Tiantai says:
According to the preceding discussion on the five great elements, all first clarify their combination and subsequently refute that combination; this passage follows the same pattern.
Because it first clarifies their combination, it says: "Perception and awareness are devoid of knowledge, existing because of form and emptiness. As for what follows in the subsequent text...

This means that cognition is triggered by objects; thus, the analysis of causes such as light and darkness depends upon the faculty of vision, which is what is meant by "having characteristics because of the faculty.
Next, within the refutation of conjunction, one investigates through the four propositions and finds them unattainable;

this means that both the characteristic (the object) and the vision (the faculty) lack intrinsic nature, being like the *kharaviṣāṇa* (a barren cow’s horn). Having refuted conjunction, there is further concern that one might cling to the notion of non-conjunction; therefore—
To refute this by following the logic of the argument: it should not be seen that the essence [of sight] emerges from nowhere on its own.

Once this refutation is complete, one then uses the sense-organ (the great element) to equalize it with the previous five great elements; thus it says, "If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect and all-pervading, it is fundamentally unmoving" (and so forth).
Within this, first the sense-organ (the great element) is used to equalize the great element of space, and subsequently the sense-organ (the great element) is used to equalize the remaining five.
"Great. This signifies that these two [aspects] unfold and excel far beyond the former. As for emptiness, it excels through immovability and signlessness;
as for the faculties, they excel through awareness and perfect integration. However, this distinction between superior and inferior is merely a conceptual differentiation according to appearances.
Since the abbreviated expression of the *tathāgatagarbha* contains no difference [from the full term], I shall now unify them and state that the nature is truly perfect and interfused;
all are the *tathāgatagarbha*, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. Having completed this unification, I then require you to achieve awakening (and so forth).
Having already demonstrated their mutual fusion, he further demonstrates that they are identical in their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is said:

"You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the seeing of nature and the clarity of awareness are one; the clarity of awareness is the seeing of nature. The "seeing of nature" is the seeing inherently present within nature;

it is what is referred to in the second fascicle as the "pure real mark" (*śuddha-bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). The "clarity of seeing" means that the seeing of nature is fundamentally luminous and requires no exertion.

The "Function" (yòng) refers to what is called "the nature-awareness is necessarily luminous" (*xingjuò bì míng*). The "awareness-luminosity" (*juèmíng*) and "awareness-essence" (*juējīng*) are precisely the seeing-division (*jiànfēn*) of the eighth consciousness (*bāshì*) which is capable of objectification.
This is the same as the "seeing-essence" (*jiànjīng*) elucidated in fascicle two and the "consciousness-essence" (*shìjīng*) indicated in the first fascicle.
This clearly points out that Bodhi and Nirvana are fundamentally the pure essence (*yuánqīngjìng tǐ*). Thus, when delusion arises from the True, the entirety of the Nature [is involved].
Seeing is taken as the clarity of awareness. If the delusory is itself the true, then the essence of total awareness is precisely the clarity of seeing.
If one follows the previous principle that the five great elements do not fail to merge the subsequent with the former, then here too it is by means of consciousness that the faculties are merged.

However, since the substance of the faculty and consciousness is identical, there is no need for further reconciliation; it is sufficient to directly apply the true and the delusory within the respective great element, and the faculty will not be lost.

Contemplate the meaning of the "Harmony of the Three. Furthermore, this [principle] fully encompasses all six sense organs; however, because it is easier to elucidate by means of the organ of sight, we have discussed it solely in terms of that root.
By using the faculty of sight as a standard, one finds that the same applies to all five. Therefore it is said: "As with the single faculty of sight, its vision pervades the Dharma-realm;
so too hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of touch—these wondrous virtues are brilliantly clear and universally pervade the Dharma-realm."
The realms are perfected throughout the ten directions; how could they have a fixed location? Speaking from this perspective, all six sense faculties are wondrous.
However, for sentient beings, the delusion of the other faculties is heavy, while that of the eyes and ears is light. Therefore, Nalipu specifically said:

"The Tathāgata has shown me the adamantine samādhi of joyful vision and illuminating clarity. And Avalokiteśvara specifically said: "The adamantine cultivation through hearing and the cultivation through hearing."
[It is] obscure. Is it not the case that by relying on these two gates, the fetters and delusions are easily destroyed?

Thus, the Tathāgata’s verses also praise [this] as the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening (*vajrarāja-bodhi*). However, these two gates still rely on the preceding six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) for entry.

If one’s faculties are now great and suited to the occasion, this is the Dharma-gate for entering the Way through the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Now, the fundamental purpose of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is—
The faculty of mind is called "I," which makes no selection but universally gathers the six faculties.
Is this not the balance of all sages and the summary of the framework of myriad practices? Amitābha and Śrī-Āvalokiteśvara universally gather all capacities;
Mount Lu and Tiantai refute the doctrines of the hundred schools.

○ (7. Brief Demonstration of the Greatness of the Seven Consciousnesses, Part 1) Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of sense organs and their objects. ○ (2. Detailed Demonstration, Part 1: Refuting Falsity by Citing Instances, Part 1: Citing Instances, Part 1:

Clarifying the Sense Organs and Objects that Produce Them) As you now survey this assembly of holy ones, your eyes move through them one by one; as your eyes look around, it is merely like reflections in a mirror, with no separate analysis.

[II. Explaining the consciousness that arises] Within this [assembly], you identify and point out in succession: "This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa; this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti; this is Śāriputra. [2.
Interrogating and refuting the consciousness. Part 1: Citing the alternatives of identity, difference, and totality to interrogate.
Does this consciousness that perceives arise from the seer, or does it arise from the perceived object, or does it arise from empty space, or does it emerge suddenly without any cause?
[Commentary] Zhenji says: "The 'root' (gen) merely illuminates the object, like a mirror; consciousness (shi) possesses discernment, thus it can point to [the object].
Wenzheng says: 'Jian' (seeing) refers to the root; 'xiang' (appearance) refers to the object."

(2. Refuting the specific positions by restating them: Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness arises within the faculty of vision, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—it would necessarily be non-existent from the start.
Since your seeing itself would not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If the nature of your consciousness arises from the objects and does not arise from the faculty of vision, then you would neither see light nor see darkness; if light and darkness do not impinge upon it, then [consciousness] would not exist.

In the formless realm, even that characteristic of emptiness does not exist; from where could consciousness arise? If it were to arise within emptiness, it would be neither a characteristic nor a vision.

Without vision, there is no discernment, and one cannot know for oneself. Light, darkness, form, and emptiness are not characteristics; when conditions cease, vision, hearing, awareness, and cognition find no place to be established.
Since these two—emptiness and non-emptiness—are equally non-existent, they are not distinct entities. Even if you were to give rise to your consciousness, what would you desire?
"If discrimination were to arise suddenly without any cause, why does it not discriminate the bright moon at midday?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: From "Ānanda" downward, it clarifies that the nature of consciousness is neither produced from seeing nor produced from the object.
"If it were produced from seeing" clarifies that it is not produced from emptiness; for if it were produced from emptiness, it would not be the object.
It is not seeing; if it is not seeing, there is nothing to be discerned. It is not a characteristic (nimitta); if it is not a characteristic, there is no object of perception (ālambana).

If there is no object of perception, how can a perceiving subject be established? Furthermore, if the substance of consciousness (vijñāna) were empty within this interval that is neither characteristic nor seeing, it would be like the hair of a tortoise.
If the substance of consciousness were existent, it would not be identical to material objects. Since it lacks its own substance, how could it possibly exist?
Therefore it is said: "What is there to be distinguished? This clarifies that [the absence of the moon] is not due to a lack of causes. Changshui says:
"Since there is no moon at midday, and thus no consciousness perceiving a moon, one should know that it does not arise without a cause."

○ (Third, Exhortation to Thorough Examination and Reprimand for Negligence) You should further examine minutely and scrutinize with great care: when the seeing relies upon your pupils, its manifestation pushes forward toward external objects;

it can be established as existing, but it cannot be established as non-existent. From what source, then, does this consciousness arise? When the consciousness moves, the seeing remains clear; they are neither blended nor joined.
Hearing, listening, feeling, and knowing are likewise so. It should not be that the consciousness arises from no source on its own.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Seeing" refers to that which is entrusted to the root; "objects" refer to that which is entrusted to the environment. If there is emergence, it can be described; if there is no emergence, it is not a characteristic.
From what, then, does consciousness emerge? Consciousness has discrimination and is called "movement";

seeing has no discrimination and is called "clarity. The natures of consciousness and seeing are separated and distinct. As it is with seeing and consciousness, so it is with hearing and knowing: all are not a harmonious union. Furthermore—
That which is not produced by nature is the true nature, perfectly interfused and not entangled with any delusions.

(II. Revealing the Truth Based on Principle; Part 1: Clarifying that the Awakened Nature is Perfectly Interfused; Section 4: First, showing that consciousness is equal to the six elements. If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it arises, one should know that its capacity for discernment, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and profound;

its nature does not originate from external objects. Furthermore, when combined with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements," for their true nature is perfectly interfused.
All these are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. (2. Revealing the Reality of the Six Consciousnesses) Ānanda, your mind is coarse and flighty;
you have not realized that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate these six consciousnesses of the sense-bases:
are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different, and neither empty nor existent?

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "If this 'consciousness-mind' refers to the aggregate of the *vijñāna-dhātu* (the element of consciousness), then 'discerning seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing' specifically refers to the six consciousnesses.
When combined with space and the other elements, they collectively comprise the seven *dhātus* and extend to all phenomena.
Since they fundamentally have no origin, they are tranquil, perfect, and pervasive. As it is so for earth and the other elements, so it is for worlds, sentient beings, and every single thing."

It is so. Not only are things like the earth called "great," but even blades of grass, thorns, dust, and hairs may all be called "great. Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing.
The detailed arguments in the preceding text all converge upon this point; therefore, from the faculties and objects, the myriad dharmas are collectively integrated and universally permeated.
As for the passage beginning with "Ānanda," it means that the substance of consciousness is profoundly latent and should be contemplated with subtle and minute reflection.
One must not observe with coarse or superficiality; if one attains its truth, one will awaken to its source, the Tathāgatagarbha. (3.

Explaining the Principle of Innate Endowment) You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminous knowing, and the awareness-luminosity is the true consciousness. (4. Explaining the Nature and Its Specific Functions—Part One: Clarifying Unchanging Nature as Seeming Spontaneity, Yet Not Spontaneity) The wondrous awakening is profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

(2. Clarifying Following Conditions as Seeming Dependent Origination, Yet Not Dependent Origination—Part One: Clarifying the Responding Capacity) It contains and exhales the ten voids; how could it have a fixed location? (2. Clarifying the Stimulating Capacity) It manifests according to karma.

II. (Reproving Deluded Sentiment for Lacking Essential Meaning): That which is known in the world—whether as causes and conditions, or as arising through spontaneity—is entirely the conceptual calculation of the discriminating mind;
it consists only of verbal expressions and lacks any real meaning.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Since both cognition and knowledge arise from the luminosity of the nature (*xing*), it is called "the nature’s cognitive luminous knowledge.
Although consciousness (*shí*) carries the fault of being a derivative of awakened luminosity, its essence is actually true; thus, it is called "awakened luminosity as true consciousness.
Because essence and function are non-dual and truth and falsehood are identical, they are mentioned alternately.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Consciousness is a flow of delusion; there has never been a flow without a source.
As it is said, "If the flow is reversed, it becomes entirely one, and the six functions cease to operate"—is this not the source? However, the Tathāgata has two modes of expression.

To reveal the True, he says there *is* a source, so as to cause one to awaken to its fundamental reality. To shatter the delusive, he says there *is no* source, so as to cause one to realize that phenomena are empty. Thus...

It is said: "Since these arise falsely from the six kinds of sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), how could they have any source? The text first clarifies the organs and objects, hence it says:

"Now you should observe the assembly of sages in this gathering. As you survey them with your eyes, your gaze passing over them all, your eyes looking around will see them merely as reflections in a mirror, without any further analysis.
The sages are the objects; observing them pervasively is the organ. This is what was discussed in the second fascicle.

In the first fascicle of the *Xianjian Jing*, the "consciousness-essence" (*shijijing*) and the "great essence" (*dashi*) referred to as the "awakened clarity" (*jue ming*) and "awakened essence" (*jue jing*) are, in fact, the perceiving aspect (*jianfen*) among the eight consciousnesses that functions as the cognitive faculty. Yet, Jiaoguang identifies these as the "true and eternal.

Thus, he claims that when the myriad phenomena are confronted and not a single thought arises, this is precisely their manifestation. He fails to realize that although it is like a mirror, there is no duality therein.
Analysis still belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); to realize non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must necessarily see the seeing.
To recognize the Path as not yet true and take the indeterminate to be non-arising is a grave error—indeed, a most grave error.

Only after the text has fully explained the faculties and their objects does it finally point out the six consciousnesses; hence it says: "Your consciousness [is] therein... sequentially indicated" (and so forth). This is correct.

Taking that which is without a pointing finger as the root and that which has a pointing finger as consciousness: once one falls into the pointing finger, one immediately descends into the objects of perception (*ālambana*).
It is from this that the beginningless cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) first arises.
This is precisely where the first root clarifies birth and death and the second root produces all conditions (*pratyaya*). Thus, to be cast aside by conditions is to be in birth and death. If...
To be able to penetrate and break through this is what constitutes wisdom and severance (*prajñā-prahāṇa*). Whether one turns it over once or twice, what other method could there be?

Within the investigation and refutation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), first we examine them by way of the existence of a cause. The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are the cause.

To have a cause apart from the sense organs and their objects is the characteristic of empty space. To have arising apart from these three is causeless arising. Since they necessarily depend upon one another, one must investigate them.
If this is so, then when consciousness moves and vision becomes clear, it is as stated in the text below: "This stillness is not the true flow; because the current is swift, it is not perceived.

Once the refutation is complete, one then correctly applies the eye-consciousness to equalize it with the other five consciousnesses, thereby simultaneously attaining the realization of the preceding Great Root.
That people do not awaken to this is precisely because they calculate that all dharmas have some place from which they originate. Indeed.

If one can thoroughly comprehend this, then the nature that is perfectly full and profoundly still will be seen. Once the consciousnesses and the faculties are made uniform, one then regards sentient beings as identical to the non-sentient (and so forth).
One may understand this by reversing the inquiry and demanding awakening. Next, in the passage concerning the original nature, it says:
"The nature-consciousness is clear knowing; the clarity of awareness is true consciousness. Here, "nature-consciousness" refers to the visual consciousness abiding in its fundamental position.

The term "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers here to the ninth, the pure white consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*). It is clearly understood that the terms "cognition" (*jñāna*) and "illumination" (*prakāśa*) set aside its formal position to refer instead to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the fundamental awakening and wondrous illumination.
In the preceding section on the six great elements, they were either combined with one another or the small was subsumed into the great.
One meets with the characterized to return to the uncharacterized; one meets with the insentient to return to the sentient; one meets with the delusory to return to the true.

Upon reaching this point, the school’s essence is fully realized and its principles are perfectly complete. It is simply that, by directly engaging the immediate experience, one realizes that these are merely different names for distinct explanations.
Specifically, it speaks of "wondrous enlightenment being profound and still" rather than "pure and originally so," because this refers to the ultimate realization of the school.

Because they differ, their expressions are distinct, yet their meaning is the same. This is because the profound stillness of the eight consciousnesses is not the ultimate reality, whereas the pure and white nature-consciousness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*) is truly profound.
Furthermore, the specific mention here of "containing and exhaling the ten voids" is intended to clarify the general and the particular from the perspective of the state of delusion.
For sentient beings have long been immersed in deluded sentiments, such that the internal and external are distinct.
Therefore, all sūtras generally clarify that the mind is the totality of all phenomena. As it is said: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates;
within all the worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind.
If one considers the stage of awakening, all phenomena may likewise be taken as the totality. As it is said: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha..."
Sentient beings, their minds, and Buddhas—these three are without distinction.

Therefore, one should know that they are fundamentally pure and originally radiant, that wondrous awakening is profound and still, and that the seven elements can all be described in this way. Do not allow the literal wording to obstruct the intended meaning.

Some may say that there is no passage regarding "responding to the mind and conforming to the measure," yet such a text does exist; it is merely concise in expression, though its meaning is [present].
Thus, there is nothing that is not encompassed. As it is said, "It contains and exhales the ten voids (*daśa-ākāśa*). "Containing" means being perfectly full throughout the ten directions;

"exhaling" means responding to the mind according to its measure. The meaning is that although the realm of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) responds to the mind according to its measure, in every thought-moment it is equal to the ten voids.
One who enters the Way by relying on this is Maitreya Bodhisattva. He said: "I, through my realization..."
Observing the ten directions as mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), the conscious mind becomes perfectly luminous and enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

One thereby distances oneself from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), attaining the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). According to this principle, the six sense-consciousnesses constitute the dependent nature;

delusions are the causal conditions, and spontaneity constitutes the imagined nature. The intrinsic awareness of the nature-consciousness, the luminosity of awakened awareness, is the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): speaking from this perspective, it is not that this text does not mention the eighth and ninth consciousnesses;
yet Jiaoguang’s claim that they are absent is a grave error. Furthermore, these three natures can be applied to all six elements mentioned previously.

Just as earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the sense faculties are all of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), while delusions acting as causes and conditions constitute the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), and the fundamental purity of the nature of form and so forth constitutes the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Thus, it can be seen that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) in this sutra is quite distinct from that in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. As for the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) and the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), [the same principle applies].
All these constitute the objects of contemplation for this sutra; however, among them, the single realm of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is uniquely intimate to this sutra.

Nevertheless, there are two different types of contemplated objects. In the first two fascicles, the clarification of the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*) and the essence of hearing observed by Avalokiteśvara take the eight consciousnesses as their objects.
As for the "great element of consciousness" (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*) inferred in the present passage, it takes the sixth consciousness as its object.

Taking other phenomena as objects of consciousness also has two meanings. First, for a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching], when the six sense faculties encounter their respective objects, they do not give rise to a second thought;
they immediately realize, right where they are, the primordially existing Buddha-nature, thus taking only the eight consciousnesses as their object.
This is what the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* means by "not giving rise to deluded thoughts at any time. Even if one were to perceive sensory objects...
If one discriminates, one takes the six consciousnesses as the object. By investigating and examining them through the three types of *śamatha*, the wild mind naturally subsides;
this subsiding is itself *bodhi*. This is what is meant in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* when it says, "one does not even extinguish or cease the various deluded minds.
In the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Great Master Tiantai, he first instructs one to rely on the six sense organs to contemplate the permanence of all Tathāgatas.
This is identical to the first intention. Furthermore, the instruction to take the six consciousnesses as the object of observation is identical to the second intention.
Jiaoguang failed to clarify this meaning and instead recklessly added his criticisms, claiming that observing the six consciousnesses alone is partial and provisional.
He did not realize that both passages in this sutra aim to penetrate delusion to reveal the true, and thus the text is entitled "Perfect, Sudden, and Definitive. If...
What Jiaoguang refers to is to abandon the false and seek the true, yet he ultimately regards the seeing-essence (*jianjing*) as being without birth.
How is this different from mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls or pointing to a mountain fowl and calling it a phoenix?

Nevertheless, the meaning of the seven elements (*qida*) converging in the hidden nature (*zangxing*) is most profound; my previous word-by-word explanation has not yet exhausted its full significance.

I have previously elucidated this meaning in the *Lengyan jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra). Now, without avoiding prolixity, I record it here in full so that readers may recognize its general outline.
Regarding the text on the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), the first four are explained in contrast to space, stating:
"The true emptiness of the nature of form; the true form of the nature of emptiness," and so forth. The fifth, the element of space, is in contrast to...
The sixth consciousness, Greatness, then countered the clarity of awareness, declaring: "The nature of seeing is the clarity of awareness;
the clarity of awareness is the essence of seeing. The seventh consciousness, Greatness, further countered the knowledge of clarity, declaring:
"The nature of cognition is the knowledge of clarity; the clarity of awareness is true cognition. Thus, their respective arguments differed.

What is the explanation for this? The answer is: This arises because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding true awakening, taking it as the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that is confined within the body, thereby neglecting external objects.
They differentiate between space and form to distinguish between the large and the small. As the sutra says: "Obscured darkness becomes empty space;

within the dark obscurity of emptiness, the binding of darkness forms matter (*rūpa*). Matter mingles with false conceptualization, and through the conceptualization of these appearances, a body is formed. Thus they aggregate...
Conditioned by internal agitation, they rush outward in wild flight; this state of dark confusion and turmoil they take to be their own mind-nature.

Once deluded, they identify with the mind and become certain that it resides within the physical body. They do not know that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It is like casting away hundreds of thousands of clear, tranquil oceans.
To take the substance of a single bubble and claim it to be the entire tide, exhausting the vastness of the ocean—such is the state of these people whom the Tathāgata pities.
To lead them from delusion to immediate awakening, he necessarily proceeds from the shallow to the profound;
first, he uses boundless empty space to contrast with the finite four great elements. Thus, through repeated discourse, he speaks of "the nature of form" (*prakṛti-rūpa*).
The nature of emptiness is true form; even so, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind.
The reason for this is that the form of the earth element possesses a solid substance and occupies a specific location, whereas empty space is pervasive and interfused, and thus has no location.
The elements of water, fire, and wind are characterized by movement and subject to arising and ceasing, whereas empty space is eternally constant.

Therefore, there is no agitation. Wherever there is arising and ceasing, coming and going, there is empty space. Because there is no arising and ceasing, nor coming and going, the nature is truly perfect and harmonious.

When it is now said that "the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form," it means that the emptiness-nature and form-nature are both true emptiness and true form; thus, between form and emptiness, there is fundamentally no distinction. Therefore...
In the fifth section on the Great Emptiness (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), it is harmonized thus:
"If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are equally called the five great elements;

their nature is truly interfused and all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, and you do not realize this regarding the four great elements."
The primordial *tathāgatagarbha* should be contemplated as space: whether it emerges, enters, or neither emerges nor enters.
Thus, the four great elements and space are equally and eternally abiding. Although their appearances seem different, their nature is fundamentally identical.
There is nothing that is not pure and original, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. Is it not fitting to call this "Great"? Furthermore, regarding form and emptiness—

Although the constant pervasiveness of the non-differentiation between body and environment is fused, they have not yet been fully integrated. Therefore, within the section on the Great Element of Space, it is said:

"The nature of awareness is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true awareness. Speaking generally, what is called "awareness" refers to both the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The reason for distinguishing them by contrasting space and awareness is that the sense organs and consciousness possess the faculty of cognitive awareness.
Furthermore, empty space is that which lacks sentience. While the phenomenon is indeed thus, the principle is actually not so.

Therefore, speaking of it through a dialectical exchange, it is said: "The nature of awareness is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true awareness. This means that the nature of awareness is emptiness, and emptiness is also the nature of awareness;
thus, true emptiness and awareness are fundamentally no different from one another. Therefore, within the passage on "seeing the Great," it says: [text continues].

Yet, harmonizing these points, it is said: "If one perceives that the nature of seeing, hearing, knowing, and cognizing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that boundless empty space, along with its movement, and earth, water, fire, and wind—collectively termed the six elements—are all in their true nature perfectly interfused;

they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. This, then, treats the sense organs and consciousnesses as equal to empty space. How much more so, then, empty space itself?

Space is not insentient, and earth, water, fire, and wind are likewise not insentient. Since empty space is equal to the sense organs and consciousness, it is not only space that is eternally pervasive;
the sense organs and consciousness are also eternally pervasive. Is it not therefore appropriate to designate them as "Great"?

Furthermore, since the internal and external have already merged and the body and its objects are perfectly interfused, yet regarding the two paths of truth and falsehood, there remains [sentient] emotion...

The "holding" (執) is like the metaphor of crown and shoes. Therefore, within the two great passages concerning "seeing-consciousness" (見識), it is said: "the nature sees and the awareness is luminous; the awareness is refined and the seeing is pure;

true consciousness knows and awareness is luminous; the nature of consciousness is awareness. These are all instances of the whole substance giving rise to function, and the whole function being contained within the substance;
thus they are expressed through such reciprocal descriptions. This is why the ancient masters said that [these distinctions] are made in relation to the various consciousnesses.
Although the gates are indeterminate as being one or many, they are all the mutual inclusion of essence and function, source and manifestation within the dependent origination of reality.
From the source toward the manifestations, it is quiescent yet constantly functioning; from the manifestations toward the source, it functions yet is constantly quiescent.

Because it is quiescent yet constantly functioning, it is still without obstruction; because it functions yet is constantly quiescent, it moves without confusion. Being still without obstruction, it is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because it moves yet is not disordered, dependent origination is suchness (*tathatā*). Because suchness is dependent origination, there is no nirvāṇa apart from saṃsāra;
that is, the eighth and ninth [consciousnesses] become the sixth and seventh. Because dependent origination is suchness, there is no saṃsāra apart from nirvāṇa;
that is, the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] become the eighth and ninth. Because there is no nirvāṇa apart from saṃsāra, [this is] the Dharma.
The realms are all birth-and-death; because there is no birth-and-death that is not nirvana, the dharma-realm is entirely nirvana (and so forth).

Since consciousness is thus, the sense organs are likewise so. How could it be otherwise? Not only are the six sense organs [thus], but even the aforementioned five great elements are none of which do not have their essence and function mutually identical.
This is because the three realms are mind-only and everything is consciousness-only. Therefore, within the passage concerning the element of consciousness:

Yet, to harmonize these points: if this consciousness-mind originally has no source from which it arises, one should know that its capacity for discernment—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—is perfect, tranquil, and its nature does not originate from anything external.
Furthermore, space, earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "Seven Great Elements";
their true nature is perfectly interfused, all being the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction. Indeed, the true and eternal nature of all phenomena is thus.
When one realizes it in this way, is it not fitting to call it "Great"? Therefore, when the Sage’s words reach this point, the elucidation of principle is exhaustive;

the ice-like attachments of those present according to their capacity likewise melt away. The above concludes the Tathāgata’s response to Ānanda’s three requests for cessation, wherein the principles of the Three Truths are finalized.
Someone may ask: "In reading Master Jiaoguang’s *Zhengmasu* (Commentary on the Correct Pulse), I encountered..."

It is said that this [teaching] merely addresses Ānanda’s false attachments by resolving each instance of the delusive back into the true, thereby subsuming phenomena into principle and harmonizing appearances with nature.
It has not yet reached the stage of arising cultivation from nature or accomplishing phenomena through principle;
thus, within the Tripiṭaka, it belongs solely to the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*. Yet some people forcibly apply the three contemplations and the three truths to it.
The one who judges this lacks thorough investigation. How can his judgment that [the Master’s teaching] constitutes the three truths be so diametrically opposed?
The answer is: In general, one who comments on a sutra must understand its fundamental structure;

if there is even a single point of failure here, the error is no small matter. Now, Master Jiaoguang’s analysis falls into six kinds of errors. First, he fails to recognize the structural flow of the text.
1. The fault of the narrative’s beginning and ending; 2. The fault of using the partial to refute the perfect; 3. The fault of self-contradictory speech; 4.

The fault of failing to recognize the nature and function [of the teaching]; 5. The fault of failing to recognize the mutual correspondence of the scriptural text; 6. The fault of refuting one’s own school. Regarding the first, the "beginning and ending of the textual momentum":
Ānanda first requested the three dharmas, and the Tathāgata had already finished answering them; it was only then that the compiler of the sutra...
The "Account of Enlightenment" states: "I clearly know for myself that I have attained the fundamental, wondrous mind, which abides eternally and is never extinguished.
Only after this does he speak a verse in praise of the Buddha. With a beginning and an end, the entire sequence of events is thus completed.

As for the matters concerning the gateway of seeing the Way (*darśanamārga*) mentioned in the subsequent text, they do nothing more than express a hope to further scrutinize and eliminate subtle delusions. If it were as Jiaoguang claims, then...
To recount one's awakening and recite verses would all become empty words; how much more so when each of the preceding three truths has its own distinct beginning and conclusion?
If one does not understand this, how can they be called a teacher who explains the scriptures? Second, as for using the partial to refute the perfect:
As the Tathāgata has thus provided a detailed and comprehensive exposition of the sublime purport in its full extent, it may be said that it is ultimate and exhaustive;
the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Truth (yuan-dun-di-li) cannot be surpassed. Yet, Jiaoguang claims that within the Tripitaka, this belongs only to the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha*.
Does he not thereby partially negate the Perfect [Teaching] and suppress the entirety of the Complete [Teaching]? This third point constitutes a contradiction with his own words.

Regarding this, the following section contains verses in praise of the Buddha. Both ancient and modern commentators, including Gu Shan’s commentary, employ the "Miaozhan" (Wondrously Profound) verse to praise the Buddha’s merit of true reality and prajñā;
Jiaoguang’s *Zhengmai* likewise adopts this approach. As it says:
"Because that which was previously shown—the equal endowment of sentient beings and Buddhas—is already realized, one then perceives the Buddha's virtues. Part One.

Within the context of resolving the root-nature (*mūlajāti*), ten inversions correctly demonstrate two views. By overturning these, one reveals the realization of the clarified ocean of awakening (*bodhi-samudra*) and the luminous sky of nature (*prakṛti-dyau*);
it is vast and boundless. This is precisely the virtue of the Buddha’s *prajñā*. Based upon this... (and so forth).

This explanation is extremely detailed; it shall be cited below. It is particularly inconceivable that you fail to realize that praising the Buddha’s three virtues lies precisely in the fact that what one has awakened to is the three truths themselves.
This is nothing but a contradiction of one's own words and a logical inconsistency between preceding and following statements—what can be called "knowing two fives but not knowing ten.
Fourth, regarding the failure to recognize the mutual resonance of the scriptural text: this sutra is wondrous, wondrous indeed.

The grand framework and its detailed sub-sections reflect one another. For instance, after first requesting the three dharmas, [the text] next clarifies the eternally abiding true mind and the two kinds of roots;

from there on, the discussion of the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the realization of the fruit—whether explained horizontally or vertically—is nothing other than an elucidation of this principle.
As for the fact that what has been seen on the path of seeing is not yet exhaustive, it is reflected and interwoven within the explanation of the path of cultivation. This is a matter of celebration.
Since the "Joy" chapter has not yet reached its conclusion, the "Shadow" and "Mutual Richness" chapters are explained.
The reason for the question, "How could that which is pure by nature suddenly arise? is threefold: first, to resolve immediately the doubts regarding the seven elements;

second, to resolve ultimately the doubts concerning how "dark obscurity became emptiness" and how "the self was deluded into becoming objects"; and third, to seek clarification on the methods of cultivation and progress in *dhyāna*.
This is to ensure that no errors are committed. Such various points are none other than the desire to exhaust the meaning of the preceding chapter.
As for the Three Truths, although this chapter is comprehensive, it still does not fully exhaust the realm realized by the Buddha;

therefore, he requested the Buddha to explain them as the foundation of the Great Samādhi. Yet Jiaoguang, unaware of this intent, simply asserts that the following text constitutes a separate [section].
This is generally understood as judging [the teaching] to be the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.

It fails to recognize that the preceding chapter explains the three Tathāgatagarbhas in a sequential manner based on what is non-sequential, while the subsequent chapter explains the three Tathāgatagarbhas in a non-sequential manner based on what is sequential.
Regarding the fifth point, the failure to understand the relationship between nature and function: Master Jiaoguang’s intention was that the empty Tathāgatagarbha belongs exclusively to...

Regarding the principle of nature (*xingli*), the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha" belongs solely to the sphere of phenomenal function (*shiyong*). One must not fail to recognize that both the principle of nature and phenomenal function each mutually possess the three types of Tathāgatagarbha.

Among these, the three Tathāgatagarbhas within the principle refer to the "empty garbha" (*kongzang*) elucidated from the beginning of the first fascicle through the second fascicle, starting from the investigation of the mind and the examination of vision.
As for the "non-empty [garbha]" within the aggregates, sense bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*), it refers to the following:
It is a treasury (*garbha*). Among the seven great [treasuries], it is the treasury of emptiness and non-emptiness.

Regarding the three *tathāgatagarbhas* within the phenomenal realm (*dharmadhātu*), they establish their objects based on causal illumination (*hetu-prakāśa*) and eliminate the three types of continuity; they merely clarify that sentient beings possess the non-empty treasury.

Within this, while there is the capacity for following defilement (*saṃkleśa-anuvartana*) and the capacity for following purity (*vyavadāna-anuvartana*), one has not yet reached the ultimate. How could these be entirely judged as being exclusively the non-empty?

Does it come from the *ālayavijñāna*? If one refers to the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, then the three functions of the Tathāgata-garbha manifest simultaneously and perfectly according to purity;

Yet Jiāoguāng did not understand this intent, but instead took only a single portion of the function associated with defilement and judged it to be the "non-empty Tathāgata-garbha. How could this be?
[He] was able to exhaust the subtle purport of this sutra. Sixth, regarding the refutation of one's own school:

observing the lineage of the "Original Non-existence" (ben wu) school as expounded by Jiaoguang, and noting his frequent use of texts from the Xianshou school, it is clear that he mostly adhered to the Xianshou school.

Among the most perfectly complete doctrines of the Xianshou school-vehicle are the fourfold dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), yet Jiaoguang’s commentary on the *Seven Greats* (Qidao) [does not accord with them].

The four categories mentioned previously were each individually integrated into principle (*li*), yet it was not stated that they collectively pervade the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); therefore, they represented only the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*).

It seems that Jiaoguang’s emotional bias is often so crude and reckless that he fails to consider what precedes or follows, leading him to such behavior as "raising a spear against one's own house."

II. Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Realization to Awaken the Perfect Mind (in two parts; first, the Master of the Sūtra describes the benefits; second, the detailed explanation of the signs of realization). Second, the detailed explanation of the signs of realization (in four parts; first, the benefit of realizing the vastness of the mind):

Each member of this great assembly individually realized that their own mind pervades the ten directions. They perceived the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in the palm of one's hand. Second, the benefit of understanding that all things are truly real: All things existing within every world...

This is the wondrous clarity of Bodhi, the original mind; its essence is pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions within. (3. The Benefit of Turning Back to Contemplate the Body One Received) Turning back to contemplate the body born of one's parents:
it is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—sometimes present, sometimes lost.

It is like a single bubble floating on a vast, still ocean, arising and ceasing without a trace. (4. The Benefit of Wondrously Attaining the Original Mind) One clearly knows for oneself that the fundamental wondrous [mind] has been attained.

The mind remains eternally and does not perish. (2. Narrating outward reverence and inward joy: Bowing to the Buddha with palms joined, he experienced what he had never known before; then, in the presence of the Tathāgata, he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: From the initial discernment of the mind and its perceptions, up to the universal entry into the seven great elements, various aspects are elucidated to cause one to realize that the myriad phenomena of the vessel-world are, in their very substance, entirely true and fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. This is called the subtle and wondrous revelation.
Since one has realized that the nature of the vessel-world is truly perfect and harmonious, body and mind become vast and empty, attaining freedom from all obstructions.
"Obstruction. Because one awakens to the wondrous enlightenment that is serene and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, each and every one comes to know that the mind pervades the ten directions.

The Wise One, in his commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, profoundly penetrated the characteristics of transgression and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions;

it is also said that the "ten directions" refers to the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). To perceive the emptiness of the ten directions means to perceive the emptiness of the ten realms as they manifest according to the karma of sentient beings.
Because delusion is empty and relatively small compared to the Truth, the palm leaf is used as a metaphor.

"All worlds and so forth" refers to the establishment of the world-systems based upon space; these are simply the phenomena of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—which manifest according to karmic actions.
"All are immediately bodhi" means that throughout the ten directions of empty space, the ten realms of both the environment and its inhabitants, not a single dharma can be apprehended;
all are my own true mind. That which "encompasses the ten directions" is this very true mind, which is fully endowed with the ten realms and is not subject to annihilation.
One who contemplates this passage—how could they doubt the teaching that insentient beings possess the Buddha-nature and that insentient beings attain Buddhahood? On the contrary...

Observe that Ānanda and the great assembly below are observing their own bodies as the primary retribution within their respective realms. The vast void and the great ocean serve as metaphors for the essence of the mind;
the motes of dust and floating bubbles serve as metaphors for one's physical substance. Because principle is identical to phenomena, it is like the arising of bubbles when dust remains;
because phenomena are identical to principle, it is like the extinguishing of bubbles when the dust vanishes. Since phenomena and principle are non-dual, it is said:

There is no other way. To obtain the fundamental, wondrous mind and thereby equally attain true wisdom, knowing the principle of original enlightenment, is to experience what has never been experienced before;
this refers to attaining the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding "obtaining the fundamental wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable," the preceding Buddha told Ānanda: one...

Because they employ various false thoughts—and these thoughts are not true—they undergo cyclic existence.

Therefore, from the first fascicle onward, everything has been based upon the eternally abiding true mind to open up the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). Now that this opening of understanding is complete, the one who is the immediate recipient [of the teaching]...

Therefore, Yuanwu concludes here by stating: "One attains the fundamentally wondrous mind, which abides eternally and is never extinguished. Previously it was said that one does not know; now it is said that one knows.

Thus, the two aspects of delusion and awakening can be clearly distinguished. However, the essence of this eternal mind is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein all phenomena are spontaneously and inherently complete.
Furthermore, the nature of all phenomena is such that they are fundamentally unborn. For this reason, he first describes the realization of awakening.
With a vast and expansive mind, one sequentially realizes that all phenomena are entirely true. Furthermore, this sequential awakening is entirely a reversal of delusion.
Previously, you falsely identified the four elements as your own body and the reflected images of the six sense-objects as your own mind;

it was like walking through thorns while wearing tattered rags—obstructed at every touch. Now, having received the Buddha’s instruction, you have attained thorough understanding that the body has no marks of a self.
This is precisely the Dharma-body. That the mind is devoid of mental characteristics is the eternal mind; thus, body and mind become utterly vast and free from all obstructions.
This is a brief account of the process of awakening. What follows provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics of awakening, which do not transcend the two aspects of body and mind.

Initially, one awakens to the vastness of the mind. This overturns the previous delusion of regarding the mind as fixed within the physical body—viewing space as large while the body was small, and the body as large while the mind was small.
Now, each person knows for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions;
they see the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in their own hand. This overturns the former view that there is something external to the mind.

The distinction between the dharma as subject and object was previously clear; now, however, one realizes that all things existing within the entire world are none other than the wondrous, luminous, original mind of bodhi.
This overturns the former state where the mind and form were internal and the great self was small;

it reveals the true existence of a self dwelling in the world, acting as a pillar supporting heaven and earth and serving as a model for a generation. Those who crave life then rejoice in its preservation.
Those who weary of death and suffer from the world find both arising and ceasing to be obstacles.
Now, however, you have realized that the essence of the mind is all-pervasive and perfect, encompassing the ten directions within.

Looking back at this body born of your parents, it is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—whether present or absent, it is like a single bubble rising and ceasing upon the vast, tranquil ocean.
Suddenly and clearly, he realized for himself that he had attained his fundamental, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and imperishable. His transcendent awakening was thus preeminent;

I hope that by this, I may fulfill my heart’s desire to repay his kindness.

"Immovable" (*budong*) praises the virtue of the *dharmakāya* according to the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).

Furthermore, because it is three yet one, it is called "Mysterious and Profound"; because it is one yet three, it is called "Total Retention"; and because it is neither three nor one, it is called "Immovable. It is venerable.

*Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is its general name; here it is translated as "The Culmination of Affairs. It is called "culmination" (*niṣṭhā*) because it darkly accords with the principle of the Three Virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

Now, this specifically cites the expressive designation (the name) to offer praise. This is what was spoken by the Tathāgata while he was in the world.

To be able to dissolve and to be able to obtain—if this is not *prajñā*, what is? Even for a beginner...

At the conclusion, he states: "One should merely praise the Buddha’s three virtues (triguṇa) and employ the three truths (tisatyāni) as an aid to clarify them.

...complete. Thus, it is only after awakening through the causes that one comes to perceive the Buddha’s virtues.

Throughout the four sections, the myriad phenomena are harmoniously integrated; through the unfolding of both the general and the particular, one awakens to the realization that all phenomena are the nature itself, and that the myriad things are fully present within the single mind.

This explanation of its meaning is most correct. If one simply employs this principle to resolve the meanings of the preceding and following passages, then the three truths, the three stops, and the nature-influenced cultivation will be as clear as pointing at one's own palm.

Yet, why is it that you instead contradict yourselves to such an extent, thereby throwing the Great Way into disorder? I have read this three times over with deep regret; I do not dare to judge based on the person.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "The inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas" refers to the beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding "not passing through *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas":

according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one practices the six perfections for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and plants the causes for the marks and signs for a hundred kalpas, after which one attains the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
Furthermore, as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, one passes through one [kalpa] prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* states that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the completion of the seventh stage constitutes two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; from the eighth stage to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) constitutes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, after which one attains the ultimate *dharmakāya*.
These are all expedient teachings concerning the vast duration of time and the great distance of the path.

Now it is said that without passing through these stages, one is identical to the Dragon Girl of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who became a Buddha in the South at the age of eight; this is like the awakening of the mind described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He immediately attained perfect enlightenment. The *Tāi jīng* states: "Ordinary beings and sages are equal, with no distinction of high or low.
It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; to realize the truth is as easy as turning over one's palm. Zizhong said:

"Because the preceding section extensively refuted the two attachments to persons and phenomena, this section reveals the Tathāgatagarbha mind. Furthermore, it is interpreted that this may be a manifestation through the supernatural power of the Buddhas.

He allowed them to see it briefly. If this was so for a bodhisattva, it is likewise so for a Buddha. Otherwise, why would Ānanda have attained only the second fruit [of the path] later on?
Changshui said: "Based on this scriptural passage, we shall first discuss understanding through realization (*jie-wu*).

As it says, 'Each and every one knows for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions'—'knowing' is precisely 'understanding. Wuxing said: "This passage has been a subject of doubt for scholars for a long time, yet much remains unresolved."
Decision. Now, let me attempt to explain this according to my humble understanding. Furthermore, the scriptural account states:

"At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, felt their minds and bodies become completely open and vast. This indicates that the verses were spoken as a collective realization by the assembly, not merely the recounting of a single individual.
Yet, commentators vie to identify Ānanda alone as the object of obstruction—is this not indeed too narrow? It should be so.

If we consider the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in relation to its realization (*adhigama*), it must belong to the category of realization; for there is no basis upon which to rely on knowledge as mere understanding (*parijñā*).

For instance, how could one who is called "the Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*) be said to possess only [conceptual] understanding? One must rely on the meaning of the verse—namely, that "the Dharma-body is attained without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*"—to verify that the preceding word "knowledge" is indeed the wisdom of sudden realization.

As for the explanation of the phrase "dissolving me": *Note: The original text contains a fragmentary sentence regarding the interpretation of "dissolving me" (*māṃ saṃkṣipati*), which appears to be an incomplete thought or a transition to another topic.*

Second, even if this were Ānanda referring to himself as "I" because he had already attained that same realization, there would likewise be no contradiction.

As for the analogy of the traveler being invited into a magnificent mansion, it is merely a manifestation of the practice intended to inspire those of dull faculties.
Great powers used to guide sentient beings must employ whatever transformation is appropriate. Some may say this is not so, but I do not know why they would say so.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Judging by Ānanda’s outward manifestation, he was still at the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna).
However, as described in the subsequent passage concerning his realization of benefit, he has now suddenly attained the Dharma-body; I cannot know the depth of his spiritual rank.

As I understand it, this sutra is perfect and sudden, intended for those of perfect and sudden capacity. Although their capacity is perfect and sudden, there are nonetheless degrees of shallowness and depth.

Furthermore, since the three stages of understanding, practice, and realization are identical in their aspect of awakening, it is appropriate to evaluate them using Tiantai’s doctrine of the "six identities."

Thus, sentient beings possess the Dharmakāya in its full perfection; names and words possess the Dharmakāya through perfect understanding; dry wisdom possesses the Dharmakāya through perfect contemplation;

the stage of the seven levels of faith possesses the Dharmakāya in semblance; from the first abode onward, one partially realizes the Dharmakāya; and at the stage of wondrous enlightenment, one reaches the ultimate Dharmakāya.
