The phrase "what is below" indicates the various phenomenal appearances (*lakṣaṇa*); the phrase "in your mind" clarifies their mutual inclusion.

When one contemplates appearances, they are fundamentally false, and their sublation is likewise false. When one contemplates the nature (*prakṛti*), it is the single reality in which nothing is not included. Thus, they manifest according to circumstances.
It is said that "different directions" refers to things such as the sun and clouds. Tianru’s Supplement states:

"Since the delusions of all marks are already beyond indication, how much less can there be any meaning of one mark subduing or extinguishing another? This would be like seeking flowers in the sky to produce fruit from the sky."

○ (2. Applying the two examples to the analogy; 1. Directly applying the preceding text) True, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this: if you manifest it through emptiness, then emptiness appears;
if you each manifest it through earth, water, fire, or wind, then each of these appears; if you manifest it through all of them together, then they all appear together.
[Commentary] Zizhong says: "Because True Suchness does not cling to its own nature, it manifests various appearances according to conditions.
Wenglung says: "This is like empty space, which possesses no characteristics yet does not obstruct their manifestation."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: At the beginning, "not rejecting" establishes the fundamental principle first. "Empty space" is a metaphor for *tathatā* (Suchness).

"Its essence is not the various phenomena" is a metaphor for immutability (*avikāra*). "Yet it does not reject the manifestation of those various phenomena" is a metaphor for following conditions (*anuparivartana*).
Next, the inquiry and explanation follow: "That great empty space" points to the essence of immutability; "the sun’s brightness, clouds’ darkness, and so forth—these eight matters" point to...

Regarding the conditions that follow [the entity]: these various conditioned characteristics from different quarters—where "different quarters" conversely reveals that the essence of emptiness is not diverse, and "conditioned" conversely reveals that the essence of emptiness is unconditioned—arise because of those [conditions], thereby investigating production from another.
Furthermore, regarding whether emptiness arises from itself or from others: although the investigations are only two, the refutations are fourfold.

If that which is produced is "going," it refutes production from another; if it is "emptiness," its clarification refutes production from self. One should know that this clarification is neither sun nor sky, thereby refuting co-production;
that it is not distinct from the sky or the sun, thereby refuting causeless production. Though the directions may differ in myriad ways, emptiness remains constant.
It is unchanging. Although emptiness is unchanging, it does not reject the myriad distinctions. "The unchanging follows conditions, and following conditions is the unchanging"—it is simply this.

In the second section on the synthesis of dharmas, the passage beginning with "First, synthesizing the following of defilement" and ending with "does not accord with the characteristics of true reality" is precisely this.
It is like inviting the flowers of the sky to form the fruit of the sky; [the text] again establishes a metaphor to clarify that which is not...
This refers to the section stating that "only when the two realities combine and are purified through conditions do they accord with the nature of suchness (tathatā) in its singular aspect.

As for the phrase "previously not," "previously" means originally. This means that the natures of water and fire are not identical; the characteristic of water and the characteristic of fire possess qualities that mutually conflict and extinguish one another.

Furthermore, the character "also" (亦) may be read as "in" (在). This means that while in their original state as natures, there is no mutual conflict or extinction. If one were to say that within the nature there is a single totality...
It is not that water and fire do not exist; rather, this is not the intended meaning of the inherent nature (*xingju*) taught in this sutra.
(2. The Analogy Demonstrating Simultaneous Manifestation) How do they manifest simultaneously? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.
When two people look at the sun in the water together and each walks away—one to the east and one to the west—each person perceives a sun following them, one to the east and one to the west.
Since there is no prior standard, one should not raise the objection: "If this day is one, how can people each perceive it as a different day?
If it is already dual, how can it appear as one? Such circular arguments are empty fabrications with no basis in reality.
[Commentary] Gushan says: The sun is a metaphor for true nature; the water is a metaphor for the deluded mind; the sun within the water is a metaphor for deluded objects;
and the two people are metaphors for deluded karma. When they walk separately, their karmic actions are simultaneously activated; as they move along, deluded objects appear together with them.
Observing them together as one proves that the two are empty; observing each individually as two proves that the one is false. Therefore, it is said they are "whirling in delusion.
[Commentary] Tiantai says:
Regarding the manifestation of both, first is the Dharma. It is said that true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this.
This refers to the fact that, following the previous point, not rejecting the dharmas that correspond to one’s own nature constitutes the second fundamental principle of simultaneous manifestation.
This means that it is not merely a matter of not rejecting one particular dharma; rather, even if immeasurable dharmas were to come forth, they would likewise not be rejected. Thus it is said:
"If you clarify emptiness, then emptiness will manifest," and so forth. It is like digging out one foot of earth and seeing one foot of empty space appear.

This is the meaning of the matter. Next is the analogy: it is like observing the reflection of the sun in a single body of water, which varies according to the conditions of defilement (*rañjana-pratyaya*).
When two people observe it together, their respective perceptions correspond to the measure of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-pramāṇa*).

To say that one is in the east and the other in the west, with no prior standard, means there is no definitive characteristic of "duality" or "oneness. Precisely because there is no such certainty, one should not raise the objection that "this sun is one."
"How is it that each moves individually yet forms a pair? This 'one' is not fixed as one.
Since both are daily paired in the east and west, how could only one have appeared previously? This 'pair' is not fixed as a pair.
These are all merely convoluted, empty fabrications with nothing to rely upon; they are all metaphors for the conceptual constructions of sentient beings, consisting of nothing but mere words."
It possesses no substantial reality. For when the sun in the sky becomes a reflection in the water, it loses its fixed point of reference.
Even if a thousand people each walk their own path, there will be a thousand reflections, each following its respective person; how much more so with only two?
Therefore, one who observes the sun well does nothing better than to discard the reflection and observe the heavens. This serves as a metaphor for skillfully observing the Dharma.
One who is thus should not contemplate the nature by discarding its manifestations.

When one is able to contemplate the nature, the Wisdom-Sun of the Dharma-realm shines brilliantly within the space between the mind and the eyes; there, one does not even reckon with "one," let alone "one" and "many.
Within this, the two metaphors carry profound significance: the first demonstrates fearlessness through non-rejection, while the second reveals [the truth] through simultaneous manifestation.
This serves to manifest the function of skillful means (*upāya*). While fearlessness represents the profound essence of *prajñā*, skillful means represents the vast application of *upāya*.
That one can follow along with pure and impure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms is fundamentally based upon this.
Nevertheless, one must understand that although the conditions being followed differ in being defiled or pure, how could the nature that follows them ever undergo rising or sinking?

This is the distinction between them. Thus, throughout the day one may follow conditions without hindering the unchanging; throughout the day one may remain unchanging without obstructing the following of conditions.
One who can understand this can realize purity within defilement and fully transform delusion into wisdom.
The wondrous gateway of perfect penetration in the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama is called the ultimate and firm; it is also based upon this. [Part Two:

Extensive Correlation of Dharmas (in two sections)] First, clarifying that the unchanging mind follows the nine realms and responds to the capacity of what is known. A. First, clarifying the principle of that which is turned away from. "Pūrṇa, you use the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and usurp one another. B. Second, clarifying the principle of that which is turned away from. "Within the Tathāgatagarbha... C. Third, clarifying the functional power of following defilement. 1. First, clarifying the substance of the defiled function.

"...and the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly becomes form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. 2. Second, clarifying the appearance of the defiled function. "Therefore, within this, the wind moves and the space is clear, the sun [shines]..."

The bright clouds darken. (3. Concluding the discussion on the faults of defilement and returning to the source: Because sentient beings are deluded and distressed, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust, they give rise to worldly toil and the phenomena of the mundane world.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Form" encompasses the four great elements; when contrasted with space, they form five. Previously, Pūrṇa asked about the nature of earth, water, fire, and wind being perfectly interfused.
He doubted that the natures of water and fire could coexist without one subduing or extinguishing the other—that is, they would mutually displace one another.

He also doubted that empty space and the great earth could coexist without one usurping the other—that is, they would mutually supplant one another. Wenzhulin says: "To lose the true essence is to engage in discrimination."

To rely on reflected images is called "turning one's back on awakening and joining with the dust. To understand that the characteristics [of phenomena] are fundamentally false and to contemplate that their nature is fundamentally true is called "extinguishing the dust and joining with awakening.
[Tiantai’s Commentary: Within the section on the "Correct Method of Application," there are two parts. First, it clarifies responding to what is known according to the minds of the nine realms.
Regarding the measure (*māna*): second, it clarifies that the mind of the Buddha-realm corresponds to the measure of the objects of knowledge.

Each of these two passages consists of three sections. First, within the defiled [aspect], there are three: (1) the mind capable of turning away, (2) the principle from which one turns away, and (3) the functional capacity following defilement.

Next, within the pure [aspect], there are three: (1) the mind capable of uniting, (2) the essence with which one unites, and (3) the functional capacity following purity. Regarding the functional capacity...
Within each of these [two] capacities, there are again three parts: first, the application of the essence; second, the application of the characteristics; and third, the conclusion and return.
Thus, the headings and subheadings of the two texts are equal in their general enumeration; however, the number of phrases within the "application of characteristics" differs.

To speak in comparison: whereas previously the deluded characteristics were extensively developed—detailed earlier through the analogy of the sun’s illumination with its eight phrases beginning with "light"—now...
Because the brief is used as a standard for the extensive, it is said that "the wind moves, the sky is clear, the sun is bright, and the clouds are dark.

Next, because wondrous functions arise profusely, it is said that "one becomes immeasurable," and so forth. Following this precedent, according to defilement, one should likewise [be understood] as being turned by objects, as in the second fascicle;
therefore, within this state, one contemplates the large as small. Thus, from the perspective of sentient beings, one becomes...
The immeasurable is simply immeasurable; the small is simply small; and the great is simply great.

Furthermore, by uniting the wondrous clarity that neither perishes nor arises with the Tathāgata—according to the principle of mutual overturning and mutual supplanting—the wisdom of wondrous clarity and quiescent illumination, which is non-dual, overturns and supplants the deluded and active mind of differentiation.
That which neither perishes nor arises is based upon the eternal mind.
By practicing the constant conduct, one realizes that mutual rivalry and mutual plundering arise from relying on deluded thoughts to pursue a state of chaotic distraction.
One aspect turns its back on awakening to unite with sensory objects; the other extinguishes sensory objects to unite with awakening. It is like two people:
one is currently abandoning his father and fleeing, left alone and weary, having no leisure for anything else; the other returns home, receives the inheritance, and rejoices.

The difference between these two states—immeasurable as it is—is such that the distance between delusion and enlightenment within the single nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is no less than that between heaven and earth.
Thus, for us sentient beings to willingly wander through birth and death is truly pitiable.
Nevertheless, one must understand that although their manifestations differ, their fundamental nature is not distinct.
For when one takes the nature as the entirety of its characteristics, then the characteristics exist entirely within the nature. Nature is like moisture; characteristics are like water.
Although the characteristic of water differs according to motion or stillness, how could the nature of moisture possess any distinction between waves and tranquility?
This analogy is most intimate for the principle of immutability. Thus, one knows that I unite the wondrous clarity, which is neither extinguished nor born, with the Tathāgata-garbha;

it is not a matter of discarding the waves to observe the moisture, but rather observing the nature through the very phenomena themselves. When the winds of the objective realm subside, the water of nature naturally becomes clear.
This is the ocean-seal radiating light samādhi (*sāgara-mudrā-prabhāsa-samādhi*), wherein the entire body and the great [ocean] are fully manifest.
That which is manifested before us is fundamentally no different from the realm of sentient beings.

(2. Explaining how the mind of the Buddha-realm responds to the measure of what is known; Part 1: Explaining the mind capable of unification. By means of my wondrous clarity, which is neither extinguished nor born, (Part 2: Explaining the principle of unification) I unify with the Tathāgata-garbha. (Part 3: Explaining the function of purity according to conditions; Sub-part 1:

Explaining the essence of the pure function) And this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. (Sub-part 2: Explaining the characteristics of the pure function) Therefore, within it, one becomes infinite and the infinite becomes one.
The small manifests the large within the medium, and the large manifests the small within the medium; the immovable site of enlightenment pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
The body contains the infinite voids of the ten directions, manifesting jewel-king lands upon the tip of a single hair, and turning the Great Dharma Wheel within a minute speck of dust.

○ (Third: Purifying the Three Bonds and Returning to the Source) Because the dusts are extinguished and one merges with awakening, one gives rise to the wondrously enlightened, luminous nature of True Suchness.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Wondrous Luminosity" refers to the wisdom of quiescent illumination. "Neither extinguishing nor arising" refers to the true and eternal essence of that wisdom;
these are all that can merge. The Tathāgatagarbha is that which is merged with. Here, "Tathāgatagarbha" restates that which is merged with.

This principle is as follows: "wondrously awakened clarity" (miaojue ming) refers to the wisdom that can unite [subject and object]; "perfectly illuminating the dharma-realm" (yuanzhao fajie) demonstrates the function of reflecting all things.
To illustrate this by analogy: the Tathāgatagarbha is like the substance of a mirror, and wondrously awakened clarity is like the light of the mirror.
The Perfect Illumination of the Dharma-realm is like images appearing in a mirror. Though three, they are one; though one, they are three.
The phrases "one becomes the infinite" and so forth all manifest this meaning. "One becomes the infinite, the infinite becomes one;

within the small appears the large, and within the large appears the small" enumerates these four meanings in general. "Without moving," and so forth, specifically demonstrates their characteristics. This is the Path of Non-movement.
"The site pervades the ten directions" means that one is immeasurable. "Dharma-site" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the ground of quiescent extinction;
based upon this, responsive manifestations arise and pervade the ten directions, just as in the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], where one ascends and travels without moving or departing from one's place.
"The body contains the inexhaustible space of the ten directions" means that the immeasurable is one; the body is the very essence of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is able to contain the ten directions of empty space; since empty space necessarily encompasses all worlds, all phenomena converge into the one.
To manifest a Jewel-King Land upon the tip of a single hair and to turn the Great Dharma Wheel within a minute speck of dust is to manifest the great within the small.
Manifesting a land on the tip of a hair is to manifest the support (the environment) within the supported (the body); turning the wheel within a speck of dust is...
The medium [state] manifests the correct [nature], while the great [state] manifests the small; since this is easily understood, it is omitted.

Regarding "extinguishing dust and merging with awakening," etc., this is a summary of the preceding meanings. It is called "arising" because inconceivable function is not something produced through cultivation.
Although "function" is not mentioned here, the mention of "nature" implies that phenomenal functions exist only because they are fundamentally inherent in principle.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The wondrous clarity and so forth are the wisdom that can unite; the *tathāgatagarbha* is the principle with which it unites.

This demonstrates that the two gates of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) within the Great Samādhi constantly support one another. For wisdom is not wisdom in itself; it becomes wisdom by illuminating the realm.
The realm is not a realm in itself; it becomes a realm by being illuminated by wisdom. It is like the analogy of the single, uniform [mirror].
Regarding the principle of the *ālayavijñāna*: ordinary beings are deluded by it and take it to be the mundane; those of the Two Vehicles refute it and take it to be biased emptiness;
Bodhisattvas bring it to rest and take it to be the "Middle Only"; and the Tathāgata illuminates it and takes it to be the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Understanding is supported by the teachings, while the principle is harmonized through understanding; wisdom arises because of the nature, yet the principle is realized through wisdom. Indeed, this perfect principle is...
The words of Master Gushan regarding the foundation of Great Samādhi are correct. Therefore, what is integrated within the *Tathāgatagarbha* fully encompasses the beginning and end of its exposition.
There are both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). As for phenomena, there are the three categories (*triskandha*), the seven elements (*saptamahābhūta*), and the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).

As for principle, there are the three truths (*trisatya*) and the three *tathāgatagarbhas*. Furthermore, these phenomena and principles can both serve as the general and the particular, as in the case of the twenty-five [realms].
When the Sages each take one phenomenon as their object to illuminate the principle of the three truths, the phenomena are unified while the principles remain distinct.
When each truth and its nature inherently contain all phenomena, the principles are unified while the phenomena remain distinct.
One who can understand this realizes that there is no principle that is not manifest and no phenomenon that is not subsumed. This is the Dharma-gate of the Three Truths of Tiantai and Xianshou.

The fourfold dharma-realm is naturally manifest without the need for artificial interpretation; thus, the single principle of "one becoming the immeasurable" and so forth is also attained as its fundamental nature.
Regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, the following clarifies the three sections concerning the function of purification:
first, the essence of the function of purification; second, the characteristics of the function of purification; and third, the conclusion regarding the virtues of purification.
Regarding "function" (*kāritra*): Wu-xing explains the first two phrases by means of "wisdom-function" (*jñāna-prayoga*).

I, however, maintain that the phrase "only the wondrously enlightened clarity universally illumines the dharma-realm" still refers to wisdom and has not yet entered the realm of function. It speaks not only of wisdom but also encompasses principle (*tattva*).
The Tathāgata’s intention was this: you have used the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and usurp one another within the *tathāgatagarbha*, whereas the Tathāgata...
The entire One Principle gives rise to the myriad phenomena; thus, according to their manifestation, they appear as form or emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
I unite with the Tathāgata-garbha through non-extinction and non-arising, yet the Tathāgata-garbha takes these myriad phenomena as its single principle.
There is nothing else at all, for it is nothing but the wondrously enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm. To speak of this is not merely to speak of wisdom.

That which also encompasses principle (*li*) is as follows: for the person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*), cultivation arises from the entirety of nature (*xing*), and the entirety of cultivation resides within nature.

Thus, wisdom illuminates the object, and the object illuminates wisdom; wisdom illuminates wisdom, and the object illuminates the object. Being free from subject and object, it transcends all relativity.

Therefore, it is called "perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm" (*yuanzhao fajie*). For this reason, the following clarifies the characteristics of pure function (*jing-yong*). Within this, [the text] points to the object...

The "one" within the Tathāgatagarbha corresponds to the "immeasurable number"; the "small" and "large" correspond to the "magnitude. The "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) and the "body" correspond to the "mind" and "physical form" (nāmarūpa).

The "single hair-pore," "land," "dust mote," and "wheel" correspond to the "support" (āśraya) and the "supported" (adhiṣṭhāna). These four constitute the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of wondrous function.
The "small" and "large" represent the limitations of that essential nature; the "one" and the "measure" further represent the limitations of the essential nature's measure.

This refers to numerical quantity. "The body, mind, and the tip of a hair" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) as actual phenomena inherently possessed by nature (*xingju*), as elucidated by Tiantai.

"Dust motes and jeweled lands" refer to the dependent retribution lands (*yipao guotu*) inherently possessed by nature. "Small and large" refers to the respective dimensions of these two types of phenomena inherent by nature.
Alternatively, a single dust mote is small and the Wheel of Dharma is large; the tip of a hair is small and the royal land is large. One...
These are provisional designations established upon two kinds of real dharmas: the immeasurable and the intrinsically endowed.
One may designate a minor portion as "one" and the entire whole as "immeasurable"; one may point to a single realm as "one" and ten realms or a hundred realms as "immeasurable";
or one may point to a single phenomenon as "one" and the underlying principle as "immeasurable," and so forth. Among these three pairs, the latter two...

Since the character "manifestation" (xiàn) is attached, it is certainly its function; this is the sphere of *parabhogika* (enjoyment for others). The first [character] is merely attached as the character itself;

it is still its essence, being the sphere of *svabhogika* (enjoyment for oneself). As for that which is exclusively self-enjoyment, one does not take the one to be one, but takes the immeasurable to be one.
One does not take the immeasurable to be immeasurable; the immeasurable is [itself] one.
Because it is one, its wondrous functions can arise in profusion: the small can manifest the large within itself, and the large can manifest the small within itself, and so forth.
This is precisely because the ten realms of beings and their environments, down to the atoms and the oceans of lands, are all phenomena possessed by my single nature.
Although these atoms and lands differ in size, how could there be any distinction in the single nature? Therefore, a single atom is but a single atom within the ocean of lands.
A single atom of the dharma-realm is not small; since the ocean of lands is the ocean of lands within a single atom, the ocean of lands is not large.
The rest may be understood by applying this principle accordingly. Thus, from the many to the few, there are the three virtues (triguṇa);
the meaning of the three Tathāgatagarbhas will then be clearly and brilliantly manifest in the following text.

○ (4. The Extensive Exposition of the Principle of What is Excluded, Part 3: First, the True Truth; 2. First, Designating the Nature of What is Affirmed and Denied) Now, the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind. ○ (2. Showing the Characteristics of What is Denied, Part 2: First, Directly Clarifying the Emptiness of the Treasury; 3.

First, Refuting the Conventional Truth) It is not mind, not emptiness, not earth, not water, not wind, not fire; it is not the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; it is not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas;

it is not the sphere of visual consciousness, and so on, up to and including the sphere of mental consciousness. (2. Refuting the Ultimate Truth) It is not illumination, nor non-illumination, nor the exhaustion of non-illumination. Thus it is.
...and so on, up to: neither old age nor death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death; neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path;
neither knowledge, nor attainment (the first of the three negations regarding the Truths);
neither dāna, nor śīla, nor vīrya, nor kṣānti, nor dhyāna, nor prajñā, nor pāramitā (the subsequent negation of the fruit); and so on, up to: neither Tathāgata, nor Arhat.
Samyak-saṃbodhi is not Great Nirvāṇa; it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity.

[Commentary] Wénlǐng says: Although one extinguishes the dust and manifests the truth within the one and the many, the small and the great, such that all things are as they are (*tathatā*), the fundamentally wondrous and perfect essence has from the beginning undergone no change or variation.
Therefore, it is neither mind nor emptiness, and so on, up to being neither mundane nor supramundane.
These are dharmas. "Neither mind nor fire" refers to neither the seven elements (*dhātu*) nor the five aggregates (*skandha*).

"Mind" is the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which subsumes the five aggregates. "Neither eye nor ear... up to neither the element of mental consciousness" refers to neither the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) nor the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
These above constitute worldly dharmas. "Neither illumination nor non-illumination... up to neither old age and death."

"Exhaustion" refers to that which is not the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas. For the Pratyekabuddha, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as having both the characteristic of arising and the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment;
these are presented here together. From the stage of the Pratyekabuddha up to Nirvana, all constitute supramundane dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*). Guishan says:
"From 'not mind' up to 'not the sphere of mental consciousness'—this collectively negates the six realms of ordinary beings. "Neither clarity nor ignorance."
These are not the realm of the Pratyekabuddhas; they are neither suffering nor its origin, and thus are not the realm of the Śrāvakas.

They are neither wisdom nor attainment, for they do not possess the wisdom and realization of the Two Vehicles—wherein attainment is itself the principle (li). They are not [the practice of] dāna and so forth, and thus are not the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
First, that which is not the "path leading toward" and not a "pāramitā" refers generally to that which is not the principle to be reached.
"Not a Tathāgata" (below) refers to the Buddha-realm; first, it is not the person who realizes [it], namely the three titles [of the Buddha].
Next, it is not the dharma realized, namely the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*. "Tathāgata" means "Thus-Come One. "Arhat" means...
"Arhat" (應供), "Samyak-saṃbuddha" (三耶三菩)—meaning "Perfectly Complete Knower" (正徧知)—are three of the Ten Epithets.
"Nirvāṇa" is the general term, while the four virtues are the specific ones.
(2. Concluding the above and introducing what follows: Because these are neither mundane nor supramundane.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Worldly fetters" refers to the six realms of ordinary beings; "transcendent fetters" refers to the four types of noble ones.
Since the nature of the treasury is emptiness and lacks the ten realms, neither of these applies. Wunling says: This connects what precedes to initiate what follows.

○ (The first part of the two-fold conventional truth: indicating the essence of that which is identical) It is the Tathāgatagarbha, the primordial luminosity of the mind, wondrous. ○ (The second part: showing the characteristics of that which is identical; first, the direct explanation of the non-empty treasury; first, establishing the conventional truth) It is identical with the mind, identical with space, identical with earth, identical with water, identical with wind, identical with fire, identical with the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind;
identical with form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas; identical with the sphere of visual consciousness, and so on, up to being identical with the sphere of mental consciousness.
(Second, establishing the ultimate truth) It is identical with luminosity and non-luminosity, and the exhaustion of luminosity and non-luminosity. Thus it is.
...even unto: birth itself is old age and death; the exhaustion of old age and death is itself suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
it is itself knowledge and attainment (the first of the three establishments of the Middle Truth);
it is itself dāna, śīla, vīrya, kṣānti, dhyāna, and prajñā-pāramitā (the subsequent fruit); and so on, even unto: Tathāgata himself is Arhat.
"Samyak-saṃbodhi is itself Great Nirvāṇa; it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says:
"Although its essence is unchanging, its function is suchness; therefore, it is the mind that is the Dharma, and the Dharma that is the mind.
Gūshān says: "The preceding passage, through 'neither... nor,' demonstrated the Tathāgatagarbha according to the True Truth (paramārtha-satya). This passage..."

"Both" refers to the demonstration of the Tathāgatagarbha according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because the principle of the Garbha is "non-existent yet existent," wherein the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are perfectly manifest.

(2. Concluding the above and introducing the following: Because these two are both mundane and supramundane. (3. The Middle Truth [in two parts]: First, indicating the essence of neither-nor-nor-both. It is the wondrously luminous fundamental mind of the Tathāgatagarbha. (2. Indicating the characteristic of being apart from both "is" and "is not. Apart from...
"It is neither identical nor non-identical.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This passage appears somewhat contradictory, yet each statement has its own primary referent. The first, "the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind," refers to the self-substance (*svabhāva*).
The second, "the originally luminous wondrous mind," refers to its function (*vṛtti*). Finally, "wondrous... [refers to its essence].
"Clarifying the mind's origin" is spoken in terms of the unity of essence and function. Changshui says:

"The fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind is neither mind nor emptiness," etc., which clarifies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of negating characteristics. "The originally luminous mind is wondrous;

it is precisely the mind and precisely emptiness," etc., which clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of affirming characteristics. The wondrously luminous mind's origin is beyond both affirmation and negation, and is neither affirmation nor negation.

"Immediate" (*ji*) refers to clarifying the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*) by means of simultaneous negation and illumination. This is based on the two gates of non-duality, which are but the single mind:

because it simultaneously negates both the ultimate and the conventional, it is said to be "neither immediate nor non-immediate"; because it simultaneously illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional, it is said to be "immediate yet non-immediate.
Since the three truths are a single essence, they are all called the Tathāgatagarbha. Furthermore, the Dharma-realm is suchness.

Fundamentally, there are no names or marks. Because of delusion, there is the false; in response to the false, the "true" is spoken of. As the true and the false define one another, names and words never cease.
Following names to cling to marks—how can such perversion ever end? Therefore, by using words to dispel words, one arrives at a state where even dispelling ceases.

At first, one employs the negation of characteristics; next, one employs the negation of that very negation. Yet, as long as one remains bound by names and words, one has not yet reached the ultimate principle of the Single Truth.
Only when one is free from both "is" and "is-not," and beyond "neither is nor is-not," do the paths of language cease and the sphere of mental activity vanish.
This clearly reveals the one true *dharmadhātu*, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
Thus, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, when the thirty-one bodhisattvas expound the gate of non-duality (*advayadharma*), they all employ words to dispel conceptual marks.
Mañjuśrī employs words to dispel words, and the Great Being Vimalakīrti employs silence to dispel words; only this constitutes the ultimate. These three meanings are likewise [as described].
"It is. Tianru’s Supplement states: "That it 'is' is precisely that it 'is not'; this is like saying 'not separate from' means 'not separate from not.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The fourth section extensively explains the principle with which [the preceding] accords; this is the essence of the pure function. Only because there is this principle does [the function arise].

There is a matter at hand. Only when there is substance can there be function. However, because the principle previously integrated—the manner in which it conforms to and yet turns away from defilement, as well as the functional capacity to follow defilement for the sake of ease of understanding—must be explained, its expression could not help but be brief.

If one were to discuss the substance of the principle that is integrated, it is the perfectly interfused Three Truths, also called the Three Tathāgata-garbhas. If this were not extensively [elaborated],...
If this were explained clearly, those who hear it would not see their nature deeply, nor would they give rise to cultivation that is subtle and wondrous.

Therefore, the Tathāgata supplements this with a section of scripture that extensively harmonizes these principles to expand upon them; thus, there will be no matter that is not perfected and no principle that is not brought to its ultimate limit.
This explanation is divided into three parts: first, harmonizing the names; second, pointing out errors; and third, the formal explanation. First, regarding the harmonization of the names:
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* all clarify the three truths: first, the truth of existence;
second, the truth of non-existence; and third, the ultimate truth of the middle way. This sūtra names these the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.
There are three [aspects]: first, the empty Tathāgatagarbha; second, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha; and third, the both-empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Regarding this present sutra, there is only the single name "empty Tathāgatagarbha. That we now speak of three is established according to their underlying meaning.
This has two points of intent: first, according to the main text, since it says that the Tathāgatagarbha is "neither all [of these] nor not [any of these],"...
This is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Yet, the *tathāgatagarbha* is all-pervasive; this is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

Furthermore, the *tathāgatagarbha* is beyond both affirmation and negation, being neither identical with nor different from them, and thus it is the *tathāgatagarbha* that is both empty and non-empty.
This is consistent with the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, which states that the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is not liberated from all afflictions.
"Affliction. The non-empty Tathāgatagarbha possesses the inconceivable dharmas of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha universally responds to all things according to their form and emptiness. Someone may ask:

"These three Tathāgatagarbhas were originally cited by the Master of Wenling. His commentary states that the latter two garbhas receive their names according to their specific functions, while the 'solely empty' Tathāgatagarbha..."
If it is designated by the name "fruit" because it is the true essence, how does this contradict what the Master has taught? The answer is:

these are words from Wenling’s temporary commentary on the text. If one generates understanding based solely on the literal phrasing while disregarding the contemplation of names and meanings, then both the name and the meaning are lost.
For instance, regarding "Amoghasiddhi" (Not-in-Vain-Treasury), it is said that he possesses the inconceivable [powers] of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding the Dharma: since this nature is the wondrous existence that is inherently complete (*xingju miaoyou*), how can it be said to belong exclusively to function?

If one speaks of the "empty" and "not-empty" treasuries (*zang*) as being "conforming" (*sui*) or "responding" (*ying*), they may seem to belong to function; however, these treasury-names take two dharmas together to constitute their essence.
The "empty" is the first treasury, and the "not-empty" is the second treasury. Even if the not-empty belongs to function, does the empty not also belong to the essence? One must...

Knowing that both emptiness and non-emptiness are the essence, one now unites these two essences to form the *garbha* (womb-treasury). How could it be appropriate to categorize them as merely functional?

Furthermore, the Middle Way possesses the merit of both negation and illumination: the terms "empty" and "not empty" represent dual negation, while the phrase "universally responding to all" represents dual illumination.
The Middle Way is suchness (*tathatā*); throughout the day it remains unchanging, yet throughout the day it accords with conditions.

Therefore, Ratnakūṭa spoke thus. Again, he asked: "If all three *piṭakas* may be called 'the essence,' why does the questioner, according to his capacity, raise only the *śūnyatā-piṭaka* as a question?

He replied: "There are two meanings to this. First, although the Venerable One has opened the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), he still abides by his former realization; therefore, he asks about the essence of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*) which was realized. Second, if..."

If one distinguishes essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) based on the three truths, then the Truths of Reality (*zhēn*) and Centrality (*zhōng*) constitute the essence, while the Conventional Truth (*sùdì*) constitutes the function.

These all clarify the essence from the perspective of the single nature; they do not refer to the arising of function from essence at the level of fruition. Therefore, the Tripitaka Master [Jizang] judged both essence and function within the nature to be the essence itself.
Now, because a partial aspect that is easy to clarify has been raised as a question, it says: "The Emptiness of the Tathāgata."
It is the *Tathāgatagarbha*. Regarding the errors in the commentaries of Ji and Liaoguang, there are two types of errors in their interpretations of the preceding and succeeding passages.

First is the error of inherited tradition: they follow Master Zizhong’s judgment that the first three fascicles refute the two attachments to persons and phenomena to reveal the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, while from the fourth fascicle onward, they reveal the non-empty *garbha*; furthermore, they add their own personal interpretation to this.
Answer: It has been concluded that water and fire are incompatible; thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is both empty and non-empty.
I maintain that such an interpretation involves two kinds of errors. First, it reveals a failure of correspondence between the question and the answer regarding the capacities of the audience.
For if Ānanda had posed his inquiry based on three dharmas, the Tathāgata would necessarily have answered with three dharmas; thus, the three [instances of] cessation...

The three truths where one abides are precisely the three *tathāgatagarbhas*. Therefore, having completed the cycle of questions and answers from beginning to end, the verse of realization is recited to mark the conclusion.
If one were to categorize them all collectively as the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, it would conversely reveal that there are three points of inquiry but only one point of response;
would this not constitute the fallacy of a discordance between the questions and the answers? Second, to manifest the non-empty...
The ālayavijñāna (ālaya) would incur the fault of being subject to defilement and arising-and-ceasing.

For since the *Ratnakūṭa* states that the non-empty tathāgatagarbha possesses the inconceivable dharmas of a Buddha as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it must be that its intrinsically endowed virtues are entirely free from falsehood and defilement.
If one were to judge that the "established object" (*ālambana*) and the three continuities (*saṃtati*) of the *Hetuvidyā* constitute the non-empty tathāgatagarbha, would this not be [erroneous]?
Does this not manifest the fault of [your view] being defiled and subject to arising and ceasing?

Third, it manifests the fault that the designation "Tathāgatagarbha" as both empty and non-empty fails to exhaustively encompass its meaning. For this Garbha is designated based on its universal responsiveness to all things through the manifestation of form and emptiness;
yet, according to your judgment, it would only encompass the single section where you describe form and emptiness as mutually displacing and usurping one another.
The remaining portions of the sutra text do not belong to this same category. Is this not a failure to fully encompass the meaning? This is the first error.
One must understand that this sutra explains the three *tathāgatagarbhas* in two places:

from the first fascicle to the second, it shows that "seeing is non-seeing" to clarify the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness, which is the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Following this, it speaks of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
The clarification that the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The subsequent explanation of the seven greatnesses—which correspond to the capacity of what is known according to the minds of sentient beings—clarifies that the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).

This constitutes the sequential exposition of the three types of Tathāgatagarbha, though not in their original order. From the first question and answer in the fourth fascicle onwards, although it follows upon the preceding chapter...

Two questions are raised; however, the primary intent is to reveal that the three Tathāgatagarbhas are not sequential, but rather constitute the object of contemplation for the perfect cultivation of samādhi and prajñā.

Therefore, the statement is made using the terms "the wondrous clarity of intrinsic awareness" (*xingjue miaoming*) and "the clarity and wondrousness of fundamental awareness" (*benjue mingmiao*), by which the three Tathāgatagarbhas have already been presented.
Once the explanation and interpretation are concluded, it then proceeds with "like... (referring to the subsequent passage).
I shall now expound, based on the perfect and ultimate Tripitaka realized within the fruits produced by their respective causes, as a foundation for the complete cultivation of future students.
For if it were not for the sequential meanings of the former three, the principle would not be revealed;
and if it were not for the final, perfectly sudden principle, the truth would not be manifest. Now that both meanings are clarified together, the eternally abiding true mind—
The pure reality-mark (*dharmatā*) is the perfect integration of the three *śamatha* and the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi; these two are raised together and attained in their perfection.
Second, pointing out errors: that commentary further states, "In this context, there is a close resemblance to the three truths and three contemplations.

Those whose minds are coarse and floating, rather than deep and settled, hastily establish [their own] truths and contemplations. They do not understand the Buddha’s profound intent, but merely point directly to the multitude."
That the mind originally possessed and now manifested is thus perfectly integrated and most wondrous.
When sentient beings are deluded and when the Buddhas have realized awakening, it is always just like this, without any increase or decrease.

This is truly because this teacher did not understand that the two terms "intrinsic nature" (*xing*) and "cultivation" (*xiu*) belong to different categories. Ancient masters such as Gushan, Wuxing, and Changshui [recognized this distinction].

Regarding those who explain all [teachings] by means of the Three Truths, they speak of nature (*xing*) but not of cultivation (*xiu*). Furthermore, the principle of the Three Truths is the innate, natural virtue of nature;

how does this differ from what Jiaoguang (Jiaofang) says—that it points directly to the mind already fully possessed by sentient beings, which, after the Buddhas have realized it, is utterly without increase or decrease?
This has already been extensively refuted in the preceding sections; those who require further detail should consult them.

[The character] "jiǎn" (to examine) is an error in both instances. ○ Third, the correct explanation is divided into two parts: first, an individual explanation; second, a collective explanation. Regarding the first, the individual explanation, there are three sections.
In clarifying the true reality (*tattva*), the initial section identifies the essence of that which is capable and that which is not, stating:

"The fundamental, wondrous, original mind. Here, the character "mind" (*xin*) is the primary subject. This is what Master Shao meant by "there are no dharmas outside the mind. Only [within] the mind...
Because they are non-existent, the ten realms are all "neither" (non-dual). This section on the characteristics of that which is negated has two parts.

First, the formal explanation that the Treasury of Emptiness does not exclude the ten realms. Second, the conclusion of the above and the introduction of the following; this concludes the section on "neither mundane nor supramundane.
Because of this, it introduces the subsequent section. As the teaching states: "When conditions are forgotten, the thousand suchnesses manifest clearly. Second, the conventional.
In the section on the Truths (*satya*), the essence that is identified as "immediate" is described as "the wondrous mind of the original clarity of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Here, the character "wondrous" (*miao*) is primary. All phenomena (*dharma*) are wondrous—this is what Master Shao meant by "blue mountains filling the eyes.

Because all phenomena are wondrous, the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are all immediately present. This precisely clarifies that the non-empty nature does not transcend the ten realms, thereby concluding the preceding discussion.
The "arising below" refers to both the mundane and supramundane fetters; it is for this reason that it arises below.

It is not that one cannot achieve the dual union because one was previously unable to be free from both; rather, it is what the teaching-gate calls the mutual fusion of the hundred realms according to conditions.
Among the three truths, the first truth marks the essence of neither-duality-nor-identity, which is called "wondrous."

In "Clarifying the Origin of the Mind," the character "origin" (*yuan*) is the primary focus. This means that the fundamental origin—the Buddha-nature—is such that there is no emotion not fully exhausted and no principle not fully perfected.
Second, it demonstrates the characteristics of being neither dual nor identical. Regarding the phrase "departing from both identity and non-identity, being both identical and non-identical":

"departing" is a synonym for "non-identity," while "being" is a specific designation for "identity. The "departing" mentioned above refers to the ten [aspects] of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The ten realms are both identical and non-identical. The former, "identical," refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), where the ten realms are all identical;
the latter, "non-identical," refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), where the ten realms are all non-identical.

This reveals that the Middle Way simultaneously negates the two extremes. Furthermore, the ten realms are inherently wondrous, yet through emotional attachment they are perceived as coarse. This [text] seeks to shatter that coarseness.
Because of this emotional attachment, all ten realms are simultaneously discarded. Once coarse emotion is shattered, the wondrous principle naturally manifests;

since every phenomenon is truly eternal, all ten realms are simultaneously identical [to that principle]. However, while deluded emotion is easy to shatter, attachment to phenomena is difficult to eliminate.

Although one initially uses the principle to discard emotion, later one may instead grasp at emotion as being the principle. When emotion is grasped as the principle, both emotion and principle become coarse. Therefore, the wondrous [attainment]...
The Middle Way discards both emotion and principle. Yet, emotion is not an emotion external to principle, and principle is not a principle external to emotion.
Therefore, when one errs, both emotion and principle are merely emotion; when one attains it, both emotion and principle are merely principle.
Thus, the wondrously luminous mind-source, being detached, is detached from detachment itself; it is both immanent and non-immanent. This is the second section of the commentary.

This consists of three parts: first, elucidating the three truths by means of a vertical classification according to the ten realms; second, elucidating the three truths by means of a horizontal classification according to the ten realms;

and third, synthesizing these two meanings to lead back to the present sutra. Regarding the first [the vertical], this terminology and its meaning originate from the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* (Renwang jing) and the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Yingluo jing).
Those texts state: "First is the truth of existence, second is the truth of non-existence, and third is the supreme truth of the Middle Way."
The Truths. First, regarding the truth of existence (*satya*): the twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*) perceived through the deluded sentiments of sentient beings are called "existence.

Because these perceptions are examined and found to be real and not false, they are called "truth" (*satya*). They are also termed "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because they are provisional and pertain to the mundane world.
They are also termed "worldly truth" (*loka-satya*), which refers to that which is perceived by ordinary people. This is what is meant by "as seen by worldly people."
This constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Here, the six realms of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*) are regarded as the mundane. Second, regarding the truth of non-existence:

it is called "non-existence" because the principle of true emptiness perceived by the noble ones of the Three Vehicles is without name and without form. It is designated as "truth" (*satya*) because it is examined and found to be real and not false.
It is also called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) because it is truly real and not false. It is also called the "truth of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-satya*).
In Nirvana, that which is seen by those who have transcended the world is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This takes the two realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas as the true reality. Among these, the ultimate truth of the Middle Way is called "middle" because it negates the two extremes.
This principle is termed the "Way" (*mārga*) because it is empty, pervasive, unobstructed, and unimpeded.
It is called "supreme" because there is nothing superior to it; it is designated as "meaning" (*artha*) because it possesses profound significance;

and it is termed "truth" (*satya*) because it is that which has been realized and seen by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as being authentic and not false. Therefore, it is called the "Middle Way, Supreme Ultimate Truth.
This takes the two dharma-realms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as the Middle Truth. Next, [this is] applied horizontally across the ten realms.

Regarding the clarification of the three truths: the meaning of these three truths originates from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. The treatise states: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty;
they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Since all ten dharma realms are phenomena produced by causes and conditions—because the Buddha-seed arises from conditions—I say they are empty. The conditions of the ten realms...
Arising is entirely true; it is also called "provisional names," for the dependent origination of the ten realms is entirely conventional.
It is also called the "meaning of the Middle Way," for the dependent origination of the ten realms is entirely the Middle.

The reason these three assemblies and two meanings are subsumed within this sutra is that the three truths of the present sutra fully encompass these two meanings. As it says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is neither mind nor emptiness."

"Up to and including 'not the eighteen realms'—that which is negated here is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as perceived by deluded minds, namely the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) mentioned in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.

'Not ignorance' up to 'not wisdom' and 'not attainment'—that which is negated here is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as perceived by supramundane sages, as described in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. Not..."

From *dāna* (generosity) up to the [four marks of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity—what is negated here is precisely the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*) perceived by the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the *Benevolent Kings’ Garland Sūtra*.
This constitutes the vertical principle (*ūrdhva-artha*) of the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*).

As for the horizontal principle (*tiryak-artha*), it is like the simultaneous negation of the ten realms; this universally takes the ten realms as the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). How is there simultaneous negation? Because...
Because the fundamental, wondrous, original mind-substance of the Tathāgatagarbha is devoid of sentimentality and artifice, the ten realms are next taken together as identical.

This generally takes the ten realms as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Why are they all identical? Because the wondrous nature of the originally luminous mind inherently possesses the ten realms.
Next, "separate from identity and separate from non-identity" means that this generally takes the ten realms as the Middle Way.
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Why is it both "is" and "is not"?

Because the wondrously luminous mind-source of the Tathāgatagarbha, though appearing as the two extremes, is devoid of those two extremes because they are not distinct from one another. First, taking the character for "mind" as primary refers to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
since one observes from the perspective of the single mind, how could there be any differentiation among the myriad dharmas? Therefore, all things are simultaneously "not. And...

To say "the fundamental wondrous primordial mind" (*ben-miao-yuan-xin*) is to speak of the conventional within the ultimate. Next, taking the character "wondrous" (*miao*) as primary refers to "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*);
when one contemplates that all phenomena are wondrous, the ten realms appear vividly, and thus everything is simultaneously identical [to the ultimate].
To say "the primordial luminous mind is wondrous" (*yuan-ming-xin-miao*) is to speak of the conventional within the ultimate. (3)
That which takes the primordial character (*yuan*) as primary is the Buddha-nature of the fundamental Middle Way.

When viewed from the perspective of the original mind-nature, it simultaneously negates both extremes, whereby both the ultimate and conventional truths are dispensed with; yet it simultaneously illuminates the two truths, whereby the ultimate and conventional shine forth clearly.
To speak of the "wondrously luminous mind-source" is to say that the conventional is precisely the middle of the ultimate. Now, since the three truths [of this sutra]...

It possesses two meanings. When the horizontal is integrated with the vertical, there is nothing vertical that is not horizontal; when the vertical is arrayed alongside the horizontal, there is nothing horizontal that is not vertical.

Since there is nothing horizontal that is not vertical, the three [truths] are perfectly distinct in their triad; since there is nothing vertical that is not horizontal, they are all termed the single, ultimate, wondrous truth.
The three truths are equally real, being but the single ten realms. The ten realms are beyond all relativity, being the solitary, wondrous mind alone.
This, then, is further called the truth of non-truth. Thus, when the True Truth (satyārtha) is expounded, the ten realms are simultaneously negated;

this is "one emptiness, all things are empty. There is nothing within the realm of non-existence that is not empty. Since the six classes of ordinary beings are all negated, their existence is also empty.
Since the two vehicles are both negated, their emptiness is also empty. Since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are both negated, the Middle Way is also empty.

Furthermore, when explaining the conventional (saṃvṛti), the ten realms are simultaneously identical; this is called "the existence of one is the existence of all. There is nothing that is not present, whether it be emptiness or the middle way.
Since the six classes of ordinary beings are all identical, existence also exists. Since the two vehicles are all identical, emptiness also exists.
Since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all identical, the middle way also exists. When explaining the Middle Way, the ten realms are all [identical].

It is neither refutation nor establishment. This is called "the one within all" and "all within the one. There is nothing that is not the center, for among the six realms of ordinary beings, there is neither refutation nor establishment;
thus, existence is also the center. Among the two vehicles, there is likewise neither refutation nor establishment; thus, emptiness is also the center.

Neither Buddha nor Bodhisattva involves refutation or establishment; this is the Middle Way within the Middle Way. Therefore, if one speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called "signlessness" (*animitta*) because it dissolves all phenomena.
While the six classes of ordinary beings are dissolved by this, they are merely said to be signless.

Since even the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are likewise dissolved, is it not the case that the true is neither true nor untrue, and that the true is itself the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)? Regarding the ultimate truth, it dissolves emotional attachments but does not dissolve [the reality].
What is meant by the Dharma as the true reality (*tattva*) being signless (*animitta*)? If one speaks of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one establishes that all phenomena possess signs;
thus, the six classes of ordinary beings are established and said to possess signs. Is the true reality established for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) also possessed of signs?
Is the Middle Way of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also possessed of signs? Regarding conventional truth, phenomena are established, but sentient dispositions (*citta*) are not.

Who would say that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses characteristics? If one speaks of the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*), it is the "mere middle" (*butian zhong*) which doubly negates the dharmas of the two extremes.
Yet, the true and conventional truths of the six classes of ordinary beings and the two vehicles are what are negated; it is merely said that they are not identical [to the Middle].
Since even Buddhas and Bodhisattvas negate them, is it not the case that the Middle is neither the Middle nor the Middle, yet is identical to the two extremes? The Middle Truth encompasses all.
How could one say that the Middle Way is not perfect? It is simply because the eternally abiding true mind is fully endowed with all dharmas.
These very dharmas pervade the great void; their mutual interpenetration is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, and their mutual omnipresence is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp.
Even within a single mote of dust, the ten realms and the three truths are not lacking; even within an ocean of lands, the ten realms [are likewise complete].
The Three Truths are not many. It is as when ten thousand kinds of incense are pounded into a single pellet; if one grain is burned, it fully possesses the fragrance of all.
It is also like cutting sandalwood or splitting beryl: whether much or little, every fragment is true. Therefore it is said:
the nine realms merely desire to speak of them, yet speaking wounds their reality; they merely desire to contemplate them, yet contemplating loses them.
This is its true essence. Thus, the Tathāgata remained silent in Magadha; Vimalakīrti closed his mouth in Vaiśālī;

and in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he did not speak despite three requests. Only now, in this present sutra, does he discuss it in full detail. The *Garbha-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-dharma is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong.
Ordinary beings, sages, and saints are equal, without high or low. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...
It is said that "the mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words," and it is further said that "this Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
What the present sutra says—that "all sentient beings fail to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature"—is precisely what these passages refer to.
This wondrous Dharma is that which has been [attained] by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
This is the truth. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The present text states: "I unite the non-extinguishing and non-arising with the Tathāgata-garbha. Only the Tathāgata, within the causal stage, is able to follow the branches back to the root;
therefore, in the resultant stage, he is able to give rise to function from the essence. For this reason, within this [reality], the one is non-dual.
The measurable and the immeasurable are one. The small appears within the large, and the large appears within the small. Within a single hair-tip, the Jewel-King Buddha-land is manifested;

seated within a mote of dust, the Great Dharma-Wheel is turned. Were it not for the fact that the essence itself is spontaneously and perfectly realized as the nature-endowment (*dharmatā-prakṛti-yoga*), how could such sovereign wondrous function be possible?
The Buddha now speaks this so that the practitioner may fully realize this truth.

This serves as the foundation for cultivating the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Having attained this as the foundation, then mind-moment after mind-moment, dharma after dharma, and phenomenon after phenomenon, all are perfectly interfused within the eternally abiding wondrous fruition.
This is precisely the gate of the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara, wherein the perfect fulfillment of the Dharma is spontaneously present at every thought.
This is what is meant by taking non-arising and non-extinction as the fundamental cause of cultivation in order to seek the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction.
Question: For one who practices the Great Samādhi based on the perfect fusion of the three truths, is this a complete contemplation (*ju-zu guan*) or a partial contemplation (*sui-fen guan*)?

Answer: For a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, having already opened the perfect understanding, both the complete and the partial are applicable; there is nothing that cannot be practiced.
Nevertheless, according to the current text, it mostly concerns the partial contemplation rather than the complete. As for the twenty-five sages, each...

Relying on a single gate is to observe according to one's capacity. For superior-stream bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, they observe according to their capacity and see [the Buddha] as complete.
As for others, whether their practice is partial or limited, they observe according to their respective capacities.

As it is with the objects of focus, so it is with the contemplations themselves. There is the partial according to the parts, there is the complete according to the parts, and there is the complete according to the whole;
these correspond to the twenty-five wheels of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*.
For one who has attained a perfect understanding, it is like rolling a ball down a thousand-fathom cliff: wherever it goes, there is nothing that is not sovereign.

○ (The fifth reproof: how ordinary and small-minded beings do not understand the three initial dharmas. How can sentient beings within the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world, use their limited cognitive minds to measure the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata, or employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?

[Commentary] Gushan says: "The reason why only ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are refuted and not the bodhisattvas is precisely because [the interlocutor] Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra belongs to the two vehicles (śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha).
In reality, even the bodhisattvas of the partial teachings (pradeśa-śāsana) cannot fathom it. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra states:
'Even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are unable to know it.'"
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The two characters "how" (jiān hé) are words of direct reproof. The phrase "the world, etc. brings forward those who do not understand.
"The mind that knows" and "worldly language" refer to the mind that does not understand. To speak of "bodhi," etc., refers to the Buddha-dharma that one does not understand.
Sentient beings within the three realms of existence are thus stuck in existence; as for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they... [text continues].

They are attached to emptiness. Not realizing that what they perceive as an obstruction is itself true emptiness, and that what they cling to as emptiness is itself wondrous existence, they fail to grasp the Middle Way and their movements result in frivolous discourse.
This is to use a mind of intellectual knowledge to measure the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata, and to employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision.
Both *bodhi* and *buddha* are translated as [Awakening and Enlightened One].
Jue (Awakening) specifically refers to the Brahma-sound entering the right ear. To measure it with the mind and express it in words is to enter through speech and action;

since both mind and action are not [the truth], one remains far removed from the Way. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are twofold: first, the capacity for knowing and seeing, which is the self as neither ceasing nor arising;
second, that which is known and seen, which is the convergence with the three Tathāgata-garbhas.
(2) Analogy: For example, although lutes, harps, *konghou*, and *pipa* possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce music.
(3) Application: You and all sentient beings are likewise so. The precious, awakened true mind is each and every one of you fully complete.
It is like when I press my finger and the Sea-Seal radiates light; yet when you briefly raise your mind, the dust of affliction arises first, because you do not diligently seek the Unsurpassed [Way].
[The text states: "To awaken to the Path while cherishing the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and considering a small attainment sufficient.

[Commentary: Changshui says: "The lute and other instruments metaphorize sentient beings; the exquisite sound metaphorizes the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; and the exquisite fingers metaphorize true wisdom (bhūta-jñāna)."

The metaphor is raised to illustrate the manifestation of function: you and sentient beings correspond to the aforementioned lute and so forth; the precious awakened true mind corresponds to the aforementioned exquisite sound.
Pressing the finger is wisdom accords with principle; emitting light is the great function manifesting before one.

"When you briefly raise your mind," and so forth, corresponds to the aforementioned lack of exquisite fingers. Zizhong said: Regarding the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgaramudrā), the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states that in Jambudvīpa...

All great oceans that possess form and appearance have seal-patterns (*mudrā*). This is a metaphor for the fact that the ocean-like nature of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* universally manifests the appearances of all worlds.
The general meaning of this passage is to resolve an anticipated objection. The objection states:
"If all things are identical to the true self (*ātman*), how is it that they do not share the same wondrous functions as the Tathāgata? Therefore, the text now explains: "You..."
Although they possess the true mind of precious awakening, they have not yet attained its wondrous function because their defiled, deluded thoughts have not been purified.
Guishan says that the phrase "due to not diligently seeking" below explains the reason why defilement arises first.
Although this specifically refers to the meaning of the Hīnayāna, it encompasses other realms; therefore, it was said previously: "You and all sentient beings are equal."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Changshui states that the lute and other instruments metaphorize sentient beings, while the exquisite sound metaphorizes the *tathāgatagarbha*.

This is incorrect. One should instead take the lute and other instruments to metaphorize the precious, awakened true mind; the exquisite sound to metaphorize the great function that is without fixed direction;

and the exquisite fingers to metaphorize the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. As it says below: "As when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light. This is an interpretation of the sūtra by means of the sūtra itself; such is the meaning.

This is extremely clear. However, although the finger is pressed against the surface as a metaphor for the mind being raised upward, it actually serves as a counterpart to the mind being raised downward.

This is because the metaphor illustrates that the essence of quiescence (*śamatha*) is the foundation of the function of illumination (*vipaśyanā*), while it reveals that the raising of the mind is the source of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).

It speaks precisely of how the Buddha attains wondrous concentration (*samādhi*) and the great function manifests before him; it is like all forms and images on Jambudvīpa being reflected simultaneously in the great ocean.
The text states: The ocean possesses three kinds of virtues: it is profoundly still and pure, it reflects the images of forms, and it is immovable and all-pervading.

This serves as a proximate metaphor for my own state—through non-extinction and non-arising, I am united with the Tathāgata-garbha, which is wondrously enlightened and luminous, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
The ten realms and the three truths are neither simultaneous nor identical; the ten realms and the three truths are both simultaneous and identical.

The ten realms and the three truths are both detached from identity and detachment, and detached from non-identity and non-detachment. This is a distant analogy for Ānanda’s praise of the Buddha’s three dharmas—wondrous clarity, total retention, and immovability—which are likewise extremely clear.
In this present passage, since the three truths are presented by citing one as being identical to the three, the three truths of the preceding passage [are likewise established].

It is also said that the three are identical to the one. What are their characteristics? If we distinguish them by way of the nature of vision (*darśana-svabhāva*): its profound stillness and purity is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones can all, through the very faculty of vision, realize this is the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

That its substance pervades the entire dharma-realm without wavering is the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*). This is how the Ultimate Truth is said to be "three yet one. [The same applies to] the aggregates (*skandha*).

The sense bases and elements are not merely nature-endowed, but are the wondrous existence (*miao-you*). Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they spontaneous; they are the true emptiness (*zhen-kong*).

Immovable, pervasive, and perfect, this wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the "perfect" within the "middle. This conventional truth (*saddharma*) speaks of the three as being identical to the one.
The seven great elements are substance that is true emptiness, and true emptiness is substance; this is wondrous existence.
Being pure and fundamental is true emptiness, and pervading the Dharma-realm is the perfect Middle Way within this. To speak truthfully, these three are one.

Since discussing the nature is intended for the purpose of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and since the truths are already perfectly interfused and mutually inclusive, cessation (*śamatha*) is likewise subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable. May readers first...
Set aside the mind of right and wrong and enter together into the ocean of the nature of harmony; with a single illumination, examine whether the fundamental truth accords with its fruit.

Because one does not diligently seek it, although one may explain the causes from which afflictions first arise, this is in fact the most diligent cultivation, serving as the gradual entry into the Way.

[Section Two: Answering the Previous Doubts (Part One: Pūrṇa Re-examines the Cause of Delusion; Part One: The Question)] Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata possess the perfect clarity of precious awakening, the true, wondrous, pure mind, which is non-dual and complete.
Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusive thoughts and have long remained in saṃsāra. Now that I have attained the Holy Vehicle, I am still not yet ultimate.
World-Honored One, since all delusions have been completely extinguished and only the wondrous, true, and eternal remains, I venture to ask the Tathāgata: among all the assemblies..."
"By what cause is birth produced? Why do they delude themselves and obscure their wondrous brilliance, thereby undergoing this drowning in samsara?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This question follows upon the previous statement that each is "perfectly complete.

Since it has already been realized that there is no duality, this further clarifies the deluded drowning; however, because they do not know the origin of this delusion, he requests an exhaustive investigation of its cause. Tiānrú supplements:

The commentary states: "Near" refers to what precedes; "far" refers to what comes before. Since the preceding text had not yet reached the meaning of "manifestation according to karma," there arose the question, "How could this suddenly arise?
The Tathāgata then answered with the passage beginning, "Taking delusion as the cause of enlightened awareness, based on that awareness, one establishes the objective realm.
Although Pūrṇa now understood that it was delusion, he still did not know for what reason this delusion exists.
Therefore, this question was asked. Gushan said: "That it is not yet ultimate has two meanings.
