What follows below relies on the eternally abiding true mind to open the perfect practice (*caryā*). Now, understanding is the understanding of the practitioner, and practice is the practice of the one who possesses understanding.
Regarding the section on Practice: the preliminary opening of the Perfect Understanding has already prepared the gateway of practice.

Now, within this gateway of practice, there is nothing more than clarifying the two kinds of determination regarding the initial aspiration for enlightenment. This serves to demonstrate the twenty-five gates as the primary skillful means for cultivating the aforementioned gateway of understanding.
Thus, we know that the ancient masters—such as those of Wēnlíng, Gūshān, Wúxīng, and Chángshuǐ—[held this view].

The great judgment is not at all the same. Who is there that does not know that "first understanding, then practicing" is what was refuted in the section where Master Jiaoguang’s *Xuanshi* (Explanatory Notes) provides his critique?
Furthermore, Jiaoguang judges that from the beginning up to this point, the response to Ānanda regarding *śamatha* has been completed;
what follows, which opens the gate of practice, is the response to the request for *samādhi*. To speak in such a manner is not only...
The Buddha-dharma cannot be understood through mere literary composition; even in the formal structure of writing, there are points that do not hold.
Generally, every literary composition has a beginning, an exposition, and a conclusion. Ānanda’s initial request for the three dharmas constitutes the beginning.

The Tathāgata’s sevenfold inquiry into the mind constitutes the exposition. Ānanda’s attainment of awakening and his praise of the Buddha’s three dharmas constitute the conclusion. Maitreya... [text continues]
The opening of the two questions constitutes another introduction; the passage from "the nature-awareness is wondrously luminous" (*xingjue miaoming*) onward constitutes another exposition;
and the scriptural account of the realization constitutes another conclusion. Thus, across these two cycles, the three dharmas are presented both in sequential and non-sequential order.
How can this be said to answer only *śamatha*? One must understand that the preceding opening of the gate of understanding was a discussion of *śamatha* and the other [two] practices.
The three dharmas illuminated are the three truths. Subsequently, opening the gate of practice involves discerning the definitive root of afflictions within these three dharmas;
this corresponds to the terminology of "selecting one gate" and "entering deeply into cause and effect.

Thus, it should be known that the three dharmas of opening and understanding must necessarily coexist, and the three dharmas of the gate of practice must likewise coexist; they differ only in the distinction between cultivation and nature, and between wisdom [and ignorance].
The distinction lies in the object [of realization]. Previously it was said that by eliminating the deluded thoughts of self and phenomena, one suddenly attains the Dharma-body;
now it is said that once doubts and suspicions are eliminated, the mind awakens to the true reality (dharmatā). If this is considered in terms of true realization, then the path has increased;

if considered in terms of intellectual understanding, then it is even more clarified. Furthermore, the previous statement was: "I hope you will further examine and eliminate subtle delusions, so that I may quickly ascend to supreme enlightenment."
Thus, having now received this instruction, my doubts have been dispelled and my mind has awakened to the true reality;
this is also one instance of the author’s illuminating reflection. To praise the Buddha as the Unsurpassed Great Compassionate and Pure Jewel King:

it is known that the Buddha’s awakening to delusion is like realizing that flowers in the sky seen by one lost in a maze are fundamentally non-existent; having realized True Suchness, the pure gold is no longer subject to the moisture of ashes.
In the state of birth, there is nothing superior; all myriad entanglements are completely cast off. Without mind and without conditions, one is able to extract suffering and bestow happiness.
Therefore, it further describes the Dharma and its benefits, saying: "It skillfully opens my mind," and so forth.
[II. Statement of the Request (divided into two; first, the statement that there is understanding but no practice;

first, the formal statement)] "World-Honored One, although I have now received such sounds of the Dharma and know that the Tathāgata-garbha—the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind—pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned, wondrously enlightened royal lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the lands of the ten directions, the Tathāgata has further rebuked me for my lack of merit in much hearing and my failure to engage in cultivation.
[II. Manifestation by Analogy] "I am now like a traveler who has taken up temporary lodging."

Suddenly, I have been graced by the Heavenly King with the gift of a magnificent mansion; though I have obtained this great residence, I must enter through its gates. (2. Explaining the formal request for the gate of practice:

I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion and reveal to me—the ignorant ones gathered here in this assembly—the path of the original aspiration for the ultimate Nirvāṇa without remainder of the Tathāgata, after casting aside the Lesser Vehicle.
Now that there are those who study, by what means shall they subdue their past attachments?

"Because you have attained the *dhāraṇī*, you shall enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and with single-minded devotion, he waited in the assembly for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "Losing one's true nature is like being a traveler in a lodging; seeing one's nature is like entering a magnificent mansion. To see one's nature and yet not cultivate it..."
Having obtained a dwelling yet not entering it, he therefore requested the path of the Tathāgata’s original aspiration, hoping to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

*Nirvāṇa without remainder* is the perfect fruit; the path of the original aspiration is the perfect cause. Since he has already seen his nature, he further seeks to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision:
seeing is what is opened and shown, while cultivation is what leads to awakening and entry. The Zhou dynasty referred to the Son of Heaven as "Heaven" (*tian*).

The King selected among the various princes. Gu Shan said: "The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that the three *dhāraṇīs* correspond to the three meanings of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way.

Now, we request [the teaching on] the practice-gate of subduing delusive thoughts through the single mind and the three contemplations (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*), so that upon entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the three types of wisdom may be manifested simultaneously;
therefore, it is called 'entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision' (*buddhajñānadarśana*)."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the account of the request concerning "having understanding but lacking practice," the emphasis lies on the single character "knowledge" (zhī). Knowledge is precisely understanding.
If one has already attained true realization, why would it be necessary to further request the gate of practice?

In short, Ānanda manifested his traces to initiate this teaching as a method for cultivation and progress in the Dharma-ending age. His mind universally encompasses and nurtures all beings, as was constant in the preceding sutra.
The points that differ from the present [teaching] are that there is a distinction between the pure and the defiled, and a difference between the living being and the Buddha.
What is expressed here is the understanding of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, which is the wondrous clarity of inherent awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*) and the clarity of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*);

it is the wondrous clarity of sublime awakening that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm and is intrinsically pure. In the metaphors used to clarify this, the Heavenly King represents the Tathāgata, the Great Treasure Dharma-King.
The metaphor of the "flowered mansion" refers to the perfectly integrated three virtues realized by the Tathāgata.
That the Tathāgata fully transfers the Dharma he has realized into the minds of others is what is meant by "the Heavenly King bestowing the flowered mansion.

Within the section on the "Correct Petition for the Gate of Practice," the phrase "Nirvana Without Remainder is originally the path of initial aspiration" is a formal restatement of the specific petition for the primary expedient means; this serves as...
The general invitation concludes. Below, from the section on "How to Subdue Past Objects of Attachment," the separate invitation opens the second determination:
a detailed examination of the root of afflictions. From "Attaining Dharani and Entering the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision," the separate invitation opens the first determination:

the correspondence between names and categories regarding cause and effect. All of this is based upon a single, fundamental root of perfect penetration; thus, one immediately cuts off the afflictions.
The root of affliction is eliminated, and one immediately attains the nature of the three universally pervasive and constant virtues.

This constitutes the attainment of *dhāraṇī* and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. When the assembly first requested instruction, the approach was first general and then particular, yet the primary intent lay in the generality;
therefore, the Tathāgata first clarified the primary intent through that general request. Now, however, the request is first particular and then general.
However, the primary intent lies elsewhere. Therefore, the Tathāgata, responding to the request concerning that which is "elsewhere," clarifies this primary intent.
What was initially called "the Tathāgata’s bodhi" is now called "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision"; the correspondence between these scriptural passages is clearly visible.

As for Guishan’s current request regarding the term "three contemplations," how does it differ from the previous general request? One must interpret and reconcile [the general] by returning to the specific.
The intent of the vision.

(2. The Tathāgata’s proclamation of the practice gate; Part 1: The Sūtra Master’s Narrative) At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly—both pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who were not yet masterful regarding the bodhicitta, and for the sake of sentient beings of the final dharma period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa who have resolved upon bodhicitta, revealed the unsurpassed [teaching].

Riding upon the path of wondrous cultivation, he proclaimed this to Ānanda and the great assembly. (2. The actual proclamation, in two parts: first, for the sake of the primary recipient Ānanda, clarifying the initial expedient means; second, [the subsequent clarification]. 1. Clarifying the initial expedient means, in two parts: first, the actual clarification of the two meanings of the initial awakening mind; second, the general statement. "You all must resolutely give rise to the Bodhicitta.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi, you should not give rise to weariness. You ought first to clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial awakening mind. (2. The specific clarification, in two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the actual explanation. 1. The inquiry:

"What are the two definitive meanings of the initial mind? (2. The actual explanation, in two parts: first, examining the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground; second, [the subsequent clarification]. 1. Examining the mind generated at the causal ground, in two parts: first, the general exhortation to examine; second, the narration of the purpose and the actual exhortation. "Ānanda, first..."

"Regarding this meaning: if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas, cultivate the bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant fruit. (2.

Showing why it must be examined) Ānanda, if you take a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice at the causal ground while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible."

Section. ○ (2. Direct Instruction on Thorough Observation; Part 1: Pointing to Phenomena and Using Analogies to Illustrate Thorough Observation) For this reason, you should illuminate that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) are subject to transformation and extinction.
Ānanda, observe the conditioned phenomena of the world: which among them does not decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space (*ākāśa*) decaying or rotting.
Why is this? Because space is not something conditioned; therefore, from beginning to end, it is without decay or extinction.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: Within emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, all are termed arising and ceasing. The middle is precisely emptiness and the provisional; this is called the Buddha Vehicle.
That the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive bodhisattvas cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom is precisely because of this.

All phenomena undergo transformation and cessation, which is a metaphor for the illusory substance being impermanent. Emptiness is without decay or destruction, which is a metaphor for the true nature being eternally abiding.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, the interlocutor requested [instruction] regarding *dhāraṇī*; now, in the response, it is called "wondrous *samādhi*.
One must understand that both names possess two meanings: the general and the specific.

As in the second fascicle, where "subtle and secret contemplation-illumination" (*dhāraṇī-vimokṣa-pratyavekṣaṇā*) refers specifically to the *dhāraṇī* of skillful means (*upāya*), whereas in the present text, *dhāraṇī*...
This collectively enumerates the three types of cessation within the single mind; these are all names established based on practice (*caryā*).
If there is a great *dhāraṇī* gate called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), this name is established based on principle (*tattva*). The same applies to *samādhi*.

If one were to request the *samādhi* of the three dharmas at the beginning, it would specifically refer to contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*); here, the mention of "wondrous *samādhi*" likewise refers to the three.
"Samatha-vipaśyanā" is a general designation for both. Furthermore, when the twenty-five sages describe their entry into *samādhi* as "entering *samādhi*," this too is a general designation.
Jiaoguang, however, restricts himself to the single phrase "wondrous *samādhi*" from this text and immediately judges that what precedes it is *śamatha* while what follows is *samādhi*.
If his judgment were correct, then there would have to be *samādhi* mentioned in the first fascicle.

To claim that the "Great Buddha-Crown" refers to all the meanings discussed since the "Seven Investigations," and that these are entirely subsumed under the contemplative illumination of *samādhi*, is yet another extreme case of being confused by the terminology and losing the meaning, failing to grasp the essential point.
"Awakening" (*pratibodha*) refers to the initial awakening at the very beginning of the process of "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*).
"Certainty" (*niścaya*) has two meanings: first, it is that which the sages, such as the Tathāgatas, have resolved; [the second is that which they cause others to resolve].

Because it is fixed, it is called "determined" (*niyata*). First, that which has already received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Tathāgata is fixed and cannot be altered; this is also called "determined.
These refer to the same meaning, differing only in the distinction between the capacity [of the recipient] and the act of bestowing the prediction.
Someone may ask: "Are these two meanings of 'determination' the same as or different from the two preceding fundamental types? The answer is: they are the same, and furthermore...

They differ yet are again the same. As for their initial sameness: when viewed at first glance, the first [point], the root of birth and death, is the same as the second, the thorough examination of the root of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The second, the root of wisdom and abandonment (*prajñā-prahāṇa*), is the same as the second [point] in that both cause and effect accord with non-arising (*anutpāda*).
There are two ways in which they differ: first, difference in name; second, difference in essence. This causes people to understand clearly.

One knows the fundamental source of birth-and-death and nirvana and thereby understands what to choose and follow. This is first called "determination," which enables one to determine between two paths as that which can choose and follow.
Second, there are differences in meaning and principle: one clarifies that the root of birth-and-death is the deluded mind that clings to conditions;
one clarifies that the root of afflictions is the six sense-faculties of experience; and one clarifies bodhi and nirvana...

"Pan" (槃) refers to inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). First, clarifying the correspondence between cause and effect names refers to cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). Regarding that which is different yet identical:

while the root of birth and death was previously explained in a broad and pervasive manner, encompassing the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), as well as the seven great elements and the ten realms, the roots of wisdom and severance likewise follow the pervasiveness of the phenomena of birth and death, such that there is nothing that is not [encompassed].

The eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of the sublime True Suchness—by means of these two definitive meanings, the root afflictions of birth and death are now definitively established as residing within the six sense faculties;

likewise, Bodhi and Nirvana are also definitively established as residing within the six sense faculties. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The root of the fetters of birth and death, and Bodhi, quiescence, and permanence [are one]."
These are simply the six sense organs and nothing else. Regarding these two dharmas, unless the Tathāgata himself were to provide a resolution, they could never be definitively settled;
therefore, it is called the "Two Definitive Meanings. In the detailed examination of the analogy of the matter, one never hears of empty space being decomposed or destroyed;
this is intended to clarify that emptiness is not something that can be produced, serving as an analogy for the wondrous nature of the six sense organs which relies [upon emptiness].
To practice in this way is what is meant by the correspondence between cause and effect, name and reality.

(2. Correctly examining the phenomena; Part 1: Distinguishing turbid delusion; Sub-part 1: Pointing out delusion as a general heading) Now, within your body, that which is solid is earth; that which is moist is water; that which is warm to the touch is fire;
and that which moves is wind. From these four entanglements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Examine from beginning to end these five layers of turbidity. (2. A detailed explanation of the meaning in two parts: 2.1. General explanation of the meaning of turbidity; 2.1.1. Establishing a metaphor. What is meant by turbidity?

Ānanda, it is like clear water that is pure and pristine by nature, while the dust, soil, ash, and sand are by their very substance obstructive and solid. These two entities are such that their natures do not accord with one another.
Yet, there may be people of the world who take that dust and throw it into the pure water; thus, the water loses its clarity and obstruction.
When water loses its purity and clarity, becoming turbid, it is called "muddy. (2. Brief Synthesis) Your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.
[Commentary] Guishan says: From these four entanglements up to the fifth layer of turbidity, the four great entanglements are collectively [referred to].

Thus the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are formed. By means of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) are formed, with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) residing in their midst.

It enables the eye to see, the ear to hear, the nose, tongue, and body to perceive, and the mental faculty (*manas*) to investigate. Because sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) arise in accordance with forms and sounds, the five aggregates are thus formed.
Form is the beginning and consciousness is the end; because the five aggregates obscure that profound and perfect [nature], they exist.
The *kalpa* and so forth constitute the fivefold turbidity (*pañca-kaṣāya*). The present text’s treatment of the five turbidities differs fundamentally from that of other sūtras.

What is elucidated in other sūtras holds that views (*dṛṣṭi*) have the five sharp [afflictions] as their essence, while afflictions (*kleśa*) have the five dull [afflictions] as their essence; thus, the sharp and dull together constitute the ten proclivities (*daśa-anuśaya*).
Sentient beings merely grasp at the retribution of views and pride to establish this conventional designation. Life (*jīvita*) refers to the continuity that sustains a single period [of existence].
Form and mind constitute its substance; because it crushes years and shortens the lifespan, it is called the turbidity of life (*āyus-kāṣāya*). A kalpa has no separate substance of its own;

it is merely named the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kāṣāya*) because the four turbidities aggregate during that time. The present text is not like this; rather, it defines the five turbidities based on the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Therefore, the subsequent text states that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) possesses the delusive thought of solidity, while the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) possesses the delusive thought of empty luminosity.

[This refers to] "delusive thoughts" (*vikalpa*) and so forth. Tianru’s Supplement states: "Various masters explain the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) by means of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.
It would be easier to understand if Master Yuan (Zhiyuan) had explained them as the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Furthermore, this would not conflict with the meaning of the passage in 'Distinguishing Demons' which says, 'When the aggregate of form is exhausted, one transcends the turbidity of the kalpa,' and so on."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, by pointing to concrete examples and metaphors, we observed that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subject to change and decay.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), however, is not something conditioned and thus never undergoes destruction. Thus, worldly phenomena are never apart from emptiness;
the conditioned and the unconditioned are eternally of one essence. Now, applying this to the Dharma for formal contemplation, it is likewise so: within your own body...
Earth, water, fire, and wind are conditioned products. The profound, perfect, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind is not a conditioned product.
Because of these four entanglements, your wondrous mind is divided into seeing, hearing, and so forth; thus, the conditioned and the unconditioned are always present together.
This is how the continuity of the world leads to the continuity of sentient beings. This, then, is the division.

Your statement encompasses what was previously clarified: that delusion is not caused by the luminosity of another's awakening, yet once the falsely constructed has been established, the underlying principle of luminosity is no longer understood.
The explanations of the "three subtleties and six grossnesses" provided by various masters may be used to trace its origin.
As for the affairs of the five turbidities in the present day, it is appropriate to follow the explanation given by Master Gushan. If one proceeds from the beginning...
Entering the final five aggregates (*skandha*), when they are turbid, there are two beginnings. The subsequent text states: "Birth arises from consciousness (*vijñāna*);

cessation results from the removal of form (*rūpa*). Now, since we are specifically discussing the process of origination, it would be appropriate to take the aggregate of consciousness as the beginning.

That the current text takes form as the first is stated with reference to the self-establishment of the five aggregates; for there are indeed the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).
It is because there is sensation (*vedanā*) after form (*rūpa*); there is perception (*saṃjñā*) after sensation; there is mental formations (*saṃskāra*) after perception;
and there is consciousness (*vijñāna*) after mental formations. Thus, Master Gushan’s [position] that form begins and consciousness ends possesses profound道理 (*yǐlǐ*, principle).

In the established analogy, water represents the profoundly perfect true mind (*tānzhuān zhēn xīn*); the ash and sand represent the entanglements of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). One is clear and the other is obstructive. By itself—
They do not conform to one another; when earth is taken and cast into water, each loses its own nature. For this reason, it is called turbidity.
Nevertheless, although the water is turbid, its essence of clarity is never forgotten; wherever turbidity pervades, there clarity also pervades.

The same applies to the five faculties and the four great elements. Therefore, the practitioner of perfect cultivation does not reject turbidity to seek clarity, but rather [seeks it] within the very state of stillness.
Furthermore, Gu Shan says: "The five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) in the present text differ forever from those in other sutras.

For example, it is said that one enters the *kalpa-turbidity* only when the human lifespan reaches ten thousand years. As for the turbidity of views, there are five types of sharp [afflictions]; as for the turbidity of afflictions, there are five types of dull [afflictions]. Sentient beings are designated by the provisional name "sentient beings" based on the combination of these sharp and dull [afflictions].
The turbidity of life refers to the destruction of years and the shortening of the lifespan. Because these four turbidities converge at this time, they are called the five.
Regarding the turbid and evil world: from the beginning of the kalpa of emptiness until now, this turbidity has existed.

It is manifested through the six sensations, afflictions through the six perceptions, sentient beings through the six volitional formations, and life through the six consciousnesses; all of these are explained by way of their respective essential natures.
One is true and one is false; from time immemorial they have coexisted. This enables people to return to the true by means of the false through very sight and hearing.
Not only do the coarse and the subtle differ, but even matters and principles, as well as the great and the small, are utterly distinct from one another.

○ (2. Specific Explanation of the Five Aspects; 5. First, the Turbidity of the Kalpa) Ānanda, you see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions. Space and seeing are not distinct; yet there is emptiness which lacks substance, and there is seeing which lacks awareness.
These two interweave in delusion to form the first layer, which is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

[Commentary]孤山 (Gushan) says: "This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Now, the four great elements, the five sense organs, and the five sense objects are collectively termed the aggregate of form.
Here, it is explained by means of the eye organ seeing the object of space (*ākāśa*) because this serves to clarify the meaning of 'turbidity.
Why is it called the *kalpa-turbidity*? Since the four phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are all termed *kalpas*, it refers to the seeing of space as the name for it."
This constitutes the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). "There is emptiness but no substance" means that emptiness lacks any essential nature or physical form.
"There is seeing but no cognition" means that when one perceives emptiness, there is nothing—neither beauty nor ugliness, neither opposition nor compliance—to be cognized.

"They are interwoven to form delusion" means that the emptiness lacking substance is interwoven with the seeing lacking cognition, and the seeing lacking cognition is interwoven with the emptiness lacking substance; thus, they are falsely constructed.

Seeing emptiness, both [subject and object] lack substantial reality; this is precisely the earth-element losing its obstructive nature. That the true nature becomes turbid—does not the fault lie here?
This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means of instruction, pointing directly to the emptiness before Ānanda’s eyes to establish the meaning of the kalpa-turbidity.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In Sanskrit, *kalpa* means "period of time. If there were no arising, it would simply not exist;

since there is arising, it must occur at its proper time, and thus turbidity is formed. Because time consists of the phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, this turbidity exists regardless of whether one speaks of antiquity or modernity, or of purity or decadence.
However, time does not exist of itself; time is established through the locus of form (*rūpa*). Therefore, this turbidity depends upon [form].
The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) exists by means of the four great elements, the five faculties, and the five objects.
Now, when it is explained by correlating the faculty of the eye with the object of space, it is as Master Guishan said: "This is done to manifest it through the meaning of turbidity.

Thus, the seeing [faculty] serves as an analogy for the other four faculties, and space serves as an analogy for the other three great elements. Within the sphere of daily life, there is nothing that is not a mutual correspondence between faculty and object.
Regarding the meaning of turbidity (*kaṣāya*): this turbidity takes the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as its substance.

Therefore, it is said that one weaves the perception of non-awakening with emptiness that has no substance, and weaves the emptiness that has no substance with the perception of non-awakening. This first layer is called the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Someone may ask: "If goodness, evil, and the indeterminate all belong to delusive thought (*vikalpa*), why is the indeterminate alone [designated as such]?"

"Are not the turbidities of good and evil themselves turbid? He replied: "Now, when the faculties and their objects meet but before discrimination has arisen, the essence of seeing, the essence of hearing, and so forth, are considered indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If the thoughts of good and evil arise, the meaning of turbidity becomes even more pronounced;

furthermore, this will be clarified within the context of the four subsequent turbidities. Nevertheless, since it is said that 'emptiness exists but has no substance' and 'seeing exists but has no awareness'..."

Weaving [these perceptions] together creates turbidity. If, at the moment you perceive seeing, you realize that this seeing is not true seeing, then its substance is empty and its perception is present;
without weaving them together and without delusion, the kalpa-turbidity can be transcended. By this principle, one may infer the following four cases:
seeing forms is equal to being blind; experiencing sensation is neither experiencing nor not experiencing, and neither non-experiencing nor non-non-experiencing.

Up to and including the five non-receptions, one thoroughly realizes that the mind is fundamentally non-existent throughout the three periods of time, and that its arising and ceasing, its coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, by means of the six receptions, one returns to sameness; through sameness, one illuminates difference.
These are all the swift paths for transcending the turbidity described in the various sutras.

○ (2. The Turbidity of Views) Your body presently manifests as a composite of the four great elements; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth revolve to produce sensory awareness.
These interweave falsely to form this second layer, which is called the turbidity of views.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "This turbidity relies upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Now, the reception of an object is called sensation, and there are six kinds.
That is to say, the six sensations arise based on the conditions of the six contacts (*sparśa*).

However, because objects are distinguished as being disagreeable, agreeable, or neither disagreeable nor agreeable, the six sensations likewise each have painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*), pleasant sensation (*sukhā-vedanā*), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukhā-vedanā*)."

This is the differentiation of sensation (*vedanā*). That which is falsely formed through mutual interweaving refers to the six sensations being obstructed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), thereby causing them to become stagnant and impeded.
Consequently, seeing does not transcend form, and hearing does not go beyond sound. Because the four great elements are rotated by the six sensations, they are made to be perceived.
These two factors interweave and falsely constitute the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); because it perceives objects and receives them as a whole.
Because it turbidizes the true nature, it is called the turbidity of views.

○ (3. The Turbidity of Afflictions): Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of recollection, cognition, chanting, and study gives rise to knowledge and vision; these appear as the six sense objects.
When separated from the objects they have no form, and when separated from awareness they have no nature. These interwoven delusions constitute the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions.
[Commentary] Changshui says: "It recollects past objects, cognizes present sensory fields, and rehearses future realms.
Gushan says: "This turbidity relies upon the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception). The objective marks (*nimitta*) of the conditions that are grasped and experienced are called 'perception.

There are six kinds; that is, taking the marks of the six sensory objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) that are grasped and experienced constitutes the six perceptions. Its nature gives rise to cognition and vision."
This refers to the ability to grasp the six perceptions, which can manifest as the six sense objects—the characteristics of the six grasped objects.

By weaving these characteristics together, one falsely constructs the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Once one becomes attached to what is perceived, the agitation exceeds that of the previous [aggregate].
Because it muddies the true nature, it is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

○ (4. The Turbid Age of Sentient Beings) Furthermore, as you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing, your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in the world, while the operations of karma perpetually shift the lands.
These interwoven delusions constitute the fourth layer, known as the turbid age of sentient beings.
[Commentary] Gushan says: This turbidity relies upon the mind of fabrication within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) that is able to proceed toward its fruit;
this is called "formation" (*saṃskāra*). There are six kinds of formations. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they are described as the "six volitions" (*ṣaḍ-cetanā*). Volition is itself karma.

That is to say, following each of the six perceptions (*saṃjñā*), one respectively gives rise to unwholesome karma, wholesome karma, and immovable karma. As for "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*)...
The six volitions constitute karma; their movement shifts according to good and evil. The realms of existence are likewise mundane.
Just as one may personally long for one's hometown yet must travel to another district due to official duties, the principle of wandering through the six paths is similarly so.

That which is falsely constructed through mutual entanglement—wherein the desire of one's perceptions remains while the movement of karma constantly departs—is the falsely constructed aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). And...
The false conjunction of coming and going that muddies the true nature is called the turbidity of sentient beings.
(5) The Turbidity of Life: You all see and hear, yet fundamentally there is no difference in their nature; yet, separated by the various sensory objects, they give rise to differences without cause.

Within their nature they recognize one another, yet in their functions they turn away from one another. Agreement and disagreement lose their standard as they interweave into a delusion; this fifth layer is called life.
Turbidity.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "This turbidity depends upon the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate). That which discerns the objects of perception is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
There are six kinds of consciousness, which are the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). 'Fundamentally there is no distinct nature' means that the mind which discerns is merely..."

Because they are one. "The various dusts are separated" means that the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are distinct; because they draw forth the production of the six consciousnesses, it is said they "arise differently without cause.
"In their nature they know each other" explains that fundamentally there is no different nature. "In their function they turn away from each other" explains that they arise differently without cause.
That the eye does not distinguish sound and the ear does not distinguish form is what is meant by "turning away from each other. They are the same...

Regarding the failure of fixed standards: when one speaks of their sameness, their functions are mutually opposed; when one speaks of their difference, their natures and characteristics are known to be identical.

Thus, there is no fixed standard. Because these elements interweave, they falsely constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). When consciousness abides, life exists; when consciousness departs, life passes away. It turbidly obscures the true nature;
therefore, it is called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

[Commentary] Tiantai said: "The first turbidity (kalpa-kṣaya) is heavy in its impact on the eon; this refers to being turbid with respect to time. The second turbidity is heavy in its impact on views;
this refers to being turbid with respect to the six faculties of sensation. The third turbidity is heavy in its impact on afflictions; this refers to being turbid with respect to the six perceptions.
The fourth turbidity is heavy in its impact on sentient beings; this refers to being turbid with respect to the provisional aggregation of coming and going."
It is turbidity. The five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) primarily reside in life, meaning they are turbidified by the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) of consciousness.
Furthermore, the first turbidity takes the essence of consciousness as its basis; the other four turbidities take the various conditions from which one is born as their basis.

These "various conditions" are a broad term: from the essence of vision, the various sensations (*vedanā*) arise; from sensation comes perception (*saṃjñā*); from perception comes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and from volitional formations comes consciousness (*vijñāna*). All of these...

Because they are called the various conditions produced from names, the five turbidities do not exist externally; rather, it is the essence of the second fundamental consciousness that is able to produce these various conditions.

As for the methods for clarifying the turbidity, there are those who clarify it starting from the initial turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which refers to the matter of entering the Way by means of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
There are also those who clarify it starting from the final turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), which refers to...

This concerns the matter of those who enter the Way through the six consciousnesses. If, like the *vaidūrya* light, one enters the Way by relying on the wind, then one clarifies the turbidity of sentient beings;
as for the perception of water and the perception of fire, one thereby clarifies all afflictions.

When wondrous fragrance is subtle and perfect, and wondrous touch proclaims clarity, then the turbidity of all views is clarified. By inferring through their meanings, each corresponds to its own category.

(2) Revealing the Constant Function (in two parts: first, the correct elucidation based on the Dharma; second, the initial section on the correct demonstration of the constant cause). (2.1) First, distinguishing the false and relying on the true: Ānanda, if you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far into accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should...
One should first select the fundamental basis of birth and death, which is established upon the nature that is perfect, profound, and neither arising nor ceasing. (2.

Using the True to Understand the False) By means of this profound stillness, one reverses the illusory cycle of extinction and birth, subduing them to restore the original awakening; taking this primordial, luminous awareness—whose nature is without arising or ceasing—as the mind for the causal ground.

(2) Subsequently, one perfectly accomplishes the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition. (2) To illustrate this cultivation and realization through a metaphor: it is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel;
when it is deep and motionless, the sand and soil naturally sink, and the pure water appears before one. This is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions.

When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance. When the characteristics of clarity are pure, all things manifest without being obstructed.
All afflictions are inherently united with the pure and wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa.

[Commentary: Wēnlíng says: "Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are the six faculties of sensory reception (*ṣad-indriya*). Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa.
Birth and death are the fundamental root; the five turbidities are their karmic functions. Now, one who wishes to turn back from delusion and accord with the Truth must first..."

One should select and eliminate the deluded root of birth and death, relying instead upon the nature of non-arising and non-extinction—the perfectly tranquil and profound essence—to achieve its fruition.
It is like clarifying turbid water; one must do so within a still vessel. Wuxing said:

"To revolve the illusory mind by means of the perfectly tranquil and profound nature is precisely to cultivate the three types of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and to illumine the realms of the three truths. This subdues and severs birth and death, realizing the Unborn."

This refers to arising and ceasing. "Subduing" refers back to the causal stage, encompassing the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). Only then does the resultant stage below proceed through its partial and complete fulfillment.
The "vessel of stillness" is the mind of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Prior to faith, one is still shallow; upon entering faith, one gradually deepens.
As sand and soil naturally settle, coarse impurities fall away first. When clear water appears, the Three Truths seem to manifest. Xie Li said: "Adventitious dust is affliction..."

All sutras and treatises designate what causes affliction as the *kleśāvaraṇa* (afflictive hindrance). Tiantai identifies this as the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realm of desire and form.
All sutras and treatises designate fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) as the *jñeyāvaraṇa* (hindrance to the knowable) or the *jñānāvaraṇa* (hindrance to wisdom).

Tiantai identifies this as the views and thoughts beyond the realm of desire and form. As for the phrase "permanently severed," this is stated in terms of the general characteristics of the path from cause to fruition.
In principle, it is only through wondrous enlightenment that one is said to have attained permanent severance; hence it is called "the pure refinement of the signs of clarity.
Guishan says: "All manifestations are forms appearing according to what is perceived by the capacities of the ten realms.
Since these are all pure functions, they are said not to constitute afflictions; since these functions are themselves the essence, they are said to be entirely in accord with *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, when opening up understanding to clarify that the essence of Bodhi and Nirvana is fundamentally pure, I pointed to the fundamental brightness of your own consciousness-essence—that which is able to give rise to all conditions yet remains beyond what those conditions can exhaust—saying that this is because "natures are similar.
Now, in establishing practice, it is said: "It is not through your diligent cultivation and realization over kalpas," and "to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence."

The [concepts of] pleasure, self, purity, and covering are distant from the characteristics of practice. The intention is to take that which is near as the nature and cultivate it toward the distant fruit;
thus, there is the initial matter of determination. This is to be near while being distant, and distant while being near, thereby accords with that which is neither distant nor near.
Tiantai distinguishes this through the six stages of "being thus" (*liu ji*); the Buddha’s intent lies herein. Regarding the phrase "one should first select," it means to select away [delusions].
...and it is based on grasping. In all matters of perfect cultivation, one should first recognize what is to be discarded and what is to be grasped.
In the preceding Fundamental Gate, one merely recognized the nature of discarding and grasping; now, in this Gate of Determination, it is precisely the time for actual discarding and grasping.

For the previous text has already shown that by means of these four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), your perfectly tranquil essence is divided; thus, one part is true and one part is false, pervading the five turbidities. Now, therefore—
In this process, one first selects and discards that which is turbid—the root of birth and death—and does not employ it;

ultimately, one takes up that which is pure—the perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound nature free from arising and ceasing—and completes [the practice] with it. By means of this very profundity, one turns back against false delusion and extinguishes birth;

this is the stage of "Dry Wisdom" and the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Regarding the phrase "subduing and returning to original enlightenment," "subduing" (*fu*) and "returning" (*fu*) are distinct questions.
The preceding stages are all cultivation based on conditions; it is only upon reaching the first dwelling that it becomes true cultivation, also termed the "true cause. Therefore, it is said:

"Having attained the primordial enlightened awareness as the mind of the causal ground, one then perfectly achieves the cultivation and realization of the fruition ground. Wuxing claims that the "still vessel" refers to the mind of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
While this is generally applicable, it is not precise. One should interpret it by subsuming the general into the specific, namely:
This refers to cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the perfect clarity of the six sense faculties. It corresponds to what is stated in the following passage:

"When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through; stillness and illumination encompass empty space. Both masters' explanations—that the pure marks of clarity are singular and that all transformations manifest—are correct.
This is precisely as stated in the preceding text: "I unite the non-extinguishing and non-arising with the Tathāgatagarbha," and thus the Tathāgatagarbha...
The wondrous, sublime, and luminous enlightenment perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm; therefore, the one becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes the one—they are equal.

[Section Two: Examining the Root of Afflictions] [Part One: General Exhortation to Examine Carefully] [Sub-part One: Stating the Purpose and Properly Exhorting] Regarding the second point: You must all resolve to give rise to the Bodhicitta and generate great courage within the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
With fierce resolve, you must utterly abandon all conditioned phenomena; you should carefully examine the root of afflictions:

who created this that has issued forth and moistened rebirth since beginningless time, and who receives it? (2. Showing the necessity of careful examination) Ānanda, if you cultivate Bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know where the false roots and objects are inverted;
if you do not even know the location [of the inversion], how can you proceed?
"How does one subdue [the afflictions] and attain the stage of a Tathāgata?
[Commentary: Wuxing says, "The 'activation of karma and moistening of birth' refers here to the afflictions (*kleśa*). 'Who acts and who receives?'—this seeks out the root.
This intends to clarify that the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) act upon themselves and receive the results themselves. Tianru’s Supplement says: First...

The first meaning is that one must examine the ground upon which the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is generated; thus, it points to the karmic activity within the five turbidities as the root of birth and death—that is, the source of delusion and the cessation of arising.
It instructs one to select and revolve [the mind] so as to rely upon the perfect, profound, and tranquil nature that is neither born nor extinguished, thereby accomplishing one's practice.
The second meaning is to examine the root of afflictions, which simultaneously includes the selection of the perfect faculty (*indriya*).

This is the intended meaning. Therefore, the text below immediately identifies the six sense organs as the "thieves' emissaries" who plunder the household, establishing them as the root of afflictions.

It then follows this with the principle of the mutual interpenetration of worlds to fully reveal the quantitative dimensions of the merits of the six sense organs, definitively determining their order of superiority and inferiority to enable one to know what to select.
Once the nature free from arising and ceasing has been attained as the mind for the causal ground, [the text proceeds].
Furthermore, one must carefully examine the root of afflictions to know what is to be subdued. Then, select those with the most perfect faculties to enter deeply through a single gate.

Thus, from the purification of the six sense organs up to the cultivation and realization of the perfected stage of fruition, there is nothing that does not emerge from these two principles of determination.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: It is discussed that the activation of karma and the moistening of rebirth are precisely the afflictions (*kleśa*).

However, there is that which causes these afflictions to arise—namely, the question of "who acts and who receives. Furthermore, it is stated below: "In what place do the false roots and objects undergo perversion?
This indicates that while the fundamental source of affliction is the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), it is not the six sense faculties themselves. The subsequent passage...
The treatise states that the source of the knots is the mind; only then is it the root of afflictions. The mutual implications of the sutra text are truly not easy to discern.

(2. Properly Demonstrating Thorough Examination [divided into two parts; first, pointing to the metaphor for thorough examination]) "Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how can they know how to untie it?"

"You hear that space has been torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because space is without characteristics or form, and thus it is neither bound nor liberated. [Section Two: Correctly Examining the Dharma in Detail] [Part One: Thoroughly Indicating the Locus of Delusion] [Sub-part One:
Generally Indicating the Faults] "Thus, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six serve as the intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family's treasures.
Because of this, from time immemorial, the world of sentient beings has given rise to entanglements and fetters, such that they cannot transcend the vessel-world (the physical environment)."

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "When you observe the explanation below, you must know its context. The citation regarding the meaning of 'emptiness' means that if there were no knots to be untied, there would be no untying;
yet who is it that has no knots? The passage beginning with 'Then you' demonstrates the inversion of the false faculties and sense-objects.
The six media, such as the eyes, are the false faculties. The six robbers they attract are the false objects. From here on...
"The nature of the kalpa is inverted. Wuxing said: "The six external sense objects and the six internal consciousnesses are all induced by and conjoined with the eyes and the other faculties;
therefore, it is said that 'the six are the mediators of thieves.

Because the afflictions they give rise to harm the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said that 'one robs one's own family treasure. It is due to the afflictions arising from the six sense organs that karma is initiated and rebirth is moistened."
Thus, there are the beginningless sentient beings and worlds, and so forth. Gushan said:

"Sentient beings and their worlds constitute the primary retribution (zhengbao), while the physical environment constitutes the secondary retribution (yibao). Because one is bound by the primary retribution, one is unable to transcend the secondary retribution;
therefore, what follows explains this solely in terms of the primary retribution."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the unraveling of knots, it is essential first to see the knot. It is not enough merely to see the knot; one must see its origin.
If one does not see that which is knotted, one is discussing the very beginning of how the knot arose.

It is like saying, "One must first know from where the knot originally began before one can now properly unravel it according to that pattern. This already implicitly points to the "origin of the knot" discussed in the following text.
"It is the mind. As for the statement, "I have not heard of empty space being torn asunder by you," it is because where there is a knot, there is a form;
where there is a form, there must be an untying. If there were truly no form, what need would there be for an untying?

Therefore it is said: "Space has no form; since there is neither knot nor untying... The subsequent text points out that which was knotted, saying: "That which is your present sense-faculties... and so forth. Thus it is stated.

"Taking the six as the intermediaries for thieves to plunder one's own family treasures" refers to the first fascicle’s statement, "recognizing the thief as one's son," which points to the six discerning consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
These six consciousnesses are fundamentally thieves, not sons; that sentient beings recognize these six consciousnesses as their master is what is meant by "recognizing the thief as one's son.
Now, when it says "the six serve as intermediaries for thieves," this points to the six faculties of reception (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
That which constitutes the essence of the pure clarity within the consciousnesses of the six sense organs is, in its original state, the true son and not a thief.

However, because the Father of Original Enlightenment lacks the merit of Initial Enlightenment and fails in his governance, the child—being immature and ignorant—instead becomes a mediator for thieves and robs the family treasure himself.
The Tathāgata cites this as a metaphor, intending to instruct him with both compassion and sternness.

It causes them to reform their evils and migrate toward goodness. When the preceding three [aspects] arise in succession, the "subjective deluder" (the perceiver) is formed based upon the "objective delusion" (the perceived);
thus it is said that once the objective delusion is established, the clear principle is not understood.

Now, to clarify that the delusion resides precisely because of this, it is due to the subjective deluder that one cannot transcend the objective delusion; therefore, it is said that because sentient beings are bound by afflictions, within the vessel-world...
One cannot transcend this interval. What is meant by "entanglement"? It is that which gathers upon objects, wavering within while rushing outward, a state of confusion and agitation—this is it.
What is meant by "unable to transcend"? It is that although sentient beings have penetrating vision, they do not go beyond a mere inch;
separated by skin, they do not see the internal organs; separated by membranes, they do not see external objects—this is it. How is one liberated?
"How can one transcend the world that binds? This refers to what is stated in the following passage:

"Now, when your faculties have been completely uprooted and the inner clarity radiates light, then these superficial phenomena and the various changing appearances of the vessel-world will, like ice melting in boiling water, transform into supreme awakening as soon as you think of it.
This section correctly elucidates the method for releasing the bonds.

II. A Detailed Explanation of the Characteristics (Two parts: First, clarifying the world by means of sentient beings; Second, first, explaining the names and defining the essence; Second, first, explaining the names). Ānanda, what is meant by the "sentient-being world"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial directions. II. Defining the Essence (Two parts:

First, pointing out the characteristics and indicating the number; Second, concluding by returning to sentient beings). You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. II. Concluding by Returning to Sentient Beings: All sentient beings...
The birth-weaving of delusive appearances forms bodies within which worlds trade and shift, mutually interpenetrating. (2. Distinguishing and Determining the Transformative Layerings; Part 1:

Distinguishing the Four Interpenetrations) Although the nature of these realms may have fixed positions clearly defined throughout the ten directions, in the mundane world one only speaks of east, west, south, north, above, and below; there is no fixed position for the center, nor is there a fixed direction for the middle. (2.

The Flowing Transformation Increases the Number) The four numbers must be clearly understood as interpenetrating with the mundane world; three times four and four times three turn back upon each other to become twelve, flowing on.

Transforming the three into one, multiplied by ten, hundred, and thousand. (2. Regarding the world to traverse the six faculties; 2a. First, showing this through the laws of flux and transformation: Summarizing from beginning to end, within each of the six faculties, there are twelve hundred merits.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: The world of sentient beings also possesses the four directions; these are simply left, right, front, and back.

"World" (*loka*) refers to the successive transition of the three time-periods (*adhvan*). "Sphere" (*dhātu*) refers to each abiding in its own fixed position. There are ten such spatial positions and three temporal periods.
Because the principle inherent within a single body naturally interpenetrates one another, it is said that "the worlds within the body trade places and their spheres interpenetrate."
Although the directions of the realms are ten, their constant enumeration is four; because the three and the four interpenetrate, they are said to be "circularly winding.

Because they flow and transform through the three periods of time, there are three layers. Starting from one layer, ten times ten makes a hundred; a hundred times ten makes a thousand; and a thousand times twelve makes twelve hundred.
The six sense organs each possess [these functions]. However, this provisional reliance on worldly treatises merely provides a general outline to manifest their wondrous utility.
As for the state where the six are liberated and the one is extinguished, such that they function interchangeably in perfect illumination—how could numerical quantity reach it? Wuxing said:
"This refers to the twelve shifting and changing flows, which together constitute three layers. 'One, ten, hundred, thousand' is a general enumeration."
This is merely the method of increasing the number—namely, increasing one to ten, ten to a hundred, and so forth. Now, to clarify the three layers as they apply to the directions and the world:
first, regarding the four directions, each is discussed in terms of the three times, totaling twelve.
Second, within the eastern direction, the three times transform the one into ten, resulting in thirty; this applies likewise to the south, west, and north.
It is also like this. Thirty in each of the four directions makes one hundred and twenty.

In the third stage, thirty in the eastern direction changes ten into a hundred, making three hundred; the same applies to the other three directions. Three hundred in each of the four directions makes one thousand two hundred.
This analogy can be understood by applying it to the worldly engagement with the directions. This is indeed the Tathāgata’s...
This refers to the six sense organs of ordinary beings, where the faculties and their objects are interwoven and the worlds intersect;
from the coarse to the subtle, it proceeds through three layers to manifest its virtue.

The general meaning is to cause one to know that the seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing of the present moment involve, at every instant, the characteristics of space, time, and the coarse and subtle. This is based on the nature of the six organs' discernment.
Because they are identical, it is said that each possesses twelve hundred merits. Below, in contrast to the function of discerning the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), there are differences;

thus, the merits are entirely absent or unequal. Does this not correspond to what was stated in the preceding text: "In their nature (*svabhāva*) they know one another, but in their function (*vṛtti*) they turn away from one another"?

and within each of those wholesome actions, the ten suchnesses (*yathābhūta*) are present, forming one thousand two hundred. However...
The Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, and human sentiments diverge toward various extremes. If there were no definitive evidence, who could determine what is most correct?

Although I have provided a separate interpretation, I also do not dare to equate it with their specific doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Let future sages remain impartial and follow only that which is good. *Tianru Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes by Tianru).
It is said that "there is no fixed position for above and below" because the terms "above" and "below" refer to the upper and lower directions of the four cardinal points.

Since there is nothing else besides these that can be designated as above or below, they are said to have no fixed position. That "the center has no fixed direction" refers to the middle of the four intermediate corners (*koṇa*).
A corner is named by the intersection of two directions; since a single corner belongs to two directions, it is said that—

Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred; three hundreds make three hundred. The transformation of these numbers was not clearly explained [previously]. Now, I shall explain their formation and provide diagrams alongside the text.

Second, concerning the transformation of the three times of the eastern direction into ten: this refers to the nine worlds within a single *kṣaṇa*. As in the *Mūla-śāstra*...
The single past eon within the intermediate [period] already transforms into three eons. Each of these, in turn, forms three sets of three eons, resulting in nine eons.
Within these transformed three eons, there are the past-of-the-past, the present-of-the-past, and the future-of-the-past;
the same applies to the present and the future. By adding the original single past eon from the fundamental [structure], ten eons are formed.
"Worlds" refers to the ten worlds of past and present, beginning and end, which do not depart from the present moment of thought.

The two worlds of the present and the future are likewise each thirty worlds. The third layer consists of thirty worlds in the eastern direction; thus, by transforming ten into a hundred, it is the same for all directions.
The Buddha’s intention was likely to state that the world of sentient beings necessarily possesses spatial orientation and temporal flux in every direction.

There are worlds; in every world there are directions. Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), there are the ten directions and nine periods of time (*navadhva*). The arising and ceasing of the positions of these worlds is naturally so.
This refers to the number of merits within a single *kṣaṇa* being thus. If one considers the merits of a single thought-moment, a single instant, or a single day, how could they have any limit?
That which is called "merit" (*puṇya*)—the term "merit" (*guṇa*) refers to power and virtue.
Regarding "function": this refers to the power and function of each of the six sense organs, which vertically exhausts [the past and future] and horizontally pervades [all space].

Although the realms of mind and objects undergo transformation and the world flows through the cycles of time, there exists that which neither changes nor migrates. This is demonstrated in the first fascicle by the finger-counting and the flying-light experiments, which verify that seeing is immovable;
throughout the ten sections, the text repeatedly reveals that the nature is all-pervasive and perfect. Furthermore, it is like the following example of striking a bell.
Examining what is constant, there is nothing that is not this matter. This is the most urgent point regarding the selection of the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
Yet Jiaoguang claims it is not the sublime function of true nature;
how is this different from Lord Ye’s fondness for dragons, which caused them to flee far away when a celestial dragon looked down upon him?

The Diagram of Using the World to Engage with the Principle. (Part Two:

Establishing Superiority and Inferiority Based on Relative Merit; Section One: General Statement. Ānanda, you should further determine superiority and inferiority among these. (Section Two: Specific Analysis of the Six; First, the Eye Faculty. It is like the eye seeing darkness behind and light before.
The front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark; when looking to the left or right, two-thirds are visible. Generally speaking, the meritorious functions performed by it are incomplete;
of its three parts, one part is said to possess merit while one part lacks it. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: First, the illusory nature of the weaving [of the faculties] is revealed in order to clarify the origin of the knots of the sense-faculties.

Next, their relative superiority and inferiority are distinguished in order to clarify the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, so that one may know which to choose. Tiānrú’s Supplemental Notes say:

If one speaks in terms of three hundred *yojanas* for each direction, then combining the front with the left and right would total nine hundred; this interpretation is not tenable. One should know that...

Each of the four cardinal directions contains two hundred [parts], and each of the four corners contains one hundred. Thus, what is currently seen by the eye—namely, the front and the three sides including the left and right—already constitutes six hundred.
Adding the two corners from before, which contain two hundred, together makes eight hundred.
Since only the two hundred parts of the rear direction and the two hundred parts of the two rear corners are not seen, it is said that "two-thirds" are visible.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In discussing merit, there are two meanings: that which pertains to direction (space) and that which pertains to time.
In definitively determining superiority and inferiority, this treatise speaks only of direction and not of time. This is because time exists only after direction;
since direction is all-pervasive, it certainly does not follow the transitions of time.

(2) The Ear Faculty: Just as the ear listens all around to the ten directions without omission—moving when sounds are near or far, yet remaining still and boundless—know that the ear faculty is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits in full perfection.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Because it is able to listen all-pervasively, its function is complete. As for "moving as they do," when one follows their movement, there appear to be distances;
yet in one's own stillness, all-pervasive listening is boundless.

○ (3. The Nose Faculty): Just as the nose smells and perceives through the passage of inhalation and exhalation—where there is out-breath and in-breath, yet the intermediate junction is lacking—one should know that when one-third of the nose faculty is missing, the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "When exiting, it can grasp fragrance; when entering, it can smell fragrance. Because there is no capacity during the interval between exiting and entering, the middle intersection is missing.
Chángshuǐ says: "Exiting, entering, and the middle intersection together constitute three parts. One part consists of four hundred [units];
because the middle intersection is missing, there are only eight hundred."
○ (4. The Tongue Faculty): Just as the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its expressions have spatial dimensions while its principles are inexhaustible;
one should know that the tongue faculty is perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The objects known by mundane and supramundane wisdom can only be expressed and manifested through the tongue.
Although its function is limited, its underlying principle is inexhaustible. Gūshān says: "We take the capacity for speech and do not consider the act of tasting flavors.
If we were to take the act of tasting flavors, its efficacy would be inferior, because it involves cognition through contact."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The merit of the tongue is extremely great, for it is able to proclaim the wisdom of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "If no one speaks the Buddha-dharma, even though one possesses wisdom, one cannot realize it.

It is like the great darkness of night: without a lamp, nothing can be seen. Conversely, the commission of offenses by means of the tongue is likewise immense; these are all the capacities of the tongue.
Now, I cite this merely to demonstrate the capacity of eloquent speech; it is not to say that one who does not proclaim [the truth] lacks virtue.

Jiaoguang has simplified the distinction between the ignorant and the wise, yet he further generalizes it by saying that "the talk of the ignorant and the worldly wisdom both reach the ultimate principle.
How cluttered and redundant are such flowery words and forced sophistry!
○ (The Body Faculty): Just as the body perceives touch-consciousness when in contact with the agreeable or disagreeable, it cannot perceive separation when apart;
since the experience of "separation" is absent in one of these three aspects of the body faculty, one should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To be separated from one part and to be complete with two parts is called 'separated from one and united with both. Gūshān says:
'Separated from one and united with both' means that while in separation, it is unaware that it is missing one part;
when united, it is able to perceive what is contrary and what is compliant, and thus possesses both parts."
○ (The Sixth, the Faculty of Mind): Just as the mind silently accommodates all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—
encompassing both the holy and the ordinary without exception and reaching their very limits— one should know that the faculty of mind is complete with twelve hundred merits.
[Commentary] Zhenji said: "Because the mental consciousness arises alone and universally conditions all phenomena, it is called 'silent containment'. Gushan said:

"The merits of the six faculties explained in this sutra differ from those in the *Lotus Sutra*. Here, the intent is to reveal the awakening of the initial mind so that one may know the locus of inversion;
thus, he distinguishes the functions of the superiority and inferiority of the six faculties, with the aim of having Ānanda choose [the correct one]."
The faculty of hearing serves as the foundation for cultivation and realization. Having relied on the sutras to practice, he has already given rise to a semblance of understanding;

thus, his six faculties become pure, and their functions intermingle without fixed direction. Although his eyes possess eight hundred merits, they likewise embody the virtues of the other five faculties, and this applies even to the mental faculty (*manas*).
This is identical to what is stated in the present text: "Once one faculty returns to its source..."
The six sense organs achieve liberation.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: As for why the mind-organ alone is called "silent containment" (*mòróng*), it means that the nature of this organ inherently possesses all merits;
it is naturally so, without depending on deliberation or conceptualization. That the Tathāgata closed his room and Vimalakīrti remained silent both arose from this.

This is derived from the character "Mu" (Silence). Tiantai’s clarification that a single thought-moment inherently possesses the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—is also established by this.
Regarding all mundane and supramundane things, whether sages or ordinary beings, there is not a single phenomenon possessed that is not encompassed.
Regarding the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is not a single phenomenon possessed that is not pervaded. To cite [the source]:...
This primarily serves to manifest the preeminence of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), which encompasses all things without exception to their very limits.

"Limit" (*yā*) refers to spatial extent, while "boundary" (*jiè*) refers to temporal duration; this signifies the meaning of the eternally abiding true mind, which vertically exhausts the past and future and horizontally pervades all space.
The mental faculty is the universal, while the other faculties are the particulars; the merits of all other faculties arise from this fundamental root. (As stated in the preceding passage)
