Not yet perfected. (2. Comparing Superiority and Inferiority) If one can awaken to this root of perfect penetration and turn back that beginningless flow of fabricated karmic delusions, one will attain circulation through perfect penetration;
compared to those with imperfect roots, the difference between day and eon will be multiplied tenfold.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The flowing roots are precisely that which is wondrously profound and immovable. When they are directed outward, they flow and escape, rushing toward objects; this is called the 'flow of birth and death.
When they are turned inward, they reverse the flow and become whole and unified; this is called 'non-arising and non-ceasing. The six faculties of reception are those explained above:
if one follows the perfect [nature], they accord with the fundamental nature and are profound; if they are not perfect, they depart from it."

The natures [of the faculties] differ in depth and shallowness. Because the distance between deep and shallow is so vast, the efficacy of their progress—whether slow or swift—differs by multiples of days and kalpas.
Now, those who wish to return swiftly must select a faculty of perfect capacity.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When sentient beings delude the truth and pursue the false, the awakening of their own nature necessarily becomes obscured by delusion.
Luminous awareness and so forth are like water flowing from its source; this is called following the stream of birth and death.

Now, by reversing delusion to return to the truth, one naturally does not follow the three kinds of continuity of discrimination; this is like tracing the current back to its source, and is called reversing the stream of birth and death.
"Root" refers to the fundamental basis; as stated in the preceding text, "the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous, and original awareness is luminously wondrous."

It is so. Although it is called the "root-source" (*gen-ti*), it has never been apart from the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Therefore, one is led to examine these six faculties of reception (*ṣaḍ-upabhoga-indriya*):

which accords with this nature and is profound, and which departs from this nature and is shallow. Regarding the two characters "accordance" (*he*) and "departure" (*li*), what was said by Wenling is correct;
there is no need to employ Jiaguang’s theory of "knowing within departure" (*li-zhong-zhi*) and "knowing within accordance" (*he-zhong-zhi*). This is because...

In this context, although the discussion is based on the faculties (*indriya*), it primarily clarifies whether the nature of the faculties is complete or incomplete; it does not speak of the faculties' function being separate or joined.
To unite with their nature and penetrate deeply is what constitutes attaining the "following of the perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*);

then every step is the path back home. It is like obtaining supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) and returning to one's hometown—the destination can be reached in days. To be separated from their nature...
Superficiality constitutes a failure to attain perfection. It is like setting out for Yan with a southern-facing carriage;
though one may ride a fine horse, one cannot avoid being delayed by years and months. That days and kalpas increase exponentially is no exaggeration.
Therefore, among those who study the Way, nothing is more precious than selecting the proper faculty, realizing one's nature, and practicing accordingly.
○ (Third, granting permission to provide illumination: "I shall now fully manifest the six profound, perfect, and luminous fundamental merits in their exact measure.

According to what you have carefully examined and chosen as being suitable for entry, I shall provide illumination so that you may advance. ○ (Second, explaining the reason why discernment is necessary:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cultivated each of the eighteen realms one by one, and all attained the perfection of unsurpassed Bodhi; yet, in the midst of this, there was also no..."
"Your inferiority lies simply in this: you have not yet attained the perfected wisdom of mastery therein.
Therefore, I shall proclaim it so that you may enter deeply through a single gate; once you have entered one gate without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once."

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The six sense-faculties are profoundly still, perfectly luminous," and so forth; this indicates that the delusory clarity and meritorious functions of the six faculties are entirely the true luminosity inherent in one's original nature.
Because it is inherently real, it is therefore delusorily present. Wenglung says:

"If one attains the wisdom of perfect mastery, then the eighteen realms are none other than perfect penetration. However, those of inferior capacity and initial stage are not yet able to attain this perfection.
Furthermore, enter through a single gate; if one faculty is free from delusion, then all six will be pure.
Not only will you awaken to the eighteen realms, but every particle of dust and every world-system will be perfectly penetrating.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, regarding the enumeration of one thousand two hundred and eighty [faculties] based on the six sense organs, it was explained that these are all the inherent merits of the six profound, perfect, and luminous [faculties], without the slightest increase or decrease. Because there is no merit achieved through cultivation, this measure remains somewhat limited.
Accordingly, you may choose whichever among them is accessible as the "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*); the World-Honored One has permitted me to further elucidate this for you.

Relying upon this, one practices, increases, and advances it. What is stated below—that "in this way, as hearing gradually increases, that which was heard is exhausted"—refers precisely to this matter.
The original merit possessed by the faculties is limited; however, as they are increased and advanced, they transcend measure.
Even the merit of the six sense organs in the *Lotus Sūtra*, though pure and characterized by mutual functioning, still possesses limits. If birth and death are extinguished and quiescence...
When cessation manifests before one, it is immeasurable. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cultivate within the eighteen realms;
they have all perfected the path of awakening without any distinction of superiority or inferiority. This is spoken with reference to those of the most supreme vehicle’s faculties.
Since there is nothing that is not the Way, it is unnecessary to select specific faculties. Since it is said "the ten directions," the Sahā world is also included therein. Therefore:
One who knows that their chosen faculties are entirely inferior will find even the various fragrances and celestial robes of other realms to be inferior as well.
For one whose faculties are not inferior, there is nowhere that is unsuitable. Those ancients of this land who entered the Way each had their own gate:
such as the direct pointing to the human mind of Bodhidharma and the exclusive contemplation of the six realms of existence by Tiantai.

Consciousness does not necessarily depend solely upon the faculty of hearing. One must understand that the six consciousnesses of the human mind constitute the "general" (the whole), while the other faculties and their respective objects constitute the "particulars" (the parts).
One may observe the particulars through the general, or observe the general by means of the particulars;

when these are perfectly integrated, they all return to a single source where there has never been two paths. This can be explained to those entering the gate, but it is difficult to discourse upon with those who compete on the road.
Indeed, this is so. Nevertheless, for those of initial capacity who have not yet attained perfect and sovereign wisdom, it is impossible not to exercise selection.

Regarding the method of such selection, if one speaks in terms of the "sentient" and the "insentient," the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are insentient and thus inferior, while the sense-faculties and consciousnesses (*indriya-vijñāna*) are sentient and thus superior.
If one speaks in terms of the sense-faculties and consciousnesses themselves, then consciousness falls into conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

The faculties are inferior; those without discrimination are superior. Speaking in terms of the six faculties, those where five are complete and one is not are inferior, while those where the ear faculty is complete are superior.
The teachings also state that when a beginner enters the Path, how could they possibly observe everything?

Therefore, among the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) are excluded. Furthermore, within the five aggregates (*skandha*), the preceding ones are also eliminated.
The fourth [stage] takes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as its object of contemplation. It is like moving from the *zhang* to the *chi*, and from the *chi* to the *cun*;
it is like felling a tree by reaching its root or treating an ailment by finding its source. Thus, thousands of branches and hundreds of maladies naturally dissolve away.
This, moreover, is the great point of convergence where the Buddhas and Patriarchs administer medicine according to the disease; there is no seeking for harmony, yet nothing fails to harmonize.

[2. Extensive Explanation Based on Doubt (divided into two; first, the request arising from doubt): Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and penetrating deeply into a single gate, one can cause all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?

[2. Extensive Demonstration (divided into two; first, the general demonstration by means of analysis and refutation, divided into three; first, the Dharma-method; first, clarifying the identity of the one and the six by means of persons): The Buddha told Ānanda:

“You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and have already extinguished the delusions abandoned through insight regarding the world of sentient beings within the triple realm; yet you still do not know that within the faculties there has been an accumulation of births since beginningless time.”

If even the cultivation of those cultivations must be attained through the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how much more so the distinctions of arising, abiding, change, and cessation, as well as their specific divisions and enumerations?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The profound and perfect [nature] is differentiated due to delusion; the one and the six arise because of delusion. This is about to be explained.

Regarding the meaning of these six [aspects], they are first distinguished from delusions. Gushan says: "The delusions severed by the vision of the Truths (darśana-heya) are the eighty-eight proclivities (anuśaya);
the delusions severed by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are the eighty-one volitions (cetanā). Birth, abiding, change, and extinction are the ignorance of the same essence (sahaja-avidyā).
As for the numerical divisions and categories, this refers to the stages from the First Abode (prathamabhūmi) up to the Sublime [Bodhisattva Grounds]."
"Awakening" refers to the forty-two stages. "Vague practice" (xū xí) is synonymous with deluded confusion (*moha*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding Mount Gushan’s statement that birth, abiding, change, and extinction are identical to the *amala* (ignorance of the same essence), if one examines their distinctions, it should follow the explanation in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Ordinary beings at the stage of the ten faiths awaken to the characteristic of extinction; those of the three stages of worthiness awaken to...

The characteristic of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The characteristic of abiding in the awakening of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-bodhi-sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). The characteristic of the arising of awakening when the stages are fulfilled (*bhūmi-paripūraṇa-bodhy-utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).

If one follows the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-kūṭa-sūtra* (Renwang jing) in clarifying the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*), one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), and realizes the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*) at wondrous awakening (*miao-jue*).

Thus, the characteristic of arising comes before and the characteristic of cessation comes after. Furthermore, as it says regarding Avalokiteśvara: "Since both arising and cessation have been extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one. Here too, the characteristic of cessation is [present].
Furthermore, the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are difficult to discern; thus, I dare not force a correspondence.

If one discusses the general meaning, however, arising, abiding, change, and cessation are fully present within a single momentary mind (*kṣaṇacitta*). Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "That which arises is immediately subject to cessation;
this is not taught for the sake of the foolish. This indicates that the subtle aspects of arising and cessation are so difficult to clarify. Students should simply understand this.
This is merely a general outline.
○ (2. Regarding Principle: Refuting the One and Six; First, the Inquiry) Now, you should observe these six faculties before you: are they one, or are they six? ○ (2. Refuting [the False];

First, Refuting the One) Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see, why does the eye not hear, why does the head not tread, and why do the feet not speak? ○ (Second, Refuting the Six) If these six...
The faculties are determined to be six, as I have now proclaimed this subtle and wonderful Dharma-door to you in this assembly.
Among your six faculties, which one comes to receive it? Ānanda said, "I hear it with my ears. The Buddha said, "Your ears hear it themselves; what concern is this for the body or the mouth?

It is the mouth that comes to inquire about the meaning, and the body that arises to show reverence. (3. Explaining the Refutation of Objections) Therefore, you should know that they are not merely one, yet they ultimately number six. They are not...

Six ends and one end are not the root of your faculties; one source and six manifestations are not the origin. (3. The Three Bonds) Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six.
Because of the inverted and fluctuating delusions since beginningless time, the meanings of "one" and "six" have arisen within the perfectly湛 (zhan—tranquil and profound) reality. (3.
Chiding the Person for Not Yet Forgetting One) You, O Srotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six, have not yet forgotten the one.
[Commentary] Gushan says: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states, "The Srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered;
they do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is the dissolution of the six [sense objects].
Yet, they have not yet eliminated the "one," which is the attachment to the existence of *nirvāṇa*. This is because that which is realized by the Hīnayāna is entirely ignorance. Zizhong says: No...

New karma created due to the six sense-objects is called "attaining the six dissolutions. Yet, because one is still deluded regarding the six faculties as being a single entity, that "one" has not yet perished.
Master Wu-xing said: "The meaning of 'single entity' as explained by Master Yun differs from that in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."

It is simply that one point has not yet been clarified. One should know that from the "essence of seeing" down to the "essence of knowing" mentioned in the following text, they are fundamentally one body.

Because of the notions of identity and difference, one gives rise to attachments of identity and difference regarding the six sense faculties. Since these attachments and practices are entirely delusions regarding the principle, it is asked:
"How can one flow against the current and enter deeply through a single gate, thereby enabling all six sense faculties to become pure at once?
The intent is that the six sense faculties form knots; one must necessarily untie them one by one in succession before liberation can be attained. How then [can they be purified simultaneously]...?
"By entering one gate, do all other faculties likewise attain purification? In the passage below, the World-Honored One answers entirely from the standpoint of principle (*li*).

This is because when principle is clarified, doubts regarding practice (*xing*) naturally dissipate; thus, answering through principle is in fact answering through practice. This section contains the thesis (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).

Within the thesis: first, he uses a person to clarify the distinction between "one" and "six"; second, he shows that according to principle there is neither "one" nor "six"; third, he rebukes the person.

First, you have not yet forgotten [the teachings]. You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and have extinguished the delusions of sentient beings within the three realms that are abandoned through insight.
Indeed, one who is called a Srotāpanna is "one who has entered the stream," yet does not enter into form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.
The statement "this has already been forgotten" refers to six. However, it is still not known what the specific measure or number of these departures is;

this clarifies that one has not yet been forgotten. Second, regarding the principle that there is neither one nor six among them: first, "Now you... interrogates; next, "Ānanda... refutes the notion of one; then, "If this...
refutes the notion of six; finally, "Therefore... concludes that they are neither one nor six. "Ānanda... below explains the shifting of the difficulty.
An objection is raised: "If, in principle, there is neither 'one' nor 'six,' why is it that sentient beings perceive six while I perceive one?

Therefore, it is explained: "Due to the sinking and shifting caused by beginningless inversion, the conceptual meanings of 'one' and 'six' arise within the perfect and profound stillness. Next, in the analogy:
"Just as when the great void of space is joined with various vessels, the space is designated as different based on the differing forms of the vessels. This is the metaphor.
The "one" refers to the arising of the six [sense-faculties]. Excluding the vessel-world and contemplating emptiness, one speaks of emptiness as being "one.

This is a metaphor for how a *srotāpanna*, although having attained the dissolution of the six, has not yet forgotten the "one. As for that great empty space, how could it be removed by you? This is a metaphor for the principle that there is neither "one" nor "six.
Thus, your understanding of the six faculties of reception is also like this; the correspondence with the teaching can be understood accordingly.
From this we know that, in principle, there is fundamentally neither one nor six. One and six arise from delusion;
thus, their arising begins with "one" originating from the non-existence of principle. What is this "one"?

It is birth, abiding, change, and cessation within the faculties, as well as the accumulated arising of empty habits. From this "one," the "six" arise—the six sense-faculties. Therefore, regarding their cessation...
One must likewise return from the six to the one, and from the one to the non-existence of principle.
Precisely because it proceeds from the one to the six, once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.

For while they are distinct when situated within the six, they are identical when situated within the one. Since beings were formerly situated within the six, the sentient person’s attachments could not help but arise.
This is called "difference. Now, because one returns to oneness through a single faculty, the Dharma of the Srotāpanna—wherein attachment remains unavoidable—is called "sameness.
If both the dual attachments to self and dharmas are forgotten, then oneness and sixfoldness, as well as sameness and difference, all vanish.
Therefore it is said: "Now you should enter deeply through a single gate; once you have entered oneness, there is no delusion, and those six faculties of cognition [will likewise be resolved]."
At one time, there was purity; yet, the single word "still" (*you*) has not been forgotten. Its doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are threefold:
namely, the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna, fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), and the numerical phenomena of the world (*lokasaṃkhyādharma*).

Masters of both ancient and modern times have never reached a profound understanding of these, but instead vied with one another in their various attachments. Thus, it is necessary to offer this one clarification. Master Gushan said: "Still..."
The first thing not yet forgotten is the clinging to the existence of *nirvāṇa*.

Since that which is realized by the Hīnayāna is entirely nothing but ignorance, this constitutes a failure to fully comprehend the numerical categories of phenomena, as it simultaneously possesses both [the notions of] duality and existence. Master Zizhong said:

"When new karma created through the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) is no longer produced, it is called 'the extinction of the six'; yet one still remains deluded regarding the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) as being a single entity."
The first [point] remains unextinguished. This refers to one who has grasped the various phenomena (*dharmas*) but has lost the essential substance (*dharmatā*) of the One.

As for Wu-xing, he takes the side of Gu-shan, saying: "Master Yuan’s interpretation of the 'One Substance' differs from that of *Nirvāṇa*; it is simply that the meaning of 'One' has not been clarified.
One should know that in the subsequent text, from the "essence of seeing" (*jian-jing*) down to the "essence of knowing" (*zhi-jing*), these are fundamentally the One Substance.
Thus, the Master of Wuxing not only failed to understand the principle of numerical categories, but moreover clung to these numerical categories without letting go.
Therefore, I offer this judgment: the interpretation of the meaning by the Master of Gushan is harmonious, while the interpretation of the names by the Master of Zizhong is correct.
I, however, shall emulate the fisherman by taking both [methods] together to benefit [the practitioner], saying: "One and six are the numbers of the world;

The six [defilements] are names that cannot be confused with one another; when the six functions of a *srotāpanna* cease to operate, the number "six" vanishes along with the substance of the dharmas.

Viewed in this light, is it not the case that the principle of Mount Gu is consistent? This is how I have studied it.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Space is fundamentally neither identical nor different; this is a metaphor for how the perfect stillness is fundamentally neither one nor six.

Combining vessels and removing vessels is a metaphor for the origin of the conceptualization of 'one' and 'six. To know the identity, difference, and right or wrong of space is to understand [the nature of the faculties]."
When there is nothing established, both "one" and "six" vanish together, and the perfect clarity remains undivided.

Since "one" and "six" no longer exist, yet the six sense-faculties appear to exist, this is because the deluded manifestation arises from clinging to that perfect clarity. Therefore, the following section traces the source of this deluded manifestation to demonstrate it.
Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state: Previously, Ānanda had not yet understood the entry into the one and the purification of the six.
Thus it was said. Therefore, when the Buddha wished to grant the beginning of illumination, he first clarified the delusions;

that is to say, because their accumulated habits from countless lifetimes had not yet been cultivated or severed, it was only natural that they did not yet understand the teaching of "one entry into the six purities.

Next, he used the "one" and the "six" to challenge them, so that they might know there is no fixed destination for either. He then directly showed them, saying: "You should know that these faculties are neither one nor [many]."
Sixth: Due to inversion, the meanings of "one" and "six" arise. In the current text, the analogy of the vast empty space illustrates how the meanings of "one" and "six" arise.

II. A Detailed Exposition of the Distinctive Characteristics of the Evolving Phenomena (divided into two parts; first, clarifying how delusion arises from the True, with six sections on the partiality of the six functions; first, the specific exposition of the cause of their arising; first, the eye-faculty): Due to the mutual contrast between light and darkness and other such dualities, within the wondrously perfect [nature], the stillness (*rasa*) becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision.

The essence of vision reflects forms, and by binding to these forms, the faculty is formed. The root-source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements"; its substance is named the "eye-body," which resembles a cluster of grapes.
This "floating root" [is composed of] the four sense-objects and flows outward in wild abandon, rushing toward forms.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The manifestation of the limpid clarity (*zhan*) through adhesion arises from the pure nature being stirred by defilements such as light and darkness.
The other cases are all treated accordingly. Xielü says: "The essence of seeing (*jian-jing*) that reflects objects refers to the *indriya* (faculty) of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

Although it takes the eight dharmas—both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived elements (*bhautika*)—as its substance, it is an invisible and resistant form (*rūpa*) that can illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness."
This is the realm known by the sages; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, unlike the coarse and shallow realms of sensory dust, and is therefore called "pure.
This is purity spoken of within the context of defilement, not the purity of untainted, wondrous luminosity.

It is called the "eye-substance" because it is the lower, ephemeral physical organ (*sāsrava-indriya*). It is also called the "conventional organ" (*saṃvṛti-indriya*), as it is coarse, shallow, and easily known; thus, it is contrasted with what precedes it.

The establishment of names likewise takes the eight dharmas—both the subjective and the objective—as its substance. What is now called the "four gross elements" (catur-mahābhūta) refers only to the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).

Question: The gross elements merely serve as the locus for the primary sense-faculties (paramārtha-indriya); they cannot themselves illuminate objects or give rise to consciousness. Why, then, is it said that they "rush out in pursuit of form"?
Answer: In principle, this refers to the primary sense-faculties; however, the gross elements are their locus. Here, the locus is being cited [to represent what is supported by it].
This clarifies the basis upon which [the faculties] depend. Furthermore, there is no error in interpreting this in conjunction with the aforementioned pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The "producers" (*bhūta*) are the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; the "produced" (*bhautika*) are the four objects—form, odor, taste, and touch.
The remaining five [faculties] follow this same principle.
○ (2) The Ear Faculty: Due to the mutual striking of the two conditions of movement and stillness within the wondrously perfect [nature], the clarity is adhered to and hearing is produced.
The essence of hearing reflects sound; by coiling back the sound, it forms the faculty. The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements. Its substance is like a newly rolled leaf;

as a floating faculty among the four objects, it flows and escapes, rushing toward sound. ○ (3) The Nose Faculty: Due to the two conditions of openness and obstruction, [the faculty] is activated within the wondrously perfect [nature].
Within the sphere of the circle, the clarity adheres to stillness, giving rise to the faculty of smelling; its essence reflects fragrance and assimilates it to form the sense organ.

The root of this organ is designated as the "pure cause of the four great elements," and its substance is named the nose, resembling two hanging claws. This peripheral organ flows out toward the four objects, rushing toward fragrances. (4) The Tongue Faculty:

Through the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and transformation, within the wondrously perfect state, the clarity adheres to stillness, giving rise to the faculty of tasting; its essence reflects flavors and gathers them in.
Taste forms the faculty; its source is designated as the pure four great elements, and its substance is named the tongue.

Like a crescent moon at dawn, this floating faculty flows and roams, rushing toward flavors. (5) The Body Faculty: Through the two modes of separation and union, it rubs against objects within the wondrously perfect state, adhering to the profound stillness to give rise to sensation.
The essence of sensation reflects contact, and by grasping that contact, the faculty is formed. Its source is designated as the pure four great elements.
Therefore, its physical form is like that of a waist-drum; the floating faculties and the four sensory objects rush toward contact. (6.

The Mental Faculty) Due to the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—it adheres within the wondrous perfection to give rise to cognition from the profound stillness. This essence of cognition reflects phenomena and grasps them to form the faculty.

The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements"; therefore, it is called the mental faculty (*manas*), like seeing within a dark chamber. The floating faculties and the four sensory objects... [as above].
"Dust flows and rushes toward phenomena.
[Commentary: Gushan says that "adhering to the profound stillness to give rise to cognition" refers to deluded deliberative cognition (*vitarka-vijñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the root-source," this takes the physical heart-mind (*māṃsa-hṛdaya*) as the locus upon which deliberative cognition relies. Therefore, the ultimate sense-faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*) is still the fourfold pure [element].

It is vast. Just as in a dark chamber, that which is seen is the physical sense organ (*bu chen gen*) serving as the locus for the mental faculty (*yi si*); it is like being situated within a dark chamber.
As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says: "It is like the opening and closing of a lotus flower."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This sutra clarifies the manner in which the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise in four places.
First, it says: "The mixture of form and deluded thought; taking these appearances as a body. Second, it says: "From the two objects of light and darkness, the faculty of seeing arises in the center;
absorbing these objective images is called the nature of seeing. These [first two] are still brief and not yet extensive; they merely serve as a foundation for the latter two.
The first point is the initial manifestation. The third is clarifying that it is not another who is at fault, but rather that the delusion arises from the luminous awareness;
once this delusion is established, the principle of luminosity does not exceed it. By this, one can trace its origin.

The fourth is that luminosity and darkness, etc., are mutually defined by their two-fold contrast. By this, one can grasp its conclusion. To clarify these together is to understand the matters of beginning and end.
This is manifested. Thus, because the two aspects of light and darkness are mutually defined, that which is falsely established arises;

within the wondrous perfection, the stillness is adhered to and vision is emitted, such that the principle of clarity is not exceeded. As for the phrase "the essence of vision reflecting color," this was not yet fully explained in the preceding text.
The character for "adhere" (黏) should be written with the radical for "grain" (黍) and the phonetic "occupy" (占); those with the radical for "grain" (米) are vulgar. If we take it as a metaphor:

It is said that just as sticky resin clings to an object once it has made contact, so too at the moment of initial conception, the nature of clarity and turbidity—the two sensory objects—clings to the perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound nature within awareness, thereby forming the "seeing-essence" (*jīng*). Once the sense organs have formed, there is no time when one is not being adhered to by the sensory objects of form.
Therefore, this character "adhere" (*nián*) is the central theme of this entire section; it contrasts with the "detach" (*tuō*) that follows.
The clinging within and the latent [nature] mutually reflect one another. Since form already clings to seeing, they respond to and penetrate each other;

thus, the essence of seeing also reflects form. This "reflecting" is like a mirror’s discernment of objects. The essence of seeing is the eighth consciousness's *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-division), while form is the eighth consciousness's *nimitta-bhāga* (image-division).
Because of the capacity to see, the objective realm falsely manifests; because of the interweaving of these images, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is formed.
The subsequent examples follow this pattern. Designating the fundamental source as the "pure four great elements" clarifies that these are the primary sense organs (*indriya*).

These consist of the four great elements as the creators and the four objects (*viṣaya*) as the created. Now, when only the "four great elements" are mentioned, it means that form, odor, taste, and touch have no inherent nature of their own;
they take earth, water, fire, and wind entirely as their substance. By mentioning only the "creators," the created objects are implicitly included.

It obtains that which is produced. The same applies to the four objects of the lower floating-root. That which is called "pure" (viśuddha) refers to the most refined substance among the eight elements;
thus it is termed "pure. This is what is meant by speaking of purity within defilement. Consequently, the substance of the eye is said to be like a cluster of grapes;
thus it extends upward to the ultimate sense (paramārtha) and downward to the floating dust-sense. For the ultimate sense is like the form itself.
"Floating dust is like a shadow. There is no shadow that does not resemble a form; because the scriptural text is concise, this phrase serves to connect the preceding with the following.
Master Wuxing, however, interprets it as the "floating-dust sense-faculties" (*rūpa-prasāda-indriya*).

How could it be that in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) the fruit lacks its own form? Therefore, Master Yunjian, relying on the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, offers this clarification: "The eye-faculty is..."
The atoms of the visual faculty reside upon the pupil; because their substance is transparent, they are like an autumnal spring or pond.
The atoms of the auditory faculty reside within the cavity of the ear, arranged in a spiral, like the rolled-up bark of a birch tree.

Furthermore, the *Purāṇa-vaibhāṣika-śāstra* states that the atoms of the gustatory faculty reside in the center of the tongue, shaped like a half-moon. The atoms of the olfactory faculty reside on the back of the bridge of the nose within the nasal cavity.

What was previously stated—that the two phases of waking and sleeping correspond to the opening and closing of the body—is also intended in this sense. If one were to define it by way of its functional characteristics, such is the formulation established in the sūtra text.
Each has its own specific significance. For example, the ear is like a newly curled leaf, yet it is specifically called "curled" (*juǎn*);

This is precisely because the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) of the eye-faculty revolve in a sphere, pure and bright like crystal grapes, and reflect and illuminate objects like an autumnal spring-pool. It is thus.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "That awakened clarity" refers to true clarity; "there being clarity within clarity" refers to delusive clarity.
Because one is deluded regarding that true clarity, it is said "one loses that essential lucidity. Because this delusive clarity is established, it is said "adhering to delusion, light is emitted."
Wenling says: "Therefore, because the preceding [passage] explains that they arise from delusion, all six are false and illusory;
if separated from the six sense-objects, they have no self-substance whatsoever.

[Commentary: Tiantai says: The previous section, which specifically demonstrated the causes for their arising, is now complete. This section concludes the discussion on their partiality and limitation.
The manifested aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is twofold. First, it clarifies that the aspect exists because of sense objects; second, it clarifies that apart from sense objects, it has no substance.

"Because that cognitive clarity possesses clarity, there is clarity-awareness" describes its beginning. "Losing that essential lucidity, it adheres to the delusive and emits light" describes its formation.

The former spoke of adhering to stillness (*zhan*), while the present speaks of adhering to delusion (*wang*). This is because so-called solitary truth cannot be established, and a solitary delusion cannot be formed.
The term "light" (*ābhāsa*) generally encompasses all six sense faculties. That which arises by adhering to form and adhering to stillness is the faculty of seeing.

Because its cause of arising depends upon sensory objects (*viṣaya*), its manifest function lacks any intrinsic substance when separated from those objects. Thus, the eye's seeing exists because of form and lacks substance apart from form;
the ear's hearing exists because of sound and lacks substance apart from sound; and this applies even to the mental faculty (*manas*).

This is what the proverb means: "The life of one who has fallen lies in his staff; lose the staff and he falls. [II. Clarifying the Mutual Functioning of the Six Faculties upon Returning from Delusion to Truth] [A.

Clarifying that Perfect Cultivation Does Not Depend on External Objects to Arise Knowledge and Vision] "You need only not follow these twelve conditioned characteristics: movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and agitation, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness.

[B. Clarifying that Perfect Realization Does Not Depend on the Sense Organs to Attain Mutual Functioning] [A. Clarifying that through Cultivation One Attains Realization] "By following and severing even one faculty, you detach from its clinging and turn inward to rest. Resting in the fundamental truth, the source is revealed."

The luminous brilliance of the nature of illumination reveals all other five attachments; they should be uprooted for perfect liberation. (2. Explaining how function arises from realization. Part One: Citing the mutual functioning of the faculties to illustrate and reveal. Part One: Citing the mutual functioning of the six faculties.

Because the cognition and vision arising from external objects do not follow the sense organs, but rather the clarity issues forth by relying on the organs, the six faculties thus serve as functions for one another.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To be 'stuck' to delusion means to follow the sense objects and trace back through the faculties; thus, obstructions are formed.
To 'detach' from being stuck means not to follow [objects] and not to trace [back], but merely to rely upon the faculties; thus, they can be used interchangeably. Wŭxīng says:
"By relying on the two kinds of faculties, the enlightened clarity is developed; therefore, each of the twelve hundred merits of the faculties can be used interchangeably. Gūshān says:
There are both the true and the semblance; the semblance is like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, while the true is like the *Avataṃsaka*.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Second, regarding the return from delusion to truth within the section on the "mutual functioning of the six sense organs," the passage beginning with "If you simply do not follow...
clarifies that perfect cultivation does not arise through the objects of the external environment to produce cognition and vision. It proceeds by uprooting one sense organ...
Thus, one perfectly realizes the mutual functioning [of the sense faculties] without following after the sense organs. Previously, one followed what is habitual and thereby lost true constancy;
now, by not following what is habitual, one attains true constancy. As for the statement that "by pulling out a single root, the stickiness is subdued within," it means:

Previously, we explained that the nature [of the faculties] becomes defiled by attachment to objects (*viṣaya*), thereby forming the sense organs (*indriya*). Thus, the organs become bound to the objects and remain eternally fixed.
Now, in reversing delusion and returning to the Truth, one does not follow after objects nor employ the organs. Not employing the organs is called "uprooting the roots.
Once the roots are uprooted, their sticky attachment is also shed. Since one no longer conditions objects and no longer employs the organs, one merely subdues them within.
It is simply primordial truth (*yuanzhen*). Once primordial truth is once again settled, fundamental luminosity manifests.
All other five "sticky" faculties are uprooted simultaneously as they are encountered, and all defilements are completely liberated. Neither before nor after, they are attained all at once.
The efficacy and swiftness of this process are such as this. From now on, one shall no longer follow after external objects.
"By giving rise to knowledge and vision. This sentence correctly concludes the previous answer to the question, "How is it that by entering one gate, all six gates are simultaneously purified?

Its function is identical to the four subsequent sections on Avalokiteśvara’s cultivation and realization, such as the disappearance of external objects, and it is also a major pivotal point of the entire treatise.
Why is this? For what is expounded throughout the entire work does not go beyond the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*). Now...
"Uprooting the roots" is the perfect cultivation of Prajñā; "shedding attachments" is the wondrous function of Liberation; and "original truth" is the fundamental essence of the Dharmakāya.
When one uproots, perfects, and sheds, the Way that is neither vertical nor horizontal is manifested.
There is no essential point for the practice of cultivation more important than this. May readers and listeners not fail to follow it. From "Not depending on the sensory objects... [downward].
The six concluding statements regarding the mutual functioning of the six sense organs are also words used to resolve a difficulty. The objector asks:

"If cognitive perception does not arise by means of the external objects before one, then there would be no six sense organs. How could one, upon attaining Buddhahood, merely realize a vague and undifferentiated True Suchness?
Furthermore, all World-Honored Ones possess the six sense organs; how could they ever fail to give rise to cognitive perception? Therefore...
The commentary explains: "Clarity does not follow the sense organs; it relies upon the sense organs to manifest.

If clarity did not follow the sense organs, then cognition and vision would not arise based on external objects (*viṣaya*). If it relies upon the sense organs to manifest, then it is not that the Sage lacks the six sense organs.
It is precisely because of this that the six sense organs function interchangeably for one another. For if clarity were to follow the sense organs, then the organs themselves would become the master.

I am a servant. When I follow the commands of my master, I am weary while the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are at ease. Because I am weary, I can focus on one thing but cannot attend to many; I am present there but not here.
When the sense-faculties are entrusted with clarity and manifestation, I become the master and the faculties become servants.
Again, when the servants follow the master’s commands, I am at ease while the faculties are weary. Because I am at ease, I can both focus on one thing and attend to many. Thus it is.
The many are identical with the one; that which is there is identical with what is here, and what is here is identical with what is there. Therefore it is said:
"By this, the six sense faculties function as one another."
○ (2. General Manifestation for Ordinary and Lesser Beings) Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees without eyes;
the Naga Baddhālana hears without ears; the goddess of the Ganges smells fragrances without a nose; Gavāmpati knows tastes with a different tongue;
and the Śūnyatā-deva perceives touch without a body—all of whom have been made to appear momentarily by being reflected within the light of the Tathāgata. Since...
For those of a windy temperament whose bodies fundamentally lack the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation, such as the śrāvakas who have attained tranquility,
within this assembly Mahākāśyapa has long since extinguished his mental faculty, yet he possesses a perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation.

the Dragon King Bhadrapāla has no ears yet can hear; the deity of the Ganges has no nose yet perceives fragrances; and because Gavāmpati received the retribution of a cowherd’s pipe, he is said to have "extraordinary tongues.
Śunyatā is the deity who presides over space; its substance is like wind, yet it is capable of perception.
Regarding "contact": when one cultivates the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and attains emptiness and stillness, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is extinguished.
Yet, as with Mahākāśyapa, although his mental faculty was extinguished, he was still able to perceive. Guishan says that *Gaṅgā* is a name for a river;
here it is translated as "Coming from Heaven," because it flows forth from Lake Anavatapta at the summit of the Snow Mountains. [The text mentions] the six persons such as Nanda and the others, or...

These are the karmic retributions of ordinary beings, or what is attained through the cultivation of those of lesser sanctity; these are all powers of delusion that do not even rely upon the sense organs.
How much less so for one who has attained perfect liberation—how could such a person lack the mutual functioning of the faculties?

[II. Explaining the reason for mutual functioning (2): First, explaining that reversing delusion is itself true permanence. Ānanda, if your various faculties were now to be completely uprooted, so that they shine forth with inner clarity and radiance, then these ephemeral phenomena and the vessel-world of all changing appearances would—like ice melting in boiling water—transform into supreme awareness at the very thought of it.

(2. Explaining Doubts to Reveal the True and Constant) Because seeing depends on light, darkness results in the absence of seeing; yet when light does not arise, seeing manifests of itself. Thus, various dark forms can never obscure it.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: True wisdom is like boiling water; delusory objects are like [cold] water. To realize that delusion is itself truth is to transform it into enlightened awareness (*jñāna*).

"Pointing" refers to the person with eyes closed. "Tracing the body" means following around another's body.

The phrase "ultimately seeing the pointing below" refers to delusion. It is not... [text ends]

This is because the sense organs, the body, and the physical world are originally the wondrous, perfect true mind. From beginningless time, due to...

it is like water turning into ice—though not inherently obstructive, it becomes obstructive. Now, as the various faculties are perfectly uprooted and their inner luminosity shines forth, it is like hot water melting ice, yet the ice returns to become ice again.

Therefore it is said: "In response to thought, it is transformed and manifested. The passage beginning with "As those worldly people" below uses inferior analogies to demonstrate mutual functioning.

Regarding the characteristics of their mutual interaction, I shall explain them: "Conditioned by seeing, it depends on light and darkness to constitute non-seeing.

This means that when it previously clung to and issued forth from light, it could see when there was light but could not see when there was darkness. When it detaches from its clinging and recedes inwardly, it brings forth the radiance of its fundamental clarity;
thus, even without light, it manifests spontaneously, and darkness cannot obscure it. The realm of sentient beings arises from the dusts of the external world triggering cognition.

II. Resolving and Clarifying Doubts and Obstructions (in two parts): A. Explaining that Cause and Effect are Both Constant to Resolve the First Meaning (in two parts): 1. Ānanda’s Doubt Regarding the Discrepancy between Cause and Effect (in two parts): a. Confirming the Buddha’s Words: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, if one seeks the permanently abiding state through the awakened mind at the causal stage, it must correspond in name and designation with the resultant stage. b. Narrating His Own Doubt Regarding the Discrepancy (in two parts): i. Generally Explaining the Asymmetry between Cause and Effect (in two parts): A. Explaining the Permanence of the Resultant Stage: “World-Honored One, within the resultant stage, there are these seven designations:

That is to say, although its distinct, pure, and perfect essence is as firm and solid as a diamond-king, eternally abiding and indestructible.

(2. Explaining that the cause is impermanent: If this seeing and hearing were to be separated from light and darkness, motion and stillness, and penetration and obstruction, they would ultimately have no substance;

just as the thinking mind, when separated from external objects, originally has nothing at all. (2. Directly doubting that the cause cannot produce the fruit. Part 1: The direct doubt. How can one take this ultimate cessation and annihilation as the practice?
"Because one desires to obtain the fruit of the Tathāgata’s sevenfold permanence.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To depart from illusion and return to the true, remaining permanent and indestructible, is called the fruit of permanence.

To attain correspondence [with reality] is indeed difficult; this is because one mistakenly identifies with conditioned objects and loses sight of the eternally abiding.

Because one deviates from the constant nature, it is difficult to accord with the fruit of permanence. Since actual cultivation and realization involve great peril, this must be explained with difficulty.

That which all Buddhas have attained is called *bodhi* (enlightenment). That which is quiescent, eternal, and blissful is called *nirvāṇa*. That which is non-false and unchanging is called *tathatā* (suchness). It is free from faults and transcends...
It is not called "Buddha-nature. To discern all things without defilement or attachment is the *amala-vijñāna*.

To establish not a single dharma while afflictions are utterly exhausted is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. To illuminate all phenomena with penetrating clarity yet remain free from discrimination is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
*Amala* here means "stainless"; it is the ninth consciousness, the pure white consciousness.

That which has already become wisdom yet is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is so called because it is capable of conceptual differentiation. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Conceptual differentiation is consciousness;
non-conceptual differentiation is wisdom. There is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "The empty *tathāgatagarbha* is free from non-liberation."
All afflictions [are thus removed]. The non-empty Tathāgatagarbha possesses the inconceivable dharmas of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha universally responds to all things according to their form and emptiness. The latter two receive their names according to their specific functions.
The solitary empty Tathāgatagarbha constitutes the true essence; therefore, it is designated by the name of the "fruit."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the correspondence between cause and effect in the titles and designations, the fact that the practitioner specifically cites seven types of titles as questions is because this constitutes a major pivotal point within the gateway of cultivation.
That is to say, within the section on the cultivation of the path, one takes the eternally abiding true mind as the basis for practicing the perfect conduct;
this eternally abiding true mind is precisely what was discussed in the preceding sutra.

To summarize the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as it is revealed: when one uses the fingers to trace light or tests whether the vision remains unmoving while observing a river, the visual faculty does not shift from childhood to old age; thus, its coming into being is nothing other than the manifestation of this mind.

This is precisely intended to reveal that the causal nature is itself the resultant nature. Therefore, [the text] employs seemingly inconsistent language to pose a counter-objection, hoping that the Tathāgata...

There is a clarification to be made. Essentially, what the first fascicle points to is that within the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-garbha*) of sentient beings, there exists an original luminosity that is quiescent yet constantly illuminating—a mirror-like wisdom clearly manifest.
It is illuminating yet constantly quiescent, vast and devoid of even the slightest emotional defilement.

This is precisely the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana realized at the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition. Because it is neither false nor different [from its nature], it is called "True."
That which is indestructible and unchanging is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). To discern all things without attachment is called the *amala-vijñāna*.
When not a single dharma is established and afflictions are utterly exhausted, it is called the empty Tathāgata-garbha.

To illuminate all phenomena through and through without discrimination is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Striking the bell below serves as a test for the constancy of fundamental pervasive penetration.
The faculties are themselves the proof. They truly constitute the fundamental basis of the gateway to cultivation. One may well refrain from emulating the poor man who counts another's treasures.
[Section Two: The Second Layer of Difficulties; Part Three:

First, Clarifying that Cognition is Unconditioned and Impermanent] World-Honored One, if vision is ultimately empty when separated from light and darkness, then like the absence of external objects, the nature of thought itself would cease. Furthermore—

Revealing the Immediate Contradiction with Former Teachings: What the Tathāgata has spoken regarding the profound, quintessential, perfect, and eternal contradicts his sincere words and ultimately becomes mere frivolous discourse.

[Section 3: Requesting the Buddha to Resolve the Doubt] "How is it that the Tathāgata’s words are 'true speech'? I pray you, out of great compassion, will deign to open my ignorance and resolve my hesitations.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Furthermore, he conjectures that the six faculties might be severed and extinguished;
yet, conversely, he takes the Buddha’s teaching of profound permanence (*zàncháng*) to be untruthful, viewing it as bordering on frivolous discourse (*kṣudra-pralāpa*) rather than true speech.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: There are two layers of refutation, each consisting of two parts. First, it clarifies that because the cause is fixed, [the effect] is impermanent.
"Advancing and retreating in a cycle" means: advancing by investigating with the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), one finds that apart from light and darkness, seeing is ultimately empty;

retreating by investigating with the mind-faculty (*manas*), one finds that in the absence of external objects (*viṣaya*), the nature of thought itself ceases. Furthermore, one advances to investigate the external objects themselves.
Retreating inward, one infers that within the sense organs there is fundamentally no self-mind or mental factors (*caitta*).

"Mind" refers to the mind-consciousness (*cittavijñāna*), and "mental factors" refer to the six sense organs, which are also the seven locations previously investigated. This second point reveals an immediate contradiction with the previous teaching:

if, as the Tathāgata previously stated, one does not follow the six objects and uproots the senses to detach from their adhesions, thereby returning to the source and becoming eternally constant, how could this not contradict [the current position]?
Is this not a transgression of truthful speech? Here, Ānanda clings to that which the Tathāgata has refuted and doubts what has been revealed.

His arguments—whether advancing or retreating in a cycle—are all based on the claim that there is no mind or mental factors, a position he raises as an objection by following the statements from the first fascicle that refute the deluded mind as being neither a locus nor a substance.
Furthermore, the principle of the profound, pure, perfect, and constant was already demonstrated in the preceding sutra.
These two dharmas coexist within the six sense faculties; therefore, it is difficult to achieve a precise discernment of them.
Thus, this question was posed in the hope that the Tathāgata might provide a definitive resolution.
Although those present at that time attained awakening, I fear that readers today have not grasped the essential point. For this reason, I shall now expound upon it as follows:
This sutra takes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as its fundamental essence.

If one gives rise to knowledge and vision by depending on sense objects, or possesses discrimination based on the sense organs, these are all delusions; they ultimately lead to annihilationism. As it says below:
"To establish knowledge within knowledge is the very root of ignorance. This refers to the knowledge that arises not through external objects, but from within.
To see the liberation from clinging and the internal subduing of the faculties, thereby perfectly uprooting the temporal knowledge and views—that is the truth.
It is the subduing that returns one to the original permanence. As it says below, "Knowledge and views being without views—this is precisely nirvana.
Even when testing for permanence by striking a bell, one must necessarily rely on this alone.

○ (2. The Tathāgata demonstrates that the causal source is fundamentally eternal; 3. First, rebuking delusion and promising to speak. The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You have studied much learning, yet you have not exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).

Ānanda, though he has not yet exhausted all outflows, his extensive learning allows him to know only that [the former], while remaining ignorant of this [the latter].

○ (2. Pointing to Specific Objects to Remove Doubts, Part 1: First, Concluding the Roots and Objects to Reveal Delusion; 2.1. Concluding the Roots and Objects; 2.1.1. Concluding the Roots; 2.1.1.1. Concluding Existence and Non-existence) At that moment, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We hear it. When the sound of the bell ceased and there was no noise, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We do not hear it. Then Rāhula struck the bell once more, and the Buddha asked again.
"Did you hear it now, Ānanda? The great assembly replied, "We all heard it. (2. Concluding the reason) The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way did you hear it?
In what way did you not hear it? Ānanda and the great assembly together said to the Buddha, "If the bell is struck, we hear it;
when the striking has long ceased and the sound has faded until both resonance and echo are utterly cut off, that is called 'not hearing'."
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "This merely means there is no sound; it does not mean there is no hearing.
The reason for striking again and asking repeatedly is to cause [the student] to discern clearly and attain awakening."
○ (2. Interrogating the Object; 2a. First, interrogating existence and non-existence) The Tathāgata again commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear the sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "There is a sound. After a short while, when the sound had faded, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear the sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly answered, "There is no sound. A moment later, Rāhula struck the bell once more, and the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear the sound now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "There is sound. (2. Interrogating the reason for this) The Buddha asked Ānanda, "What do you mean by 'sound' and what do you mean by 'no sound'?
Ānanda and the great assembly replied to the Buddha together, saying, "If the bell is struck, it is called having sound;
when the striking has long ceased and the sound has faded until both the resonance and the echo have utterly vanished, it is called no sound."
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: The previous answer was inverted; this answer is correct. This is because sound has arising and ceasing while the nature of hearing is ever-present;
through deluded sentiment, one fails to realize this and mistakes the hearing for the sound, thereby taking the permanent to be intermittent.
[2. Refuting Evasive Confusion] The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly: "How is it that you now engage in evasive confusion? The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha:

"In what way, World-Honored One, is this called 'evasive confusion'? [2. Demonstrating the Cause of Permanence Based on the Nature of Hearing (in two parts: first, refuting attachment to demonstrate the correct understanding; within this, first, refuting the attachment to impermanence)] The Buddha said:
"I ask you about hearing, and you say 'hearing. Again I ask you about sound, and you say 'sound. Your answers regarding hearing and sound are inconsistent."

In this way, why would this not be called evasive confusion? (2. Revealing that the nature of hearing is eternal; Part 1: The direct demonstration. Ānanda, when sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say there is no hearing.
If, in truth, there were no hearing, then the nature of hearing would have already ceased, becoming like a withered tree. When the bell is struck again, how could you know it?

To know "there is" or "there is not" is simply the response to the dust of sound—whether that sound exists or does not exist. How could that nature of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence for you? It is hearing.

[The opponent] truly says: "Who knows that there is no knower? (2. Conclusion and Clarification) Therefore, Ānanda, it is the sound itself within the act of hearing that possesses arising and ceasing;
it is not the case that your hearing arises when sound arises and ceases when sound ceases. Now, is this nature of your hearing existent or non-existent?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The object of sound may sometimes exist and sometimes not, yet the nature of hearing has never been subject to existence or non-existence.
That which is called 'when sound is absent, there is no cessation; when sound is present, there is no arising'—this is precisely the true, eternal nature that is neither born nor extinguished."
Now, the knowledge of non-existence also depends upon the faculty of hearing; one cannot say that because there is no sound, there is no hearing.

Therefore, Ānanda cites the preceding [passage] below to manifest the permanence [of the faculty]. Wuxing said: Previously, Ānanda had resolved his doubts regarding the six faculties being without substance when separated from their objects;

how could he now take this state of annihilation as a cause in the hope of attaining the fruit of permanence? As for what the Tathāgata... [said]: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
To specifically reveal that the nature of hearing is eternal is truly intended to awaken the potential for the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding section established the response through guidance, and only then did it refute his prevarication.
That sound and hearing are indeterminate in their response constitutes prevarication. How is it indeterminate? "When sound is extinguished, there is no echo"—this is my question.
Regarding sound, you said "there is no sound," which is correct. But was it not an error when, at the outset, you were asked "is there hearing?
and you replied "there is no hearing"? If one follows the former answer, then since there is no sound and no hearing, when the bell is struck again, one should not hear it further.
If one follows the latter answer, then even if sound exists or does not exist, there is no absence of hearing. To respond in such a way—without a fixed position—is not evasive sophistry.
Therefore, he rebuked him, saying: "When the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say that you do not hear.
If it were truly the case that you do not hear and the nature of hearing had already ceased, you would be like a withered tree. When the bell is struck again, how could you know it?

To know that there is knowing or that there is no knowing is simply a matter of whether the auditory object (the sound) exists or does not exist; it is not that the nature of hearing itself comes to be or cease to be for you" (and so forth).
The meaning of this passage is to clarify that hearing is permanent. It unfolds through a sequence of four stages—sound, hearing, cognition, and nature—and ultimately returns to its source.

First, hearing is manifested by means of sound; yet since sound itself is merely a sensory object that may exist or not exist, how could that nature of hearing be subject to existence or non-existence for you?
Although hearing has thus been manifested, it is still not yet sufficient [to establish permanence].
"True. Next, one manifests knowledge through hearing; that is, when it is heard that 'there is nothing,' who is it that knows there is nothing?

Yet, although this knowledge is manifested, it is still not yet sufficient to constitute the truth. Next, one manifests the nature through knowledge: namely, within hearing itself, sounds naturally arise and perish;

it is not the case that the arising of sound causes your faculty of hearing to arise, nor the perishing of sound causes your faculty of hearing to cease, such that your hearing-nature would become either existent or non-existent."
This is the ultimate principle of the fundamental nature of hearing. Therefore, one should know that manifesting the eternal is not merely a matter of discarding the dust;
it is essential that both the hearer and the knower are discarded, leaving only that which cannot be discarded—like the salty taste within water or the lacquer-blue within color.
It is never obscured even in dreams and is never forgotten even in moments of haste; it must necessarily be present within the pure ocean.
Those with eyes can perceive this; otherwise, many would surely pass it by right before their faces, and many would mistake the derivative for the fundamental.
Nevertheless, these four stages generally correspond to the four sections of the Ear-Root Dharma Gate.
To speak further, while the former text establishes them vertically within the four practices (*xiū*), the present text situates them horizontally within the single nature (*xìng*).

(3. Refuting through analogy and concluding with an exhortation) If you are already deluded by inversion such that you mistake sound for hearing, how can you be surprised that you are so confused as to take the permanent to be intermittent?

Ultimately, you must not say that hearing has no intrinsic nature apart from movement and stillness, or closure and openness. (2. Citing examples to conclude and demonstrate [the permanence of the nature]; Part 1: Citing the example of deep sleep to reveal the permanence of the nature) Suppose there is a person in a deep sleep on a bed and pillow;
while they are sleeping, someone in the house pounds silk or husks rice. In that person's dream, they hear the sound of pounding.

The sound of the pestle was mistaken for something else—perhaps the beating of a drum or the tolling of a bell—and while in the dream, he wondered at the sound of the bell as if it were that of wood or stone.

Suddenly waking up, he immediately realized it was the sound of the pestle and told his family, "While I was dreaming, I was deluded by this sound of pounding rice and took it to be the sound of a drum.
Ānanda, how could one recall stillness or movement within a dream?

Whether opening or closing, penetrating or obstructing, although its form may be in sleep, the nature of hearing does not grow dim. (2. Concluding the demonstration that the form dissolves but the nature is not extinguished:
Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of life were to pass away, how could this nature ever be extinguished for you?
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The example cited regarding sleep serves to verify that while deluded consciousness reaches the point of extreme obscurity, the true nature remains unobscured.
Furthermore, fearing that those who are confused might say, 'If it is not obscured during sleep, does it not perish at death? he therefore reiterates the teaching, saying:
'Even if your physical form dissolves,' and so forth."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: To mistake the sound of pestles pounding for something else is a delusion within a dream.
That one perceives a strange bell as the resonance of wood or stone while dreaming proves that the nature of hearing is not obscured.

How could this person, while dreaming, recall whether sounds were still or vibrating, or whether the ear-organ was open, closed, unobstructed, or obstructed? "Still and vibrating" refers to the object of sound; "open, closed, unobstructed, and obstructed" refers to the faculty of the ear.
This passage clearly demonstrates that the nature of hearing is eternally so and does not depend upon the sense organ or its objects.
If cognition depends upon the organ and its objects, it belongs to the realm of impermanence; if cognition exists independently of the organ and its objects, it is truly eternal.
Therefore, this text reveals that while the nature of hearing is extremely easy to manifest, it is most difficult to realize.

○ (Third: The Convergence of the Three, with a Conclusion; Part One: Clarifying that because it is distant, the permanent is itself impermanent. Because all sentient beings, from time without beginning, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing and turning with every thought, they have never awakened to the pure, wondrous permanence of their own nature.

Instead of following that which is permanent, they pursue all that arises and perishes; thus, life after life, they flow through defilement. ○ (Part Two: Clarifying that because of awakening, the impermanent is itself permanent.

If one abandons arising and perishing and maintains the true permanence, the light of permanence will manifest before them, and the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will respond in accordance with the moment.

When the characteristics of conceptualization have dissolved and the emotional attachments of consciousness have been cleansed as defilements—having distanced yourself from both—then your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that moment;
how could you fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because they do not awaken to the permanence of the nature, they pursue all that arises and perishes. If one can maintain this constant nature, the fruit of permanence may be hoped for.
Previously, it was commanded to carefully discern the constant nature as the mind of the causal ground; Ānanda has raised a difficulty regarding this, hence this summary and declaration.
Wǔxīng says: Both the pervasive and specific delusions are termed "dust and grime"; these are what is realized through the true and the semblance [levels].
All are termed the "Dharma-eye. This eye, when endowed with the five directions, is called "clear and tranquil.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This section generally synthesizes and concludes the teaching. Because sentient beings depart from clarity and fall into delusion, the permanent is impermanent.
If one abandons arising and ceasing and departs from clarity toward awakening, the impermanent is permanent. Thus, permanence and impermanence—
The constant nature dwells within the six sense faculties like two birds flying together. If one follows after forms and sounds to engage in discrimination, there is defiled saṃsāra;
if one discards birth and extinction to maintain the constant, then the light of permanence manifests before one.

Therefore, know that the nature of transformation perceives the sense organs, objects, and self; it is not another. That which transforms the sense organs and objects into the nature of awakening is likewise the self;
it is not another. Rising and sinking, defilement and purity, depend solely upon delusion and enlightenment—should one not strive to turn back from the false and return to the True?
To conceive of appearances as objects is the dust of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); for consciousness and emotion to become defilements is the mind (*manas*).

"Consciousness. This is stated for the time being with reference to Ānanda’s discrimination of objects. However, regarding the coarse and subtle nature of these defilements, the words of Master Wuxing concerning the general and specific [delusions] possess profound道理 (principle).
For if one were to merely shatter the general delusions, one would only realize the *prajñā-cakṣus* (eye of wisdom).
Now, it is said that the *dharma-cakṣus* (eye of dharma) requires the knowledge that both the general and specific delusions have been shattered; only then can it be called the eye of dharma.
