(2) Resolving the Non-duality of Binding and Unbinding (Second Section). (A) Directly Clarifying the Non-duality of Binding and Unbinding (First Sub-section). (B) Expressing Doubts and Making a Request (First Sub-section). (C) Stating the Doubt (First Sub-section):

Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie the knots, if they do not know the origin of what was bound, I believe such people will ultimately never succeed in untying them.”
“World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: from beginningless time, we have co-arisen and co-perished with various forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left the home life,’ we remain like those suffering from quotidian malaria.
[Second Request for Instruction] “I only pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us who are drowning in the depths. Today, regarding our bodies and minds, how do these fetters arise?”
"What is meant by 'liberation,' such that it enables sentient beings suffering from the hardships of the future to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly, shedding tears and waiting with uplifted sincerity for the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: In the preceding second meaning, the text states, "If one does not see that which is bound, how can one know its release?

Therefore, he cites this here to request further explanation. Gū-shān says: Since the categories and numbers of coessential ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) are extremely numerous, and since the objects of delusion are not uniform, it is called "various" (*zhū*).
Because arising and ceasing, going and coming, are always present within the midst of delusion, it is called "together" (*jù*). Tiān-rú...

The supplementary note states: "In this world, malaria fever recurs every other day because its underlying cause has not been eliminated. This serves as a metaphor for the śrāvakas in training (*śaikṣa*):
although their pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have been destroyed, the disease-causing root of their specific afflictions (*pṛthag-āveṇika-kleśa*) has not yet been eliminated."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the previous fascicle, the Tathāgata revealed the second determination, first commanding a thorough examination of the root of afflictions (*kleśa*).
He then asked: "Observe those in the world who untie knots; if they do not see what was knotted, how can they know how to untie it?
The root of afflictions is precisely that which is knotted. Now, the one who is suited to receive this teaching wishes to deeply understand this knot.
"I request that the World-Honored One clarify this for me. Thereupon, he added the two characters "Yuan" (Original). "Yuan" means the fundamental source;

it refers to the original source from which [the state] was first bound. This has both distant and proximate aspects. The distant aspect refers to how, through the illumination of causes, an object was established; once that object was falsely established, your false subjectivity arose.
The proximate aspect refers to the essence of consciousness, the original clarity, which pervades the gates of the sense organs and is called the "original source of what is bound."
From the beginningless past, it has arisen and ceased simultaneously with all forms of ignorance; this is called innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*), and it is also this very same entity.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* clarifies that there are briefly two types of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*): first, the innate, and second, the discriminative.
Innate self-grasping, due to the internal causal force of false habitual tendencies accumulated since time immemorial, is constant...
It arises simultaneously with the body. Because it functions spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination, it is called "innate" (*sahaja*).

This is further divided into two types: First, that which is constantly continuous, residing in the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). It takes the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as its object, giving rise to the appearance of its own mind and grasping it as a real self (*ātman*).

Second, that which is intermittent, residing in the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). It takes as its object the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) transformed by the [eighth] consciousness.

One grasps at the characteristics of the aggregates—whether collectively or individually—as a real self arising from the appearances of one's own mind. Because these two forms of self-grasping are subtle, they are difficult to sever;
they can only be eliminated by repeatedly cultivating the superior contemplation of the emptiness of persons during the subsequent path of meditation.

Therefore, taking this as an opportune analogy for the present context, the "tertian malaria" is used precisely because, although the *darśana-heya-kleśas* (afflictions to be abandoned by insight) have been severed in a *srotāpanna*, the underlying disease-root of the *bhāvanā-heya-kleśas* (afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation) has not yet been removed.

If one were to apply this analogy broadly to the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it refers to the fundamental ignorance of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which grasps at the objects of the seventh consciousness (*manas*); this is called innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*). Although...
This most subtle root of illness is likewise not outside of this very thing. For this reason, the relationship between the knots and their source is extremely profound.

Nevertheless, although the inquiry into the source is fundamental, the focus now lies in the present; thus it is said: "Today, regarding your body and mind, what constitutes a knot, and from what is it called 'untying'?
Therefore, as the Tathāgata shows in the passage below: "For this reason, you now establish knowledge upon your knowing-and-seeing."
This is precisely the root of ignorance. To know that there is no seeing—that is itself Nirvana. The character "now" (今) at the end of the phrase is exactly the point of illumination and reflection.

(2. The Revelation [in two parts; first, the manifestation of auspicious signs]) At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training, also for the sake of those who had not yet...
He comes to serve as the cause for all sentient beings to transcend the world and to act as their eye for the future.
He then rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand, which was like Jambūnada purple-gold light;

immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and from the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds—each as numerous as motes of dust—there issued forth precious lights, which simultaneously appeared in those worlds.
When the waters from the various realms came to the Jeta Grove and poured over the Tathāgata’s crown, the great assembly experienced what they had never known before. (2. The Main Exposition; 2a.
All Buddhas Proclaim in Unison) Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly all heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, speaking with one voice:
"Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and understand the innate ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death—"
The root of bondage is none other than your six sense faculties; there is no other thing.

Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peace, liberation, tranquility, and wondrous permanence—that too is nothing other than your six sense faculties. It is not any other thing.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "First rubbing his crown signifies the supreme revelation.

The six types of quaking—moving, rising, leaping, roaring, shaking, and striking—signify the breaking of the delusive knots of the six sense organs. The light from the crowns of all Buddhas pouring over Śākyamuni’s crown signifies that they have together realized the supreme Dharma of the Crown.
Their speaking with one voice signifies that all Buddhas have attained liberation."
The realization of *bodhi* within birth-and-death all proceeds from this essential point. "Co-arising" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

Regarding the statement that birth-and-death and wondrous permanence share the same cause—the six sense faculties: when one establishes "knowing" upon knowing and seeing, one revolves in birth-and-death;
when there is no "seeing" in knowing and seeing, one realizes wondrous permanence, as will be explained below.
[Tiantai’s Commentary: Tiantai says: This sutra is titled "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" precisely because it reveals the supreme Uṣṇīṣa Dharma.
It is that which all sentient beings inherently possess and that which is venerated as the ultimate fruit. The fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness transcends the realm of principle;
those who perceive the Way perceive this, those who cultivate the Way cultivate this, and those who realize the Way realize this.
For this reason, when wishing to reveal this Dharma, one first touches the crown of the recipient’s head to signify it.

Furthermore, the reason each of the Buddhas emits light from their own crowns to consecrate the Tathāgata’s crown is to clarify that the primordial luminosity within the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-śukra*) of the recipient is identical to the ultimate luminosity of the Tathāgata’s fruition stage; they share a single crown.
That "the Dharma is neither dual nor differentiated" is indeed expressed with the utmost thoroughness and detail.
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata, having illustrated this through analogy, further declared it clearly: birth-and-death, nirvāṇa, afflictions, and bodhi are nothing other than the six sense faculties;
there is no other entity whatsoever. This is precisely sufficient to elucidate the point.
The coughing and clearing of the throat by the Originator of Bonds serves as the introduction to the instruction on untying the knots;
as for the words of realization, there is further text below.

○ (2. This Buddha’s Personal Explanation: 2a. Initial Inquiry) Although Ānanda had heard such a Dharma-sound, his mind was still not clear, so he bowed his head to the Buddha and asked: "How can one..."

My cycle of birth and death, my turning and returning, my peace and happiness, and my wondrous permanence—all these are nothing other than the six sense faculties; they are not some other thing. (2) The second part: The Answer and Explanation (divided into two sections). First, the prose section (divided into three parts). First, clarifying that the roots and objects are fundamentally true:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "The roots and objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. Second, clarifying that the nature of consciousness is empty (divided into two parts). First, the direct clarification: "The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky."

[Commentary] Wuxing said: The three—sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—encompass the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). Because they are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*) of the Tathāgata-garbha, they are said to have a common source.
Ordinary beings are bound because they are deluded regarding the truth; sages are liberated because they have awakened to the truth.

Although delusion and awakening differ, the principle from beginning to end is one; thus, they are said to be non-dual. Since they share a common source, they must necessarily include the nature of consciousness; since it is false and illusory, [it must be understood as such].
The faculties and objects are present, their patterns interwoven.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Wuxing held that since they share the same source, they must necessarily include the nature of consciousness; and since they are false and illusory, they must necessarily possess both faculties and objects.
This interpretation may be acceptable regarding the proximate meaning; however, if one claims it refers to distant external objects, I fear it is not so.

For within the second fascicle, when the Buddha demonstrates his own abiding in *samādhi*, he speaks of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as follows: "The seer and the conditions of seeing, along with all perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky.
Are they not of the nature of consciousness, false and illusory, just like flowers in the sky? Subsequently, he demonstrates wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-sattā*).
Setting aside the conceptual characteristics of the six consciousnesses, it is simply stated that this seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.

Is this not the same source as the sense organs and their objects? Thus we know that the shared source of the organs and objects possesses both the real and the delusory, and can therefore be bound or liberated.
The nature of consciousness is purely delusory; it is merely said to be like flowers in the sky, and is not spoken of in terms of a shared source or bondage.
[This concludes the section on] "Liberation. ○ (2.

Explaining the Accomplishment) Ānanda, because cognition arises from objects and characteristics exist due to the faculties, the nature of both the perceived characteristic and the seeing faculty is non-existent;

they are like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. [Commentary] Wuxing says: "Objects and characteristics" generally refer to the six sense-objects. "Cognition and seeing" briefly indicate the two faculties. Thus, the faculties and objects correspond.
The treatise subsumes the twelve bases (*āyatana*). All of these involve two factors that interpenetrate, and because they lack intrinsic nature internally, they are likened to "crossing reeds.

It is incorrect for some to explain this metaphor by means of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness; for they fail to recognize the subtle artistry of the sūtra’s language, which proceeds from the broad to the narrow.
Above, it subsumes the meaning of the elements (*dhātu*), and thus there are three; here, it subsumes the meaning of the bases (*āyatana*), and thus there are two. As for the following passage:
Furthermore, by abbreviating the objects and speaking only of their faculties, it says, "To establish cognition within seeing and knowing," and so forth.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding this section, Wuxing claims that the phrasing of the sutra is skillful, proceeding from the broad to the narrow; however, this explanation is also incorrect.

One must understand that all three locations—seeing, hearing, and smelling—equally possess the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness, yet the primary intent lies in refuting consciousness. This is because...
The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are of the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*); they are inherently faultless.

Only the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), serving as the root of birth and death; therefore, they must be destroyed. Thus, the first section specifically states that "the nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky.
The subsequent section states that "subject and object lack intrinsic nature, being like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. This must be cited below again.
The verse states that there is no real nature in between, and thus it is like a bundle of reeds. To explain this, the analogy of the reeds makes the nature of consciousness (vijñāna) extremely clear.

Regarding the three sections: "the establishment of knowledge and vision" is the very root of ignorance. "Knowledge and vision" refers to the sense organs (indriya), while "the establishment of knowledge" refers to consciousness (vijñāna).
Although the objects (viṣaya) are not explicitly mentioned, how could there be knowledge without objects? They are merely omitted for brevity. Thus, one should understand these three locations.

All these passages encompass the meaning of the realms (*dhātu*) while primarily serving to refute consciousness (*vijñāna*). As it is said: "To establish knowledge within seeing is the root of ignorance;
to see no seeing within seeing is itself *nirvāṇa*. How could this not be a refutation of consciousness?

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if one follows the explanation of Wu-xing from the broad to the narrow, then [the text] would be identical to the two-fascicle version, with four omissions occurring in succession.
[This section] is weighty. First, it reveals the true emptiness, stating: "The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived forms are like flowers in the sky;
fundamentally they do not exist. This corresponds to the first section, where all three [elements] are fully enumerated. Next, it reveals the wondrous existence, stating:

"This seeing and its objects are originally the essence of wondrous, pure, and luminous substance. This corresponds to the subsequent section, which omits the "consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*) and speaks instead of the "seeing and clarity" (*jien*).
The passage "At that time, seeing is not this clarity... corresponds to the third section; it speaks only of establishing knowing and seeing, thereby discarding the six sense objects.
Next, "When seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing" corresponds to the fourth section; it states that knowing and seeing are without seeing, thereby discarding the essence of seeing.
Although there is this interpretation, the first [interpretation] is taken as correct.
○ (The Three Clarities: Binding and Unbinding Share the Same Cause) Therefore, if you now establish cognition upon your knowledge and vision, this is the very root of ignorance;
if you perceive no object within your knowledge and vision, this is Nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could any other thing be admitted therein?
[Commentary] Gushan says: The preceding passage speaks of establishing knowledge while omitting seeing; the following passage speaks of the absence of seeing while omitting knowledge.
These lines in the sutra text mutually reflect one another. To cling to knowledge and seeing as being real is called "establishing knowledge and seeing";

this is precisely the deluded mind, which is the root of birth-and-death saṃsāra, and is therefore said to be the very basis of ignorance (*avidyā*). To realize that knowledge and seeing have no inherent nature is called "non-knowledge."
Seeing this is precisely the true mind, peaceful, blissful, wondrous, and eternal; therefore it is said that "this is itself nirvana, the untainted and truly pure.
This means that there is only the single true mind and no other dharma; thus it is asked, "How could anything else be admitted within this? Furthermore, another interpretation is:
to establish cognition upon seeing is to be deluded regarding true knowledge; to establish cognition upon conditions such as sense objects is false cognition.

Therefore, ignorance itself is the realization that there is no seeing; this is the penetration of true knowledge and vision because it is free from false knowledge and vision regarding objects and conditions, and is thus *nirvāṇa*.
Hence, the preceding text speaks of "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Outside of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, there is no other dharma;
therefore, nothing else can be admitted. The previous explanation, based on the constant mind, shows that all things are extinguished in stillness.
The latter explanation, based on the constant mind, shows that there is true knowledge and vision that illuminates [reality]. Therefore, both of these explanations accord with the Buddha’s intent.
Tianru’s *Supplementary Notes* asks: "How can other things be admitted within this?

This is because, as the aforementioned Buddhas told Ānanda, the wheel of birth and death and the realization of wondrous permanence are none other than your six faculties; they are not other things. Ānanda—

Having doubts regarding this, he raised them to question the Buddha. The Buddha then provided an explanatory analysis by drawing upon the triad of faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as they interrelate, concluding with the words, "Establishing knowledge based on knowing and seeing" (*zhìjiàn lìzhī*).
The two characters "knowing and seeing" (*zhìjiàn*) comprehensively encompass the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
To say that there is nothing other than the six sense organs for what constitutes ignorance or nirvana—how could any other entity possibly be admitted?
This is intended to resolve Ānanda’s doubts and to corroborate the words of the Buddhas. Furthermore, Ānanda previously stated:
"If one does not know the source from which the knot was tied, I believe such a person will never be able to untie it. He further said: "Now..."
Raji asked, "What constitutes a knot of the body and mind, and from what is liberation named? Therefore, the Tathāgata replied:
"To establish cognition based on knowing and seeing is itself the knot; this is the very source of that which is bound. When knowing and seeing are without seeing, it is called liberation."
[Tiantai’s] Commentary states: Mount Gu’s interpretation of the two statements regarding "establishing knowledge within knowledge and views" is correct in both cases.

The former explanation, based on the constant mind as quiescence, is the realization that delusion is fundamentally empty. The latter explanation, based on the constant mind as illumination, is the understanding that true reality possesses its own essence.

Thus, the very place where one realizes that delusion is fundamentally empty is precisely where one understands that true reality possesses its own essence; and the very place where one understands that true reality possesses its own essence is [the same].
This is precisely the realization that delusion is fundamentally empty. Thus, stillness is itself illumination, and illumination is itself stillness.
Stillness and illumination are fused as one; stillness and illumination both vanish. It is like clouds dispersing and the moon becoming bright: as the clouds disperse, the moon becomes bright;
there is no sequence of before and after, nor any difference in time. However, the object confronted by this stillness and illumination has not yet been explicitly stated; it is not known.

Where should the practitioner apply their efforts? One must understand that the Tathāgata previously indicated that birth-and-death, afflictions, bodhi, and nirvāṇa are all identical to the six sense faculties, with nothing else existing apart from them. Because Ānanda had not yet realized this, he again posed his question.
The World-Honored One now resolved it, saying: "To establish a cognition within cognition and vision is the very root of ignorance. Cognition and vision...
The absence of such views is itself nirvana. How could any other entity possibly exist within it? For what reason?

Did we not say previously that the sense organs and their objects share the same source, and that bondage and liberation are non-dual? That the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky;

and that knowledge is triggered by objects while appearances arise through the sense organs, yet both appearance and perception lack inherent nature, being like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another. It is indeed as follows:
First, it demonstrates the reason why [the state of bondage] is as it is, and subsequently, it correctly demonstrates the reason why [the state of liberation] is as it is;
therefore, the sequence of its discourse is thus. Why is this? For birth and death are bondage, while nirvāṇa is liberation.
The cause of bondage arises from afflictions and discrimination, whereas the cause of liberation arises from the illumination of bodhi-wisdom. Once one truly attains the source, [then...]

The root can be restored; if one attains its source through the realization of its falsity, then the flow can be checked. Therefore, in the study of the Way, nothing is more essential than knowing the source.
The source is the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). For fundamental clarity is the source of the True, while the essence of consciousness is the source of the False.
These two dharmas dwell together in confusion within the six sense faculties, which is called "sharing the same source. If one relies upon consciousness...
When the essence gives rise to discrimination based on objects, it becomes affliction (*kleśa*).
When one relies on the essence-consciousness to perceive, seeing that which is not seen and transcending thought to illuminate the fundamental reality, it becomes awakening (*bodhi*).

Once the true source is attained, how could one regard that nature of consciousness as anything other than a flower in the sky or a clump of reeds standing together? Therefore it is said: "Therefore, you now establish knowledge upon your knowing and seeing."
This is precisely ignorance; when one realizes that there is no seeing, this is itself nirvana.
It is solely the single, untainted, truly pure state—how could anything else be admitted within it?

[Verse 2] (The second section consists of two parts: first, the verses on the formal exposition; second, the initial reiteration. First, the reiteration of the source of the faculties and objects; third, the initial clarification of how the Middle Way simultaneously negates both bondage and liberation. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "In the true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty; conditions..."
Because they arise, they are like illusions; being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they have no arising or ceasing and are as unreal as flowers in the sky.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "True nature" (*tathatā*) is the source of the sense organs and their objects. "Conditioned" refers to the characteristics of bondage and liberation.
If true nature remains in delusion and can give rise to the characteristics of the sense organs and objects within the nine realms, it is called "bondage. If...
When the true nature emerges from its entanglements and is able to give rise to the functions of the ten realms—the faculties and their objects—it is termed "liberation.

Since both this bondage and this liberation are identical with the ultimate while appearing as the conventional, they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*); yet, since they are also identical with the conventional while being the ultimate, they are called "empty" (*śūnya*).
The statement "arising from conditions, they are like illusions" explains and establishes the meaning of existence and emptiness. All conditioned phenomena arise from conditions:

ordinary beings take delusion and karma as their conditions, while noble ones take responsive resonance as their conditions. Since that which is produced by these two types of conditions is in both cases merely a provisional designation, it is said to be "like an illusion.
This verse [demonstrates] that the sense organs and their objects share the same source, and that bondage and liberation are non-dual. There is no...

The following verse states that the nature of consciousness is illusory, like a flower in the sky; the previous statement that it is "like a phantom" merely served to support the meaning of emptiness.

Now, by saying it is "like a flower in the sky," the verse directly reveals its illusoriness. Furthermore, the nature of consciousness is a conditioned phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, whereas true nature is the opposite;
thus, it is called unconditioned and devoid of arising or ceasing. Since it is described as illusory, it is therefore—

Because they are unreal, they are like flowers in the sky. The *Pāṇy-aratna-śāstra* (Treasury of the Hand) states that the first two lines refute the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the latter two lines refute the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

[The Commentary] says: Tiantai notes that the *Wuxing Xunwen Ji* (Record of Fragrant Hearing from Wuxing), citing the *Xieli Zhengzhen Chao* (Notes on Verifying Truth from Xiali), states that the first half-verse...
To establish that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty is precisely the true nature. Conditioned phenomena are existent things; "they are certainly empty" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they arise from conditions. The concordant example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "like illusory phenomena. The latter half of the verse establishes that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) have no arising or ceasing and are unreal like flowers in the sky;

this also possesses the three members of a formal inference (*trirūpa-linga*). If one wishes to follow the logical convenience of the meaning, the term "unreal" must be moved [to the end of the thesis].
The two characters [“true nature”] are moved to the preceding clause, and the three characters “without arising or ceasing” are moved to the following clause.

Since "unreality" constitutes the meaning of emptiness within the thesis (*pakṣa*), one should formulate the syllogism as follows: "Unconditioned true nature exists; it is established that its nature is empty."

The reason given is that there is no arising or ceasing; the concordant example is like a flower in the sky. Question: Since the latter half of the verse does not contain the term "true nature" (*tattva*), why do you now insist on adding it?
Answer: The term "true nature" mentioned above must be understood as extending down to apply to the subsequent line (and so forth).

The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhen-lun) presents four lines that differ slightly from this: "True nature is empty of the conditioned because it arises dependently like an illusion; the unconditioned is [empty of]..."
That which exists substantially does not arise, being like a flower in the sky. Later it says: "If conditioned phenomena exist, then unconditioned phenomena exist;
since conditioned phenomena do not exist, how can unconditioned phenomena exist? (and so forth). This treatise consists of two fascicles:
the first fascicle extensively elucidates that true nature is empty of the conditioned, while the second fascicle extensively elucidates the latter two lines [of the verse].

[2. Dispelling the Unconditioned Middle Way: By speaking of the false to reveal the various truths, both the false and the true are equally false. [3. Analogizing the Senses, Objects, and Liberation as Equal to Emptiness: Since it is neither real nor unreal, how can there be a seer and that which is seen?
In between, there is no substantial nature; therefore, they are like bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The preceding prose section merely refuted the false; now, fearing that one might abandon the false and grasp at the true, it is once again dispatched [as non-existent].
Gushan says: 'Zhu' (諸) is a particle used for emphasis. By stating that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are empty and false, it reveals that *nirvāṇa* is real and true.
Because truth is spoken of in opposition to falsehood, and because the relationship of mutual dependence never ceases, even truth becomes false; therefore, it is called 'the two.'"
Delusion. Nāgārjuna said: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that very phenomenon remains dependent; thus it cannot yet be dispelled. The 'real' is not what dispels the 'unreal.

Since the 'non-real' is precisely deluded perception—wherein perception itself is the faculty and that which is perceived is the object—and since even the 'real' is spoken of only in contrast to the 'unreal' and must likewise be swept away, how could there still be faculties and objects within delusion? This refers to the intermediate state."

Within the essential nature of both the sense organs and their objects, there is no inherent existence. This verse shows that the lack of inherent existence in the perceived and the perceiver is like two interlaced reeds.

(The second verse explains that the path for binding and untying is the same. Binding and untying share the same cause; there are not two separate paths for the holy and the ordinary. You should observe that within the nature of the interlaced reeds, both emptiness and existence are neither.
When one is deluded and obscured, this is ignorance; when one’s intrinsic luminosity is revealed, this is liberation.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: To clarify the method for untying the knots, he generally cites their cause. The "cause" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

The previous statement by all the Buddhas—“If you wish to recognize the root of the knots of birth and death, and even to swiftly realize the liberation of peace and bliss, it is none other than your own six faculties, and nothing else”—is precisely identical to this meaning. Gushan said: “Observe...”

The following section reiterates the previous analogy to encourage careful contemplation. To say it is "empty" implies that the reeds possess external forms; to say they "exist" implies that the interior of the reeds is fundamentally empty.
This metaphor illustrates how the sense organs and their objects are falsely grasped as having substantiality, whereas they are originally empty.

The subsequent lines on "delusion and obscurity" (míhuì) summarize the verses concerning "establishing cognition within cognition and vision" (*zhījiàn lìzhī*) and "the absence of vision within cognition and vision" (*zhījiàn wújiàn*).

II. (The Second: The Three Stand-Alone Methods; First, Causing One to Select the Gate of the Faculties) "Unraveling the knots follows a sequence of six; when one knot is untied, all are gone. By selecting the faculty that is perfectly penetrating, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment."

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This takes up the meaning of the preceding "untying the knots" to initiate the subsequent passage on "perfect penetration. When the six knots are untied, the sense-faculties are uprooted;
when the one [knot] is lost, there is profound stillness and perfection. By selecting the perfect faculty, one enters the stream of the sages and realizes the fruit of sagehood.

(2. Showing that discernment must be precise: "The *ādānavijñāna* is subtle; its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent. Fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it."

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: The following verses on *dhātu* (the root-element) explain the origin of the initial arising of the knots of the faculties. *Dhātu* here is translated as "grasping and maintaining" (*zhíchí*).
It grasps and maintains seeds to initiate active manifestations; this is precisely the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*.

Containing and storing seeds constitutes "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); the accumulation of waves of consciousness constitutes the "flood. From this stillness [of the substrate], differentiation arises, and from this, the knots arise.

This consciousness relies upon True Suchness (tathatā) to arise as a mixture of the conditioned and the unconditioned, existing between the true and the false; therefore, it is said that "the true is not truly true.

If one were to take it as truly real, one might fear becoming deluded by false habits and thus erring on one's own account. If one were to take it as not truly real, one might fear becoming deluded regarding one's own nature and seeking it externally.
For this reason, it is not revealed in the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "O Ānanda..."
The *ādāna-vijñāna* is extremely subtle; it consists of all seeds and flows like a torrent.

I do not reveal this to the ignorant and foolish, fearing that they might conceptually grasp it as a self. The "divine self" (*puruṣa*) postulated by the non-Buddhists is precisely this consciousness.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: According to the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings), the meaning of *ādāna* is translated as "grasping and maintaining" (*zhichih*).

It is able to grasp and maintain the seeds and the body of the faculties (*indriya-kāya*), thereby producing the sense of continuity. There are three types of grasping: first, grasping and maintaining the body of the faculties so that it does not decay;
second, grasping and maintaining the seeds so that they are not lost; third, grasping and taking up the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*).

The meaning of "continuity" (*pratisandhi*) refers to the moment when a sentient being, in the final stage of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), undergoes rebirth for the first instant of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
At that time, there is the sense of "grasping" (*upādāna*) and "linking continuity. "Linking" (*sandhi*) means to bind or to belong;

for at the very instant of taking birth within the mother’s womb, one becomes bound and attached to that [new existence]. This is also like a magnet or a lodestone attracting iron; the iron is like...
The two drops of the parents' vital essence and blood are grasped and held by the eighth consciousness in a single kṣaṇa, like a lodestone attracting iron filings;

simultaneously, the seeds of the sense organs and their objects also arise as manifest activity from within its own consciousness, which is termed "grasping" (upādāna) and "linking birth" (pratisandhi).
As for the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* referring to it as the "ninth consciousness," this is merely a distinct designation for the pure portion (śuddhabhāga) of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma generally consists of three types:

first, the defiled portion; second, the purified portion; and third, the portion that is both defiled and purified. For example, within gold-bearing earth there are three elements: first, the earth element; second, the gold; and third, the layer of soil.
Taking earth as a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it possesses both the defiled and purified portions. This refers to the eighth [consciousness].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). Taking "earth" as a metaphor for the nature of differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it constitutes the defiled portion of saṃsāra; this refers to the seventh consciousness.
Taking "gold" as a metaphor for the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it constitutes the pure portion of nirvāṇa; this refers to the ninth consciousness.

Now, according to what is taught in various sūtras and śāstras, the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) serves as the general name for these three consciousnesses; thus, it is the consciousness indicated at the beginning of the first fascicle.
The "essence of the spirit, luminous and correct" refers specifically to this consciousness. The essence of consciousness is the eighth consciousness, which possesses both defiled and pure aspects;
it is like the element of earth. The "original luminosity" is the ninth consciousness, the purely pure aspect; it is like pure gold.

That which "can give rise to all conditions" refers to the seventh consciousness, which takes external conditions—form and emptiness—to produce the six consciousnesses; it is like the layer of soil. If all sentient beings...
Although it possesses the ninth [consciousness], it is intermingled with the eighth, because what is called "true" is not truly true.
If one perceives seeing as non-seeing and hearing as non-hearing, one immediately escapes the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and becomes purely the ninth. This is the Tathāgata’s intention:
he considers that if a practitioner perceives the nature as not yet true, they will cling to this essence of consciousness, taking its seeing-essence to be devoid of discrimination.
Because it is truly eternal, this verse is spoken as a profound admonition not to give rise to grasping or attachment; thus it is expressed in this way.

Furthermore, the *Zhengmo shu* (Commentary on the Correct Pulse) explains the two characters "subtle" (*wei-xi*) as follows: "Profound and hidden rather than shallow and manifest is called 'subtle' (*wei*");

"refined and wondrous rather than coarse and superficial is called 'minute' (*xi*). One should know that what was shown during the first ten inversions at the beginning of the sutra fully exhausts its subtlety and minuteness.
It is so. One does not realize that the two characters "subtle" (*wei-xi*) merely indicate the state of this consciousness’s habit-energies (*vāsanā*) as a torrential flow, which is not real.

The subsequent section on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) states: "This limpidity is not real; it is like a rushing stream that appears tranquil from afar, yet its current is swift, and thus it is not seen.
This is because the nature of seeing can only be described as unmoving and all-pervasive. If one were to call it "subtle," [it would be a misunderstanding].
How is this different from "carving a likeness of the ugly Yan-yan" or "rudely interrupting Xi Shi"? (2.

Admonition not to give rise to grasping: To take one's own mind with one's own mind is to turn the non-illusory into illusory dharmas. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not non-illusory;
since even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory dharmas be established?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This verse explains the essential method for resolving the knots and entering the Perfect [Nature]. All dharmas are manifested solely by the mind;

yet within them, through grasping and attachment, one falsely forms the "root-knots. This is the case where the self-mind grasps the self-mind, whereby non-illusory phenomena become illusory phenomena.
Because of false grasping, there is the illusory and the non-illusory; if one does not grasp falsely, even the non-illusory would not exist.

If even illusion does not exist, how could illusory phenomena exist? When illusory phenomena do not arise, the sense organs and their objects are suddenly purified, and perfect penetration manifests before one.
○ (2. Praise by way of function; Part 1:

Praise according to the essence of the Dharma) This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Adamantine King, the Jewel-Awakening, and the Illusion-like Samādhi. ○ (2. Praise according to function) A mere snap of the fingers transcends...
No further training is required. (3. Quotation in Agreement with the Buddha’s Praise) This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This is a concluding verse. This Dharma-gate is called the "Wondrous Lotus" because it is unstained by purity and untainted by defilement.
It is called the "Vajra-King Awakening" because when the faculties, objects, fetters, and delusions encounter it, they are dissolved. That is to say—
When one is without conditioned activity, has extinguished deluded emotions, and severed all conceptual understanding, it is called the "Samādhi of Illusion-like Correct Reception.

By practicing and advancing according to this, one may transcend the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) in the mere blink of an eye and enter the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*). The *Abhidharma* calls this the "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*).
It is through this alone that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have transcended birth and death and swiftly realized quiescent permanence; therefore, it is said: "The ten directions..."

The Bhagavān is the single path to the gate of *nirvāṇa*. "Bhagavān" is a title that possesses six meanings: sovereignty (*vaśitā*), brilliance (*tejas*), majesty (*śobhā*), renown (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*prabhutva*).
Guishan said: "Transcending [the stages] with a snap of the fingers surpasses the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), manifesting the merit of the three cessations (*śamatha*).
If one enters the stages (*bhūmi*) and abidings (*vihāra*), one then transcends the rank of the *arhat* of the Lesser Vehicle. Even if one enters the realm of signs...
It appears that [this stage] also transcends the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). This is because they are equal in that both eliminate the four abodes of existence (*catur-vāsa*);

however, in terms of suppressing ignorance (*avidyā*), the Three Piṭakas are inferior. Furthermore, even while remaining in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), it transcends the stage of no-more-learning.
It is like a prince in the womb whose nobility already surpasses his ministers, or like a *piṅgala* chick in its shell whose cry exceeds that of all other birds.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: In India, there are two types of flowers, the "strung" and the "scattered," used as metaphors for the sūtras spoken by the Buddha.
The prose sections, with their interconnected meanings and principles, are like flowers strung on a thread in an orderly sequence.

The verses, however, with their expansive diction and reasoning, are like flowers that have not been strung and yet compete in their brilliance. Yet, there are those where the strung and scattered elements emerge together in profusion, such as in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such scriptures are examples of this. There are those that are coherent yet lack dispersion, and those that are dispersed yet lack coherence, such as the various single-translations of sūtras and verses.
Only this *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is both highly coherent and minimally dispersed;

its meaning is profound and its intent far-reaching. Therefore, the verse passages from three locations therein do not fail to encapsulate the entire sūtra and extensively gather its great principles. That is to say:
Although this verse is said to be a mixture of *geya* and *gāthā*, refined and brilliant, it is actually composed mostly of *geya* with few *gāthā*.
Therefore, one may extract the distant meaning of the preceding sutra to explain it. The text is divided into two parts: first, the verses of the formal exposition; second, the verses of praise.
Within the formal exposition, there are two sections: first, the repeated verses (*anugīti*); second, the independent verses (*udāna*). Within the repeated verses, there is first the initial verse.
The two verses on "the roots and objects sharing the same source" conclude that bondage and liberation follow the same path. In the first of these, there are three parts:
first, the verse simultaneously negates both the middle way and bondage/liberation; second, the commentary simultaneously negates the middle way and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the simultaneous negation of the middle way and bondage/liberation in the first part, the phrase "the true nature is empty of the conditioned" uses the two characters "true nature" (*zhenxing*) to indicate the middle way—this is precisely what was mentioned twice in the preceding sutra.
The three truths taught in their perfect interpenetration all take the Middle Way of the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as their substance.

Although it is said that they "illuminate both," they actually reside in "negating both"; thus, both bondage and liberation are discarded. Because bondage is discarded, it is said that "conditioned phenomena are empty.
This establishes the meaning of emptiness through dependent origination, for all dharmas arise from conditions and their causes and conditions are empty and without a master. They are like illusions.

This illustrates the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). All phenomena arising through dependent origination are like illusions and transformations. Because illusions and transformations lack substantial reality, they are empty.
Because they are free from [conceptual] removal, they are called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and without arising or ceasing.

This refers to the fact that within true nature (*tathatā*), the Middle Way exists such that not only is the bondage of the conditioned empty, but the liberation of the unconditioned is likewise empty; therefore, it is said to be "unreal. That which is unreal is precisely emptiness.
Regarding the meaning: Why is non-existence not real? Because it lacks arising and ceasing.

If even conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), which possess arising and ceasing, are empty, how much more so could that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and devoid of arising and ceasing be real? It is like the metaphor of flowers in the sky;

all unconditioned dharmas are like flowers in the sky and lack substantial reality. One should know that the former emptiness empties persons and dharmas, while the latter emptiness empties [that] emptiness.

Both are empty. This verse correctly states that the faculties and their objects share a common source; when it speaks of the "Middle Way True Nature," it specifically refers to the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana.
Fundamental luminosity is the true source of the faculties and objects, while the essence of consciousness is the delusive source of the faculties and objects.
Here, it specifically points to the true source, so that those who seek to return to the origin may know what to grasp. Below this...
This verse now sets forth the source of delusion so that those who return from delusion may know where to go. By speaking of delusion, all that is real is revealed;

in the two expositions of "going," both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are discarded. One might wonder: since there is doubt regarding the conditioned state of birth and death, it is appropriate to discard the unconditioned state of *nirvāṇa*;
why, then, is the latter also discarded? The verse explains this through two meanings, first discarding the unconditioned by stating "delusion."

This reveals that all that is "true" is spoken of as false only in dependence upon the "True. As Nāgārjuna’s verse says: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself is dependent.
Therefore, it is said that both the false and the true are equally two kinds of falsity. Next, the conditioned is negated; hence it is said:
"It is neither true nor not-true; how could there be a seer and what is seen? In the middle, there is no real nature; therefore, they are like bundles of reeds leaning against one another."
That which sees is the faculty (*indriya*); that which is seen is the object (*viṣaya*); and that which is between them is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This means that even true nature (*tathatā*) is not truly existent within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), let alone the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness—which could possibly not be empty? The simile of the "intertwined reeds" will explain this clearly below.

The two verses conclude that bondage and liberation follow the same path; as for the statement that "bondage and liberation share the same cause, and there are no two paths for the noble and the ordinary," the prose commentary [explains as follows]:
The Buddhas collectively declare that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally the six sense faculties. Thus, the verse says: "They share the same cause; there are no two paths.
Although they speak of the six faculties, the primary intent lies in destroying the six consciousnesses.

Therefore, it is said: "Observe the nature within their interaction: emptiness and duality are both negated. Furthermore, although it speaks of destroying consciousness, the intent lies in revealing the true through the delusive. Therefore...

One proceeds by means of emptiness, existence, and the negation of both; "emptiness" refers to the aforementioned unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and "existence" refers to the aforementioned conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

By analogy, that which lies between them is the Middle Way, the true nature (*tathatā*). This is precisely what the preceding text clarifies: the simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence within the Middle Way.

This specifically refers to the root and source of the bonds of birth and death, namely the *vijñāna-essence* (識精) and the fundamental luminosity (元明). Fundamental luminosity is the true nature of the Middle Way;
the *vijñāna-essence* is the source of the knots of the sense-faculties. When it gives rise to various conditions, it constitutes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

when one maintains the *vijñāna-essence*, it is termed the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The unconditioned *nirvāṇa* realized by the two vehicles is precisely this consciousness. It is based upon consciousness...

The rest is as explained in previous commentaries. Regarding the "Single Path to the Gate of Nirvana," although it is said that there is no way to transcend birth and death and swiftly realize quiescent permanence other than through this, one must understand what is meant by "path" and "gate.

Essentially, it is the six sense faculties themselves, yet it is not the six sense faculties. This Dharma-gate is like honey; were it not for the Bodhisattvas who act as king-bees, [it could not be gathered].
Yet they are unable to partake of this ambrosia. The Sūtras call it the "fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness," and the titles refer to it as the "esoteric cause of the Tathāgatas.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha-Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction—composed of *geya* and *gāthā*, refined and pure, subtle and clear, penetrating to the heart and mind—were enlightened and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him: II. (Ānanda’s humble words: “Now that I have heard the Buddha’s unobstructed great compassion, which is intrinsically pure, wondrously eternal, and true.”
The Dharma-verse has not yet reached my mind; the six have dissolved and the one has vanished.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: *Geya* is called "Responsive Verse" (*ying song*) and also "Repetitive Verse" (*chong song*); it is a verse that reiterates the preceding prose (*chang xing*).
