Because these two verses clarify [the subject] together, they are described as "intermingled yet refined and brilliant. This refers to the *vācaka* (the expressive words).
"Subtle, pure, and transparent" refers to the *vācya* (the expressed meaning). Wēnlíng says: "Unobstructed great compassion" describes its universal salvation.

"The nature-purity, subtle-permanence, and true dharma-phrase" means that both the real and the delusive are forgotten; it is discourse that accords with the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). As for "sinking defilements and subtle... [text fragment].
The "subtle knots" refer to the delusions of affliction. Changshui said: This doubt arises because the preceding verse states, "The method for untying the knots follows a sequence;
when the one is untied, all are gone.
[Tiantai’s] Commentary: Tiantai says: When it comes to realizing and understanding the profound exposition, the sūtra’s narrative places the subject first and the object later. It should be...
When the occasion calls for discourse, that which is subsequent may be placed first. The wondrous principle is the nature of pure, wondrous permanence;
it refers to the principle of the Middle Way—which simultaneously negates both existence and non-existence—as expounded in the preceding *geya* and *gāthā*. This is liberation within bondage itself.
To take a metaphor: like the wondrous lotus, the Vajra King, and illusory transformations, there is nothing that is not pure and wondrous.
It is utterly pure, bright, true, and eternal. Were it not for the Buddha’s unobstructed great compassion, how could it be thus?
My mind and eyes have been opened; this I have already realized. As for that which remains unrealized: the six being resolved, the one vanishes—this is the sequence for loosening the knots.
Regarding the intent of the question here, although the text consists of two phrases, there are six meanings. These six interpretations are as follows:
first, disappearance; second, non-existence; third, unfolding; fourth, formation; fifth, categorization; and sixth, sequence.
Categorization takes its meaning solely from formation, whereas sequence encompasses the meanings of both formation and dissolution. As for the single meaning of categorization:
As in the metaphor of the six knots, the six sense organs are like siblings whose order of birth is not confused. Regarding the meaning of "sequence":
for each knot tied, the strands cross from left to right, proceeding from the root toward the tip;

this represents the manner in which the six sense organs arise, following a sequence from the subtle to the coarse without confusion. If one first understands this, then the answer provided in the subsequent text will be clear.
There is the fault of using metaphors that fail to match [the point being illustrated]. This is not the case;
rather, some people either place the blame on the metaphors themselves or arbitrarily engage in forced interpretations, thereby causing the meaning of the sutra to become obscured.

○ (2. Revealing [the Truth]) (i. First, the analogy of tying a cloth to illustrate delusion) (a. First, tying the cloth to establish the analogy) (1. Tying the cloth as a general demonstration) At that moment, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne, adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robe, gathered his *saṃghāṭī*, and took hold of a seven-jeweled desk.
Reaching out his hand over the desk, he took the flower-cloth presented by the *Kāpila* devas and, before the great assembly, tied it into a single knot.
He pointed to it and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called..."
Having tied it thus, the Tathāgata again folded and knotted the flower-cloth, forming another knot, and asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying, "This too is called a knot.

In this manner, he successively folded and knotted the flower-cloth until six knots were formed in total; as each knot was completed, he took the knot produced in his hand and held it up to ask about it.
"Ānanda, what is the name of this? Ānanda and the great assembly likewise replied to the Buddha in succession:
"This is called 'knotting'.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is the inner robe; *saṃghāṭī* is the outer robe; *kambala*...
It is said that the "time-period" (*kāla*) refers to the Yāma Heaven. As the supplementary note states:

because Ānanda had not yet realized that the six [knots] dissolve when the one is gone, nor understood the sequence of loosening and tying knots, the Tathāgata manifested a single cloth forming six knots to lead him to realize that when the six are dissolved, the one vanishes;
and he demonstrated the sequential order of tying the knots to lead him to realize that there is a systematic order to loosening and tying them.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The Tathāgata’s tying of the precious flower-cloth into a single knot first serves as a metaphor for the meaning of sequential order.
Thus, tying it into six knots in succession serves as a metaphor for the meaning of categorical classification. Speaking in terms of sequential order, then...
The meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) is vertical. Regarding the sense of "category" (*jāti*), it refers to the horizontal arrangement of a series.
For example, when first tying a knot, the interlacing of the left and right strands with an intervening space—is this not a sequence?

And if one, two, three, four, five, or six knots are tied in an identical manner, is this not a category? It is like, for instance, six children being born together from a single womb over the course of ten months.
To nurture its meaning is "vertical" (竪); to manifest it simultaneously is "horizontal" (橫).

Since they are born together and likewise die together, the arising of birth and the occurrence of extinction do not obstruct one another; thus, verticality and horizontality are identical, and horizontality and verticality are identical.
This section first clarifies the formation of categories and the sequence of the three meanings.

[2. Determining the Knots by Way of Binding] (First: The Analogy of Delusion Forming the Six Sense Organs) The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "When I first tied this cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded silk cloth was originally a single strand;
as for the second and third [ties], why do you all again call them 'knots'? Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, although this precious folded silk cloth was woven into a handkerchief and was originally a single entity, according to my contemplation, when the Tathāgata tied it once—"
If one knot is called "one," and if a hundred were tied, it would ultimately be called "a hundred knots"—how much more so with this cloth, which has only six knots?
It will never reach seven, nor does it stop at five. Why, then, does the Tathāgata allow that only the first is called a knot, while the second and third are not?
(2. The Metaphor for the Sequential Order of the Six Faculties) The Buddha told Ānanda: "This precious flower-cloth—do you know that this cloth originally consists of only one [piece]?"
“When I tie this cloth six times, there are six knots; you should examine this closely. The substance of the cloth is the same, yet because of the knots, they appear different.
What do you think? When the first knot was tied, it was called the first. And so on, up to the arising of the sixth knot.
Now, if I were to take the name of the sixth knot and call it the first, would that be possible? “No, World-Honored One. “If these six knots...”
To maintain this sixth name is ultimately not the first; even if I were to exhaust my eloquence throughout all future births, how could I cause these six knots to change their names?

(2. Summary by way of analogy) The Buddha said: "In this way, although these six knots are different, if one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth.
To make them disordered would ultimately be impossible. Thus it is with your six sense-faculties as well, in the end..."
"Arising together, they are ultimately different.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The same" refers to the nature of the single truth, which fundamentally has no differentiation, like the substance of a cloth.
"The different" refers to the essence of the six sense organs, whose functional applications are distinct, like the knots made in the cloth. (Tianru’s Supplement)

He said: "This means that as long as these six knots exist, their sequence cannot be confused or disordered. What follows says that if the six knots are untied, then both the 'one' and the 'six' vanish together. [Section 2:

The Metaphor of Untying the Headcloth to Realize the Threefold Nature] First, the metaphor for the six knots vanishing when one is untied. Second, first establishing the metaphor. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you truly find fault with these six knots and do not wish for them to remain as such, and instead desire them to become a single unity, what would you do?"
Ānanda said: "If this knot exists, disputes arise; it arises spontaneously from within. This knot is not that, and that knot is not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and if they do not arise, then there would be neither 'this' nor 'that.
Since they could not even be called 'one,' how could they become 'six'?"
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Not forming" means that when right and wrong arise in sharp conflict, they do not form a single unity.
To wish for and delight in a single formation is nothing other than the removal of fetters. When delusive attachments do not arise, identity and difference are perfectly extinguished;
therefore it is said: "If one cannot even be called 'one,' how can there be six? Wǔxīng says: The essence of the six sense organs is originally the nature of the One True Reality. Because...
Following conditions, that which resides in the eye is called the "essence of seeing," and that which resides in the ear is called the "essence of hearing," and so forth.

These are all like a second moon produced by pressing [the eye]; if one can follow the faculties to detach from their adhesions and turn inward to settle, then as the six [faculties] merge, even the "one" perishes.
It is like when the knots have been untied, the cloth is no longer needed.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding section clarified moving from the root toward the branches; when viewed from the perspective of the branches, the six sense organs cannot but be different.
Thus it was said: "Thus your six sense organs are also like this: ultimately identical within the midst of difference.
This concludes the meaning of establishing their common category. This present section clarifies returning from the branches to the root. If the six [organs]...
When they are resolved, even that "one" perishes. Therefore it is said: "If one cannot even be called 'one,' how can there be 'six'? Thus, the method of unification states:
"Six resolving into one and the one perishing" is likewise so; this concludes the establishment of "six resolving into one and the one perishing."

○ (2. The Integration of Dharmas) The Buddha said: "The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one are likewise thus. From your beginningless nature of mind, which is deranged and chaotic, deluded perceptions arise.
Because these delusions do not cease, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust. It is like when the eyes are strained, there appear floating flowers;
from within the serene and luminous clarity, these arise without cause due to confusion. All worlds—mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and nirvana—all are [thus produced]."
This refers to the delusory, exhausting, inverted appearances of flowers.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The arising of false knowledge and vision belongs to the aspect of the perceiving subject (*neng-jian*). The exhausting vision giving rise to dust refers to the objects perceived (*suo-jian*).
Thus, through mere falsity and exhaustion, the five abodes of ignorance are fully present. This is as explained below in the passage beginning with "exhausting the eyeball."
This serves as an analogy for its meaning. "All worlds" below indicates the characteristics of worldly afflictions (*rajas*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This section precisely accords with the sequence of the six knots arising. The four phrases beginning with "the nature of the mind" correspond to the three subtle and six coarse states.
"The nature of the mind is deranged" refers to falsely taking what is not awakening to be awakening. Affliction...
To see the stirring of dust is precisely what gives rise to worldly toil and afflictions; the intermediate stages may be understood accordingly.
As in the metaphors of the fatigued eye and so forth, there is no substantial reality.

That both birth-and-death and nirvana are all merely the appearance of flowers means that what is called "delusion" reveals the various aspects of the Real, and thus delusion and truth are equally two forms of delusion. Since birth-and-death is the appearance of flowers, the six [sense faculties] are as they should be.

Explanation: Since nirvāṇa is itself the manifestation of a flower, it should be discarded; furthermore, since saṃsāra is itself the manifestation of a flower, there is the emptiness of persons, and since nirvāṇa is itself the manifestation of a flower, there is the emptiness of phenomena—both are empty.
○ (2. Explaining the Unraveling of the Knot through the Mind; Part 1: Directly Showing it is Done through the Mind) Ānanda said, "This weariness is like the knot; how is it to be untied?
The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand and pulled it to the left, asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.
He then turned the cloth over and pulled it to the right, again asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I have now tried pulling with my hands from both the left and the right, but I cannot untie it. What skillful means might you employ to untie it?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, one should untie it at the very center of the knot; then it will immediately fall apart. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot."

[Commentary] Wuxing said: "Pulling from the left and right, one cannot untie it in either case. This is a metaphor for how observing either of the two extremes cannot destroy fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
Ordinary people and non-Buddhists take permanence and annihilation as the two extremes; the practitioners of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas take emptiness and existence as the two extremes.
Although these [extremes] may be suppressed or severed, the knot in the cloth still remains. If one wishes to remove the knot, one must...

Regarding "the binding of the mind": when one perceives and establishes cognition within [the mind], this is called "binding. To contemplate that cognition as the Middle Way is termed "the binding of the mind.
Binding does not depart from the cloth; once untied, it becomes one. Cognition does not differ from the Way; once lost, the center remains. Tianru’s supplementary note states:
"The preceding passage on 'the nature of the mind being deranged' and so forth demonstrates the origin of the root-binding and its successive layers of delusion."
This pulling of the cloth and so forth demonstrates the method for untying the knots.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Wuxing’s interpretation—that pulling to the left and right corresponds to the two extremes and the center of the knot—is vague and imprecise.
One must know that "pulling to the left and right" metaphorically represents biased contemplation; neither contemplating the sense organs nor contemplating the objects can [lead to liberation].

Explanation: "One should resolve it at the knot" means one should break through consciousness within the contemplation of the center. This takes the fundamental essence of the primary clarity of the second root-consciousness as the object of contemplation.
The preceding text’s statement that "seeing seeing is not seeing," and the subsequent text’s statement that "hearing hearing is not hearing," constitute resolving it at the knot.
To apply this to the previous analogy: it is like when tying a knot, a single cloth is on the left...
Tie the knots by crossing the right over the left; while the center must remain empty, the left and right form knots, yet the empty space in the middle is not a knot.
This serves as a metaphor for the union of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), which constitutes consciousness conditioned by objects.

Within this, that which is not conditioned by objects is the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*). Therefore, this sutra consistently takes the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness as its primary focus.

This constitutes the foundation of Great Samādhi. Now, when a knot is tight and its center is not hollow, making it difficult to untie, this may be compared to the heavy attachments of ordinary, ignorant people, which are ultimately difficult to liberate.

When a knot is loose and its center is empty and cavernous, making it easy to untie, this may be compared to those with innate roots and great resolve who enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata in a single leap.
It is so. The previous passage stating that "knowing and seeing are non-seeing" is precisely this meaning, which is *nirvāṇa*.

However, the application of function herein is profound, subtle, and extremely difficult to definitively determine. I shall now re-establish three meanings to elucidate it: first, clarifying the "middle" by way of the object of contemplation;

second, clarifying the "middle" by way of the means employed; and third, clarifying the "middle" by way of what is to be eliminated. First, clarifying the "middle" by way of the object of contemplation:

Regarding "clarity within": although it is said that one contemplates the faculties and their objects separately, neither can truly be understood; one must instead rely on the faculty to transcend the faculty.
Thus, while the nature of the faculty being contemplated depends upon the faculty, in reality it does not use the faculty.

One directly contemplates the essence of seeing which reflects form and the essence of hearing which reflects sound; this nature abides between the faculty and the object, and is called "abiding at the center of the knot."

The explanation is thus dispersed. Second, regarding the clarification of "the Middle" in terms of its application: although this sutra fully expounds the three dharmas, its primary intent lies in the Middle Way of *dhyāna*.
Therefore, within *śamatha*, it has already clarified the definitive meaning of the Middle Way as the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
As it says: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi; there is no [duality]."

This is not so. Within samādhi, arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, unmoving, and all-pervading nature of true suchness (tathatā).

It is precisely because the clarity within the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is taken as the object of observation that one who can observe in this way is "arising cultivation from the entirety of the nature.
By observing through the midst, this constitutes the point where the knots are untied at the heart, which is the moment of discernment.

[The section on] "Dispelling. Third, regarding the clarification of the "intermediate" [level] based on what is to be destroyed: this has both the fundamental and the derivative, as well as the primary and the secondary.

The fundamental is the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-śukra*), which belongs to the eighth consciousness; the derivative is the capacity for cognition (*ālambana*), which belongs to the sixth consciousness.

If one examines the meaning of the preceding and following passages, it is primarily intended to refute the mind that takes objects as its conditions within the six consciousnesses. This consciousness dwells between the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*); as it is said, "knowing."
To see non-seeing is itself nirvana. This means that when the knots of the mind are untied, they immediately disperse.

One simply employs the practice of seeing-seeing to directly contemplate the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-sāra*) in order to manifest the primordial luminosity. Once the primordial luminosity is manifested, the essence of consciousness is immediately shattered.
Thus, it is not only the conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*) that is produced which is destroyed; the very essence of consciousness that is capable of producing it is also destroyed.

This is also refuted accordingly. This constitutes using the primary to encompass the secondary, observing the root to refute the branches. As previously stated in the analogy: "It is like splitting bamboo;
first opening its tail, and then, driven by the wind, it all tears asunder. It is also like felling a tree; once the root is reached, the thousand branches all perish.
This is precisely what is meant here. Someone may ask: "Regarding that which is refuted, you only mention 'six' and 'eight,' but do not state the specific [numbers]."
"What are the seven? He replied: "The seventh consciousness abides between the two [other] consciousnesses; it externally conditions form and emptiness, while internally it conditions the eighth.
If the conditioning of the mind is destroyed, then there is nothing external for it to employ. Only the subtle half-portion of the manas remains, internally conditioning the essence of consciousness.
Now, as the essence of consciousness is destroyed along with it, there is likewise no internal object of condition, and it becomes subtle."

The subtle is likewise extinguished. Therefore, in a general discussion on the refutation of consciousness, one need only refute the six or eight [consciousnesses], for the seventh has no inherent substance of its own.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Under the ruins of a overturned nest, there are no intact eggs."

○ (2. Pointing to the True Causes and Conditions and Exhorting [the Audience], Part 1: Pointing to the True Causes and Conditions) Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse appearances of worldly conjunctions.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: Since one is commanded to untie the knots, it must be done at the very center of the knot. Because [the Buddha] wishes to lead [practitioners] to select their faculties and cultivate the perfect practice (*yuanxing*), he demonstrates that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This serves as a counter-illustration that if there were no causes and conditions, the Buddha-dharma would have no way to arise.
As stated in the preceding text: "For example, although a lute or a zither possesses exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers [to play them], [the sound will not be realized]."
In the end, they were unable to produce [the fruit]. This, then, is the present causal condition for the perfect cultivation of both samādhi and prajñā.
As for the matters within the Tripiṭaka, such as the six pāramitās and so forth, these are all mundane, compounded, and coarse characteristics.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunction.
This distinguishes the mundane to reveal the supramundane; it is not a case of distinguishing the heterodox to reveal the orthodox.
For in the preceding text, having already refuted both causes-and-conditions and spontaneity, those things refuted were all the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunction. Now, this clarifies...

If one wishes to eliminate the fetters, one should do so within the very mind of the fetters, which likewise belongs to the realm of causes and conditions. This is what is meant by "destroying the emotional attachments but not destroying the dharmas.
The Buddha feared that those who did not understand his intention might cling to what was previously refuted and find it difficult to accept what is now established;
therefore, he spoke thus to make known the purpose behind both the refutation and the establishment.

(2. Exhorting the Selection of Faculties for Cultivation) The Tathāgata has revealed the mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes as they emerge according to their respective conditions.
Thus, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its number;

and the various things appearing before him—whether pines straight or thorns crooked, cranes white or crows black—he fully understands their origins. For this reason, Ānanda, you should, according to your own mind, select one of the six [faculties].

If the fetters of the sense-faculties are severed, the marks of defilement will naturally perish; when all delusions have vanished, what need is there for anything that is not true? [Commentary] Gushan says:
The mundane world refers to the six realms of ordinary beings, while the supramundane refers to the four types of noble ones. One knows that these ten realms all arise from the mind:
following the defiled conditions of ignorance, one produces the nine realms; following the pure conditions of teaching and practice, one...
They emerge from the Buddha-realm. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says, "There are also causes and conditions;
by extinguishing ignorance, one obtains the blazing lamp of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Wuxing said: "The Buddha possesses two kinds of wisdom:
provisional and ultimate. Ultimate wisdom darkly accords with principle; provisional wisdom mirrors phenomena. It illuminates mundane and supramundane dharmas, even unto the point of knowing..."
The various origins of these [distinctions] are all discerned by expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Since one has already clearly and unerringly realized both the sentient and the insentient, the method for untangling the knots and the principle of selecting the faculties (*indriya*) as now explained are entirely the discernment of what is appropriate for each thing;
