Now, this perfect penetration specifically resides in the sense of fragrance. As it is said: "I see the bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense.
Next, the contemplation of its expansion and contraction is explained in four parts. First is the core principle of the Buddha’s intent, which explains what was realized.

The initial statement, "He instructed me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena," refers generally to the twenty-five objects of perception, directing one to observe principle within phenomena;
because truth is encountered in every matter, it is called "thorough contemplation. This constitutes receiving the ultimate teachings of the Mahāyāna gate in their entirety.
Next, it says: "I saw the bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense, the fragrance of which came in silently and tranquilly."

Within the nose. This describes what was practiced in former times: when the habitual objects appear before one, one uses the supreme teachings received to contemplate the phenomena of the olfactory realm.
Taking wood as the cause and fire as the condition, smoke is the phenomenon produced;
emptiness is the locus upon which it depends. When it comes, there is that from which it proceeds; when it goes, there is that to which it adheres. [This is] the cause.

When dust arises, smelling occurs; because of smelling, consciousness is produced. The five consciousnesses and the five mental consciousnesses arise in succession without end, leaking and falling into the three realms of existence.
To speak in terms of the subtle fragrance’s secret perfection:

if this fragrance were produced from wood, then its fragrant substance would become smoke upon being burned, and if the nose were to perceive it, it ought to be enveloped by that smoke. Yet now, the fragrance is tranquil and enters [the senses] directly.
Within the nose, smoke has never been encountered, nor does it arise from wood. If it were to arise from space, then because the nature of space is eternal, fragrance should be eternally present;
why then rely on burning this withered wood in a brazier? It does not arise from space. When one smells the remaining smoke and fire, there is no fragrance;
thus it does not arise from the smoke or the fire. It is neither self-caused, nor other-caused, nor both, nor without cause.

Coming, it has nowhere from which it comes; going, it likewise has nowhere to which it attaches. Thus, by turning back what is provisional, one enters emptiness, meeting with all things and returning to oneself.
Thereby, the mental constructs dissolve, and the untainted (anāsrava) is manifested; this is called "wondrous fragrance" and "mysterious perfection.

The names and characteristics may be known. Regarding the three meanings related to the four teachings: the contemplative gates of the four teachings do not go beyond the methods of analysis and substance.

Those of the Tripiṭaka teaching must analyze fragrance in order to clarify emptiness. Now, in this Mahāyāna gate, although the four natures are refuted, there is nothing that is not the wondrous essence.
The distinction between the three teachings is made according to the differences in the realization of the true and conventional aspects of the *dharmatā*.
What is described by Xiangyan here is equal in principle to the Perfect and Sudden; it merely speaks in terms of what has been realized, which resides solely in...
The four fruits of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) involve hearing the Perfect [Teaching] yet realizing the Partial; or, following habitual tendencies, they borrow the stages [of the Shared Teaching].

Because he was adorned with exquisite fragrance, thereby adorning his Dharma-body, he was named the Youth of Fragrance Adornment (Xiangyan Tongzi). "Youth" (tongzi) is an alternative name for a Bodhisattva.
This means that they are all of the nature of *kumārabhūta* (the eternally youthful), being entirely devoid of even a trace of artifice or falsehood; it is not a term referring to mere childhood.
Regarding the point that the principles of the four schools of the Tripiṭaka are harmonized and converge into the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]:

when the境 (*viṣaya*, object) contemplated is manifested through the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to reveal the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is subsumed under the sense-object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*). When the *tathāgatagarbha* is manifested through the seven elements (*saptadhātu*), to which element should it be assigned? Now...
Speaking in terms of the four—wood, emptiness, fire, and smoke—they are subsumed within the three great elements of earth, fire, and space.
They are none other than "the true emptiness of the nature of form" and "the true form of the nature of emptiness," which are fundamentally pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
According to the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the capacity of their cognition, they manifest according to karma as wood, fire, emptiness, or smoke. Grasping...
Taking the three dharmas as the object, one manifests the nature of smelling and enters the Way; thus wondrous virtue shines brilliantly, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. (4.

King of Medicine Contemplating Taste, Part Two: First, Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) The two Dharma Princes, King of Medicine and Superior King of Medicine, along with five hundred Brahmā deities present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats.
Rising, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Throughout beginningless kalpas, I have served as a skilled physician for the world.
Within my mouth, I have tasted every herb, wood, metal, and stone of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand.

Thus I know thoroughly all tastes—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their combinations, those produced by natural growth, and those resulting from transformation, whether they are cold or [hot]."

They fully understand all that is hot, whether it possesses poison or is without poison; they serve the Tathāgata and thoroughly comprehend the nature of flavors as being neither empty nor existent, neither identical to the body and mind nor separate from the body and mind.

Having awakened through this analysis of the causes of flavor, they were granted the seal of approval by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who bestowed upon my brothers the names of the two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; they now stand within this assembly as Dharma Kings.

Son. (2. Citation of Evidence and Conclusion of the Answer) Because I attained awakening through the faculty of taste, I ascended to the rank of Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect method of penetration, I replied: "According to what I have realized, the cause of taste is supreme."
[Commentary] Gushan says: These are the six flavors, such as bitter and sour. When various flavors combine, they are called "harmonized flavor" (*saṃyukta-rasa*).
To take them directly as they are is called "innate flavor" (*sahaja-rasa*). To refine, roast, or cook them is called "transformed flavor" (*vikāra-rasa*).

Wuxing says: Because one serves the Buddha, one will inevitably hear the True Dharma; thus, regarding the nature of flavors, one realizes their arising and non-arising, and designates emptiness and existence as "flavors."
It is also dust. "Body and mind" refers to the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*). Since taste is known through contact, they are spoken of in relation to one another.
Because taste is not empty, it is not separate from body and mind; because taste is not existent, it is not identical to body and mind.
It is herein that the nature of the Middle Way is revealed.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the fourth explanation regarding the perfect penetration of the sense-object of taste (*rasa*). First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of this object.
Generally speaking, food and drink that possess the five flavors are all objects encountered by the tongue-faculty.

Now, specifically, he takes the nature of medicinal herbs—plants, grasses, minerals, and metals—as the flavor, much like Shennong’s tasting of the hundred herbs. This is discussed as recorded in the medical classics of this region.
Cold, heat, warmth, coolness, and harmony comprise ten thousand varieties; yet that which is taught in India numbers one hundred and eight thousand.
Thus, what exists here may be absent there. For example, the King of Medicines from the Snowy Mountains illuminates the internal organs, causing all ailments to burn away;
the *gośīrṣa-candana* cures chronic illnesses, such that other medicines lose their efficacy. In this region...
This is something physicians have never known before. To say "one hundred and eight thousand" is by no means an exaggeration; it is a clear observation of their increase and decrease.
First, following the intent of the Buddha’s teaching, I shall explain what these two bodhisattvas realized. These two bodhisattvas were originally excellent physicians of the world;
they served the Tathāgata through this very path, and by constantly hearing the essentials of the Dharma, they came to understand its flavor.

The nature is non-arising. Regarding the statement "neither empty nor existent," Wu-xing says that "empty" and "existent" refer to the flavor-object and the body-mind, while "tongue-consciousness" refers to the tongue-faculty consciousness.
Now, I say that this too should be examined by applying the four-fold nature (*catuskoṭi*) as before.

If the food were produced [by the tongue-consciousness], since the food would not exist within the consciousness, how could it know itself? Furthermore, if the food knew itself, it would be identical to the food of another; what concern would it have with [the eater]?
You call this the cognition of taste. If it were produced in empty space, what flavor would you experience while devouring that void?

Suppose that empty space were salty; if your tongue were salty, your face would also be salty, and the people of this world would be like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness and never knowing sweetness.
If they did not recognize sweetness, they would likewise have no perception of saltiness.
If you truly have no cognition, how can you know the taste?

Furthermore, if this taste arises from your tongue and there is but one tongue within your mouth, then at that time your tongue would already have become the flavor of ghee; when encountering black rock honey, it should not change.
If it does not change, it cannot be called "knowing the taste. If it does change, then the tongue is not a single entity. How...

How can many tastes be known by a single tongue? If consciousness arises dependent on [taste], then consciousness itself would be the taste; in that case, it would be identical to the tongue-organ and should not be able to taste itself.
How, then, could consciousness know whether something is a taste or not a taste? Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance.

Since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise have multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were a single entity, then it would necessarily be produced by a single taste—whether salty or bland.
When sweet and bitter flavors are blended together, all the various transformations arise as a single taste and should be without distinction.
Since there is no distinction, it is not called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Within the Dharma-body Middle Way, the "taste" is the true cause.

Awakening to this cause of taste is what is meant by [the realization of] names and marks; these may be understood accordingly. Regarding the three meanings related to the four teachings, the Bodhi of the *Zàng* (Āgama) teaching...

The analytical discernment of the causes of flavors must involve the disintegration of dharmas (*dharmapra-bheda*). Now, this [discernment] based on the four propositions already belongs to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) approach.

If one realizes "mere emptiness" (*śūnyatāmātra*), it is judged to belong to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). "Mere Middle" (*madhyamātram*) belongs to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), while "not merely Middle" (*na-madhyamātram*) belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-śāsana*).
Regarding the convergence of the principles of the four schools of the *pitakas* upon the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]: these two bodhisattvas have already entered the higher stream;

thus, the dharma-gates they have realized are identical to the true flavor of the nature, the emptiness of nature, and the true flavor of emptiness—pure from the very beginning and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
It does not hinder them from distinguishing flavors according to pure conditions, nor from manifesting the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) by following the nature of karma.
This is the nature [of things].

○ (5. Bhadrapāla’s Contemplation of Touch, Part Two: First, Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. While bathing the Sangha..."

At that time, as I followed the custom of entering the chamber, I suddenly awakened to the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the midst of this, one finds peace and attains non-existence.
My former habits were not forgotten, and even until the present day, I have followed the Buddha into the homeless life and attained the state of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla. (2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) "The sublime touch proclaims clarity, and one becomes established as a son of the Buddha. Thus the Buddha asked.
"Among the various gateways to perfect penetration, that which I have realized—touch—is the foremost.
[Commentary] Gushan says: Bhadrapāla means "Worthy Protector" (Xiánshǒu) or "Worthy Guardian" (Xiànhù).
He protects his own virtuous qualities and also protects sentient beings. Zizhong says: According to the *Lotus Sūtra*, he possesses twenty trillion majestic powers.

The Buddha Ghoṣarāja appeared in the world both before and after [the present Buddha]. During the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of that former Buddha’s image-form, these individuals such as Bhadra and others, due to their overweening pride (*abhimāna*), reviled the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta;
consequently, for a thousand kalpas they fell into the Avīci Hell. Once their retribution was exhausted, they encountered the subsequent Buddha and left the household life.
Wu Xing says: "Water" refers to the cause of what is touched; "dust" (*rajas*) refers to the substance, which is the condition (*pratyaya*) of the toucher.
Since dust cannot defile it, its essence is eternally pure. Subject and object are like illusions, and both extremes are empty;
thus, the mind that perceives through contact dwells in tranquility, in accord with its true nature. Lektan said: "Contact involves the threefold harmony.
Here, these are reversed to signify the secret treasury of the Three Virtues; therefore, it is called 'the marvelous touch proclaiming clarity.'"

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the fifth explanation regarding the perfect penetration of the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.
Generally speaking, all phenomena in the world—such as clothing, cold, and heat—are objects of touch encountered by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Now, in reference to the bathing of the Sangha, he sets aside the general to follow the specific, hence the phrase "the water as cause. Furthermore, one must clarify the distinction between harm and benefit; for instance, if one is wounded by a poisonous thorn...

If one encounters that which is coarse, it causes harm; if one encounters that which is soft, subtle, and smooth, it brings benefit. At present, while relying on the occasion of bathing, matters of harm and benefit are incidental.
It is precisely because these matters are incidental that the emptiness of their nature is easily revealed. Second, the fourfold contemplation of expansion and contraction.
The initial thesis explains the Buddha’s intent regarding what has been realized: that contact does not contact itself because it is known through the sense organ;
and that cognition does not cognize itself because cognition exists by means of contact.

Now, at the time of bathing, one is actually washing away the defilements from the body-organ (*kāyendriya*), yet you say, "I wash neither the defilements nor the body. This is because that which defiles the body is form (*rūpa*).
That which defiles the substance is the superficial dust (*pāṃśu-rajas*).

While the objects of form (*rūpa-āyatana*) may be cleansed and the superficial dust may certainly be washed away, as for the sense-faculty of the body (*kāya-indriya*)—which perceives cold and warmth in their ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)—how can it be washed? Furthermore, how can that which is known as warmth and cold be cleansed?
Viewed in this light, the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) is fundamentally empty and the sense-faculty of the body is fundamentally quiescent. Consequently, [the middle...]
The intermediate state arises from body-consciousness; how could it possibly exist? Therefore it is said: "In the middle, one rests in peace, attaining non-existence.
When the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is shed in this very moment, the illusory and empty body is revealed as the very essence of the Dharma-body.
Thus it is said: "Marvelous touch is proclaimed and made clear, and one dwells as a child of the Buddha. However, since it is already said that one has suddenly awakened to the cause of water—
It is further said that "past habits are never forgotten. What was practiced? Awakening was attained under the Buddha Vipaśyin, yet the habits were forgotten under Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
thus it is fitting that the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions of thought remain entirely intact. Alas!

Such is the ease with which the Way is realized, and such is the difficulty with which habits are forgotten. This is why Ānanda did not have to pass through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to attain the Dharma.

As for the body: when discussing what has been realized, one has only just attained the third fruit (*trtīya-phala*). From this, it can further be known that there is a disparity between the two paths of realization.
While names and characteristics may be understood, the three [aspects] accord with the timing of the teaching and pertain to the meaning of the four *yānas*.

To say, "At present, having left home following the Buddha, one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*)," and thus calls it the *pāryāyika-yāna* (the universal vehicle), and to clarify the nature of form as being emptiness—this is permissible. However, [it is not yet sufficient].
It is said: "When wondrous touch is proclaimed and clarified, one attains the station of a Buddha’s son. This may be termed either the "Middle Alone" (Danzhong) or the "Perfect Middle" (Yuanzhong).

Regarding the convergence of the principles of the four schools of the Tripitaka into the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun): since this principle is most profound and mysterious, there is no need for further reconciliation.

Should one wish to reconcile them, one may cite that through the awakening to touch and the awakening to cognition, wondrous virtue becomes brilliantly clear, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm in its perfection.
If the ten directions truly possess no fixed location, then in principle nothing is not profound, and in phenomena nothing is not sublime.

(6. Kāśyapa’s Contemplation of Dharmas, Part Two: First, Narrating the Circumstances of Awakening) Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and others immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Sūryacandraprabha."

"Dīpaṃkarā, when I drew near to you to hear the Dharma and practice it, and after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when I made offerings to his relics and continued the light by lighting lamps, I anointed a Buddha image with purple-gold light.
From that time forth, in life after life and birth after birth, my body has always been perfectly full, a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs, such as the one named Purple-Gold Light, were my kinsmen who simultaneously resolved [upon enlightenment]."
With my mind contemplating the world, I saw that the six sense-objects are subject to decay and transformation;

by cultivating extinction through emptiness and stillness alone, my body and mind were able to traverse hundreds of thousands of kalpas as easily as a finger-snap. By means of the dharma of emptiness, I attained Arhatship.

The World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta. (2. Citation of proof and conclusion of the answer) The Wondrous Dharma has been clarified and all outflows have been extinguished. As for the question of perfect penetration, it is as I have described.
"The dharmas realized serve as causes for the higher [stages].
[Commentary: Wēnlíng says: Mahākāśyapa is "Great Drinker of Light. His body was golden in color, its radiance eclipsing the sun and moon.

Because he contemplated the transformation of sensory objects (*dhātu*), he awakened to the emptiness and stillness of all phenomena (*dharma*). He subsequently cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to extinguish the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*). Not...
By taking the dharma-objects as conditions, he attained the state of non-arising and non-ceasing; thus, he transcended hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the space of a finger-snap.
He remains now on Mount Kukkuṭapāda awaiting Maitreya before entering this samādhi. *Dhūta* is newly translated as *duo-duo*, which means "shaking off";
it is named for its ability to shake off the dharma-objects. Guishan said that those who cultivate the cessation of all mental activity...
Among the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), the ninth is the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).

Changshui says that Ziguangjinian was his wife during his time as a householder. Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state that since Ziguangjinian and [the Buddha] simultaneously resolved their minds for enlightenment, they were not merely relatives of a single lifetime.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This explains the perfect penetration of the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) through six methods of interpretation. First, it clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.

"General" means it universally encompasses all six objects, as when it is said: "I observe that the six objects in the world undergo transformation and extinction. "Specific" refers exclusively to the dharma-object.
It is as if one were to say, "I have attained Arhatship through the dharma of emptiness. Yet, the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) has no separate intrinsic nature;

rather, it takes as its substance the residual shadows of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Thus, while they are always distinct in terms of their general temporal continuity, they are always continuous in their specific temporal manifestations.
Second, the explanation of the expansion and contraction of contemplation: first, the primary school elucidates the Buddha’s intent regarding what was realized. Since it says, "I..."
That one attains the state of an Arhat through the dharma of emptiness is clearly explained in the Hīnayāna. Second, to briefly clarify the terminology and characteristics for practical purposes:
it should be understood as the ninth meditative attainment, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), as stated by Guishan.
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate this attainment must first practice the preceding eight attainments as a preliminary means. These eight attainments...
Having achieved these, one then cultivates the final concentration. Regarding the nine successive concentrations: first is the successive concentration of the first dhyāna.
When one enters the first dhyāna concentration—free from all desires, evil, and unwholesome states; with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*);

and possessing the joy and bliss born of seclusion—at that time, the observation (*vipaśyanā*) within this first dhyāna concentration is perfectly balanced. One recognizes one's own mind and enters it successively, without any [distraction].
When one enters the first dhyāna concentration amidst scattered thoughts during meditative cultivation, this is called the sequential concentration of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the sequential concentration of the second dhyāna: when one enters the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna, within that state the meditative observation of the second dhyāna is perfectly balanced.
Recognizing one's own mind, one enters sequentially; without a single moment of distracted thought intervening, one enters the second dhyāna-samādhi.

This is the sequential attainment of the second dhyāna. [The same applies to] the sequential attainment of the third dhyāna, the sequential attainment of the fourth dhyāna, the sequential attainment of the sphere of infinite space, the sequential attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sequential attainment of the sphere of nothingness.
The successive attainments (anupūrva-samāpatti) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are all similar to those explained for the first and second dhyānas.
Regarding the ninth, the successive attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception (*nirodha-samāpatti*):

when entering the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one recognizes one's own mind prior to this attainment, resolving with a sharp mind so that each moment of consciousness follows the next in succession.
One enters [this state] such that there is not a single moment of distracted thought intervening before entering the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

This is the sequential meditative concentration of the cessation of sensation and perception. Regarding the third point, the meaning of the sequence of explanations in relation to the four teachings: if one enters by means of the analytical method (*prabheda*), it belongs to the Tripitaka Teaching;

if one enters by means of the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it belongs to the Shared Teaching; if one enters by means of the Middle Way of the "mere substance" (*tathatāmātra*), it belongs to the Distinct Teaching; and if one enters by means of the Perfect [Middle], it belongs to the Perfect Teaching.

Entering through the twelve *āyatanas* belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As for the principle that the four schools and the three collections (*piṭaka*) are harmoniously integrated into the Perfect and Sudden:
within the twelve *āyatanas*, one examines each instance—whether as identical to the mind or distinct from the mind—and finds that neither can be apprehended.

Since phenomena (*dharma*) and the mind both have no locus, both the faculty of mind (*manas*) and phenomena are equally illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature; they are eternally [such].
Abiding in wondrous brilliance and immovability, the pervasive and perfect nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is revealed.

[Section Two: Awakening through the Contemplation of the Five Faculties] [Part One: Aniruddha’s Contemplation of the Eye] [Sub-part One: Narrating the Circumstances of His Awakening] Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first left the household life, I was always fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I was of the same class as animals. Hearing the Buddha’s rebuke, I wept and..."
"Rebuked for not sleeping for seven days, I lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination;
no longer relying on the eyes to see, I perceived the ten directions with essential clarity and brilliance, as clearly as looking at fruit in the palm of one's hand.

The Tathāgata sealed me as an Arhat. (2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) "The Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the faculties. According to what I have realized, it is the revolving of vision and returning to the source that constitutes it."
First. [Commentary]:
Changshui says that Naluo (那律) is Aniruddha, which is translated as "Free from Poverty" (Wupin) and also as "As One Wishes" (Ruyi).
He was the prince Śuklodana. In a past life, by offering a single meal to a pratyekabuddha, he experienced bliss at will for ninety-one kalpas.
Guishan [Zongmi] says that the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to the assembly in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, Nanda (Naluo) fell asleep there. The Buddha rebuked him with a verse, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep?"
Shellfish such as snails, clams, and oysters sleep for a thousand years without hearing the name of the Buddha. At that time, Aniruddha remained awake until dawn;
consequently, his faculty of sight was lost. Because of this, he cultivated dhyāna and attained the four great pure forms (*mahābhūta-rūpa*) covering half his head, through which he could see.
He observed the trichiliocosm as clearly as a fruit in the palm of his hand. Now it is said that through the Vajra-samādhi, one observes and sees the ten [directions].
That which is now refined, true, and profoundly clear—differing from the past—is because this sutra reveals and clarifies [the truth], and thus speaks by way of the inner secret.
Previously, when guiding sentient beings according to their capacities, it was taught by way of the manifest small [vehicle]. Wuxing said:
"The Āgamas speak of 'cultivating dhyāna' as a general and abbreviated indication; here, speaking of the 'Vajrasamādhi' specifically reveals its name. It does not mean that [it is] gold..."
"Vajra" is used as a metaphor for Great Samādhi; for example, when Ānanda entered the *vidyut-prabhā-samādhi* and severed his final afflictions of thought, it was also called the "Vajra Samādhi.
This, however, is merely a metaphor for the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the Hīnayāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) of Nandika consists of the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), and is pure over half the head. The Buddha’s divine eye consists of the four great elements and derived matter, and is pure throughout the entire head."
[The Buddha’s vision is] pure. The Tiantai Master Zhiyi said that in the Tripitaka [teachings], the Buddha’s physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) perceives everything without obstruction.
Thus we know that the designations "whole" and "partial" merely refer to the contrast between the incomplete and the complete; they do not differ in terms of being "small" or "great.

Furthermore, if one were to rely on the *Āgamas* where he observes the trichiliocosm, or this sutra where he sees the ten directions, to claim there is a superiority or inferiority [between these visions], it would certainly not be appropriate.

Furthermore, that sutra states: "Does not Nanda’s divine eye see the realms of the ten directions? Since the analogy of the fruit in the palm is identical, how can the expression "refined truth" differ?
The subsequent passage clarifies that even for the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, it is said that "refined truth is manifest before one, and its transformative molding is unimpeded.
How much more so for an Arhat who has manifested true outflowlessness; could it not be called "refined"?
Is this not truly and clearly so? To revolve one's views back to the source means to revolve the views of the great trichiliocosm back toward the discourse on true emptiness;
when seeing is exhausted and ignorance is ended, perfect penetration is attained.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the second section on the perfect penetration of the five faculties, this first explains the perfect penetration of the eye faculty.

First, it clarifies the general and specific aspects of its objects. Generally speaking, cognition arises because of sensory objects; thus, light, darkness, space, and obstruction are all objects manifested by the eye faculty.
Specifically, when the Venerable Aṭnāṭa lost both his eyes, the World-Honored One showed him the samādhi.

It is because of darkness that seeing exists. Second, regarding the expansion and contraction observed through light: the primary tenet explains the Buddha’s intent as it pertains to what was realized.
When Nanda heard the Buddha’s reproach, he wept and reproached himself, remaining awake for seven days until he lost both his eyes.
The World-Honored One revealed to him the Samādhi of the Adamantine Illumination of Delightful Vision, saying:
"I do not perceive the ten directions by means of the eyes. This is to lose the physical eye yet attain the celestial eye;

it is called the Samādhi of the Adamantine Illumination of Delightful Vision because one turns back from seeing to follow the source of vision, such that seeing is no longer seeing. From this, one attains Bodhi."
The path leads to the thorough penetration of the pure true reality (*dharmatā*). Second, regarding the brief analysis of names and characteristics:

this sutra explains the eternally abiding true mind (*nitya-citta*) in relation to the faculty of the eye with extreme detail. As at the beginning, it tests that the seeing is immovable by bending the fingers and flicking a light;
next, it shows that the seeing of the river does not shift from childhood to old age; and finally, it demonstrates that when one perceives the act of seeing itself, that seeing is not [the object].

This is the vision. However, all such instances are distinguished by contrasting it with the appearance of forms against empty space. If this Venerable One has already lost both eyes, then his vision must have returned to its source;
one should therefore clarify its nature by referring to the moment he perceives darkness. It must be understood that although the objects differ, the seeing itself remains without distinction.
For this reason, at the beginning of the assembly where the mind was brought back to its source, the World-Honored One demonstrated [the nature of] blindness.

When people perceive that this darkness is the mind and not the eye, they abide permanently within the ten categories [of the *Zhongyong*], where those without eyes share the same path as those with eyes.
By turning one's vision back toward this very state and tracing it to its source, it is called the "Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination.
Suddenly, the lacquer bucket is shattered, and the heavenly eye manifests in its entirety. Now, having attained half of it, it is said to reach as far as the eyebrows.
The superior [vision] can penetrate and see the great trichiliocosm. Regarding the three meanings related to the four teachings:

although Nanda was a śrāvaka, such a dharma-gate as this certainly does not involve the analytical breaking down of form (*rūpa-vibhāga*). However, because he attained the vision of emptiness, it is appropriate to call him a śrāvaka who "embodies the dharma" (*tǐfǎ*).

Furthermore, because he also saw that which is not empty—distinguishing between the *butianzhōng* (limited-middle) and the *bùdànzhōng* (unlimited-middle)—it is appropriate to call him one of the Distinct or Perfect [teachings]. This concludes the fourth assembly.
For those who return to the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], the Sūtra has already revealed its perfection; yet if one wishes to meet with it once more,

one may do so by citing the nature-as-seen-through-awakening-clarity, the awakening-as-seen-through-pure-clarity, and the pure-naturedness that pervades the Dharma-realm— thereby reaching its ultimate domain.

[2. Cūḍapanthaka Contemplates the Nose] (Part 1: Narrating the Circumstances of His Enlightenment) Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and possessed no nature for extensive learning.

When I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I could remember a single verse of the Tathāgata, yet after a hundred days, I would forget the latter part upon remembering the former, or forget the former part upon remembering the latter. The Buddha took pity on my folly and instructed me.”

During the summer retreat, I regulated my inhalation and exhalation. At that time, I observed the breath until it became subtle and reached its ultimate limit, exhausting all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—in every moment (*kṣaṇa*).
My mind suddenly opened up and attained great non-obstruction;

eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat, sitting beneath the Buddha’s seat and sealing myself as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). (2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, I reversed the breath and followed the void. This is my method.
"He is the foremost. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says: *Panthaka* here means "successor of the Way," referring to the bhikṣu Sūci. Chángshuǐ says:
*Tarka* is also called "Snake-Slave" (*Sarpa-dāsa*); he was born by the roadside. In the past, he was a great Dharma Master who was stingy with the Buddha's teachings.

Because he was unwilling to teach others in his past lives, he subsequently experienced dullness of intellect. Due to the merit of his former goodness, however, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life.
Although five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse for ninety days without success, the Buddha instructed him to practice counting the breaths to collect his mind;
through this, he attained realization.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the second explanation of the perfect penetration of the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya-pariśuddhi*). First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of its object.
Generally speaking, the nose is pervasive throughout both exhalation and inhalation; exhalation can grasp fragrance, while inhalation can smell fragrance.

Taking this as its functional capacity, [the practitioner] here does not take the grasped or the smelled as the object of contemplation, but specifically takes the grasper and the smeller as the object of contemplation.
Second, the explanation of the expansion and contraction of contemplation is divided into four parts. First, the core intent of the Buddha’s teaching is explained to clarify what has been realized.
However, this Venerable One, due to his past stinginess regarding the Buddha-dharma, received a retribution of dullness and lacked the nature of extensive learning.

The Buddha, pitying his ignorance, instructed him in the regulation of breath (*ānāpāna*). Since ignorance arises from mental distraction, the regulation of breath is the means by which that distraction is gathered and controlled. [From] the Sūtra...
It is said that if one places the mind in a single location, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished; by means of this, one attains concentration (*samādhi*) and becomes suddenly unimpeded.
This is called "reversing the breath and following emptiness," which constitutes the liberation of the six sense faculties once the faculty of the nose has returned to its source.

Second, to briefly clarify the terminology and characteristics for the sake of convenience: the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) serves as an essential gateway for entering the Way. As stated in various sutras...
The methods presented differ. Now, the Six Wondrous Gates of Dhyāna established by the Great Master Zhiyi are similar to this.
First, counting, and second, following, are the initial stages for regulating the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.

Third, cessation, and fourth, contemplation, involve contemplating the breath’s subtlety to exhaustively investigate the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—namely, their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. Fifth is returning.
The six purities are the reversal of the breath and the following of emptiness. 1. The Gate of Counting the Breath (*gaṇanā-mukha*).

Concentrating the mind upon the breath from one to ten is called counting. A practitioner who seeks to cultivate the true Dharma free from outflows must first harmonize the mind and enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Since the coarse and distracted states of the desire realm are difficult to restrain and cannot be pacified by anything other than counting, one must skillfully regulate the body and breath, beginning from one.

Upon reaching ten, coarse and distracted thoughts subside and the mind comes to rest; this is the essential method for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus counting the breath is considered the wondrous gateway.
2. The Gateway of Following the Breath (*Anāpānasmṛti*). Because the subtle mind relies on the breath to know its entry and exit, it is called "following.
Although the practitioner’s mind may abide due to counting the breath, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) has not yet arisen. If [the mind] still...
If one dwells upon counting, the mind incurs the fault of giving rise to discursive thoughts; therefore, one must relinquish counting and practice following (*anugama*).
When the mind rests upon the breath, one knows it as it enters when it enters, and knows it as it exits when it exits. One fully perceives its length, its shortness, its coolness, and its warmth.
If the mind becomes settled, bright, and pure, the various dhyānas will spontaneously arise through this means; thus, "following" is taken as the gateway. 3. The Gateway of Stopping (*sthāpanā*).

The stilling of the mind and tranquil contemplation is called *śamatha* (cessation). Although the practitioner, by means of following the breath, attains clarity and purity of mind, concentration has not yet been fully aroused.
If the mind remains dependent on [the breath], there will still be a slight disturbance of arising conceptualizations.

Nothing is more clear, stable, and peaceful than *śamatha*; therefore, one abandons the practice of following [the breath] and cultivates *śamatha*. Within this, the "stabilizing the mind" (*nirodha*) method of *śamatha* is primarily employed. Stabilizing the mind...

When the mind is stilled through contemplation and free from fluctuation, the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) will naturally unfold; therefore, "stopping" (*śamatha*) is taken as the gateway.
Fourth is the gateway of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). The mind that discriminates and analyzes is called contemplation.

Although a practitioner may realize the various meditative concentrations by means of stopping, if wisdom has not yet been awakened, then while abiding in a concentrated mind, there remains the flavoring attachment of ignorance.

This is incorrect; therefore, one must investigate and analyze it. Within this state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) that has been realized, there frequently arise the sixteen inverted views of "self" and so forth.

Once these are clearly discerned, one knows that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are deceptive and false. By destroying the four inversions, one employs the true contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
If one contemplates that the mind is non-existent, the expedient means of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state will thereby be developed. Therefore, by means of...

Contemplation is the gate. ○ Fifth, the gate of returning. To turn the mind back and reflect upon itself is called "returning. Although the practitioner cultivates contemplative observation, true illumination has not yet arisen.

If they calculate that there is a self capable of observing and thereby analyze and break down delusions of inversion, then the delusion of calculating a self will instead attach itself to the contemplation and arise from it, becoming identical to those of the external paths. Therefore, it is said: "These various external paths..."

If one becomes attached to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, one will not attain liberation. If one perceives this affliction, one should immediately turn the mind back to reflect upon the observing mind itself.
If one knows that the observing mind is illusory and lacks substantial reality, then the inversion of clinging to a self through attachment to contemplation will naturally vanish.
Consequently, the untainted expedient means will spontaneously become luminous; therefore, this is termed "returning."
Section Six: The Gate of Purity. When the mind has no basis and the waves of delusion do not arise, it is called "purity.

When a practitioner cultivates the practice of returning [to the source], although they may be able to break through the inversions of contemplation, if true illumination has not yet arisen and they dwell in a state devoid of subject and object, they will perceive sensation and mindfulness;
this causes the mental faculty to become turbid. Having realized this, one should neither dwell nor cling.

It becomes utterly pure and serene. Through the development of this true illumination, one immediately severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the triple world and realizes the path of the Three Vehicles.
Thus it is said: "One who attains a single-minded state of purity shall have all evils extinguished. The intent of taking purity as the gateway lies herein.
Third, regarding the meaning of the timing of the teaching in relation to the Four Teachings: as is commonly explained, this refers to the *Śūramgama-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Heroic Progress).

The method of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) belongs only to the Hīnayāna. However, the interpretation of the wise maintains that it penetrates all four teachings (*catur-yāna*), for a sutra states that *ānāpāna* is itself the Mahāyāna;
thus, whether it is Great or Small Vehicle depends on the person.

It is like a person of great merit who sees earth, stones, tiles, and rubble as nothing but precious jewels, whereas a person of meager merit, even upon seeing a hidden treasure, calls it a tiger or a snake.
He departed in haste. As for the convergence of the principles of the four schools of the Tripiṭaka into the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]:

from the perspective of reversing the breath and following emptiness, it is no different from the "nature-awareness as true emptiness" and "true awareness as nature-emptiness," which are primordially pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
From the perspective of exhausting the moments of all conditioned phenomena—birth, abiding, change, and cessation—one’s mind suddenly becomes clear and expansive.
Having attained great non-obstruction, his speech is such that the true wind of the nature of emptiness and the wind of the nature of emptiness are non-dual.

(3. The Vision of the Tongue of Kauṇḍinya-vatsīputra; Part 1: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) Kauṇḍinya-vatsīputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In past kalpas, I committed verbal karma by lightly mocking śramaṇas; consequently, in life after life, I have suffered from the disease of ruminating like an ox. The Tathāgata..."
I have attained this Dharma-door of the single-flavored, pure mind-ground; I have achieved the extinction of the mind and entered samādhi.

Observing the cognition of flavors, I find it is neither a substance nor a thing. In a single thought-moment, I transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*); internally, I am liberated from body and mind; externally, I leave behind the world.
Far removed from the three realms of existence, like a bird escaping its cage, defilements are dissolved and dust is wiped away. My Dharma-eye is purified, and I become an Arhat.

The Han Tathāgata personally sealed my attainment of the path beyond learning. (2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, returning the flavors and revolving the faculty of cognition is the foremost method.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: *Kauṇḍinya* (Gavāmpati) means "ox-chewer. Just as an ox often makes a hollow sound even when not eating, this man’s mouth made a sound like an ox’s rumbling;
it was a frivolous manifestation of his retribution. The Buddha, to ward off slander, gave him a rosary and commanded him to constantly recollect the Buddha.
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Mind-ground, by which one can extinguish mental conditions and attain [liberation].

One enters into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, by means of the teaching that observing the tongue-root tasting flavors leads one into the Way, one does not cling to mundane tastes and does not follow deluded cognition.
This is called "returning to flavor and revolving the cognition. Guishan said: "To realize that flavor is flavorless is called 'one-flavor' (*ekarasa*).
Although he mentions the object of flavor, it is intended to reveal the function of the tongue; therefore, he speaks of "observing the cognition of flavor. As for this capacity to know...
The tongue and the ear are not the substance of the tongue, nor are they the substance of flavors. Internally discarding body and mind is liberation of the primary retribution;
externally discarding the world is liberation of the environmental retribution.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the third explanation of the tongue faculty as the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.
Regarding the cognition of tasting flavors: generally speaking, it penetrates all flavors; specifically speaking, it resides within each of the five flavors.

This is precisely what is meant by the story of Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King), who manifested his inherent nature through the act of tasting medicine. Now, this Venerable One speaks of "observing the cognition of flavor. Although...

It is not necessary to distinguish between the universal and the particular; rather, one knows flavors with a distinct tongue. This "distinct tongue" is the particular, while "knowing flavors" is the universal.
This is an instance of the same principle as [the statement that] when it is universal, it is always particular, and when it is particular, it is always universal.

Second, clarifying the expansion and contraction of contemplation: first, the primary tenet explains the Buddha’s intent regarding what has been realized. For this Venerable One possessed the "ox-chewing" [habit].

When the Buddha was ill, he bestowed a rosary upon him to prevent slander, for people saw that he was reciting the Buddha’s name with his mouth and could not perceive any sign of "ox-chewing" (rumination).
This was the first way he prevented slander. Furthermore, because of the karmic retribution of his extraordinary tongue, this sensory object was most intimate to him.

The Buddha observed it from the perspective of what was currently manifest and intimate; by observing it, the mind became peaceful and the sensory object became still. When the sensory object is still, [the afflictions subside].
His tongue does not move, and there is no appearance of rumination whatsoever. This is the second point regarding the refutation of slander.

Furthermore, it is said that the cognition of taste is neither the substance nor the object; "substance" refers to the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), and "object" refers to the flavor-obstacle (*rasa-viṣaya*). Since flavors are of three kinds...

Sweetness, bitterness, and blandness are to be understood according to the preceding [analysis] in order to reveal the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*). One should investigate this by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Thus, when tasting bitterness or blandness, one knows that it does not come from sweetness, nor does it exist because of the blandness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from empty space (and so forth).
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is such that its teaching is invariably central; therefore, by reflecting upon this, one attains transcendence of all worldly outflows (*āsrava*).

One realizes that the cognition of flavor is neither the essence nor a substantial entity. Thus, internally one is liberated from body and mind; externally, one casts off the world as if it were not a thing.
One distances oneself from the three realms of existence like a bird escaping its cage—such is the joy of attaining liberation.

The names and characteristics may be known thus. Regarding the three meanings related to the four teachings: by contemplating that the cognition of flavor is neither the essence nor a substantial entity, one becomes an Arhat.

The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is now clear. If one takes the Middle Way as merely the substance, it becomes the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao); if one takes the Middle Way as the perfect substance, it becomes the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Regarding the four assemblies returning to the Perfect and Sudden: they clearly perceive that the nature of hearing and knowing is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving.
That very nature is ever-present, clearly aware, and luminously pure; it is fundamentally quiescent and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

(4. Conclusion of the Contemplation of the Body, Part 2: Initial Account of the Conditions for Awakening) Piliṅgavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

I reflected that there must be a cognizer who knows this deep pain; though I am aware of the awareness of the pain, the awareness is pure, and within the mind there is neither pain nor the awareness of pain.
I further contemplated: how could there be two simultaneous cognitions in such a single body? Before long, as I focused my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty for twenty-one days.
In midday, all outflows were exhausted in emptiness as I became an Arhat; I received the seal of personal certification and manifested the state of No-more-learning. (2.
Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, that which I have realized—pure awareness transcending the body—is the foremost.

Generally speaking, sensations such as cold, heat, pain, and itchiness all belong to the body-faculty; here, however, he specifically takes the sensation of pain as the object. Second...

Clearly contemplating its expansion and contraction, one first clarifies the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teachings to explain what has been realized. One frequently hears the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be enjoyed;
generally speaking, these are the eight types of suffering. One contemplates these phenomena that are not to be enjoyed.
When one encounters an unpleasant object, the entire body experiences pain, which is inherently suffering. One whose every thought remains fixed on the Path does not cling to this pain;
rather, they take that very pain as their meditative object. This object is most intimate. One observes it with contemplation, examines it, and investigates it.
As it is said: "I am mindful and possess cognition; I know this deep pain. That which knows the pain is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
It is the sensation-object of painful touch. At first, one perceives this perceived painful touch through the awakening of the body-faculty;

the perceiver and the perceived are clearly distinct. This is the first point for examining one's doubts. Precisely at such a time, one further awakens to the fact that the pure true mind is fundamentally devoid of both subject and object.
Therefore it is said: "Though one awakens to the awareness of pain, one awakens to the pure mind as being without [subject and object]."
The sensation of pain is perceived. This is the second point of my critical inquiry into doubt. Furthermore, I reflect: how could there be two simultaneous sensations within this single body?
That is to say, a single body possesses only one sensation. How could there be one sensation that possesses both subject and object, and another sensation that lacks both subject and object?
This is the third point of my critical inquiry into doubt. As for the Dharma taught by the Buddha...
He administered medicine according to the capacity of each individual, knowing that their faculties were ripe and they would surely attain awakening through this.
Anticipating that they would encounter painful sensations, he preached the Dharma on the nature of things as being undesirable to guide them forward.

Thus, after a short time of investigating doubt, examining himself, and collecting his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty; within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted and he attained realization.
"Arhat! This is the dharma-gate of the pure awakening that leaves behind the body. Someone asked:

"Regarding 'pure awakening,' is there a distinct pure awakening that exists apart from the awakening of subject and object? Or is it the very awakening of subject and object that constitutes pure awakening?
He replied: "It is both identical with and separate from; it is both separate from and identical with—this is called pure awakening. Why? If..."
If it exists as something separate, how could there be a dual awareness within this single body?

If it exists as something identical, then since the pure mind of awareness is free from pain, there would be no awareness of pain. One must realize that the awareness of subject and object is fundamentally devoid of subject and object.
To awaken to this is called "pure awareness. Regarding its relation to the four teachings: although it is like the realization of the Venerable Śrīlāta, [the text continues...]
In Xuánzàng’s preface to the *Sādhana*, it is clearly established that the realization of the body of the Arhat pertains to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
