"The awakening to touch and the awakening to cognition are of wondrous virtue, brilliantly radiant, pervading the Dharma-realm and filling the ten directions; how could there be any fixed location? This is the non-empty-as-emptiness (*śūnyatā-aśūnyatā*).
This is the Perfect Enlightenment of the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*.

(5. The Contemplative Intent of the Five Emptinesses; Part Two: First, Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Throughout kalpas past, my mind has attained non-obstruction. I recall my successive births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; even while first in my mother’s womb, I already knew emptiness and stillness."
In this way, even until the ten directions become empty, he causes sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness;
they receive the Tathāgata’s awakening to the true emptiness of their nature, and through the perfect clarity of that emptiness, they attain Arhatship.

They suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-bright emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and are sealed as those of the stage of no-more-learning whose nature is empty. I am the Unsurpassed One. (2. Restating the Evidence and Concluding the Answer) The Buddha asked about the Perfect...
"Penetratingly, as I have realized, all marks enter into that which is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; when the non-existent is exhausted, phenomena revolve back to the Unconditioned—this is the foremost.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Among all the Śrāvakas, it was only this Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti), along with the three below him, Śāriputra, Pūrṇa, and Maitreya..."
When people recount their past causes, they say, "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind has attained non-obstruction," and so forth;

yet when discussing what they have realized, they are merely Arhats. The distinction between the provisional and the ultimate is not easily discerned. One should attempt to resolve this by clarifying two points:
first, if one relies on the claim that the mind attained non-obstruction since the beginningless kalpas, it would seem to refer to the period prior to this present body.

Having once attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), you have now encountered the Buddha and been inspired to awaken to your inherent nature; this is certainly not the path of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

This is likely because, during the past period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, amidst the censure and refinement [of those with inferior capacities], you heard the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) openly and secretly realized its Great Way.

Since you have already entered the provisional means (*upāya*), the manifestation of your realization of the ultimate truth (*bhūtārtha*) is now evident; thus, the title of "Arhat" is identical to that of the Dharma.

Huāzhēn was indeed an Arhat. Second, if one interprets this according to the principle of inner secrecy and outer manifestation, taking it as a provisional teaching, there is likewise reason for such an explanation.
This is because a Śrāvaka who has attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) can know events of eighty thousand kalpas;
thus, speaking in reverse order of what he perceives is called "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*). Although it is said that while in the womb he knew emptiness, and so forth...
Because he had not yet severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) despite having realized his nature, it was only upon receiving the Buddha’s inspiration that he became an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*).

If this is so, then from the passage on "awakening to the true emptiness of nature" down to the later section on "profoundly penetrating the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is no fault in interpreting these according to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) school.
There are many such instances where the names are identical but the underlying substance differs. Thus, Master Yuan also maintained that [the monk] saw the Buddha in the stone chamber.
The *Fashen* (Dharma-body) commentary explains this meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Zizhong says: "First, by means of single emptiness, one empties all marks;

therefore it is said that 'all marks enter into non-being. Next, by means of double emptiness, one empties the mark of emptiness itself; therefore it is said that 'that which is non-being is also exhausted.'"

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the five explanations of the faculty of mind (*manas*) as the universal penetration (*yuan-tong*), the first clarifies the universality and particularity of its objects.

The mental objects (*dharmas*) perceived by the faculty of mind, when categorized by their nature, do not exceed the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). If one employs the samādhis of various sūtras to break through them, they are each perceived according to whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral;
thus, the objects are particular. [In contrast,] the Tiantai "Awakening the Mind" (*jue-yi*) samādhi involves three matters...
The objects of all conditions are universally pervasive. Now, this "Perfect Penetration" (Yuan-tong) does not specify which particular nature it conditions;

rather, it simply speaks of "revolving phenomena back into non-existence," which is an observation made from a universal perspective. Second, clarifying the expansion and contraction of the contemplation:

first, following the fundamental intent of the Buddha, he explains what he has realized, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind has attained unimpededness; thus it continues... up to the tenth [stage].

Only then is emptiness truly established. Thus, it is clear that this Venerable One has long used the contemplation of emptiness to empty his own mental objects (*dharmas*). His station in the stage of "understanding and practice" (*adhimukti-caryā*) is evident.
Furthermore, he causes sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness; this is to teach people by means of the dharma of emptiness so that they may shatter their delusions and realize emptiness.
Having received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the true emptiness of the fundamental nature, his realization of the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness was attained.
Only upon becoming an Arhat does one finally enter and personally realize the stage of the Path within this world.
To suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness and share in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—wherein does the teaching lead?

It is simply because one attains the seal of Arhatship that the nature of liberation is perfected as non-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and emptiness; regarding this as my supreme contemplation, who among those of the former Hīnayāna could [attain it]?
It is not said that being born from the Buddha’s own mouth, being transformed by birth from the Dharma, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are themselves merely empty.

As for the statement that “all marks enter non-being”: the various marks refer to the objects of the mind (dharma-dhātu); to “enter non-being” is to enter emptiness. Regarding “that which is negated is exhausted”:
it means that not only are the marks that are negated exhausted, but the emptiness that performs the negation is also empty. As for the object...
This means that just as fire burns all the wood and fuel and then naturally extinguishes itself, the meaning pertains to the four teachings.
Since what is described therein does not speak of analyzing the substance of dharmas to reveal their emptiness, it is clear [this refers to the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings].

If one elucidates the Middle Way and the nature-awareness of true emptiness, then one receives the transition from the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. Thus, returning to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching becomes perfectly clear.
To realize that nature is true emptiness and that true emptiness is nature, and that this purity is inherently so and pervades the entire Dharma-realm—
remaining unchanging while following conditions, and following conditions while remaining unchanged— is to enter the principle of the equality of emptiness as taught in this sutra.

[Section Three: Awakening through Contemplation of the Six Consciousnesses] [Part One: Śāriputra’s Contemplation of the Eye-Consciousness] [Sub-part One: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening] Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, my mind and vision have been pure. Thus have I taken birth, and through various mundane and supramundane transformations, a single glance has brought me universal penetration and the attainment of non-obstruction. While traveling on the road, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa, who were walking together."
He proclaimed the causes and conditions for awakening to the boundlessness of the mind;

he left the household life under the Buddha, beheld the perfect clarity of enlightenment, attained great fearlessness, and became an Arhat as the Buddha’s eldest son—born from the Buddha’s mouth and born through transformation from the Dharma. (2.

Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the mind and vision emit light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing; this is the foremost.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The mind sees" refers to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). That "the light of the mind's seeing shines forth, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing" means that through the illumination of the mind's seeing, one manifests a perfect illumination of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom and preeminent in his reputation for virtue;
therefore, he is called the "eldest son. Wǔxīng says: [This refers to] the realm of the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) of both the mundane and supramundane worlds. Of various kinds...
This refers to the characteristics of transformation, arising, and ceasing. Because visual consciousness is clear and sharp, it is said that "upon seeing once, one attains penetration," and so forth;
this is stated for the time being in terms of intellectual understanding. Master Yuan (Yuán) remarked:

"Other sutras all state that Śāriputra encountered Aśvajit on the road and, upon hearing that 'all phenomena arise from conditions,' attained realization of the Way. Why does this [text] say he encountered Kāśyapa? That [account] was in relation to the Small Vehicle..."

It is said that those of limited capacity hear only the Lesser Dharma, whereas those of great capacity hear the Great Way; since what they hear differs, the persons from whom they hear must also differ.
This, however, is likely not the case. Considering Śāriputra’s status as a householder prior to the twelve years [of the Buddha’s teaching], one cannot allow the person to differentiate the Dharma.
Moreover, the present text states that hearing the exposition of the meaning of causes and conditions is the same as [hearing it] from Aśvajit.
The expression "dependent origination" refers to awakening to the boundlessness of the mind, which is the Path of Seeing of the first fruit (*srotāpatti*).

Thus, the Āgamas clarify that upon first hearing the Dharma taught by Aśvajit, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and subsequently, upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, one thoroughly masters the Buddha-dharma within seven days.
It is further stated that one attains Arhatship after fifteen days. Judging from this, the statement that "the clarity of insight becomes perfect" is also spoken from a provisional perspective.
If one were to provide a grand interpretation, the aforementioned awakening of the mind would have to encompass all four fruits of realization;

it is only when one subsequently becomes an Arhat that they truly receive their name. Tianru’s *Supplementary Notes* states: "Other sutras say that Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others [attained it]..."

If Aśvajit heard that the meaning of *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) differed from what is explained here, it may be that the teachings on the meaning of dependent origination were not limited to a single person, but were mutually presented by various individuals.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Within the third section on the perfect penetration of the six consciousnesses, this first explains the perfect penetration of the eye-consciousness. First, it clarifies...

Regarding the general and specific aspects of the object-field (*viṣaya*): generally, one discriminates between light, darkness, form, and space; specifically, one takes one of these four as an object.
However, form is manifested through these three factors—light, darkness, and space; thus, by mentioning "form," the other three are already included. Within form, there are no more than five types.
Taking all five types of form as objects is called "general" (*sāmānya*); taking each one individually is called "specific" (*viśeṣa*). Now...
As for its objects of perception, their scope is even broader, comprising a portion of the ten bases (*āyatana*).

It does not only take form as its object, but also takes mind as its object, because it perceives all four truths. This is because it belongs to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and is distinct from the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
Next, the expansion and contraction of contemplation are clarified. First, the core intent of the Buddha’s teaching is explained to interpret what has been realized.
Since it is said, "My mind and vision have been pure throughout kalpas of antiquity," this cultivation based on visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is certainly not limited to a single lifetime.

What is called "purity" means that [the mind] does not engage in the discrimination of objects through the conditions of visual consciousness. The causes and effects of the twenty-five states of existence constitute worldly phenomena. Three...
Riding upon cause and effect constitutes the supramundane Dharma. When one discriminates based on sensory objects, suffering is seen as suffering and its accumulation as the origin;
thus the Path and Cessation are not perceived. It is precisely because one perceives the mundane dharmas in a single view and knows them to be suffering that one cuts off their origin;
conversely, this constitutes the cultivation of the Path and the realization of Cessation. Therefore it is said: "In a single view, one attains penetration and is free from obstruction. Nevertheless—

However, although one may practice based on this alone, true realization has not yet been attained. Thus, while traveling upon this worldly path, one encounters a virtuous friend who proclaims the teachings on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), whereby one awakens to the boundless nature of the mind.
Indeed, causes and conditions serve as the marvelous medicine of a new physician for destroying false views. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, who was not practicing?
Yet in the end, it was like the medicine of an old physician—it lacked superior efficacy. Therefore, one must encounter the "Golden Scalpel" (*Suvarṇa-śalākā*).
The cataracts are instantly dissolved. To see and perceive is the mind seeing; though at first one sees and perceives, one has not yet attained luminous perfection.

Now that you have awakened to the mind, you possess great fearlessness. When it is said that "the mind-seeing emits light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowledge and vision," it means that once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties become fearless. This is identical to the dharma-gate of Nalakūvara.
As for the differences: the samādhi of the eye-faculty takes non-discrimination as its function, and is thus called "revolving the vision and following the source.
The samādhi of the eye-consciousness takes discrimination as its efficacy, and is thus said to be "the mind-vision emitting light, where the light reaches its limit in knowing and seeing."
Regarding the three meanings as they relate to the four teachings: according to the single perspective of "seeing," one universally attains non-obstruction;

this refers to the essence of the teaching, which clarifies that phenomena are empty. If one realizes that phenomena are themselves the Middle Way, one should understand that this encompasses the Distinct and Perfect teachings, as well as their respective stages of transition.

Regarding those who return to the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]: if one integrates this through the principle of the Treasury [of the Tathāgata], then the nature-consciousness is luminous awareness and the awareness of luminosity is the true consciousness;
this wondrous awakening is profoundly still, encompassing and exhaling the ten voids—how could it have any spatial location?

[2. Universal Worthy’s Contemplation of the Ear-Consciousness] (Part 1: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I have previously served as a Dharma Prince to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions instructed their disciples whose faculties were those of bodhisattvas, they taught them to cultivate the practices of Universal Worthy;
thus, I was named after him. World-Honored One, I employ the hearing of the mind to discern the various states of sentient beings.”
If there is one who possesses knowledge and vision such that they perceive, even beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions,
a single sentient being who has awakened the practice of Samantabhadra within their heart, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of emanations,
arriving at that very place. Even if that person’s obscurations are so deep that they do not yet behold me, I will secretly stroke their crown, protect them, and comfort them.

Regarding its accomplishment: (2. Citing the testimony and concluding the answer) The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; I have explained my fundamental cause. Through the illumination of "hearing with the mind," discernment became sovereign;
this is the foremost.

[Commentary] Xielǐ says: "Pervading the entire dharma-realm" is called *pú* (universal). "Ranking adjacent to the ultimate sages" is called *xián* (worthy). This is not the worthiness of those prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*);
rather, it refers to the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), where one dwells at the summit of all those who have subdued their afflictions—this is what is termed "Worthy.
Wēnlíng says: Generally, anyone who possesses great roots and cultivates the bodhisattva path is said to perform the practices of Samantabhadra. [This is] heard by the mind and heard by the ear.
It is consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Discriminating the knowledge and vision of sentient beings" means selecting the practices of Samantabhadra and bringing them to fulfillment.
Gusuan says: "The mind-hearing that brings forth illumination is internal realization; discriminating with sovereign mastery is external function."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: There are two explanations regarding the perfect penetration of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of its objects.

While the discernment of ear-consciousness is restricted to sound alone—this meaning being limited—this Bodhisattva states, "I employ the hearing of the mind to discern all the cognitions and views of sentient beings.
This meaning, therefore, should pervade all six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). As it is said, "to know... [and so forth].
When seen, it pervades the objects of the dharma-dhātu; if one prostrates and recites the name, such that it can evoke the Bodhisattva, then it pervades form and sound.

The rest may be understood by analogy. Second, explaining the expansion and contraction of contemplation: first, according to the primary school, I shall explain the intent of the Buddha’s teachings regarding what is realized.
Although Mañjuśrī says that "hearing with the mind penetrates the ten directions," this arises from the power of great causes and is not the skillful means of the initial mind.
While it may be said that this does not apply to the skillful means of the initial mind in the Sahā world, how could there be an end to that which has no beginning?
Therefore, among the hundred and eight samādhis of the *Śūraṅgama*, there is the samādhi that discriminates the number of dharmas and sentient beings; this is essential.
One should know that in the discernment of all sentient beings through the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), there is likewise a process from the subtle to the manifest.

When the mirror is pure, clarity arises and its essence manifests of itself. If one were to discuss the similarities and differences between this and the "ear-hearing" of Avalokiteśvara, there are three distinctions:

first, the difference in cause, which refers to the skillful means of the initial mind; second, the difference in object, which refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*); and third, the difference in hearing, which refers to the uprooting of suffering.

Regarding the preceding four teachings, the definitive point lies in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Since the entire body is the *tathāgatagarbha* nature (*zangxing*), there is no need for further reconciliation.

(3. Sudhana Observes Nose-Consciousness, Part Two: First, Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) Sudhana Nanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first left home and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated within *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained [realization]."
The World-Honored One, who is free from outflows, instructed me and Kūṭadanta to contemplate the white [light] at the tip of the nose.
When I first began this earnest contemplation, after three weeks had passed, I saw the breath entering and exiting through my nostrils like smoke. Within my body and mind there was inner clarity;

the world became a perfectly hollow and transparent sphere, as pure as lapis lazuli. As the appearance of smoke gradually vanished, the nasal breath became white, the mind opened, and the outflows were exhausted. Thus did I emerge.
The inhalation was transformed into radiance that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions; I attained Arhatship, and the World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Bodhi.

(2. Citation of evidence and conclusion of the answer) The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; I replied that by dissolving the inhalations, after a long time clarity arose, becoming perfectly full and extinguishing the outflows—this is the foremost method.
[Commentary] Gushan says: *Sundarī* means "beautifully beloved"; it is the name of his wife. *Nanda* means "joy"; it is his own name.
At Ci'en Monastery, both names are translated as "Glorious Joy. To distinguish him from Nanda the cowherd, [the text] specifies his wife;
he was, in fact, the Buddha’s own younger brother. Wénlíng says: The preceding practice of counting breaths relies on the sense organs (*indriya*) in order to collect the mind.

This contemplation on white is based on consciousness; it is for the purpose of stabilizing the mind. Respiration arises from wind and fire, and because it stirs up the turbidity of afflictions, its appearance is like smoke.
Those who are deluded do not perceive this, but through diligent observation one can see it.

When the six elements interact, the fire of perception burns the breath, producing black smoke and purple flames; these are all manifestations of afflictive turbidity. When pure contemplation brings forth illumination, however, [the state changes].
Because turbidity gradually subsides, the interior becomes clear while the exterior is empty; as the smoke vanishes, it becomes white.
When the outflows are exhausted and afflictions no longer exist, the inner clarity emits light, and thus the inhalation and exhalation are transformed into radiance. Wuxing said:
"By observing the nose-consciousness, it resembles the development of the sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*) of dhyāna. This dhyāna begins with the knowledge of the exhalation."
Entering [the stages] up to and including the contemplation of relinquishment encompasses the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because one is able to perceive the realized realms of the three worlds and nine stages, it is said that "one thoroughly penetrates the world" and so forth.

Furthermore, because within each stage one uses contemplative observation to realize and shatter the four inversions, thereby giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), it is said that "the mind opens and outflows are exhausted" and so forth. This may also be considered a general [attainment].

The characteristics of the transmission of illumination (*prabhāsvara*) are fully contained within the gate of *śāsana*. The record was then sealed and authenticated; it remains thus even now. *Bodhi* means "the Way.

As stated in the preceding text regarding "attaining the personal seal and record (*mudrā-śāsana*) and manifesting the realization of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)," if one were to interpret this as a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that one shall attain the fruit of *bodhi* in the future, it would then refer to either the secret prediction of the two *sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Avataṃsaka*) or the explicit prediction of the *Amṛta* (the *Lotus Sūtra*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: There are three explanations regarding the perfect penetration of the nose-consciousness. First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of its object.

The nose takes smelling fragrance as its function and governing the breath as its gateway; this is the general object. Now, for the purpose of treating distraction, one contemplates the white light at the tip of the nose;

this is not originally the primary object, as it is merely that which is confronted by the eyes. However, the concluding text of the contemplation states: "I have extinguished the breath... [and so forth].
It has long been clarified that this constitutes the primary object of focus.

Is it not the case that one first borrows the white [mark] at the tip of the nose as a condition to make the mind subtle, and subsequently uses this as a basis to observe the breath? Next, the expansion and contraction of the observation are explained.
First, following the Buddha’s intent, the realization is interpreted: for those whose minds are constantly distracted and moving during *samādhi*, once the object of focus...

Because there are many [distractions], the mind is not unified. To unify the mind by observing the white at the tip of the nose means that when the mind is placed in a single location, there is nothing it cannot accomplish;
this is the primary gateway for treating mental scattering. After a long time, the mind naturally becomes subtle.

When the mind is subtle, the inhalation and exhalation of the breath become self-evident. The breath is driven by the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*), which stirs up the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore—
The scattering and movement of the mind are governed by the wind of the breath.

It is for this reason that the contemplation of the realm, the world, the body, and the mind by Vairocana-prabha—wherein all movements are non-dual and are merely driven by the power of the wind of delusive conditions—is the sublime gateway for treating such scattering.
After twenty-one days, one will see the breath entering and exiting through the nostrils like smoke. Up to this point...
When the contemplation is perfected, all inhalations and exhalations are transformed into radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions.
This may be studied alongside the two methods of Vairocanaprabha and Ucchuṣma. Briefly explaining the names and characteristics:

this is the *ṣoḍaśānupūrvasamāpatti* (the sixteen stages of special excellence), which is the meditation of the sixteen special victories (*ṣoḍaśaviśeṣa-dhyāna*). 1. Knowing the inhalation is the beginning of practicing the special victory; it is precisely based on following the breath.
Therefore, taking the awareness of the inhalation as the gateway serves as a substitute for the initial method of counting breaths to harmonize the mind.
The reason for this is that when one counts the breaths, the mind remains obscured by the act of counting, and thus contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) is not clear;

whereas now, by being aware of the inhalation, the breath is clearly illuminated, and thus liberating wisdom (*prajñā*) easily arises. For this reason, the awareness of the inhalation is employed as the method for harmonizing the mind.

If one were to correlate the sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*) with the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), then from "knowing the inhalation" onwards, there are five stages of special excellence that belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Second, "knowing the exhalation":

for one practicing the stages of special excellence, this knowledge of the exhalation should replace the counting of breaths; this is the initial method for regulating the mind. The meaning is as explained previously. If [this] is correlated...
The foundations of mindfulness still belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Third, knowing the length and shortness of the breath:
those who cultivate the *viśeṣa* (special) method rely on contemplation to regulate the mind. Once the mind is purified and subtle, its illumination gradually becomes clear.

If one attains coarse abiding (*sthūla-sthiti*), subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-sthiti*), and the concentration of desire (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), the obscurations within that concentration will thin out, and one will immediately perceive the long and short duration of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.

This is the mark (*nimitta*). If contrasted with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). 4. Knowing that the breath pervades the entire body:
Those who practice the *viśeṣa-vidarśana* (special insight) enter the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) supported by the meditative absorption of desire (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).

Therefore, upon realizing the stage of not-yet-reached concentration, they perceive that both the body and the dharmas of concentration are entirely empty and false. The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pervade [the body].
The body becomes as if slightly present and as if non-existent; since one clearly perceives within meditative concentration, the mind of defiled attachment becomes thin.

If this is categorized among the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the application of mindfulness regarding the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). ○ Fifth, the removal of all bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*):

One who cultivates the *viśeṣa-mārga* (the path of distinction) should constantly practice analytical observation from the stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) when intending to enter the first dhyāna. Because of this, if [the breath] should arise...
When the factors of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna arise, the body and mind suddenly become clear and luminous.

It is like a person with clear vision opening a granary and immediately seeing clearly everything within it. One discerns that the realized realm is entirely false and empty, devoid of self or person (*pudgala*).
Since there is no self or person, who performs these various activities, and who receives the meditative absorption? This, then, is a perversion.
All bodily actions that have arisen are completely destroyed; therefore, it is said, "removing all bodily activities.

If one correlates this with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Sixth, regarding the joy of feeling (*vedanā-sukha*):

Since those who cultivate the "Special Excellence" (*viśeṣa*) are constantly associated with contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), they are able to clearly discern it as soon as they realize the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*) of the first dhyāna. Because of this joy, no fault arises.

Therefore, it is said that one "experiences joy. If, in relation to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are these three special excellences (*viśeṣa*), they all belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
○ Seventh, experiencing pleasure: One who cultivates the special excellences is constantly in association with contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).

When realizing the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*) upon attaining the first dhyāna, one is immediately able to discern it and thus does not give rise to views or attachments regarding that factor of pleasure. Because [there is no...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*

Because one experiences the sensation of pleasant contact, it is called "experiencing pleasure. If this is categorized according to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

○ Eighth, regarding the various mental activities: since those who cultivate the *viśeṣa* (special) [meditation] are constantly supported by contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), when they realize the factor of "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*) in the first dhyāna, they are immediately able to illuminate and understand that this one-pointedness does not give rise to perversions. Regarding this one...
Because one attains correct meditative absorption within the mind, it is said that "one experiences all mental activities.

If this is compared to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). 9. Generating Joy in the Mind:

When one who practices *viśeṣa-labdha* (the distinguished attainment) leaves the first dhyāna and enters the second dhyāna, they constantly maintain self-illumination and awareness. Consequently, if the inner purity and joy of the second dhyāna arise, it is true joy.
Because it arises from the wisdom of contemplation, it is called "the mind producing joy.

When applied to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these three special excellences (*viśeṣa*) all belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the mind. 10. The Mind Producing Concentration:

Having attained the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) of the second dhyāna through the wisdom of contemplation while practicing the special excellences, one thereby illuminates and realizes this one-pointedness of mind. Consequently, inverted perceptions (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*) do not arise.

Therefore, it is said that the mind performs the act of gathering. If this is contrasted with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
○ Eleven: The Mind Performs Liberation. One who cultivates the "Special Excellence" (*viśeṣa*) enters the third dhyāna from the second dhyāna while maintaining constant contemplative observation.

For this reason, upon arising in the third dhyāna, one is immediately able to illuminate and realize [the truth]. Although one attains sublime bliss, the mind does not become attached to it, remaining free from entanglement.

Because it is sovereign, it is said that "the mind creates liberation. If one correlates this with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Twelfth, the Contemplation of Impermanence: Those who cultivate the *viśeṣa* (special) [meditation] constantly practice contemplative observation when departing from the third dhyāna to enter the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, when the immovable concentration (*āniñjya-samādhi*) of the fourth dhyāna arises, they immediately observe and penetrate the state within that concentration.
Because the mind-consciousness is deceptive and arises and ceases moment by moment, it is called "contemplating impermanence.

If one proceeds from the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are five further "special excellences" (*viśeṣa*), all of which belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). ○ Thirteenth: Contemplating the Emergence and Dispersion.

When one who practices the special excellences enters the sphere of infinite space from the fourth dhyāna, they further cultivate contemplative wisdom to illuminate both internally and externally. This is...

Therefore, when one realizes the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one knows that the consciousness which can detach from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and takes emptiness as its object is freely dispersed, deceptive, and unreal;
because the mind does not feel attachment, it is called "contemplating emergence and dispersion.

If categorized according to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). ○ Fourteenth: Contemplating Detachment from Desire. Those who cultivate the *viśeṣa-labdha* [special attainment] detach from the unreal.
When entering the sphere of infinite consciousness from the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, one constantly uses the wisdom of contemplation to examine within oneself.

With the desire to leave behind the sphere of infinite space, the mind becomes free from craving; therefore, one gives rise to the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Because one is then able to contemplate and penetrate that the concentration of consciousness is empty, deceptive, and unreal, and the mind does not harbor attachment, it is called "contemplating the departure from craving.
If categorized according to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this still belongs to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Contemplation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. Fifteenth, Contemplation of Cessation.

When one who practices *viśeṣa-uttara* (the Distinctive Excellence) leaves the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and enters the Sphere of Nothingness, they use wisdom to clearly illuminate both the object being cultivated and the mind that cultivates it.

Therefore, as soon as the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness arises, they personally observe and penetrate that the Sphere of Nothingness is deceptive and unreal; because the mind does not dwell in attachment to it.

This is called the contemplation of cessation. If it is contrasted with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it still belongs to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the abandonment of the sixteen contemplations:

when one who cultivates the "special excellence" (*viśeṣa*) enters the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by departing from nothingness, they personally observe with wisdom both the dharma being cultivated and the mind that cultivates it. Therefore, if the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises, [one observes it].
At that time, one clearly contemplates and realizes that even the meditative absorption of equanimity in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception still possesses subtle perception;
that it arises from the combination of the four aggregates and is thus deceptive, unreal, and not the true Dharma of the blissful Nirvana. Thus, the mind does not become attached to it.
For a practitioner of the "Special Attainment" (viśeṣa-bhāgīya), if they cultivate contemplation and achieve clear realization at each stage, then for each stage—

Without giving rise to inverted views in the interim, the mind remains unstained by attachment. Following the convergence of its causes and conditions, one immediately gives rise to true, outflow-free wisdom upon this ground and realizes the path of the Three Vehicles.
This concludes the brief explanation of the distinctive excellence; for when words are too few, the intended meaning is difficult to perceive.

The reader must carefully compare these points to understand that, although the stages within each level and the fundamental dhyānas and four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) may appear similar at first glance, there are distinctions in their contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*). Regarding the third point, the omission of the four teachings from the perspective of realized fruit:
it is stated that one "attains the fruit of Arhatship," yet it is also said that one "shall attain Bodhi. This refers to the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-yāna*).
The realization that all phenomena are empty is clear. If one realizes that phenomena are themselves the Middle Way, then one receives the guidance of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
For those who ultimately return to the Perfect and Sudden, the wind-element is the fundamental nature-wind; the turbidity of afflictions is the fundamental nature-fire;
and the nose-consciousness is the fundamental nature-consciousness—all are fundamentally the wondrous true thusness of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is like the nature of purity, fundamentally such and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Upāli Contemplates the Body-Consciousness, Part Two: First, Narrating the Conditions for Awakening) Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all the māras."
I have subdued all non-Buddhists and liberated myself from worldly greed and the outflows (*āsrava*).

Having received the Buddha’s teachings and precepts, I have purified everything down to the three thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle categories of natural and proscribed offenses (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), until my body and mind were stilled and I became an Arhat.
I am the pillar of the Tathāgata’s assembly; he personally sealed my heart, and I maintain the precepts and cultivate the person.

The assembly acclaimed him as supreme. (2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; I replied that by clinging to the body, I attained mastery over the body, and by successively clinging to the mind, I attained penetration of the mind;
thereafter, both body and mind became universally efficacious, and thus this was ranked first.
[Commentary] Gushan says: Upāli is translated here as "Foremost" (*śreṣṭha*), because by upholding the Vinaya, he served as the guiding framework for the assembly.
Alternatively, it is translated as "Attendant" (*upasthāyaka*), because when the Buddha was a crown prince, he served as his close attendant official.

Wenglun says: The terms "intimate follower," "intimate observer," and even "receiving the teachings" all clarify that the physical consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) reverently received [the instructions].

Furthermore, there are two hundred and fifty rules of discipline (*vinaya*) for each of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. When these are applied to the three categories (*tripuñja*), they become three thousand.

These three thousand are then multiplied by the seven branches of body and speech to become twenty-one thousand. Finally, when these are applied to the four types of afflictions (*kleśa*), they become eighty-four thousand.

Regarding the "intrinsic offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, these are rooted in one's nature. As for the "prohibited offenses" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), namely...
Regarding the prevention of faults arising from the transgressions of the branches and the extremities: in the Vinaya, Upāli was foremost in attaining mastery;

among the Saṃgha, Dharmapāla (Cen-na) was the first to attain mastery. Therefore, in this hall, the altar for Dharmapāla is placed, and the altar for Upāli is placed, each establishing its own foundation.
Wuxing said: "Master Yuan [Zhiyi] held that the mind follows a sequential order, because it is through the purity of the precepts (*śīla*) that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arises."

This refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). This [interpretation] is likely incorrect. As the subsequent text states: "First, one maintains the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules of the Śrāvaka, holding the body motionless;
later, one practices the pure discipline (*vinaya*) of the Bodhisattva, holding the mind so that it does not arise.

Thus, it is clear that "holding the mind" is not established by means of both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Nevertheless, the assignment of body and mind to the Great and Small Vehicles is based on the distinction between the coarse and the subtle.
This is divided according to their respective scopes. It is not that the Bodhisattva does not restrain the body; nor is it that the Śrāvaka does not guard the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

For instance, when the various *Varga* (collections) prescribe the preliminary practices (*pūrva-prayoga*) for distancing oneself from unwholesome states, are these not matters of the mental ground? What is being described here specifically refers to the "small" [vehicle].
Therefore, by governing the body and mind from the coarse to the subtle, one guards against the subtlety of bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). Once bodily consciousness has ceased, the truth...
Wisdom manifests before one. This is what is meant by: "When the precepts are pure and wisdom is present, one attains the foremost path.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the fifth explanation regarding the perfect penetration of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). First, he clarifies the general and particular aspects of its objects.
Speaking generally, body-consciousness discriminates between tactile sensations that accord with the emotions, those that oppose the emotions, and those that are neither—neutral sensations.
Regarding this contact: now, by upholding the precepts and restraining the body, one attains mastery over the body.

One abandons favorable contact and relies solely upon adverse contact, remaining cautious and diligent, so as not to fall into indeterminate contact as a distinct object of perception. Next, the expansion and contraction of contemplation is clarified;

first, the fundamental tenets and the Buddha’s intent are explained to interpret what has been realized. First, the reliance on the body and consciousness is described, reverently receiving [the teachings] as they are.

Come. Next, we shall describe the reliance on the body-consciousness to uphold the precepts; the explanation of their meaning may be understood as it was previously. Next, to briefly clarify the terminology and characteristics:
although the precepts are numerous, they do not exceed the five categories (*pañca-vastu*) and seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*). As for the five categories:

first, the *pārājika*—namely, sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying—which consist of four rules for bhikṣus and eight for bhikṣuṇīs. Second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, which consists of ten... [text continues]
There are three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: thirteen for bhikṣus and seventeen for bhikṣuṇīs.
There are three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* categories, namely thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and ninety *pāyattikas*: one hundred and twenty for bhikṣus and two hundred and eight for bhikṣuṇīs.
There are four *pratideśanīya* offenses: four for bhikṣus and eight for bhikṣuṇīs. There are five *prāyaścittika* offenses, namely *duṣkṛta*. For bhikṣus...

For a *bhikṣu*, there are one hundred rules; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, one hundred rules. Regarding the seven groups of offenses: first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *sthūlātyaya*; fourth, *pāyattika*;
fifth, *pratideśanīya*; sixth, *duṣkṛta*; and seventh, *durbhāṣita*. As for the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva precepts, they consist of ten *pārājikas* and forty-eight minor transgressions.
Regarding the fact that their meaning pertains to the four teachings: I [the author] shall now take up the body...
When one attains mastery over the body, one gradually masters the mind; when the mind attains penetration, the Three Piṭakas may be understood.

Upon reaching the stage where both body and mind are entirely proficient, and through hearing the Vaipulya sūtras that censure and rebuke, one gradually comes to embody and believe the characteristics of the mind;
thus, the Vinaya of a bhikṣu becomes the three clusters of precepts for a bodhisattva, and one may ascend through the Separate and Perfect Teachings until finally returning to the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding "sudden": if even the ordinary six consciousnesses are already identical to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, how could the pure essence of upholding the precepts not be a perfectly sudden dharma-gate?
Its wondrous virtue is brilliantly radiant, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it is perfect throughout the ten directions, having no fixed location.
