Maudgalyāyana Observes Consciousness, Part Two: Initial Account of the Conditions for Awakening) Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I was first on the road begging for food, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—as they were proclaiming the Dharma."
Through these causes and conditions, I suddenly attained realization and achieved great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe;

as soon as it touched my body, my beard and hair fell away of their own accord. As I traveled through the ten directions, I attained unimpededness, and my supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) were so manifest that they were ranked as unsurpassed.
I became an Arhat—not only was the World-Honored One pleased, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also praised my spiritual power as perfect, pure, and luminous.
Purity, mastery, and fearlessness. (2. Citation of evidence and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:

"I attained it by reversing the flow of the tranquil mind, causing its light to manifest and proclaim itself, like clearing a turbid stream until it becomes long-lasting, pure, and crystalline; this is the foremost."
[Commentary] Gushan says: *Uruvilvā* means "papaya" (*moguǒ*). Because there was a papaya-shaped protuberance on his chest, he was so named.
*Gayā* is the name of a mountain; it is Mount Elephant Head (*Gajapṛṣṭha*). It is also called a "city," because the city was near this mountain.
The name of the Nadi River is [Nadī]. There were two younger brothers of one elder brother; thus, Śāriputra said that those encountered were the Kāśyapa brothers.
Wēnlíng says: "The profound meaning of causes and conditions refers not to the coarse phenomena of worldly conjunction, but rather to the elucidation of mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, by means of this, one awakens the mind and attains great penetration, with supernormal powers as one wishes."

Furthermore, "revolving the stillness" means revolving the consciousness to restore its wondrous stillness; thus, after a long time, it becomes clear and crystalline, and one attains the power of penetration that is perfectly bright, pure, and sovereign.
Wuxing said: "Spirit" is named the mind-heart (*tianxin*), and "penetration" is named the nature of wisdom (*huixing*).

This nature of mind is precisely the manifestation of the mental consciousness. In the Mahāyāna, this brings forth the *tathāgatagarbha*; in the Hīnayāna, it brings forth the fundamental [consciousness].

Dhyāna. Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), only the power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) is an internal realization; the remaining five powers all belong to external applications.
[Commentary] Tiantai says:

Regarding the six explanations of the universal penetration of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), first is the clarification of the universality or limitation of its objects. As for the objects of the mental consciousness—
The objects of focus (ālambana) of this samādhi pertain to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva). Other samādhis may each focus on only one nature;
for example, the *Caryā-apagata-sūtra* states: "Lust itself is the path; hatred is likewise so. Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained."

This [samādhi] takes only evil as its object, as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. However, if one recites the *Lotus Sūtra*, contemplates Avalokiteśvara, or practices counting the breaths, these all take wholesome natures as their objects, as in the *Bodhyaṅga-samādhi*; thus, the three natures may be universally taken as objects.

Now, this samādhi—wherein "I" cause the luminous mind, which has revolved into stillness, to manifest—is likewise of the same category as the *Bodhyaṅga-samādhi*. Second, the fullness of contemplation.
*Suǒ*. This initial section explains the Buddha’s intent regarding the realization attained by the protagonist.

First, it describes how he encountered a superior friend on the road and heard an exposition of the causes and conditions (*nidāna*), whereby he suddenly attained thorough penetration; thus, the conditions for his renunciation lay with the three Kāśyapas.

Next, it describes how he later saw the Tathāgata, who bestowed upon him the *kāṣāya* robe, whereupon his beard and hair fell away of their own accord and he became an Arhat; this constitutes his attainment of the Way.

The causal condition lies precisely with the Tathāgata. Recently, there have been some lecturers who do not believe that the Tathāgata’s supernatural power caused his hair and beard to fall off naturally;
they claim that if it were as described, it would be a strange anomaly. How utterly contemptible!
Third, the account of attaining the spiritual powers to roam freely throughout the ten directions and achieve unimpededness is all a peripheral narrative, not the primary account.
The conclusion states: "I have turned back the stillness of the mind, causing its light to radiate forth, like clearing a turbid stream until it becomes permanently limpid and bright.

This is precisely to set forth the perfect penetration entered through the mental consciousness. To speak of "turning back the stillness" means to reverse the laws of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—which are the modes by which the objects of the mental consciousness are produced—and to return from these to the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, the perfectly still and pervasive essence, thereby turning away from delusion and returning to the source.
This is the true meaning. Once the swirling stillness has persisted for a long time, the supernatural powers and radiant light inherently present within the mind will spontaneously manifest.
This is as clear as the analogy of settling turbid water until it becomes pure and translucent; the metaphor is most explicit.
What is called the "pure essence of luminosity" can manifest all transformations without becoming affliction, for all are in accord with the wondrous virtue of the purity of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, one should know that although this gate differs from the samādhis of the ear-gate, it likewise possesses four kinds of extraordinary merits:
first, because it is the universal capacity of all dharmas, being both the possessed and the creator; second, because it is what is elucidated and revealed by the Mahāyāna sūtras;
third, because it is directly pointed out by the patriarchs of the Chan and doctrinal schools; and fourth, because it is [the subject] of this very sūtra.

Because it was shown in secret, Mañjuśrī’s verse of selection states only: "Since supernatural powers are fundamentally due to past causes, what connection have they with the discrimination of dharmas?
If thoughts and conditions do not depart from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration? One [line] selects the past cause, and one selects mental attention (*manasikāra*);
he never says that the revolving within the profound stillness (*zhan*) is incorrect—the general intent is thus clearly visible. As for its relevance to the four teachings:
The turning of the turbid toward clarity and the realization of the partial truth are clearly explained in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

If one awakens the mind directed toward the Middle Way, it can be known that the light of wisdom will be received by those of the Distinct (*pratyekabuddha*) and Complete (*vaipulya*) Teachings, whether their realization is partial or universal.

As for those who ultimately return to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*), if they awaken to and clarify the six bases of consciousness within this sutra—transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations—then their fundamental consciousness becomes luminous awareness, and their cognitive clarity becomes enlightened illumination.
The true consciousness of wondrous enlightenment is profoundly still and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

[Section Four: Awakening through Contemplating the Seven Elements] 1. Ucchuṣma’s Contemplation of Fire 2. Part One: Narrating the Circumstances of Awakening A. Part One: Meeting the Buddha and Hearing His Teaching Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, during a kalpa long ago, I was by nature full of greed. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kūṭa."
The King said, "A person of excessive lust becomes a mass of fierce fire. (2. Cultivating Contemplation Based on the Teaching; Part One:

Attaining Enlightenment through the Completion of Contemplation) He instructed me to contemplate universally the hundred bones, four limbs, and all the cold and warm vital energies, so that the spiritual light would coalesce within and transform the mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom. (Part Two:

Reiterating and Explaining the Accomplishment) From this point on, all Buddhas have called me by the name Huatou (Fire-Head). By the power of the *prabhāsvara-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi), I have attained the state of an Arhat.

"I made a great vow that when the Buddhas attain enlightenment, I would become a *mahāpuruṣa* (powerful being) to personally subdue their demonic adversaries. (2. Citing evidence to conclude the answer:

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed with clarity that the sensations of warmth within my body and mind flowed unimpededly; once all outflows were extinguished, a great jewel-flame arose, and I ascended to supreme enlightenment. This is the foremost."
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: *Ucchuṣma* means "Fire-head," referring to the Vajra Fire-head. Those who indulge excessively in lust are fundamentally impelled by the sensation of warmth (*sparśa*).
While alive, this becomes the fire of desire; after death, it becomes the fire of karma. Because the power of karma increases and blazes, it becomes a mass of fierce flames.
Wú-xīng says: "Observe everywhere that the four great elements are all the object-field of touch."
The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is the ground of the hundred bones and four limbs. The various sensations of cold and warmth are precisely the elements of water, fire, and wind.

Because *samādhi* has been firmly established, it is said that "divine light condenses within. Since for those with great desire the element of fire (*tejas*) is particularly predominant, the fire of lust is transformed into the fire of wisdom.
To "attain the fruit of an Arhat" refers below to attaining the lesser fruit; subsequently, one gives rise to the Great Vow. Is this not so?
Is it that the Universal Manifestation Body (Samantavyūha-rūpakāya) manifests through the Vajradhara deity assisting the Buddha to propagate his transformation?
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the fourth of the seven great perfect penetrations, the first explains the perfect penetration of the fire element (*tejas-mahābhūta*).
First, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of its realm. Generally speaking, there is the fire of the insentient and the fire of the sentient. Now...

Do not seek the realization of universal penetration (*yuan-tong*) by observing the fire-element among the four great elements within the body. Next, clarify the expansion and contraction of this contemplation;
first, explain the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teachings to interpret what has been realized. The Dharma taught by the Buddha varies according to the capacities of those to be trained.

For those of the Hīnayāna capacity who possess a predominance of desire, he instructed them to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Now, it is for the sake of those of the Mahāyāna capacity...
It causes the transformative mind of much lust to become the fire of wisdom. Now, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It accords with the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know.

Since the beginning, it has never changed, yet because it follows conditions, it manifests as the fire of the four great elements within the body; likewise, it follows conditions while remaining unchanged.

If one follows the conditions of sexual desire and passion, they become a mass of fierce fire; this accords with the nature of greed and runs counter to the nature of wisdom, and should be measured against what is to be known.

If one accords with the nature of wisdom and runs counter to the nature of greed, one should universally observe the cold and warm vital energies throughout the hundred bones, four limbs, and various parts of the body.
Having observed for a long time, the divine light will coalesce within, transforming the many lustful minds into [purity].
The fire of wisdom—whether moving contrary or in accord, ascending or descending—is nothing other than this;
what other dharma could there be? Thus, the *Apocryphal Scripture on Non-Action* says: "Lust is itself the Way; hatred is likewise so. Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are complete.
The Buddha-dharma specifically refers to the nature that remains unchanging while following conditions. Only one who can embody this Way is truly [a practitioner].
When the nature of greed and other afflictions arises, one does not conform to that nature;

rather, one employs wisdom in a contrary manner to universally observe that the nature of greed is unchanging while it follows conditions, and though it follows conditions, it remains unchanging. As Ucchuṣma said... (and so forth).

Thus, it is established that desire itself is the Way. As for why all the Buddhas have called me by the name "Fire-Head" (Agnimukha), it is because my nature was characterized by abundant desire, such that my fire was fiercely blazing;
this is because those with a mind of much lust become a mass of fierce flames. Now, having transformed a mind of much lust into the fire of wisdom, the nature of its flames has thus been changed.
The fire-light is likewise due to this. It is argued that all seven elements are possessed by the human body. When one element manifests, it is called "actualized creation" (*shizao*);

when the other six elements remain latent, they are termed "inherent principle" (*lizhi*). Now, speaking from the perspective of what is manifested through actualized creation, it is named the Fire-Head Vajra.

[2. The Second: Observing the Great Element of Earth] [2.1. First: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening] [2.1.1. First: Encountering Buddhas and Receiving Their Teachings] [2.1.1.1. First: Successively Meeting Various Buddhas and Fully Cultivating Meritorious Deeds] The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.

Whenever there were important roads, ferry crossings, fields, or narrow passes that were uneven or otherwise unfitting, causing damage to carts and horses, I would level them all, or construct bridges over them.”
I carried sand and earth on my back, undergoing such diligent toil for immeasurable eons as Buddhas appeared in the world.
Or there were sentient beings in marketplaces who required someone to carry their goods; I would first carry them to their destination, set them down, and then depart without taking any payment.
During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine, and I served as a porter.

"Whenever people asked me for money, regardless of whether they were far or near, I would take but a single coin. Or when ox-carts were mired in the mud, I used my supernatural powers to push their wheels and rescue them from their suffering.
At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast;

I leveled the ground at that moment to await the Buddha. [2. Specifically meeting the Vaisya relative and receiving his instruction: "The Tathāgata Vaiśravaṇa rubbed the crown of my head and said to me: 'You should level the mind-ground, and then the world will be level.'"

All realms and lands were entirely level. (2. Attaining Enlightenment through the Teaching; Part 1: Directly Stating the Realization of the Principle) My mind was immediately opened, and I perceived that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles that constitute the world are equal and without distinction.
These particles of dust do not touch one another in their essential nature; even weapons do not come into contact with them. (2. Attaining Enlightenment through Realization; Part 2:

Describing the Attainment of Realization) Through this realization of the Dharma-nature, I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and became an Arhat; having now turned my mind [toward the Mahayana], I enter [the Bodhisattva path].

While in the stage of a Bodhisattva, I heard all the Tathāgatas proclaim that the ground of the Buddhas’ wondrous Lotus Flower of knowledge and vision was for me first to witness and certify, acting as their foremost leader.

(2. Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction;

they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, from which delusions arise to manifest as dust. As this dust dissolves, wisdom becomes perfect, and I accomplished the Unsurpassed Way. This is my [method].
1. [Commentary] Wuxing said: "From the atoms of the body-realm up to weapons and armies—all these are forms produced by the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
They are, therefore, phenomena born of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). The non-differentiation of atoms is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
It does not touch the middle [truth] either. Are the three truths not fully present in the *tathāgatagarbha*?

Awakening to non-arising and so forth occurs because one has partially realized the *dharmakāya* and provisionally attained the lesser fruits; thus, it is distinguished by means of "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
First one liberates oneself, and subsequently one transforms others—this is called "turning the mind. *Viśvabhū* signifies being omnipresent and sovereign over all.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: There are two explanations for the great element of earth as perfect penetration. First, clarifying the general and specific aspects of the object.

To speak specifically, there is the great element of earth within the body and the great element of earth as the environment (dependent retribution). Now, this Bodhisattva contemplates both internally and externally:

the minute particles of the world constitute the environment (dependent retribution), while the minute particles of the body constitute the self (primary retribution); these are equal and without distinction.
Distinct things do not touch one another; they are perfectly interfused and converge in the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Second, the explanation of the expansion and contraction of contemplation.

First, the primary tenet and the Buddha’s intent explain what has been realized. First, the aspiration to benefit sentient beings is presented; second, the conditions for encountering the Buddha are presented.

Within the context of benefiting beings, leveling the treacherous and narrow paths is the primary focus, while supporting objects and pushing wheels are secondary. Furthermore, regarding those encountered below...

The Buddha’s expedient means (*upāya*) for entering the Way through correct speech is as follows: generally, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he guides beings according to their habitual tendencies and what is most suitable for them.

For example, teaching the son of a goldsmith to practice *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and teaching the son of a dyer to practice *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) are instances of this. Therefore, the Tathāgata Viśvabhū [taught] him to repeatedly fill [the vessel].
If one levels the ground now by means of the teaching on leveling the mind, then the ground of the entire world will become level.
The Buddha’s intention was that leveling the ground to benefit others, while waiting for the Buddha to level it himself, would surely be a beautiful practice of benefiting both self and others.
However, sentient beings in the world are boundless and immeasurable; how could one hope to achieve this with such limited supernatural power alone?
This is the mind that can widely propagate the Way of universal salvation; therefore, it causes one to attend solely to the root and not seek after the branches.
This is precisely what Vimalakīrti meant when he said, "If the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure.
If the Buddha-land is indeed pure, then all sentient beings will be gathered and brought back to this wondrous land—how could there then be any inequality? One must understand these words.
Furthermore, there are both general and specific aspects. Generally, the mind is the totality of all phenomena; when the mind is level, all things are level.

Specifically, that which corresponds to this sutra’s teaching—that the nature of form is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true form, being inherently pure and pervading the Dharma-realm—is taken as the "ground of the mind.
That which follows the minds of sentient beings and accords with the measure of what they know is taken as "all things."
Not understanding that the unchanging follows conditions is called "the unevenness of the mind-ground. Not understanding that the unchanging follows conditions is called "all-encompassing unevenness.
If one can understand this, it is the leveling of the mind-ground, whereby the world-ground becomes level as well.
Because one attains awakening in accordance with what is heard and practices contemplation that accords with the nature, the mind immediately opens up and realizes entry into the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The subtle atoms of the body are the earth-element of the *pratyaya-phala* (the retributive fruit); the subtle atoms that constitute [the world] are the earth-element of the *adhiṣṭhāna-phala* (the environmental support).

These correspond to the capacities of sentient beings' minds and accord with the measure of what they know. They are equal and without distinction; the self-nature of these subtle atoms does not obstruct one another.

Regarding "touching," "rubbing," and so forth: this awakening that remains unchanging while following conditions is precisely the realization that the nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself true emptiness.

When I speak of "awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within the dharma-nature," it means that I have awakened to the Tathāgata-garbha within the material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) of the earth element.
The dharma-gates described in this treatise may be called supremely perfect; one merely attests to them by awakening to the patience of non-arising.
As for the Arhat, he is properly a bhikṣu who maintains the appearance of a śrāvaka. Although he is able to benefit others, his own mind is primarily focused on its own realization;
thus, although he has destroyed the afflictions and eliminated ignorance, he achieves only the fruit of arhatship.

He is also heard of as one of those who constantly take up the fruit [of their practice]. Having first emerged from the triple world to complete his own self-benefit, he subsequently enters the world to benefit others.
Therefore it is said: "Having turned their minds, they now enter the stage of the Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the passage, "I was the first to witness and certify that which the Tathāgatas proclaim as the ground of the Buddha’s wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, acting as their leader," this is found at the end of the Universal Gate Chapter (Pumen pin).
This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* is for the sake of the one great cause and condition, desiring to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s wisdom and vision.
Seeing this, one realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. What the Earth-Holding Bodhisattva has now awakened to is but a single dharma within the true mark of all phenomena;
yet the one is the all. Having personally realized it himself, he knows that the Buddha’s teaching is not false;
thus, he serves as a witness to the true mark for the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra gathering. Some may cling to these words and judge that this sūtra belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

As for the latter [point]: it fails to recognize that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* consists of a preceding and a succeeding section; that while the preceding section is sequential, the succeeding section is not.

Although the latter is non-sequential, it subsumes what follows back into what precedes, leaving no further discourse to be made. The concluding text is self-evident; there is no need to elaborate on the remaining sections.

○ (Part Three: Contemplating Water as Great; Section One: Narrating the Circumstances of Awakening; Subsection One: Encountering the Buddha and Receiving His Teaching. The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Jaladeva.

He taught all the bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water and enter samādhi. ○ (Section Two: Cultivating Contemplation According to the Teaching; Subsection One: Fully Describing the Practice; Part One: Stilling the Mental Fabrications. "Observe the watery nature within the body, which cannot be displaced. First, begin with the mucus and saliva..."
Exhausting the津液 (tissue fluids), *sūkṣma-rasa*, *śukra*, and blood, as well as the large and small excretions, the water-nature within the body circulates and returns;

it is identical [to external water]. When seeing water, one perceives no difference between the water within the body and the various fragrant water-oceans of the Floating Banner King Lands (*Ucchraya-ketu-rāja-kṣetra*) outside the world.

(2. Narrating the Partial Realization) At that time, when I first accomplished this contemplation, I saw only the water and had not yet attained the state of being bodiless. (3. Encountering Conditions upon Entering Contemplation) I was then a bhikṣu.

While I was in meditative absorption within my chamber, a disciple of mine peered through the window and observed that the room was filled with nothing but clear water, with no other objects to be seen.
Being ignorant and childlike, he took a piece of tile and threw it into the water;

the water splashed and made a sound, whereupon he looked around and departed. (2. Observing and Knowing Illness) After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt a pain in my heart, as if Śāriputra had suffered a violent injury.
"O Ghost, I reflected within myself: 'I have now attained the path of Arhatship; it has been long since I was parted from the conditions of illness.

Why does a heartache suddenly arise today? Could it be that I am falling away from my realization? (3. Examining the Conditions to Attain Peace) At that time, the youth quickly came before me and reported the matter as described above.
I then told him: 'If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove [the pain].'"
After receiving these instructions, the Child of Debris entered meditative concentration; upon emerging, he again saw the water, and the debris was restored exactly as it had been.
He opened the door and emerged, and after I had left, he emerged from his concentration with his physical body restored to its original state.

He encountered immeasurable Buddhas in this manner until he reached the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Unhindered Penetration of Mountains and Seas, whereupon he finally attained the dissolution of the self-body and became one in nature with the fragrant waters of the oceans throughout the ten directions.

In ultimate emptiness there is neither duality nor distinction; I have now attained the name of "Celibate Youth" (*kumārabhūta*) from the Tathāgata and am included in the assembly of Bodhisattvas. (2.

Citation of testimony and conclusion of the answer) When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I attained the patience of non-arising through the single-flavored circulation of the nature of water, thereby fulfilling Bodhi;
this is the foremost.
[Commentary] Zizhong says: According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean there is a great lotus flower.
Within that lotus flower are various fragrant waters; each of these fragrant water-oceans serves as the seed for the worlds of the Buddha-fields.

Since the Flower Treasury World resides within these fragrant waters, it is called the "Vimalacchatra-rāja" (Pure Canopy King) realm. The Flower Treasury consists of twenty tiers, stacked one upon another.

As high as a banner, it is called a "king" because it is the most lofty and great. Now, observing that the water of one's own body is identical to that ocean, it is called the "Floating Banner King Land" among the various fragrant water-oceans.
When first accomplishing this contemplation, seeing only the water is the result of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which transforms according to the mind;
just as when entering the ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), there is [water] upon entering and [it disappears] upon emerging from concentration.
There is none. It is not the same as the matter of the fruit of karma, for through common karma one is collectively affected; only by not creating worldly karma can one attain purity.
Regarding the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities)—blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—all ten of these totalities are present therein.
For instance, when one forms the perception of blue, then all places are entirely blue. Wuxing said: "One attains Arhatship."

"Having long been free from the conditions of illness," and so forth. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is clarified that all noble ones (*ārya*) experience physical suffering, such as Śāriputra’s wind-disorder and Pindola Bharadvāja’s eye pain.
To now claim that one who has attained arhatship and is long free from the conditions of illness [experiences no suffering] is truly difficult to reconcile.

This is likely because they previously attained only the minor fruits [of the śrāvaka path]; since they lack the afflictions (*kleśa*) and karmic actions of both *darśana-heya* (to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (to be abandoned by cultivation), [their remaining suffering is merely residual].
This matter is the condition for departing from the suffering of the illness of the segmented body. At that time, he turns his mind back toward entering the triple world;

because there was originally no actual disease, he doubted it. However, the samādhi cultivated by this Bodhisattva is largely the same as the previously mentioned method of the Earth-Holding Contemplation (*dhāraṇī-bhūmi-vipaśyanā*);
it is only because ignorance (*avidyā*) still remains and he has not yet attained the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) that he emerges from meditative absorption.
Not understanding the causal conditions of the illness, there are those who attempt to resolve it through the crude method of analytical disintegration; this is truly unacceptable.
Only by attaining the initial realization of the Dharma-body—wherein one loses the self and the body—is one able to transcend the body of change.

Within this body, the nature of the water-element merges with the nature of the Fragrant Ocean and unites with the nature of the Treasury of True Suchness and Emptiness. Wénlǐng says: "The Moon is the Yin essence; it is the crystalline essence of water."
Furthermore, in the past, my teacher Water-Heaven (Jaladeva) practiced the contemplation of water. Because the nature of water is perfectly luminous, he was named Moonlight (Candraprabha).

Regarding the fact that the nature of water cannot be superseded: though the internal essence of semen and blood differs from the external nature of the waters of the oceans, their natures do not conflict with one another.
At that time, my physical body returned to its original state; this describes the conditions under which I performed this contemplation. Śāriputra.
While entering meditative absorption on the banks of the Ganges River, he was struck by a malevolent spirit and emerged from samādhi with a headache;
this was because he had not yet attained the body of no-form (*amūrti*). The traces of Master Shui Guan of Mianzhu County in Hanzhou were similar to those of Candraprabha.

The *Fo-tuo ben-zhuan* (Biography of Buddha-datta) states that when the Master entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), his chamber seemed to be ablaze; this is of the same category as the aforementioned "malevolent spirit" (*vyādhāta*).
"He should act as a harmful one. The name of this yakṣa king was actually that of Śāriputra’s enemy from a past life. [Commentary] Tiantai says:
This is the third explanation of the perfect penetration of the water element (*āpas*). First, it clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.

To speak specifically, there is the water within the body and the water of the external environment (*niśraya-vipāka*). Now, this bodhisattva contemplates both internally and externally with universal penetration.

It is like observing within the body that the nature of water does not differ from the water of one's primary retribution; the various fragrant seas of the Floating Banner King lands are the water of one's secondary retribution.
When these are equal and without distinction, then the internal and external natures are identical. Next, the expansion and contraction of this contemplation is clarified.
First, the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teaching is explained to interpret what has been realized. The master of this method is the Bodhisattva named Moon.

The Tathāgata whom Guang takes as his teacher is named Sudarśana (Water Heaven). This refers to the fact that the Way is one throughout antiquity and the present, and the realization of cause and fruit is one and the same.
There are three points in which this differs from the visualization of water in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*: first, the difference between the environment and the body;

for that [sūtra] visualizes the environmental retribution (*niṣyanda-phala*), whereas this [text] visualizes both the environment and the body. Second, the difference between phenomena and principle; for that [sūtra] concerns only phenomenal characteristics, whereas this encompasses both phenomena and principle. Third, the difference in direction...
This is indeed a different reality. Because he wishes to contemplate the jeweled ground, he first relies upon the water of a great pond as a skillful means for his contemplation.
By contemplating this nature of water, he reveals that the nature of water is empty of true existence;
the emptiness of the nature of water is itself true water, pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds to the minds of sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
Knowing the measure and taking it as the basis for what is correct, the distinction between the sentient world (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*) arises.

Thus, speaking from the perspective of one's own *svabhāva-bhāga* (the objective portion of one’s own nature), there are internal and external, small and large, red and white, fragrant and foul, impure and pure—ten thousand variations that differ from one another.
Now, observing this from the standpoint of one’s own *dharmatā-bhāga* (the essential nature of phenomena): first, observe that the water-element within the body cannot be displaced. At the outset...
From saliva to such things as the exhaustion of fluids, essence, blood, excrement, and urine, the water element within the body circulates and returns, being identical [to external water];
this contemplation shows that the nature of the primary retribution (the body) is equal [to external water].

Next, one sees that the water within the body is no different from the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King World-system (*Sudharman*) in the external world; this contemplation shows the equality of the primary retribution and its support (the environment).
The nature of retribution is uniform. However, because deluded sentiments have persisted for so long, it is difficult to achieve uniformity between the dependent and the primary.

Therefore, when first establishing this contemplation, one sees only the water and has not yet attained the state where there is no body. If one were to extinguish the body, then the water would be the body and the body would be the water;
if the water is the body, it may be called "only water," and if the body is the water, it may be called "only body."

This is also possible. Since both the body and water are called the Dharma-body, after one has attained the dissolution of the body, they will merge with the true emptiness of the nature of the various fragrant water-seas throughout the ten directions, becoming non-dual and without distinction.

[4. The Section on the Wind Element of the Vimalaprabhāsamādhi (Second Part): 1. Narrating the Circumstances of Awakening; 2. Following the Teaching to Practice Contemplation. The Dharma Prince Vimalaprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa.
He revealed to the Bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening, teaching that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all turned by the power of the wind of false conditions."
At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the movement and stillness of the body, and the movement of thoughts in the mind;
I saw that all movements were non-dual and without distinction. At that time, I realized the nature of these manifold movements:
they come from nowhere and go nowhere; the sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are equally deluded and illusory—thus it continues even unto the end.

All sentient beings within the single world-system of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds were like a hundred mosquitoes and gnats contained in a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together, creating a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.

It is shown that the Bodhisattva’s fundamental awakening—wondrous and luminous—is to be directly realized by contemplating the eternally abiding true mind, which is neither arising nor ceasing.
Yet, to say that "this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all turned by the power of the wind of false conditions" is precisely to demonstrate that within movement there is immovability;
it intends for one to contemplate movement in order to manifest the immovable.

This is their inherent nature. Therefore it is said: "At that time, I observed the establishment of the realms, observed the movement of the world, observed the movement and stillness of the body, and observed the movement of thoughts in the mind;
all movements were non-dual and without distinction. For the establishment of the realms is sustained by the wind-wheel, and its movement is great;
the flux of the three periods of time is its small movement; and as for the body—
Whether in movement or stillness, the stirring of the mind and the arising of thought—whether small or large, though they differ in degree, they are all equally movements.
At that time, I clearly realized that the nature of these manifold movements comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; this is what Master Sengzhao meant when he said:
"The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet they remain eternally still; the rivers rush together in their torrents, yet they do not flow; wild horses gallop and flutter, yet they are but dust."
Yet the sun and moon do not move, nor do they traverse the heavens in their entirety;
they do not exceed the dust-motes of the ten directions, for all inverted sentient beings are but a single instance of delusion. Therefore, he further clarifies this through a dharma-parable:
"In this way, even within a single world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, all sentient beings are like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel."
The chirping of insects clamors in confusion within a space of but a few inches, drumming up a frantic noise.
This uses the small vessel of a few inches to metaphorize the great chiliocosm of worlds; the immeasurable sentient beings are likened to a hundred mosquitoes.
The chirping of insects clamoring in confusion and drumming up a frantic noise is a metaphor for the collective agitation of the body and mind within the world. Yet, as for these mosquitoes—
Although the vessel moves, its emptiness remains unmoving; likewise, although the deluded conditions of sentient beings move, my fundamental nature of awakening remains unmoving.
It is not merely that the unmoving lacks motion, but rather that that which moves is fundamentally non-moving.
This means that by observing the directions, one knows the destination, yet the traveler does not arrive at the direction itself.
Thus, having encountered the Buddha not long ago, he awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When it is said that "at that time his mind opened and he beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the east, serving as a Dharma Prince for the Buddhas of the ten directions," it is because the east is the head of all movement, while the name of the Buddha-land is "Immovable" (*Akṣobhya*).

"Movement. Is this not precisely to reveal that within movement there exists that which is unmoving? When body and mind emit light, penetrating and unobstructed—this is exactly what is meant by the origin of its name.

By observing that the world, body, and mind are one and the same in their emptiness and delusion, realizing they possess nothing at all, they are identical to fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi), tranquil yet ever-illuminating, like pure lapis lazuli. [End] of the final section.
Regarding the statement, "The Buddhas of the ten directions transmit one wondrous mind":

among the Buddhas of the ten directions, who is there that does not transmit the mind by means of fundamental enlightenment’s wondrous luminosity? Furthermore, who is there that does not manifest stillness within movement?

Yet, when Manjusri subsequently examines this, he says: "If one contemplates the nature of wind through movement and stillness, they are not without their opposites; yet these opposites are not without [their own nature]."
How does the Supreme Awakening attain perfect penetration? Yet, it alone does not say that the nature of sound—whether in motion or stillness—is present within hearing, nor that it is absent.
To claim there is no hearing when there is no sound is not true; for hearing has no inherent nature. When there is no sound, hearing does not cease;

when there is sound, hearing is not born. Birth and cessation are both transcended in their perfection; apart from these, there is the eternal reality. This may be understood by borrowing the words of Subhūti.
These words were spoken by the Dharma Prince Vairocana-prabha as a rebuttal to the criticism.

**[5] The Contemplation of the Great Emptiness of Ākāśagarbha:** 1. **Narrating the Circumstances of Awakening.** a. **Sharing in What the Buddha Attained.** The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I and the Tathāgata attained the Boundless Body together with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. 2. **Fully Manifesting His Spiritual Powers.** At that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminated...
I clearly perceive the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, transforming into empty space.

Furthermore, within the great round mirror manifested from my own mind, I emit ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights that flow and drench all the realms of the banner-kings throughout the reaches of empty space.
These realms enter into the mirror and penetrate my body; my body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction, and is able to skillfully enter into the subtle.

I perform Buddha-works extensively throughout the lands of the dust-motes and attain great accordance with reality. (3. Attainment through Contemplation) This great spiritual power arises from my profound contemplation that the four great elements have no basis, that false thoughts arise and perish, and that empty space is non-dual;
thus, the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical. By illuminating this identity, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
(2. Citation of Realization and Conclusion of the Response) When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that by contemplating the boundlessness of empty space, I entered *samādhi*.
"The marvelous power of the earth is perfectly bright and complete; this is the foremost.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: Because one has realized the boundless Dharma-body through the observation that the material substance of the four great elements is empty, in order to manifest that this body universally permeates and fuses with all things, one grasps a precious jewel to illuminate the ten directions and so forth as a symbolic representation. Since—

The jewel represents form (*rūpa*), and the mirror further represents the mind (*citta*). Form is created from the mind; its entire substance is the mind. Therefore, it emits precious light that bathes the ten directions and so forth.
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all. "The body is identical to space" refers to the Dharma-aspect (*dharmatā*).
"The body enters into lands within the dust-motes" refers to the responsive aspect (*nirmāṇa*). To preach the Three Vehicles constitutes Buddha-work (*buddhakārya*). This is called...
The four *siddhāntas* serve as the means of accommodation.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the fifth explanation of entering the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) through the great element of space. First, it clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.
Specifically, one contemplates only empty space to reveal the hidden nature; now, one generally contemplates all four great elements to reveal the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

This is also the universal contemplation of the sentient and the insentient. Next, the expansion and contraction of this contemplation are clarified. First, according to the fundamental intent of the Buddha, the realization attained is explained:
that "I" and the Tathāgata King Dīpaṃkara obtained the "boundless body" (ananta-kāya) refers to the same as Śākyamuni’s initial realization of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
At that time, the holding of the four great precious jewels in one's hand and so forth refers to the [jewels].
The jewel must be a *maṇi*, demonstrating that the possession of jewels is boundless, giving rise to them inexhaustibly.
It is precisely because the *dharmakāya* is named Vairocana that it pervades all places; there are no phenomena whatsoever that are not the Buddha-dharma.
All phenomena are the four great elements, the ten dharma-realms, and all dharmas. When one realizes this Buddha-dharma, there is not a single phenomenon that does not [participate in it].
It accords with the nature [of reality]. Because it is as boundless as empty space, he is titled the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha (Space-Treasury).

Thus, after realizing this body, his right hand holds four great precious jewels that illuminate the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, transforming them into empty space.
This serves to manifest that the four great elements and emptiness are each in accord with the nature and are all-pervasive. This is because...

The four great precious jewels represent the wisdom that contemplates the four great elements; the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions represent the objective realm of the four great elements being contemplated.
Their transformation into empty space signifies the use of wisdom to dissolve the objective realm, subsuming phenomena into principle.
This refers to such passages as: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form. Pure and inherently so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, within the Great Perfect Mirror manifested by one's own mind, ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light are emitted, flowing and pouring throughout the ten directions to the very limits of empty space;
all the various banner-kings and lands enter into this mirror and penetrate my body.

The body is identical to empty space and does not obstruct one another. This signifies that the single mind is fully endowed with the ten realms, such that the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are of one essence, and sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual.
It is like the thousand jewels of Indra’s net, wherein each reflects the others in mutual fusion, and every phenomenon is all-pervasive.
The above has described the essence of what is realized, which is the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*). Next, the manifestation of spiritual powers describes this essence.
The characteristics possessed therein are such that the body is able to skillfully enter lands as minute as motes of dust to extensively perform Buddha-works, attaining great accordance (*anuloma*).
This describes how function arises from the essence. It is precisely because this is so that the concluding exposition states:
"This great supernatural power [is realized] through my contemplation of reality" (and so forth). What has been expressed may indeed be called exhaustive. The preceding...

The four bodhisattvas each realized one of the four great elements; now, however, by connecting this with what preceded, the principle that "one is all" is fully integrated, identical to the principle of perfect realization in the third fascicle.
Thus, it may be known that the gate of contemplation here is even more transcendent and superior.

[6. Maitreya’s Contemplation on the Greatness of Consciousness, Part One: Narrating the Conditions for Awakening] Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, after the passage of atoms of kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness;
however, my mind was heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in visiting noble families. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the contemplation of ‘mind-only.’”

Consciousness is fixed as it enters samādhi. (2. Cultivating Contemplation in Accordance with the Teaching; Part 1: Long-term Cultivation and the Cessation of Faults) Throughout kalpas past, by means of this samādhi, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
the seeking mind for worldly fame has ceased and no longer exists. (Part 2: Attaining the Way through the Perfection of Contemplation; Part 1:

Realizing Mind-Only) When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind, extending even to the lands of all Tathāgatas throughout the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent.

"All these are manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind. (2. Manifesting All Buddhas) World-Honored One, because I have realized that all is but the consciousness of the mind, the nature of consciousness has flowed forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas;

I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed them in the place of Buddhahood. (2. Citing Evidence and Concluding the Answer) When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of dhyāna], I observed with clarity that the ten directions are but consciousness;
the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature and remaining far removed from the *paratantra* (dependent) nature."
Furthermore, to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of universal conceptualization is the foremost.
[Commentary: Wēnlíng states: Maitreya is correctly called *Maitrīyaṇa*, which is translated as "Kindly One" (*Cishi*).

Because his kindness flourishes in the present world and his compassion reaches the future kalpas, he manifests traces to illuminate the truth for those who pity sentient beings yet are deluded regarding consciousness. This is the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

It is said that because they do not realize that the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is fundamentally empty and the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is illusory existence, they are addicted to worldly fame and delight in frequenting noble families.

As for those who maintain that "only mind-consciousness exists," this merely negates the existence of external objects; by distinguishing consciousness from the mind, it asserts that only one's own mind exists and that there are no phenomena outside of it.
Wuxing says: "Exhausting emptiness" refers to all the Buddha-lands throughout the entirety of the realm of space.
All are manifestations of what is perceived by the mind alone. If we speak in terms of the four lands (*bhūmi*), the mind itself is the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*);

the transformation land (*nirmāṇakāya*) corresponds to the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala-bhūmi*), the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), and the Land of Shared Residence (*sahā-vāsa*). Purity and defilement are merely the characteristics of these three lands; because they arise and cease in alternation, they are described as "existence" and "non-existence.
That which "flows forth from the Tathāgata" refers to the emanation of the Reward and Response Buddhas (*saṃbhoga- and nirmāṇa-kāya*) from the consciousness-nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
[This refers to] the body. Guishan said: "The cessation of the mind that seeks worldly fame until it no longer exists" refers to the stage of semblance (xiangsi-wei).

"Attaining the unsurpassed, wondrous, perfect, and complete samādhi of the cognitive mind" refers to the stage of partial realization (fenzhen-wei). Zizhong said: "Perfectly accomplished reality (yuan-cheng-shi) and so forth" refers to the three natures (trisvabhāva):
first, the nature of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva), which is the horizontal grasping at sentient beings, life-span, and self.
Furthermore, because [they] perceive a substantial reality in everything from "mine" and "self" down to sentient and insentient beings, they engage in pervasive conceptualization.
Second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): they conceive of the existence of causes and conditions through which the world is established as a combination of names and signs;

they cling to these provisional appearances as definitely arising from seeds, even though there is no self-clinging and they are naturally devoid of seed-nature, yet they falsely take form, mind, and so forth as [real].

The "seed" gives rise to phenomena such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Third is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the essence of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the *dharmadhātu* of true thusness (*tathatā*).
The perfected nature is like the hemp; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like the rope; and the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like the snake.
Now, entering into the perfected nature is to realize the principle of true thusness.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the sixfold analysis of the Great Consciousness as the entrance to Perfect Penetration: first, he clarifies the general and specific aspects of the object.

Generally speaking, the six consciousnesses, the seventh consciousness, the eighth consciousness, and the ninth consciousness can all serve as objects. Now, because he specifically takes the ninth consciousness as the object of contemplation, he says:
"I have contemplated with clarity that the ten directions are but consciousness; the conscious mind is perfectly luminous, entering into the Perfectly Accomplished Nature."
[This is] indeed so. Next, I shall clarify the expansion and contraction of contemplation. First, I will explain what has been realized according to the fundamental intent of the Buddha.

Regarding those who have left the household life following the Buddha yet whose minds value worldly fame and delight in frequenting noble clans: this admits of two interpretations. First, in terms of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):

it refers to those like the present-day person who, though having left the household life, does not let their mind be colored by the Way but only frequents aristocratic gates. This may be compared to a small district... [text fragment].

To compare [him] with base and vulgar monks: if a bodhisattva has already encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara after passing through kalpas as numerous as atoms, one should explain this according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) mentioned in the subsequent text.
To value worldly fame is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); to delight in visiting noble families is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Just as the phenomena of the triple world—both the primary and secondary elements of birth and death—are all dependently originated and lack intrinsic existence.
They arise through clarity. The eighteen *dhātus* and so forth each have their own lineage; this is called "clan" (*gotra*).

Within this nature, one perceives objects and discriminates them, reckoning them as a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span—these sixty modes of cognition and view constitute the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

All of these arise because one fails to understand that the dependent nature (*paratantra*) exists as an illusion and that pervasive conceptualization is fundamentally empty; thus, the mind becomes heavy.

The world calls me one who travels among all clans; now the Buddha has taught me the excellent remedy for its direct counteraction: the meditative concentration on the mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti-samādhi*).
This is indeed the medicinal dharma that accords with the disease, intended to bring about the thorough realization that all phenomena are created solely by the mind and consciousness.
As for the so-called "Ultimate Reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*), it merely negates the existence of objects while distinguishing the emptiness of the mind; there is only this.
"Within one's own mind, there are no phenomena external to it; throughout kalpas, by means of this samādhi and so forth. Changshui says:

"Once this contemplation has been first cultivated, one attains the counteractive measure (pratipakṣa). The upper phrase dispels the aforementioned characteristic of exhaustion; the lower phrase is the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness itself. "Awakening" refers to the act of awakening and illumination, which is the essence of wisdom.

Fourth is the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): it is the ultimate perfection of the awakening to emptiness, wherein both emptiness and that which is emptied by emptiness are extinguished.
The preceding phrase reveals the wisdom of the non-dual emptiness (*gnyis su med pa'i stong pa nyid*); the following correctly extinguishes the principle of non-dual emptiness. Question:

Since the principle is fundamentally quiescent and extinguished (*śānta-nirvṛta*), what further extinction could there be? Answer: If one says it is already quiescent and extinguished, this consciousness still arises;

however, one merely destroys its emotional attachment (*saṃjñā*) rather than destroying its principle. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One does not destroy the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages," because for those who have not yet...

Those who grasp at attainment cling to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, it must be refuted. The above constitutes four sections. If one speaks in terms of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*), from the initial entry into the stream of liberation, their meaning must be fully present;

one must not lose sight of the yet-unarisen aspects of reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). If one were to dogmatically insist on a fixed sequence, one would likely damage the underlying logic and textual structure.

[The passage] concerning "arising and ceasing" and so forth concludes the preceding discussion on the faculties and objects of both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). Since arising and ceasing have already ceased—
One immediately attains the first stage (*bhūmi*), partially realizing the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the second of the five explanations of the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ. First, the common and specific characteristics of the object are clarified.

The characteristics of the objects distinguished by this organ are extremely difficult to discern; when it issues outward, it is easily confused with the objective sound-dust (*śabda-rūpa*), and when it enters inward, it is easily confused with the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). Correctly...
One should separately take that which neither issues forth nor enters—that which is capable of hearing—as the object of contemplation.

For if one falls into the objects of the sense-fields, it becomes ear-consciousness along with the five mental consciousnesses; furthermore, when these grasp objects and subsequently recollect what was previously perceived, it becomes mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and is not the object of contemplation in this perfect penetration.
Second, clarifying the expansion and contraction of contemplation. First, the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s teaching.
To explain what he has realized: the Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is also named Avalokiteśvara;
as the Wénlǐng commentary states, this is the correspondence between cause and effect, a single path throughout past and present.

His statement, "That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation," refers to the dharma-gate for entering the Way at the very beginning of upholding the teachings. The three wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation together constitute...

The essential gateway for entering the Way differs from the conventional path in that it does not fall into the tracks of conceptual meaning, but is rather a direct, illuminating, and perfect cultivation.
Since the previous teachings of the Buddha were already matters of hearing and reflection, the three types of wisdom discussed here pertain solely to cultivation;
as Wēnlíng said, "hearing" refers to reaching the ears, "reflection" refers to fixing the mind, and [cultivation] refers to refining habitual tendencies.
This refers to cultivation. The third is perfect clarity; these are called the three wisdoms.

The first section, from "In the midst of hearing, entering the flow and losing the object" to "the state of quiescent extinction manifests," precisely clarifies the three wisdoms' ability to realize contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) as well as their shallow and deep stages.
This explanation is divided into two parts: first, analyzing the text to explain the meaning; second, correlating the meaning to determine the stages. Regarding the first part:

This consists of two parts: first, the division, and second, the explanation. First, within the section on "hearing," the two lines beginning with "entering the stream and losing the object" provide a general heading.
The eight lines beginning with "since that which is entered is already tranquil" provide a detailed explanation. The two lines beginning with "arising and ceasing" provide a summary.

Within the initial line of the general heading, only the commencement of entering the stream is indicated; the single line "entering the stream and losing the object" specifically distinguishes the power of perfect penetration.

"Use. The meaning and intent of this phrase are profoundly comprehensive; therefore, it is categorized as the general heading. Second, within the detailed explanation, one should follow the textual divisions of Wuxing, which establish four sections:
1. "The loss of external objects": This refers to the fact that what is entered is already quiescent, such that the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.
"What is entered" refers to the stream of objects mentioned above. "Already quiescent" means to directly follow [the nature of reality].

When the faculty of hearing enters the stream of the Dharma-nature and reaches the nature of awakening—which is wondrously luminous—and the fundamental awakening which is luminously wondrous, this is true *āraṇya*.

This place of the stillness of cessation (*śamatha*) and the field of the Way (*mārga-kṣetra*), the site of correct cultivation, is called "already stilled. This is what is meant by "tranquil and unmoving."
Although this is the first step of practice, it must accord with the profound principle of "extinction" (nirodha) in the lower stage of cessation;
only then can it be said that the names of cause and effect correspond. The two characteristics of movement and stillness are the sense-object of sound: when there is movement, there is sound;

when there is stillness, there is no sound. To bifurcate this into two kinds of "knots" (grasping at signs), as Master Jiaoguang does, shows he does not understand the nature of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa).
Ah! Regarding the meaning of "clearly non-arising," there are varying depths. To speak of it briefly: the nature of sound consists of movement and stillness;
within hearing, these may be said to exist or not. When there is no sound, one speaks of "no-hearing," yet this is not a case where the nature of hearing itself is absent.

Therefore, when one first enters the stream within hearing, being able to follow that which is constant and not following the dust of sound to give rise to discrimination—this is called [the state of non-arising].

Regarding "thoroughly understanding non-arising": speaking deeply, for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom who have entered the stream—entering once and entering forever—and who attain profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), forgetting self and what belongs to self, and no longer perceiving the marks of the desire realm such as sounds and objects, this is called "thoroughly understanding non-arising.
Second, the exhaustion of internal faculties: in this manner, as they gradually increase, that which is heard and that which hears are both exhausted.
Indeed. Now, knowledge arises from objects and appearances exist because of the sense faculties; these two phenomena form a pair, and the existence of either one alone is impossible.
Although the preceding faculty was shown to perish because it depends on the object, if the faculty itself were not extinguished, one would ultimately fail to reach the goal;
therefore, it is necessary to exhaust both the faculty and its root. As for the phrase "thus gradually increasing," "thus" refers back to the aforementioned term "already stilled. This is because...
The distinction between the true and the semblance of the contemplative understanding of quiescence is extremely profound. For now, we shall discuss the essential application of contemplative wisdom:
it causes the nature already attained through quiescence to gradually increase and expand. Since hearing this brings all that is heard to an end, it is said:
"Thus gradually increasing, what is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted. This means that even the one who hears and the object that is heard [are likewise exhausted].
It is exhausted. The wisdom of the three contemplations of emptiness is precisely the exhaustion of hearing, which is the non-abiding wherein both the perceiver and the perceived are empty.

"Exhaustion of hearing" reiterates the aforementioned characteristic of the internal faculties having already been exhausted; "non-abiding" clearly elucidates that the wisdom of contemplation should be empty.

For contemplative wisdom is the agent of emptiness, while the faculties and sense objects are the objects to be emptied. Just as medicine is prescribed in response to an illness, once the illness has departed, the medicine should likewise be discarded.
When the illness has vanished, if one continues to take the medicine, then holding onto the medicine will perpetuate the illness.

Therefore, the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness must itself be emptied. Only when one brings about the realization that the very wisdom which contemplates and perceives is also empty can it be called "the illness gone and the medicine discarded," returning once more to the original vital energy (*prāṇa*).
This is the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): emptiness, awakening, and ultimate perfection.
Emptiness is the extinction of that which is empty. The awakening to emptiness is precisely the awakening of the wisdom of the superior contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

This awakening and the principle of truth realized therein possess distinctions that are fundamentally different. If one has not yet attained ultimate perfection, the principle of the "repeated emptiness" will not have been forgotten.
One must require that this emptiness itself be empty to attain the principle of ultimate perfection; therefore, it is said that "the emptiness and that which is emptied are both extinguished.

Regarding these four sections of the text: the first section emphasizes the two characters "already tranquil" (jì jí); the second section emphasizes the two characters "gradually increasing" (jiàn zēng);
the third section emphasizes the two characters "not abiding" (bù zhù); and the fourth section emphasizes the two characters "ultimate perfection" (jí yuán). All other [points] are as follows.
This merely explains and completes the auxiliary clarification. Third, regarding the summary: "When arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests.
The single phrase "entering the stream and losing the object" from the preceding general heading already encompasses the following four sections.
That is to say: first, one enters the stream of hearing and loses the object of sound; next, one enters the stream of contemplative wisdom and loses the locus of the faculty of hearing.

Third, entering the stream of profound emptiness, one abandons the locus of contemplative wisdom. Fourth, entering the stream of quiescent extinction, one abandons the locus of the principles of the Truths.
The summary of this section is likewise so: first, by abandoning external objects, the object of sound ceases and the faculty of hearing arises;
this is merely arising and ceasing, not non-arising. Next, by exhausting the internal faculties, contemplative wisdom arises and...
When the faculty of hearing ceases, this too is a process of arising and ceasing, not a non-arising.

When the wisdom of the threefold contemplation of emptiness arises and the contemplative wisdom itself ceases, this too is a process of arising and ceasing, not a non-arising. Fourth, as for the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):

although the aforementioned repeated contemplation of emptiness belongs to the principle of the Truth, it still possesses subtle marks of arising and ceasing, and thus must also be extinguished. As it is said:
Only when these coarse and subtle arisings and ceasings have ceased does quiescent extinction (śānti-nirvāṇa) manifest before one.

Therefore, the intent of the preceding four fascicles—which, by means of the four propositions of "caused by conditions" and "arising spontaneously," eliminate [misconceptions]—lies herein. Second, regarding the determination of stages according to their meaning:
first, the external objects are lost; second, the internal faculties are exhausted. As stated in the preceding text: "This faculty first attains liberation..."

1. "Attaining the emptiness of persons" belongs to the stage of the first faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), where one breaks through the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). 2. "The wisdom of the contemplation of the threefold emptiness" corresponds to the preceding passage on the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness;
"attaining liberation from dharmas" belongs to the stage of the seventh faith of the Perfect Teaching, where one breaks through the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). 3.

"The principle of the Truth of Cessation" corresponds to the preceding passage on how, once the dharmas of liberation are attained, both [person and dharma] are empty and do not arise; this belongs to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching, where one breaks through... [the delusions of ignorance].
This is the stage of ignorance; therefore it is said: "This is called the Bodhisattva entering the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from samādhi.

To speak of this again according to the concluding text: "When arising and ceasing have both ceased"—if the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) were to cease, one should realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

Furthermore, it says: "When quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*) manifests before one, one should realize the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-kṣānti*). Now, regarding these two patiences...

In the end, where does it reside? Therefore, I shall explain this according to my own understanding: speaking in terms of the five *kṣāntis* (patiences), the manifestation of quiescence (*śānti*) corresponds precisely to the stage of the fruit of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Now, the provisional judgment that it enters the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) is because the Bodhisattva of the first *vihāra* (abode) has already destroyed the afflictions of the aspect of cessation;
thus it is said that "quiescence manifests. Second, a brief explanation of the names.

Regarding these characteristics: when words involve many avenues, practice follows the explanations of those words and thus remains unexamined; yet when principle returns to the ultimate truth, contemplation follows that principle and enters it, becoming easy to clarify.

I have humbly investigated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and although its textual meanings are numerous, upon examining its essential purpose, they are all established for the sake of the Venerable Ānanda’s earnest request for the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. However—

Practice depends on understanding for its advancement, while understanding relies on practice for its fulfillment. Only when understanding and practice support one another can one realize entry into the stage of fruition (*phala*).

Therefore, the sūtras establish the sequence of first attaining the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and subsequently the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), followed by the realization of the fruit.

Although there are three divisions [of the teachings], one takes the gate of practice as the primary subject. While there are twenty-five gates of practice, they are further categorized by means of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

The dharma-gate cultivated through sound serves as the sovereign lord. Thus, the four characters "entering the stream and losing the object" constitute the main axis of this entire scripture and the profound pulse of its ten fascicles.
From the perspective of intellectual understanding, the single character "stream" (liú) fully encompasses it;
from the perspective of establishing practice, the single character "entering" (rù) comprehensively includes it; and from the perspective of realizing the fruit—
Thus, the two characters "nothing" (wu-so) encompass everything; therefore, one may synthesize and understand them by means of two meanings.

First is the section on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and second is the section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). At the beginning of the section on the Path of Seeing, the primary recipient first makes a request based on three dharmas.

In the past, Master Gushan once explained this by means of the Three Kinds of Cessation (*tri-śamatha*) of Tiantai, which accorded perfectly with the Buddha’s intent. However, regarding what this sutra...
