If one distinguishes them according to the three dharmas in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), they appear clearly and orderly, as has already been explained through detailed analysis in the preceding text.
Now, I shall merely synthesize them according to their meaning; furthermore, the sūtra contains two successive responses, the first of which concerns non-... [text truncated]
Next, in succession, he recompenses Ānanda. First, there was the general indication, such as the eternally abiding true mind, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the fundamentally pure essence;
this refers to the single character "flow" (*liú*) within the object of contemplation of the ear-faculty. Within the specific indications:

Just as a blind person stares into the darkness, this is the mind and not the eye. Having set aside [the physical organ], one first tests that seeing is immovable by counting fingers or waving a light;

finally, at the moment of seeing-seeing, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing. These ten sections provide a profound demonstration of the nature of seeing, all of which belong to the realm of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) where *śamatha*—the cessation that realizes the true essence—comes to rest.
As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, this is what is meant by "awakening to the pure, perfect [enlightenment]."
Awakening consists in taking stillness as one's practice by means of a pure awakened mind. When a practitioner first enters this stream, they must realize this nature of hearing.

Just as with the nature of seeing—which is neither moving nor shifting, and even where "seeing the seeing" is not seeing—one should contemplate in this manner so as to eliminate external objects, empty the internal faculties, and extinguish the wisdom of contemplation within the principle of the Truth of Cessation.

This constitutes ceasing by realizing the true essence and taking stillness as one's practice, coming to rest within the True Truth (*satyadharma*). This is precisely what Master Sengzhao meant when he said, "To encounter phenomena and realize their truth;
to embody this is the numinous. Furthermore, it is like the two kinds of discernment that perceive delusion:

by removing [delusion], one sees that the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. When examined through the analysis of the four modes of being (*catuṣkoṭi*), they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they self-existent.

However, all these involve practicing "stopping according with conditions" (*suiyuanzhi*) within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), one awakens to pure, perfect enlightenment;
with this mind of pure awakening, one realizes that both the nature of the mind and the sense bases (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are all illusory transformations.
Thus, one gives rise to various illusions in order to eliminate the illusionist. When the practitioner enters the stream [of the Dharma], they must first...

One should know that the nature of the ear, as well as the faculty and its object, are all produced by illusion; thus, one gives rise to various illusory investigations to eliminate the illusionist itself.
For instance, within the sensory object of sound, one should examine whether the sound comes to the ear or the ear goes to the place of the sound.
Furthermore, when auditory consciousness arises conditioned by these factors, one should investigate each one individually: does this consciousness arise because of the ear?
When arising, it takes the ear as its realm; when produced by sound, it takes sound as its realm.

Furthermore, one should investigate each instance within the ear-entrance (*śrotra-āyatana*) and know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.

By investigating in this manner, one can eliminate the external objects (*viṣaya*), exhaust the internal organs, and realize the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) through the wisdom of contemplation. This is...
To cease through skillful means in accordance with conditions is precisely to give rise to various illusions in order to eliminate illusion.

Furthermore, the principles of the great nature of the seven elements—namely, that the nature of form is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true form; that they are pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;

and that they respond to the capacity of what sentient beings know according to their minds—all illustrate the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging."

Dhyāna brings to rest the dualistic discriminations of the two extremes, halting within the realm of the Middle Truth. As stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, this means awakening to pure perfect enlightenment;
with a mind of pure awareness, one does not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness.

One thoroughly understands that both body and mind are hindrances, and that the luminosity of non-cognitive awareness does not rely on any such obstructions, thereby forever transcending both the obstructed and the unobstructed.
The objects of perception, the world of experience, and the characteristics of body and mind exist within the realm of sensory dust, like the sound of a bell emerging from within a vessel.

When the practitioner enters this stream, they must employ a mind of pure awakening that neither grasps at the mundane extreme of illusory transformations nor clings to the true extreme of quiescent signs;
they must clearly realize that both body and mind are but entanglements.
Having forever transcended the two extremes of obstruction and non-obstruction, it is like the faculty of hearing:

when a drum is struck in the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm, one hears it in all ten places upon merely hearing once. This wondrous virtue is luminous and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, filling the ten directions;
how could it have a specific location? It is truly as the saying goes: "The form resides within the realm of dust, like the resonance within a vessel."

Emerging from the external, one is able to contemplate in this way: that the external objects have perished and the internal faculties are empty, such that the wisdom of contemplation realizes the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
This is called "stopping by ceasing the discrimination of the two extremes" and not grasping at them as practice;

it is to abide in the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Next, by means of the sequential and non-sequential Three Truths, he responds to Pūrṇa’s [inquiry] regarding the fundamentally pure nature.
How is it that this "sudden arising" question precisely clarifies the principle of the aforementioned "the unchanging following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging"?

At the outset, it generally indicates the true *āraṇya*—the locus of correct practice—as the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodha*) and the fundamental awakening’s clarity-wonder (*mūla-bodhi-prakāśa-vicitra*).

Furthermore, the single character "flowing" (*liú*) refers specifically to the object of contemplation for the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as described here. It separately demonstrates how, by means of my own...

The cessation of non-arising is identical to the Tathāgatagarbha; the ten realms are neither together nor separate, yet they are both together and separate, and thus detached from being either together or separate.
This is the perfect interfusion of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) as observed: to mention one is to include all three, and to speak of three is to include all one.
Thus, the single character "flow" (*liu*) perfectly embodies the three truths as well as the ten realms. However...

The specific mention of "streams" is a metaphor used to reveal the Dharma. It means that sentient beings, having been deluded regarding the Truth since beginningless time, have pursued the false as if flowing from a source.
Now, returning from the false to accord with the Truth is like tracing back to the source from the stream.
When one flows from the source, the root becomes adhered to sensory objects, rushing outward and escaping, thus forming a thousand streams.
Ten thousand streams flow into it; upon entering, one sheds their attachments and lies dormant within, following the current to trace back to the source, where the One Way is serene and level.
You must know that the inherent awareness (*xing-jue*) is necessarily luminous as the root of the source, while delusion (*wang*) is the beginning of the flow of luminous awareness.

Because of this luminosity, an objective locus is established; once that locus is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. From these three subtleties (*san-xi*), the six coarsenesses (*liu-cu*) subsequently emerge.
The characteristics of the six sense organs together constitute the end of the flow.

Now, when one speaks of "entering the flow," it means to go against that beginningless flow of woven delusive karma, returning to the root of the flow until reaching the state of non-arising and non-extinction. To summarize:
this is precisely the essence of the two aforementioned roots—the fundamentally pure body of Bodhi and Nirvana—which is your present consciousness-essence, the original luminosity.

That which is capable of giving rise to all conditions yet is overlooked by those conditions is the primordial purity of the essence of wisdom; it is the inherent clarity of the fundamental awakening.
That which is capable of giving rise to all conditions refers to the auditory faculty of the present moment acting as the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses.

If one follows sounds with discrimination, then that which gives rise to all conditions overlooks the original luminosity, resulting in deluded luminosity. If, however, one enters the stream and turns the hearing inward...
Prostrate and return to the original, true nature of non-arising and non-extinction. By returning thus without ceasing, the preceding sensory objects vanish and the internal faculties become empty;
as contemplative wisdom realizes the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), arising and ceasing are extinguished, and quiescent extinction (*śānti*) manifests before one.

Is not the scope encompassed by the single character "flow" (*liu*) truly vast? Second, the Section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The meaning of the text has no other purpose than to clarify certainty.
Regarding the meaning: the path previously perceived, which is called "cultivating the path" because it illuminates and realizes in accordance with the nature, is as follows:

for instance, when one first makes a definitive and careful observation to see whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is the same as or different from the awakening of the resultant stage—if, while at the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for cultivation and yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.

Furthermore, it is said: "If you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death and rely upon the nature of the non-arising and non-perishing perfect stillness to achieve this.

By means of that stillness, you should revolve the false and extinguish arising; thus you subdue and return to original enlightenment, taking that fundamental luminous enlightenment as the mind for the causal ground. Only then—"
The fruit of the stage of perfection is the realization of the fruit-stage awakening.
This differs from the seven categories cited by Ānanda below to question the Tathāgata regarding the nature of the cause of doubt and its cessation.

The Tathāgata then commanded the Venerable Rāhula to strike a bell to test for permanence, thereby demonstrating that the faculty of hearing does not perish. Furthermore, it is like a person in sleep or a dream, although—

this is the second definitive and detailed examination of the root of affliction. Since beginningless time, who has created and who has received the karma that initiates action and moistens rebirth?
It is your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six that act as the intermediaries for thieves.
From the plundering of one's own family treasures, up to the discernment of what is seen and heard, the fundamental point of the conclusion is to bind the mind.

To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; to see no-seeing within seeing and knowing is itself nirvana. This is also the single character "flow" (liu) within this very stream.
It is because this essence of the auditory consciousness within the ear-organ can give rise to various conditions, flowing outward from its source; thus it becomes affliction and birth-and-death.
If one relies on this original clarity of the ear-organ—the hearing that hears both hearing and non-hearing—and traces back from the flow to the source, then it becomes bodhi and nirvana.
Therefore it is said: "The binding and the untying share the same cause; the holy and the ordinary are not two."

The "stream" (pravāha) refers to the word "stream" (*liu*) in the verse, which indicates that the true nature—in which both the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as bondage and liberation, are simultaneously discarded—is ultimately resolved within this very stream. It shows that the discernment [of this] must be precise;
for fear of confusion regarding what is truly real and what is not, I have never extensively expounded upon it. This also refers to the word "stream. If...

When I do not see, if one can transform objects, then at the moment of seeing the seeing, one realizes that the conditions are not the cataract. One must examine the four natures.

if that ceases, the knots at the heart will immediately unravel and disperse. This occurs merely through these few points. For this perfect principle is the foundation of Great Samādhi.

Practice relies upon understanding to advance—this is precisely what is meant. Third, regarding the judgment of the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*): the treatise on Bodhi...

For instance, in the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings, those who have attained the stage of *Srotāpanna* are called "those who enter the stream," yet they do not enter into form, sound, taste, touch, or dharmas.
Is this not precisely "entering the stream while losing the object"? Furthermore, this "entering the stream" is also termed "hearing what is heard. And...
When the Venerable Aniruddha turned back to see the source of his vision, he called it "seeing-seeing.

Since both seeing-seeing and hearing-hearing are the perfect penetration of the six sense faculties, yet the Venerable only realized the fourth fruit of Arhatship, does this not mean that its meaning belongs to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao)?
If there are bodhisattvas who, relying on this, cultivate practice such that they see only the "Middle" (zhong) and not the two extremes, does this meaning not also apply to the Separate Teaching?
Thus, the principle of "Perfect Penetration" (yuantong) here ultimately belongs to the Perfect Teaching; it must be discussed in terms of perfect principle and perfect practice.

II. Extensive Manifestation of the Two [Attainments] (First: Transcending the Nine Realms) Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds. II. Attaining the Two Sublime Victories The ten directions become perfectly luminous, and one attains two sublime victories:
First, above, one merges with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, becoming one with the Tathāgatas in their power of universal compassion;
Second, below, one merges with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, becoming one with all those beings in their shared sorrow and yearning.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: Regarding the phrase "the power of compassion" mentioned above, since compassion bestows happiness, it must necessarily be able to extract one from suffering;

This does not refer to the Responsive [Buddha], but rather speaks of the capacity of the sentient being. Therefore, when one feels weary of and afflicted by the path of suffering, this is due to "compassion."

Now, you clarify that [the Buddha] manifests activity based on realization;

why, then, does he still descend to respond to the Two Vehicles? The answer is: This clarifies that the karmic capacity (indriya) of the Two Vehicles still remains latent within the sixth consciousness.
In general, one feels compassion for the suffering of the aggregates and severs their accumulation; one looks up toward the bliss of cessation and cultivates the Path.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva manifests an emanation body to preach the Dharma, they extract suffering from beings and bestow upon them bliss; ultimately, this is not a path of union.

○ (2. Manifesting worldly bodies; 2a. Celestial bodies; 2aa. Heavenly kings) If there are sentient beings whose minds are clear and awakened regarding desire, who do not transgress the dust of desire, and whose bodies are pure, I appear before them in the form of a Brahmā king and preach the Dharma for their liberation.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become celestial lords and exercise sovereignty over the heavens, I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma so that they may achieve it.
If there are sentient beings who desire to travel freely through the ten directions with their bodies,
I appear before them in the form of Īśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve this. If there are sentient beings who desire to fly through the void with their bodies at will,
I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve this.
[Commentary] Gushan says: The Brahmā King is the lord of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), named Śikhin, which translates as "Crest.
The *Ābhāsvara-alaṃkāra-sūtra* clarifies that there is a king for each of the four dhyānas; the one mentioned here as "Brahmā" should be the pinnacle of the first dhyāna.

Because he possesses the dharmas of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and speech, he serves as the sovereign of a thousand worlds. One who preaches the Dharma is like [the Buddha in] the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
It is said that the Great Brahmā Heavenly King expounded the *Discourse on Transcending Desire*. "Liberation" means causing one to depart from the dust of desire.
Śakra is the lord of the second heaven within the Desire Realm; that heaven consists of thirty-three heavens situated side-by-side, over which Śakra presides.
His preaching of the Dharma refers to the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Śakradevendra [expounds] various discourses on the wholesome."
This is so. Īśvara is the zenith heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In full, he is called Vaśavartin, which means "Mastery over Others' Transformations" (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*);
he achieves his own pleasure by making use of what others have created, and is thus the Māra King.

Alternatively, it is said that there is a separate dwelling for the Māra King on the sixth heaven, which is also subsumed under the Īśvaras. Maheśvara, however, is the zenith of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Maheśvara is the deity described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as having three eyes, eight arms, riding a white ox, and holding a white fly-whisk.

Wēnlíng says: "First Maheśvara is mentioned; then, by leaping from the Desire Realm to the Peak of Form, the formless realms are implicitly included, thereby clarifying that there is no land where he does not appear."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Question—Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, it is acceptable to call the first four "transcendental" (lokottara) as they constitute liberation.
However, although the Brahmā King presides over the three realms, he has not yet transcended the world;
why then is he also called "liberated"? Answer: Lust is the deep root of birth and death and the evil karma of sinking into saṃsāra. This sutra, by means of...
It was on account of the defilement of Ānanda that the Great Teaching was vigorously promulgated;

this is why every exhortation found within the sūtras is expressed in terms of abandoning desire and attachment. Thus, the Brahmā King is the foremost of those who ascend to purity and the precursor to emerging from desire;
although he has not yet transcended the mundane world, he is capable of bringing about detachment.
The *Shiben* (Origins of the World) states that its words are earnest, incisive, and clearly manifest: "One desires the mind to be awakened;
one desires not to transgress the dust of desire; one desires the body to be pure. For the body is the mate of desire, the dust is the counterpart of desire, and the mind is the mechanism of desire.
Therefore, for those who hope to escape desire, there is nothing more fundamental than to dismantle this mechanism. Desire—
When the mind attains clear awakening, one has already attained the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). With a single awakening of the mind, the mechanism of desire (*kāma*) perishes;

with the perishing of the mechanism of desire, one takes nothing from sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Once one truly attains this state of non-appropriation, the body becomes like a wooden cock, and one no longer encounters the dust of desire.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests his body and teaches the Dharma so that beings may be liberated from desire.
This refers to the body and mind of the realms (*dhātu*). Since this is the case for the first dhyāna, the subsequent three dhyānas become increasingly superior.

The Sūtra does not mention "attainment" (*samanvāgama*) because it cites one instance to represent all others. Because those in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) lack a body, "attainment" is not mentioned;
as for the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they differ from these cases, and thus it simply says they "possess" (*sampanna*).

(2. Belonging to the Celestial Realm) If there are sentient beings who desire to govern spirits and deities to protect their lands, I appear before them in the form of a Great Celestial General and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.

If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect all living beings, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and command ghosts and spirits,
I manifest before them in the form of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma to them so that they may achieve their goal.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: The former passage cited the orthodox lineage; this passage cites the ministers and assistants.
The Heavenly General serves as the supreme general of Śakra-devendra, commanding ghosts and spirits. The Four Heavenly Kings are subjects of Śakra-devendra and command the world.
The princes of the Four Heavens—such as Nāṭa and his peers—are capable of driving away ghosts and spirits.

○ (2. The Human Body: Part 3, Initial Section on Noble Lineage and Pure Conduct) If there are sentient beings who delight in being kings of men, I manifest before them in the body of a king of men and preach the Dharma for them, so that they may achieve fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who love the status of a head of a clan and are esteemed by the world, I manifest before them in the body of an elder (*śreṣṭhin*) and preach the Dharma for them, so that they may achieve fulfillment. If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing fame...
If there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling in purity, I appear before them in the form of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and teach them the Dharma so that they may achieve accomplishment.

If there are sentient beings who love to govern a kingdom and adjudicate the affairs of a state, I appear before them in the form of a high official (*kṣatriya-amātya*) and teach them the Dharma so that they may achieve accomplishment.
If there are sentient beings who love various arts and sciences for the sake of self-protection and maintenance...
He dwelt before me, manifesting in the form of a *brāhmaṇa*, and preached the Dharma for him so that he might achieve success.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: From the *cakravartin* kings down to the minor rulers, all are kings of men.

"Minor rulers" (*xiù sàn*) refers to the small kingdoms and local princes scattered throughout the world as numerous as grains of millet. A "householder" (*gṛhapati*) possesses ten virtues; these refer to noble lineage and high status...
Tall, noble, wealthy, majestic, profound in wisdom, advanced in years, pure in conduct, and perfected in ritual, he was praised by those above and venerated by those below;

thus, as the head of his clan, he was esteemed by the world. One who lives in seclusion to pursue their aspirations and practices righteousness to reach the Way is called a *gṛhapati* (lay practitioner).
He delighted in discussing renowned sayings, that is, elegant and refined speech. He served as a high minister of the Three Dukes, a prime minister, a provincial governor, or a district magistrate.
They were all titled as officials. A *brāhmaṇa*—here translated as "Pure Practice"—is one of the four castes.
They delighted in various arts of calculation, namely the synthesis of divination, physiognomy, and the推算 (calculation) of the waxing and waning of celestial bodies.

○ (2. The Fourfold Assembly of the Dharma of Transformation) If there are men who delight in study, have left the household life, and uphold the various precepts, I shall manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are women who delight in study, have left the household life, and uphold the various prohibitions, I shall manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment. If...
If there are men who delight in upholding the five precepts, I manifest before them in the form of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I manifest before them in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.
[Commentary] Gushan says: *Upāsaka* means "male lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*); *upāsikā* means "female lay follower" (*jìnshì nǚ*).
Because they maintain themselves by means of the five precepts, they are capable of serving as attendants to the two groups of the ordained community.

○ (Third: Female Rulers and Virgins) If there are women who govern internal affairs and establish themselves as pillars of their households and nations, I appear before them in the form of a female ruler, a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
If there are sentient beings who do not damage their male organs, I appear before them in the form of a young man and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
If there is a maiden who delights in dwelling in her body and does not seek to be violated,
I shall manifest before her in the form of a young girl and preach the Dharma to her so that she may achieve accomplishment.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "The female ruler" refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven.

According to the *Rites of Zhou*, the consort of the Son of Heaven establishes six palaces, consisting of three ladies, nine concubines, twenty-seven women of the generations, and eighty-one attendants.
A "State Lady" is as described in the *Analects* regarding the wife of a feudal lord, called the "Lady Consort. A "Commanded Lady" refers to a wife who attains honor through her husband.
As for the term "Dajia" (Great Lady), there was, for example, the wife of Cao Shishu of Fufeng during the Later Han dynasty;

she was the daughter of Ban Biao of the same commandery, named Zhao and styled Huiji. Emperor He repeatedly summoned her into the palace and ordered the Empress and the noble ladies to take her as their teacher, whereupon she was titled "Dajia."

○ (Section 38: The Threefold Assembly; First, Clarifying the Four Classes) If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial status, I manifest in a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve fulfillment.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their original class, I appear before them in a yakṣa body and preach the Dharma for them.

If there are those among the gandharvas who desire liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment.

(2. Explaining the Three Families) If there are asuras who desire liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma for them so that they may achieve accomplishment. If there are kinnaras...
If those who delight in liberation from their own kind appear before them in the form of a kiṃnara and preach the Dharma for them, they shall achieve accomplishment.
If mahoragas delight in liberation from their own kind, I appear before them in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them, so that they may achieve accomplishment.
(The third section on the latter part: If there are sentient beings who delight in being human and practicing as humans, I manifest as a human.
Manifesting in bodily form, I preach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment. Whether they be non-human beings with form or without form,
with perception or without perception, who desire to transcend their own kind, I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma to bring them to accomplishment.
[Commentary] Gushan says: *Yakṣa* is translated here as "light and agile. *Gandharva* is translated as "fragrance-aggregate" (*xiāngyīn*);
in the new translations, it is rendered as "seeking-fragrance-goer" (*xúnxīngháng*). He is the music deity of Śakra. *Asura* means "not upright";

because the women are beautiful while the men are ugly, the name is designated according to the male. In the new translations, they are called "non-gods" (*fēitiān*), because they lack the conduct of gods due to their flattery and deceit. According to...
In the eight classes of the "Universal Gate" (Pumen pin), this [text] omits the *garuḍa*, which is the golden-winged bird (*suparṇin*).

The *kiṃnara* has a form resembling a human but with horns on its head; for this reason, it is called the "Doubtful Deity. It is the deity of the celestial emperors' string and bamboo music, and is slightly inferior to the *gandharva*.
The new translation calls them the "Singing Deities. Regarding the *mahoraga*, Master Shi says they are "earth dragons. Master Zhao...
It is said that these are like great pythons crawling on their bellies. Changshui says: "Those with form include those such as the *xiujiu jingming* (spirits of portents);
those without form include those such as the *kong sanxiao chen* (those who disperse, dissolve, or sink into emptiness); those with consciousness include spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings;
and those without consciousness include those where the spirit transforms into earth, wood, metal, or stone—all of whom are not human."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The thirty-two transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of this sutra are identical to those in the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet the teachings they deliver differ.
That [sutra] was for the purpose of circulating the *Lotus Sutra* and thus speaks exclusively of the Buddha-dharma; hence its text states:
"By whatever body one should be delivered, by that very body he shall preach the Dharma. This sutra, however, is intended to manifest...
From the wondrous essence arises the wondrous function; there is no land where it does not appear, and no dharma that it does not expound.

Speaking in terms of its universal response, the application of *samādhi* (Lengyan) is vast; speaking in terms of its great essence, the foundation of the true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is great.
One [sūtra] bestows the provisional while the other reveals the real; their matters are not redundant. One narrates the causes, while the other narrates...
The fruit and the path are not distinct from one another.
(2. Summary and Demonstration) This is called the wondrously pure body of the thirty-two manifestations entering various lands;
all are accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrousness, cultivated by hearing and practicing what has been heard through samādhi.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The traces manifest as being of the same class, while the mind is free from attachment and views; this is called 'wondrous purity.

Relying on non-acting wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) to give rise to great spiritual power is called 'wondrous power. Being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and acting spontaneously in accordance with conditions is called 'the accomplishment of mastery.
Wŭ-xīng says: "Although the thirty-two manifestations differ in their appearance and disappearance when compared to the *Pumen pin* (Universal Door Chapter), the general principle is the same."
These are the same. Generally speaking, there are no more than ten realms. Within these ten realms, both sutras lack mention of the bodhisattva body and the hell-being body.
Some say this is merely an abbreviation of the holy word; others say that since Avalokiteśvara is already a bodhisattva, why would he need to manifest such forms?
Furthermore, the suffering in hell is so heavy that it cannot be saved. The Wise One (Zhi-zhe), relying on the True Dharma...
The flowers manifest the bodies of the Bodhisattvas within the ten realms. Furthermore, according to the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shìlùn), Bodhisattvas also transform the hells;
thus, one knows that the ten realms must not be omitted.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These thirty-two responses are the bodies of the ten dharma-realms. The lands are adorned with the true retribution (*vipāka*).

The "Expedient Means" (upāya) refers to the realm where ordinary beings and sages dwell together. If the capacities of the ten realms are arranged horizontally within a single land, then Bodhisattvas enter this realm of common dwelling (*sahā*) by means of thirty-two kinds of bodies.
If they are arranged vertically across the three lands, then Bodhisattvas enter the Land of True Reward (*niṣyanda-vipāka*) with the body of a Buddha;
they enter the Land of Trace (*nirmāṇa*) with the bodies of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas; and they enter [the realm of ordinary beings] with the bodies of the six paths of existence.

They enter the Land of Common Abode (*sāmbhogika-kāya*). That Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-dharmadhātu*) is the land wherein Bodhisattvas dwell, having partially realized the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

"The permeation of hearing through samādhi" and "the cultivation of hearing" manifest the non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) of causal practice. "Sublime power" manifests the non-action of the fruition-function.
To summarize the preceding text: the Perfect, the Penetrating, and the Universal encompass the ten realms and the three truths as their fundamental nature.
The non-action of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is the entry into the stream where the object of perception is lost.

Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, it harmonizes upward with all Buddhas and downward with the six realms of existence; this is the non-action of the wondrous essence of the nature-endowed fruit-realization.
The thirty-two manifestations respond to the nature and the capacity [of beings], and in a single day, as the sun is in the sky, its reflection descends upon ten thousand things.

This is the effortless, wondrous function of water. From cause to fruit, relying on the essence to give rise to function, the merits of the Bodhisattva are accomplished with such sovereign mastery; how could one not believe this?
"O World-Honored One, furthermore, by means of this power of the effortless and wondrous Vajra-samādhi— perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—
and because I share in the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings of the ten directions and three periods throughout the six realms,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness within my body and mind."
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "Because I did not [fixate on] my own sounds, others were able to escape suffering;
because my faculty of knowledge and vision was reversed, they were not burned. Therefore it is said: 'I have attained the virtue of fearlessness within my own body and mind.'"
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the *Fahua Xuanyi*, it is discussed that there are four permutations regarding the relationship between the capacity (*jī*) and the response (*yìng*).

These are: manifest capacity with manifest response; manifest capacity with hidden response; hidden capacity with manifest response; and hidden capacity with hidden response. The preceding explanation of the thirty-two transformation bodies refers to the case where both capacity and response are manifest.
The subsequent explanation of the fourteen fearlessnesses refers to the case where the capacity is manifest and the response is hidden. If [the response is] hidden...

Regarding the manifestation of response through latent capacity (*mijian yingzuo*): although sentient beings may currently lack the capacity to "strike" the Buddha, there are those whose past seeds for cultivating the eighth consciousness have matured.
When a Bodhisattva perceives that such a person can be delivered, he manifests a response.

As for the case of a latent capacity meeting a latent response, this refers to a practitioner of the present who, without receiving instruction from a teacher, is nonetheless able to practice virtue with vigor.

That one is able to penetrate and understand the essential principles of the Dharma without having heard them is entirely due to the presence of hidden mechanisms within and the secret response of Bodhisattvas without that brings it about.
○ (II. Specifically showing the manifestation of benefits according to capacity;

Part One: General explanation of how the wisdom of contemplation bestows grace upon those who observe their capacity, enabling them to attain fearlessness amidst all sufferings. First: Because I do not contemplate myself, but rather contemplate the one who contemplates, I cause those multitudes suffering in the ten directions—
When one gives rise to contemplation of its sounds, one immediately attains liberation.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Not contemplating the sound itself" means not following the cognitions and views that arise from the sensory object of sound.

"Contemplating by means of contemplation" refers to turning back the mechanism of inverted hearing to reflect upon one's own nature. When such cognitions and views do not arise, there is nothing [to be grasped].
If one turns back to reflect upon that which is falsely grasped, then the self-nature is entirely true and quiescent, and no further suffering or affliction can be found.
This is the True Contemplation, the Pure Contemplation, and the Contemplation of Great Wisdom; it can shatter the darkness of ignorance and subdue calamities.
Therefore, it causes suffering sentient beings to receive this True Contemplation of mine and immediately attain liberation. Wu Xing said: "The Sage has no self; there are only things."
This is the benefit. Therefore, by applying the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara to the capacity of those who contemplate his voice, they shall be liberated from suffering before their feet have even turned.

As for those who merely recite the name while remaining ignorant of the cultivation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), such that the skillful response has not yet been reached and they instead accuse the words of the Sage of being empty—this is like sprinkling a single cup of water to extinguish a fire of accumulated firewood; the fire will not...
To say that when extinguished there is no water because it does not overcome fire is a most profound delusion. Tianru’s supplementary note states:

"Master Huan’s interpretation places the contemplation of sound in the response; Master Yue’s interpretation places the contemplation of sound in the capacity [of the practitioner]. Since these two views cannot be discarded unilaterally, they are preserved together.
One should know that the meaning of the preceding text is no different from this."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Because I do not observe the sound by means of the observer, the observed sound resides in the response (*yìng*).
Causing those sentient beings to observe that sound, the observed sound resides in the capacity (*jī*) [of the practitioner].

Since the meaning of the following text is no different from this, the title of this section is established as "A General Explanation of How the Wisdom of Observation Bestows Its Power upon the Observation of Capacities and Attains [the Goal]."
They are fearless regarding all sufferings. (2.

Specifically explaining the empowerment of contemplative wisdom and its application to sentient beings so that they attain fearlessness toward all sufferings, in thirteen parts; first, knowing and seeing the reversion [of the faculties], resulting in fearlessness toward the calamity of fire. Second, by the reversion of knowledge and vision, even if all sentient beings enter a great conflagration, the fire cannot burn them.

(Second, the reversion of hearing and contemplation, resulting in fearlessness toward the calamity of water. Third, by the reversion of hearing and contemplation, even if all sentient beings are swept away by a great flood, the water cannot drown them.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The four elements of the internal and external realms are constantly interacting and influencing one another. Vision and cognition belong to fire; hearing and listening belong to water.

Therefore, when the karma of vision interacts, one perceives fierce flames; when the karma of hearing interacts, one perceives surging waves. Now, because one knows that vision has revolved back [to its source], there is no karma of vision;
because one observes that hearing has revolved back, there is no karma of hearing. Thus, water and fire cannot [disturb them]."

"Shao" means to burn; "ni" means to drown. Regarding the phrase "listening to words and contemplating," the pronunciation of "yan" (words) is the same as "guan" (contemplation). When it says "drifting on great waters," the meaning includes the calamity of wind.

Xielǐ said: According to the Tiantai interpretation, there are three kinds of fire calamities: first, the fire of karmic retribution, which extends from the hells below up to the First Dhyāna Heaven above;
second, the fire of evil karma, which pervades the Three Realms; third, the fire of afflictions, which pervades the Three [Realms].
Since the difficulty of the fire-vehicle is thus resolved, all others may be released accordingly.
○ Third, by severing and extinguishing delusive thoughts so that the mind is free from killing, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts, where the ghosts cannot harm them.

○ Fourth, when the six sense-faculties are dissolved and restored, one is fearless even amidst weapons and warfare; fifth, by perfuming the hearing until it becomes true hearing, the six faculties are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to the hearing of sounds, which can cause—
When sentient beings are about to be harmed by weapons that cut them into pieces, their nature remains as unshakable as water being sliced or light being blown away.
[Commentary] Guishan says: "The false hearing is perfumed until it becomes the true hearing-nature. Wenglun says: "Once one faculty is perfected..."

Then the six sense organs are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to hearing sound, such that there are no longer any obstructions to their functioning; thus it is like cutting water or blowing light.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Generally, when ghosts kill people, they must wait for an opportune moment when the victim is susceptible to being killed before they do so.
Thus, when the Bodhisattva cuts off and extinguishes deluded thoughts, the mechanism of slaughter becomes silent.
People also learn from the Bodhisattva to contemplate his voice; the Bodhisattva then bestows the wisdom of Avalokiteśvara upon them.
Whether demons come to harm them or they enter the realms of various ghosts, they cannot be harmed. Sentient beings, by hearing this, give rise to [faith].
Because consciousness is formed from the six sense organs, it remains subject to conditions; thus, a blade can cut it and a spear can slice it.
The Bodhisattva, however, reverses the hearing to hear his own nature, perfuming the hearing until it becomes true hearing. What, then, is the mark of this fruit of hearing?

After a long time, the six sense organs are dissolved and restored to a state where they listen like sound itself—formless. Not only can a blade not destroy them, but they will even become identical [to the ultimate].
Vajra-like, it is firm and indestructible. Like water being cut by a blade and light being blown by the wind, its nature is unwavering;
indeed, it is trustworthy. (5.

Dispelling the Darkness of the Dharmadhātu Ghosts through the Five Sciences): Sixth, when the brilliance of hearing and cultivation pervades the entire dharmadhātu, the nature of all profound darknesss cannot prevail.
It causes yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and the like to be unable to even look upon sentient beings when they are near them.

(6. The Reversal of Hearing and Listening Enters the Locks and Shackles, Fearlessness) Seventh, as the nature of sound is completely dissolved and hearing and listening are reversed back into their source, one becomes free from all defilements and delusions;

this enables one to remain unaffected by the shackles and fetters that bind sentient beings. (7. Universal Arising of the Power of Compassion, Fearlessness Toward Robbers) Eighth, as the cessation of sound is perfected...
Hearing [this name] generates the power of universal compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths where bandits cannot plunder them.
[Commentary: Guishan says that *yakṣas* are as previously described. Master Sengzhao says there are three kinds: first, those on the earth; second, those in the void;
and third, those in heaven. *Rākṣasas* means "the fearsome. *Kumbhāṇḍas* are ghosts who cause loathing and bewitchment. *Piśācas*...
The *piśāca* spirits that devour vital essence; the *pūtana* spirits of feverish disease. Wēnlíng says:

"When the refined brilliance of hearing permeates and illuminates those dark obscurities, [the spirits] are unable to see. When the nature of sound is completely dissolved, there is nothing within to which one is bound.

When seeing and hearing are turned back inward, there is nothing without to which one is entangled. Thus, the shackles fall away of their own accord. When sound and hearing stand as two, then self and other...

They become enemies. Now, when the sound ceases and hearing is perfectly pervasive, there is no dependence on either internal or external; thus, one can universally generate the power of compassion, and there will be no further enmity or opposition.

(8. Fearlessness of Not Being Robbed by Form: Greed and Desire) Ninth: By perfuming the hearing and departing from sensory dust, one is not robbed by forms; this can cause all sentient beings with excessive lust to distance themselves [from it].
[They] depart from desire. ○ (The ninth: The Perfect Fusion of Roots and Objects; Fearlessness Regarding Anger and Resentment. Tenth: The Sound is Pure and Free of Dust;

roots and objects are perfectly fused so that there is no opposition between the perceived and the perceiver, enabling all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to leave behind all forms of hatred. ○ (The eleventh: Dust is Eliminated and Clarity Revolves; Fearlessness Regarding Delusion and Darkness. Eleventh: Dust is eliminated and clarity revolves;

the dharma-realm, body, and mind are like lapis lazuli—luminously penetrating and unobstructed—enabling all those with dull natures and karmic obstructions to [attain liberation]. Arhats... [text continues]
*Dingjia* (the *pārājika* offense) is forever free from the darkness of delusion.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Sentient beings are "robbed of their color" (*sèjié*) because their habitual tendencies of desire unite with sensory objects.

If one can use the *vajra-samādhi* to permeate the faculty of hearing so as to perfect its nature, then one will be able to leave behind sensory objects and perfect that nature; thus, the craving of desire will dry up and one will be separated from sensory objects.
Thus, because the sense faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, even though there may be seductive forms, they cannot cause agitation.

Hatred arises from the violation of one's emotions and is produced in response to external objects; since the nature of sound is pure and free from delusive dust, it is perfectly integrated, without conflict, and devoid of subject and object.
Without conflict and without opposition, there is no hatred. Delusion is formed by the obscuration of delusive dust; [it does not exist] here.
It is obscured by ignorance. When the dust is dissolved, there is no obstruction; when the light is turned inward, there is no covering.

Thus, the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind become concentrated, pure, and brilliantly penetrating, departing from the darkness of delusion. The "obstruction of nature" (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*) is precisely this delusion.
*Adīnaka* means "lacking a virtuous mind. Among the ten internal karmas, it is lust, anger, and delusion alone that destroy and annihilate the Dharma-body.
Because these are the most prominent, three are cited to include the rest. Wuxing says: "According to the Tiantai interpretation, the three poisons pervade both the internal and external realms.
'Internal' refers to the delusions of thought (*sahakleśa*), while 'external' refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). For those of the Two Vehicles, delighting in *nirvāṇa* constitutes greed;

loathing birth-and-death constitutes hatred; and being deluded regarding the Middle Way constitutes delusion. For Bodhisattvas, extensively seeking the Buddha-dharma constitutes greed, while reviling the Two Vehicles constitutes hatred."
"The Buddha-nature is realized as being entirely the three poisons.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The pure sound is free from dust. Now, sound (*śabda*) is the root that gives rise to delusion;

whereas *yin* (sound/resonance) refers to lingering, trailing vibrations, and thus the principle of giving rise to delusion is more remote. This is like the Tang dynasty poem: "The reflection of the pool empties the human heart," where by means of the pool...
Is it not far-fetched to say that the reflection appearing in the empty clarity of water is merely a phenomenon of form?
Yet, when a person gazes down into it, their thoughts and emotions suddenly vanish without expectation. Those who say this poem approaches Zen are indeed close to the truth.
It is like a Bodhisattva who does not hear the sound, but seeks only the resonance; one hears nothing.
Regarding that sound, observe it alone. If one observes the sound alone, the karmic consciousness loses its causal basis and cannot reach [the object].
That pure sound leaves behind all hearing—how could this deceive me? For this reason, when the name "Bodhisattva" is used in the context of contemplation, form is not mentioned.
To not speak of "hearing" while being amidst sounds—is this not to easily place the faculties and objects of sentient beings in different realms?
It is for this reason that I do not first believe in the fruit of the Dharma-gate of the mutual functioning of the six faculties, but rather believe in the causal mind of the Bodhisattva.
How much more so when one turns hearing back toward one's own nature, such that it penetrates the ten voids and the resonance of sound is fully manifested.
In my own nature and lot, I have heard that the principle of the Dharma-realm is revealed through sound alone;
thus, Zao Bo possessed the teachings of Avalokiteśvara, and the *Vajraśekhara* contains the words of "hearing with the eyes. All these accord with the same principle as the voice of Great Compassion.
Eleventh, [the fearlessness of seeking a son endowed with both merit and wisdom]: Twelfth, he manifests a fused form and hears the immovable place of enlightenment;
he enters into the mundane world without destroying the world-systems, and is able to universally make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.

At the side of each Buddha, he serves as a Dharma Prince, enabling those sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who lack sons and desire to seek a male heir to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.

○ (Twelfth: Attaining the Dharma-foot of Wisdom by Seeking a Daughter Free from Fear) Thirteenth: When the six sense faculties are perfectly interfused and clearly illumined without duality, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions, one establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha.
By reverently following the secret dharma-gates of the dust-mote-like Tathāgatas of the ten directions, one receives and maintains them without loss.
This enables those sentient beings within the dharma-realm who have no children and seek a daughter to give birth to one who is upright, endowed with merit and virtue, gentle and compliant.
The multitude loves and honors this woman who possesses the marks of excellence.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "When the fused form is extinguished, the obstruction ceases; yet when one again hears, the nature is true. Thus, though she engages with the world, she is neither moved nor destroyed.
She is able to go throughout the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, receiving and upholding their teachings for each."

Dharma-heirs, by making offerings to the Buddha, they possess the merit; by receiving the Dharma, they possess the wisdom. Thus, they are able to succeed the Dharma King and possess the way of a true son of man;

therefore, they can respond to such requests. Regarding the "six faculties being perfectly penetrating" (*yuan-tong*): "perfect" (*yuan*) means there is no duality, and "penetrating" (*tong*) means encompassing the realms.
This luminous illumination is the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). As for "encompassing the realms," it refers to the emptiness of the Tathāgata.
This is the essence of the *Zang* (Storehouse). Possessing this, she is able to accord with and receive the Dharma-gates without error.

"Accordance" refers to the gentle virtue of the *Kun* (Earth) hexagram; "receiving" refers to the domestic duties of the inner chambers. Because she possesses the way of a woman, she is able to respond to those who seek her. Wuxing says:
"The Wise One (*Zhìzhě*) cites the *Āgama* to clarify that [the realm] from the hells upward, up to the heavens of desire..."
All suffer the pain of childlessness; to enable those who seek [offspring] to have their hearts' desires fully satisfied is likewise to extract that suffering.
Xielü said: "To enter into the mundane world without destroying the world is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Skillful means belongs to the provisional (*prajñapti*);
because the provisional can manage affairs, it gives rise to males. To establish the Great Perfect Mirror-like *Tathāgatagarbha* is..."
She belongs to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). True wisdom accords with principle (*li*); because principle is able to contain and nurture all things, she is born as a woman.
This is the meaning of what is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas, and upāya is their father. This is precisely that point.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The male possesses the yang-nature, which has the capacity for authority and governance; the female possesses the yin-nature, which is endowed with the way of containment and nurturing.
Yet, function is not manifested without substance, and substance is not verified without function.
To "fuse forms" and further "hear without moving from the site of enlightenment" is first to attain its substance. To "enter the mundane world" without destroying the world is subsequently...
This manifests its function. Possessing the yang-path of a man and being fully endowed with both merit and wisdom—this is the realization of the provisional within the real.
Thus, it can respond to whatever is sought. The six sense faculties are perfectly penetrating and luminously illumined without duality;
this is first attaining the provisional. It encompasses the ten directions of space and establishes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the empty Tathāgata-garbha.
This is subsequently attaining the reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, to receive and accept [the teachings] while remaining compliant with them is precisely the provisional (*upāya*) within reality.
Thus, one is able to respond to whatever is sought.

(13. One Confronts Many: The Title "Fearlessness") Fourteenth: All those currently dwelling in this world-system of three thousandfold great thousand worlds, including the ten billion suns and moons...
Among the Dharma Prince sons, there were as many as sixty-two Ganges-sands who cultivated practices to serve as models for teaching and transforming sentient beings;
their skillful means and wisdom, which accorded with the capacities of sentient beings, were each different.

However, by means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I attained—the wondrous Gate of the Ear—my body and mind subsequently became subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, enabling me to cause sentient beings to uphold [this teaching].
"My name and that of his are equal in merit, no different from those of the sixty-two Ganges-sands of Dharma-princes whom they both uphold;
World-Honored One, my single name is no different from their many names.
Because I have practiced and attained true and perfect penetration, this is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, providing all beings with merit."
[Commentary] Gushan says that the *Lotus Sūtra* also contains such a comparison. Only upon examining the present sūtra does one come to understand its intent.
This is because the beings of this region have sharp faculties of hearing and thus many receive the Way; therefore, the transformation of Avalokiteśvara is superior.
Because the other faculties are dull, those who receive the Way are few; therefore, the transformations of the other sages are inferior. Thus, one knows the stages of practice and realization.

Although there are differences depending on the specific capacities of those being taught, since the total number of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is countered by the single person that is Avalokiteśvara alone, the two merits of these two practices are exactly equal.
Based on this teaching, one has already implicitly distinguished the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
For those who have not yet understood, I shall further await Mañjuśrī’s detailed discernment. “Ten billion suns and moons” refers to ten billion *kṣetra* (buddha-fields);
this is the concluding summary of the name. ○ (34.

Inconceivable [Chapter], Part 2: Initial General Clarification of Arising Function Based on Realization) "World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and cultivated the realization of the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully attain the four..."
"Inconceivable, Unconditioned, and Wondrous Virtue.
[Commentary] Wénlíng says: "Manifesting a multitude of forms, each recited mantra gathers and transforms sentient beings, perfectly responding to their needs.
Its principle issues from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and its spiritual response is unfathomable; thus it is named 'Inconceivable, Unconditioned, and Wondrous Virtue.'"
However, while the previous [section] also manifested forms in response to seekers, it was only this that is termed "inconceivable.

The former merely provided a brief indication, whereas this further clarifies the matter in depth; for instance, manifesting eighty thousand heads and arms within a single body is truly beyond the reach of thought.

○ (2. Specifically showing the benefits manifested according to individual capacities; 4. First, enabling the attainment of mastery) First: Because I initially attained the wondrous and sublime mind of hearing, wherein the essence of the mind left behind all hearing, and because seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned, forming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and preach boundless secret divine mantras.
Among these, I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, or nine heads.
There are eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, one thousand heads, ten thousand heads, and eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads.
There are two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four;
and so on, up to one hundred and eight arms, one thousand arms, and ten thousand arms.
He has eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms; his eyes are two, three, four, nine, and so on, up to one hundred and eight, a thousand, ten thousand, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes.
Whether manifesting as compassion, majesty, meditative concentration, or wisdom, he rescues and protects sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The phrase 'initially obtained' refers to the fundamental cause. The head represents the totality of the six faculties;
the arms symbolize the compassion that uplifts and receives; the eyes symbolize the wisdom that illuminates and comprehends.

Each follows its original number and is expanded to eighty-four thousand to represent responding universally to sensory objects based on the fundamental six faculties and the fundamental wisdom and compassion."
Through diligent effort, one attains great mastery. These eleven stages constitute the sublime practice of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Prior to the ten stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, one still relies upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to nurture great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Upon reaching the eleventh stage, the cultivation of merit reaches its consummation;

it becomes purely great compassion, which serves as the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, wherein wisdom manifests in its full perfection. Therefore, the hands and eyes of Avalokiteśvara are pervasive throughout his entire body.

He is thus designated by the name "Great Compassion. Within his single essence, the myriad phenomena of worldly afflictions, as well as compassion, majesty, meditative concentration, and wisdom, are fully present without exception.
His manifestation as the twenty-four sages clarifies that although each of those manifestations represents but a single aspect, when perfectly integrated, they all culminate in this very state.
Thus, he enables those who awaken and enter his teaching not to stop at merely the twenty-five gates.

The eighty thousand phenomena of the realm of afflictions (*kleśa-dharmadhātu*), both in their facts and principles, are suddenly realized as never having been separate from my single, perfectly interfused, pure awakening-body.
Capable of being identical and capable of being different, being simultaneously one and many, the oceanic functions and uses pervade throughout boundless lands.

The physical realms and lands of the ten directions interpenetrate one another; so too do the arts of the heterodox and orthodox, the auspicious and inauspicious, and the methods for nourishing life and bringing peace to all things.
Every dharma is perfectly interfused and every dust mote is fully endowed [with all dharmas]. Someone may say: "The eighty-four thousand [dharmas] merely represent the teachings;
what can they possibly apply to a single body? This is simply because one uses a conceptualizing mind to gauge the Bodhisattva’s realm of perfect penetration.
Indeed, the body contains the ten voids, and within a single hair-tip, world-systems appear. Those voids and world-systems are more than just mere metaphors.
It is merely like a head or an arm. Those eighty-four thousand heads and arms are just like a person’s eighty-four thousand pores;
there is nothing extraordinary about them. The words of the Sage correspond both to phenomena and to principle.
Since they are called "inconceivable virtues," one cannot fathom or deliberate upon them with a limited mind. *Śakrāla* (Skt. means "vajra-like," signifying firmness and solidity.
"Ruài" means to destroy. "Mudrā" means seal; each possesses its own wondrous seal. "Pure Jewel Eye" signifies being free from dust and attaining awakening through union.
"Compassion" is used to gather and transform beings, while "awe" is used to subdue them. "Samādhi" serves to restore the profound stillness, and "wisdom" serves to open the way to awakening.
This collectively refers to the many wondrous countenances.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding "the wondrously wondrous mind of hearing," the first "wondrous" refers to the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Truths; the second "wondrous" refers to the fundamental organ of Perfect Penetration.
This Perfect and Sudden teaching is for the sake of those with the corresponding capacity; it is the most profound among the profound and the most subtle among the subtle.

Therefore, these words are reiterated as "wondrously wondrous. Furthermore, the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is inherently wondrous because it possesses the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of completeness, pervasiveness, and constancy.
When a Bodhisattva is able to hear with inconceivable, wondrous wisdom, they attain this very wondrousness;
this is called the "wondrously wondrous mind of hearing. When the wondrously wondrous mind of hearing reaches the state where objects vanish and the faculties are exhausted, it enters into emptiness.
When wisdom extinguishes principle, it may be said that they are refined and non-dual; thus, once a single faculty returns to the source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
Therefore, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing cannot be partitioned, forming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious body of awakening.
By this, the great function arises without fixed direction, manifesting many wondrous forms—this is the benefit of form—and proclaiming many divine mantras—this is [the benefit of sound].

Regarding the "increased sounds": the eighty-four thousand [pores] on each of the head, hands, and eyes are because the pure, jewel-like awakening takes perfect permanence as its essence and pervasive interpenetration as its characteristic.
It is like a lantern within a thousand-eyed cage, where light permeates every opening; it is also like the boundless treasury of space, wherein every dharma is entirely true.
Thus, the eighty-four thousand gates of defilement are transformed into eighty-four thousand [gates of wisdom].
Because there are four thousand gates of liberation, one is able to employ eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi to correspond to the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*).

For each and every affliction of sentient beings, one manifests a hand and an eye to rescue and uplift them, illuminating and bringing them to realization until they finally reach the adamantine, firm, and indestructible state. This is the compassion of this Bodhisattva.

To gather and transform beings through majestic power is to subdue them; to stabilize them through concentration is to restore their stillness; and to employ wisdom through hearing and awakening is the great function [of the Bodhisattva].

(2. Causing others to obtain fearlessness): Second, because I have emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing and reflection—just as sound passes through a wall without being obstructed—I am able to manifest every form and recite every mantra with wondrous skill.
These forms and mantras are capable of bestowing fearlessness.
For this reason, all sentient beings in the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions call me the "Bestower of Fearlessness.

(3. Causing the Relinquishment of Stingy Food) Third, because I have cultivated the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, in all the worlds where I travel, I cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies' treasures and seek my compassion.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "When the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment whatsoever; thus, one can cause sentient beings to abandon all forms of stinginess and attachment.
To those who seek my compassion, I receive them with compassion and perform the Buddha-work for them."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: To discriminate according to sounds is to be stuck by them. To turn back the hearing toward one’s own nature is to detach from the stickiness and inwardly settle it.
Once a single sense-object is no longer received, all five sense-objects are liberated. When attached to objects, there are faculties; when detached from objects, there are no faculties.
Only when the false faculties are absent are the faculties like sound—formless. This was the supernormal power of the ancients.

It is for this reason that the walls and barriers of the sages are traversed directly. When one cultivates the fundamental, wondrous, perfect penetration—the pure original root—one does not receive even a single speck of dust.
Precisely because of this non-reception, one is able to cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures, seeking my compassion to accept them.
Thus, the Bodhisattva takes non-reception as the means to receive the multitude.
One should practice giving by means of non-giving; in this way, one may accomplish the offering of the Dharma.

(4. Fulfilling All Requests) Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, one is able to offer various precious treasures to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and extend them to all sentient beings within the six realms of the dharma-realm:
those seeking a wife shall obtain a wife, and those seeking a child shall obtain a child.
Seeking samādhi, one attains samādhi; seeking long life, one attains long life; and so on, up to seeking great nirvāṇa, one attains great nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Attaining the Buddha-mind" refers to the fulfillment of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Offering precious jewels" refers to the fulfillment of merit (*puṇya*). Merit...
Because wisdom is complete in its two aspects, it extends laterally to sentient beings, causing their various aspirations to be fulfilled according to their wishes. Wuxing said:

"Of these four inconceivables, the first two pertain to the response [of the Buddha], while the latter two correspond to the capacities of the sentient beings. Within the response, both benefits of form and voice are fully manifested.
Although the initial passage mentions the recitation of mantras, it primarily demonstrates the benefit of form, which is precisely the function of the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body). Next...
Although the text manifests in form, it primarily demonstrates the benefit of sound; that is to say, its fame is universally renowned.

Within the capacity of sentient beings, both cause and fruit are fully elucidated. First, the cultivation of causes is explained, briefly citing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) among the six perfections to encourage the seeking of merit.
Subsequently, the realization of fruits is explained, wherein all mundane and supramundane aspirations are fulfilled, and one now attains happiness.
Therefore, [the *Sūtra* says: "I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate. Thus, there is no principle that is not perfect and no dharma that is not complete.

It is like a *sattva* who obtains a *maṇi* jewel and places it atop a high banner; whatever the people require [is provided]. [The *Commentary*] states: Tiantai said, "When I attain the Buddha-mind and realize the ultimate, there is no principle that is not perfected and no dharma that is not fully possessed. This is like a *sattva* obtaining a *maṇi* jewel and placing it upon a lofty flagpole, such that it accords with whatever the people need."
There is nothing that is not fully provided for: looking upward, it is sufficient to nourish one’s parents; looking downward, it is sufficient to provide for one’s wife and children;

and in between, it is sufficient to reach all other people. It is the same with the Dharma; therefore it is said: "One is able to provide various precious offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the dharma-realm," and so forth.

[2. Citing evidence and concluding the answer (with two parts: first, concluding the answer to the question)] The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; I [attained it] through the gateway of the ear. By means of the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination, my mind attained mastery over its objects.

Because I entered the aspect of the stream, I attained Samādhi and achieved Bodhi; this is the foremost method. [2. Narrating the praise and the receipt of the name] World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration.
In the midst of the great assembly, he conferred upon me the prophecy of the name Avalokiteśvara.
"Because I observe and listen to the perfect clarity throughout the ten directions, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "First, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the flow and loses the objects; this is attaining perfect illumination through the gateway of the ear.
Because one has attained perfect illumination, one responds to conditions and manifests transformations, attaining great sovereign mastery. Wŭxīng says: "According to the *Guān*"...
The *Ghoṣa-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* both state that this Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood in the distant past under the name Zhengfaming (Saddharmaprabhāsa).
Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* records that in the past, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha bestowed a prediction upon Prince Animiṣa, naming him Avalokiteśvara.
Thus, both the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* and the present sūtra describe the concealment of his fundamental nature (*mūla*) and the manifestation of his traces (*vyañjana*).
He was named Er. His present attainment of perfect penetration is his subsequent incarnation as the Crown Prince.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Now, the conditions of sensory objects and the conditions of the mind are equally forms of conditioning. When one conditions sensory objects, one engages with the myriad differences;
therefore, such conditioning is laborious. When one conditions the mind, one returns to the single principle; therefore, such conditioning is effortless.
Moreover, the samādhi of the ear-gate surpasses all other gates. Wisdom illumines the object, and the object illumines wisdom;
wisdom illumines wisdom, and the object illumines the object. Thus, conditions forget their conditions, being without dependence or opposition.

Therefore, it is called the "Perfectly Illuminating Samādhi," wherein the mind of conditions attains universal mastery. Upon the attainment of the fruit, the name "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes Sounds) becomes universal.
The Ten Directions. (4.

Emitting Light as an Auspicious Sign of Approval; Part 10: Initial Light Pours upon the Buddhas' Crowns) At that time, from his five limbs while seated upon the lion throne, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light that reached far to pour over the crowns of the Tathāgatas and the Dharma-Prince Bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions. Those Tathāgatas likewise [emitted light] from their five...
Their bodies being identical, they emit precious light that comes from the direction of a single mote of dust to pour over the Buddha’s crown.
(2) It simultaneously pours upon the great bodhisattvas and arhats within the assembly. (3) The forest trees, groves, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma.

(4) The intermingling lights entwine with one another like a net of precious threads. (5) This great assembly attains what they have never experienced before; everyone universally obtains the Vajra Samādhi.

6. (The Heavens Rain Jewel Flowers): Immediately, the heavens rained down hundred-jeweled lotus flowers, intermingled and variegated in blue, yellow, red, and white. 7. (Empty Space Becomes Jewel-Colored):

The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures. 8. (Mountains and Rivers Disappear): The mountains and rivers of the great earth in this Sahā world simultaneously vanished from sight.

9. (The Merging of Nine Lands): One perceives only the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, merging together to form a single realm. 10. (The Spontaneous Performance of Chants): The chanting of *brahmā*-songs and hymns is spontaneously performed and presented.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "The intermingling of precious lights symbolizes the mutual fusion of the principles of self and other.

The sounding of voices from the trees reveals that the nature of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) is non-dual. This seals what was previously realized, fully accords with the Buddha-mind.
Wenglun says: "The preceding explained the method of perfect penetration; this manifests the auspicious omen of perfect penetration in response to it. The five limbs of all Buddhas..."
The simultaneous emission of precious light symbolizes that when the luminosity of the realized nature reaches its ultimate limit, the precious awakening manifests as a perfectly integrated whole.
That they mutually bestow consecration—wherein the crown represents the mark of perfect ultimacy—symbolizes that the realization of the Buddhas regarding the nature is thus perfectly ultimate.
The Bodhisattvas and Arhats within the assembly are the peers of the twenty-four sages; the Buddha’s light likewise consecrates them.
