As for "their summits," this signifies that their cultivation and realization are equal, without superiority or inferiority. Regarding the phrase "forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of Dharma, with interlacing lights forming a lattice":
once perfect penetration (*yuantong*) manifests before one, then all sounds are the Buddha’s voice and all forms are the Buddha’s form;
there is nothing that is not a point of awakening and entry, and nothing that is not the principle of perfect penetration. Great!
As for the multitude universally attaining the Vajra Samādhi: by means of this, they are all able to shatter the obstacles of delusion and realize perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).

As celestial rain showers jeweled flowers, the sky manifests jeweled colors, the earth conceals mountains and rivers, and the world-systems within the dust motes are contained therein—this signifies the realization of the nature of perfect penetration, whereby the wondrous practice of non-action naturally unfolds. The luminous clarity of jewels and the empty awareness naturally manifest.
Conditioned formations, habitual tendencies, and outflows shall no longer arise; the myriad dusts of the world will become vast and empty, with no further obstructions or separations.
As for the chanting and singing of the Brahma-voice performed by the assembly, it can cause the Dharma-realm to forever depart from all suffering and constantly attain wondrous bliss.
The profound meaning and subtle benefits of the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration expounded by the Sage are as detailed as this. Therefore, the assembly...

The auspicious signs appeared in detail, and he responded accordingly. [Commentary] Tiantai says: There are ten manifestations of auspicious signs that serve as seals of approval. First, the auspicious sign of light pouring over the Buddha’s crown.

Second, the auspicious sign of the light simultaneously pouring over the entire assembly. Regarding the light first emitted from the five limbs: this refers to the light of the six sense faculties being without obstruction.

Yet he does not release it. That he sprinkles the crowns of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions signifies that this Dharma-gate of the ear-organ is none other than the supreme crown-dharma of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
That those Tathāgatas likewise emit light to come and sprinkle the crown of the Buddha as well as the assembly signifies that the path and fruit of all Buddhas are identical.

This is the first seal. The treatise states that while Bodhisattvas are not without this light, it is specifically to reveal the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), which is the primary principle of the ultimate fruit.
This constitutes the mutual correspondence between self and others. It is the third auspicious sign of the preaching of the Dharma by insentient things:
that forests and ponds all proclaim the sound of the Dharma. As it is said, "Once perfect penetration has manifested before one, all forms are the form of the Buddha."

All sounds are the voice of the Buddha. The auspicious intermingling of the lights of the four jewels symbolizes that the principle of the birth of Buddhas is fundamentally identical, and that the wisdom of self and others is not separated.
It is like a thousand lamps in a single room or a thousand pearls in an Indra’s net, where each reflects the other in a mutually fusing, infinitely layered manner.
This constitutes the correspondence of the mutual integration of the environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and the *adhiṣṭhāna*). This is the fifth assembly.
Regarding the auspicious sign of obtaining benefit: the statement that "all universally obtain the Vajra Samādhi" reveals that even insentient things can thus preach the Dharma;

if so, how could the pure assembly not obtain realization upon hearing it? The auspicious sign of the six heavens raining jewel-flowers signifies that all who have obtained benefit within the assembly attain entry into the forty stages of the true cause, for there is none who does not transcend the ocean of fruition.
This means that the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. This constitutes the mutual correspondence of the dharma-positions.

The seven kinds of emptiness form the auspicious sign of precious color, symbolizing that after the realization of perfect penetration, all the empty spaces of the ten directions are entirely dissolved and transformed into the precious awakening of true emptiness.
The eighth is the auspicious sign of the mountains and rivers no longer appearing. This signifies that the various sense faculties have become perfectly liberated;

their inner luminosity shines forth, and the various changing phenomena of the mundane world of floating dust are like ice melting in hot water, transforming according to thought into unsurpassed awareness.

This constitutes the correspondence for the simultaneous dissolution of the realm of space. The ninth is the auspicious sign of the lands merging into one. This signifies that after returning to the source through the manifestation of truth, the defilements...
Since the realm of emotion is empty and lacks any non-inherently endowed nature, the body and land are all the more manifest.

When the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, merge into a single realm, it constitutes nothing other than the Sole Real Reward Land of Adornment and Purity. Ten kinds of *brahman* hymns were performed to present auspicious signs;
these *brahman* hymns and songs are all musical instruments. "Music" (*yue*) means "joy"; it causes those who hear the music to experience delight.
It is bliss. This represents the time of manifesting true return to the source and the perfect realization of the wondrous bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
This first correspondence represents the excellence of the expressive means (*vyañjana*). The next correspondence represents the excellence of that which is expressed (*artha*).

Furthermore, the subsequent correspondence represents the excellence of causal practice. The following two correspondences represent the excellence of the fruition and realization. The realm of space represents true emptiness. The body...
The "Earth" (chapter) thus manifests the wondrous existence of a single period, and its auspicious omens and responses are sufficient to encompass the entire sutra.

V. The Five Buddhas Command Mañjuśrī to Distinguish and Discern (Part One: The Five Buddhas Command Mañjuśrī; Sub-part One: Narrating the Instruction to Address the Assembly). Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
"Now, observe these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the expedient means by which they first attained the Way, all saying:"
Cultivating the true and perfect penetration. (2. Showing that those paths are equal. Their practices are in reality without distinction of superior or inferior, or of priority or sequence.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: Now, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha originally has no different vehicles (*yāna*). Because there are sharp and dull faculties among sentient beings, the teachings are divided into Great and Small.
Speaking in terms of the Three Truths, that which is expounded by the Small Teaching is the Truth of Reality (*satya*). The Great Teaching...
That which is signified is the Middle Way. This true Middle pervades all conventional truths—namely, the eighteen realms and the seven great elements previously realized.
One should know that the complete presence of these three truths is called the Tathāgatagarbha.

Conventional truth is not empty; within the ultimate, both are empty. Therefore, among the twenty-five sages, whether the śrāvakas realize the ultimate by analyzing the conventional or realize the ultimate by taking the conventional as its substance, they all partially enter the treasury of emptiness.

Whether the bodhisattvas manifest the ultimate by departing from the conventional or manifest the ultimate while remaining within the conventional, they all fully enter the treasury of emptiness. Now, by means of this...

The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha integrates all parts without distinction; it is identical to the Lotus Sūtra’s opening of the gate of expedient means to reveal the true aspect, definitively resolving that the teachings for śrāvakas are the king of all sūtras.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "In their cultivation, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence.

This interpretation by Master Wuxing is extremely appropriate. However, it is erroneous to judge this sutra as being identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Rather, as I have judged it, it is identical to the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) class.
This is because the *tathāgatagarbha-nature* (zàngxìng) harmonizes the entire portion [of the teaching] without any difference. Indeed, the *tathāgatagarbha-nature* is like a hall.
The inner sanctum (*āvaśyaka*) also has its degrees of depth; how could one differentiate between the hall and the inner sanctum based on such depth?
It is simply that although the hall and the inner sanctum are identical in their depth, those who enter the gate do so with varying degrees of speed.
Since Mañjuśrī was asked to select among those who were slow, and as their progress differs by factors of ten thousandfold over eons, it was impossible not to exercise such selection.

III. (Stating the Intent to Distinguish Between the Two: First, Identifying the Appropriate Capacity for the Present) I now wish to cause Ānanda to awaken to the twenty-five practices; who among them possesses the appropriate capacity?

II. (Easy Awakening in the Future) Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, what skillful means will allow the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed Way to achieve success with ease?

[Commentary] Wuxing said: Above, [the Buddha] followed the realization of the nature to demonstrate the convergence of all as perfect penetration. Now, for the sake of accommodating various faculties, he seeks to simplify the expedient means.
The nature is like a flowered mansion; the faculties are like the entrance. Only by finding the door can one receive its bounty. Worldly people take intellectual understanding to be realization;
please consider which of the twenty-five sages provided the initial expedient means for entering the Way.
How appropriate! (2. Receiving the Mandate:

A Detailed Discussion in Two Parts; First, Describing the Ritual of Reverence) Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate decree, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: From this point forward, he intends to select the "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*). First, he clarifies the nature of awakening; next, he examines delusion and falsehood;
finally, he demonstrates the return to the source. Within the process of returning to the source, the faculty of hearing is chosen as the most accessible.
Since Mañjuśrī has already attained realization alongside Avalokiteśvara, his act of following the Compassionate One’s instructions has a long-standing precedent.

[II. The Actual Exposition of the Verses (2): First, a verse on the unchanging essence of True Suchness to indicate the source of reality. The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; its limpid perfection makes awakening fundamentally wondrous.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "This person is one whose nature is originally and universally penetrating. Wǔxīng says: "The nature of true awakening is like the great ocean;
its clarity, tranquility, and perfect fusion all serve as metaphors for being quiescent yet ever-illuminating.

He then reiterates the awakening illustrated by the metaphors of "perfect" and "clear," showing that it is originally illuminating yet eternally quiescent; therefore, it is called "primordially wondrous. This is of the same category.
In the preceding passage, "the nature of the mind is wondrously enlightened" and "original enlightenment is luminously wondrous," the dharma and the metaphor are merely intermingled.
[The Commentary] Tiantai says: The explanation of this verse is divided into two parts. First, the verse on the unchanging essence of *tathatā* (Suchness) to mark the source of truth.
Second, the verse on the capacity of *tathatā* to follow conditions to clarify defilement and purity. Within the first part, the character "enlightened" (*jue*) marks the beginning.

The eternally abiding true mind, bodhi, nirvana, and the fundamentally pure essence expounded in this sutra are precisely what are referred to in the fourth fascicle as "intrinsic awakening" and "original awakening.
Because this constitutes the source of the single true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is likened to the ocean.
Just as the waters of the four rivers have the pond as their source, and that pond further has the four seas as its source.

Therefore it is said that the ocean possesses three secondary virtues: it is the source from which all streams arise, and it is the destination to which all streams return. It possesses three primary virtues:
its water is clear and limpid, its volume is vast and circular, and it reflects the forms and images [of things].

Now, as we are precisely clarifying the essence, we briefly set aside its functions. By analogy, because the nature of awakening is luminous yet eternally still, it is called "clear and circular" (*ting-yuan*); being still, yet eternally...

Because it illuminates, it is called "perfectly clear" (*yuánchéng*). This refers to what is explained in the third fascicle: that the nature of awareness is fundamentally wondrously luminous and that fundamental awakening is necessarily luminous and wondrous.

This is precisely the essence of the unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is described as the true emptiness of the nature of form and the true form of the emptiness of nature—pure and self-so, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Mañjuśrī, having deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent, first raised the point regarding the faculty of sight.

The principle and essence elucidated within the "Section on the Distinctions of the Path" serves as the foundation for the "Unchanging Yet Adapting to Conditions" section of the subsequent "Section on the Cultivation of the Path.

Because defilement attains its root therein, one can achieve purity through that very defilement; because purity attains its root therein, one can provisionally establish manifestations according to conditions.

[Verse 2: Explaining the capacity of True Suchness to follow conditions, clarifying the two aspects of defilement and purity; the first verse shows how it issues from the source following defiled conditions. Original clarity shines forth, giving rise to that which is perceived; once the perceived is established, the nature of the shining light is lost. Through delusion and falsehood, empty space arises;
based on space, the world is established. As thought becomes still, the land is formed; as cognition develops, sentient beings come into being.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Original luminous illumination" is precisely the nature of the aforementioned fundamental luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Zhenji says:
Upon that nature of original luminosity, one falsely gives rise to the function of illumination, thereby manifesting objective forms. When there are forms, they accord with the mind;

when there are no forms, they are hidden, and thus the nature of illumination perishes. Wuxing says: Of these two interpretations, that of Master Jie is superior, for the meaning of the character "illumination" (*zhào*) is comprehensive.
Regarding "Reality and Delusion," Wénlǐng says: "Since the true nature is obscured, empty awareness becomes divided.

Consequently, the two realms of the faculties and their objects are established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, when false conceptualization coagulates, it forms the insentient realm of land;
when false consciousness perceives and cognizes, it forms sentient beings. Therefore, that which is limpid and wondrous cannot be made perfect, nor can it be attained."
And thus they are interconnected.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These two verses clarify the capacity of True Suchness (tathatā) to accord with conditions, thereby manifesting the two aspects of defilement and purity.

The first verse describes how, by following defiled conditions, one flows outward from the source. The second verse describes how, by following pure conditions, one traces back from the flow to the source.
The phrase "from the beginning, primordial clarity and illumination" refers to what was previously stated as "the nature of awakening is necessarily luminous.
If this primordial clarity and illumination were such that its shining was eternally quiescent, then how could anything arise?

It is simply because, from the beginningless past, there has been only the virtue inherent in the nature and no achievement through cultivation, yet upon the substance of this primordial clarity, one falsely gives rise to the function of illumination. Thus, this present illumination...
The term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the previous delusion that was taken as luminous awareness.

Because there is the illuminating reflection of the subject that shines upon the objects of illumination, what is now being illuminated is precisely that which previously arose from "establishing an object based on luminosity. Since the characteristic of the object has already conformed to the mind, the capacity of the subject to illuminate likewise becomes concealed;
thus one falls into the state of non-definedness (*avyākṛta*), which is why it is said that "the nature of illumination is lost. This refers to the preceding passage.
This refers to "obscuration and darkness. From this point onward, there is no longer [the state of] "sameness and difference," but rather a blazing manifestation of difference;

because that which is differentiated is established as different, and based on that difference, sameness is established. Therefore it is said: "Deluded ignorance gives rise to empty space; depending on space, worlds are established.

Because the manifestations of sameness and difference are clarified, based upon this, the states of "neither same nor different" are further established. Therefore it is said: "The clarification of thought forms the land; know [this to be so]."
"Awakening" refers to sentient beings. The *Wuxing Xunwen Ji* states: "The clarity of perception forms the land; awakening refers to sentient beings.

This means that both the sentient and the insentient are produced by deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). As Vasubandhu says, both that which possesses discrimination and that which lacks discrimination are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
That which possesses discrimination is called "discriminating consciousness," while that which lacks discrimination is called "that which resembles the object" (*viṣayābhāsa*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, when one contemplates that the formation of the land is like dust and consciousness, this refers to the consciousness of sentient beings, which is "consciousness-consciousness.

Those who take Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*) as their fundamental tenet merely claim that this consciousness does not share the same source as True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is a single mind.
Therefore, they assert that True Suchness is devoid of sensation and cognition, remaining quiescent and unchanging, and do not permit it to follow conditions (*pratyaya*). They speak only of...
The eight consciousnesses give rise to all phenomena; for this reason, they are as incompatible with the tenets of the Dharma-nature school (Faxingzong) as water and fire.

If one understands that our school, having already refuted the four modes of being (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), teaches according to what is appropriate such that its intent is subtly harmonious and all contentious calculations are lost—this section is titled "Following Defiled Conditions:
Flowing from the Source. There are two sources: first, the True [Source], and second, the... [Defiled Source].

Delusion. The fundamental luminosity is precisely the True; the illumination is precisely the delusive. As the ancient masters have said: "A solitary truth cannot be established, and a lone delusion cannot be formed.
It is only when the two dharmas of True Suchness and Ignorance, and non-arising-extinction and arising-extinction, are joined together that they can give rise to all phenomena.
This is also what was stated in the preceding text: "The essential luminosity of the consciousness-essence can produce all conditions. For indeed...
The unchanging essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel; it is capable of both good and evil.
Now, following along with defiled conditions, it manifests as capable of evil. Precisely because it is capable of all, it remains unchanging while responding to conditions.

Therefore, subsequently tracing the flow back to its source and returning from delusion to truth is called "thoroughly understanding that while responding to conditions, it remains unchanging. The teachings clarify the full nature.
That cultivation arises from and is entirely contained within the nature—this is precisely what is attained here.

Since this constitutes a major pivotal point for those practicing the Great Samādhi and is something that must not remain unknown, I have categorized it according to the meaning of the Sūtra in this manner.

[Section Two: Following the Pure Conditions from the Flow Back to the Source (in two verses)] [Subsection One: A Verse Responding to the General Request to First Realize the Path of Seeing and Then Cultivate the Path of Meditation] [Sub-subsection One: A Verse on Realizing the Path of Seeing to Open Understanding] Emptiness arises within Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; the lands of conditioned beings, as numerous as motes of dust, all depend upon emptiness for their birth. [Sub-section Two:

A Verse on Cultivating the Path of Meditation to Realize the Fruit] When the bubble ceases, the emptiness was originally non-existent; how much more so, then, are the various realms of the three worlds?

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This section cites the preceding [passage] to clarify how delusion takes the pure and perfect [nature] to form the sense organs and their objects. To integrate the sense organs and their objects is to return to the pure and perfect.

Within the great ocean of Great Awakening, there is fundamentally no existence of either emptiness or being. Due to the tossing and stirring of the winds of delusion, false bubbles of emptiness arise, and from these, all sentient beings come into being.
Once the winds of delusion have subsided, the bubbles of emptiness also perish. As for that upon which they depend...
When existence can no longer be grasped, emptiness and awakening become perfectly interfused, and one returns once more to the original subtlety.

"The three realms of existence" (trai-dhātu) refers here to the three realms within every atom of the lands of the ten directions. Wu-xing says that "existence" (you-lou) includes both sentient beings; the "three realms of existence" encompass both the world of sentient beings and the physical vessel-world.
Chang-shui says: "As for the phrase 'the bubble vanishes,' it is like the saying: 'If one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the ten directions become void.'"
"Emptiness completely causes all things to perish," and so forth.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These two verses follow the pure conditions; they trace the source from the flow and are divided into two parts.

The first verse responds to the general request regarding the Path of Seeing followed by the Path of Cultivation. The second verse responds to the specific request regarding the Path of Seeing followed by the Path of Cultivation.
In the verse, the first four lines explain the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the final two lines explain the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the realization of the fruit.

Generally speaking, when sentient beings have not yet seen the Path, they are not only deluded regarding the fundamental emptiness of all phenomena, but are also ignorant that the objective world is vast and the self is small.
These two types of delusion arise through mutual dependence; it is precisely because they do not understand this that [delusion persists].
Because all phenomena are fundamentally empty, there exist heaven and earth, and there exist the dependent and the primary.

Once one falls into the realm of existence, one claims that the dependent is great while the primary is small, or that the body is large while the mind is small; this is what is meant by the saying: "The One, deluded, becomes the mind; it is certain that the delusion is within the physical body.
Those who are able to perceive the Way realize that the nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect, and that this perfect, limpid nature is awakening itself.
The Primordial Wondrousness. From Great Awakening, empty space arises; relying on empty space, the great earth is established; relying on the great earth, sentient beings find their station.
This is because they do not realize that everything from the physical body outward—the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all an object within the wondrously luminous True Mind.
It is like abandoning a hundred thousand clear, tranquil oceans and—

To recognize the substance of a single bubble as being the entire tide is to exhaustively comprehend the vast ocean. Therefore it is said: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea;
the myriad dust-like worlds of outflows are all produced in dependence upon emptiness.

Herein, for now, we refute the notion that the object is large while the self is small. Furthermore, the refutation that all phenomena possess [intrinsic nature] occurs in the following two lines. Hereafter...

Regarding the second verse on the cultivation of the path and the realization of the fruit, which states: "When the bubble is extinguished, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three worlds?

The preceding text says: "Now, if your faculties are completely uprooted, their inner clarity will emit light, and these superficial phenomena as well as the vessel-world and all its transformed appearances will—like ice melting in boiling water—dissolve at the moment of thought into supreme wisdom."
[This is] the realization. The subsequent passage states: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions is entirely dissolved;

how much more so the lands that exist within that space? To extinguish the bubble is what constitutes the cultivation of the Way; the extinction of the bubble is precisely the expression for realizing the fruit.
These two lines directly refute the existence of being (*bhava*). When being is refuted, the essence of the myriad dharmas is empty.
When the essence is empty, the calculations of "great" and "small" are forgotten, and one returns to the nature of the original source—the single precious awakened true mind.

II. Verses Responding to the Separate Request to See the Path of Insight (Darśanamārga) First, the General Exposition of the Intent (divided into two parts; first, clarifying that the principle toward which one proceeds is no different). 1. Verse on the Non-differentiation of the Nature to Which One Returns: The nature of returning to the source is non-dual. 2. Clarification that the Gateways through Which One Returns Are Diverse: The skillful means have many doors. 3. Clarification of the Reason Why This Must Be Discerned (divided into two parts; first, regarding the fact that there is truly no difference among the various sages):

The sagely nature is all-pervasive; whether following or reversing [the sequence], both are skillful means. 4. Clarification that There Is Superiority and Inferiority According to the Capacity of the Practitioner: When those of the initial resolve enter samādhi, their speed differs beyond comparison.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The twenty-five sages share one and the same perfect penetration; this is what is meant by 'non-duality' and 'many gates.

It depends on the nature of the sages that both the 'contrary' and the 'conforming' are equally effective, such that no selection can be made between them. However, because beginners differ in their aptitude regarding speed and slowness, it is necessary to choose.
Gūshān says: "For Guanyin, the ear-faculty is the conforming [path]; for the other sages, the various [faculties are the contrary path]."
"The roots are contrary. This is said in response to the spiritual capacities of those in this region. [Commentary] Tiantai says:

These two verses respond to a specific request regarding the Path of Seeing followed by the Path of Cultivation as two stages. The first part excludes what is not [the case] and reveals what is. This is divided into two: first, a general statement of the intent;

second, a detailed analysis and distinction. The first of these is further divided into two: first... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist treatise, likely from the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue* (The Great Decision on the Practice and Realization of the Stopping and Contemplation) or a similar work by Zhiyi. The translation reflects the technical terminology of Chinese Buddhist scholasticism.)

The second section clarifies that there is no difference between the two in terms of the principle toward which one proceeds; it further clarifies the reason why they must be distinguished. This first section has two parts:

first, the verse shows that the nature to which one returns is without distinction, meaning the fundamental nature to which one returns is non-dual. Second, the verse shows that the gates through which one returns differ, meaning there are many expedient means.

Regarding the "returning to the source," this pertains to the principle; how could the nature of the principle be different? As for the "expedient means," these accord with the capacities of sentient beings (*yathābhavyatā*).
The phenomena (dharma) are necessarily unequal; however, principle (*li*) is the nature of non-change, while phenomena are the conditions that follow [that nature].

To know that the unchanging follows conditions means that principle follows phenomena, such that they are two yet not-two. To know that following conditions is unchanging means that phenomena follow principle, such that they are not-two yet two.
Only by realizing this can one cultivate the Way. Second, it must be clarified that...

The reason for this twofold distinction is as follows: first, it concerns the fact that among the various sages there is actually no difference; second, it clarifies that when confronting specific capacities (*mārga*), there are degrees of excellence and inferiority.
Regarding the first, there are two points: first, because individuals and their dharmas differ, they cannot be treated as a single uniform category—this is spoken of in terms of differentiation.
Second, because the Buddha accords with their past roots and adapts to what is appropriate for their inclinations—this is spoken of in terms of non-differentiation.
Therefore it is said: "The nature of the Sage is all-pervasive; both the favorable and the adverse are skillful means. Next, there are also two meanings:
first, that practitioners in the末法 (mofa) age cannot discern the capacities [of beings]; second, that what they encounter should be broad, so that all may enter. Therefore it is said:
"When those of initial resolve enter samādhi, their speed differs beyond comparison. Below, the second section is clarified through specific distinctions and analysis.

There are four [sections]: first, distinguishing the contemplation of the six sense objects; second, distinguishing the contemplation of the five sense organs; third, distinguishing the contemplation of the six consciousnesses;

and fourth, distinguishing the contemplation of the seven elements. One must know that among the fundamental roots of perfect penetration of the various sages, there are cases where the method is superior while the realization is inferior.
For example, although Nālada’s vision of the nature was profoundly clear—as was most fully revealed by the Tathāgata in the preceding sutra—he realized only the fourth [stage].

Is it not the case that the fruit is not realized by those of inferior capacity? There are dharmas that are inferior while their realization is superior. For example, the medicinal king’s flavor and other sensory objects are far more inferior when compared to the nature of seeing;
yet, because one has already deeply entered the stage of perfection, is this not a superior realization?

Thus, if a dharma-gate is indeed superior to those of ordinary beings and sages, it nevertheless shares the same path with them. Just as one who ranks high in the civil service examinations shares the same status as both children and the elderly.
They share the same register. If one relies on what Mañjuśrī has selected, then by relying solely on the "one is," one generally eliminates the "hundred non-is.
Even veteran masters must fold their hands and submit to this command. The verse consists of four lines:

the first two lines eliminate the "non-is" by means of the "non-is," while the third line eliminates the "non-is" by means of the "is. Students should briefly set aside what is non-is and preserve [the is].
This is what is meant. One should know that the Dharma-gate of the ear-organ is not merely the perfect penetration of the three virtues;
it must indeed be ranked alongside Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

(2. Specifically distinguishing and clarifying [the four stages]; first, distinguishing the contemplation of the six sense objects. The conceptualization of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) binds one into a dust-field (*rajas*), such that the essential clarity cannot penetrate through. How could one not attain perfect penetration by failing to understand this? Thus, one obtains the perfect.
The faculty of hearing perceives sounds mixed with speech; yet it consists only of a single name, phrase, or flavor, and does not encompass all things.

How, then, can it attain perfect penetration? The faculty of smell knows through contact; when separated from its object, it fundamentally ceases to exist. Since what it perceives is not constant, how can it attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not inherent; it exists only at the moment of tasting. Since this awareness is not constant or singular, how can it attain perfect penetration?

The faculty of touch is clarified by means of what is touched; yet there is nothing it does not touch. Since its nature involves both contact and separation and is not fixed, how can it attain perfect penetration?

The faculty of smell is called an internal object; since it must rely on an object, there is necessarily that which acts and that which is acted upon. As it does not pervade all things, how can it attain perfect penetration?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Kauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, and others each attained enlightenment through one of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), yet these are all excluded here.
That which is called 'the holy nature' is universally pervasive; this which is called 'the initial mind' is not of the same category.
Thus, whatever is not selected is because it is unsuitable for the initial mind; the intention is to select the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) alone as being uniquely suitable."

Now, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are being distinguished. Form (*rūpa*) can give rise to conceptual fetters (*saṃjñā-saṃyojana*), causing the essential nature of the spirit to fail to penetrate through it.

Sound (*śabda*) is restricted solely to names, phrases, and syllables; it is neither comprehensive nor universal. "Wei" (味) means "flavor" (*artha*). "I" (伊) is equivalent to "only" (*kevalam*). Flavor, odor, and touch are as explained in the text.

As for the object of mental phenomena (*dharma-viṣaya*), it has no external form; only the mind (*manas*) can take it as its object. Because it lies hidden within the internal faculty of the mind, it is called the "internal object. — Guishan.
Question: It is said that the awakening of Dharmapāla to the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) and that of Avalokiteśvara to the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) are similar in meaning.

Why, then, did Mañjuśrī reject the former as being incorrect? Answer: Sound is the speech of the Buddha, whereas the faculty is one's own mind. To recognize the object is to become attached to the language of others;
to contemplate the faculty is to realize the nature of one's own mind. For this reason, even hearing sound was rejected.

[Commentary] Lord Jing said: "Names (nāman) express intrinsic nature (svabhāva). For example, the word 'fire' expresses only fire and does not express water, wind, and so forth, nor what kind of fire it is.
Phrases (pada) express distinctions (viśeṣa), such as charcoal fire, moxa fire, and so on.

Syllables (vyañjana) are the characters (akṣara), serving as the basis for these two. The ancients took syllables to be the 'flavor' (rasa); that is, characters can manifest both [names and phrases], just as flavor [manifests taste]."
It can manifest the salty or bland flavors within food. The dharma-object serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*), while the mind serves as the perceiving subject.

However, the mind cannot engage two objects simultaneously; for instance, if it perceives wholesome mental factors, it cannot simultaneously perceive unwholesome ones. Therefore, it is said to be "not universally pervasive.
Since it is not universally pervasive regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings, how could it attain perfect penetration? If one were to speak of the perfect penetration of Kāśyapa, it would be said:
How can the elucidation of the Wondrous Dharma be dismissed by claiming that the subject and object do not pervade everywhere?

○ (2. Discerning the Five Faculties through Contemplation) Although the nature of seeing is luminously clear, it sees what is before and not what is behind; its four dimensions are deficient by half. How, then, could one attain perfect penetration?
The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pass through the present without intersecting; they are fragmented and do not involve mutual entry. How, then, could one attain perfection?
The tongue-faculty is not a gateway to liberation; it arises without end from flavors to produce cognition, yet when flavor perishes, the cognition vanishes.

Since there is nothing remaining, how can one attain perfect penetration? The body and its objects of touch are likewise each distinct from perfect enlightenment; their boundaries cannot be observed through contemplation, and they do not meet in silent harmony.

How can one attain perfect penetration? The various faculties are confused and entangled; though the mind may be still and clear, ultimately no vision of thought-objects exists. Since such conceptions cannot be shed, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Penetrating. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because the nose lacks a central junction, it is called "fragmented" (zhīlí). That the tongue is able to perceive and discern without depending on flavors is what is meant by "without cause" (wúduān).
Wŭxīng says: The tongue-root is that upon which consciousness relies; it is also called the tongue-base (jihvā-āyatana). Now...

The phrasing is inverted; however, it is simply that the sense-field of the tongue is not without cause. When internal body and external objects touch as subject and object, there is sensation and reflection (*vitarka-vicāra*);
since these are absent when they are separated, it is said that "each is not [the other]," and so forth. If one were to claim that [sensation] exists within their conjunction, how could this be?
Since the object is not the essence of cognition, they stand as two opposing entities; thus it is said that "their limits" and so forth are "profoundly clear," yet ultimately non-existent.

To see [the nature] as merely clear and distinct is not to penetrate it thoroughly. Because one uses distracted and chaotic thoughts toward the nature of profound clarity, one will ultimately be unable to see it.
[Tiantai’s] Commentary: Although the seeing-nature is luminously penetrating, the Buddha has revealed and deeply affirmed it. This clarifies [the point].
In front it was not bright; behind, the four intermediate directions were deficient by half. Following what the Buddha taught, the front was entirely bright while the back was entirely dark;
looking to the left and right, two-thirds were visible, though slightly diminished. Based on this, it can be said that Mañjuśrī’s general simplification was intended for beginners.
If one attains even a small measure of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), then the ten directions will be clearly penetrated.
How much more so for the nature of the Sage! Whether in opposition or accord, all are skillful means; how profoundly flavorful are these words! [Section Three:

Examining the Six Consciousnesses] The consciousness and the seeing are mixed with the three harmonies; when one interrogates their root, they are called "without marks. Since their own substance was originally non-existent and lacks fixed definition, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions and arises from the power of great causes; yet the beginner cannot enter it—how then can one attain perfect penetration?

The practice of the nose-perception was originally a provisional means intended only to cause the mind to settle; once settled, it becomes a mental state—how could this lead to the attainment of perfect penetration?

The preaching of the Dharma involves playing with sounds and texts, which first brings enlightenment to those who are already accomplished; yet names and phrases are not themselves untainted—how could this lead to the attainment of perfect penetration?

Upholding precepts and violating them merely binds the body; where there is no body, there is nothing to bind. Since this does not pervade all things, how could it lead to the attainment of perfect penetration?

"Regarding the supernormal powers, what was the fundamental cause in past lives? How do they relate to the discrimination of dharmas and the conditions of thought? Since they are not detached from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?

[Commentary] Xielǐ says: The treatise states that consciousness arises from the conjunction of two factors; that is, consciousness is produced within the union of the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*).
The present mention of the "conjunction of the three" refers to the synthesis of the subject and the object. Wēnlíng says:

"Because the conjunction of these three, when traced to its root, is found to have no intrinsic substance, it is called 'non-characteristic' (a-lakṣaṇa). Because Samantabhadra employs the faculty of hearing with the mind, he is able to know things beyond the sands of worlds in other directions;
this arises from the great cause of practicing the dharmadhātu-conduct, and is not something that can be entered by those at the initial stage of the path.

Furthermore, Sunda was distracted; the Buddha wished to collect and stabilize his mind by having him contemplate the tip of the nose, which was merely a provisional expedient for that specific occasion.
For the true mind has no abiding place; to have an abiding place is delusion. Wuxing said:

"The awakening of the gustatory consciousness belongs to those who have previously accomplished mastery over sounds and texts. For example, Pūrṇa’s eloquence [has been cultivated] since remote kalpas."
Cai Wuai preached the Buddha’s teachings and attained arhatship; was he not one who had already achieved awakening?

However, the substance of the names and phrases he spoke was not yet the supramundane, untainted Dharma. This too is one case where [the teaching] does not encompass all [aspects], and for this reason it is excluded.
Question: Does Pūrṇa attain mastery over both body and mind simultaneously, or does he first master the body and then the mind?

[The questioner asks: "It is comprehensive and penetrating. Why do you now say it merely involves 'restraining the body'? [The answer is: "Even the mental adherence of a Śrāvaka prevents the faults of the six groups and seven branches [of transgression].
How much more so when we speak now of the 'body,' for consciousness is contained therein. Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers were obtained through past habituation;
although it is said that his mind's radiance was manifested by returning to the stillness of the ocean, this was not produced through the discrimination of dharmas."

Furthermore, the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Hīnayāna are all produced through deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*); they exist when directed toward objects and cease when separated from them. [Commentary] Tiantai says:
Among the various forms of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) attained by the sages, those that are lofty and beyond reach are exemplified by the passage:
"The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, born of the power of great causal roots. Those that are humble and not suited to the highest capacity are the other gates. Only Avalokiteśvara...

This Dharma gate is appropriately suited for those who, even in the brief interval between a bow and a prostration, may above attain equal enlightenment and below benefit those at the stage of the initial resolve;
it can thus be practiced for a long time. It is truly what is called "teaching the Dharma equally to both the shallow and the deep."

○ (4. Examining the Seven Elements) If one contemplates the nature of earth as solidity and obstruction rather than penetration, it is not the nature of the sages; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates the nature of water as conceptual thought rather than true reality, it is neither suchness nor contemplative awareness; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates the nature of fire as aversion toward existence rather than true detachment, it is not the expedient means of the initial resolve; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate through the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without their opposites; since opposition is not the supreme awakening, how can you attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate through the nature of space, its dullness and obscurity were originally not awakening; since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how can you attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate through the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining a mind [of attachment] is a delusion; how can you attain perfect penetration?

"Penetrating all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as being impermanent is a nature of mindfulness that fundamentally arises and ceases; since cause and effect are now distinct, how can one attain perfect penetration?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Holding the earth level and filling it in still involves the conditioned (saṃskṛta); it is not the true nature of the sages. Moonlight and water..."

To contemplate while not yet free from conceptual thought makes it difficult to accord with suchness (*tathatā*). This is because the principle of suchness is not a phenomenon of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
When Ucchuṣma hears the teaching on the fire of desire and gives rise to weary detachment, this is a weariness toward existence (*bhava*).

When Vairocanaraśmipratimaṇḍita contemplates that the nature of wind is movement, he perceives movement as being in opposition to stillness; this duality of opposites is not true awakening. Obscured darkness constitutes space (*ākāśa*).

Therefore, it is said that they are dull and obscured. Maitreya cultivates the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), yet the consciousness he contemplates arises and perishes from moment to moment;
if even his mind dwelling upon this contemplation is already false, how much more so would attaining perfect penetration be? Wuxing says:

"In the case of Śrī-Ālokakāra’s mindfulness of the Buddha, which universally gathers the six sense faculties, the object of mindfulness must necessarily encompass the three bodies (*trikāya*). However, as for the analogy of the mother and child remembering one another..."
These [teachings] are mostly spoken from the perspective of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Therefore, they point toward [the truth] as being identical to impermanence, arising, and ceasing.
How could one expect to elicit the fruit of the eternally abiding, unarisen, and undying through such causes?

The above twenty-four sages were all excluded because the fundamental root of their attained *pariniṣpanna-samādhi* was not the appropriate faculty for this land. One must know that the exclusion of these sages is entirely...
This is a selection of capacities. How could it be that Mañjuśrī harbors a mind of pride, or that the various sages possess a sense of shame?
To say, as the ancients did, "How can those who fail to pass through this Dragon Gate not sigh deeply? is truly base.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: The twenty-four sages are like physicians who have long been ill; they certainly cannot treat all manner of ailments with a single prescription.
Guanyin Bodhisattva is like one who uses an elixir of immortality (*huan dan*) to heal both others and himself;
with a single dose, he can universally cure all maladies. Thus, while the Dharma-gate of Guanyin is indeed divine and wondrous...
It alone excels in its practical application; even the various perfected methods of penetration (*samyak-pratipad*) among the sages are not without their utility as specific remedies.

Mañjuśrī’s selection, however, takes the entirety of Avalokiteśvara’s perfection to universally exclude the hundred negations, while using a single negation among the other sages to generally obscure their hundred affirmations.
This is just like a refined medical prescription that touches upon many points of taboo.
Is it not the case that each of the various sages fell into a particular "non" (error), thereby becoming a hundred-fold cautionary example for the Avalokiteśvara Dharma-gate of the Ear-organ?
Those who later cultivate the Perfect Penetration must certainly preserve what is correct and discard what is erroneous.
Not only will their own faculties become sharp and clear, but the Dharma-gates of all the sages will likewise be fully contained within my medicinal casket to respond to needs at any time.
This is what is required for the illness. The previous detailed explanation of each of the twenty-four gates was intended for this very purpose.

Thus, the Dharma-gate of Avalokiteśvara is not merely characterized by its perfect penetration (*yuantong*). If one takes visual forms as something that obstructs the faculty of hearing, such that refined discernment cannot penetrate through, it is not perfect penetration.
If one takes sounds as [the object of the ear]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
That which is averse to the sense-faculties is not one that encompasses all; thus, it is not universal penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
To take the object of fragrance as something averse to the ear-faculty means that what is perceived therein is not constant; thus, it is not universal penetration.
To take the object of flavor as something averse to the ear-faculty means that its perception is not consistently uniform; thus, it is not universal penetration. To take the object of touch...

If the nature of water is treated as something to be avoided by the faculty of hearing, then such conceptualization is not true reality and is not universal penetration.
