first, violating the precepts but not the views; second, violating the views but not the precepts; third, neither violating the views nor the precepts; fourth, violating both the views and the precepts. As follows:

When a person has already violated the precepts, yet feels dread regarding their future transgressions and is able to give rise to shame and remorse, repenting and reforming, this is a violation of the precepts (*śīla*) but not a violation of the view (*dṛṣṭi*).
There are those who, though they do not violate the precepts, do not believe in cause and effect and do not understand sin and merit, heaven and hell;
to sweep all of these away at once is a violation of the view but not a violation of the precepts.

Furthermore, there are those who naturally maintain the prohibitive precepts as if guarding a bright pearl, and who are not deluded regarding cause and effect, deeply understanding the nature of transgression and merit;

such individuals possess both insight and preceptual integrity without impairment. Yet there is another class who indulge their passions in eating and drinking, and give free rein to their desires for lust and killing, yet claim, "The Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna has no precepts to uphold or transgressions to commit.
They show no outward fear of the worthy and the enlightened, nor do they have any secret dread [of retribution].

To fear ghosts and spirits is to break both one's precepts and one's views. While breaking the precepts without breaking one's views may lead to falling into sin, there is still a principle by which one may be excused.
However, while breaking one's views without breaking the precepts may involve no formal transgression, there will never be an opportunity to attain the Way.
Those who nowadays speak of the Mahāyāna have broken both their views and their precepts; they are truly *nāraka* (hell-beings).
The life-span of the *kāya* is like the hard substance of the *pāṭala* flower. How can this great ocean of the Buddha-dharma remain amidst such a corpse?

(2. The Exhortation Regarding the Period After Extinction; Part 1: Māra Causes the Violation of Precepts) After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), many of these followers of Māra will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed.
Sexual desire is a false friend that causes all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views, thereby losing the path to Bodhi. (2. You Teach Them to Firmly Maintain:

You should teach the people of the world that when practicing *samādhi*, they must first sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: In various sutras, the precept against killing is placed first because the establishment of transformation takes compassion as its foundation.

In this sutra, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first because true cultivation takes the departure from desire as its foundation. Indeed, the energy of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity;

the habit-energy of desire is wild and deluded, easily causing one to lose right reception (*samyag-samādhi*). There is nothing more extreme than this for perpetuating birth and death and losing the true permanence.

Therefore, it is necessary to take the primary precepts as the foremost instruction for purification. Observe how Ānanda, when he began his teaching mission, encountered defilement by improper taints;
yet at the very outset of his resolve, he first felt revulsion for the turbidity of desire.

Only after applying corrective measures one by one throughout the three gradual stages did his body and mind become wondrously perfect and attain great peace and stability. This was the initial stage of the ten levels of faith.
Because sensual craving has been dried up, the nature of wisdom becomes perfectly luminous, and one thus ascends through the stages of the Equal and the Sublime.

Ordinary people of the world, because their minds do not flow outwardly but remain clear and crystalline, give rise to illumination and gradually reach the six heavens. Therefore, true cultivation and internal integration must first involve the departure from desire.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: That there are so many such followers of Māra during the age of the Semblance Dharma (mofa) is because the True Dharma (zhengfa) has already been obscured while the winds of heterodoxy are now blazing.
There are three categories of these followers of Māra: first, those dispatched by Māra who belong to his lineage;
second, those who have gradually converted and practiced under him to become his subjects; and third, those who have violated both view and precepts and thus join his ranks of their own accord.
Is it not a clear foresight of the future that those who flourish in this world by widely practicing greed and lust act as "good spiritual friends"?
Indeed, the True Dharma and false dharmas are opposites; the path to Bodhi and the pit of craving and views are contradictory.
If the True Dharma is practiced, the path to Bodhi can exhaust the waters of desire. False [dharmas]...
When the Dharma is thus inflamed, the pit of craving and views can sever the path to Bodhi.

(II. Second Section: Further Elucidation; Part One: Violating Precepts Obstructs Cultivation and Realization) Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cut off lust yet cultivates meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and stones hoping they will become rice;
even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they would only be called "hot sand. Why is this? Because these are not the basis of rice; they are merely sand and stones.
If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its foundation, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape; by what path could you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata? (2.

Attaining Bodhi through Abstinence) You must cause the mechanism of lust to be severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of severance is non-existent; only then can you hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha. (2. Concluding the Distinction between the Deviant and the Correct) As I have said...
"This is called what the Buddha has spoken; that which is not so spoken is the speech of Pāpīyān. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says:
"The 'trigger' (*jī*) is that which is spontaneously aroused by the mind of lust; the nature of its severance is not non-existent, for it is aroused upon encountering the trigger.
Pāpīyān is a name for Māra."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Practicing dhyāna is like desiring to prepare rice. To practice dhyāna while harboring lust is like using sand and stones as the base for one's rice.
This is because, in order to achieve Buddhahood, one must obtain the root; if the root is pure, then the branches and flowings will also be pure.
It is for this reason that all four types of restraint are called "pure and clear instructions. They are like rice [as the foundation].
To use sand and gravel as the basis for making rice is to lose its very essence.
To seek Buddhahood while maintaining a body of lust is to lose its very essence. The mechanism of lust resides in the mind;

though the body may be severed, if the mind is not severed, it is like a wooden puppet—its internal mechanism does not cease even if its various faculties are temporarily stilled—and thus it cannot be considered true cessation.
However, although the functioning of the faculties may have ceased, as long as the nature of cessation remains, it is not yet sufficient to constitute true severance.
Only when both the faculties and their functioning are forgotten within the Buddha’s bodhi can one truly hope for liberation.

○ (2. The Precept Against Killing, Part 2: First, Distinguishing and Demonstrating Observance and Violation; 2.1. Direct Explanation; 2.1.1. Proclaiming the Benefits and Harms; 2.1.1.1. Observance Means Not Following the Continuity of Birth and Death) Ānanda, furthermore, if the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor the intent to kill, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. ○ (2.1.1.2.

Violation Means One Will Certainly Fall into the Realm of Spirits) If you practice samādhi with the aim of escaping worldly toil but do not eliminate the intent to kill, you cannot transcend the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the intent to kill, you will certainly fall into the realm of spirits—this applies even to those of superior grade.
Those of superior power shall become great spirits; those of middling capacity shall become flying yakṣas and various ghost generals;
and those of inferior capacity shall become earth-walking rākṣasas. These ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

[II. Exhortation and Admonition Regarding the Period After My Extinction (divided into two parts: first, spirits causing violations; second, spirits and ghosts deceiving the world)] After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi.
[II. The Tathāgata’s Discrimination and Clarification (divided into two parts: first, clarifying what is correct)] Ānanda, I have permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat;

these meats are all produced through my supernatural power and originally possess no life-force. You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the ground is mostly humid and damp, further compounded by sand and stones.

"Herbs and vegetables do not grow [as meat]; it is through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power, and by means of great compassion, that it is provisionally named 'meat,' so that you may obtain its flavor.
[Commentary] Gushan said: "Question: All the Vinayas clarify that fish and meat are *kāla-bhojana* (food for the proper time). Only the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Nirvāṇa*..."

Furthermore, why does this present sutra universally proclaim the cessation of meat-eating? The answer is: in the teaching of the Dharma, there are matters of sudden and gradual according to the capacities of the recipients.

This is true for both concentration and wisdom, and it is likewise so for the precepts. Therefore, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, meat-eating was suddenly prohibited for those with the capacities of the Separate and Complete Teachings (*vyāvṛtta* and *pariniṣpanna*), who have long since ceased eating meat.

However, from the Deer Park onwards, the *Vinaya* was gradually established for those with the capacities of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings; thus, for their sake, the "three kinds of pure meat" were permitted as a skillful means of conversion.
As the Path was nearing its end, the gradual approach was withdrawn and the sudden approach was emphasized. Consequently, three scriptures all proclaimed the cessation of meat-eating;
while the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* restricted it to Bodhisattvas of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* vehicles, this scripture restricts it universally for all three vehicles.

Thus, it states below that "pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not tread upon living grass," and so forth. Upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the restriction was further specifically applied to the Śrāvakas with great earnestness.
I have diligently provided this instruction. Question: Within the Brahmajāla Sūtra’s Bodhisattva precepts, it was originally established that one may eat meat;

why is it that only in the Laṅkāvatāra and other Vaipulya (fangděng) sūtras is it stated for the first time that from now on Bodhisattvas must not eat meat? Answer: The Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka and Shared (tōng) teachings have no distinct bodhisattva precepts;
they receive the same Vinaya-piṭaka as the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas). Therefore, the prohibition found in the Laṅkāvatāra and in the present sūtra serves as an illustration [of a new standard].
All [of these] are declared to be prohibited. Regarding the five kinds of pure meat, the Vinaya clarifies the "three purities":

not seeing that it was killed for one's sake, not hearing that it was killed for one's sake, and not suspecting that it was killed for one's sake. The present mention of "five" adds two more: meat from animals that died naturally and meat left over by birds.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* lists nine kinds of pure meat; this is because each of the three types of pure meat is further divided into the meat of animals that have not been seen, heard, or suspected of being killed for one's sake, as well as the meat of those killed through the actual transgression and its preceding or subsequent preparatory stages.
Jueli said: "Furthermore, among pure meats, ten species must be excluded—namely, humans, snakes, elephants, horses, donkeys, dogs, lions, foxes, pigs, and monkeys.
This is because even if these ten are not seen, heard, or suspected of being killed for one's sake, it is still impermissible to consume their meat."

[This refers to] food. Wēnlíng says that "not seeing, not hearing," and so forth, constitute five [aspects]. That which is transformed by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is called "pure" (*śuci*) because it fundamentally lacks the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
This, however, is a provisional teaching of the Hīnayāna; if one speaks of true compassion and true liberation, these [impurities] are all that must be severed.
"Pure conduct of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇacarya*) is a general designation. Among the four castes in the West, the Brāhmaṇas are considered superior; therefore, they...
The five regions of India are all called the Kingdom of the Brahmins; the monastics there are also called Brahmins. [Commentary] Tiantai says:
Now, killing takes the mind as its primary mechanism (*mēi*) and body and speech as its conditions (*yuán*).
Only when the mechanism is activated do the body and speech then engage in action. Therefore, in severing killing, nothing precedes the mind. Thus it is said: "If one's mind does not kill, then..."
One does not follow along with the continuity of birth and death. Although the capacity for action is rooted in the mind, that which is actually performed resides in the body and speech;
what benefit, then, is there in the mind? How grave it is! Among the sins committed by the sovereign of the mind, none is greater than the karma of killing.
Consequently, one brings about retribution and must repay prior offenses by having one's own body and mind butchered, sliced, roasted, and grilled to match them.
Both are destroyed. This is what is meant by "inflicting great harm through that which is of no benefit. Those who study the Way of the Buddha should not fail to take heed of this.
Regarding the claim that if one does not cease killing, one will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits (*shendao*):

after a person dies, those whose bodies are extended become *shen*, while those whose bodies are bent become *gui*. If these are spoken of together, *shen* is simply *gui*; for they share a single path.

The general heading refers to the "Chapter on the Division of Spirits," yet it speaks specifically of ghosts (*preta*). Although these four precepts are all fundamental, there are differences in their gravity when expressed in terms of the realms of downfall.
For instance, sexual misconduct leads to falling into the path of Māras, killing leads to falling into the path of ghosts, and stealing leads to falling among the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*;
is this not because the offenses become increasingly base, and thus the retributions become progressively more subtle? As for false speech, however—
Their roots of goodness will perish forever, and lacking further knowledge or vision, they will sink into the ocean of the three sufferings.
This not only means losing the lineage of the Tathāgata, but they will also dwell eternally within the three evil realms.

In the *Gushan Guxiang Chao*, it is clarified that the Nirvāṇa Sūtra speaks of nine kinds of pure meat by assigning three aspects to each of seeing, hearing, and suspecting. Furthermore, regarding the three aspects within "seeing," "seeing" refers to:
When leading away an animal, up until seeing it being held with a blade and on the verge of slaughter, is called the preliminary stage (*pūrvaprayoga*).
Seeing the actual slaughter is the fundamental primary offense (*maulāpatti*). Seeing that it has been slaughtered and feeling joy is called the subsequent stage (*paścātprayoga*).

Meat not involving these three stages is termed "pure meat" (*viśuddhamāṃsa*). The same applies to hearing [of such acts]. Regarding the three types within doubt: the first, the mere initial stirring of the mind, is called the preliminary stage.

The preliminary preparation (*upāya*) consists of deliberating and reflecting with doubt as to whether [the meat] was killed for one's own sake; this is termed the fundamental primary offense (*maulapāpa*).
To feel joy while doubting that it was for oneself is termed the subsequent preparation (*pṛṣṭha-upāya*). Meat free from these three doubts is called "pure meat.
To claim that such meat is pure is like a Brahmin who goes to a defiled land and eats a cake made of a festering ulcer, regarding the impure as pure, only to realize later what it truly is.
Only then will you beat your breasts and retch in grief, but by then it will be too late for regret.
(2. Refuting Deviance) Alas! After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, how can those who eat the flesh of sentient beings call themselves disciples of Śākya?
You should know that even if such meat-eaters should attain mental clarity resembling *samādhi*, they are all great *rākṣasas*; when their retribution ends, they must... [fall into the hells].
Those who sink into the bitter sea of birth and death and are not disciples of the Buddha—such people kill one another, devour one another, and eat one another without ceasing;
how could such people ever escape the three realms? (2. You Teach Them to Firmly Maintain) You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, and next to sever the taking of life;

this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past. (2. Re-explaining the Two [Points]: First, the transgression obstructs the Holy Path; Second, the direct reprimand for violating the precepts. This...

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking for others not to hear them;
such a case is called "seeking to hide what is instead made even more manifest. (2.

Raising the fault of holding onto the precepts) When pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas travel along a forked road, they do not tread upon living grass, much less pull it out with their hands; how could this not be great compassion?
They take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy their hunger.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: To practice meditation in order to avoid sin, yet instead commit acts of killing;

to plug one's ears to avoid others, yet instead raise one’s voice loudly—this is to seek concealment while making it even more manifest. Even those who do not intentionally trample or pluck [plants] possess the utmost benevolence and compassion.
How much more so for grasses and trees—let alone eating the flesh of sentient beings!
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Although grasses and trees lack sentience, they possess a lush, flourishing life.
Even those who study Buddhism maintain a compassionate heart toward them, refraining from treading upon or plucking them; how much more so for wriggling, moving creatures endowed with spirit!
"Does one who possesses the Buddha-nature and whose vital breath is so majestic as to be unshakable truly wish to kill it?
(2. Attaining Liberation through Observance): If bhikṣus do not wear silks, cotton, or floss from the East, nor the boots, shoes, or furs of this land..."

From wool to milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*); in this same way, such a bhikṣu has truly attained liberation from the world and has repaid his karmic debts from past lives, no longer wandering within the three realms.
Why is this? Because by consuming their physical parts, they have become conditions for those beings;

just as a person who eats the various grains of the earth cannot lift their feet off the ground, one must cause both body and mind to be so for all sentient beings, whether through the physical body or its constituent parts, or through both the body and the mind.

"One who does not accept and does not eat—I declare such a person to be truly liberated. (2. Concluding the Distinction between the Erroneous and the Correct) "What I have thus spoken is called the teaching of the Buddha;
that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān."
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The East is not without furs and wool; the Western lands are not without silk and cotton. These are spoken of according to what is predominant in each region.
Regarding the phrase "repaying past debts and no longer wandering in the three realms," the first clause should have been placed below [the second]; the translator’s phrasing is inverted.
"Feet do not leave the ground" refers to the people at the beginning of the kalpa, whose bodies possessed a flying radiance and whose feet were as if driven by it.
Yun said: "Because they consume the fat of the earth and feast upon fragrant rice, their bodies become solid and heavy, and their feet do not leave the ground.
Their bodies consist of flesh, blood, marrow, and bone; their bodily parts consist of furs, wool, milk, and curd.
Because they serve and eat with a mind of greedy seeking, these are called the 'two paths. Both must be severed together."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The *Wuli lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Things) states that "grain" (*liang*) is a general term for millet and panicled millet;

"rice" (*dao*) is a general term for non-glutinous and glutinous rice; and "beans" (*shu*) is a general term for various legumes. Each of these three types of grain has twenty varieties, totaling sixty.
When the fruits of vegetables and trees—each also numbering twenty—are added, they constitute the "hundred grains."

○ (3. Precept Against Stealing, Part 2: First, Distinguishing and Demonstrating Observance and Violation; 2.1. Direct Explanation; 2.1.1. Proclaiming the Benefits and Harm; 2.1.1.1. Observance Means Not Following the Continuity of Birth and Death) Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings within the six realms of the world do not harbor a mind of theft, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.

○ (2. Violation Means One Will Certainly Fall into Deviant Paths) If you cultivate samādhi to fundamentally escape from worldly toil, yet do not eliminate the mind of theft, you cannot transcend the dust of the world.
Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the mind of theft, you will certainly fall into deviant paths as a superior-grade spirit.

Those possessed by mid-grade malevolent spirits and low-grade heterodox persons and various demons—these various evil ones also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To take what is not given constitutes theft. Even if one has already received more than the payment due, it is still considered a debt to be reclaimed."
Furthermore, when one has stolen and acquired [wealth] without facing retribution, this is why the cycle of birth and death continues.
Because of the deceit and fraud of heterodox paths, the thief will inevitably fall into their own kind.

○ (2. Admonition for after my extinction; Part 1: Heretics Disturb the Orthodoxy; Sub-part 1: Demons Deceive the World) After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demons and heretics will flourish in the world.

They will secretly harbor deceit while claiming to be "Good Knowledge-Holders" (*kalyāṇamitra*), each asserting that they have attained the "Dharmas of a Superior Man. They will delude the ignorant and cause them to lose their minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit will suffer depletion and ruin.

○ (2. The Tathāgata’s Discernment and Revelation; Part 1: Revealing the Orthodox and Reproaching the Heretical; Sub-part 1: Revealing the Orthodox) I instruct my bhikṣus to wander from place to place begging for food, so as to...

Having abandoned greed, they have perfected the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook for themselves; they sustain their remaining lives by relying on leftovers, dwelling as travelers within the three realms.

They demonstrate a single coming and going, departing once and never returning. (2. Condemning the Deviant) How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata like merchandise?
They perform all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma, yet they instead revile those who have left the household life and possess the precepts.
The path of the Hīnayāna causes immeasurable sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell due to such doubts and errors.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Fāngfǎ" (Method) means the means. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that begging for food is called "fēnwèi" (distribution and protection), meaning that by distributing it to the Saṃgha, one protects the power of the Path.
Dharma Master Zhào says that there are briefly four intentions for begging for food: first, for... [text continues].
First, to bring benefit to sentient beings; second, to subdue arrogance; third, to realize that the body is subject to suffering;
and fourth, to eliminate attachment. This sutra causes one to abandon greed by not cooking for oneself, which is precisely the elimination of attachment.
To accomplish the path to Bodhi is itself to protect the power of the Way and bring benefit to sentient beings.

To know that the body is but a temporary lodging and the world but a transient sojourn, and to have no concern for hoarding or any lingering attachments—this is what is meant by "following the proper direction."
Unable to follow the Dharma, they greedily commit karmic offenses; because they destroy the Dharma and violate its precepts, they are called "thieves.
Though they wear the robes of the Buddha, they do not lead a pure life. They merely don the garments of the Buddha as a pretext to exploit and trade for offerings and sustenance.

[Commentary] Xunwen says: To conceal one's deceit and fraud is to harbor the mind of a thief; to claim the title of "Good Spiritual Friend" (kalyāṇamitra) is to steal the name of the sages and worthies.
If, according to each individual, they claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma), this already constitutes a grave falsehood (mṛṣāvāda).
Now, such claims are merely used as a pretext for acquiring wealth. To substantiate this, he cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
There are six kinds of thieving intentions: taking through harsh treatment; taking by feigning a pitiable appearance; taking with an air of contempt while manifesting an imposing demeanor;
taking by using others' names, claiming "I am a spiritual friend"; taking by bullying and insulting to force others into submission;
and taking what was entrusted by exploiting the confusion of another regarding a deposit. Taking on interest refers to demanding money from others as a loan.
Regarding these "breaths," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* lists four types: namely, a mind of flattery, a mind of crookedness, a mind of anger, and a mind of fear.
The *Caturvargika-vinaya* lists ten types: a mind of darkness, meaning ignorance of cause and effect;

a mind of perversity, meaning failure to recognize correct principle; a mind of crooked tears, meaning sycophancy; and a mind of terror, meaning constant apprehension of loss. These are always present.
Regarding the mind of stealing another's property, since it is said to be constant, one certainly intends to steal regardless of the quantity.

This involves a definitive taking; whether by forceful seizure, disregarding what is permissible or not, or by taking entrusted items, or by taking through intimidation—meaning to frighten someone with words, such as speaking of the retributions received in other hells or of being shaken [by hell-wardens] to take their wealth—or by taking upon mere sight.
This refers to spying for an opportunity to seize what can be taken and then stealing it. "Taking by relying" means using one's influence or power as a pretext.

As the Sūtra says, "fearing that they might lose their minds" refers to taking through intimidation; "losing their minds" means causing the person before one to lose their right mindfulness and fall together into false views.
Now, I say that this Sūtra conceals such craftiness and deception; although its words are brief, they are sufficient [to reveal it].

This obscures all things. Is it not the case that those who point one-sidedly toward the so-called "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) do so because the Tathāgata foresaw that in the末法 (mofa), the end of the Dharma, his followers would indeed be numerous?
Those who uphold this sutra should reflect upon themselves accordingly.

○ (2. Showing the Method for Expiating Offenses; Part 1: Encouraging Practice and Revealing the Benefits) If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi and is able, before an image of the Tathāgata, to light a single lamp with his own body, burn a finger joint, or incinerate a single stick of incense upon his person—I declare that such a person will at once repay all karmic debts from beginningless time, take a long farewell to the world, and forever escape all [sufferings].
Although his outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been extinguished and he has not yet clarified the path to supreme enlightenment, this person’s mind regarding the Dharma is already resolved. (2.

Not for the sake of signs: Even if one does not perform such minor acts of self-sacrifice, should they nonetheless attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they will inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay their past debts, just as in my own case with the horse-barley, exactly the same and no different.
[Commentary] Gushan says: A thief takes another’s *upabhoga* (objects of enjoyment) for his own body.

Now, by sacrificing one’s *vipāka* (the physical body as karmic retribution) to provide for the Supreme Sages, one is able to overturn and destroy the karma of theft accumulated since beginningless time. Wenglung says: Among all things difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one’s own body.
If one can relinquish what is most difficult to relinquish, then all other forms of greed and attachment will certainly be abandoned. Therefore, it is said: "This..."

When a person has reached a state of certainty regarding the Dharma, if they can relinquish the body while the mind does not decisively relinquish it, they will merely increase the suffering of karma without benefiting the Path.
Therefore, it is said below that one must cause both body and mind to be completely abandoned.
Because the Buddha was reviled by his former enemies, he was permitted to eat horse barley; thus, after realizing the fruit of enlightenment, he ate it at the village of Veḷudvāra.
This demonstrates that past debts must inevitably be repaid.
[Commentary] Gu-shan says: A thief takes another’s *pariṣkāra* (external requisites) for his own body;

now, to damage one’s *ātmabhāva* (physical existence) to provide for the Supreme Sage is precisely what the Great Teaching permits regarding the burning of the body. The *Shiyao* states: Someone asked about the prohibitions of the Vinaya...
Burning the body incurs a *thullaccaya* offense, while burning a finger incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. Regarding this, how is it that burning the body is praised? To answer this now:

the regulations of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and the Greater Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) differ in their prohibitions and permissions. The Lesser Vehicle establishes offenses, whereas the Greater Vehicle mandates burning.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Present karma is easy to restrain, so one may deviate from it in one's own practice; however, long-standing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are difficult to eliminate and must rely upon spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
Now, practitioners may prefer what is correct yet remain stubbornly attached to the perverse, or desire purity yet remain biased toward defilement.
They act without being taught and do so without wishing to; there seems to be something secretly driving them that they cannot stop—this is the power of long-standing habitual tendencies."
It is as if one’s virtue is exalted yet one’s fortune is meager; though one practices goodness, one’s person suffers misfortune.

To have many obstacles and many grievances, to suffer frequent illness and constant vexation—this state that persists as if bound by a mechanism and cannot be released of its own accord—is summoned by past habits (*vāsanā*).

This is not a condition arising from the causes of a single lifetime or a single kalpa, but rather that which has been perfumed moment after moment since beginningless time. Therefore, it is not something supernatural.
No power can liberate [one from it]. *Mahā-sattva-paraṃtara*—which is translated here as "Great White Parasol"—is the very essence of the heart-mind (*citta*).

Its magnitude pervades the realms of sand; thus it is called "Great. Its substance is utterly free from delusive defilement; thus it is called "White. Its function covers all things; thus it is called a "Parasol.
Because this divine mantra flows forth from it, it is named the "Heart-Mantra. "The Unseen Summit" refers to the flower.
Yanjing of the Ninth Ground personally declared himself to have been the Buddha’s wet nurse; at the time of birth, he held him in his hands and gazed closely, yet could not see the crown of his head.
He demonstrated that the Dharma of the Crown cannot be seen by means of seeing. Changshui said:

"The previous explanation concerned how concentration and wisdom destroy the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, it clarified that the study of precepts merely stops sinful karma. Now it is explained that divine mantras can destroy past calamities."
It also eliminates the obstacle of retribution. If these three obstacles are truly extinguished, what need is there to wait for realization?

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The previous discourse on the Vinaya rules was intended to restrain present karma; the current discourse on divine mantras is intended to eliminate past habitual tendencies.

This not only demonstrates the completeness and perfection of the established teachings, but also reveals that the Buddha’s compassion reaches all beings. Had it not been for this provision, how could those with past... [text truncated]
When habitual tendencies manifest before us, what dharma should be used to counteract them?
According to the words of Master Wenling, there is that which is impelled by past habits and that which is summoned by past habits;

while in the scriptural text, "impelling" is explicit and "summoning" is implicit, if one can uphold this divine mantra, then transgressions will be extinguished and blessings will arise—the intent of the scripture truly encompasses both. However, regarding these past habits...
To store this within the mind, it will not be altered by non-mind mantras; though habitual tendencies may exist, they will neither act nor fail to act, and thus cannot be remedied.
Now, by employing the essence and characteristics of the Great White Parasol to confront them, the three delusions shall be forgotten together and the four māras shall be extinguished simultaneously.
How then could habitual tendencies dare to conceal their traces therein?

(2. Manifesting the Benefits) Furthermore, regarding your karmic conditions and the habitual tendencies of affection shared with Mātanga over many kalpas—tendencies that span more than a single lifetime or a single kalpa—I have now proclaimed them, and your lustful hearts were forever liberated, enabling you to become Arhats.

If even she, a courtesan who had no intention to practice, was secretly sustained by my spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), how much more so for you, the sons of the Buddha, gathered here in this assembly?
To hear and seek the Supreme Vehicle with the determination to achieve Buddhahood is like raising dust in a favorable wind; what difficulty or peril could there be?

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: If even one with the carnal nature of Puṇḍarīka (Daṅgiā) can still realize it swiftly, how much more easily can those who possess the vessel of the Śrāvaka attain profound realization!
"Provision. How can one say "how much more so"? Wuxing said: "The heart of attachment is forever liberated" refers to attaining the stage of Anāgāmin upon first hearing the mantra.
"Becoming an Arhat" refers to the passage in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter where the perfect path is distinguished from the others.

If this is so, since one only becomes one beyond training (aśaikṣa) by virtue of hearing the Dharma, why speak of the "mysterious provision of spiritual power"? It is truly because of the secret... [text ends]
Relying on the power of the mantra and manifesting through the support of the Dharma-sound, with internal cultivation and external perfuming, one is able to realize [the fruit] swiftly.
If it were due to the mantra alone and not due to the Dharma, why was it previously stated that the bhikṣuṇī Śīlavatī became an arhat upon hearing the recitation of a verse?
Dust represents past habitual tendencies, and the wind is like the divine mantra; when dust is blown by the wind, it is easy to disperse. [Thus, one should] recite...
It is not difficult to eliminate habitual tendencies through mantras and attain liberation.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Within this passage, there are four distinct points regarding the superior power of mantras as compared [to other methods].
First, the difference in the thickness of past habitual tendencies. For example, the woman Mātangī’s habituation to affectionate attachment was not formed in a single lifetime.
"Through practice, one becomes thick [in virtue]. You who are gathered here have taken the body of a bhikṣu, yet your practice is thin.
Thus, the two of you differ in status, noble and base. Caṇḍā was a courtesan; as a person, she was base. You are the sons of the Buddha; as for your rank, you are noble."
Third, their mental resolve differs in terms of superiority and inferiority. The courtesan Mātaṅgī has no aspiration for practice, and thus her mind is inferior;
you bhikṣus seek the Supreme Vehicle, and thus your minds are superior. Fourth, there is a difference between those of wrong determination and right determination.
The courtesan Mātaṅgī takes the primordial Brahmā as her primary object and belongs to the category of those with wrong determination; you bhikṣus are determined [in the right].

Attaining Buddhahood belongs to the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Therefore, when you recite mantras to eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is like scattering dust with a following wind;
when Mātangi received the mantra and realized the fruit of enlightenment, it was like catching a fragrance against the wind.

In the analogy of the sutra, the wind is used to represent the mantra and the dust to represent the habitual tendencies. In my own view, however, the wind represents the habitual tendencies and the fragrance represents the mantra.
This is by means of the aforementioned mantra. (2.

Briefly showing the procedures for the site of practice; 2a. The preliminary expedient. If there are those in the final age who wish to sit at the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they must first uphold the pure prohibitive precepts of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, they must select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher. If they do not encounter one who is truly pure...

"O Bhikṣu, you must first perfect the discipline of the precepts. Once the precepts are established, don new, pure robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion to recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times.

(2. The Main Practice, Part 1: First, Clarifying the Cultivation) Thereafter, perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), establish the *maṇḍala*, and pray that the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions will emit great rays of compassionate light and descend to consecrate you."

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The observance of this precept should apply universally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the preceding section, the exhortation to recite and uphold [the text] was shown to reveal its benefits; it is called "brief" because it is contrasted with the subsequent passage which extensively reveals them.

In this present section, the regulations for the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) are presented; it is also called "brief" because it is contrasted with the following passage which provides an extensive demonstration.

The text on these regulations consists of two parts: first, the preparatory practices (*upāya*), and second, the actual cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The current text specifically clarifies the preparatory practices.

The *Zhengzhi Guan* (Correct Stopping and Contemplation) possesses twenty-five kinds of expedient means prior to formal cultivation: first, the possession of five conditions; second, the reviling of the five desires;

third, the discarding of the five hindrances; fourth, the adjustment of the five matters; and fifth, the practice of the five dharmas. These correspond to the present text and are all fully present therein.
For example, the statement "first maintain the pure prohibitive precepts of a bhikṣu" refers to the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, having perfected the precepts and donned new, pure robes, one possesses both clothing and food.
Establishing the *maṇḍala* by choosing a secluded forest or deep valley means dwelling in a quiet and solitary place.

Entering the altar with single-minded devotion and practicing the Way with a focused heart means ceasing all worldly affairs. Selecting a foremost *śramaṇa* as one's teacher means drawing near to the virtuous.
This is knowledge. The Sūtra says: "If these four matters are not lost, the mind will no longer take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch"—this is a rebuke of the five desires.
For the first twenty-one days, he practiced the Way in six periods of the day and night without sleep.
Thereafter, he sat upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days, thereby abandoning greed, anger, and sloth.
Restlessness, regret, doubt, and the five hindrances [must be abandoned]. When sitting upright in tranquil meditation, one must harmonize the mind so it is neither sunken nor agitated;
harmonize the body so it is neither too lax nor too tense; harmonize the breath so it is neither constricted nor slippery; harmonize sleep so it is neither restricted nor indulgent;
and harmonize food so it is neither hungering nor satiated—these are the five things to be harmonized. At the time of sitting in meditation, one must be fully endowed with joy.
Desire, diligence, mindfulness, skillful wisdom, and single-mindedness constitute the practice of these five dharmas.
Thus, this sutra not only accords with the "Yong-hui" [Hui-yung] on correct cultivation and śamatha-vipaśyanā, but its expedient means (*upāya*) are likewise largely identical.

Prior to the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), one should first recite the divine mantra one hundred and eight times, and only then perform the delimitation. Regarding the method for delimiting the boundary, this sutra does not...
It is taught that one should establish the boundary either by drawing it with a blade as prescribed in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*,
or by scattering white mustard seeds in the four directions, or by taking the extent of one’s mental visualization as the boundary. Now,
the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) in my mountain retreat follows the latter method, using visualization to define the boundary.
○ (2. Clarifying the Verification) Ānanda, if in the final age there are pure bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors, who extinguish greed and lust in their hearts and uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts;
who make bodhisattva vows within a place of practice (*maṇḍala*); who enter and exit for bathing and perform the path during the six periods of the day;
and who thus remain awake for twenty-one days—then I shall personally manifest my body before such a person and touch them.
[The Buddha] comforts him from above and causes him to attain awakening.
[Commentary: Tianru’s Supplement states: Previously it was said that he "seeks the Buddha’s consecration. Now, the Buddha manifesting his body is called "resonance" (yinggan).
Having attained this resonance, his mind will necessarily awaken. If he were to see other objects, it would contradict his original vow.
Furthermore, that which lacks any awakening is not a true response to conditions. Gushan said: "The Buddha is fundamentally mindless;

because he is pure, he exists. When the water is clear, the moon appears; such responding and inducing are spontaneous. If you encounter this situation, you should contemplate emptiness and stillness."
This Buddha clearly manifests as a Māra, and then he vanishes.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the sutra, the assembly is divided into three groups: first, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs;
and third, upāsakas, who are lay donors (dānapatis). However, laymen who are *upāsakas* may perhaps advance in their practice together with those on the same altar.
If a bhikṣuṇī truly wishes to practice the Way, she should establish a separate site for practice (daochang) of her own.
According to the ancient methods of the holy nuns of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are established precedents for this.

As for Jiaoguang’s allowance that laywomen may also participate in the altar, this internally violates the Vinaya regulations and externally invites public censure; what was intended as beneficial instead results in harm. How can one speak so clearly [of such matters]?
"Pure bhikṣus and others" indicates generally that all four types of discipline must be pure.
"With a mind that extinguishes greed and lust, one upholds the Buddha’s pure precepts" emphasizes, among the four precepts, the first precept above all.
"To give rise to bodhisattva vows within the site of enlightenment" refers to the ten great vows as taught in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

This focuses specifically on the precept against sexual misconduct. Regarding the four fundamental precepts, it is because the first—the precept against sexual misconduct—is easy to violate yet difficult to maintain—that such urgent and earnest instructions and admonitions are given.
As for "entering and exiting for bathing," some say that one must bathe whenever entering or leaving an impure place;
according to the *Fangdeng Daochang* (Mahāyāna Ritual Manual) of Mount Nanyue, however, this refers to performing repentance upon both exiting and entering [the ritual space].

One must bathe thoroughly. "Practicing the Way during the six periods" refers to the passage below concerning the constant recitation of mantras and circumambulation of the altar during the six periods.
"Thus remaining awake for three times seven days" is equivalent to the Buddha’s establishment of the *samādhi* of constant practice without sleep.
According to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the *samādhis* of various sūtras do not exceed four types. First:
1. The Samādhi of Constant Sitting (*niṣadyā-samādhi*): As described in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, one sits constantly and does not lie down;
a period of one hundred days constitutes one session. 2. The Samādhi of Constant Walking (*caṅkramaṇa-samādhi*): As in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, one walks constantly and does not sleep;

a period of ninety days constitutes one session. 3. The Samādhi of Half-Walking and Half-Sitting: As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one practices walking and sitting in equal measure; a period of twenty-one days constitutes one session.
Regarding the period: the four practices that are neither walking nor sitting—that is, the *bodhyanga-samādhi* (awakening-intent samādhi)—are not limited by a specific number of days.

In this sutra, during the first three seven-day periods at the site of practice (*dharmāyatana*), one focuses exclusively on constant walking; thereafter, for one hundred days, one dwells in seated retreat (*an-gu*), focusing exclusively on constant sitting.
Thus, this single sutra encompasses both practices. Jiaoguang’s *Zhengmo* states that these are the six periods.

He practiced walking meditation during the six periods of the day and sat in stillness to balance dullness and agitation, believing that walking meditation would remedy dullness while sitting would remedy agitation.
I say: if one exerts effort in such a manner, how could one possibly remain awake for twenty-one days without sleep?

Thus, if one practices walking meditation intending to remedy dullness, it only serves to increase distraction; if one sits in meditation intending to remedy distraction, it only serves to increase dullness.
In this way, there is either dullness or distraction, and if not dullness then distraction—how can one possibly prevent sleep?

To force this into human speech is truly laughable. Gushan said, "The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent" means that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas has no form or characteristics by which they could see one another;
it refers to what is called the *dharmakāya* pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
"Because the mind is pure, [the Buddha] exists" means that the practitioner, through a pure mind, evokes the presence of the Buddhas.

The Buddha necessarily responds to this; that which is called "responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli without exception" refers to this. Thus it is said: "When the water is clear, the moon appears; the response and stimulus are spontaneous.
If one perceives this correspondence, one should contemplate emptiness and stillness as the manifest form of the Buddha.

This is precisely because the Buddha exists due to the purity of the mind. When one is able to contemplate emptiness and stillness, the mind becomes increasingly pure and the marks of the Buddha become increasingly manifest. If...
The deeds of Māra defile the mind, while the opposite reveals the purity of the mind and causes such defilements to perish.

It is like the glass *laṅgamani*, which at first glance seems genuine but upon closer examination proves to be counterfeit; this may serve as a clear mirror for distinguishing between the Buddha and Māra.

[The Threefold Enlightenment: Binding the Altar and Establishing Practice, Part Two; First, Extensively Showing the Methods for the Site of Practice; First, The Inquiry] Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, having received the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Tathāgata, my mind has already attained awakening.

I know for myself that the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) has been realized and perfected. Now, regarding the practice during the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), when establishing a site of practice (*maṇḍala*), how should one bind the boundaries so as to accord with the pure rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?”
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "I ask for a detailed explanation of the ritual rules for establishing the altar.

As for the statement "knowing for oneself [the stages of] cultivation and realization," it means that one knows the mantra’s power provides secret assistance, and the attainment of the sacred fruit can be expected.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: For those who know for themselves that they have attained realization and perfected the path of no-more-learning—that is, Buddhas during the Buddha’s lifetime—it was not necessary to establish an altar.
This was because there were four reasons: they personally beheld the compassionate countenance; they directly received the sacred teachings; their faculties and capacities were mature and profound;
and they had already attained the first fruit [of the Path]. In the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age, it is the opposite; therefore, one must establish [the altar]. There are also four reasons for this.
Because he sought to see the Buddha manifest his body, because he received the touching of the crown of his head, because he accomplished the capacity as a vessel for the Dharma,

and because he was admitted into the stream of the Dharma— this "stream of the Dharma" refers precisely to those of sharp faculties who, after dwelling in seclusion for one hundred days, realized the stage of Srotāpanna without rising from their seats.

[II. Answering and Demonstrating (with two parts: first, the specific demonstration; first, clarifying the altar ritual; first, the method for establishing the altar)] The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the final age wish to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*, they should first seek a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fragrant herbs of those mountains.
This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle.
One should take this dung and mix it with *candana* to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the ox’s dung will be foul-smelling."
The impure ground being unfit for coating, one should select a level plain and excavate five feet beneath the surface.

From below that depth, take the yellow earth and mix it with the ten kinds of incense—sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *kunduruka*, saffron, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *sāla* resin, *candana*, *jātī*, and clove—and grind them finely into powder. Combine this with the earth to form a paste to coat the site.
Make a square altar sixteen feet in circumference with eight corners.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The Dharma King’s words of Dharma are such that phenomena are identical to principle; phenomena do not arise in isolation, nor are phenomena established in vain.

It is like the Dharma-gate of a single word in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which could not be fully recorded even if one used the ink of the oceans. The characteristics of the five stages of practice are likewise..."

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is thereby made manifest. Whatever is established therein must necessarily possess symbolic significance; thus, every implement and provision used for this maṇḍala is none other than a representation of the Dharma.
The mountain represents the elevated ground. The Snowy Mountains represent pure, supreme faith. The powerful white ox represents the pure, great root.
The fragrant herbs and clear water represent wondrous, virtuous, and pure wisdom. The lush growth signifies fulfillment.
This is the remnant. Sandalwood is the foremost of the ten fragrances and the crown of the ten pāramitās and myriad practices.

Originally, it represents faith within the level ground; the surface soil has not yet been purified. Among the five numbers and among the five colors, yellow is taken to represent the purity of the central-center faith.
The ten fragrances are the Dharma-fragrance of the ten pāramitās. It is finely woven.
It is ground and refined to constitute the subtle and wondrous myriad practices.

Now, one who wishes to attain the Tathāgata’s field of quiescent extinction must fundamentally rely upon vast faith and be sustained by pure wisdom and sublime goodness to cultivate a single, pure root.
When this is fully developed and overflowing, it is sufficient to accord with the Dharma-fragrance and crown the ten perfections; therefore, one may—
This is to solemnly perfect the site of the field of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣetra*). Those of superior faith and great capacity find that there is nothing to be attained;

thus, they seek the next level. Therefore, one takes the "middle-of-the-middle" faithful mind. Although it may not yet surpass the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) and myriad practices, one who is able to embody them can likewise solemnly perfect [the practice].

[Commentary] Tiantai says: As for the necessity of using incense when coating altars and making offerings to the Buddhas, it is a sublime substance for repelling impurities and a divine object for honoring the sages.
According to the *Gantong zhuan*, Tianren Fei said that the foul odors of human beings rise upward to permeate [the heavens].
In the forty thousand *li* of empty space above, there are pure devas who do not fail to find it refreshing;
yet, because they have received the Buddha’s entrustment to protect the Dharma, even though the Buddha dwells together with humans, these devas dare not fail to come.
Thus, within the Buddha-dharma, incense serves as a Buddha-activity, established for the purpose of clearing away impurities and invoking the sages. (Translated)
The *Mingyi ji* (Compendium of Names and Meanings) states that "ox-head sandalwood" (*gośīrṣa-candana*) is sometimes left untranslated because it does not exist in this region;

alternatively, it is translated according to its meaning, as the wood acts as a medicine capable of eliminating disease. The *Ci'en zhuan* (Biography of Xuanzang) notes that the tree resembles the white poplar (*pappus*), its substance being cool and cold, and that many snakes frequent it.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that ox-head sandalwood originates from Mount Malaya.
If one applies it to the body, even upon entering a pit of fire, one cannot be burned.

When the devas and asuras are engaged in battle and are wounded by weapons, if they apply ox-head sandalwood to their wounds, they are immediately healed. For this reason...
The mountain peak is shaped like an ox’s head; because sandalwood trees grow on this peak, it is named Ox-Head (Goviśāna).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that no sandalwood grows except on Mount Malaya. White sandalwood cures febrile diseases, while red sandalwood removes wind-swelling.

Although sandalwood originates from foreign lands and exists in two varieties—red and white—its nature is hot, its efficacy is limited to treating qi (vital energy), and its substance is inferior;
it possesses no other qualities whatsoever. Whether these are genuine or counterfeit is beyond my knowledge.
