And yet it grows again. Tiantai said: "Recently, from the garden planted at Bodhi Peak, I was able to harvest quite a bit;
after drying it in the sun and storing it in my chests and baskets, its fragrance has overwhelmed me.
Tiantai said: "Gansong (Cedrus deodara) comes from Guangzhou. That it is now widely used by perfumers is easily understood. [The fifth: Chicken-Tongue.]
*Maizhou* (Horse Island) produces it. The *Nanzhou Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things from the Southern Continent) states that when this grass withers, it can be used to compound incense tablets.
Foreign Hu people say that various fragrances are all from the flowers of a single tree, which is called *jishé* (chicken-tongue). ○ *Touluopo* comes from the Ghost-Demon Kingdom (*Guishen Guo*).
Since this is not found in our own region, it is not translated; alternatively, it is translated as "fragrant herb. Formerly, it was called *baimeoxiang* (white mugwort incense). — Tiantai.
It is said that *baibaoxiang* (white-moss incense) is found everywhere on Mount Tai; that which grows on Mount Xianglin is the finest.

[Section 2: Methods of Offering, Part 1] [A. Offerings within the Altar, Part 1] [B. Constant Offerings Day and Night, Part 1] [C. Adorning the Center of the Altar] Place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood at the center of the altar.
Upon the flower, place an alms bowl (*pātra*). Within the bowl, first pour dew collected during the eighth month; into the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available.
[Commentary] Changshui says: "A *tan* (altar) is made by clearing the ground; it is what we call a *shan* (levelled mound) today. Wuxing says: "Not so.
Since the previous passage states that the site of the field may be 'like its *shan*,' and since it is now specifically named a *tan*, one must necessarily raise earth to construct it."
This means that first the ground is cleared to form a site, after which yellow earth is separately taken and mixed with incense to form mud;
this mud is applied to the site to raise it up and create the appearance of a maṇḍala. Wēnlíng says: "The maṇḍala is the essence of tranquil extinction, level and solid.
Because its essence possesses the Eightfold Noble Path, it has eight corners. Because it subsumes the eight heterodoxies, it is sixteen feet square. This is the maṇḍala.

The "Lotus in the Mind" represents the wondrous practice of the Middle Way. That the lotus, as a thing, possesses fruit and flower as one substance and defilement and purity as a common source symbolizes the general principle of wondrous practice.
Those made of gold, silver, copper, or wood represent the wondrous conduct of practice.
Gold and silver, though refined a hundred times, become ever more pure yet do not change; copper is hard yet capable of being tempered—these are metaphors for the meaning [of the practice].
Furthermore, wood can grow upward while grass covers what lies beneath; this is the image of benevolence (*ren*).

Now, when conduct arises based on the essential nature, it is refined yet unchanging, firm yet capable of harmony. Whether one restrains with righteousness (*yi*) or covers with benevolence, there is neither excess nor deficiency;
all converge upon the Middle Way. This is precisely what constitutes wondrous conduct. The alms bowl (*pātra*) is the vessel appropriate for a monk, symbolizing compliance.
The measure corresponds to the object. The dew serves as the moisture for the Yin, descending in autumn. August is the middle month of autumn.

The blossoms and leaves upon the water represent the conduct of benevolent coverage, following wherever the moisture is bestowed. This, moreover, is a manifestation of how the Yin benefits things through subtle transformation according to their respective measures.
(2. Adornment of the Eight Directions) Take eight circular mirrors and place each in its respective direction surrounding the flower bowl.

Outside the mirrors, establish sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners, interspersed with flowers as an adornment. The incense burners shall burn only aloeswood (agaru), ensuring that the flames are not visible.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The 'Perfect Mirror' refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The fact that each is placed within a lotus bowl surrounded by the eight directions signifies that wisdom and practice depend upon one another, responding perfectly to each quarter.

As for the sixteen lotuses and incense burners arranged alternately outside the mirror: the flowers symbolize wondrous practice, and the incense symbolizes wondrous virtue. 'Outside the mirror' means outside of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*)."

This is established through skillful means so that the heterodox and the orthodox may mutually embrace one another and their virtuous practices may mutually perfume one another; it is hoped that after a long time, both will be transformed together such that heterodoxy and orthodoxy are both forgotten.

To burn pure aloeswood without allowing anyone to see the fire is to reverse the functioning of the treasury of virtue and extinguish and subdue discursive thought (*vitarka* and *vicāra*), whereby one can subsequently accord with the ground of quiescent extinction. Someone said: "The manifestation of the Dharma is indeed thus, but what of the ancients?"
The Virtuous One did not understand. Is this not a mere speculative theory? I replied: "That which I follow is the *Avataṃsaka-mahā-śāstra*.
If one studies it thoroughly, one will know that this is not a speculative theory.
(Third: Arranging the Offerings) Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels; prepare milk pancakes along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, and milk [cakes].
With *mṛdvīkā*, saffron, honey, and ginger, as well as pure ghee and pure honey, each surrounding the lotus flower sixteen times;
outside the flowers, these were offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The outer [offering] presents the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna to the Two Honored Ones. While the provisional teachings permit milk and curd, the definitive teachings prohibit them;
yet, they are nevertheless taken up for offering. The intention behind this is to harmonize the provisional and the definitive, and to unify the heterodox and the orthodox.
Thus, the eight flavors are each surrounded by sixteen [petals], symbolizing on the outer surface the method of harmonizing the provisional and subsuming the heterodox."
This is the ritual provision for practicing with joy. (2.
Separate Offerings at Two Times) At every mealtime or during the middle watch of the night, take half a jin of honey and three he of ghee.
Before the altar, separately install a small fire-pit and boil *turuṣka* incense to produce scented water; bathe the charcoal with this and kindle it into flame.
[One] takes this ghee and honey, casts it into a blazing furnace, burns it until the smoke is exhausted, and offers it to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary: Wēnlíng says: "Because the Buddha accepts food at midday, he is always offered sustenance at midday. Midnight follows the same principle as midday.
Honey is produced from flowers, symbolizing the harmonious and integrated practice of the Dharma. Ghee is produced from milk, symbolizing..."

The harmonious fusion is the flavor of the Dharma. Five is the intermediate number, and three is the number of completion. The small incense burner represents the square inch of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*).
Using incense to moisten the charcoal is the method for generating awakening. King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his own body after first consuming *turuṣka* incense;
his intention was to cause flames to erupt. Therefore, one takes the moistened charcoal and burns it until it blazes fiercely, then casts ghee and honey into the flames.
Regarding "smelting in the furnace until the smoke is exhausted": once the practice of the Dharma has been accomplished, one must not remain stagnant.
One should forge and refine the awakened mind with vigor, causing habitual tendencies to be melted away entirely and the shadows of conditions to vanish together.

Only when it is as sudden and clear as "a snowflake falling into a red-hot furnace" will one be worthy of the Buddhas' enjoyment. Indeed, those who dwell in the field of cessation yet have not yet partaken of the bliss of meditation—how could they attain this?
In this matter, one should exert every effort. (II.

Adornment Outside the Altar, Part 1: Arrangement of Various Images) One should cause banners and flowers to be hung everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the altar chamber, images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions should be displayed;
specifically, Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Maitreya should be installed facing the main entrance.
The great transformations of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Avalokiteśvara, along with Vajragarbha,
are installed at their left and right; Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, Lambodara,
the various Mañjuśrīs, Vighnāntaka, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka are arranged on both sides of the entrance.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The four outer banners and flowers represent the adornment of external conduct. The Lord of the True Field, Vairocana, occupies the central position facing south.
Maitreya is the future Lord of the True Field. Akṣobhya resides in the east and Amitābha resides in the west;
they are the Lords of True Wisdom and Compassion. The various great transformations and the forms of Avalokiteśvara correspond above and below."
He is the True Lord (*bhagavān*). Vajragarbha constantly leads the vajra-protectors who uphold the mantras, subdue māras, and sever obstacles;
he is the True Lord. On the left and right sides of the gate are the hosts of Śakra, Brahmā, and others, who provide powerful external protection.
In the Dharma-ending age, practitioners of the path rely entirely upon these; if even one is lacking, success will certainly not be achieved. Ucchuṣma, the Fire-Headed Vajra.
Nīladaṇḍa is the Blue-Faced Vajra; he is another name for Krodhacaṇḍa. Bhṛkuṭī is also a deity of great supernatural transformations;
she is the one described in the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* as being on the left side, three-eyed and holding her hair in a topknot.
Pīṇākī and Yakṣa are the two messengers with the heads of a boar and an elephant, respectively.

○ (2. Hanging Eight Mirrors) Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in space, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual arena, so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The mirror within the altar is mixed with things and has a basis; it is the wisdom of the practitioner.
The mirror in space is detached from things and has no basis; it is the wisdom of the Buddhas.

That which is mixed with things and has a basis can only illuminate objects but cannot yet illuminate itself. One must attain that which is detached from things and without basis, so that the abiding wisdoms may mutually interact."
Thereupon, things and self illuminate one another, and the mirror of the mind and its reflection merge into a single unity. The bodies and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate;
without moving a step and without waiting for a thought to arise, every dharma is omnipresent and every phenomenon is unimpeded.

At a glance, the thousand sages appear together; wherever one touches, the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest. With a single flower or a single incense offering, one makes universal offerings to all lands within the dust motes. A single act...
The single characteristic is expansive and infinite; it does not rely on supernatural powers nor involve conceptual thought. Such is the fundamental nature of all dharmas in the tranquil field.
Herein, the subtle culmination of the cultivation and realization of the secret cause is reached.

[II. Showing the Ritual for Recitation (divided into two: first, the preparatory practice; second, the actual practice). First, the preparatory practice (divided into two: first, practicing the path; second, clarifying accomplishment). First, clarifying the auxiliary practices: During the first seven days, one should perform prostrations with utmost sincerity to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the titles of Arhats.

Constantly throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should recite the mantra while circumambulating the altar, practicing the path with a sincere heart. During each period, one should constantly perform one hundred and eight recitations.
During the second seven days, one should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the Bodhisattva vows, maintaining them without interruption. My Vinaya...

Yaśas, previously there was a vow: during the third seven-day period of instruction, by reciting the Buddha’s *Bhadrā* mantra continuously throughout the twelve periods of the day until the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where mirrors reflect one another’s light, and you shall receive the Buddhas’ touch upon the crown of your head.

(2. Explaining the Primary Practice) One should then cultivate *samādhi* within the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), which can cause those who practice and study in this manner during the final age to [purify] their body and mind.
"Brilliant and pure, like lapis lazuli.
[Commentary] Wénlǐng says: "In all that one aspires to, taking refuge in the Triple Gem is the primary expedient.
Therefore, during the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the names of the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats. This is why one relies upon them..."
The inconceivable power initiates the practice that aids the Path. However, without the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), there would be no means to sustain it;
therefore, during the second seven-day period, one relies on the Vinaya teachings to single-mindedly formulate aspirations. When practice and aspiration are firm and strong, one attains great valor;
thus, during the third seven-day period, one recites and maintains the mantra without interruption, without limit, and with single-minded devotion.
Thus, one is able to move the divine through sincerity and, by exerting effort, achieve merit. When mirrors reflect one another’s light, the Buddha-wisdom arises;

this is the mutual resonance of the path of response and stimulus. That body and mind are bright and pure means that the obstacles of past habitual tendencies have been completely eradicated down to their finest details;
this is the matter of achieving merit through response and stimulus. Wuxing said: "Those who previously possessed the vow to teach are like the Brahma-net [Sūtra]."
This refers to the "Ten Great Vows" and other such texts.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The ritual altar for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as a symbolic representation of the Dharma began with Wang Jinggong (Wang Anshi). Ancient masters had never heard of it.
By the Yuan dynasty, the Master of Wenling also followed this elegant tradition. However, Wang Jinggong’s approach was characterized by a predominance of substance over form.
In the case of Wen (the literary) at Wēnlíng, the literary aspect excels the substantial;

yet when it comes to being practical for conduct and in accord with the core of the scriptures, where interpretation and practice follow the same path and the manifest and the esoteric share the same track—such that the meaning of *jingguan* (contemplation of the objective realm) is perfected and the Way of resonance is made manifest—I have never heard such a claim.
Therefore, I am able to once again set forth this representation of the Dharma to serve as a basis for veneration.
This is a guide for those on the Way; yet I do not dare claim it to be necessarily correct. I only ask that the wise and enlightened examine it once to see what it truly is like.

Now, while the net of principle and the management of affairs constitute a single Way, they are not obstructed by their myriad differences. When affairs accord with principle, even though ten thousand...

The myriad differences are not separate from the single nature; how much more so when the ten thousand differences are phenomena within the principle, and the thousand disparities are not a mind external to those phenomena.
Phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, and the one and the many are without obstruction: the cause transcends the sea of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.

I have seen this clearly in the ritual methods of the *Śūraṅgama* altar. Why is this? It is because without the subtle myriad differences, there would be no means to clarify the resonance [between cause and effect].
It is so. Without the subtle single principle, there would be no way to establish the interpenetration of phenomena. The single principle is precisely the myriad particulars;
a small room contains boundless Buddhist activities. The myriad particulars are precisely the single principle; the various vessels do not obstruct empty space.

Thus, as sentient beings and Buddhas are in constant, dark harmony, and as response and stimulus are perfectly manifested in every thought-moment, all established arrangements do not lie outside this dynamic of response and stimulus.

Thus, by taking the eight mirrors above and below as the primary elements, they are explained and manifested. Now, the umbrella upon which the eight mirrors above rest symbolizes the ultimate reality (paramārtha) heaven of all Buddhas.
The ritual platform upon which the eight mirrors below rest symbolizes the ever-abiding ground of the mind of sentient beings.
As the reflection of the ritual platform descends upon the upper mirrors, the ground of the minds of sentient beings is itself the [Buddha-realm].
The Buddha is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The shadow of the parasol enters the lower mirror, wherein the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas is precisely the ground of the minds of sentient beings.
This serves as the representation of the fundamental source, the locus upon which the various adornments below are entrusted.
As for the initial act of taking the dung of a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains to smear the ground, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Snow..."
On the mountain there is a herb called "Patience" (*kṣānti*). If a cow eats it, she immediately obtains *sarpis-maṇḍa* (the finest essence).
*Sarpis-maṇḍa* is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). Since the herb is the root of *sarpis-maṇḍa*, all that is consumed therein is the pure source of Buddha-enlightenment.
This sandalwood from this shore is worth as much as the great trichiliocosm; when six *zhu* are burned, its fragrance pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Using this in combination with *ru-tui* to smear the ground demonstrates that those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom employ the Buddha’s awakening exclusively as their own mind;
thus, the self-nature is pure, and the root of precepts is fundamentally free from defilement. If one lacks such superior faculties...
Thus, one cannot help but adopt the neutral nature. One distinguishes this from the plains by piercing the ground and removing the surface soil;
at a depth of five chi or more, one takes the yellow earth. Now, earth is the center of the elements (*dhātu*), five is the center of numbers, and yellow is the center of colors.
This constitutes the root of the neutral nature. By radically discarding the ordinary sentiments of the broad world, one proceeds by means of this.

It flows inward from within the heart. As for "harmonizing with the ten fragrances," this means relying on the ten precepts—such as being complete, upheld, unbroken, and without leakage—as the foundation for entering the Way through the Middle Dharma.

However, the specific statement that "if it were not from the Snowy Mountains, its cow would be foul-smelling and unfit even to smear upon the ground" is precisely intended for those in the degenerate age who lack the precepts.
The admonition for a bhikṣu who claims to have attained the state of a superior man (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) is as follows:
Those who nowadays speak of the Mahāyāna rely solely on their own wild wisdom (*unmatta-prajñā*). They claim that the precepts need not be maintained and that conduct need not be established.
Their foul stench is even worse than the remains from a wild ox's anus. The World-Honored One predicted from afar that they will never possess the principle of attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, it is said in extreme terms that this filth and impurity is unfit even to be smeared upon the ground.
As for the eight-cornered altar measuring sixteen feet in circumference: in terms of its corners, it cannot help but be square; yet in terms of its eight sides, it cannot help but be circular.
This represents the foundation of the Perfectly Sudden (Enlightenment), which is square on the outside and circular within. Its square exterior signifies majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
And it serves as a standard for measuring objects. Internally, it is circular, thereby harmonizing the mind through the wondrous principle.
This further demonstrates that although practitioners of the Mahāyāna realize the perfect fusion of the single nature, they do not lose the orderly discipline of the three trainings.

As for the term "sixteen feet," it simply means that using eight feet directly would be insufficient to accommodate the ritual implements for offerings; therefore, those eight feet are doubled to become sixteen.
The direct path never forgets its root. Within the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood;
this too is determined by the abundance or scarcity of one's offerings (*dāna-pāramitā*) and has no fixed form.

Placing the alms bowl within the flower and placing water within the bowl signifies that the Tathāgata relies upon great wisdom (*mahā-prajñā*) of equality to respond to sentient beings, even though his transformative manifestations are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Transformation after transformation produces further transformations; all these manifest various modes of deportment without arising from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Without moving from the tranquil site (*śānta-maṇḍala*), they traverse the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, although it is said that concentration (*samādhi*) is brought forth from wisdom (*prajñā*), there is nothing that is not itself wisdom and itself concentration.
Therefore, he placed lotus petals upon the water to manifest this principle. He took eight circular mirrors, each...
Regarding the arrangement of the methods [as described in the text]: the number of circular mirrors within the altar corresponds to the lotus incense burners.
Eight mirrors are suspended above; this is the way through which the Buddhas respond. Eight mirrors are placed below; this is the way through which the practitioner is moved.
One mirror is provided for each direction, according to the Eightfold Noble Path. The flowers and the burners are likewise ten in number.

Regarding the sixfold enumeration: the Way of the Buddha’s response to sentient beings’ resonance has no other [foundation] than taking the incense of precepts, the flowers of wisdom, and the mirror of meditative concentration as its basis.
Specifically, because a mirror can be hung while the flowers and the ritual vessel cannot, these two are provisionally entrusted to the ever-abiding mind-ground for their placement.

As for the light of the mirror, when it manifests in successive layers of mutual penetration, these three [elements]— [...are unified.]* *(Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point.)*
From the beginning, there is no interval between the upper and lower [realms]. Within the furnace, one burns pure agarwood so that the fire itself is not seen;
whereas other incenses require the fire for their fragrance to begin to rise, agarwood, though it relies on fire, does not actually depend on it for its fragrance to become clear and bright.
This illustrates that the precepts of the other vehicles must rely on the activities of body and speech before they can be maintained, whereas in the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], they are otherwise.
Although the wondrous precepts of the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna) rely upon signs, they do not in reality dwell upon signs;
thus, the fragrance of these precepts is rich and pervasive, filling the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding the taking of white ox milk and placing it in sixteen vessels:

the white ox milk takes the "suffering-grass" (*kṣānti-tṛṇa*) of the Snowy Mountains as its essential basis. One must know that this milk is itself the clarified butter (*ghṛta*, *sarpis*). To necessarily obtain the white ox, one must...
These may be offered to the Buddha; if such are lacking, one should follow the aforementioned rules, for milk that is still "milky-smelling" (fresh) and impure is unfit for offering.
In my family’s altar ritual, we separately substitute worldly delicacies for milk and gruel.

Specifically, we use pure white rice, wheat flour, bean flour, or fern flour to make fried cakes (*bianshi*). Perhaps it was with this that [the donor] informed the Buddha, and the Buddha likewise [accepted it].
I trust you will grant me your permission. As for the "Eight Flavors" (Hachi-mi), it employs the Eightfold Noble Path as the foundation of all myriad practices.
Furthermore, by combining the dew of the eighth month with the charcoal fire thereafter, one forms the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, wherein the primary and auxiliary practices are cultivated in tandem.
This is precisely what is meant by the title "The Secret Cause of Myriad Practices. Indeed, the dew of the eighth month represents the essence of Yin, while the red furnace [represents Yang].

Fierce flames are the essence of Yang; Yang can produce things, while Yin can nurture them. It is for this reason that the myriad things of the world rely on the sun to be born and on the night to be nurtured.
The circular image [of the sun] symbolizes the cultivation of Samādhi and Prajñā:

Samādhi serves to restore one's nature, while Prajñā brings about awakening. Thus, the Great Master Tiantai said: "Cessation (śamatha) is the excellent provision for nourishing the mind and consciousness."
"Contemplation is the subtle art for stimulating spiritual understanding. How profound these words are! "The time of eating is the midpoint of the yang;
midnight is the midpoint of the yin. This demonstrates that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do not depart from the Middle Way.

"When the fire ignited by fragrant water has burned so fiercely that the smoke is exhausted," this signifies that concentration and wisdom melt away dullness and distraction until nothing remains. Cause it to...
The four outer directions are universally draped with banners and flowers; this further constitutes auxiliary practice, leaving nothing unexhausted.
Regarding the instruction that one should hang [images] facing the sun, such as Vairocana and others: Vairocana is the *vipāka* (retribution) image, while Śākyamuni is the *nirmāṇa* (response) image.

The reason it does not mention Vairocana as the *dharmakāya* is that the *dharmakāya* is the realm of those on the ten stages of practice, who, like the Venerable Ānanda, do not pass through the stages of the *śrāvaka*.

"Having suddenly attained it all" refers to the Dharmakāya, which has already been realized as identical [to the ultimate]. That which has not yet been made identical is the Nirmāṇakāya and Saṃbhogakāya.
Therefore, when the Venerable Ānanda had already attained the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he immediately made this vow:
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King. This vow was fulfilled as the Tathāgata Ratnajñāna, who in turn saved beings in such a manner.

The multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall fulfill this vow to become Response-Bodies (nirmāṇakāya) Tathāgatas. Those who have not yet attained this are to be perfected through offerings;

those who have already attained it truly have no need for offerings. Furthermore, since the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is formless, if one insists on representing it in form, how could one ever capture its likeness?
Now, exalting compassion in the present world and bringing forth pity in future kalpas, he shall be the Lord of the coming age.
This is Maitreya. His unconditional compassion is that which I must devote my whole heart to and serve.
Akṣobhya is the Venerable Immovable One of the East; Amitābha is the Immeasurable Life of the Western Land.
My mind is wondrously profound and tranquil, and as the Dhāraṇī-Immovable One, it is of the same essence as them. Since he is the true refuge of the present moment, he is also...
This is a supreme refuge for rebirth; these five Buddha-Tathāgatas are those to whom practitioners who have perfected their cultivation should take refuge, and thus they are specially venerated.
As for the various great transformational images of Avalokiteśvara, they are those who, upon achieving perfect penetration (*yuantong*), manifest infinite transformations.
As for Vajragarbha-rāja, he is one who, while perfect penetration has not yet been achieved, secretly awakens my spiritual power.
This is for those who possess wisdom. As for the remaining images, some protect and uphold the True Dharma while others subdue Pāpīyān.
Furthermore, it is essential that my mind be well-entrusted and well-guarded, like a golden city with its moats and walls.
Moreover, take eight mirrors and suspend them in the void, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual arena so that they correspond to one another in all directions.
As for the manner in which forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in layers, this is the manifestation of the primary intent of the altar’s resonance.
Indeed, the altar is established with sixteen mirrors as its core; all other elements arranged in successive, intersecting layers can only be sustained by these mirrors.
This represents the Great Dharani of the Perfectly Penetrating, Wondrous Nature.
The Gate is able to sustain all things as the fundamental basis for the mutual resonance between sentient beings and Buddhas; it is precisely the inconceivable realm expounded by this sutra.
Regarding the practice of performing one hundred and eight circumambulations at one time while prostrating to the Buddha, reciting mantras, and practicing the Way during the first seven days:
this is the initial contemplation of the inconceivable realm to shatter the one hundred and eight afflictions. Second...
"Devoting one's mind for seven days to making vows" refers to the second stage: truly generating the bodhicitta to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below.
"Single-mindedly reciting mantras for twenty-one days" means again employing the inconceivable mind to contemplate the inconceivable realm, thereby making the dull and distracted free from confusion;
this serves as a skillful preliminary for settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Below...
It is said that after twenty-one days, one sits upright in *an-guo* (summer retreat) for one hundred days. Skillful methods for settling the mind are all centered upon this.

As the Sutra says, at the end of the third seven-day period, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions appear simultaneously at the place where mirrors reflect one another’s light, and they stroke one's head.
Were it not for the fact that the beginning and the fundamental are unified, such realization and entry into resonance could not be achieved through sincere devotion alone.
Since the response to their influence is never erring, how could it be that they do not resonate with the Buddha-mind in such a manner?

Furthermore, by taking what Avalokiteśvara has realized—the two kinds of extraordinary excellence—and clarifying them together, the way of resonance and response becomes as clear as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand.
He said: "Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains two kinds of extraordinary excellence; the first is..."
First, above, they harmonize with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same power of compassion;
second, below, they harmonize with the sentient beings of the six realms, sharing the same aspiration for pity. This is because Avalokiteśvara abides within the Path;
thus, there is the teaching of "harmonizing above" and "harmonizing below" based on the individual self. As for the beginner practitioner of today who abides within the Path...
At the beginning, one unites with the Way of the Buddhas above through sorrowful yearning;

at the end, the Buddhas likewise unite with the way of the practitioner below through the power of their compassion. Because they unite above, they seek to bestow joy by manifesting their responsive descent;

because they unite below, they seek to extract suffering by mobilizing their compassion. Thus, the subjective capacity and the objective response merge in obscurity, where the light of the mirrors intersects.
Having received the prediction of enlightenment through the touching of my head, my task of cultivation and realization for this single lifetime is now complete.
Therefore, I have further composed this scripture on practice and conduct to clarify the Way of resonance and response.

Thus, the ritual methods of the three-week altar and the hundred-day period of Chan meditation are entirely encompassed within the symbolic arrangements of the eight mirrors above and below, as well as the principles and practices elucidated in this scripture.
A single principle of practice enables one to contemplate both the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three truths (*satya*) that are their objects.

Thus, when Ānanda attained wondrous insight, he spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha: "O Wondrously Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One. "Wondrously Profound" praises the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom) within the truth of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

"All-Holding" praises the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*) within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). "Immovable" praises the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) within the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). These are the virtues of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
Possessing these is called the Three Truths. Cultivating virtue to illuminate them constitutes the Three Stills (Samatha). The Buddhas realize them as the Three Virtues (Guṇas).

Although the cultivation and the nature are divided into two gates, the essence of the Dharma has fundamentally no difference between them. Now, this altar-mirror establishes images that in reality embody all three:
the mirror’s substance is limpid and transparent both inside and out, representing the essence of the Truth of Reality (Paramārtha-satya) and True Stillness.
When the Buddha abides in the virtue of wondrous, profound *prajñā*, he uses the mirror-like function to reflect images such that even the finest hair on a mountain is revealed without interval;

this is the cessation in accordance with conditions within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When the Buddha abides in the virtue of *dhāraṇī* and liberation, he is brilliantly lucid yet unimpeded in his reflection of things;
he reflects things yet remains unmoved by that lucidity. This represents the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*), wherein the two extremes cease and one comes to rest.
The Buddha is the merit of the immovable Dharma-body; does this not manifest the cultivation and realization of a single lifetime?

The practitioner takes the three types of cessation as the capacity to evoke response, while the Buddhas take the three merits as the capacity to respond. Is it not the case that the mutual resonance of evocation and response is but a single principle?
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* is named the "Great White Parasol," its measure encompassing the realms of saṃsāra and its essence [pervading all].
It severs the function of delusive defilements and covers all things; furthermore, one should contemplate the meaning by reflecting upon the names.

Thus, the upper and lower parts of the altar, as well as its four sides, represent the Four Holy Ones: the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas. The various devas who have attained the Dharma, the fourfold assembly, and the six classes of ordinary beings who practice the Way likewise reside there.
As the light from the eight mirrors reflects and enters one another from above and below, it symbolizes the inner minds of all Buddhas.
Sentient beings attain liberation in every moment; within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas realize the Truth in every thought-moment.
Above, they merge with the Buddhas of the ten directions through the same power of compassion, thereby merging with the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings.

Below, they merge with the sentient beings of the six realms through the same shared sorrow and longing, thereby merging with the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas. This is the birth [of the Bodhisattva].
Before the Buddha and the image have merged, the principle is already fully present; once the living Buddha and the image have merged, the phenomena are then perfectly manifested.
Through unconditioned compassion, he constantly provides rescue and extraction; through effortless resonance, they are mutually related in every thought-moment.

As for the interlacing of banners and streamers, they symbolize the unfolding of the myriad practices; as for the surrounding array of offerings, they symbolize the perfect completion of the myriad virtues.
The Dharmakāya is all-pervasive, yet it does not hinder its reflection being grasped within the space of a single room.
The great illumination of Prajñā may properly be observed by means of the eight mirrors set within the altar. With every step, one attains liberation in every dust mote;

through every phenomenon, the Dharma is perfectly interfused. This further depends upon the practitioner planting the Eightfold Noble Path to destroy the eight heterodoxies and clarifying the three types of cessation.
This is for the purpose of illuminating the three truths.

○ (2. Showing that it is not accomplished) Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus in the assembly there is even one who is impure, such a place of practice will for the most part not be accomplished. ○ (2. Sitting Meditation) After the three seven-day periods...
He sat upright in meditative retreat for one hundred days. (2. Verification) There were those of sharp faculties who, without rising from their seats, attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*;

even though their physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they knew with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood would be unerring. (2. Conclusion) Such was the manner in which you asked about the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "One who attains *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) refers to having entered the stream of the sages; it does not refer to a minor fruit. Gūshān says:
"Regarding the stage of *srotāpanna*, according to the [Lotus Sūtra] stages, this is the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect [Vehicle].

If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is the initial entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) and dwellings (*vihāra*) of the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles]. Were it otherwise, how could one know for oneself that their attainment of Buddhahood would not be erroneous?"—Wǔ.
Xing said: "Regarding the ritual procedures for the altar, their practice in this land during the final age is extremely difficult.
However, the text of the incantations to be recited also permits one not to enter the ritual arena. Thus, those with the karmic affinity may receive benefit according to their capacity."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "There are those of sharp faculties who, without rising from their seats, attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer).
This is a provisional designation used to manifest the Dharma. For the perfect cultivation of the Path-field (*bodhimaṇḍa*) resides in the faculty of hearing.

To turn the hearing back toward one's own nature is called "entering the stream. This precisely corresponds to the fruit of *srotāpanna*, which is the name for "entering the stream"; it is not merely a matter of not entering into forms and colors.
It consists merely of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas. As for the previous interpretation:
"The former refers to entering the stream of the faculty of hearing and losing the object of sound, continuing until entering the stream of cessation and losing the object of profound emptiness.

This indicates that the stage of "entering the stream" (ru liu) extends through the first bhūmi. Thus, one knows that the designation "entering the stream" covers a very long period of practice, even if [the afflictions] have not yet been suppressed.

The five stages of abiding may also be called "entering the stream," because in each case one is able, for the first time, to turn the hearing back toward one's own nature within the midst of hearing.
Therefore, even if the holy fruit has not yet been realized, one who knows with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood will not be in error—

knowing that the essential method for attaining Buddhahood lies in turning the hearing back— is clearly one who has already attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) and has thus entered [the path].

Regarding the flow of the Dharma, from this point one may follow the current to enter it; indeed, for the Great Samādhi to manifest before one and for Buddhahood to be attained is truly not difficult.
Master Wuxing said, "The ritual procedures for constructing the altar are extremely difficult to practice in this land during the Final Dharma Age.
I say that it is not only the construction of the altar that is difficult, but finding a qualified person is likewise extremely difficult. As for the so-called ten...
If among the bhikṣus there is even one who is impure, the *maṇḍala* will thus largely fail to be accomplished.

Seeking this in the final age—is it not indeed difficult? Furthermore, it is said that the text of the incantations to be recited also permits not entering the *maṇḍala*, so that those with the karmic affinity may receive benefit according to their capacity.
Since it is permitted not to enter the *maṇḍala*, [the benefit] follows the capacity.
One receives benefit. How could it be that one is not permitted to enter the Dharma hall and receive benefit according to one's capacity?
An ancient said, "If you gain an inch, act upon an inch; if you gain a foot, act upon a foot"—this is precisely the practice for those walking the path in this degenerate age.
I pray that all my fellow practitioners will each exert yourselves.

[II. Reiteration of the Buddha’s Recitation of the *Uṣṇīṣa-mantra* (3): First, Ānanda’s Request (2): First, Ānanda’s Brief Statement (1): First, Describing the Power of the Mantra] Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha:

“Since my renunciation of the world, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate affection and seeking much learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Consequently, I was obstructed by the evil arts of that Brahmā. Although my mind was clear, my power was not autonomous.
Fortunately, I encountered Mañjuśrī, who enabled me to attain liberation. Although I have received the secret *uṣṇīṣa* divine mantra of the Tathāgata...”

Although we have obtained its power, we have not yet personally heard it. (2. Requesting the Recitation of the Mantra) We only pray that the Greatly Compassionate One will once again proclaim it for the sake of the practitioners in this assembly, as well as those in the future who remain within saṃsāra, so that by receiving the Buddha’s secret voice, their bodies and minds may attain liberation.
[II. The Entire Assembly Pays Homage] At that time, the entire assembly in the gathering prostrated themselves universally, waiting to hear the secret verses of the Tathāgata.

[II. The Tathāgata’s Proper Exposition (in two parts): First, the Manifested Transformation Buddha Preaches the Dharani; Second, the Manifested Transformation Buddha] At that time, from within the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewel-lights.

From within these lights, there emerged thousand-petaled jewel lotuses, upon which manifested Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious flowers. From their crowns, they emitted ten streams of hundred-jewel radiance, each and every one...
The radiance universally manifested ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of Vajrapāṇis, who held mountains and wielded maces, filling the entire realm of empty space.
(2. Recitation of the Divine Mantra) The great assembly looked up in awe and affection, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection.
With single-minded attention, they listened as the Tathāgata Alokamukha, from his invisible crown, emitted light and proclaimed this divine mantra.
[Commentary] Tianru’s Supplement states: "In the past, Ānanda secretly relied on the power of the mantra to resolve the difficulty of his lustful encounter;

therefore it was said that he 'attained it in secret without hearing it. Now he requests a further explicit explanation, his intention being to compassionately rescue those in this assembly as well as those of the future."
