"Dhāraṇī" refers to incantation (*zhùzǔ*) and is also called a prayer of aspiration (*zhùyuàn*).

The Buddha uses these words to invoke blessings for sentient beings so that they may produce goodness and extinguish evil, transforming from ordinary beings into sages, just as the *gǒuluó* wasp incants over the *mínglíng* caterpillar. It is also this.

The esoteric exposition of the meaning of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi is no different from the previously mentioned exoteric explanation regarding its power and function; it differs only in the manner in which it reaches sentient beings.
Some say that the exoteric explanation causes understanding and thus gives rise to wisdom, while the esoteric explanation causes recitation and thus gives rise to merit;
this is generally true. Guishan said: "As a rule, divine mantras in all sutras are not translated. Since ancient times, many masters have held this view."
Regarding alternative interpretations, Tiantai harmonizes them such that they do not exceed the four *siddhārtha* (fourfold benefits). First, it is said that a mantra is the name of a ghost-king;
by invoking the king’s name, his subordinates revere their lord and dare not commit transgressions—this is the meaning of the *lokadhātu-siddhārtha*.

Second, it is said that a mantra is like a secret password within an army; those who chant the password in accord are not questioned or interrogated, whereas those who are not in accord are... [punished].
To govern and rectify it—this is the principle of humanity. Third, as for "incantation" (*mantra*): it refers to secretly and silently warding off evil, while others remain unaware.
It is like a lowly person who flees to a foreign land and falsely claims to be a prince; consequently, he marries a princess, yet she is prone to anger and difficult to serve.
A wise man comes from that country, and the husband goes to him to complain. That man says:
It is said that when one is about to become angry, one should recite this verse: "Having no kin, you have gone to another land and deceived all people;
coarse food is your constant sustenance—why trouble yourself with anger again? When this verse is spoken, the anger subsides in silence; this is the meaning of "antidote.
Fourth, as for "mantra," these are the secret words of the Buddhas known only to the sages. It is like a king’s command... [text ends].

The term *saindhava* has a single name yet possesses four actual referents: salt, water, a vessel, and a horse. Among the subordinates, none understood this, but only the wise minister could explain it.

Mantras are likewise: though they consist of a single dharma-word, they universally possess manifold powers—curing illness, eliminating transgressions, generating goodness, and harmonizing with the Way;
this is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Because they embody these four meanings, their original sounds are preserved.
Among the five reasons for not translating, this is "not translated because it is secret. Among the four categories [of translation], this is "translating the characters but not the pronunciation.
Regarding the term *tian* (heaven), Supplement says: "The 'four *si*' cited by Gushan refers to the four *siddhāntas*.
*Si* means 'universal' (*prabhūta*), and *tan* means 'bestowal' (*dāna*). The Buddha universally bestows these four dharmas upon sentient beings. First is the *loka-siddhānta*:"
The first is the benefit of generating joy through teaching according to different dispositions; the second is the benefit of generating goodness through the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta*;
the third is the benefit of destroying evil through the *pratipakṣasiddhānta*; and the fourth is the benefit of entering into principle through the *paramārthasiddhānta*.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Gushan’s application of Tiantai’s four *siddhāntas* to interpret the divine mantra is highly consistent with the intent of the sutra.
First, he interprets it through the *loka-siddhānta*, stating that "mantra" refers to the name of a king of spirits.
By invoking the name of the king, his subjects revere their lord and dare not commit transgressions. This is roughly like the case of the *piśāca* Kharaka and the *kumbhāṇḍa* Kharaka.
Rāhu and the others are all names of ghost-king deities; it is not only these.
As in the first assembly, *namo bhagavate* and so forth are all the names and titles of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This causes them to hear the names and be moved by their grace, such that they dare not commit transgressions. Furthermore, as at the end of the first assembly, there was Vajraśṛṅkhala.
"Bha" and so forth are all names for Vajrapāṇi, the Secret Keeper. This means that by causing them to hear these names and stand in awe of his majesty, they do not dare to commit wrongs;

this is the meaning of the world-siddhānta (loka-siddhānta). Second is the person-siddhānta (pudgala-siddhānta), such as when secret signals are used within an army and the calls correspond to one another.
Third is the therapeutic siddhānta (pratipakṣa-siddhānta), wherein one silently restrains evil through secrecy so that others remain unaware. Fourth is the... [text fragment].
The *ekārtha-siddhānta* (the definitive teaching of a single meaning), which is the secret language of all Buddhas, is known only by the Buddhas themselves.
This is like the conclusion of each assembly, or like a secret code within an army, or like a silent gesture used to ward off evil; it is indeed the secret language of the Buddhas.

There is nothing about it that does not aim to cause those who uphold it and those who hear it to rejoice, to give rise to goodness, to extinguish evil, and to enter into the principle. Therefore, one should know that this is no different from explicit teaching.

Although there are differences between the expressive words (*vācaka*) and the expressed meanings (*vācya*) when explained esoterically, their purpose in bringing about spiritual benefit is one and the same.
Regarding the five reasons for not translating: first, "secret" non-translation, which refers to the mantra-syllables used today;
second, "multivalent" non-translation, such as *bhagavat*, which contains six meanings; third, "non-existent here" non-translation, such as the Jambu tree.
...and so forth. Fourth, there are those that follow ancient precedent and are not translated, such as *anuttara-bodhi*, which has been preserved in its Sanskrit sound since antiquity.
Fifth, there are those that are not translated to generate wholesome roots, such as *prajñā* (wisdom), for if it were translated as "intelligence," it would be deemed slight and trivial.

However, regarding "secret" non-translation, which refers to *dhāraṇī* mantras, this is not necessarily the case in all instances; for example, within this *Śūraṅgama-mantra*, there are various Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and [deities]...
Even among the "stiff" (untranslatable) spirits and deities, there are cases where they may be translated according to their meaning.

This is roughly similar to how *Amitābha* is translated as "Buddha of Immeasurable Life," yet one must take its general sense, as it is a secret term left untranslated. Furthermore, regarding the four categories:
first, translating the characters but not the phonetics, such as the dharanis in various sutras; second, translating the phonetics but not the characters.

The *svastika* (卍) is a script that translates the form of this region’s characters yet remains a Sanskrit sound; this is the case for those three-syllable characters whose texts in all the various scriptures have been translated.
As for those four-syllable characters that are not translated, they remain as the Sanskrit manuscripts brought from the West.

Regarding the previously mentioned "not translating the secret," this refers to translating the characters while not translating the sounds; however, among these cases where the sounds are not translated, it is not only [the case] here in this region...
People do not know what this refers to; even all ordinary and holy beings in the Western Land of India have things they do not know, and for this reason it is called "secret."

II. Describing the Merits and Exhorting to Uphold (in two parts): A. Clarifying the Resultant Virtues by means of this mantra, thereby encouraging its upholding through both self-cultivation and the transformation of others (in three parts): 1. Directly demonstrating [the merits] (in three parts): a. Enumerating all the various meanings (in two parts): i. General clarification of the resultant virtues produced. Ānanda, this *Sītātapatrā-guhya-gāthā*—the subtle and wondrous syllables of the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-raśmi-sañcaya*—produces all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

ii. Specifically demonstrating the ten kinds of functions: 1. Attaining Buddhahood through this because of this mantra-heart. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by virtue of this mantra-heart, have attained supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
2. Subduing demons by holding this mantra-heart. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by holding this mantra-heart, subdue all Māras.
It subdues all non-Buddhists. (3) The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, mounting this mantra-heart, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
(4) The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-heart, turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.

(5) The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, are able to bestow the consecration of their heads and grant predictions of enlightenment throughout the ten directions; even for those whose own fruits are not yet accomplished, it likewise applies.

Throughout the ten directions, they receive the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas. (Six: Relying on this to Eradicate Suffering) By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to rescue and deliver all beings from suffering throughout the ten directions—namely, the sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals;
the sufferings of blindness, deafness, and muteness; the suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of being separated from those one loves;
the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and the burning intensity of the five aggregates—all such great and small calamities are simultaneously liberated.
Calamities caused by bandits, military conflict, kings, prisons, wind, fire, or water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty, shall be dissolved and dispersed upon mere recollection.

(7. Following this Matter of the Master) The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the four modes of deportment in the ten directions;
they are honored as Great Dharma Princes within the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. (8. Practicing This to Receive [Protection]) The ten directions...

The Tathāgatas, by practicing this mantra-heart, are able to gather and sustain their karmic causes throughout the ten directions, ensuring that those of the Lesser Vehicle do not give rise to alarm or fear upon hearing the Secret Treasury.

(9) By reciting this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Unsurpassed Enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa. (10) After their parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart.

Entrusted with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma, they shall ultimately maintain and uphold it, strictly purifying the precepts until all are completely cleansed. (The second is the broad binding of the names.

If I were to speak this *Bhadrakarāṇī* mantra of the Glistening Mass of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa from dawn until dusk, with its sounds linked in continuous succession and its syllables never overlapping, even after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I could not reach the end.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: To speak of the "mantra-heart" (*zhòuxīn*) in general refers to what was stated in the preceding text:
"This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Buddha of the Unconditioned Mind, who possesses the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown.

It is also called the "mantra-heart" because it is the most essential dharma within the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). Wenzheng says: The "mantra-heart" is the Great White Parasol (*Mahāsitātapatrā*). Broadly...
This is the secret dharma-gate of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, which is great, untainted, and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Because it is vast and all-pervading as the Tathāgatagarbha, by upholding and relying upon it, one is able to give birth to all Buddhas,

achieve unsurpassed enlightenment, subdue Māras, manifest transformations, and rescue sentient beings from their myriad sufferings, along with other meritorious qualities, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It cannot be fully described. Among the hells, hungry ghosts, and so forth, four of the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) are briefly cited.

Among enmity, resentment, separation from loved ones, and so forth, four of the eight sufferings (*aṣṭau duḥkhāni*) are briefly cited. According to the *Guanding jing* (Consecration Sūtra), there are nine major calamities and innumerable minor calamities.
"Grasping the direct cause" means encompassing all those with whom one has a karmic connection.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The first four fascicles of the sutra clarify the exposition of the *cittagarbha* (storehouse mind).

From the entry into the jeweled house onward, one cultivates this *cittagarbha*. Now, the teaching of the divine mantra is the esoteric exposition of the *cittagarbha*. Entering the altar and reciting it...
One cultivates this *garbha-citta* (storehouse mind). For this reason, the mantra is named *Mahāsitātapatra*, which is translated as "Great White Parasol.
The previous praise regarding the explicit teaching (*nītārtha*) states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions all share the single path to Nirvāṇa.
The present praise regarding the implicit teaching (*neyārtha*) states: "It gives birth to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Thus, the former and the latter illuminate one another.

They correspond to one another like a seal and its impression. Some say that explicit teaching leads to understanding and thus gives rise to wisdom (*prajñā*), while esoteric teaching leads to recitation and thus gives rise to merit (*puṇya*).
Why not say instead that explicit teaching causes people to sever their attachments through understanding, and esoteric teaching causes people to sever their attachments through non-understanding?
From these, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom arise, and through them, the fruit of Buddhahood is attained.

Indeed, because this sutra was established through the earnest and persistent requests of those whose capacities were suited to it, leading to the attainment of Bodhi and the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, the Buddha therefore expounded the three Tathāgatagarbhas.
This is precisely because the three types of Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit are accomplished by means of three dharmas, and those three dharmas are cultivated by means of the three Garbhas;
thus, even the mantra-heart is explained in accordance with the explicit teachings. [End of] Text.

There are eleven sections. The first section provides a general explanation of the arising of the fruits and virtues; the subsequent ten sections separately open up ten kinds of functional capacities.
Within these separate openings, nothing is excluded that does not fall within the eight aspects [of Buddhahood]. The first four aspects pertain to the causal stage and are therefore omitted here.
The first refers to attaining the Way by means of the cause; the second refers to subduing Māra by grasping this [attainment]; the third refers to turning the Wheel of Dharma.
The meaning of the single characteristic of the wheel is expanded into six aspects: first, mounting this to manifest responsive transformations; second, containing this to turn the wheel of Dharma;

third, maintaining this to confer empowerment and bestow predictions of enlightenment; fourth, relying on this to rescue beings from manifold sufferings; fifth, following this to practice causes while carrying the fruit;
and sixth, acting upon this to embrace the proximate causes—all these are none other than the activity of turning the wheel of Dharma. First.
The fourth refers to reciting this mantra-heart to enter the meaning of Great Nirvāṇa, which is divided into two parts:
transmitting this mantra-heart as the matter of entrusting the Buddha-dharma, and the ultimate maintenance of it; both are indeed matters of entering Nirvāṇa.
The claim of ancient masters that these constitute "ten kinds of mantra-hearts" is incorrect. One must understand that although there are ten matters, they are [all] the heart.
It is of only one kind; yet this single mind possesses three meanings. Its magnitude pervades the realms of sand [sands of the Ganges], which is called "Great" (*mahā*);
this is the mantra-heart of the *śūnyatā-aśūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*. Its essence is utterly free from delusive defilement, which is called "White" (*śukla*);

this is the mantra-heart of the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*. Its function covers all things, which is called "Parasol" (*chattra*); this is the mantra-heart of the *aśūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*. If explained according to these meanings...

To explain this further, it should be said as follows: The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of the mantra of the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*, attained the realization of true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

By means of the mantra of the *aśūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*, they attained the realization of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By means of the mantra of the *śūnyatā-aśūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*...
The mind attains the true nature of *bodhi*, the unsurpassed, perfect, and universal enlightenment. Since *bodhi* belongs to the category of the fruit, it is here referred to as the cause;
that is to say, the cause arising from the entirety of the nature is itself contained within the fruit.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold the *dhāraṇī* of the Tathāgata-garbha as their heart-essence to subdue the four māras of the segmented birth within the realm where ordinary beings and sages dwell together.
The four views and afflictions of the four types of externalists cling to the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha;

by means of the mantra-heart, they subdue the four māras of the transformational realm in the expedient lands outside the [true] realm and restrain the various *catur-asamkhyeya-dharmas* (dust-like sands) of the four views and externalists.

Those who cling to the empty and non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, by means of the mantra-heart, subdue the four māras of the transformational realm in the stage of true retribution and restrain the various stages of ignorance.

When observing the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), the Vajra-subduer of Māras invariably grasps a precious vajra; because the meaning of the Vajra-King’s precious awakening is likewise, it is said that he "grasps" it.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, riding upon the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness, sit upon precious lotus flowers through the mantra-heart;
they respond to the cohabitation of ordinary beings and sages within lands as numerous as motes of dust. Riding upon the *tathāgatagarbha* of non-emptiness, they sit through the mantra-heart.

The *ratnapadma-pratibhāsa-upāya-śeṣa-rajas-pramāṇa-lokadhātu* (the land of subtle atoms of residual skillful means appearing as precious lotuses) corresponds to the *ākāśa-anākāśa-tathāgatagarbha-mantra-hṛdaya* (the mantra-heart of the Tathāgata-garbha, both empty and non-empty), which corresponds to the *svasaṃbhoga-nirāvaraṇa-rajas-pramāṇa-lokadhātu* (the land of subtle atoms of the unobstructed self-reward). One sits upon the precious lotus, resting upon its very foundation.
Because one possesses that which is mounted before one mounts the person [who rides it], it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). The Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain space within themselves.
The *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* of the Tathāgatagarbha turns the Dharma wheels of the fourfold Four Noble Truths and so forth in the lands of motes of dust where ordinary beings and sages dwell together.

Containing the *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* of the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, it turns the Dharma wheels of the threefold Four Noble Truths and so forth in the lands of motes of dust of the stage of remaining with skillful means (*upāya-śeṣa*).
Containing the *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* of the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, it [turns the Dharma wheels] in the land of true recompense (*bhoga-niṣpatti*).
In lands as numerous as motes of dust, he turns the Dharma wheel of the two kinds of Four Noble Truths and so forth.
Because the Sun-Disk (Sūryamaṇḍala) expounds the Dharma, it is said to "contain" [the teachings]. What is taught accords with practice and does not deviate from the Tripiṭaka.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions uphold the *śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha-mantra*, by which they can touch the crown of one's head in the ten directions and bestow the prediction of the Bodhi of true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). One upholds the *aśūnyatā-*.
The *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* of the Tathāgatagarbha can bestow the prediction of expedient bodhi by means of touching the crown of the head throughout the ten directions.

The *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* of the Tathāgatagarbha, which upholds both emptiness and non-emptiness, can bestow the prediction of true-nature bodhi by means of touching the crown of the head throughout the ten directions.
To comfort others by touching their crowns is entirely based on holding [the mantra]; thus, the act of recording the person also constitutes the "bestowing of the hand. (10)

By relying on the *dhāraṇī-heart* of the *Śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*, one is able to rescue ordinary beings and sages alike from the sufferings of the eight difficulties within the three realms of segmented existence throughout the ten directions.

By relying on the *dhāraṇī-heart* of the *Aśūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*, one is able to rescue those in the three realms of transformation through skillful means and with remainder from the sufferings of the eight difficulties throughout the ten directions. By relying on the [dhāraṇī-heart] of both emptiness and...

The heart-essence mantra of the *Śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha* can rescue and deliver beings from the sufferings of the three realms—the realm of retribution for true deeds, the realm of transformation, and the eight difficulties—throughout the ten directions.
It is just as one must rely on a boat to save those drowning; only by relying on these Three Pitakas can one truly deliver others from suffering.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following the heart-essence mantra of the *Śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha*, are able to [act] throughout the ten directions among all...
In the four modes of conduct while serving spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the Land of the Sages’ Co-residence, one’s offerings of both material wealth and the Dharma are fulfilled at will.

Following the heart-mantra of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi, one is able to serve spiritual friends in the four modes of conduct within the lands of skillful means in the ten directions, where offerings of both material wealth and the Dharma are fulfilled at will. Following the [mantra of] Emptiness...
The heart-mantra of the Śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha enables one to serve spiritual friends within the lands of actual recompense and adornment throughout the ten directions;
it fulfills all wishes regarding the four modes of deportment and the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma. In serving one's teacher, one follows their instructions without opposition.
Regarding the three kinds of Dharma-offerings, there is nothing that does not accord with one's mind. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this Śūnyatā-tathāgatagarbha.
The mantra-heart of the Tathāgata Garbha can, throughout the ten directions, gather in those with whom one has a karmic affinity,

causing those of the Hīnayāna to not give rise to alarm or fear upon hearing the secret treasury of the virtue of *prajñā*. The mantra-heart of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi can, throughout the ten directions,
gather in those with whom one has a karmic affinity, causing those of the Hīnayāna to not give rise to alarm or fear upon hearing the secret treasury of the virtue of liberation.
The mantra-heart of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is both empty and non-empty, is able to gather and sustain its direct causes throughout the ten directions;
it enables those of the Hīnayāna who hear the virtues of the Dharmakāya’s secret treasury not to give rise to fear or alarm.
It causes oneself and others to enter the secret treasury, and I too shall soon enter therein. Therefore, it is called "practice" (*xing*). Thus do the Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite it.
By reciting the Heart Mantra of the Śūnyatā Tathāgatagarbha, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment, sits beneath the Bodhi tree, and enters the perfectly pure nirvāṇa.
By reciting the Heart Mantra of the Aśūnyatā Tathāgatagarbha, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment, sits beneath the Bodhi tree, and enters the nirvāṇa of skillful means.
By reciting the Heart Mantra of the Śūnyatā-aśūnyatā Tathāgatagarbha, one attains unsurpassed enlightenment and sits beneath the Bodhi tree...
The tree enters the nature of pure nirvana; the reciter follows this, which also means "to approach" the text. Approaching it and following it is to accord with nirvana.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit the heart-essence of the *Tathāgatagarbha-śūnyatā-mantra* after their parinirvāṇa, entrusting it to the Buddha’s prajñā-virtue and dharma-activities, so that they may ultimately abide in and maintain the majestic purity of the precepts, attaining complete purification.
He transmitted the heart-essence of the mantra of the Tathāgatagarbha that is non-empty;

after my parinirvāṇa, he shall entrust it to the Buddha’s virtue of liberation, so that the dharma-activities may reach ultimate completion, and the upholding and purification of the precepts may all become perfectly pure. He transmitted the heart-essence of the mantra of the Tathāgatagarbha that is both empty and non-empty;
after my parinirvāṇa, he shall entrust it to the Buddha’s virtue of the Dharma-body, so that the dharma-activities may reach ultimate completion and be strictly and purely maintained.
Their precepts shall all become completely pure. Since the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, he transmits the Way to others so that it may ultimately be maintained;
because this does not go beyond the Three Piṭakas, it is called "transmission. Next, regarding the extensive enumeration of names:
if I were to speak of this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Garbha-Pāṭala Dhāraṇī from dawn until dusk, its sounds would be continuous, and even within the intervals between its words and phrases—

That which cannot be exhausted even after reciting it incessantly for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is like this: the mind that recites the mantra is like a valley, and the words of the mantra are like an echo.
The sound produced by striking the valley has an end, but the valley that answers the echo is infinite.

Now, these secret chapters of the Five Assemblies consist of four hundred and twenty-seven phrases and two thousand six hundred and sixteen characters; they are intended to accord with the capacities of beings.

The appropriateness of detail or brevity depends on what one strikes upon. If the essence of the mantra is inconceivable, it may be called "empty," like the voidness of objects within a mountain valley.
It may be called "not empty," as it responds to sound with an echo. It may be called both "empty and not empty," as these two aspects coexist.
By using this analogy to illustrate the Dharma, one can understand that no single description is exhaustive, even after passing through kalpas.

How could my proclamation ever exhaust [the meaning]? Formerly, Dharma Master Yinhai once used the wondrous contemplations of the Ten Vehicles of Tiantai to resolve the ten causes of the *Zhuxin lun*.

He held that the first, "entering the ocean of universal knowledge," corresponds to the inconceivable realm, and so on, up to the tenth, "entrusting the dharma and strictly observing the precepts," which corresponds to the absence of craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). I have carefully compared these with the text, and their meanings all coincide.
I have been studying this matter and have further attributed its elucidation to Siming, claiming that the Great Master Fazhi once explained it in this way.
Yet, upon a thorough review of all the works composed by Siming, I find no such statement. Is this not a case where the intention to attribute merit instead results in attributing blame?
I have often marveled at how various masters of the Mountain School (Shanjiao) frequently force a correlation between *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and [the text].
The explanations of the names and meanings of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* are for the most part inconsistent with one another; they are like trying to catch the wind or grasp a shadow.
Consequently, they fail to satisfy scholarly discourse, causing even those whose Tiantai teachings fundamentally accord with the *Śūraṅgama* to become estranged from it.
Is this not a case of seeking to circulate [the teaching] while instead creating obstruction? Recently, there has been one master who also... [commented].

By means of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), this work is neither of the Tiantai school, nor of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), nor of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (*Léngyán jīng*). One does not know to which category it belongs.

I have repeatedly savored its flavor and feel deep regret for it. Generally speaking, if one wishes to explain the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* through the teachings of Tiantai, it must necessarily accord with the textual meaning;
it should then be integrated with the three contemplations of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* and confirmed by the original [text].

There is the Mind-Only school (*cittamātra*), which is as harmonious as a box and its lid, and as indistinguishably blended as water and milk. Though they initially unite, in the end they are forgotten;
one does not know who is the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and who is the Tiantai teaching. This is like forgetting the trap after catching the fish.
To take the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* alone and reduce its essentials to no more than what is established by Tiantai in the "Ten Modes of Practice" (*daśayāna*)—this is precisely it.
Regarding the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*): there is only the first, the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), which has two aspects—the manifest and the secret.
The manifest is as described from the first to the fourth fascicle, wherein the perfect understanding is opened by means of the eternal mind;

the secret is as in the ritual methods for the altar’s adornment and the various representations, all of which constitute the inconceivable realm. Second is the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta, the text of which is seen [in the following].
There are two instances. The first is when the practitioner praises the Buddha and subsequently makes a vow, saying:

"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This encompasses the four great vows in their entirety. The second is within the ritual altar, where one single-mindedly makes the Bodhisattva vow;
this is because our Vinaya already contains instructions for such vows. Third is the skillful arrangement [of the ritual].

The practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) also has two aspects. The manifest aspect consists of everything from the time he requested entry into the "Flower Hall" up until his realization of the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-organ, and even throughout the period of his sitting upright and settling for one hundred days;
all of this was nothing other than skillful means for settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The secret aspect consists of relying on the altar to recite mantras. The altar represents the inconceivable image, and the mantra is the inconceivable sound.

As for the essence: by contemplating it and relying upon it, one forgets emotions and severs conceptual attachments; this is precisely to settle the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the inconceivable realm.
Fourth is the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas. Viewed vertically, there is not a single of the three delusions clarified in this sutra that is not destroyed.
Viewed horizontally, there is not a single thing among the ten realms of the perfectly interfused three truths that is not [destroyed].
No. Fifth is the penetration and obstruction of consciousness. If all dharmas are none other than nirvāṇa, yet one establishes knowledge within knowing and seeing, this is the very root of ignorance;
thus, what is penetrating becomes obstructed. If one knows and sees without seeing, this is precisely nirvāṇa;
thus, what is obstructed becomes penetrating. Therefore, those who cultivate the Great Samādhi must break through any obstructions and [realize] any penetrations.

One should guard them. Sixth is the "Harmonization of the Factors of Enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa-dharma). If the path of awakening is open and unobstructed, one must ensure that the factors of enlightenment are harmonized along this level path;
thus, among the myriad practices, each of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment accords with the nature of reality, treading upon the Great Vehicle with even and upright steps.
Seventh is the "Aids for Counteracting and Opening," which concerns the faculty of hearing and the Dharma.
The gates are indeed the primary practice; yet if there are defects or ailments, they must also be countered.
One may use the six perfections to remedy the six defects, such as using the four types of discipline to counteract greed, or reciting mantras to eliminate past habitual tendencies.
As the Sūtra says, "When one is complete in the myriad practices, what practice would not be cultivated? Eighth is the knowledge of stages and positions; the following clarifies the fifty [stages].
The five stages of the true path to Bodhi are precisely this matter. The ninth stage is the ability to practice patience (*kṣānti*);
preventing the manifestation of the fiftyfold layers of the *skandhas* is precisely this matter. The tenth stage is the departure from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments, one perfects Bodhi and returns to non-attainment; thus, there is no attachment to dharmas that is not abandoned. This is because...
The ten modes of contemplation constitute the great highway for the Tathāgata to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and the essential key for penetrating the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Without these, one cannot be called a follower of the Mahāyāna; if even one is missing, it is insufficient to constitute the Perfect Teaching.
Thus, even within the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, there are none that do not involve the principles of teaching, wisdom, cessation, practice, stages, cause, or effect.
It is not complete. As it is said, whether it be the Śrāvaka-yāna, Pratyekabuddha-yāna, Bodhisattva-yāna, Buddha-yāna,

or the Supreme Vehicle (Anuttara-yāna)— any single mention of a "vehicle" must, like that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, be fully endowed with the ten vehicles before one can personally employ them to transport others to the site of enlightenment.
○ (Third watch: Explaining another name) This mantra is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata. ○ (Second:

Exhortation to uphold) For you who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship but do not uphold this mantra while sitting in the bodhimanda, it is impossible for your body and mind to remain far removed from the works of Māra.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: The preceding section reveals the realm of the Tathāgata; this section clarifies that it also encompasses gradual cultivation; the following section reveals the benefits of upholding the mantra.
[Sub-commentary] Tiāntái says:
It was previously stated that "Buddha-Topknot Radiant Mass" (*buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-jāla*) is a designation established based on its locus of reliance. This is because...

The divine mantra relies on what is taught by the emanation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha); the emanation Buddha relies on the manifestation of light; and the light relies on the crown of the head for its expression.
Thus, because this *Mahā-sāttvatatrarahasya-gāthā* relies upon the crown of the head, it is called "Buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-ghana" (The Buddha’s Crown, Mass of Radiance).
Now, when it says "named the Tathāgata’s Crown," it refers directly to the dharma of the crown itself.
Therefore, my previous explanation of the two meanings—phenomenal application and principle—of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata precisely accords with this.
Thus, both the exoteric and esoteric expositions possess these two meanings:
it may be said that this secret cause is the secret cause of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata; it may also be said that this secret cause is the unsurpassed Uṣṇīṣa Dharma itself.
The treatise states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all practitioners are subject to the harassment of Māra.

For example, during the Buddha’s lifetime, a bhikṣu who was practicing the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) felt such profound revulsion and loathing that he sought death but could not obtain it.

He then hired someone with his robes and bowl to end his life, yet Māra commanded an outsider to seize a blade and kill him instead. Furthermore, during the first hundred years of the True Dharma (saddharma),...
Māra was able to harass the Venerable Kuṭadanta; during the period of the Semblance Dharma, Māra was able to harass the Great Master of Tiantai—how much more so for people of this final age?
However, during the time of the Buddha and during the periods of the True and Semblance Dharmas, the monks possessed extraordinary spiritual power (*mārgabala*);
thus, even when demonic activities occurred, they could not cause them harm. Now, in this age of the Final Dharma, we possess neither the power of the Path nor the power of patience (*kṣāntibala*).

If one does not rely upon the power of this mantra, how could one possibly keep all demonic activities at a distance? Therefore, the Tathāgata has repeatedly and earnestly exhorted its diligent retention. (2.

Explaining the causes and conditions by which, through this mantra, evil is extinguished and goodness is produced, thereby encouraging its retention. Part 1: Extensively explaining the production of goodness and the extinction of evil. Sub-part 1: General exhortation to receive and uphold it. Ānanda, if in all worlds, according to whatever lands there may be, all sentient beings born in those lands—whether on birch bark...
Written upon leather, conch, palm leaves, paper, or fine white silk, this mantra is to be stored in a fragrant pouch.

If a person’s mind is clouded such that they cannot recite or remember it, yet they either wear it on their person or keep it written within their home, you should know that throughout their entire life, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to harm them.
(2. Specifically explaining the efficacy; first, the heading: Ānanda, I now speak further for your sake regarding how this mantra provides protection and rescue.

In the world, they attain great fearlessness and achieve the supramundane wisdom that delivers sentient beings. (2. Explaining the first of the eleven [benefits]: being able to eliminate all calamities.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings in the final age are able to recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such sentient beings who uphold and recite it cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by great or small poisons; this extends even to [the harm of] nāgas.
No evil spells of devas, ghosts, spirits, deities, or māras can take hold; one attains right concentration (*samādhi*).

All curses, enchantments, poisons, gold poisons, silver poisons, and the poisonous vapors of plants, trees, insects, snakes, and all manner of things, upon entering this person's mouth, become the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding all malevolent stars and various ghosts and spirits who harbor cruel hearts and seek to harm others—
Such a person cannot give rise to evil; the various malevolent *piśāca* and kingly ghost-lords, along with their retinues, all recognize this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Fire cannot burn them," and so forth, refers to what is called "protecting the world and attaining great fearlessness."
It is out of fear. Because the recitation of mantras benefits others, all the evil ghost-kings (rākṣasa-rājas) feel a profound sense of gratitude.
Gold and silver, when introduced into medicine, may even trigger toxicity.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the second major section of the preceding [text], "Cultivating Perfect Practice Based on the Permanently Abiding True Mind," there are two general divisions.
The first clarifies the initial expedient means for the immediate disciple Ānanda; the second is for practice in the final age.

This clarifies the formal establishment of the *maṇḍala*. First, there was a discussion on the manifest cultivation alone; next, there was an exposition on the combined cultivation of the manifest and the secret.
Now, this is the third major section, which distinguishes the stages of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*) based upon both manifest and secret practices.
Thus, the preceding [section] relied upon the ordinary mind to fully clarify the perfect principle and the *śamatha* contemplation of the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.
This is the realm of the Truths (*satya*). Next, relying on the constant mind, the *Zhenglun* (Correct Treatise) reveals the perfect practice by cultivating the three dharmas.
However, the *Jiaoguang Zhengmai Shu* (Commentary on the Correct Pulse of the Interwoven Light) divides these three dharmas into three distinct sections.

From here below, it is said that he explains *dhyāna* to cause [the practitioner] to abide in perfect concentration (*samādhi*), and details the stages of cultivation and realization in response to Ānanda’s request for the "Wondrous *Dhyāna*. Regarding this, I [have already discussed] previously.
In my present commentary, I have repeatedly refuted the errors of [Mao].
Those who read the *Zhengmai* should not follow its mistaken interpretations, lest the great meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* be further obstructed within the True Pulse and fail to circulate.

○ (3. Distinguishing the Stages of Perfection Based on the Two Practices of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings; 4. First, the Request; 2. First, Describing the Faults and the Benefits. Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition, yet our minds remained full of outflows, failing to seek liberation. Having received the compassionate instructions of the Buddha, we have attained correct cultivation;

body and mind are refreshed, and we have gained great benefit. ○ (2. Requesting the Stages Based on Practice. "World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s samādhi, yet it has not yet reached [the ultimate state]."
"What is meant by the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*)? From what sequence of the forty-four minds does one gradually attain the vision of cultivation?
To what destination must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)? And what is meant by an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bodhisattva*)?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; the great assembly waited with single-minded devotion for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed, rapt attention.
[Commentary] Gushan says: There are two intentions behind Ānanda’s request. First, since he has received the practice-methods (xingmen), there must necessarily be a sequence of stages;
just as one who enters a house through its gate must know the depth and arrangement of the halls and rooms, he therefore makes this request.

Second, at the beginning of the sutra, the Buddha spoke to Ānanda using direct mental discourse; therefore, [the text proceeds] from the beginning up until the final stages of the spiritual positions (bhūmi).

In the interim, there are eternally no signs of deviousness. Since the preceding practices of understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*) are perfectly integrated, the mind and speech are straightforward.
As for the stages (*bhūmi*), their lack of deviousness is not yet known; therefore, this is requested.

Regarding the "forty-four minds," this refers to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). Below, the Buddha’s response consists of five parts.
Regarding the fourteen minds: within the first stage (*bhūmi*), ten faiths are opened horizontally, yet when combined, they constitute only the first stage.

This differs from the "ten faiths as a semblance stage" found in other sutras; thus, the present "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*) is already established as a collective name that subsumes the ten faiths of other sutras.
Changshui said: "Faith, abiding, practice, and direction, along with the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), are called the forty-four [stages]."
[The text] says: "It is the mind. Master Wu-xing said that the explanation by Master Xuan is correct. Next, it states:

"Going to a certain place and being named 'entering the middle of the ground' refers only to the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi). The interpretation that the initial dwelling (prathamā vihāra) horizontally opens up the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā) is not correct."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the preceding section, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had finished selecting the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), the Sūtra author narrates the benefits obtained by the primary interlocutor, stating:
"He clearly understood the path leading back to the home of the Buddha-bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa.
However, any path leading back to one's home must necessarily have its stages and distances. Therefore, following the two practices of the Exoteric and Esoteric [teachings],...
He then inquired: "If one has not yet reached *nirvāṇa*, why is it called the stage of 'Dry Wisdom' (*śuṣka-prajñā*)? (and so forth).
If explained by way of analogy, it should correspond to the path to the "Jewel Treasury" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is five hundred *yojanas* long.

Of these, three hundred *yojanas* represent the stages for destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts; this corresponds to the preceding seven mental states, namely the stage of the Seven Faiths (*sapta-śraddhā*). Fourth...

A hundred *yojanas* represent the stage for shattering the dust-like realms within the boundary and the dust-like realms outside the boundary; this corresponds to the final three stages of the *śraddhā-citta*.
A five-hundred *yojana* represents the stage for shattering the forty-two grades of ignorance (*avidyā*) that follow;

this corresponds to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This occurs at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi within Equal Enlightenment.
Entering the Gate of Profound Emptiness, one destroys the final grade of subtle ignorance—the parents of all delusion.
Only when these successive three grades of affliction are exhausted and purified without remainder does one pass the five hundred *yojanas* to reach the precious abode of Bodhi and Nirvana.
However, regarding the existence or non-existence of the stages (*bhūmi*), the debates and calculations of ancient and modern scholars have been manifold. [The school of] Tiantai...
Zhiyi’s two explanations follow the perspective of the interlocutor, as already discussed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Now, I shall further integrate these with the present sutra.
The text below states: "As for principle, one attains sudden enlightenment; with enlightenment, all is simultaneously extinguished—what need is there for stages?
Yet it also says: 'Phenomena are not suddenly eliminated; they are exhausted through successive stages,' which does not preclude the establishment of stages. This is because...
From the perspective of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), because the principle is fundamentally true, delusion is fundamentally empty.

From the perspective of the secondary meaning (*saṃvṛti*), because there are degrees of thickness to the removal of delusion, there are levels of depth in the realization of the principle. Thus, one understands that principle is precisely phenomena and phenomena are precisely principle;
existence does not obstruct non-existence, and non-existence does not hinder existence. As the Master of Wuxing said: "It is like the vast blue sea..."
The vast void is surely without limit or measure; yet, because those who steer the boat or spread their wings differ, the number of *li* arises—this statement is indeed correct.
(2. Praising and Approving) At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have been able to universally [benefit] the Great..."

For the sake of the assembly and all sentient beings of the future ages who cultivate *samādhi* seeking the Great Vehicle—from ordinary persons up to the ultimate Great Nirvana—I shall reveal the path of supreme, correct cultivation. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. [The third section:

Acceptance] Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, emptied their minds, and silently received the teaching. [The fourth section: The Proclamation (divided into two parts; first, the general clarification; first, clarifying that the Principle transcends names and marks)] The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you should..."

Know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; fundamentally, there have been no worlds and no sentient beings. (2. Explaining how awakening is established in contrast to delusion. Part one: Delusion arises from the truth.

Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction; birth and extinction are called "delusion. (Part two: Extinction of delusion is called "truth. The extinction of delusion is called "truth";
this refers to the titles of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa, which are the two designations for the transformation of the basis.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Birth-and-extinction, truth-and-falsity, bodhi, and nirvāṇa are all what are called "various names and marks.
Within the wondrous nature, these are fundamentally and perfectly transcended. Due to the causes of deluded appearances, there is cultivation and realization.

Thus, by turning away from non-awakening and relying upon bodhi, and by turning away from birth-and-death and relying upon nirvāṇa, they are called the "two transformations of reliance" (dvividha-āśraya-parāvṛtti).
[Title].
[Commentary] Tiantai says: *Kū* (刳) is pronounced like *kū*. The *Zēngyùn* (增韻) states it means to split open or to hollow out the interior. The *Yìjīng* (易經) says, "Hollowing wood to make a boat.
What is meant here by "hollowing the mind" (*kūxīn*) is that when a disciple receives the Dharma from a teacher, it is like drawing water from a jar.
Regarding the reception of water: one must first empty the mind before anything can be attained. The main exposition is divided into two parts:

first, a general clarification; second, a specific demonstration. The first part is further divided into two. First, from "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous," it clarifies that the ultimate principle transcends names and forms.
Second, from "Due to delusion there is birth," it clarifies how awakening is established in contrast to delusion. This, in turn, is divided into two. First, delusion regarding the truth.

The arising of delusion is called "false," while the cessation of delusion is called "true. Speaking from this perspective, within the single principle there is fundamentally no such thing as stages or positions (*bhūmi*).
What is now described as "stages" is established through the cessation of delusion; having no choice but to do so, one forcibly establishes these names and characteristics.

Regarding the second term, "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): for sentient beings, it means transforming enlightenment (*bodhi*) to rely upon afflictions (*kleśa*), and transforming nirvāṇa to rely upon [saṃsāra].
Birth and death: these are name-and-form that arise delusively from within the principle that transcends name and form.

The Buddhas, however, transform afflictions and rely upon bodhi; they transform birth and death and rely upon nirvana. This is returning to the principle that transcends name and form from within the name-and-form that arises delusively.
Furthermore, one should know that this does not mean reaching directly up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).

When one realizes that principle is without name or mark, one must, within the stage of names and marks in the Perfect Teaching, understand that while there are names and marks, they are fundamentally without name or mark.
If one can know in this way, then cultivation is itself non-cultivation; although stages and positions are spoken of, fundamentally no such stages or positions can be found.

○ (2. Specific Explanation; Part 1: Clarifying how delusion regarding the Truth gives rise to false thoughts, forming the twelve categories of inverted births; Subsection 1: Stating the Intent) "Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true Samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion within the world of sentient beings.
When inversion does not arise, this is the true Samādhi of the Tathāgata."
[Commentary] Changshui says: "The preceding section clarified the three kinds of continuity; the present section clarifies the two kinds of perversion (*viparyāsa*).

This is because the perversion of sentient beings inherently subsumes karma and its fruit. Wuxing says: "The preceding 'continuity of the world' referred solely to the *pariṇāmanā* (recompense) environment, namely the arising of the four great elements and so forth.
The present 'perversion of the world,' however, refers specifically to the *upabhoga* (recompense) body, that is, the twelve [links of dependent origination]."
This is analogous to birth. The reason for this is that the previous response addressed Pūrṇa’s question regarding how the mountains, rivers, and great earth suddenly arise;
the present response addresses Ānanda’s inquiry concerning the stages of realization entered through the cultivation of *samādhi*.

Why is this so? For the stages are attained through awakening, yet awakening must necessarily proceed from delusion. Delusion constitutes the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while awakening constitutes the state of a sage (*ārya*). Both are the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*).
This matter concerns the phenomena of sentient beings rather than the characteristics of the vessel-world (bhājanaloka), and is therefore different from the previous explanation.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Within the second section, "Specific Indication," there are two parts. First, it clarifies how delusion regarding the Truth gives rise to falsehood, forming the twelve types of inverted births.
This is divided into two: first, the statement of the intent. The intent is that since the two names for *parāvṛtti* (transformation) on the level of the fruit are already based on the cause...
To extinguish delusion in order to realize the True, one must not fail to understand the causes of that which is empty, false, and inverted.
For while emptiness, falsity, and inversion are indeed the causes of birth and death, these states of emptiness, falsity, and inversion themselves possess their own causes.
If one knows these causes, then delusion can be extinguished; if delusion can be extinguished, then inversion will not arise. Not...
Because arising is itself non-arising, it is said that this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi. This is what is meant by the analogy:
"Suppose a king is invaded by bandits and dispatches troops to eliminate them; those troops must first know the location of the bandits. This is precisely that.
However, the seven locations previously examined were the sites of this deluded mind; now we clarify the essence of that deluded mind.

Furthermore, while it is both similar to and different from the deluded essence refuted in the three locations of the first fascicle—wherein those [locations] merely pointed out its falsity in a general sense—here we directly identify it as the six types of disordered deluded thoughts.
This speaks precisely of the emptiness of the six sense faculties of sentient beings.
The characteristics of deluded thought are like a monkey peering through six windows; because it does not remain fixed on any one, they are called the "six disturbances.

(2. Correctly Clarifying the Three [Aspects]. First, General Clarification. Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion" of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly full, based upon this luminosity, the nature is activated, and from this, deluded seeing arises.
From that which is ultimately non-existent, there is established that which is ultimately existent; thus, there is "having something."
There is that which is neither cause nor the basis of causes, neither abiding place nor the characteristic of abiding; it is understood to be fundamentally without root.
From this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
[Commentary] Wenling says: "The nature of luminous mind" refers to the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The nature of luminous perfection" means not clinging to its own self-nature.
This is the nature [of reality]. Because it does not maintain its own nature, it gives rise to a deluded nature due to false luminosity;

because of this deluded nature, deluded views arise. Thus, from the markless reality, the deluded marks of existence are formed; hence it is said that "from ultimate non-existence, absolute existence is established.
However, this capacity for existence and the objects of existence, as well as the capacity for abiding and the locus of abiding, are all not caused by anything.
The causes are all understood to be entirely without root; this is seen through the mutual correspondence of the texts. Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and sentient beings are established;
thus one knows that these two are without cause and without root, being nothing more than total delusion and falsehood.
Wuxing said: "Based on this non-abiding"—abiding is reliance—and by tracing from the root to the branches, one finds there is ultimately nothing upon which to rely.
This passage provides a general indication of the two inversions; below, the two aspects will be explained separately according to their spatial divisions.
The reason for stating them individually here and concluding with both together is that the world is being described in relation to sentient beings.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The second part correctly clarifies two points. First, a general clarification of the 'middle nature. 'Clarifying the mind' refers to the eternally abiding true mind.
Regarding 'the essence of the pure and luminous nature is perfectly complete and pervasive': 'perfect' (yuan) means perfect possession and perfect pervasion.

This is what Tiantai calls the 'inherent possession of the ten realms,' which is precisely what this text describes as the 'great elements'—wherein nature is form and emptiness is true form, and nature is emptiness and form is true emptiness."

This refers to the state of being inherently pure and pervading the entire dharma-realm. When clarity gives rise to its nature, it is like the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s principle that [the mind] can follow defiled or pure conditions to fully create the ten dharma-realms.
This corresponds to what is said in the present sutra: "according to the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of their cognitive capacity.
Here, "clarity" (*ming*) refers to the "clarity of deluded awakening" mentioned in the preceding text, which marks the beginning of defiled conditions. As for "giving rise to its nature":

Luminosity is that which initiates, and the nature is that which is initiated. It is like a grain that possesses the potential for growth, which can be brought forth through the causal conditions of water, soil, and the harmony of the sun’s warmth.
If one follows the meaning of "conforming," then the nature is that which conforms and luminosity is that which is conformed to.

It is like a gentleman who is not limited to a single function and is capable of both good and evil. When the nature gives rise to false views, it immediately establishes an objective realm based upon luminosity; once that objective realm is established...

To falsely establish "arising" is to falsely attribute agency to you. To claim that from ultimate non-existence one achieves ultimate existence is to violently create differentiation within that which is devoid of both identity and difference.
This existence and its possessor are shown to be fundamentally empty in their essence; this is merely a general indication.
One must ask: does this existence—which arises from ultimate non-existence to become ultimate existence—possess any actual fruit, or does it not?
He explained this, saying: "It is not that the causes of causes can cause sentient beings to dwell; the worlds in which they dwell are utterly without foundation.
This must be understood by citing the preceding text: such delusion arises because the cause of delusion is itself delusion;
consciousness is deluded without a cause, and being falsely without support, there is not even arising—what, then, could there be for cessation? Without a cause, there is no dwelling."
Non-abiding is fundamentally emptiness. Since both sentient beings and the world are entirely like flowers in the sky, what characteristics could they possibly possess?
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "All phenomena are established based on the root of non-abiding. This is precisely what that means.

II. A Detailed Explanation of the Three [Phases] (Part 1: Sentient Beings’ Delusion; Part 2: The Initial Correct Explanation of Deluded Response) Deluded regarding their own fundamental perfect luminosity, they give rise to false delusion.

This delusive nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies. As they seek to return to the truth, that which they seek as "truth" is already not true. Since the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not something to be sought after, their pursuit of its restoration merely results in the manifestation of non-existence.

II. The Infusion of Pleasure Draws Forth the Fruit Neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma, they mutually generate one another. The power of this generation manifests through illumination, and through infusion, karma is formed. Through common karma...
"Mutual resonance arises because there is karmic activity of resonance; mutual extinction and mutual generation arise from this, and thus there is the delusion of sentient beings.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "In the phrase 'about to restore to the true,' etc., this raises the case of practicing in accordance with reality as an illustration to clarify the characteristics of practicing in opposition to it—that is, delusion.
This means that if one practices through perfect contemplation and desires to revolve back toward the true nature, even this is already not the true [nature]."
The nature of True Suchness (tathatā). Why? Because apart from True Suchness, all practices and entries into the path belong to the provisional.

Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng) states: "If one attempts to discern Complete Enlightenment without having escaped saṃsāra, that nature of Complete Enlightenment will itself be subject to the cycle of transmigration."
If even practicing in accordance [with the nature] is thus, how much more so practicing in opposition? Therefore it is said, "not truly seeking restoration," and so forth.

One should know that those of the gradual teaching’s three vehicles, up to the ranks of the external paths, all turn their backs on the nature and become deluded; they are all termed "not truly seeking restoration.
This collectively reveals their perversion, hence it says, "clearly constituting non-characteristics. Next, the listing of the four "non-" [characteristics] is merely a detailed classification.
This merely indicates their characteristics. Because there is a body, there is birth; because there is sensation, there is abiding. The mental factors (*citta-dharma*) are easy to understand.
The birth and abiding of mental factors arise successively throughout all states of existence (*bhava*); this refers to the aforementioned continuity of the results of karma.
Regarding "the power of birth reaching the completion of karma": birth is the result, while power is the karma. "Perfuming" (*vāsanā*) refers to the delusion that moves karma.

It takes greed as its root. Just as the body born in the present life is manifested by the power of past karma, so too does one give rise to delusions in the present, thereby perfuming future karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome. Regarding "beings with identical karma reaching birth together":
among the sentient beings of the seven realms of existence, each, according to their delusive afflictions, has karmic affinities that mutually induce one another; this is due to [the act of] killing.
Regarding the karma induced by theft, sexual misconduct, and the three [other transgressions], there are matters of mutual generation and mutual destruction. Changshui said:
"Because of lustful desire, they mutually generate; because of killing and theft, they mutually destroy."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The fourfold demonstration that the delusion of the originally perfect luminosity is fundamentally empty in its essence serves as the basis for the wondrous practice of *śamatha*.
This is because those who realize the Perfect Body understand that there was originally no delusion, yet it appears as if there were, due to the awakening to delusion.

This is because the nature of delusion has no substance and thus has nothing upon which to rely. Indeed, the nature of delusion is without substance, like flowers in the sky seen by one with cataracts.
Fundamentally there is no obscuration in the sky, nor are there any flowers; there is only the vast, clear void, utterly devoid of anything at all.
If one awakens to this, what delusion could there be to be removed, and what reality could there be to be restored?

Next, regarding the three phrases—"desiring to restore the real," "the real already being non-real," and "the nature of True Suchness"—these clarify that those following the partial teachings (p'ien-chiao) recognize that there is a reality to be attained and a delusion to be known.

This can be discarded. Although it differs from the "not truly seeking restoration," it is still far removed from the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), because it does not realize that the nature of delusion is without substance and has nothing upon which to rely. Next are the three phrases concerning "not truly seeking restoration."
It is explained that all those who practice among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, celestial māras, heterodox paths, and ordinary people are called "seeking restoration through what is not true.
This is because they do not know the Middle Way and Buddha-nature; that is to say, they do not know the two kinds of fundamental roots and thus practice in a state of confusion.
Wuxing, however, says: "If one possesses the true desire for perfect contemplation and seeks to restore [the original state], then this is already..."
It is not the true nature of *tathatā*. If the result were as described, then all the gates of cultivation in this present sutra would belong solely to the provisional (*upāya*).
This shares the same underlying intent as the Wēnlíng commentary on the title. That [commentary] clarifies that there is neither cultivation nor realization, which pertains only to ultimate truth;
thus it says, "no cultivation, no realization, no understanding, and no lack of understanding. This is the true *śūraṃgama*, the ultimate and adamantine.
Furthermore, it says: "The Tathāgata within the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings is not revealed except through the secret cause;

sentient beings and bodhisattvas revolve through the seven realms of existence and do not achieve cultivation except through the ten thousand practices. Is this not to say that all cultivation and realization within the mundane realm belong to the provisional?
One must realize that this Sūtra’s Perfect and Sudden teaching is such that there is cultivation without cultivation, and realization without realization—just as the Sūtra states.
This means that the seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent;
how could there be any delusion to be removed? Furthermore, it says: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi;
what 'truth' could there possibly be to return to? Moreover, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "To know illusion is itself liberation; no expedient means need be employed."
"To leave illusion is itself awakening, and there is no gradual progression. Furthermore, it says:
"If a Tathāgata, while in the causal stage, cultivates Perfect Awakening (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra), he knows these are like flowers in the sky and thus has no cyclic existence.

Why does the Master of Wuxing not cite this passage to prove the meaning of perfection within the gate of interpretation, yet still cites the cultivation gate of Vajragarbha to prove that this sutra is of incomplete meaning?

Therefore, one should know that interpreting the scriptures requires the essential eye of the school (zongyan). Otherwise, amidst what is largely correct yet slightly flawed, one will obstruct perfect cultivation;
such a failure is no small matter. Tiantai designated Wuxing as "Outside the Mountains" (Shanwai);
speaking from this perspective, it was not an excessive censure. That which is neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharma, he explained by means of body, sensation, mind, and dharmas.
Nor is it so. This "non-existence" (非) arises from the two characters of "non-characteristic" (非相). It speaks of delusion but does not yet speak of karma or sentient beings;
for it means that instead of seeking the true, one adds delusion upon delusion, and thus it is said that "it completely constitutes a non-characteristic.
"Arising and abiding" refer to its characteristic while omitting "change and extinction"; "mental phenomena" refer to its substance while omitting [the physical].
"Body and sensation" (kāya-vedanā) refers precisely to the fact that the root from which sentient beings give rise to delusion lies in the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
The characteristic of giving rise to delusion resides in arising and abiding; at the very moment a mental phenomenon gives rise to delusion, it is precisely in the state of arising and abiding.
As for difference and cessation, there is nothing to be said regarding its delusion. The four "non-"s all express its falsity; they are the "non-" of negation, not the "non-" of denial.

This arises from seeking further rebirth based on what is not real. Since the root of what is not real is already false, and all states of mind are further false upon that falsehood, it is said that they "completely constitute non-characteristics.
As for the phrase "arising through successive transformation," this does not refer to the sequential meaning of the arising and abiding of mental phenomena;
rather, it is identical to the "six types of deluded false thoughts" mentioned in the text below, and is therefore so designated.

They arise one after another in succession. Regarding "the power of arising brings forth illumination": these six types of deluded conceptualization possess great functional power and can serve as the cause for manifold karmas;
therefore, it is said that they "perfume" [the mind] to form karma. This means that karma exists because of afflictions.
Regarding "those of the same karma resonate with one another": this refers only to birth from a womb or an egg and does not mention moisture-born or transformation-born beings;

it speaks thus because it describes those whose power of karmic formation is greatest. Regarding "because there is the resonance of karma, there is the cessation of characteristics and the arising of characteristics":

"cessation of characteristics" refers to the two [karmas] of killing and stealing among the fruits of karma, while "arising of characteristics" refers to sensual desire among the fruits of karma. Because of karma...
Because there is the fruit of suffering, it is said that for this reason sentient beings are subject to inversion.

Thus, one knows that the meaning of the mutual generation of the three paths is very clearly elucidated by this passage. If one were to explain the preceding text by means of body, sensation, mind, and dharmas, the three paths would lose their established positions;
how could this possibly be acceptable?
○ (2. Worldly Inversion) Ānanda, what is meant by "worldly inversion"? It is that which exists as having something to possess, where fragmented delusions arise;
because of this realm, one establishes what is not a cause as a cause, and what has no abode as an abode. Through this constant flux and lack of stability, the world is formed. ○ (3.

The Three Times and Four Directions Interpenetrate to Produce the Twelve Categories [of Beings]) The three times and four directions harmoniously interpenetrate, transforming and giving rise to sentient beings to form the twelve categories. (Note: The text contains two initial headings for the section on the three times and four directions, with the first being a general indication and the second a general heading.)
[Commentary] Gushan says: Because that which was ultimately non-existent becomes ultimately existent, there arises the segmentation of east, west, south, and north.
This segmentation is designated as "dhātu" (realm). However, since its existence is fundamentally without cause, it is said to be "not caused by a cause.
Because this abides only in delusion, it is said to be "non-abiding. Since that which is dwelt upon is not the true nature, [it is called the realm of delusion].
If they were eternally abiding, there would be no past, present, or future; it is through their constant flux and non-abiding that the three periods of time are established.

When the periods of time intersect with the directions and the directions intersect with the periods of time, both together constitute the twelve [divisions]. Thus, the integration of the primary retribution of sentient beings with cause and effect also constitutes the twelve.
Wu Xing says: "In the fourth fascicle, the mutual intersection of directions and periods adds the three transformations."

[The text] repeats. That [previous section] contrasted the *adhiṣṭhāna* (environmental retribution) to reveal that the merits of the six sense organs (*indriya*) as part of the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (primary retribution) are each one thousand two hundred.
Herein, they interpenetrate; by taking the environment from the perspective of the primary retribution, it clarifies how the world’s inversions establish the twelve classes of living beings.
Since the previous section spoke of "merits" while this speaks of "inversions," can the ancient masters' use of this to explain the first three repetitions be considered correct?
"Accordingly.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Prior to Wuxing, it was stated that "merit" here refers to "inversion.
It is certainly correct that one should not use this to explain the principle of the three layers; nevertheless, apart from the six sense organs, there is neither merit nor inversion.
[This is] inverted. Thus, the nature of both permanence and impermanence dwells within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), like two birds flying together or two wheels yoked side by side.
It is because these six faculties possess the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-sāra*) that is capable of generating all conditions.
From the perspective of the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness itself, it is called "merit" (*guṇa*); from the perspective of its capacity to generate all conditions...

To speak of them [in this way] is called "perverted. What was stated previously—that birth-and-death, afflictions, bodhi, and nirvana are all identical to the six sense faculties and there is nothing else—its meaning lies herein.
○ (2. Showing the two [aspects]; first, establishing the twelve causes: Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form;

touch arises from fragrance; flavor arises from touch; and mental objects (*dharma*) are known through flavor. Because these six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this cycle.
Thus, the world’s sounds, fragrances, flavors, and touches exhaust the twelve transformations to become a single rotation.
Furthermore.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: This takes the sensory object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) as the cause in its own essence.

From "sound being the cause of form" up to "taste being the cause of knowing phenomena," these are successive causes used to reveal the characteristics of the sixfold confusion. Finally, there is the "knowing of phenomena."

"Knowing" refers to the faculty of mind (*manas*), and "dharmas" refers to the objects of the mind (*dharmāyatana*). By applying this later case to the preceding ones, there is the same principle for hearing sounds, seeing forms, and so forth;
how much more so when it speaks of the "six disordered delusions. Thus, one knows that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all ultimately resolve into delusion. Wénlǐng says:
"Because these six objects give rise to the six faculties, they are called the 'six disordered delusions. This is precisely what constitutes affliction and karma."
Because it is the fundamental source [of karma], it is called the nature of karma (*karmatā*). The twelve classes of beings revolve through this cycle.
