The worldly objects of sound, fragrance, taste, and touch refer to the aforementioned six types of deluded conceptualizations.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the previous introduction to the meaning, it was stated:

"Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world;
when inversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata. This [point] is identical to what was previously stated in the text regarding ignorance.
Regarding the root of what is bound, I believe that these people will ultimately be unable to unravel it; the intention is the same, though the meanings differ.
This is because the preceding section merely clarified the inversions, whereas the present section correctly clarifies the causes of those inversions.

Therefore, the sutra first explains the two kinds of inversion, and subsequently, through their mutual interpenetration, elucidates the production of categories. It is solely due to the primary retribution of sentient beings and...
The world and its dependent retributions interpenetrate one another, giving rise to the six types of disordered delusions, which serve as the cause of inversion.
Therefore it is said: "Thus, the world has sound because of movement" (and so forth), up to "exhausting the twelve transformations as a single cycle of return.
The term "six types of disordered delusions" is used because they are chaotic and lack order. As it says:

Because movement gives rise to sound, the mind takes sound as its superior object. In an instant, because sound gives rise to form, it again transforms into a mind that takes form as its superior object;
this continues until, because of form there is fragrance, and because of flavor one perceives dharmas.

This is how the sensory object of sound serves as the primary cause for the arising of six types of deluded false thoughts. Alternatively, because of movement there may be form, continuing up to the point where because of dharmas there is [form].

This is called the second transformation. Continuing in this manner, taking the knower of phenomena as the subject until the tasting of flavors through contact is called the exhaustion of the six transformations, which constitute the six revolutions (*ṣaḍ-āvarta*).

As for the term "revolution," it refers to the sequential arising of six disordered deluded thoughts as one passes through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and their objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena. If one tastes flavors by means of phenomena...

From taste there arises touch, and so on, up to from form there arises sound; this is called "reversion" (*fu*). In this way, one exhausts the six transformations, which are called the "six reversions.
As for the term "reversion," it refers to the six chaotic delusions arising in reverse order, with one's own dharmas as the primary cause.
Therefore, the concluding summary states: "For this reason, the world of sounds, smells, tastes, and touches exhausts twelve transformations to become one."
It revolves back. The initial character "movement" (dòng) generally governs the following five; the final character "knowing" (zhī) likewise extends through the preceding five.

This is because all six types of deluded thoughts are fundamentally rooted in movement. As for "knowing," as the Master of Wuxing stated, it follows the previous logic to include the meanings of hearing sounds, seeing forms, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because they constitute the nature of karma": "karma" refers to the twelve perversions, such as desire and the rest.
Taking perversion as the fundamental cause, one creates the false karma of the ten non-virtuous actions, such as killing; their nature is precisely the six types of deluded conceptualization.

As for the statement that the twelve divisions revolve by means of this, it is because the six types of deluded conceptualization serve as the cause from which the twelve perversions arise, and these twelve perversions in turn serve as the conditions for creating the ten non-virtuous actions and so forth.
Karma follows its ascent and descent, and through this, the twelve divisions revolve. Alas! The deluded thoughts and the sixfold confusion of sentient beings are such as these.
Were it not for the Tathāgata illuminating them for them, sentient beings would spend their entire daily lives using these very things without ever attaining awakening or knowledge;
one might truly say that their delusion is extreme. Now that they have awakened to this inversion—
Since this is the cause, how can one not strive to ensure that such inversions do not arise, thereby entering the Tathāgata’s true samādhi?
Now, the fundamental cause of inversion is ignorance (*avidyā*); from this, the world arises. From the world, sentient beings arise. Therefore it is said:
"Falsely taking what is not-enlightenment as enlightenment, one establishes an object based on that enlightenment. Once the object has been falsely established, you [the mind] are born."

This is the power of delusion. Since the beginning of the world must fundamentally derive from movement, it is said: "The interaction between the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness creates agitation;
thus there is the wind-circle that sustains the world. For movement belongs to wind, and wind necessarily possesses sound.
Therefore, among the six sense objects, sound arises first; thus it is said that sound exists because of movement, and form exists because of sound.
This is why, for the twelve classes of living beings, movement is placed at the beginning—the inverted intention lies herein.
Since the arising of delusion from the truth takes movement as its basis, the return to truth from delusion must take non-movement as its basis.
Therefore, as the occasion required, [Śāriputra] followed the flow of sounds and fell into erroneous thoughts; he then earnestly requested the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.
The Tathāgata then revealed to him the eternally abiding true mind and the site of tranquil extinction—the true *āraṇya*.
This is indeed the excellent medicine for the disease and the essential gate for stilling agitation. Regarding this,孤山 (Gushan) [said]:...
The three types of cessation (nirodha) eliminate [the afflictions] and are appropriately suited to the text.
○ (2. The Twelve Fruits of Sentience) Because one rides upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth;

those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with form nor without form; and those who are neither with perception nor without perception.
"Perception that is neither perception nor non-perception.
[Commentary] Tianru’s Supplement states: This is a general heading.

Because the twelve divisions exhaust transformation and return to the source, the cycles of transmigration and inversion each possess twelve aspects, thereby transforming sentient beings into twelve classes.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The nature of revolving and inverted delusion" refers to the six types of chaotic false thoughts, which, when traced through the twelve transformations, constitute a single cycle of return.
"The marks of revolving and inverted delusion" refer to everything from the inversion of false and agitated movement up to the inversion of enmity, harm, and killing.
It is because of these natures and marks of revolving and inverted delusion that [this state arises].

There are the three realms, the six paths, and the twelve classes of living beings. Their fundamental nature and characteristics constitute the causal karma, while the twelve classes of living beings constitute the resultant karma.
Once deluded appearances suddenly take form as color and suddenly take form as sound, the twelve inversions arise from these causes;
they likewise manifest all at once as movement and all at once as desire, eventually summoning [the cycle of existence].
As for their retributions—whether as oviparous or viviparous—they undergo mutual transformations; thus, there are six disordered states without fixed destinies.

If one synthesizes the essential purports of the preceding sutras to clarify this, it is because within the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of the inverted world, each one mutually contains the five objects, thereby drawing forth the birth of sentient beings within the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of inversion.

These result in the six types of deluded conceptualization. When these six deluded conceptualizations grasp at the six sense-objects, one may, through them, give rise to the delusion of false and empty saṃsāra and its fluctuations;
or, through them, give rise to the delusion of hostile and harmful saṃsāra and its killings.
This extends from committing acts of lust, killing, theft, and lying, up to engaging in divisive speech.
It is because of harsh speech that one creates karma as vast as the heavens and incurs infinite transgressions; few do not do so through this means. Therefore it is said:
"Riding upon this wheel of revolving and inverted appearances, there are thus the twelve classes of beings in the world.

This is identical in meaning to the three types of continuity described in the four-fascicle [version], though they differ in their respective details and brevity. One must necessarily cross-reference them with one another.
Only by observing these can one fully comprehend the essential purport of the twelve classes of living beings. Yet, these twelve classes do not transcend the six realms of existence.

As stated in the following text, they all arise from compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; conversely, by turning away from these three, one gives rise to a state free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Those who possess names belong to the category of ghosts, while those without names belong to the realm of heaven. Within the heavenly realm, however—
Regarding the term "desire-realm devas" (*kāmadeva*): it is because the six types of distracted delusions exist only within the desire realm.
If one has already attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the first heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how could there be such sixfold distraction?

Therefore, the obstructions of hindrance, saṃsāra, barriers, inversion, conjunction, attachment, the formation of auspicious or inauspicious signs, and spiritual brilliance exist only in the first heaven of the desire realm, being equal to the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*). If...
However, this refers to the dissolution of saṃsāra and the resulting transformation of inverted darkness into empty dispersion and sinking;

this is merely a general discussion concerning the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It certainly cannot be compared or discussed on the same footing as the ten types of beings described in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*.

○ (2. Specific Manifestation of the Two; First, Showing the Twelve; First, the Category of Movement) Ānanda, because of the delusory cycle of the world caused by the movement of inversion, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus, there exist egg-born beings (*aṇḍaja*), such as the *kalala* stage, who circulate through the lands as fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, filling all categories.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The egg-born are produced solely from thought; this delusion is precisely 'thought' (*saṃjñā*). The essence of thought is light and buoyant, which is termed 'movement' and 'inversion.

The egg is formed through the intermingling of vital energies (*qi*), termed 'harmonious blending of energies. When thought is excessive, there is rising and sinking, termed 'confused thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus, one感召 (ganshào—induces) the various species of fish and birds that fly or sink. As for the eighty-four thousand [types of afflictions] for each of the twelve classes:"
Each is produced by the transformation induced by eighty-four thousand afflictions. *Kalala* means "congealed fluid";
it is the state at the initial stage of entering the womb, when the embryo and the ovum have not yet differentiated.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Falsehood" refers to the cause of deluded movement and inversion. "Harmonious conjunction" constitutes the condition.

Fish, birds, turtles, and snakes are the phenomena produced. However, a single cause cannot be established, and a solitary condition is difficult to perfect; it is only through the harmonious conjunction of causes and conditions that phenomena can be produced.
This is the same as what was previously discussed regarding the perception of light and form within the continuity of sentient beings.

The explanation of "manifesting through seeing and thought" establishes that their meanings are identical. "Manifesting through seeing" refers to false, deluded movement; "vapor" (qi) refers to the emergence of form.

Since it is said that they are formed by the combination of vapors, the eighty-four thousand chaotic thoughts of flying and sinking are analogous to the chaotic thoughts produced upon the fruit of birth, rather than the six types of chaotic deluded thoughts such as false movement within the causal state. This is what is meant by "using chaos [to produce chaos]."
Because they invite the fruit of chaos, within the realm of sentient beings there is nothing but the sixfold chaotic delusions.
Thus, when viewed from the perspective of the fruit back toward the cause, these sixfold chaotic delusions are fully possessed by eighty-four thousand [beings], with some flying and others sinking.
The following passage clarifies that those with many emotions and few thoughts are heavy as the fur-bearing beasts, while those with few emotions and many thoughts are light as the feathered birds.
Regarding their lineages: according to the present state of affairs, those that fly belong to the feathered lineage, while those that sink belong to the fish, tortoise, viper, and snake.
Their flight or submersion is distinguished by their delusions, and their lightness or heaviness is divided according to their karma.

(2) Regarding the category of desire: due to the inversion of desire within the defiled cycle of the world, beings combine and flourish through eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts.
Consequently, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of gestation as they transmigrate through various lands;
humans, animals, dragons, and immortals fill these categories.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The womb is defiled by emotion; this 'emotion' is precisely *kleśa* (affliction). Emotion arises from craving and is termed the 'perversion of desire.
The womb is formed through the union of semen and blood, termed 'harmonious integration and growth. Emotion has its biases and correctness, termed 'horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts.
Thus, one is reborn as humans or animals in horizontal or vertical categories. *Ātapa-tunda* refers to the 'blister'; this is when the embryo and egg gradually divide."

This is their characteristic. Empty delusions, defilements, attachments, and obstructions are possessed by all sentient beings; they merely manifest as various types according to what is predominant in each individual.
Wuxing said: "That which arises depending on an egg is called birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*); that which emerges from being contained within is called birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*);

that which arises through reliance on moisture is called birth from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*); that which exists suddenly where it was previously non-existent is called transformational birth (*upapāduka*). It is thus.
The four modes of birth have internal volitional karma as their cause and external conditions—namely, eggs, wombs, moisture, and warmth—as their supporting factors.

The sequence is established according to the degree of these supporting factors. Egg-birth possesses all four [conditions], and is therefore mentioned first; womb-birth possesses three; moisture-birth possesses two;
and transformation-birth possesses only one, namely volitional karma. This is according to the interpretation found in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of deluded thoughts arise as defiled desires and inverted states, there are both the perverse and the correct.
If one’s disposition is correct, one is born vertically as a human or a celestial being (ṛṣi); if one’s disposition is incorrect, one is born horizontally as an animal;
if the perverse and correct are half-and-half, one becomes a dragon, for its physical form is sometimes horizontal.

Or perhaps it is because they are upright. What constitutes correctness? For the Confucians, it is the Three Bonds and the Five Constant Virtues; for the Buddhists, it is the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Furthermore, when combined with the Ten Wholesome Actions, this constitutes the Way of Heaven.

When augmented by the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections and myriad practices, and the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, this is the most correct of the correct; these then constitute the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.
This is the path of the Bodhisattva, the Buddha-path.

(The Three Classes of Beings) Because of the world of causes, through attachment to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) and inverted views, the combination of warmth produces eighty-four thousand types of confused and fluctuating thoughts.
Thus, there exist lands of flowing moisture where beings with moist characteristics—such as *piśāca* spirits and wriggling insects—evolve and transmigrate.
Their kind moves and fills all space. [Commentary] Wēn-líng says:

"Moisture" refers to union through resonance; "attachment" is precisely this union. Union arises from the stagnation of craving; as one pursues and clings to objects upon contact, it is called the "perversion of inclination.
Moisture, generated by Yang, is named "harmonious union" (*saṃyoga*) and is completed by "warmth. That which is inclined toward has no fixed destination.
It is named "overturned and chaotic thought" (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*); thus, it brings about rebirth among the wriggling and crawling classes of beings.
*Bhṛśa* (or *piśita*) refers to soft flesh; this is the initial sign of moisture-born birth. Since these beings do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages [of embryonic development].

All ten modes of birth are rooted in sexual desire and arise from emotional thoughts. Because deluded emotions become increasingly false, the transformation of principle becomes ever more discordant, leading to—
The dissolute becomes empty and scattered; the stubborn becomes like wood or stone. Although the branches of delusion differ, the root of delusion is one.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of chaotic delusive thoughts arise, giving rise to attachment and pursuing perversions, they oppose the mind and turn their backs on faith.
They turn over and over according to their whims, thereby affecting all creatures, whether wriggling or moving;
their forms may be overturned or upright, and their movements may be flying or walking, with no fixed direction. What is called "attachment" does not refer to being merely cautious or diligent;
rather, it means being stingily clinging and unable to let go regarding the objects of the six sense-fields, and [being bound] by the six types of chaotic delusive thoughts.
This refers to turning over and over while following one's own emotions.

(4. Category of the Four Falsehoods) Because of the false inversion caused by the world’s transformation and the cycle of rebirth, the conjunction of conditions produces eighty-four thousand types of new and old chaotic thoughts;
thus there exist the transformed phase, the *kalala*, the flowing through lands, and the metamorphosis of flying creatures.
Their activities fill their respective categories.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Transformation through responding to change is precisely *li* (separation). Departing from this and entrusting oneself to that is called "false inversion.
Touching upon various categories and transforming is called "harmonious contact and formation. Because the old turns and the new approaches, it is called "the confusion of the new and the old."

Because the perception is such, the retribution experienced is likewise so. Because one sheds [the old], one proceeds toward the new. It is like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, whereby the movement shifts from crawling to flying;

or like a sparrow becoming a clam, whereby the shedding shifts from flying to submerging. Generally, whenever different forms are transmitted to one another, it is all a process of transformation and shedding (*parivartana*).
*Kalala* refers to "hard flesh"; once shed, it becomes a physical body and no longer possesses the characteristic of softness. From here below...
The term *kalala* used by all [stages] is merely a general designation for these various types.
If one speaks of the fifth stage, *praśākhā*, as "formation of shape," then it refers specifically to each according to its particular appearance and is not a general designation. Guishan says:

"Transformational characteristics" (*huàxiàng*) does not mean that something previously non-existent suddenly comes into being through transformation; rather, it is like a grubs (qícháo) shedding its old skin and joyfully assuming a new substance. The intention is...
Because they fly and soar, it is said that they "molt and travel by flight. Wuxing remarked:
"Molting and traveling by flight does not necessarily refer only to creatures such as the *qichao* (maggot); rather, it is an image used for analogy regarding transformational birth (*upapāduka*).

As the *Liezi* says, 'Heaven and earth cast off their molts,' and the subsequent passage, 'If one’s thoughts are purely [of flight], then one flies,' all take these as metaphors. Thus, 'molting' is used as a metaphor for the physical form."
Its ease of shedding [the old] is like flight, which metaphorically represents the light elevation of a new substance. That "what was not suddenly exists" finds its logical correspondence here.
Tianru’s supplementary note states: "The explanations of the two masters Huan and Yuan regarding 'transformation-birth' (upapāduka) certainly accord with the meaning of the sūtra.

However, if one considers that the heavens, hells, hungry ghosts, and so forth all possess the characteristics of transformation-birth, then Master Yue’s statement that 'what was not suddenly exists' also holds true."
This is the principle; one should appropriately take this into account.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Someone asked me, "I have heard that the three realms and six paths of existence do not go beyond the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
Now, you further speak of eight kinds of birth outside of these four. Is it that the four modes of birth fail to encompass everything, such that there must be something else?"
Are these born from different types [of birth]? The answer is: the latter eight types are likewise not outside the four modes of birth (*catasro yonayaḥ*).
However, the intent of the Sūtra is that these eight types differ from the ordinary; yet those whose minds are coarse and superficial cannot infer the matter of cause and effect.
Therefore, they are explained in detail beyond the four modes of birth, so that sentient beings may understand their own delusions.
When one contemplates that false conceptualizations have no place where they do not cease to exist, and thus breaks through them, this constitutes the path of *śamatha*.
Nevertheless, it should be known that following this, the eight kinds of birth are predominantly transformational (*upapāduka*).

This is because "transformation" includes both the sudden manifestation of what was previously non-existent—such as the heavens and the hells—and the transformation of the very substance of existence itself, such as the gates of the various realms.

This refers to the transformation and flight [of insects]. As for the following cases of auspicious and inauspicious portents, or the manifestation of spirits, these do not belong to the category of "suddenly existing where there was nothing," as one might ask what gave birth to them.

The spirits, ghosts, and essences, or the transformation of the spirit into earth, wood, metal, or stone, and the production of curses and incantations—all are transformations of that which was previously non-existent yet suddenly comes into being.
It is like the *puluo* (wasp) that takes a worm as its offspring, or the earth-owl...
Those who form offspring by attaching to a mass all undergo transformation through the alteration of their physical substance;

only those such as the *śiśumāra* (water-mother) can be reasoned out as being born from moisture and transformation. Is this not because the principle of "transformational birth" (*upapāduka*) broadly encompasses all modes of birth?
Thus, it is only when combined with the explanations of the four masters that the way of transformational birth becomes manifest. If one relies solely on the immediate text...

To speak of this: the six types of chaotic deluded thoughts undergo transformation and are falsely inverted; as temporal sentiments and mental conceptions diverge, the new and the old shift and change.
Thus, at the time of receiving birth, one may transform from a crawling creature into a flying insect, or from a flying insect into a burrowing creature;
through mutual borrowing of characteristics and the extension of these categories, the signs of transformation—the *kalala*—are formed.

○ (The Five Classes of Obstructions): Due to the obstruction of inverted views caused by the world of causes—which involves lingering and hindering within saṃsāra—sentient beings combine and become attached, forming eighty-four thousand types of confused thoughts regarding radiant energy.

Consequently, there are physical forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands; these include those possessing auspicious or inauspicious spiritual brilliance, whose kinds fill the world.
[Commentary] Zizhong said: "To fixate upon and refuse to let go of the union of sun, moon, water, and fire, such that they obstruct and block one another, is called 'obstruction' (liu-ai).
Because the essence and brilliance become manifest and distinct through this, it is termed 'form-characteristic' (se-xiang).
Regarding stars, sun, and moon: what is auspicious is called 'rest' (xiu), and what is inauspicious is called 'calamity' (jiu). This extends even to the chewing of fire and the [use of] clam pearls."

Regarding this category, Wénlǐng says: "All spirits of refined brilliance (*jīngyào*) are manifestations of quintessential radiance. Because their mental conceptions have already coalesced into refined radiance, they possess only form.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the eighty deities are all formed from this refined radiance due to the fundamental element of obstructive conceptualization.
Although these beings are most refined and most spiritual, they have not yet transcended being carried by that wheel."
This refers to the transformation of inverted characteristics.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of chaotic delusive thoughts give rise to the obstacle of stagnation and obstruction during times of inversion, one falsely generates attachments within these worldly inversions, taking them to be essential radiance and chaotic conceptions. Therefore, at the time of rebirth, the characteristics of cause and effect—
The *fu* (spiritual talisman) ultimately represents the clarity and precision of auspicious and inauspicious signs.

○ (Section on the Six Delusions): Because of the world’s dissolution and the cycle of rebirth driven by delusive inversion, the union with darkness forms eighty-four thousand obscure and chaotic thoughts;
thus there exist the formless *kalala* realms of transmigration, where [beings] disperse and dissolve into emptiness.
Their kind sinks and fills [the world].
[Commentary: Wēn-líng says: "To loathe existence and cling to emptiness, to extinguish the body and return to non-being, is called 'dissipation' within saṃsāra.

To be deluded, leaking, and without hearing is called 'confusion' and 'inversion. To loathe existence and return to non-being is to rely on the dark and obscure emptiness; therefore, it harmonizes with darkness."
When it is formed, it is named "obscure and hidden chaotic thought" (*ābhāsvara-vikṣipta-saṃjñā*). This refers to the class of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because this possesses perception yet lacks the formation of a karmic body, it is also called *kalala*.

Furthermore, when afflictions and karma are heavy and obscuring, physical form is worn away, and the substance merges with the void and darkness such that consciousness clings to the obscure and hidden; this is also of the class of those who are empty, scattered, dissolved, and submerged.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of deluded thoughts arise and the confusion of inverted views dissipates, one regards the physical form as having dependencies and the body as the root of affliction.
One contemplates with single-mindedness and seeks to still and disperse these thoughts.

Unaware that this is the retribution of hidden and chaotic thoughts—which are themselves dispersed and dissolved into emptiness—it is also a principle that they rely upon the dark and obscure emptiness. However, this...

For now, we shall discuss only the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is not necessary to speak of non-Buddhist practitioners of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) using the example of the *śūnyatā* spirits.

(7. The Category of Shadows) Because the world’s causes produce illusory cycles of rebirth and inverted shadows, through their harmonious conjunction and recollection, eighty-four thousand [dharmas] are formed.
Because of these thousand hidden, disordered thoughts, there exist the *kalala* (embryonic stage) characterized by perception, which flows through the lands of spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings;
their various kinds fill [the world].
[Commentary] Zizhong says: "The categories of those who follow tracks and cling to shadows are all born from recollective thought (*smṛti-saṃjñā*). This discusses the causes.
Just as non-Buddhist commoners offer sacrifices to deities and rely upon images, serving them for their entire lives with the aspiration to attain spiritual communion;
because cause and effect repay one another, they are born into that same class. Wēnlíng says: "They are deluded and lose the truth, becoming perversely attached to shadows and images.
Having no basis in the *āśraya*, these forms arise from recollections and latent impressions, secretly forming appearances within the realm of the non-existent."
When the spirit is not clear, it becomes a ghost in its obscurity; when the essence is incomplete, it disperses as a numen (*ling*).
There is no substantial form, but only conceptual appearances.
[Tiantai’s Commentary: The Sixth [Sense] gives rise to chaotic and delusory thoughts, like shadows from a phantom image. At times of inversion, one recollects and imagines spirits and ghosts.

Such are their shadowy manifestations. As for what is called the way of ghosts and spirits, I too find it difficult to clarify; yet the principle of spiritual resonance (*yinggan*) must not be doubted.
Therefore, they are termed "phantom-like" (*wangxiang*) beings in the cycle of rebirth. Because they dwell upon memories, they form latent and chaotic thoughts.
The people of the world are muddled and unaware of this, vainly giving rise to admiration and aspiring to grasp at the elusive and the mysterious. How can they disregard the law of cause and effect?
Having completed their false accusations, they fall into their own kind.

(8. The Class of Delusion) Because of the delusive inversions that cause the cycle of rebirth for those who are dull-witted within the world, they combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts;
thus there exist the spirit-transformed *kalala* of the non-percipient realm, which flows through the lands.
"Earth, wood, metal, and stone—these types fill [the world].
[Commentary] Zizhong said: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon that insentient things possess life; that metal and stone are firm and solid;

or that through the practice of meditative concentration, ash congeals, and through focused thought, the withered mind transforms according to its environment, taking form upon encountering objects, such as when a spirit is born from a flower-pedestal."
This refers to cases such as those whose heads have turned to stone. Wēnlíng says: "Failing to comprehend the principle of ultimate truth, one stubbornly clings to ignorance.
When this dullness and stupidity reach their extreme, one becomes obstinate and devoid of cognition, and the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six kinds of chaotic delusions arise—when one is ignorant, dull, transmigrating, deluded, and inverted—one might think that the mind can certainly be made like extinguished ashes and the body can certainly be made like metal or stone, as a plan for the pursuit of longevity.
Consequently, the mind becomes identical with its environment, and the environment follows the mind; through this union of the stubborn, they form a withered pair.
Through chaotic thoughts, the spirit eventually transforms into an insentient and solid object.
One fails to realize that although metal and stone are hard, they ultimately return to exhaustion; and although the spirit remains present, it ultimately falls into folly.
Chen Na was destroyed by a single shout, and Zhang Hua was exposed by a single mirror. It is not only that the physical form cannot be preserved forever, but—
The spirit likewise perishes along with it; the deluded and dull cycle through saṃsāra because they believe in delusion and dullness.

(9. The Nine Pseudo-Categories) Because of the world of causes, which is a false and inverted cycle of mutual dependence, the combination of defilements forms eighty-four thousand thoughts of causal reliance and disorder.
Thus, there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics, becoming *kalala* and flowing through various realms.
The various soil-sponges (*sphaera*) and similar creatures take shrimp as their eyes; their kind fills [the world]. [Commentary: Zizhong said:
"Through the artifice of combination, they alter the old to create the new. Sometimes they falsely rely on causes and conditions to alternately provide each other with support.

Sustaining their bodies and nourishing their lives, the fruits of their karma follow one another in succession. Because they do not receive a body from their own kind, they are called 'non-[sentient]' (*asattva*)."
Regarding those with form and so forth: within the bodies of sentient beings, there are eighty thousand families of worms, all of which belong to this category.

Wenling says that creatures such as the *jalamdhara* (water-jelly) take water foam for their body and use shrimp for eyes; they originally have no form of their own, but acquire form by depending on other things.
They cannot function independently, yet they become functional by depending on others. Thus they lose the true nature of heaven and cling persistently to floating falsehoods. As for them...
Because these disparate and defiled conditions combine, they are called "causal dependence" (*hetv-āśraya*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of deluded thoughts arise in mutual relation, within this false and inverted cycle of saṃsāra, they successively depend upon one another and act as mutual supports.
Thus, in their expedient and provisional conduct, there is no limit to where they may go. It is because of this...
Through the combination of defiled causes and conditions, they eventually become the species of the *siphonophore* (the "water-jelly").
Yet, among the rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, and brothers of this world, who is there that does not rely upon one another to carry out their way? They simply seek to ensure it is correct.
If one says it is not correct, few will avoid falling into this very category. The *siphonophore* is commonly called the [water-jelly].
The shrimp-snake is also called the *fēi*; its shape is like that of a sheep’s stomach.

(10. Class of Natures) Because the natures of the world of causes lead one another into saṃsāra through inversion, they combine with incantations to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning;
for this reason, there exists the realm of the non-material, formless *kalala* that flows and turns.
Earth-dwelling beings, born through curses and incantations, fill the world.
[Commentary] Zizhong said: there is a class of beings whose nature is formed by being summoned and induced through sound, such as frogs that attach their eggs to sound.
Regarding the cause, it may be that they delight in lewd sounds and, through habituation, become attached to them; from this—self-...

The nature and category [of these beings] do not depend on others for their formation, yet their names are not devoid of form and appearance. Because they manifest their substance by means of sound, they are called "formless" (*arūpa*).
Wēnlíng says: "Driven by evil karma, their dispositions and natures are inverted; they ride upon incantations to entrust their consciousness.
Not following the laws of natural physiology, they perversely respond to summoning. Thus, through worldly sorcery, curses, malevolent spirits, and objects of ritual suppression, they come to be."
There are those who are born [into this state].
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of deluded thoughts arise, they mutually induce the nature of perversion.

At that time, through lustful sounds, they harmonize with one another, never forgetting it; thus, through habituation, it becomes their very nature. The spiritual consciousness of the deceased becomes inverted and bewildered.

There is confusion. Some hear the sound of frogs and are deluded into perceiving it as the music of a lute; others hear the sounds of incantations and curses and are deluded into perceiving them as seductive melodies.
Thus, through the power of harmonious mantras, there arise spells for summoning and confused thoughts of cursing and subjugation, such that their kind fills every space.

○ (Eleven: The Class of Deceptive Beings) Because the world of causes involves the delusory cycle of inverted views, various combinations produce eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and confused thoughts.
Thus, there exist those who perceive what is non-existent as existent, forming the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages that circulate through the lands.
Among them, creatures such as the *pulu* (parasitic insects) form their bodies by assimilating the substance of others, and their kind fills the world.
[Zijung] said: "To falsely claim another's property as one's own is *wang* (deception); to invert the natural order is *meng* (delusion).

To turn one's back on kin and follow what is deemed righteous, to entrust one's death to others and rely on them for the orphaned lineage, to forget one's own ancestral sacrifices while claiming the succession of another—these are its causes.

[Wenling] said: "When these two delusions combine, the nature and emotion become obscured; disparate substances form a single entity, and the principles of life and growth become inverted, just like that."
The *pulu* (wasp) was originally a mulberry worm; it did not possess the notion of being a bee, yet it came to have the notion of being a bee. Wuxing said:
"Because its substance is different, it does not possess the characteristic of [inherent] thought; because it is formed through characteristics, it becomes the *kalala* of thought."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six types of deluded thoughts arise and merge with the cycle of false saṃsāra, it is not only the case of turning one's back on kin and seeking profit, or entrusting the dead and relying on orphans;
rather, all instances of deceiving others and taking what belongs to them as one's own are manifestations of this.
Therefore, although cause and effect are manifest, they ultimately harmonize with the disparate to form a state of mutual inversion and confusion.
They are thought to belong to the class of gall wasps and similar creatures.

(Twelfth: The Class of Killers) Due to the cycle of mutual enmity and killing within the world, and because of the inversion of perception regarding killing, these beings combine to form eighty-four thousand types of monsters who harbor the thought of devouring their own parents;
thus, there exists the realm of the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages where beings flow through states that are neither with nor without perception.

There are creatures such as the earth-owl (*kṣitighoṇa*) that attach themselves to clods of earth to raise them as their offspring, and the mirror-breaking bird (*ādarśabhañjana*) that embraces the poisonous fruits of trees to raise them as its young;
once the offspring have matured, both parents meet their end by being devoured by them, and such species abound everywhere.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "When resentment and harm are requited, and injury and killing oppose one another, the natural course of life becomes strange and perverse, severing the bonds of human righteousness;

thus, creatures such as the earth-owl (tǔxiāo) are produced. They take form from earthen clods or poisonous fruits. It is not that they lack the perception of a bird, yet fundamentally they possess no [human] consciousness.
Zī-zhōng says: "When parents have affection for their child, this is called 'not lacking the mark of consciousness. In enmity, there is none."

Because of attachment, it is said that there is no perception (*asaṃjñā*). Question: Since these are enemies who lack the conditions for generating a feeling of affinity, how can they be attached to one another and harbor love within their enmity?
Answer: It is like raising pigs or sheep; because one craves their slaughter, one keeps them. Is this not evidence that even among enemies there is attachment? Guishan says:
Regarding the "earth-owl" (*tǔxiāo*) and the "shattered mirror," according to the *Shiji*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu": [The text continues with the historical account.]
In the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one uses a *xiāo* bird and a *pòjìng*. Mèng Kāng says: "The *xiāo* is the name of a bird that eats its mother; the *pòjìng* eats its father.

The Yellow Emperor wished to exterminate their kind and therefore mandated that they be used in all sacrifices to various spirits. The *pòjìng* resembles a wild boar (*chú*) but has the eyes of a tiger.
The current description as a "bird" likely results from an error by the translator; perhaps the character "bird" (*niǎo*) should actually be "equal to" (*děng*). [End of] Later [Dynasty].
It is people who have erroneously altered [the text].
(2. Conclusion) These are called the twelve kinds of sentient beings.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "These all fail to realize the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; they are deluded and trapped in emotional desires, and their accumulated falsehoods give rise to [these states]."

Birth arises from delusion, leading one to revolve in saṃsāra; without correct cultivation, none can escape it. Therefore, the following text demonstrates the method for eliminating delusion and attaining realization through cultivation.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the six chaotic delusions arise, bringing forth resentment, harm, saṃsāric killing, and inversion, one is severed from principle.
To subvert human relations and act contrary to the natural order is a strange occurrence. For instance, how could the killing of a superior by an inferior not be considered strange?
Thus, one might conceive of eating one's parents, like the earth-owl (*ulūka*) and its kind. Yet this is not the only case; it applies to all instances where those above exploit those below.
At first they treat one with intimacy, but in the end they distance themselves; at first they nourish one, but in the end they kill one.

Intimacy and nourishment are surely acts of affection, yet when one distances oneself and kills, that affection turns instead into resentment. Among the species of the earth-owl (*tuchao*), at first they appear as a father and son—is this not the retribution for being nurtured?
In the end, they must devour him; it is not that they possess a conscious intent [to do so].
They eat them. That form and shadow follow one another, and that karmic retribution does not err, is not something expected but is brought about by necessity.
Formerly, the Yellow Emperor wished to sever his kinship with them and thus used their flesh for all sacrificial offerings to the various spirits.

Yet, while a bird that is an *oxiao* (owl) is an *oxiao* in form and can certainly be severed from its kind, how can a person who is an *oxiao* in heart be severed? How could one ever sever such a person?
Therefore, there is nothing that reforms the owl-creature (the wicked) like reforming the person; and there is nothing that reforms the person like reforming the heart. Alas!
How could one lead all people in the world to collectively reform their hearts so as to become loyal ministers and filial sons? Wuxing said:

"The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* encompasses all beings—whether born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation, even up to the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought—throughout the three realms. Now, the ten..."
The meaning of these two categories must certainly not differ. Examining the current text, it appears that only the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of the formless realm are mentioned;
however, all eleven types [of embryonic development] are actually characteristics of the desire realm.

This is likely what the Tathāgata taught according to the needs of the occasion, briefly indicating those aspects that can be verified through both the hidden and the manifest as they appear before us. The "hidden" refers to such things as ghosts, spirits, and numinous beings.

This is illustrated by examples such as fish, birds, turtles, and snakes. If one were to interpret the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) according to the views of the non-Buddhist practitioners at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it would not necessarily be so;
for one might fear that such beings also exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). How could Śūnyatā (the "void-being") possibly reside within the four formless absorptions?
One should know that the subsequent passage discusses the seven destinies (*gati*) at length precisely because the characteristics described herein were not yet complete;

it is only when the preceding and succeeding sections are integrated that the intent of the sutra becomes clear. Within this [section], although the enumeration of births is numerous, the characteristics of the destinies are brief.

If one observes these twelve classes of beings through the lens of the seven destinies over a single lifetime, they still lack the two destinies of hell-beings and asuras. However, as for the remaining five...

The destinies (*gati*) have also not yet been explained in detail. For the time being, it is said in general that because delusion regarding the Truth gives rise to falsehood, there are various classes of beings;
and because the breaking of falsehood reveals the Truth, there are the various stages (*bhūmi*). The intent behind the mutual reversal of delusion and awakening lies in awakening.

By explaining the stages from the perspective of awakening, this serves as a response to the request of Ānanda in the preceding text. Tiantai remarked: "This explanation by Wuxing is most appropriate in principle; only—"
If one were to claim that the statement regarding the *kalala* (embryonic stage) being "formless" (*ārūpya*) implies it pertains to the higher realms, that would be incorrect.

Generally speaking, this text explains the causes of the twelve inversions as being rooted in the six types of deluded conceptualization; however, this is discussed solely with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and thus the destinies therein are limited to the first heaven.
As for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and above, although conceptualization exists there, it is not necessarily like that of sentient beings in the lower stages.
Regarding these six types of confusion, one must rely on four propositions to clarify the relative gravity of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

First, those who possess both deluded thoughts and the six confusions are the sentient beings of the lower realms. Second, those who possess deluded thoughts but lack the six confusions are those in the two upper realms, as well as those in the desire realm who possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such as devas and humans.
Third, those who possess neither deluded thoughts nor the six confusions are those who have transcended the three realms.
This refers to the Sage. It is only lacking the fourth [category], which is the "six types of confusion that are not delusive thoughts.

*Commentary on the Perfect Penetration by the Tiantai Mountain Śramaṇa Chuandeng* **II.

Clarifying the Return from Delusion to Reality and Establishing the Shallow and Deep Stages** **1. General Explanation of the Gradual Stages as the Method for Entering the Path** **2. Concluding the Previous and Introducing the Subsequent** **A. Concluding the Causes of Inversion** Ānanda, within each and every class of these sentient beings, there likewise exists twelve types of inversion.
It is like pressing one’s eyes and seeing illusory flowers; from this, inversions arise. The wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind is fully possessed of such emptiness.
"Delusive and chaotic conceptions.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The twelve inversions range from the inversion of movement and the inversion of desire up to the inversion of killing.
Gūshān says: "'Each possesses' means they mutually possess one another; for within each and every category of mind, the delusive seeds are fully present."
One aspect is manifest and is termed "actualization" (shiqiao); the remainder is latent and hidden, termed "inherent principle" (lizhi).
Since delusion has no inherent substance and is fundamentally the true mind, that which is inherently possessed by delusion is fundamentally the inherent possession of the truth.
When the characteristics of possession and non-possession are both absent and all is empty, only through such realization can one begin to discuss the Way.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding passage uses the metaphor of "pressing on the eyes to see phantom flowers" to illustrate delusion (*mṛṣā*) but not reality (*satya*).

The following passage on the "wondrous, perfect, true, pure, and luminous mind" clarifies reality but does not clarify delusion. This is because the text of the Sūtra is concise yet comprehensive in its meaning;

it employs metaphors to mutually reflect the Dharma and the Dharma to mutually reflect the metaphors. If one were to take the Dharma alone to satisfy the metaphor, [the meaning would remain incomplete].
Then the wondrous, perfect, true, pure, and luminous mind is like the clear sky.
One should take from within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) the analogy of a person with clear, bright eyes looking at a clear sky, seeing only a single, vast, empty clarity with nothing at all;
this is what is called wondrous emptiness, perfect emptiness, true emptiness, pure emptiness, and luminous emptiness—wherein there is nothing that is not possible. And when it reaches its...
When a person stares fixedly at empty space without cause, their eyes become fatigued and they perceive wild flowers appearing out of nowhere in chaotic profusion.
Thus, the original clarity of the eye becomes coarse rather than subtle, biased rather than circular, false rather than true, defiled rather than pure, dark rather than bright.
To apply this analogy to the Dharma, sentient beings are likewise so; they are deluded.
When luminous awareness, based on the manifest, establishes the objective realm, and that objective realm has already been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises.
Within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed. Thus, that precious awakening, the true void, cannot attain its wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous state.
Therefore it is said: this inverted, wondrously perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind is fully possessed of such empty and delusive discursive thoughts.

(2. The Dharma of Gradual Cultivation) You who now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi must establish three gradual stages upon these original causes of your fundamental delusive thoughts, so that they may be eliminated—just as one removes poisonous honey from a clean vessel by using various hot waters mixed with ashes.
After purifying the vessel with incense, one stores the nectar therein. (2. Marking and Listing; 3. Correctly Explaining. First, marking and listing: What are called the three gradual stages?
First, cultivation to eliminate their auxiliary causes; second, true cultivation to excise their primary nature; third, advancement to counteract their manifest karma.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Removing the poisonous honey" is a metaphor for eliminating its auxiliary causes and excising its primary nature.

"Hot water" represents the primary practice (*maulī-pratipatti*), while "ash and incense" represent the auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). "Amṛta" (sweet dew) is an analogy for the principle realized. Gushan says:

"To speak of gradualness" refers to the gradual process of phenomena leading to the perfection of principle; it is not the same as the gradualism of the partial teachings (*pradeśa-śāsana*). Question: Regarding these three...
To which stage among the "Six Degrees of Attainment" (*liujie*) in the Tiantai system does this gradually belong? The answer is:

within the stage of "Name and Word" (*mingzi*), one is able to cultivate *guanxing* (contemplative practice) and give rise to the "True" and "Semblance" [stages]. Changshui says: "The previous question asked at what gradual stage one attains the designation of 'cultivation' (*xiuxing*);
now, as this second [point] is precisely named 'cultivation,' it is called 'true cultivation' (*zhenxiu*)."
[Commentary] Tiantai said: Someone asked, "What are the characteristics of the relative depth and shallowness of the three gradual stages? He replied:

"If one observes the three sections of practice from a general perspective, the stage of 'cultivation through practice' (*xiuxiwei*) is limited to the level of names and words (*mingzi*). The stage of 'true cultivation' (*zhenxiuwei*) corresponds to the stage of 'dry wisdom' (*ganhui*), where contemplative practice (*guanxing*) has become mature.

The stage of 'further advancement' (*zengjinwei*) begins from the first stage of faith (*shixin*) onwards. If one observes the final summary at the end [of the text], [the distinctions are further clarified]."
Thus, by means of these three progressive advancements, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi;

this constitutes the complete possession of all three types of shallow and deep levels. Indeed, within each stage there are both paths of subduing (*vītarāga-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Whether it be the preceding stages up to the "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-sambodhi*), the subsequent mind of "Vajra-Dry Wisdom" (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*), or the "Sublime Enlightenment" (*pravarabodhi*), [each contains these paths].

Regarding the Path of Subjugation (*vītarāga-mārga*): according to the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, within the nature of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*), there is a person named Vajradhvaja-prajñā who, by the power of his great vows, dwells for a hundred kalpas while practicing the conduct of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) in reverse order.

How could it not be that in terms of effort there are also distinctions among the three types—subtle and manifest, shallow and deep, and the cultivation of true cultivation and progressive advancement? If one discusses this...

There are three kinds of things to be abandoned. First, one eliminates the auxiliary causes by first renouncing the five pungent vegetables; this can be permanently severed at the very moment of initial resolve.
As for other auxiliary causes, there may be many types. As the following text states: "Food purified by fire should not be eaten if it possesses a living essence";
thus, all causes that assist the three poisons should be strictly and completely severed. If the second [category] is to be excised...
Regarding its fundamental nature (*dharmatā*): the body and lust are easy to restrain, but the fundamental nature is difficult to excise;

one must sever both the mechanism of lust and the nature itself so that neither remains. However, observing the following passage which states that "the physical bodies of parents do not require the divine eye," it can be known that this [stage] also occupies a position between the internal and external.
Third, it contravenes their manifest karma; if one observes the present text, then...
Beginning with the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) and culminating in the First Abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), one knows thereby that karma is not easily transgressed.
As for Bodhisattvas, they possess the greed of seeking the Buddha-dharma extensively, the anger of vowing to sever ignorance, and the delusion of failing to realize the Buddha-nature.
Śrāvakas were unsettled by the sound of the Great Tree Lute, and Kāśyapa perceived the five sensory objects as the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
And they rise and dance. Since the beginning is verified by the end, how could there not be such things?

Thus, to excavate one's true nature and contravene manifest karma is precisely to align with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Therein, that which was originally confused by causal conditions—the deluded thoughts—is clarified as the object of contemplation.
The establishment of the three gradual stages clarifies the contemplation that is the subject of observation. Now, regarding the object of contemplation in this sutra...

The objects of perception are the same as those elucidated in the *Tiantai Zhiguan*: there are both the delusory and the true. The delusory refers to the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
the true refers to the Three Truths and the Three Tathāgatagarbhas. Indeed, the power and function of this sutra consist in destroying delusion to reveal the truth.
Although it is said that the purpose of destroying delusion lies in realizing the truth, everything elucidated in the preceding sutra is none other than this matter.

Now, the text merely speaks of "establishing the three gradual stages" based on the original disordered thoughts; this follows the momentum of the literary style and is stated in terms of that which is to be destroyed.
The original state of confused thoughts does not go beyond the six types of consciousness. This, moreover, is identical to the initial contemplation of the six consciousnesses in the Tiantai school.
Is it not the case that the statement regarding the establishment of the three gradual stages (*sanzhianci*) encompasses the entire sutra, detailing its beginning and end?
However, if one has profound realization of their ultimate convergence, there is no need for further clarification; yet, if one clings to the vessel [the words], [one must proceed].
Fearing that [previous] explanations of the fish may not have fully exhausted the original intent, I shall therefore explicate these two phrases without avoiding prolixity.

I will extensively collect passages from the entire scripture and apply them through the Tenfold Contemplation Method (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna*) of Tiantai, so that those who seek to advance along the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi may have something upon which to rely.
As for the "Ten Vehicles," they are: 1. Contemplating the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*).

If one proceeds from the *zhang* to the *chi*, and from the *chi* to the *cun*, then the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is taken as the realm of phenomena (*dharma*), while its perfect, pervasive, and constant nature is taken as the realm of principle (*li*). The identity of phenomenon and principle is inconceivable.

By contemplating in this way, the fundamental deluded thoughts within the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) are extinguished. Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
This is liberation. This constitutes the first contemplation of the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), wherein perversions do not arise and one enters *samādhi*.

If, while contemplating this realm, one’s conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) cannot be extinguished and the principle cannot be entered, one should feel compassion for oneself and others, seeking the Way above and transforming those below.
Why? Because when the practitioner contemplates this realm, they know that it is necessarily due to the six types of distracted deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

Sinking into the evil realms, there is suffering and lamentation; yet because one possesses the perfect, universal, and constant [nature], one shall attain the Buddha-way, where there is joy to be looked up to.
Out of compassion for oneself, he makes a vow: "May I dissolve my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas and hope to further scrutinize and eliminate even the subtlest delusions.
Out of compassion for others, he makes a vow: "As long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never [rest]."
In this state, one attains nirvāṇa. Out of compassion for oneself, one makes a vow to attain the fruit of becoming a Treasure King;
out of compassion for others, one makes a vow to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Because these four great vows are made, the six types of deluded conceptualization are extinguished. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka*, at the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment]...
One then attains perfect enlightenment. This is the second [stage]: the true and correct arousal of the bodhicitta, wherein no inversion arises and one enters samādhi.
Regarding the third [stage], skillful settling of the mind in concentration and wisdom:
if one has truly aroused the mind yet still cannot enter samādhi, one should observe each instance of which among the six types of deluded conceptualizations one is currently engaged in.
Perceptions are numerous; yet, although there are many types of perception, they do not transcend the states of dullness and agitation.

If agitated thoughts are prevalent, one should employ the three methods of *śamatha* (calming) to bring them to rest. If dullness and torpor are prevalent, one should employ the three methods of *vipaśyanā* (insight) to illuminate and clarify them.

Dullness and agitation are the diseases; calming and insight are the medicines. Just as taking medicine brings peace to the body and the physician achieves efficacy, if one does not apply the remedies where they are needed, [the cure will fail].

Yet the medicine, conversely, becomes the illness. If quiescence (*jiji*) is excessive, it easily gives rise to drowsiness; if alertness (*xingxing*) is excessive, it easily gives rise to distracted thoughts.
One should therefore balance them to suit the proper occasion. Thus it is said: "Quiescence that is [merely] quiescent is distracted thought; alertness that is [merely] alert is not."

"Vigilant yet tranquil" refers to a state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*), which is not [the goal]. When the mind is thus settled and finds its proper place, it becomes pure, and the ultimate radiance penetrates through;
tranquil illumination encompasses empty space. This is the third skillful method for settling the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, wherein inversion does not arise and one enters *samādhi*.
Fourth, regarding the "Pervasiveness of Dharma-Destruction": previously, one proceeded by means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* toward...

The upper [aspect] descends; the upper should enter *samādhi*, while the lower should be inverted so that it does not arise. If one neither enters nor breaks [this state], what obstacle or covering could there be?

Furthermore, the dharma that is broken would not be all-pervasive. Moreover, one must investigate and break through the six deluded妄 (delusive) thoughts regarding the realm of the Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).
Since the fundamental [reality] is not identical to the ten dharmas, how is it that it suddenly becomes identical to the ten dharmas? For this reason, it is necessary [to investigate].
To break [the delusion] by unifying wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the *tathāgatagarbha*, one must realize that the ten realms are all "neither" (non-existent).
This serves to break through the pervasive nature of dharmas. Since they were originally not separate from the ten dharmas, how could they suddenly become separate?

Therefore, they must be realized as "immediate. By unifying wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the *tathāgatagarbha*, one realizes that the ten realms are all "immediate. Yet, this realization of immediacy necessarily involves both immediacy and separation; it is immediate while being separated.

Detaching yet immediately uniting—by joining the wondrous clarity that neither ceases nor arises with the Tathāgata-garbha—one realizes that throughout the ten realms, there is detachment and immediate union, detachment and non-being, being and non-being, and immediate union and non-union.
By means of this, one breaks through the pervasiveness of phenomena. When neither uniting nor detaching, the path of Bodhi is accomplished;
this is the fourth stage of breaking through the pervasiveness of phenomena, wherein inverted thoughts do not arise, and one enters samādhi. The fifth is the penetration of consciousness.
As for "stopping": since the three types of cessation have already destroyed the six kinds of distraction, this mind ought to accord with principle; why then does it still not do so?
You should further examine minutely that within all dharmas there is the nature of peace and bliss; why then do you suddenly discard them? Therefore it is said:
"To perceive seeing as non-seeing—this is itself Nirvana. Within all dharmas, everything is the net of Māra.
Suddenly they are taken together. Therefore it is said: "To establish knowledge within seeing is the very root of ignorance. It is also said:
"Because one is turned by external objects, within this state, the great is viewed as small; this is to be open yet obstructed. If one can turn objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata;
this is to be obstructed yet open. This is called the fifth consciousness: penetrating openness and obstruction so that delusions do not arise, thereby entering [the Way].
This is samādhi. Regarding the sixth [section], the "Excellently Cultivated Factors of the Path":

once the practitioner has recognized what constitutes penetration and obstruction, how should they cultivate the factors of the path upon the level ground? Within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is both the primary and the auxiliary.
The primary refers to the secret cause, such as śamatha and so forth; the auxiliary refers to the myriad practices, such as the perfect and sudden four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
The Sūtra says: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices.

Because one skillfully cultivates it, the six types of distracted delusive thoughts are extinguished. This is the sixth stage: skillfully cultivating the factors of the path so that inversion does not arise, thereby entering samādhi.
Regarding the seventh stage, the "Aids for Counteracting and Opening": having already been able to skillfully cultivate the path...

This chapter will certainly enable one to flow into the three gates of liberation. If difficulties arise before one has entered [the path], or if difficulties arise while one is attempting to save others, how should these be countered?
If the difficulty of the affliction of stinginess (*mātsarya*) arises, one should contemplate that stinginess itself is bodhi.
Whether it is accepted or not accepted, both accepted and not accepted, or even the fivefold non-acceptance—this non-acceptance is itself *dāna*. The meaning of *dāna* encompasses...
Sixth: The Dharma of Fearlessness for Requisites. Herein, the first, second, and third [types of] corruption are likewise [treated].
Furthermore, if one has difficult-to-guard latent tendencies from past habituation regarding the corruption of sexual misconduct, the Buddha enjoins the exclusive recitation of divine mantras.

This constitutes the seventh remedy that assists in opening [the path) so that perversions do not arise and one enters *samādhi*. Eighth: Skillful Knowledge of Successive Stages. If the practitioner...

If one does not understand the stages [of the fivefold teaching], there is the fault of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), whereby one claims to have attained what has not been attained and realized what has not been realized.

One should know that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha; this is the stage of the Principle (*li-ji*). To be able to understand it in this way is the stage of the Name (*ming-zi-ji*).

When the object of contemplation accords with the principle, it is the stage of Contemplative Practice (*guan-xing-ji*). When the six sense faculties are purified, it is the stage of Similarity (*xiang-si-ji*). Constantly...
The manifestation of the mind’s divisions is the stage of identity with reality (*tathatā*). Perfect enlightenment is the stage of ultimate identity.

This constitutes the eighth [stage], wherein one enters *samādhi* by not giving rise to inverted views regarding the sequence of stages. As for the ninth, the accomplishment of patient endurance (*kṣānti*):
When a practitioner walks the path, if they are not yet mature, many obstacles and difficulties will arise; one must always practice patient endurance (*kṣānti*).
The Tathāgata, in his *Self-Explanatory Teaching Without Question*, clarifies the fiftyfold realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) precisely to demonstrate the method of patient endurance.
Therefore it is said: "The accomplishment of disruption arises from your own aggregate-mind. If the host is deluded, the guest gains the advantage. One should remain in *dhyāna* at that very spot.
When one awakens to this, there is no fault; thus, those demonic activities can do nothing to you. This is the ninth [stage]:
being able to practice patience so that inversions do not arise, thereby entering samādhi. Regarding the tenth, "being free from attachment to dharmas":

one is able to cultivate all vehicles and abide in both the forceful and the gentle methods. One must have a corresponding resonance with the constant mind; if attachment to dharmas arises, one will remain [stuck] therein.

This is like being on the verge of ascending when one collapses, or on the verge of passing through when one falls. Therefore it is said that sentient beings are deluded and confused, failing to reflect upon themselves;
each rests according to their own habitual deluded minds, claiming this to be the ultimate ground of refuge and peace, and declaring themselves to have attained the unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Thus, the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* fail to progress further. You all—

Maintain the mind and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata. Transmit this Dharma-gate to future generations after my parinirvāṇa, so that their bodies and minds may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, perfecting Bodhi until there is nothing further to be attained.

This is what is meant by departing from the delusion of attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path, thereby not giving rise to it and entering samādhi. Furthermore, the original distracted thoughts are themselves the head [of the matter].
In the first fascicle, it was stated that those who take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀緣心 or "clinging-and-conditioning mind") as their own nature are using the root of birth and death.

When they cultivate true cultivation and progress, they realize that the second root—the original, pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana—is the *vijñāna* (consciousness) which is fundamentally bright and capable of producing all conditions, yet is itself left behind by those very conditions.
This is precisely what the current text refers to as the fundamental deluded thoughts, which expand upon the preceding discussion.
The various conditions arising from the root of birth and death— such as the conditions of form, sound, and so forth— are the six distractions that lack any underlying order.
As for the method of true cultivation, it simply consists in directly pointing to the perfect penetration of the six sense faculties,
turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature, and restoring this original luminosity.

II. The Correct Explanation of the Three [Practices] (First: Cultivating Practice to Eliminate Its Contributing Causes; First: The Inquiry). What are the contributing causes? II. The Explanation (First: General Clarification of the Four Kinds of Food). Ānanda, all beings of the twelve classes in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power; they dwell in dependence upon the four kinds of food, namely:
morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact food (*sparśa-āhāra*), volition food (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*), and consciousness food (*vijñāna-āhāra*).

Therefore, the Buddha says that all sentient beings dwell in dependence upon food. II. The Specific Severing of the Five Pungent Herbs (First: Stating the Intent). Ānanda, because all sentient beings eat what is sweet, they give rise to it; because they eat poison, they suffer.

Death. ○ (2. Proper Abandonment; 2a. First, Exhorting Abandonment to Reveal Assistance and Open the Way) These sentient beings seeking *samādhi* should sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world.
If these five pungent vegetables are eaten cooked, they arouse lust; if eaten raw, they increase anger. ○ (2b. Clarifying Faults and Sufferings According to Persons; 2ba.

First, Faults and Sufferings of the Dharma-Preacher) In such a world, those who eat pungent things—even if they can proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures—will be loathed for their foul stench by the devas and ṛṣis of the ten directions, who will all distance themselves from them. All...
Hungry ghosts and the like lick their lips and mouths after eating that food; they constantly dwell with such ghosts, their merit daily diminishes, and they gain no benefit.
(2. Faults of the Seated Meditator) When those who consume pungent foods practice samādhi, Bodhisattvas, devas, seers, and the virtuous deities of the ten directions do not come to protect them;
instead, a powerful Māra gains the opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to preach the Dharma to them.
Those who revile the prohibitions and precepts, praising lust, anger, and ignorance, will at the end of their lives become members of the retinue of Māra;

when their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell. (Three Conclusions) Ānanda, for one who cultivates Bodhi, the permanent severance of the five pungent roots is called the first progressive stage of cultivation.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Regarding the four types of nutriment, "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) among humans refers to that which must be taken in distinct portions.

Ghosts and spirits have "nutriment by contact" (*sparśa-āhāra*); they are satisfied merely by inhaling the scent of contact. Those in the *dhyāna* heavens have "nutriment by volition" (*manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra*); when nutriment arrives, they are satisfied simply by thinking of it.

Those in the realm of consciousness have "nutriment by consciousness" (*vijñāna-āhāra*); as they lack form or color, they subsist solely through conscious ideation. This directly clarifies that all sentient beings [are sustained by these].
One dwells in dependence upon food; yet, because of this food, one must sever the five pungent plants through the precepts without needing to be led by others.
Within, the five pungent plants give rise to lust and anger, while externally they attract malevolent spirits; therefore, they are called "auxiliary causes. Wuxing said:

By mentioning the benefits and harms of eating sweets and other foods, he intends to eliminate the auxiliary cause that consists of the five pungent plants, for the five pungent plants are capable of inciting lust and anger.
It is like poisoned food that leads to death. Regarding the "five pungent vegetables," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states they are leek, garlic, scallion, onion, and *hiṅgu*.
Master Ying said that *hiṅgu* is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound; its correct form is *xingyi* (興宜).
The Tripiṭaka Master Cimin stated that its root is like a radish, and it emits a pungent odor when exposed above ground. Cimin had not yet reached that land by the winter solstice.
Seeing that the seedlings [of this term] exist here [in China], it was not translated [into Chinese].

[Commentary: The *Yunjian Buyi* states: "The *Cheng weishi lun* [identifies four types of nutriment]: first, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), which has transformation and decay as its characteristic;

second, contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*), which has the contact with objects as its characteristic; third, volition-food (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*), which has longing and hope as its characteristic; fourth, consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*)."

Their characteristic is grasping. The three—edible food consisting of odors, tastes, and tangibles—are able to function as nutriment at the time of transformation, because at the time of transformation, visible form is no longer functional.
Contact-food refers to tainted contact; it is able to function as nutriment at the time of seizing an object.
Volition-food refers to tainted volition; it is able to function as nutriment by longing for desirable objects. Consciousness-food refers to...
Contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) functions as nutriment through the power of growth conferred by morsel-food, contact, volition, and consciousness.

Xīlìyún states that all four nutriments have the meaning of providing sustenance and benefit. "Morsel" (*kavaḍīkāra*) refers to physical segments, having the three objects of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility as its essence.

Upon entering the abdomen, it undergoes transformation and decay, thereby nourishing the sense faculties. In ancient translations of the sutras and vinayas, this is often termed "lump food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), but its meaning is thus restricted;
