It is also like being born from the womb. Because they perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas, they are said to be "direct sons of the Buddha. Wēn-líng says:

From the initial generation of the mind until birth in the noble state, it is called entering the holy womb (*āryagarbha*). From the fulfillment of skillful means until the stage of the youthful prince (*kumārabhūta*), it is called nurturing the holy womb.
Since the merit of this nurturing has now reached its completion, it is metaphorically likened to a prince emerging from the womb.
○ (The Stage of the Ten Consecrations): This represents the completion of one's personhood, just as a great king of a nation delegates various state affairs to his crown prince;
when the son of a Kṣatriya king has reached maturity and is presented for consecration, it is called the "Stage of Consecration."
[Commentary] Gushan says: "This signifies that he has become a full person capable of performing the Buddha-work. The terms 'Prince' (Taizi) and 'Heir Apparent' (Shizǐ) differ only in their phrasing.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* states: 'The Prince was met at Shouzhi. The *Book of Rites* refers to the 'Wenwang Shizǐ' (The Heir Apparent of King Wen). These were all sons of the Son of Heaven.
Regarding the arrangement of the consecration (Abhiṣeka), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'Born of a Wheel-Turning Sage King...'"
The mother and son possess the physical marks of a sovereign queen; she sits upon a precious golden throne supported by white elephants.
A great net-curtain is spread, various musical instruments are played, and the waters of the four great oceans are taken and placed within a golden vase.
The king holds this vase and pours it over the crown of the prince’s head; at that moment, he is said to have received the royal office. The Bodhisattva’s reception of his office was likewise so.
It is so. Because the water of the Buddhas' wisdom is poured upon their crowns, they are called "Bodhisattvas who have received the office of Great Wisdom.
That tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), is named the "Anointed Bodhisattva" (*abhiṣeka-bodhisattva*); now, this [stage of] the Ten Abidings also partially attains this.

Nevertheless, from the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-tathatā*) onward in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there is always the application of wisdom; regarding the power of that wisdom, there is no lack of distinction in its excellence or inferiority. Therefore, at the beginning—
Abiding in the worlds of a hundred Buddhas, they manifest the images of ten realms to benefit and assist sentient beings. In each successive stage, they enter deeper and become increasingly superior.

What is elucidated in the sutras does so according to a single specific meaning; however, if one considers how a single stage possesses the merits of all stages, then all ten meanings are fully present.
As it is with the Ten Abidings, so it is for all that follow.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is already called "cultivation by conditions" (*yuānxiū*), because one has not yet seen the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
From the time one ascends to the stages onward, it is called "true cultivation" (*zhēnxiū*), because one truly sees the Buddha-nature. The first stage is named "arousing the mind" (*fāxīn*);
this arises through the merit of the tenth *praṇidhicitta* stage in destroying one grade of ignorance (*avidyā*), thereby manifesting the Buddha-nature of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
This dwelling merely signifies that the Buddha-nature has manifested before one, yet true cultivation and practice have not yet been added.
Upon reaching the second dwelling, one treads upon the previously wondrous mind to form the ground;

thus, with the beginning of "partial true awakening" (fen-zhen shi-jue) illuminating "partial true original awakening" (fen-zhen ben-ju), the process of cultivating and rectifying it is named the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (zhi-di zhu). Upon reaching the third dwelling...

When both the ground of mind and its cognitive activity are clearly understood, and when both the beginning and the fundamental source are simultaneously forgotten, one is then able to traverse the ten directions without obstruction;

this is called the "Abode of Cultivation. These two abodes constitute the true cultivation of the successive stages of practice, just as a person of the world must first complete their worldly affairs before entering [the path].
The parents provide the womb; once one has entered the womb, there is nothing more to do than to nurture and sustain it, thereby expanding upon prior accomplishments.

Therefore, the fourth stage is called "Noble Birth," the fifth is called "Perfected," the sixth is called "Right Mind," the seventh is called "Non-retrogression," the eighth is called "Candala" (Childhood Purity), and the ninth is called "Dharma Prince"—all of which refer to growth and development.

As for merit, there is no further mention of the matter of progressive cultivation. Even if such were to exist, it would not go beyond the fundamental and initial objects and wisdom of the second and third stages (*vihāra*).
Having emerged from the womb of the sages and manifested as a perfected person, the entrustment of the transformative path is termed the "Consecration Stage" (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).
It is, for example, like a person in the world who, by virtue of the karmic actions of previous lives, attains the state of being human. This signifies...

This demonstrates that the man is capable of inheriting the family business; it is only upon reaching the tenth stage of practice (*daśabhūmi*) that the deeds performed by the Dharma Prince are clarified.
○ (The first of the forty stages: the Stage of Joy). Ānanda, once these good sons have become children of the Buddha, they are fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas.
To accord with all things is called the Practice of Joy. (2) The Practice of Benefiting Others: To be skillfully able to benefit all sentient beings is called the Practice of Benefiting Others.
[Commentary] Wénlǐng says: Because he possesses the wondrous virtues of a Buddha, he is able to accord with all things throughout the ten directions, such that there is nothing he cannot adapt to.

Since he is fully equipped with the benefits for both self and others, and both the capacity and the response are joyful, it is named "Joy. He skillfully dedicates his wondrous virtues to benefit others.
Therefore, it is called "Beneficial.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding ten stages of abiding clarify that the Dharma Prince’s own awakening is already perfected.

From the ten practices onward, it clarifies the guidance and benefitting of all sentient beings. Someone may ask: According to the Three Contemplations elucidated by Tiantai, starting from the stage of "Names" (nāmamātra)...

One comes to cultivate the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional; reaching the stage of the seventh faith, one destroys the delusions of views and thoughts as a practice for self-benefit.

From the eighth faith onward, one cultivates the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional to destroy the delusions of "dust-sand" (infinite) phenomena as a practice for the benefit of others.

From the tenth faith onward, one cultivates the contemplation of the Middle Way to destroy the delusions of ignorance; ascending to the first dwelling (*prathamābhūmi*) and beyond is termed benefiting both oneself and others.
Question: The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* clarifies that one benefits sentient beings only upon reaching the stage of the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*).

Why is this so? Answer: The statement that the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) break delusions to distinguish between self-awakening and awakening others is merely a provisional explanation.
Furthermore, this refers to a sequential meaning rather than a definitive discourse. Why?

This refers to the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, who cultivates the three contemplations within a single mind, destroys the three delusions within a single mind, and manifests the three enlightenments within a single mind.
How could there be such a sequential order? For example, when one first practices the five grades of faith, their sympathetic joy, reading, and reciting are for self-benefit;
yet in the middle stage they preach the Dharma, and in the final stage they concurrently practice both types of the six perfections (the six perfections of correct practice).
Is this not the awakening of one who seeks the benefit of others? Nevertheless, within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*), there is no absence of gradual stages.
As it is said: "Though the principle is suddenly awakened, all delusions are extinguished simultaneously"—this reveals the path of perfect cultivation and perfect destruction.

"Matters are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through successive stages"—this clarifies the meaning of gradual cultivation and gradual destruction. Without the gradual, there would be no way to ascend.
Sudden. Without the sudden, there would be no means to harmonize the gradual; when both are fully integrated, the Way of the Perfectly Sudden (yuantun) is finally complete.

Nevertheless, there is a sequence for contemplation and practice, namely the Five Ranks (wupin). There is also a sequence for the stage of semblance (xiangsi), from the seventh faith downward, wherein one destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (jiansi-huo) to realize the principle of emptiness (kongli).
At the eighth and ninth faiths, one destroys the delusions of "dust-sands" (chen-sha-huo) to...

Realizing conventional truth: this refers to breaking through the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) during the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) to enter the first stage of abiding (*prathama-vihāra*), thereby realizing the middle truth. This is the sequence for attaining partial realization of the true.
In the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one breaks through ten grades of ignorance to abide in the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

In the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one breaks through twenty grades of ignorance to emerge from the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). In the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), one breaks through thirty grades of [ignorance]...

This refers to the process of further cultivating the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to ascend to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), thereby realizing the principle of the Middle Way;

this is the sequence for ultimate realization. Once the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) has realized the True Principle, they further dwell for a thousand kalpas and practice in reverse the conduct of ordinary beings to shatter and sever the subtle, dust-like shadows of conditions. Thus, regarding all dharma-gates, there is nothing that is not... [realized].
It is not yet exhausted. One must further shatter one grade of fundamental, subtle ignorance to enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment;

only upon attaining perfect bodhi and returning to the state of non-attainment is there ultimate consummation. This present discussion concerns the sequential order within the "partial realization" (fenzhen) stage, specifically within the midst of what is otherwise non-sequential.
A Bodhisattva of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*) is already able to manifest as a Buddha across the hundred realms to guide and benefit all beings.

How could birth [in this stage] wait until the tenth practice before benefiting sentient beings? Having become a child of the Buddha, one is already fully endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas;
this summarizes the merits of the Abiding of Consecration (*abhiṣeka*). To "accord with the ten directions" clearly elucidates the characteristics of the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*).
It is like a crown prince of a kingdom who, having already perfected his own virtue, leads all under heaven.
There are none who do not look up to his virtue and partake of its fragrance, following him and complying with him. Not only do others rejoice, but he himself also finds joy in this;
therefore, such conduct is called the "Practice of Joy. He then employs this virtue to renew his people, so that all sentient beings receive benefit;
this is called the "Practice of Beneficence."
○ (The Third: Practice Free from Hatred) To awaken oneself and awaken others so as to achieve freedom from opposition and rejection is called the practice free from hatred.
[Commentary] Wenling says: "Hatred arises from opposition. Changshui says: "Because one awakens oneself, ignorance cannot oppose wisdom;
because one awakens others, sentient beings cannot reject their transformation. Since both self-benefit and benefit for others are accomplished simultaneously, there is no hatred."
Regret.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The practice of joy is self-awakening; the practice of benefiting others is awakening others.

Although one initially awakens oneself, ignorance may still not be in accord with that wisdom. Furthermore, although one subsequently awakens other sentient beings, it is not necessarily the case that...
They reject its transformation. Now, however, they do not oppose it nor reject it, and thus they are free from anger and resentment.

(4. Inexhaustible Practice) To give birth to all categories [of beings] throughout the limits of the future, to be equal across the three periods of time, and to penetrate the ten directions—this is called inexhaustible practice.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "The birth of various types" refers to manifesting bodies within the ten realms, where these manifestations further produce further manifestations.
Exhausting the limits of the future, they benefit sentient beings without end; vertically pervading the three periods of time and horizontally encompassing the ten directions.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The birth of various kinds" refers to the realization of the essential virtues inherent in the nature.

This is to give rise to function from this very essence, like a sovereign mani-jewel raining down fruits without end. At all places throughout the ten directions and at all times throughout the three periods, there is nowhere that is not the locus of the Bodhisattva’s responsive transformations.
These transformations further produce further transformations; thus, the names of these inexhaustible practices are endless.

○ (5. The Practice of Being Free from Delusion and Confusion) To attain non-erroneous understanding of all various dharma-gates as being identical is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "Exquisite wisdom thoroughly penetrates that although the myriad dust-like dharma-gates have different names and distinct explanations, they all return to a single principle;
therefore, one is free from delusion and confusion."
[Tiantai’s Commentary: Above, we proceeded from the single essence to give rise to the myriad functions; viewed from the perspective of their differences, it seemed as though there were errors.
Now, we unify all things to return them to the identical essence; when speaking from the standpoint of universal sameness, there is no delusion or confusion.

○ (Sixth, the Manifestation of the Good): Within the identical, a multitude of differences manifests; because each distinct characteristic is seen as being uniformly named "good," it is called the "Manifestation of the Good.

[Commentary] Guishan says: "To manifest difference within identity is to realize principle through phenomena; to see identity within distinct characteristics is to realize phenomena through principle."

This is because it is the principle itself. Wēnlíng says: "Because there is no delusion or confusion, one is able to manifest various dharma-gates in mutual correspondence, responding appropriately with perfect fusion and mastery;
this is what is called 'skillful manifestation' (sukhāvatī/sunyata)."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding "Inexhaustible Practices" may be said to manifest a multitude of differences within the identical.

However, although they manifest difference, they have not yet manifested identity. Next, the "Practices Free from Delusion and Confusion" may be said to perceive identity within each and every distinct characteristic.
Yet, while they manifest identity, they do not necessarily manifest difference. Now, having already manifested [identity] within the identical...

That which appears as the same within the different, and that which appears as different within the same, may be called "manifesting difference within sameness" and "manifesting sameness within difference.
Because there is no mutual obstruction between difference and sameness, it is called "skillful manifestation."
○ (Seventh: Practice of Non-Attachment) Thus, even unto the atoms that fill the empty space of the ten directions—within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions appear;
yet the appearance of the atoms and the appearance of the worlds do not obstruct or hinder one another. This is called the practice of non-attachment.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This arises from the expansion and perfect integration of the excellent practices of Subhūti. Manifesting lands within the sensory objects is called "manifesting realms";
not destroying the characteristics of the sensory objects is called "manifesting objects."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding "Inexhaustible Practice" is spoken of in terms of the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The "Practice of Departing from Delusion and Confusion" is spoken of in terms of the principle dharma-realm.
The "Practice of Skillful Manifestation" is spoken of in terms of the dharma-realm of both principle and phenomena.

Now, the "Practice of Non-attachment" refers to the ten realms of sentient beings and their environments (*āśraya*) manifesting as realms and objects (*viṣaya*) that do not obstruct one another; this is spoken of in terms of phenomena-interacting-with-phenomena (*shishi*).
This refers to the unimpeded Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). These four types of Dharma-realms may be correlated with the Three Truths of Tiantai:
the Principle Dharma-realm corresponds to the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the Phenomenal Dharma-realm corresponds to the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

and both the Phenomenon-Principle Dharma-realm and the Phenomenon-Phenomenon Dharma-realm correspond to the Middle Way, which simultaneously negates and illuminates the two extremes. When conditions are forgotten, the thousand suchnesses manifest brilliantly; thus it responds to things.
This refers to the mutual fusion of the hundred realms.
(8. Honored Practice): The various manifestations that appear before one are all called the "First Pāramitā," and this is termed the "Honored Practice."
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "All that is manifested is the unconditioned, wondrous power of the inherent virtue of *prajñā*, spontaneously and sovereignly accomplished;
therefore, it is called 'venerable. That which is termed the foremost *pāramitā* by the *Vajra* [Sūtra] is precisely *prajñā*."
Wuxing said: "Wisdom (*prajñā*) is light and thin, whereas *prajñāpāramitā* is honored and respected;
hence it is so named. [Commentary] Tiantai says: "The various manifestations refer to the four kinds of manifestations mentioned above.
Because there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all are *prajñāpāramitā*; thus they are called the 'Honored Practice.'"
○ (9. Practice of the Nine Wholesome Dharmas) Thus, this perfect integration that can accomplish the norms of all Buddhas of the ten directions is called the practice of wholesome dharmas. ○ (10.
Practice of Reality) Each and every one of these is pure, untainted, the single true, unconditioned nature that is primordial; therefore, it is called the practice of reality.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The superior practice of the Dharma takes the entirety of nature as its basis for cultivation; thus it constitutes the Dharma-standards. This true practice takes the entirety of cultivation as being nature;
thus all are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Wenling says: "Summarizing the preceding practices, none are not the wondrous functioning of the original nature.
Although their manifestations are myriad and diverse, their essential nature is one and true; therefore, they are called 'true'. Thus it is.

From the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) up to the final stage, one does not depart from the preceding dharmas; yet, they are established as distinct stages following one another so that the practitioner may progress through each level,
expand their innate awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*), purify the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and bring the fruit of Buddhahood to maturity.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Rules" (*gui-ze*) refer to wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). For if that which is produced were subject to exhaustion, it would be insufficient to serve as the rules for all Buddhas.
If it could not be skillfully manifested, it would likewise be insufficient to serve as the rules for all Buddhas.

If manifestations of sense-fields (*viṣaya*) and realms (*dhātu*) were subject to obstruction or limitation, they too would be insufficient to serve as the rules for all Buddhas. [Thus, it must manifest in various ways.]
The former [view] falls into frivolity, and its wisdom is insufficient to serve as a model for the Buddhas.
Only when there is such perfect interfusion can it be considered a wholesome dharma for attaining Buddhahood.

If one contemplates the four kinds of dharmadhātus but fails to realize that they are intrinsically possessed (*prakṛti-prakṛta*), and instead treats movement as something produced through effort, it cannot be regarded as true practice. Only when...
Because one deeply realizes that each and every [practice] is pure, untainted, the single true unconditioned nature, and is thus inherently so, it is called "True Practice.
Regarding these ten types of practice, there should be two expositions: the vertical and the horizontal.

The vertical corresponds to what is taught in the Sūtra—the sequential order of the stages, where each successive level is increasingly superior and none are transgressed. The horizontal refers to the ten...

The positions of the dharmas each possess [all others] in their respective stages; yet, were they not arranged in sequential order (xingbu), it would be insufficient to exhaust the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).

Were they not perfectly interfused (yuanrong), it would be insufficient to manifest the inherent completeness of nature. Thus, every single aspect of the dharmas is like a linked chain that cannot be untied, and like the constellations in the sky that cannot be diminished.

○ (The Second of the Fifty Dedications: First, the Dedication of Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings) Ānanda, when these good men have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of attaining Buddhahood—being pure, refined, and true, and having distanced themselves from all lingering afflictions—they shall deliver sentient beings while eliminating the very notion of "delivering" them.

Turning their minds toward the unconditioned and heading toward the path of Nirvāṇa, this is called the Dedication of Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: In the preceding ten abodes and ten practices, the mind for transcending the mundane was great while the practice of great compassion was deficient.

Here, one must be aided by compassionate vows to dwell in the mundane world to benefit living beings. By turning the true toward the mundane and turning wisdom toward compassion, the true and the mundane are made perfectly interfused and wisdom and compassion are non-dual.
This is called the Ten Dedications, also known as the Ten Vows. It fulfills the spiritual...

This refers to the matter of penetrating to the far reaches where all lingering afflictions are eliminated, as documented previously regarding the non-obstruction between present objects and present realms.

That is to say, when this practice is fulfilled, one should cultivate the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Because the practice of dedication possesses the deepest compassion and vows, its function lies in the deliverance of sentient beings.

However, if one perceives that there are beings to be delivered, one immediately enters the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and turns away from the path to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is necessary—
"Eliminating and transcending signs means turning the mind away from the unconditioned toward the path of Nirvana.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Although the preceding ten practices describe various wondrous functions, in essence they are all the Bodhisattva preparing the instruments for saving sentient beings before actually delivering them. Thus, although there is the act of saving beings, it is simply called "skillfulness."

"Benefit" refers merely to the practice of bringing others prosperity. Now, having fulfilled the supernatural powers and completed the work of a Buddha, such that all Buddha-activities are pure, refined, and true, and have distanced themselves from all lingering afflictions, only then can one say:
"I shall deliver sentient beings. However, if one does not realize that the four marks of sentient beings are fundamentally empty, there will be no sentient beings to be delivered.
To deliver [beings] while remaining within the realm of signs is contrary to the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus, the path to nirvāṇa is far removed.
One must, while delivering sentient beings, eliminate the very notion of "delivering," and furthermore, turn this unconditioned mind back toward the path of nirvāṇa.
To be able to practice in this way is called the dedication of saving and protecting all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings.
This is precisely the meaning of Master Zhiyi’s statement: "The Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have been devoured by me in a single mouth;
what sentient beings are there to deliver?"
○ (2. Non-destroying Dedication) Destroying that which can be destroyed and remaining far removed from all forms of negation is called the non-destroying dedication.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Destroying that which can be destroyed" is explained in terms of the objects to be destroyed; "remaining far removed from all negations" is discussed with respect to the wisdom capable of destroying.
Not perceiving the characteristics of anything that can be destroyed is what is termed "non-destroying."

[Commentary] Tiantai said: "That which can be destroyed refers to the sentiment that there are sentient beings to be saved; that which cannot be destroyed refers to the Dharma for saving sentient beings.
To be far removed from all things to be abandoned refers to dwelling in a mind of non-action (asaṃskṛta) while abandoning the attachment to the city of Nirvāṇa;
that which cannot be abandoned refers to turning the mind of non-action back toward Nirvāṇa."
In the progression of the Path, at the beginning one turns from principle toward phenomena; at the end, one turns from phenomena back toward principle.
Whether they exist or whether they perish, they cannot be named. Yet naming does not destroy this turning toward [the ultimate].

○ (The Dedication Equal to All Buddhas): Original enlightenment is profoundly still, and its awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas; this is called the dedication equal to all Buddhas. ○ (The Dedication Reaching All Places):
Through the brilliant manifestation of essential truth, the ground is like the ground of the Buddhas; this is called the dedication reaching all places.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The 'awakening' mentioned above refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), while this stage refers to principle (*li*). Since the essence of cause and effect is identical, it is called 'equal' (*sama*) and 'reaching' (*prāpta*).
[Tiantai’s Sub-commentary] Tiantai says:
From the time the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Abode, the Consecrated (*abhiṣikta*), first ascended to the position of the crown prince, by means of the non-... [text continues]

Through the practice of functional cultivation (*prayoga-caryā*), one masters all dharma-gates; having achieved this, one should deliver sentient beings, whereby the path of benefiting oneself and others is complete.
Having shattered the twenty-two grades of ignorance, the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) that is realized is profound, tranquil, and eternally abiding.
This enlightenment is equal to that of the Buddhas and is named as such; it is dedicated to being identical with all Buddhas. This is explained from the perspective of the capacity for realization.
This is spoken from the perspective of the wisdom that realizes it. When the awakening that awakens to this is refined and truly illuminated, the stages become like the Buddha-stages;
this is called the dedication "Reaching All Places. This is spoken in terms of the principle realized.

○ (The Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit): Because the worlds and Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction, it is called the dedication of the treasury of inexhaustible merit.
[Commentary] Tianru’s Supplement states: According to the interpretation of Wuxing, the world is the principle (*li*) and the Tathāgata is wisdom (*jñāna*).
[Sub-commentary] Tiantai says: When the principle of the world and the wisdom of the Tathāgata mutually interpenetrate, then wisdom illuminates.
When objects are illuminated by wisdom within their respective spheres, and when object and wisdom are mutually fused so as to attain unimpededness—
like two mirrors reflecting one another such that images and light are layered upon each other in infinite succession— it is therefore called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.

○ (The Dedication of Roots of Goodness in Accordance with Equality): Within the stages that are identical to the stage of the Buddhas, each gives rise to the causes of purity; by relying on these causes and manifesting them, one takes up the path to Nirvana—this is called the dedication of roots of goodness in accordance with equality.
[Commentary] Gushan says: Within the ground of principle of all Buddhas, one gives rise to the true cause of the myriad practices.
Relying upon this true cause, one manifests and radiates [virtue] pervasively throughout the Dharma-realm to attain the path of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Because these practices arise from principle, they are called "conformity to equality. That which can produce the fruit of the Path is termed "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The pure causes produced within each stage" refers to the merits of the myriad practices (saṃbhāra) developed within the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*) from the moment of self-realization of the truth onward.
This is what the Sūtra means by "being fully endowed with the myriad practices.

Tiantai clarifies that when the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is manifested at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), all the merits of the myriad practices appear simultaneously. Now, regarding this...

This is recounted retrospectively within the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Because it relies upon causes to manifest and take up the path to *nirvāṇa*, it is called the "Dedication of Wholesome Roots that Accord with Equality.

(7) The Dedication of Contemplating Sentient Beings with Equanimity: Since the true roots have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own original nature; this nature being perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings.
"Birth" is defined as the dedication that accords with the contemplation of all sentient beings.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The nature of impartial roots of goodness is truly perfect and harmonious, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Therefore, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature. Since my own goodness is perfected, I am able to bring the goodness of all sentient beings to fulfillment."
Because the faculties are without omission and without distinction of high or low, it is called "conformity with equal contemplation.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Since the true faculties have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own original nature.
One can see that in the preceding stage, the various causes for producing purity arise solely from the inherent nature. This is Tiantai’s elucidation of the Dharma-gate of the inherent nature.

There is self and there is other. Previously, when discussing equality and the faculties, I spoke of the "self"; now, saying that all sentient beings are my own original nature, I speak precisely of the "other.
Because this nature is perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings.
Not losing sight of sentient beings means observing self and other with equanimity; this is called "conforming to the equal contemplation of all sentient beings."
Dedication.

○ (The Dedication of the Aspect of the Eightfold True Suchness): This is the dedication of the aspect of true suchness, wherein all phenomena are free from all marks, and both "conforming" and "detaching" are non-existent. It is called the dedication of the aspect of true suchness.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "That all dharmas are provisional" refers to the emptiness that is free from all marks;
"the Middle" refers to non-attachment to these two.
[Sub-commentary] Tiantai says: "That all dharmas" means the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*) manifest brilliantly; "free from all marks" means...
The hundred realms are mutually interfused. For one who is free from attachment to both identity and difference, there is nothing that is not the wondrous nature.

Thus, when the Tathāgata reveals his own realization, stating that the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous primordial mind, and so forth, are "neither identical to nor different from" all things—this meaning is the same as the principle of being simultaneously identical to and different from, and neither identical nor different.

(9) Unbound Liberation Dedication (*abaddha-vimokṣa-pariṇāmanā*): Truly attaining suchness so that there is no obstruction throughout the ten directions is called the dedication of unbound liberation. (10) Infinite Dharma Realm Dedication (*dharmadhātu-apramāṇa-pariṇāmanā*):
The perfect fulfillment of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) such that the measure of the dharma realm is extinguished is called the dedication of the infinite dharma realm.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "The wondrous nature of the three virtues is here perfectly realized; because one no longer perceives the distinctions of high and low among the ten realms, it is said that 'the measure of the dharma-realm ceases.
Wenglun says: 'Initially realizing the nature-virtues, one considers them equal to the Buddha, identical to the Buddha, and reaching all places.
All of these involve the persistence of the perception of measure; thus, the nature of the dharma-realm has not yet [been fully realized].'"
One departs from the limited. When the inherent virtues are perfected, one then extinguishes the perception of limitation and attains the unlimited.
This generally counteracts the limited mental views of the preceding stages. Once these inherent virtues are perfected, one may enter the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "To be identical with all phenomena while remaining detached from all marks—wherein both identity and detachment are without attachment—can be called truly attaining the 'as-it-is' (tathatā).
What further hindrance or bondage could there be? This is true liberation."
When one reaches the state of being unimpeded and unbound, attaining true liberation,

then the nature of the three virtues becomes perfectly fulfilled and the dimensions of the dharma-realm are extinguished. Only when the dimensions of the dharma-realm have been extinguished can one ascend to the first stage (bhūmi).

○ (2. Four Kinds of Preparatory Practice; Part 1: General Introduction) Ānanda, these good sons have all exhausted the forty-one pure minds and subsequently achieve the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practice.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The forty-one minds" refer to the one stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), the ten stages of Faith (*śraddhā*), Practice (*caryā*), Abiding (*vihāra*), and Direction (*abhimukha*)—each being ten.
While the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) both possess these four preparatory stages (*prayoga-bhūmi*), they are neither wondrous (*pranīta*) nor perfect (*pariniṣpanna*).

Therefore, this [text] specifically designates them as the wondrous and perfect preparatory practices. Jùlǐ says: According to sutras such as the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (瓔珞經), the four preparatory stages are not separately enumerated. If...

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), the forty minds prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) are designated as the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) of the provisions (*sambhāra*).

Following the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are separately clarified as the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) of the application (*prayoga*). Wuxing remarked:

"The four stages of application (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*) here are precisely as described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. However, that [text] distinguishes between the internal and external ordinary person stages prior to the [first] stage."

The meaning of teaching [the stages] as a single application is that the "stages" (*bhūmi*) constitute the noble rank of the bodhisattva; because this noble rank is difficult to enter, these preparatory practices (*prayoga*) are opened up. Question:

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the present sutra, what purpose does it serve to establish distinct stages? Answer: There are precedents for borrowing the names of the distinct [stages] to express the Perfect [Teaching].
For example, the *Renwang jing* states: "The three worthies and ten sages abide in the retribution of fruition. — Master Min.
This means that this sutra is not necessarily complete in itself and must be supplemented by other meanings; the error [of failing to do so] is indeed grave.

(2. Specifically showing the four stages; first, the stage of "Heat") Taking the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind—though it has not yet emerged, it is like drilling for fire when the wood is about to ignite;
this is called the stage of Heat.

[Commentary] Changshui says: "Buddha-awakening (*buddhabodhi*) is the wisdom of the fruition. Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state: Although the aforementioned Buddha-awakening is said to be capable of equalizing [the stages], it has not yet been directly realized (*sākṣātkṛta*).

Now, as one is about to advance toward the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*), one takes that Buddha-awakening as one's own causal mind and further applies effort and practice to seek direct realization.
This is because, upon first entering the stage of the cause (*hetvavasthā*), one does not immediately attain the fruit.
It is like drilling for fire until the sign of warmth is attained.

(2. The Stage of the Summit) Furthermore, when one’s own mind becomes the path trodden by the Buddhas—whether relying on something or not relying on anything—it is like ascending a high mountain and entering the void;
yet because there remains a slight obstruction below, it is called the Stage of the Summit.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Relying on the mind of the stage of 'Heat' (uṣmagata), one cultivates the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit by contemplating the mind; thus it is like a foot treading upon the ground.

Because the characteristics of the mind are nearly exhausted, it is both 'relying' and 'not relying. The high mountain is a metaphor for the mind of its own stage, and empty space is a metaphor for the principle upon which it relies.
Because ignorance is not yet fully exhausted, there remains a slight obstruction below."

○ (The Stage of the Three Patiences) When the mind and the Buddha are identical, one skillfully attains the Middle Way; because this is like enduring a person, it is neither harboring resentment nor seeking fame, and is thus called the Ground of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "When one's own mind and the Buddha’s awakening merge into a single entity, they are said to be 'identical' (*dītóng*). Cause and effect are both forgotten."

The non-establishment of the two extremes is called the Middle Way. As for this Middle Way, because it is on the verge of being realized but not yet fully realized, it is like a person practicing patience (*kṣānti*):

neither inwardly harboring [resentment] nor outwardly expressing it. Wuxing said that "patience" carries the meaning of trust and compliance. Now, the equality of the two—mind and Buddha—is precisely such trust and compliance.
It is like one who manages affairs within the Sangha: if they practice patience, they remain silent; since they harbor no doubt, they are likewise compliant.
It is not something that can be expressed in words.

(4. The First Stage of the World): When the quantity of delusion and awakening has been extinguished within the Middle Way, and there is nothing to be designated, it is called the "First Stage of the World."
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "If one is deluded regarding the Middle Way or awakened to the Middle Way, both are matters of numerical quantification;
this is the meaning of the mundane world (*loka*). Now, since these two have been extinguished and there is nothing more to be designated, it should be called supramundane (*lokottara*).

Yet, because one has not yet entered the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is named 'Supreme of the World' (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Wenzheng says: "If one advances through the ten grounds to the ultimate state of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmasaṃbodhi*), then..."
This is the foremost state transcending the world.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "All these forty-one minds" clarifies that one must first take these various minds as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) for ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, one must subsequently accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect practices as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Only then can one fully realize the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). For those of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, having cultivated the three kinds of provisions may be considered the ultimate;

yet, if they wish to ascend to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), they face the difficulty of the separation between the ordinary person and the sage, and must further cultivate the four kinds of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
These present four minds are by no means comparable to those of the Small Vehicle. As for the three levels of the Sages (*tri-śaikṣa*):

The ten stages of the sages are distant and profound, yet their intent largely resembles this. That is to say, these four minds take the Buddha’s awakening of the first stage as the initial awakening (*śikṣā-bodhi*) of the ten dedications;

they take one's own mind as "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*); and they take the initial awakening of one's own mind as the fulfillment of the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of the Buddha as the path to be traversed.
Regarding the ignorance of the lower stages, whether it is relied upon or not, it constitutes the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
Furthermore, because the mind of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) and the Buddha of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) are identical, one skillfully attains the Middle Way;
being on the verge of realization yet not yet fully realized, it is like a person enduring hardship who is considered "enduring.

Moreover, as the various quantities of the Middle Way regarding former delusion and awakening are all extinguished, there is nothing for the two to refer to, which is termed the Stage of the World’s Foremost (*loka-agradharmika*).
Once these four minds have been transcended, one may ascend to the first bhūmi and penetrate to bodhi. Now, these four minds consist of both the dharma and its metaphors.
The first preparatory stage consists of taking the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind; this is the dharma of "having emerged yet not having emerged.
To apply the dharma to the metaphor: the Buddha’s awakening and bodhi of the first bhūmi serve as the fire. Now, however—
Taking this as one’s own mind, one investigates and examines it by regarding original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) as initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
As that fire of awakening is about to emerge but has not yet emerged, it is like first obtaining warmth when approaching a fire;

therefore, it is metaphorically called the "Warmth Stage" (*uṣmagata*), named for the desire to kindle wood by drilling for fire. If one seeks the Dharma through metaphors, there are four meanings. First, the capacity...
1. The act of drilling is used as a metaphor for employing the Buddha’s awakening as the wisdom of one's own mind. 2.
The wood being drilled is used as a metaphor for the ignorance (*avidyā*) that obstructs the first stage (*bhūmi*), as described in the thirty-first chapter. 3.

The presence of the nature of fire within the wood is used as a metaphor for the fact that this very ignorance is itself the Buddha’s awakening of the first stage; that is to say, although it is obscured, blind, inverted, and deluded, its essence remains the same.
This is the principle itself. Fourth, "First Attaining the Warmth" uses this as a metaphor for true awakening (*tathatā-jñāna*) about to manifest; it first attains a semblance of awakening.

However, the primary intent within the Dharma lies solely in *bodhi*, while other meanings serve merely as auxiliary support. Second, "The Application of Effort" (*prayoga*) takes one's own mind as that which the Buddha has traversed.
This is based on the non-dharmic [aspect], not the dharmic. To apply the Dharma to the metaphor: by means of...
The cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) that is obstructed by the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) serves as its summit.
By understanding and liberating oneself from it, that birth and death—whether dependent or non-dependent—is like having already reached the peak of a mountain.

Therefore, it is metaphorically likened to ascending a high mountain where the body enters the void, yet there remains a slight obstruction below; this is called the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhabhūmi*). If one seeks the Dharma through metaphors, it is likewise so.
There are four meanings. First, the person ascending is metaphorically represented by one's own mind attaining the wisdom traversed by the Buddha.
Second, the mountain to be ascended generally represents both the *pariṇāmanika* (segmented) and *nirmāṇa* (transformative) types of birth-and-death.

Third, the summit with slight obstruction below specifically represents the subtle *nirmāṇa* birth-and-death that constitutes a portion of the obstacles to the first stage (*bhūmi*). Fourth, the body enters [the summit].

Space is used as a metaphor for the nirvāṇa realized in the first stage (*bhūmi*). However, just as level ground and high mountains always depend upon space, so too can birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) be metaphorically understood as being identical to nirvāṇa;
this refers to the fact that even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) possess the characteristic of liberation.
Yet, within the Dharma, the primary intent lies solely in nirvāṇa, while all else serves merely to assist in its manifestation. Third, the addition...
The practice of the mind and the awakening of the Buddha are identical; this is the skillful attainment of the Middle Way.
To apply the metaphor to the Dharma, one takes the realization of Bodhi and Nirvana at the first stage (*bhūmi*) as the object of endurance.
Because one's own mind and the Buddha’s awakening are both identical and in accord, one skillfully attains the Middle Way. Thus, there is neither the doubt of afflictions nor the [fear] of birth.

This is the explanation for the emergence of death. Therefore, it is likened to a person who practices patience: because they neither harbor nor give rise [to anger], it is called the "ground of patience.
If one seeks the Dharma through this analogy, there are also four meanings: first, the object of endurance is used as an analogy for the bodhi and nirvāṇa realized in the first ground;
second, the doubt harbored is used as an analogy for the afflictions that obstruct the first ground; third...
The statement that "it emerges" is used as an analogy for the birth-and-death of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

The fourfold "neither harboring nor emerging" is used as an analogy for the identity of the mind and the Buddha, whereby one skillfully attains the Middle Way. "Attainment" refers to *kṣānti* (patience/acceptance).

This means that what is accepted within the mind is realized by oneself alone and is difficult to explain to others; yet, the correct intent within the Dharma lies precisely in this "neither harboring nor emerging."
All others merely serve to assist in its manifestation. Fourth, the "quantities of practice that eliminate delusion" refers to the two aspects of the Middle Way regarding awakening and delusion.
Applying the Dharma to the analogy: from the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and below, these are the quantities of delusion regarding the Middle Way;
upon ascending to the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*), one correctly attains the Middle Way, which constitutes the quantities of awakening regarding the Middle Way. Both are worldly.

These belong to the intermediate and inferior classes. Now, because the quantitative measures of delusion and awakening within the Middle Way have all been extinguished, and there is no longer any objective referent for these two, they are people of the foremost class in the world;
therefore, they are metaphorically termed "the World-First" (Lokāgra).
If one seeks the meaning of the Dharma through metaphors, there are also three types: first, those who can be compared to people of the third class in the world.
To be deluded regarding the Middle Way may be likened to the second type of person among the two classes of worldly beings;
to be awakened to the Middle Way may be likened to the highest type of person among the three classes of worldly beings.

When neither delusion nor awakening can be predicated of the Middle Way, this constitutes a man of immeasurable capacity, and is therefore called the "World-First" (Loka-agra) stage. It is precisely because of this immeasurability that one can give rise to the first bhūmi.
These four types of preparatory practice (prayoga) employ analogies based on bodhi for the first stage, *ūṣmagata*;
analogies based on nirvāṇa for the second stage, *mūrdhan*; analogies based on the synthesis of both dharmas for the third stage, *kṣānti*;

and analogies based on the absence of reference to either dharma for the fourth stage, *laukikāgra-dharma*. Here, "bodhi" refers to initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*), and "nirvāṇa" [refers to ultimate cessation].
This refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). First, one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind, whereby the entirety of the original is made the beginning.
Second, one further takes one’s own mind to become that which the Buddha traversed, whereby the entirety of the beginning resides in the original.

Third, when the two—mind and Buddha—are identical, one properly attains the Middle Way, such that the beginning and the original are unified. Fourth, within the Middle Way of delusion and awakening, both are non-existent.

When the eyes and their objects are both forgotten as they were originally, only then can one thoroughly penetrate Great Bodhi and awaken to the universal penetration of the Tathāgata’s entire Buddha-realm; this is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

○ (The First of the Ten Stages: The Stage of Joy) Ānanda, when these sons of good family have thoroughly attained mastery over great bodhi and their awakening has penetrated the realm of the Tathāgata to its full extent, it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary] Gushan says: "Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata" means that one's wisdom is identical to the Buddha-wisdom; "exhausting the Buddha-realm" means that one's principle is equal to the Buddha-principle.

The perfect fusion of the three truths is called the Buddha-realm. Compared to what preceded this, it is said that although [the practitioner] has exhausted [the realm], they have not yet truly exhausted it.
Because one first attains the joy of the Dharma, it is called "Joyful" (Pramuditā). Wēnlíng says:

As for the "Ten Grounds" (daśabhūmi), they are so called because the preceding dharmas are accumulated until they reach fulfillment, and all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them; thus, they are termed "grounds.

From the stage of the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā) downward, the positions all follow one another in succession, mutually supporting each other as they advance directly toward Sublime Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi); within this process, there is no lack of both abandonment and realization.
These are all cases of severing what is not severed and realizing what is not realized.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "This good son" refers to the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Because he further cultivates four kinds of preparatory practices (*prayoga*), he is able to achieve thorough penetration into Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). There are two meanings to Great Enlightenment.
First, the wisdom that is capable of awakening is the Bodhi of the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); therefore, it is called "Awakening that penetrates the Tathāgata.
Second, the principle that is awakened to is the Nirvāṇa of the quality of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); therefore, it is called "exhausting the realm of the Buddha.

The quality of wisdom is like the radiance of the moon, while the quality of cessation is like the darkness that is extinguished. The place where light arises is the very place where darkness is extinguished.
The very place where light arises is itself Bodhi, and Bodhi is itself Nirvana; they are a non-dual realm.

In this passage, it simply says that one has "well attained thorough penetration into Great Bodhi," while in the subsequent passage, it simply says that "the wondrous cloud of the Compassionate Shade covers the ocean of Nirvana.
Although these two dharmas appear alternately in the preceding and following sections, they must necessarily coexist.
○ (Second, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement): Entering into sameness from difference, and the extinction of that very sameness as well, is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the ultimate reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is said that because one has previously attained excellent penetration into Great Bodhi, this is termed "entering into sameness from difference."
"Even that which is similar is extinguished; if one perceives similarity, it becomes a defilement. The *Avataṃsaka* says:
"For example, when genuine gold is placed in alum stone and refined according to the proper method, it becomes free from all impurities."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When one has not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), one cannot avoid the distinctions between the natures and characteristics of sentient beings and Buddhas;
this is called "different natures" (*visabhāga*). Once one has ascended to the first stage, one realizes that these distinctions return to sameness;

therefore, one attains immeasurable joy, and it is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). However, the essence of wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally neither identical nor different. This is thus—
It is held that while difference is a defilement, similarity is likewise a defilement. Now, only when even this similarity is extinguished can one be free from defilement;
thus it is named the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*). Furthermore, it is not only this [similarity] that is so; even the presence of joy is a defilement.
When one is free from this defilement as well, it is again called "Freedom from Defilement."

○ (The Third Ground, Luminous): Because purity gives rise to supreme clarity, it is named the Luminous Ground. ○ (The Fourth Ground, Blazing Wisdom): Because clarity reaches the fullness of awakening, it is named the Blazing Wisdom Ground.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The Radiant" means that when the defilements of emotional perception are purified, the brilliance of wondrous enlightenment arises.
"Blazing Wisdom" means that when clarity reaches its ultimate limit and awakening is full, it is like a great mass of fire that completely incinerates and severs all conditioned shadows.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Having attained freedom from defilement, the purity of nirvana reaches its ultimate limit and the brilliance of bodhi arises.
Precisely because this brilliance arises, it is named "Radiant" (Prabhākari). When this brilliance reaches its peak, the awakening of bodhi becomes full;
it is like gold that, once freed from impurities, further emits its own luster. When the radiance is perfectly complete, the "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī) arises. Therefore, [it is so named].
It is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
○ (5) The Ground Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā-bhūmi): It is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer because it cannot be reached by anything either similar or dissimilar.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Developing" refers to the wisdom of this ground; "prior" refers to the wisdom of the preceding grounds. "To reach" (zhì) means to attain. —Wen.
Ling said: "Because the preceding [stage] has already incinerated and severed [delusions] with the fire of wisdom (jñānāgni), nothing—neither identity nor difference—can reach it.
Since even 'reaching' itself cannot reach it, who could possibly surpass it?

[Tiantai’s Commentary: Regarding the first stage, the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi), although one is free from the nature of difference; and regarding the second stage, the Stage of Purity (vimalā-bhūmi), although one is free from identity.
In its essential nature, there still appears to be some distinction between similarity and difference, as it remains within the sphere of conditioned reflections (*pratibimba*).

However, after the stages of Radiance (*prabhākari*) and Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī*), both similarities and differences, along with all conditioned reflections, are completely extinguished; therefore, nothing can reach it. How could the preceding four stages surpass this?
Thus, it is named the "Difficult-to-Conquer Stage" (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

○ (The Sixth Ground, the Ground of Presence): Because the unconditioned nature of true suchness is pure, luminous, and manifest, it is called the Ground of Presence. ○ (The Seventh Ground, the Ground of Far-Going): Because it reaches the limit of the realm of true suchness, it is called the Ground of Far-Going.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: When identity and difference do not arrive [at their limit], the pure nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is revealed and manifests before one.

When True Suchness manifests and is partially realized, it is still localized; only when reaching the ultimate limit is it truly "far. Because it transcends all bounds and reaches the pinnacle of achievement, it is named "Far-Going" (dūramgamā).
Wuxing said: "That which reaches the limit of true thusness (bhūtatathatā) is precisely the limit of the limitless. Since the principle is already limitless, how could practice approach it?
[Tiantai] Commentary:
When the shadows of conditions—whether identical or different—have ceased, the unconditioned nature of true thusness is revealed; this is called "manifestation."
The preceding stage. Although it was already manifest, it was not yet exhaustive; by applying further effort to bring it to completion, it is named the Stage of Far-reaching (Dūraṃgamā).
○ (8. The Immovable Stage):
The mind of true suchness is called the Immovable Stage (Acalā).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Having exhausted its ultimate limit, one then fully attains its essence; because the single truth is concentrated and constant, it is named "Immovable.
[Sub-commentary] Tiāntái says: After the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) has been revealed, one further exhausts it through the practice of "far-reaching conduct" (dūramgamā-caryā).
Thus, it is the single, wondrous mind of True Suchness (tathatā). Having truly attained that which is such, what could possibly move it? It is therefore named the Immovable Ground (acalā-bhūmi).

○ (9. The Ninth Ground, Good Intelligence; Part 1: Correct Explanation of its Name) Because it brings forth the function of True Suchness, it is named the Ground of Good Intelligence (sādhumatī-bhūmi).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Having attained the true essence, one then manifests the true function. Whatever is illuminated and responded to is entirely true and nothing is not as it should be;
therefore, it is called 'Excellent Wisdom' (Sudhī). Zīzhōng says:

"In the *Avataṃsaka*, this Bodhisattva is said to possess the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and act as a Great Dharma Master, expounding immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without end."
Because it exhausts [all phenomena], it is called the manifestation of the function of True Suchness.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: From the immovable essence of True Suchness, the immovable function of True Suchness arises.
Because its essence and function are mutually identical, its wisdom is excellent; thus it is called the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi).
(2. Further listing alternative names: Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and their merit becomes perfected;
therefore, this ground is also designated as the Stage of Cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This concludes what preceded and reveals what follows. From the initial arousal of faith up to the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*), these are all matters of cultivation.
Now, this "Good Wisdom" (*sādhumatī*) has already transcended the eighth stage’s path of non-effort (*anābhoga*).
Since wisdom and compassion are both perfected, the work of cultivation reaches its completion here; therefore, it is called "Cultivation" to conclude the ten stages.
The cause; subsequently, there is the fruit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), wherein there is no further cultivation.

In the *Avataṃsaka*’s exposition of the ten stages, Vajragarbha represents the cause and Vimukticandra represents the fruit. This is because there is cultivation on the causal stage, whereas there is no cultivation on the resultant stage.
Question: Since there is no longer cultivation in the subsequent stage, how can there still be the matter of severing hindrances? Answer: This clarifies...

The fruits of wisdom, compassion, and merit culminate only in the attainment of the tenth bhūmi. However, if one discusses the severance of hindrances, even the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) still involves cultivation;
therefore, it is only upon reaching Sublime Enlightenment (*mārgajñatā*) that one is termed "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Tianru’s Supplementary Notes state:

"Regarding this section, various masters have linked it to the subsequent description of the Dharma-cloud Bhūmi (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). Now, examining the meaning of the text, I shall follow the sequential interpretation."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: According to what Master Huan has explained, since it is stated that "one thereby forms the causes for the ten stages," from this point onward, one should refer only to the preceding nine stages.
This is because all fifty-five positions possess the meaning of being mutually related as fourfold fruits;
for example, the first stage takes the ten faiths as its cause, while the ten faiths take the first stage [as their fruit].

It is the fruit. That the forty-four moments of mind in the first stage constitute the cause, and that these forty-four moments of mind constitute the fruit of the first stage—this is precisely the matter at hand.
Furthermore, regarding the meanings of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and "severing hindrances" (*āvaraṇa-prahāṇa*), on one level they are equivalent;
on another level, from the ninth stage downward, there is the sense that cultivation and the severing of hindrances occur simultaneously. From the tenth stage upward, however, [they are distinct].
Thus, there is only the severing of hindrances and no further cultivation. For the ultimate fulfillment of the merit of wisdom and compassion lies solely in benefiting others;
yet, when the function of benefiting others is not yet perfected, it is termed the hindrance of subtle ignorance (*sūkṣmāvidyā-āvaraṇa*).
This is precisely why, at the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), one covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa* with the wondrous cloud of the compassionate canopy.
○ (The Tenth Stage: Cloud of Dharma) The stage named *Dharmameghā* is so called because the wondrous cloud of the shade of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "By means of unconditioned loving-kindness (*apratihata-maitrī*), one universally shades sentient beings with their fundamental *nirvāṇa* nature, like a cloud covering the ocean.
Wenling says: "The wondrous cloud of the shade of loving-kindness is the fruition-virtue of the tenth stage; the ocean of *nirvāṇa* is the fruition of wondrous enlightenment."
It is like the ocean. When the fruit of the ten stages is fulfilled and the merits of wisdom and compassion are perfected, there is no longer further self-benefit;

it is purely for the benefit of others. Thus, the aggregate of great kindness pervades the entire Dharma-realm; without thought or objectification, it responds to the minds of others, performing acts of benefit and profit.
Yet, being fundamentally quiescent and without fabrication, it accords with the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction; therefore, it is said to "cover."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Master Yue’s interpretation of the meaning of the "Nirvana Ocean" lies in its aspect as the productive cause (*janakahetu*);

Master Huan’s interpretation of the meaning of the "Nirvana Ocean" lies in its aspect as the fruition virtue (*phalaguṇa*). Although both interpretations are generally valid, Master Yue’s interpretation is more frequently adopted.
Originally, the Bodhisattva was intent on benefiting others; however, because wisdom and compassion were not yet perfected, his great vow was not fulfilled.
Now that his cultivation is complete, he focuses solely on benefiting others.
Thus, he uses the wondrous cloud of pure compassion to cover the ocean of the inherent nirvana of sentient beings, granting them innate bliss and extracting their innate suffering.

○ (The seventh stage of Equal Enlightenment, Part One: The Direct Explanation of Equal Enlightenment) As the Tathāgata flows against the current, so does the Bodhisattva proceed with the current until they reach the boundary of enlightenment; when these two meet, it is called Equal Enlightenment.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The principle has neither opposition nor conformity; it receives these two names based on the wisdom of provisional means (*upāya*) and ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Because the Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom descends to respond to the karmic conditions of sentient beings, it is called 'opposition' (*ni*). Because the Bodhisattva’s ultimate wisdom ascends to accord with the awakened mind, it is called 'conformity' (*shun*').

What is stated in the *Yíngluò jīng*—that 'Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness' (*zhào-jì*) and 'Sublime Enlightenment is stillness within illumination' (*jì-zhào*)—is precisely this meaning. Upon reaching this point...
The stage is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-sambodhi*) because it occurs at the juncture where two wisdoms intersect. Wēnlíng says:

"The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages mix with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, which is the same as the Tathāgata; however, they differ from the Tathāgata in their direction—whether moving against or with the current.

For while the Tathāgata flows out against the current to be identical with all things, the Bodhisattva flows along with the current toward Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). Having already reached enlightenment..."
Because it reaches the limit, it is called "entering the intersection" (*rùjiāo*). Because it is without interval from the Buddha, it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*děngjué*);

this refers to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) preceding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Although this is equal [to the Buddha], it has not yet reached the ultimate subtlety; it merely consists in being able to accord with and enter [the truth].

One must emerge against the current from the great ocean of quiescent extinction (*mahāśānti-samudra*), where one's subtle identity with all phenomena is perfected, before it is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*miàojiào*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In discussing the source and flow of the ocean of enlightenment, there are two meanings: first, the flow of the True (zhenliú);

second, the flow of the Delusory (wàngliú). Speaking in terms of the delusory flow, the Bodhisattva goes against the flow of birth and death to enter among sentient beings, while following the flow of birth and death to emerge from them.
Speaking in terms of the true flow, the Tathāgata goes against the flow of Nirvāṇa to emerge [into the world].
The Bodhisattva enters by following the flow toward Nirvana; the Tathāgata has already entered and is now emerging, while the Bodhisattva wishes to enter and is about to do so.
At the precise moment when one emerges and the other enters—the intersection of entry—these two aspects of awakening, the final and the initial, become equal.
For this reason, it is called the meaning of "Equal Awakening" (Samyaksambodhi). Nevertheless, as for the Bodhisattva’s entry:
One necessarily proceeds from the shallow to the deep; the appearance of a Tathāgata necessarily proceeds from the deep to the shallow.
Thus, for those of perfect capacity (*yuanren*), every stage possesses the significance of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*).
That it is named specifically here is because both the beginning and the source are explained in terms of the ultimate.

(2. The Subsequent Mind of Vajra): Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, one has already awakened; it is only upon attaining the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Subsequent Mind of Vajra that true awakening is first realized.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This clarifies the path of subduing [delusions] during the mind of ultimate awakening (miàojué) following the stage of equal awakening (děngjué). The path of ultimate awakening has no distinct phenomenal characteristics;

it merely involves, from the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (qiánhuí) up to Equal Awakening, once again giving rise to the Vajra-mind to re-traverse all the stages from the beginning, thereby shattering and severing subtle residual images and the final ignorance so that not even a speck of dust remains.
Only then can one enter the Subtle. Because it begins again from the initial stage, it is called the "Initial Stage of Dry Wisdom within the Vajra-mind.
When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s Vajra-dry-wisdom; this refers precisely to that.

It was previously called "Dry Wisdom" because it had not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma; it is now called "Dry Wisdom" because it has not yet [connected with... [the subsequent stages].
The "Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Sublime Adornments" (Rúlái miàozhuāngyánhǎi) connects [to this stage]. Although the names are momentarily identical, their meanings are vastly different.
Wùxīng said that Xìngfú designated this stage as a distinct position following Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi).

Zīzhōng classified it as being within Sublime Enlightenment (Prativedha-bodhi). Zhēnjì judged it to belong to the preceding stage of Equal Enlightenment; Lǐjiāng was likewise of this view. As for Gūshān, furthermore—
The general intent is the same, yet there are differences in the textual divisions as explained by Changshui.

He maintains that the section from Ānanda up to the "diamond-like mind" (*vajropama-citta*) belongs to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), while the initial "Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*), together with the subsequent passages such as "thus, in layers upon layers," is subsumed under the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).
His intention is that the initial Stage of Dry Wisdom merely serves to recapitulate the preceding text. Such are the various explanations.

Those who hold conflicting views have, to this day, been unable to determine which path to follow. I have examined the matter and believe that adopting the explanations of the two masters Jie and Min is the most appropriate.
As the *Yingluo jing* states, "Within the nature of Equal Enlightenment, there is a person named Vajradhvaja-prajñā.
Thus, we know that this stage cannot be established as a separate ground. As for what is called the "initial stage of dry wisdom," it arises from this bodhi...
Sākyamuni, by the power of his great vows, remained for a hundred kalpas cultivating a thousand samādhis; since he has now only just attained this, is it not indeed the beginning?

If you suspect that the name "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) applies only to the stage prior to faith and should not extend to subsequent stages, consider that the name "Patience of Subjugation" (kṣānti-avaivartika) also belongs to the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana).
How then could [the Buddha] have attained the Vajra-samādhi while still in that state? One should know that regarding this—
The "submissive patience" (*kṣānti*) is what we now call "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

This is because the ignorance that obstructs wondrous enlightenment has just begun to dry up, and one has not yet connected with the ultimate flow of the Dharma-water of the Tathāgata. Tianru’s Supplement states:

"The 'diamond dry wisdom' should follow Master Yue’s interpretation and be classified as belonging to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); furthermore, if one carefully savors the scriptural text, it says: 'Having reached Equal Enlightenment... already.
It is said that "Awakening first attains the Vajra-mind," which refers to the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*kandhī*).

Since it is stated that this is what awakening first attains, one knows that the Vajra-stage of Dry Wisdom definitely belongs to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). Although it belongs to Equal Enlightenment, it is nonetheless the very method for entering the Subtle [Truth].
As the master of the ring-maker said: "Having already attained Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), one again gives rise to the Vajra-mind and re-traverses the various stages;
only by shattering and severing the shadows of conditions can one enter the Sublime. This may indeed be accepted.

However, this merely refers to the arising of this mind once more within the stage of Equal Enlightenment itself; it cannot be designated as a "subsequent mind" that opens up a separate stage. If one were to rely on such a distinction...
If one opens [the text], it lists from twelve single and double positions up to fifty-five stages of true Bodhi; I fear these may be difficult to harmonize.
[Commentary] Tiantai says:
Regarding the "Vajra Dry Wisdom" (*vajra-śuṣka-jñāna*), from ancient times until the present, there has been no fixed interpretation among the various masters.

On this treatise, I maintain that it is correct to establish a separate stage based on Master Huan. For since the scriptural text states, "having reached the stage of Equal Enlightenment," how could Equal Enlightenment not be a distinct stage?
Furthermore, this awakening is where one first attains the Stage of Initial Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind;
how then could the Stage of Initial Dry Wisdom not also be a distinct stage? Master Tianru [only failed] because of the following...
The twelve single and multiple [categories] of the text and the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi are difficult to reconcile;
therefore, I have not adopted them. It is not realized that it would be very easy to open up a separate stage to achieve such reconciliation.

This must be done by harmonizing principle with emotion rather than allowing emotion to obstruct principle. The meaning of this reconciliation is fully seen in the following text. Thus, he rose again.
The adamantine mind repeatedly traverses the various stages to shatter the shadows of conditions; not only is its meaning profoundly correct, but it is also evidenced as being no mere fiction.

For instance, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the ninth of the nine great meditations—the ninth being the "meditation of purity that is clear and free from all views"—the Buddha testified that through this meditation, all afflictions, whether general or specific, whether manifest or latent, are entirely eliminated.
Because it is utterly purified, it is called the "purely pure dhyāna. From the lower stages downward, all possess residual habits (*vāsanā*). As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, transcending the practices of all bodhisattvas;
this 'purity' refers precisely to this. Furthermore, as the Great Master Tiantai’s *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra* states: "In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), beginning from—"
From the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) up to the final Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), although all views have been completely severed, residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remain.

Upon entering the Gate of the Double Profundity at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one undergoes renewed cultivation for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; while the realization of principle is clear, the residual habits are as slight as a faint wisp of smoke.

Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* cited in the commentary explains only the "view-habit" (*dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*), whereas the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states that it is severed at the tenth stage, [the two sources differ].
Regarding the habituation of craving: since the Ten Stages constitute Equal Enlightenment, how could one not have entered the profound mystery?

Thus, we know that after the final mind of Equal Enlightenment, one again traverses the various stages to destroy both the pervasive and specific views and afflictions, as well as their respective fundamental and habitual tendencies; this principle is beyond doubt.
