Thus, both the Esoteric and the Exoteric, as well as the Tathāgatagarbha-mind, the eternally abiding true mind, the secret cause of the Tathāgata, and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas, all take their beginning from this and reach their ultimate consummation in this. By taking their beginning from this, the cause transcends the ocean of fruition;
by reaching their ultimate consummation in this, the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. There is not a single phenomenal phenomenon that does not [partake of this].
Because it is ultimately firm and solid, it is titled *Śūraṅgama*. This name is established solely from the perspective of its essential principle (*mūla*).

The current title, however, preserves three elements while concealing two, condensing them into a brief designation; that words possess spatial divisions (or sequential parts) is also inherent in their underlying logic.
This is the skillful artistry of the translators of the scriptures. Yet, Wu-xing said: "One who cultivates this samādhi possesses the One Mind."
The myriad practices have been fulfilled yet remain hidden and unmanifest. I shall now cite the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* to clarify this meaning.
In that sūtra, the Buddha asks the bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati: "How does one practice the six perfections within a single thought-moment? He replies:

"When a bodhisattva relinquishes everything and the mind is free from attachment and craving, this is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). When the mind is well-peaceful and extinguished, ultimately free from evil..."
To know the characteristic of the exhaustion of phenomena and to remain unharmed amidst all sensory objects is called *kṣānti*.
To diligently observe and discern the mind so as to know the characteristic of detachment is called *vīrya*. To ultimately attain sublime tranquility and subdue the mind is called *dhyāna*.
To know that the mind is no-mind and to penetrate the characteristics of the mind is called *prajñā*. This is the Great Samādhi of the present.

When, through the samādhi of the ear-gate, one contemplates the objects of the external field and the faculties within, and the wisdom that perceives the principle of reality relinquishes all things—this is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
Since that which is entered is already tranquil, the two marks of motion and stillness clearly do not arise;

this is the mind’s excellent quiescence and ultimate absence of evil, named the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā). To thoroughly realize that the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and realms are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous True Suchness.

The nature itself is the knowledge that all phenomena are ultimately characterized by exhaustion; to remain unharmed amidst all sensory objects is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

To thoroughly comprehend perfect penetration so as not to be defiled by the sense organs or their objects, such that one flows into [enlightenment] moment after moment through diligent contemplation and discernment, and the mind is able to know the departure from marks, is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
When arising and ceasing have both ceased and quiescent extinction manifests before one, this is ultimate, sublime tranquility.

To subdue the mind is called the perfection of dhyāna (meditation). To realize that the faculty of hearing is not produced by causes and conditions, but is naturally the wondrous true suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha, and thereby to know that the mind is no-mind and to penetrate the characteristics of the mind, is called the perfection of prajñā (wisdom).
These six perfections are the foundation of all practices; once the six perfections are complete, all practices are naturally encompassed. This concludes the general outline of this sutra.
The practitioner first requested instruction on the Great Samādhi. The Tathāgata first showed him how to develop the perfect understanding by relying on the eternally abiding true mind;
next, he showed him how to cultivate the perfect practice by relying on the eternally abiding true mind;

and third, he showed him how to distinguish the stages of perfection by relying on both the manifest and secret causes. Thus, understanding and practice support one another, and the eyes and feet are both provided.
Having prepared the direct path, one enters the Cool Lake. The Great Sutra’s essential principle begins and ends with this;

the task requested by the immediate occasion has been completed. Thus, Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the names and their upholding can be said to have perfected both name and essence, and the trap and the fish are both brought to their ultimate excellence.
Now, the fifth chapter continues by extensively discriminating the seven destinies. As for this...
One uses the precepts as a safeguard against error so as not to become lost upon the divergent paths. There are, however, two such divergent paths:
first, sinking and falling, which refers to the three evil realms; second, ascending and purifying, which refers to the four wholesome realms.

As for why the three evil realms are also called "divergent paths of cultivation," it is as in the case of the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, who secretly engaged in sexual misconduct yet falsely claimed she had none.
If one commits a transgression, both [one's view and] precepts are simultaneously destroyed.
Is this not because for those who have received the Bodhisattva precepts in the Mahāyāna, a single erroneous view or a single defiled action constitutes a direct path to the Avīci Hell?
Furthermore, it is like the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, who falsely claimed that all phenomena are empty and that there is neither sin nor merit; yet, due to a single moment of error...
Is it not the case that seeing [them] as false constitutes a bypath leading directly to the Avīci Hell? Following this track, one seeks [rebirth]: once the period in hell ends, one becomes a ghost;
once the period as a ghost ends, one becomes an animal; and once the period as an animal ends, one becomes a human—all these categories arise from riding upon the force of past habits.
Even if one attains the state of a human being, it is certainly not merely for this reason that one should take the experience of losing one's way on this long journey as a warning. (Yuan)
Those who practice the sudden path must be cautious! Next, regarding the four wholesome paths leading upward: first is the deviation into the path of the celestial immortals (*ṛṣi*).
This occurs when the aggregate of sensation has already been broken and the aggregate of perception manifests. Within *samādhi*, one’s mind becomes attached to longevity;

through arduous investigation of subtle principles, one greedily seeks eternal years, abandoning the coarse birth of the segmented realm and suddenly aspiring for the subtle marks of the transformative realm.

It is eternally abiding. Furthermore, just as when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has ceased and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) manifests before one, if one were to regard this as a perfect, constant, and solid body that abides eternally—identical to the perfection of the vital essence (*ojas*) that grows long and never declines—then all those Āsuras who seek longevity would become one's companions.
Would this not mean that the practitioner of the Perfect Way has fallen onto the divergent path of the Immortals (*ṛṣi*)? As for the heavenly realms, moreover...
For a practitioner of the Sudden and Perfect [Teaching], it is unavoidable that there must be stages for ascending vertically out of the triple world.
If one were to become attached to this single lifetime, would that not be falling onto a bypath leading toward the heavenly realms?
As for harboring suspicion and jealousy while practicing the ten wholesome deeds, or engaging in strife while cultivating the three trainings—would these not cause one to fall among the asuras?

This is the divergent path of the worldly way. Speaking from this perspective, those who comment on the scriptures and categorize them as "preparations for avoiding errors" have deeply grasped the meaning beyond the words.

Thus, to specifically clarify the various realms of rebirth, prepare for the avoidance of errors, and provide detailed analysis of demonic states to deeply guard against deviance and delusion, is an urgent task for correct cultivation; it is directly consistent with what was previously observed.
It would be appropriate to categorize this into six major sections: the Path, Cultivating the Path, Realizing the Fruit, and the Compilation of the Sutra.

To claim that these are all collectively for the purpose of "assisting the path" (zhudao) is likely not the case. For instance, within the ninth stage, "Able to Practice Patience" (*neng anren*), of the Ten Vehicles (*shicheng*) in Tiantai’s *Zhiguan*, and within the four objects—afflictions, karma, meditative concentration, and various views—among the Ten Objects (*shijing*), all are things that are stimulated and brought forth by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If one does not anticipate this in advance, many errors and delusions will arise; this is a fundamental principle for correct cultivation.
How could the present sutra be any different? (5.

Extensive Discrimination of the Seven Realms: Preparing Against Errors and Delusions—Part One: Questions and Doubts; Part Two: Hearing the Dharma Increases the Path. Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the secret.
The meaning of the seal *pranidhāra* encompasses hearing this sutra’s definitive title, which brings about sudden awakening to the stages of holy advancement in the cultivation of *dhyāna*,

the superior and wondrous principle of the mind’s contemplation becoming void and concentrated, the severing of the three realms, and the elimination of the six grades of subtle afflictions through mental cultivation.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This section concludes the description of how the assembly present at that time obtained benefit; what follows is the expression of praise and gratitude.
"Revealing the secret seal" through to "the supreme and wondrous principle" refers generally to the profound meanings of the preceding sutra.

Regarding the delusions to be severed through the cultivation of the path, the Lesser Vehicle divides the three realms into nine stages (*bhūmi*), with each stage containing nine grades. Having severed the first six grades of the desire realm...
One realizes the second fruit by abandoning the latter three grades; one realizes the third fruit by abandoning the nine grades of each of the two upper realms;

and one realizes the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) by abandoning them. Now, because these superior [faculties] abandon [the defilements] all at once, it is said that the six grades of the three realms are abandoned.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Having received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Pañcarakṣā* (Bhadrakarātrī)"—this refers to the instruction received since the construction of the altar and the hearing of the mantra.
In this scripture, there are two seals: the manifest and the secret.
The three *tathāgatagarbhas* are called the manifest seal; the Great White Parasol is called the secret seal. Both of these dharmas...

Taking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*), while simultaneously hearing the names of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), surpasses the previously mentioned benefits of being shown the five types of sūtra titles.
"Sudden awakening to *dhyāna* and advancing through the stages of sainthood" follows upon the previously mentioned benefits of being shown the stages (*bhūmi*).
The true mark, the secret seal, *dhyāna*, and the stages of sainthood all represent the ultimate fruit of principle, transcending the person.
The principle that transcends the ordinary grades is called the "superior and wondrous truth"; this is the truth entered.

Because one attains realization in accordance with what is heard and the wondrous samādhi manifests before one, it is said that "the mind and its deliberations are void and congealed"; this is the samādhi that enters.

When the beginning accords with the source and the object accords with the contemplation, its sharpness is like gold and its hardness is like steel, capable of suddenly severing fundamental ignorance.

Now, to briefly indicate the迹 (traces) [of the teaching]: because it suddenly severs the branch-like and secondary afflictions of thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is said that "the six grades of subtle afflictions of the mind in the three realms are severed.
This is what Master Wenling refers to as "superior sudden severance" (*zēngshàng dùnduàn*). It is like cutting a handful of silk threads:
when one is cut, all are severed. Not only are the first six grades of the desire realm severed, but those of the two higher realms as well.
Because the six grades of each of the realms were simultaneously severed, it is said that "the six grades of the three realms" were abandoned.

(2. Arising from his seat to pay homage and resolve lingering doubts; Part One: Arising from his seat to pay homage and describe the benefit. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with his head, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, whose compassionate voice is all-encompassing, you have skillfully opened up for sentient beings their subtle and deep-seated delusions, enabling my body and mind this day..."
I am filled with joy, having obtained great benefit. (2. Doubts regarding the Buddha’s remoteness; 2a. Directly expressing those doubts; 2aa. General doubt concerning the various realms of existence.

World-Honored One, if this wondrous, bright, truly pure, and sublime mind is from the beginning all-pervasive and perfect—such that even the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and sentient beings are fundamentally True Suchness, which is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood—and if the Buddha-essence is truly real, how can there further exist the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals? How could these be cultivated?

"World-Honored One, regarding this path of the various classes of beings, including humans and devas—is this path inherently possessed from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The previous teaching stated that the true, pure, and wondrous mind is originally pervasive and perfect; thus, the dharma-realm is the single truth."

Since the myriad movements are of one essence, there should be no distinction between the various realms of existence (*gati*). Yet, as they currently manifest today, this remains a point of doubt for ordinary people.
Consequently, some cling to the various realms and become deluded regarding the wondrously perfect essence;

others cling to the wondrously perfect essence and deny the karma of the various realms, thereby falling into error and ruin. Therefore, I specifically request your instruction, hoping that practitioners may gain a detailed and clear understanding.

Thus one knows what to guard against and prepare for. Wuxing said: Previously, Ānanda asked about the stages, and later the Buddha stated that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks;
fundamentally there have been no worlds or sentient beings. Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction.
Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called the True, and so forth. Thus, [the text] first establishes this based on the existence [of phenomena] due to delusion.
The two types of inversion, "birth" and "clarity," have been explained. Subsequently, regarding the cessation of delusion, the various stages of the gradual progression toward true clarity are named.
However, within the discussion of the inversions of the world, the twelve classes of beings were presented merely as a general indication of the causal characteristics of the Desire Realm;
in reality, the explanation of the realms and destinies was not exhaustive. Now, as the response concerning the stages has concluded, [the text] follows upon the previous "Subtle" section.
The meaning of "nature" (prakṛti) encompasses all categories of beings as being entirely True Suchness (tathatā).

Since the Tathāgata initiated this teaching to provide a detailed discourse on the various realms of existence (gati), to regard it as merely a remnant of the orthodox main body (siddhānta) is not appropriate.

It is likewise untenable for the two masters Kuò and Jié to judge it as belonging to the section of "Circulation" (liú-tōng) based solely on its inclusion since the passage where Mañjuśrī inquires about the name [of the Lotus Sūtra].
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The interpretations of these two masters—Wenling explains the meaning based on the specific text, while Wuxing explains it by connecting it to what precedes.
Although these two explanations complement one another and neither can be dispensed with, it appears that Wuxing’s insights are more extensive.
However, not only was the previous explanation incomplete regarding the twelve classes of beings and their destinies, but even...

The retributions for the six types of deluded false thoughts have not yet been fully revealed. Now, within the hells, they are explained in detail through the ten causes of habitual practice and the sixfold mutual retribution;
the meaning of these six delusions accords perfectly with their results, like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound, without the slightest discrepancy.
Thus, when the Buddha speaks of the wonders of the world, he never utters anything that is not true.

○ (2. Specific Inquiry on the Hells) World-Honored One, for instance, the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, while upholding the Bodhisattva precepts, privately engaged in sexual misconduct and falsely claimed that "sexual intercourse is neither killing nor stealing, and thus carries no karmic retribution.

Having uttered these words, a great, fierce fire first arose from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires blazed through every joint of her body as she fell into the Avīci Hell. So too were King Vairūḍyaka and Sunakṣatra.
The bhikṣu Vairāṭya, having falsely proclaimed that all dharmas are empty, was executed along with the Gautama clan and Saṃjīva;

his physical body fell into the Avīci Hell. Do these various hells have fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously such that each person receives their retribution according to the specific karma they have produced?
[2. Requesting to Hear the Dharma] I pray that you will bestow great compassion and enlighten the ignorant, so that all may uphold [the teachings].
When sentient beings hear this definitive meaning, they rejoice, receive it upon their heads with reverence, and maintain it with purity, never violating it.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: The Crown Prince of King Virūḍhaka usurped the throne from his father and, harboring long-standing resentment, slaughtered the Śākyas.
The Buddha prophesied that he would enter hell within seven days. The king sailed out to sea to escape, but while in the water, [the earth] spontaneously...
[They] are incinerated. The bhikṣu Shanxing was able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures and attain the fruit of the four dhyānas;
yet, because he associated with evil friends and falsely claimed that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no nirvāṇa, he fell into the Avīci Hell.

These are all cases of those who perversely cling to the subtle and perfect [nature] while denying karmic retribution and the realms of existence. Wuxing said: "The intent of the question is twofold, namely, individual karma and common karma."

"Retribution for individual karma is individual retribution. The initial inquiry regarding lust, killing, and falsehood constitutes "individual karma"; the question of whether there is a fixed location constitutes "common retribution.

Furthermore, the subsequent inquiry concerning "natural [retribution]" and so forth refers to "individual karma and common retribution. According to the intent of the following answer, these are all instances of individual karma resulting in common retribution.
As the text says: "Though one invites [suffering] by following the creation of evil karma, it is shared by the multitude."
Within the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous class), there are also the original lands; it continues until it says that the three karmas are not interrupted and each has its own private [nature].
Because each has its own private [nature], the collective *sabhāgatā* of these privates is not without a fixed location.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Herein, combined with the previous [section], two questions are posed regarding ordinary beings.
The first is a general inquiry as to whether the six realms of existence exist inherently from the beginning, or whether they arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings.

This establishes a single principle as the starting point; hence it says, "If this wondrous clarity... and so forth. This implies that since the principle is true, there should not be the delusion of phenomena.

This constitutes the question. First, there is the specific inquiry as to whether hell has a fixed location or whether it arises spontaneously such that individuals create their own karma and each privately undergoes its retribution.
This inquiry takes a present matter as its starting point, hence the mention of "the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā and others.
Thus, within the context of false conduct, the question concerns how collective karma leads to shared retribution while individual karma leads to distinct retribution.
The reason these three individuals are singled out is that they were identified as the primary culprits due to the three root poisons of greed, anger, and delusion.
For instance, Baolianxiang was driven by greed, Liuliwang by anger, and Shanxing by delusion;
all of them committed high-grade karma through high-grade afflictions, which is why they fell into the Avīci Hell in their very bodies.

Regarding the hells: as for those born with their physical bodies, their other offenses are light; however, because this offense is so grave that their consciousness falls [into hell] without waiting for the casting off of the body, it is said they are "born with the body.
In the case of Jewel-Lotus Fragrance, both her view and her precepts were violated.

In the case of Sunakṣatra, only his view was violated; we do not hear of his violating the precepts. Is this not because the offense of violating the view is lighter than the offense of violating the precepts? If...
Vaiḍūrya is neither view nor precept; it is merely the power accumulated over many years through long-standing resentment and a single moment of anger, unleashed to commit slaughter.
It uses a subordinate state to oppress a superior state, inflicts evil upon virtuous people, and harms the disciples of the Triple Gem with its petty, vulgar folly—killing indiscriminately.

In the act of regicide, there is no greater crime; yet many people of the present age do not understand this ultimate principle, and they recklessly slander the Holy Way, claiming that there is neither sin nor merit.
To believe lightly in Buddhist principles while asserting that violating the precepts incurs no guilt—when reading the scriptures to this point, how could one not feel a chill in one's heart?
○ (2. Exposition [Part 1: Praising and Granting Permission]) The Buddha told Ānanda: "Excellent indeed is this question! It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views.

Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. ○ (2. The Actual Explanation [Part 1: General and Specific Exposition] [Part 1: Clarifying the General and Specific] [Part 1: General Clarification Based on Sentiment and Perception] [Part 1: General Clarification Divided into Two] [Part 1: Identifying Both Based on Delusion of Reality]) Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure.

Because of that deluded vision, deluded habits arise; because of this, they are divided into the internal portion and the external portion. ○ (2. Specific Demonstration Based on Internal and External [Part 1: The Internal Portion] [Part 1: Explaining its Characteristics]) Ānanda, the internal portion is precisely the multitude...

The internal causes for the arising of existence are the various defilements of craving that give rise to deluded sentiments; as these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they are able to produce the water of desire.
Therefore, when sentient beings think of delicacies, water flows from their mouths; when they think of people from the past, whether out of pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes;
when greedily seeking wealth and treasures, love-saliva issues forth, moistening their entire bodies; and when the mind is attached to sexual intercourse with men...
In women, the two organs naturally discharge fluids. (2. Concluding Summary) Ānanda, although various forms of craving differ, their underlying fetter is the same:
they moisten and do not rise, but naturally fall downward; this is called the "internal portion" (*antar-bhāga*).
[Commentary] Wuxing asked: "It may be that pity arises from affection and thus gives rise to tears; however, why does resentment arise from hatred and give rise to tears? The answer is:
"In this context, all internal divisions are discussed in terms of emotion (*qing*). To take 'affection' as the representative emotion is merely to speak of one partial aspect."
Just as joy, anger, grief, pleasure, love, and hatred—these six—are all human emotions (*qing*), resentment and hatred likewise belong to the realm of emotion.
When emotion is intense, it gives rise to sorrow; sorrow, in turn, results in tears. The meaning of the internal division (*neifen*) is difficult to understand within the context of the text itself;

therefore, one must rely on the external division (*waifen*) that follows to clarify it. Furthermore, the external division states: "When the mind upholds the prohibitive precepts, the entire body becomes light."

Regarding those who desire to be reborn in the heavens through purifying the mind, or who dream of flying and ascending, one should know that those who follow the vehicles of humans and devas—by virtue of maintaining precepts and cultivating meditative concentration—belong to the outer division.
All those below this level belong to the inner division. A question is raised:
since the subsequent text states that those with an equal balance of emotion and thought are born as humans, does it not follow that the human vehicle belongs to the outer division?

If these are purely of thought, how can their sentiments be said to be uniform? Answer: It is precisely because in the human realm the phenomena of upholding and reviling are entangled, and good and evil remain mixed, that one speaks of "uniformity.
As for the degree of sentiment and thought, these all follow the ascent or descent determined by good and evil.
Only when birth in the heavens arises from pure thought does one transcend the internal division.
Master Yuan took the arising of attachment toward the body as "internal" and the delighting in superior external matters as "external"—how close this is to the truth!

○ (2. The External [Section], divided into two; first, explaining the characteristics) Ānanda, the external section refers to the external sphere of sentient beings. Due to various causes of yearning and aspiration, they clarify and manifest empty conceptions (*śūnyasaṃjñā*).

As these conceptions accumulate without ceasing, they are able to produce a superior vital energy (*viśiṣṭavāyu*). For this reason, when a sentient being’s mind maintains the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), their entire body becomes light and pure.

When the mind maintains mantras and mudrās, their gaze becomes heroic and resolute. When the mind desires to be born in the heavens, one dreams of flying aloft. When the mind dwells upon the Buddha-lands, one perceives the holy ones.

The objective realm merges with manifest phenomena; the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) disregards their own body and life. (2. Conclusion and Instruction) Ānanda, although these various perceptions differ, their lightness and elevation are the same.
They soar and move without sinking, naturally transcending [the mundane]; this is called the "external division."
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Thought can produce excellence, yet those born from eggs are produced by thought because of the difference between defilement and purity.
Wǔxīng says: "Furthermore, it refers to the conceptual mind of humans and devas as being 'external factors,' not the wisdom of the three vehicles that transcend the world.
Why? Because in the preceding text, due to Ānanda’s question regarding the paths of the hells up to those of humans and devas..."
Thereupon, the Buddha taught that the deluded habituation is opened into two divisions. Next, he distinguished the various realms of existence based on these two divisions.
Following the discussion of the realms, he concluded by showing: "These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of saṃsāra.
Therefore, one knows that the external division does not transcend the triple world. Although the text states that the mind dwells in the Buddha-land, [it refers to the internal division].

"The realm is darkly manifested; this is a general description of the signs of superior qi. If discussed in terms of cultivation, it is merely the phenomena and perceptions of the shared world throughout the ten directions.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the Sutra states that "internal divisions are the internal divisions of sentient beings," it refers to the sentiments of the world.
Desire consists of all objects enjoyed by a sentient being’s single body; this is what Master Yuan meant when he said that "attachment arises conditioned by the body.

As clarified in the following examples: when the mind recollects delicacies, when the mind recollects a former person, when one greedily seeks wealth and treasures, or when the mind is attached while engaging in sexual intercourse—is this not the enjoyment of the body?
Nevertheless, although these are internal [experiences], they actually depend upon external [objects]. Thus, they tend toward the external.
Restlessness is its characteristic. When discussing its conditions, it may also be called "external to the self.

Since the conceptual mind arises from emotion, it is likewise nothing other than an internal aspect of emotion. Therefore, the internal and external divisions of emotional desire are constantly opposed to one another:
for the sake of various internal states, one seeks them externally; yet seeking them externally, they are instead realized internally. Thus, emotion...
Because the mind associated with perception is both external and internal, it is called the "division of internal and external. This refers to sentient beings;
that which is external to sentient beings refers to those who practice and aspire to the Way, for all these are matters outside the body of a sentient being.

As Master Yun said, "To rejoice in those superior matters is to be 'external. As clarified by the following examples: the mind upholding the prohibitive precepts, and the mind upholding the seals (*mudrā*).
When one recites mantras with the desire to be reborn in heaven or dwells the mind upon the Buddha-lands, is this not something external to the body?

Nevertheless, although it takes external things as its object, it actually abides within. To manifest these empty conceptions is precisely what constitutes their characteristic. If one discusses its internal conditions, it may be called "internal";
yet since it arises by taking an external object as its condition, it is none other than "external" to the body. Therefore, the conceptualizing mind—
The distinction between the internal and external is always contrary: one acts for the sake of the external and instead gains the internal;

one gains the internal and instead completes the external. Thus, when emotion transforms into thought and both the internal and external become externalized, it is called "externalizing the internal."

[2. Specific Explanation of the Destinies and Births (divided into two parts): First, General Clarification; Second, the Two Habits. Ānanda, in all worlds, the succession of birth and death proceeds such that birth arises from habitual conformity and death arises from transformative flux.

At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one’s entire lifetime manifest simultaneously. Death is contrary [to the flow of existence] while birth is conformable [to it];
thus, these two habits intersect.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Birth follows habitual tendencies while death follows the flow of transformation" is because all sentient beings love life and loathe death.
Therefore, birth accords with their habits, whereas death opposes them. Thus it is further said that "death is contrary and birth is compliant;
these two habits intersect. This is merely a matter of mutual abbreviation in the phrasing. It is simply this.
Birth proceeds from the persistence of existence, thus it accords with habitual tendencies; death proceeds from transformation and flux, thus it opposes habitual tendencies.
"Not yet having abandoned warmth and tactile sensation" refers to the end of the present *skandhas* and the beginning of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Wēnlíng says:

"The intersection of the inverse and the accordant" refers to the interval between the moment of death and the moment of birth. At this very time, all karmic actions—whether good or evil—manifest according to one's mental dispositions.
One perceives lightness or heaviness and thereby experiences transformation.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "When one is at the point of death and has not yet abandoned warmth and tactile sensation," for a person, consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*) constitute the three dharmas that form life.
At the time of birth, consciousness first enters the womb, coagulating the father’s semen and the mother’s blood to serve as the seed. Next...
There is respiration only after there is warmth. Through the conjunction of these three factors there is birth, and through their separation there is death.

At the time of death, one first relinquishes warmth and subsequently relinquishes respiration; once respiration is relinquished, consciousness departs. That which is called "the master who comes last and goes first" is consciousness.
Now, it is said that as long as warmth and tactile sensation have not been relinquished, one is on the verge of dying.

In the interval before death, all the good and evil deeds performed throughout one's life manifest simultaneously and instantaneously. Now, craving life and fearing death are the common sentiments of humanity;
thus, death is contrary to human nature while life is its natural inclination. As these two habitual tendencies intersect, the dying person is unable to devise a plan for themselves.
It is like a person burdened by debt, whom the stronger creditor first drags away; therefore, according to the degree of their mental inclinations and conceptions, [they are led accordingly].
The distinction between ascending and sinking is thus determined. (2.
Specifically revealing the five modes of rebirth; first, those with pure thought: Those with purely virtuous thoughts will immediately fly upward and be born in the heavens.

If within that flying mind there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands, being reborn therein according to one's vows.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "Those who will certainly be born in the heavens are based on having few afflictions and much pure thought, yet they remain below the Four Heavenly Kings.

Examining those currently born from pure thought alone, they should be in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or above. If one practices only the meditative concentration of good deeds, one is born only in the upper realms;
if one combines various merits and wisdom, one proceeds to the ten directions according to one's inclination. Regarding the "flying mind":
Since this is a collateral discussion regarding merit and wisdom, the term "combined" (*jiān*) is used in both cases.
[The *Shu*] states that Tiantai says there are two paths within those who possess pure thoughts: first, rebirth in the heavens; second, rebirth in the Pure Land.

The thought of being reborn in the heavens takes the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions as its karma. According to the sutra, this involves thought alone and lacks [the cultivation of] merit.

Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*) and aspiration (*praṇidhāna*): according to principle, even when born into the Inner Court of Tuṣita, there is both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom, as well as pure aspiration.

If one is born into the Form or Formless Realms, these are likewise accompanied by the merit of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). For those born in the Pure Land, all four meanings are fully present;
yet it is said that one "is born there in accordance with aspiration" because, in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, faith, practice, and aspiration are essential.
The three dharmas serve as the primary foundation, and within these three dharmas, the vow for purity serves as the guiding principle.
Both the Pure Lands of Bhaisajyaguru and Amitābha contain methods for exhorting one to seek rebirth there; however, it is the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī that is most widely followed.
If one possesses pure thoughts, merit, wisdom, and the vow for purity, the Pure Land will naturally manifest before one at the moment of death. Do not—
One will not attain rebirth in accordance with one's vows.
(2. Little emotion and much thought: With little emotion and much thought, one is lightly elevated;

though not far away, one becomes a flying immortal, a powerful ghost-king, a flying yakṣa, or a land-walking rākṣasa, roaming through the four heavens without hindrance. Among them, if there are virtuous vows and virtues...

Those who protect and uphold my Dharma with their minds, or protect the prohibitive precepts according to those who maintain the precepts; or protect divine mantras according to those who maintain the mantras;
or protect meditative concentration and preserve the patience of the Dharma—these individuals dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Because their superior thoughts are not pure and they are slightly hindered by deviant emotions, they give rise to this class [of beings].

"Among them, the lower grade" refers to those who, despite being hindered by deviant emotions, possess virtuous vows; thus they attract virtuous conditions, namely the classes of the Eight Divisions of Devas and Dragons (deva-nāga-aṣṭakula).

Zhēn-jì says: "Emotions are few and thoughts are many"—this is a general statement. In principle, it is appropriate to divide these into four categories according to their relative degrees of superiority and inferiority.
With one emotion and nine thoughts, one becomes a flying immortal; with two emotions and eight thoughts, one becomes a powerful ghost-king;
with three emotions and seven thoughts, one becomes a flying yakṣa; with four emotions and six thoughts, one becomes a terrestrial rākṣasa.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Among those with "little emotion and much thought" (qíng shǎo xiǎng duō), there are also two paths.

First, those who possess wholesome vows and a wholesome mind, yet take only the ten wholesome acts of an inferior grade as their practice. Second, those who possess wholesome vows and a wholesome mind, but for whom the vehicle is urgent while the precepts are lax;
such individuals are able to dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata to hear the Great Dharma.
Furthermore:

(3. Equalization of Sentiment and Thought) When sentiment and thought are equalized, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans; if thought is clear, one is intelligent, and if sentiment is obscure, one is dull-witted.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Present acuity or dullness is induced by past emotional conceptions (*qingxiang*).
Thus, we know that what is called 'equal' refers to karma of collective retribution (*zongbao*), while what is called 'darkness and light' refers to karma of individual retribution (*biebao*).
Due to the relative strength or weakness of the emotional conceptions one has habitually practiced, differences such as acuity and dullness arise."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When emotion (*qing*) and thought (*xiang*) are equal, they likewise divide into two paths. Although thought consists of five parts, there is a distinction between brightness and darkness.
Those who are bright are clever; thus, they possess much wisdom. Although emotion also consists of five parts, it likewise divides into heavy and light.
Those whose emotion is heavy are dull; thus, they are mostly ignorant and deluded. Although dark thought is close to emotion, emotion is still thought. Although light emotion—
"Near-thought" (*jìn-yǎng*) is still like "emotion" (*qíng*).
(4) When emotion is predominant and thought is scarce, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth; the heavy become the fur-bearing beasts, and the light become the winged tribes.

When the seven emotions are dominant and the three thoughts are weak, one sinks below the water-wheel and is born at the limit of fire, receiving a breath from fierce flames and becoming a hungry ghost (*preta*), constantly consumed by fire.

Boiling water can harm oneself; for a hundred thousand kalpas, one has neither food nor drink. With nine feelings and one thought, one descends through the wheel of fire, the body entering the ground where wind and fire intersect.
From this light birth in the *sāntara* (intermediate) hell, one is reborn in the *avīci* (uninterrupted) hell—these being the two types of hells.

[Commentary] Zhenji said: "When emotion (*qing*) is predominant and thought (*xiang*) is slight, one should likewise divide them into four categories. With six emotions and four thoughts, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth (*hengsheng*).
With seven emotions and three thoughts, one falls as a hungry ghost (*preta*). With eight emotions and two thoughts, one is born in the *sāntara* hells.

With nine emotions and one thought, one is born in the *avīci* hells. Wénlǐng said: "As for 'horizontal birth,' because emotion is predominant, one undergoes transformation while still carrying thoughts."
Therefore, they fly upward; yet because their karma is heavy, they cannot remain merely among the flocks of beasts.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the very bottom of the great earth are the wheels of gold, water, and wind, with the eight cold and eight hot hells situated above these three wheels.
This text, however, speaks of sinking down through the wheels of water, fire, and wind, which suggests that the hells might be below the three wheels. This is a point of doubt.
What is indicated here is not the three wheels beneath the earth, but rather the three wheels of hell. The phrase "the water wheel at the limit of fire" refers to the eighth cold hell.
Regarding "receiving the fierce fire," this means receiving fiery vapors to form one's body, thereby being constantly burned by fire;
even if one obtains water to drink, it transforms into fire, hence it is said that "water can harm oneself. Below is the cave.
The "wheel of fire" refers to the eight hot hells. "The body enters the ground where wind and fire intersect" means that one transcends the cold hells and enters the hot hells.
The eighth of these hot hells is named the Five Uninterrupted (Avīci) Hells; the others, numbering seven, are those with intervals.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"Within the seven hot hells themselves, there are naturally degrees of lightness and heaviness; however, this 'uninterrupted' [hell] is not one of the five."
[Interval. In the following text, the Avīci hell is specifically identified as the eighth hot hell and is called the "Five Uninterrupted [Hells].

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Sentient beings with a predominance of passion and a scarcity of wisdom are divided into four categories; however, regarding their rebirth destinies, there are only three types.
Regarding the three types [of offenses], each is divided into light and heavy to discuss the resulting retribution. Two clarify the opening [of the teaching], while one has its meaning obscured.

If one were to differentiate them, the light refers to those with possessions (*sāpateya*), and the heavy refers to those without possessions (*anāpateya*).孤山 (Gushan) further states that the "Seven Hot Hells" refer to the seventh of the eight great hells. The *Dīrgha Āgama* says: "These four..."
The world-system consists of eight thousand worlds surrounded on all sides. Beyond these, there is further a great ocean that encircles them.
These eight thousand worlds are, in turn, surrounded by a great Vajra-mountain that encompasses the waters of the great ocean.

Outside of this Vajra-mountain is a second great Vajra-mountain. The *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra) states that these two Vajra-mountains are also called the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
Mountains. Between these two mountains, it is so deep and dark that even the sun, moon, and celestial deities cannot illuminate it.
Therein lie eight hot hells. Each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary hells. The first great hell is named Sañjīva (Reviving); the second is Kālasūtra (Black Rope);
the third is Saṃghāta (Crushing); the fourth is Raurava (Screaming); the fifth is Mahāraurava (Great Screaming); the sixth is...
The seventh is *Tāpana* (Scorching), and the eighth is named *Avīci* (Uninterrupted). Their respective characteristics are fully detailed in the nineteenth fascicle.
Furthermore, the newly translated *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Where are the hells located? It answers:
"For the most part, they are beneath this Jambudvīpa. How are they established? Some say that forty thousand *yojanas* below this continent..."
The *yojana* extends down to the bottom of the Avīci Hell. The Avīci Hell is twenty thousand *yojanas* in length, breadth, and height.
Above this, within a space of nineteen thousand *yojanas*, the remaining seven hells are established. That is to say, above it is the Pratāpana (Extremely Hot) Hell;
above that is the Tapana (Hot) Hell; above that is the Mahāraurava (Great Wailing) Hell; and above that is the Raurava (Wailing) Hell.
Above [these] are Saṃjīva (Reviving), above that is Kālasūtra (Black String), and above that is Saṃghāta (Crushing).
Each of these seven hells is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Some say that the Avīci (Uninterrupted) Hell surrounds them all, just as a great city is surrounded by its villages.
(And so forth. It is only within this [Avīci] hell itself that there are degrees of lightness and heaviness; however, this [distinction] does not exist [in the others].
If the "interval" (*antara*) were not the five *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses, then the sixth should also be considered "with interval" (*sāntara*) and the seventh "without interval" (*anantara*).
In that case, the two elements of wind and fire would intersect, and the earth element would extend through both the sixth and seventh stages. Tiantai said:

"The locations of the hells are not what is being discussed here as being 'different'; rather, they merely appear to one another in alternating fashion. It must be between the two mountains of diamond (*vajra*)."
Furthermore, that which is light is below the great earth, while that which is heavy is above it. Moreover, it is not only this;
even in vast wildernesses and deep mountains, there are places where spirits and deities punish offenders, such as Fengdu in Sichuan and Mount Tai, the Eastern Peak.
Likewise, the City God (Chenghuang) and the Local Deity (She-ling) also possess prisons like those found in the human world, which people frequently encounter. It is not so? No, it is indeed so.

Those who claim to have seen King Yama and the hells, or say that a certain person became King Yama after death, should know that King Yama, the Dharma King, has his own abode between the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
It is not easy for humans to see him, nor is it easy to become him; what they have seen and what they have become are merely manifestations of the underworld.
The Officer of the Ears.

(5. Pure Sentient Beings) Those of pure sentiment sink directly into the Avīci Hell. If, while sinking, their minds harbor slander of the Mahāyāna, violation of the Buddha’s prohibitions, deceptive and false preaching, hollow greed for offerings of faith, or unwarranted acceptance of reverence;
or if they commit the five heinous crimes or the ten grave offenses, they will further undergo ten [rebirths].

Now, regarding the Avīci Hell: (2) A detailed exposition of the seven hells based on karmic retribution. (3) First, the realm of hell-beings: (a) Concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; (b) First, concluding the preceding: Although one invites [rebirth] through the performance of evil karma, within the commonality of sentient beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), there are also the original lands.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: *Avīci* (阿鼻) means "Without Interval" (*mūrcchā*).

This refers to the five things—namely, the suffering of retribution, the instruments of punishment, the physical dimensions of the body, the duration of the kalpa, and the lifespan—all of which lack any intervening gap; thus it is called the "Five Without Interval.

Only those whose emotional karma is most heavy fall into this realm and remain until the kalpa is destroyed before they emerge. If their offenses additionally include slandering the Mahāyāna and so forth, then even when this kalpa is destroyed...

Furthermore, they enter the Avīci hells of the ten directions with no prospect of escape, because by slandering the Dharma and violating the precepts, they cause countless people to fall into false views.
As to the previous question regarding whether the hells have fixed locations or arise spontaneously:

the answer is that although the pure state of emotion (the karma) is personally incurred, the resulting experience is not without fixed locations, as it is induced by shared karma. As for the "original lands," each...
According to the original source.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Even within the Avīci Hell of pure affliction, there are two categories.

First, those who do not slander the Mahāyāna and so forth, who may reach the end of their existence when the kalpa is destroyed. Second, those who slander the Mahāyāna and so forth, who do not emerge even when the kalpa is destroyed.

The uninterrupted continuity of these acts is inexhaustible. As for the offenses of slandering the Mahāyāna and committing the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) or the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), their transgressions pertain to both the monastic and the lay.
However, regarding the violation of the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, excluding the four grave offenses (*catvāraḥ pārājikāḥ*), they pertain solely to the monastic path.

Therefore, for those on the monastic path who have not yet emptied their conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), it is appropriate to first empty their passions (*kleśa*). Once one is entangled in passion, it constitutes a lapse of conduct.
This is the gradual progression. How much more so for those of pure emotion who reach the inexhaustible Avīci Hell?
Furthermore, emotion and thought should be analyzed through a fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*). Those with pure thought and no emotion are born in celestial palaces or Buddha-lands.
Those with pure emotion and no thought fall into the Avīci Hell. Those possessing both emotion and thought are divided into nine categories. Those with neither emotion nor thought...
This constitutes supramundane true cultivation. If one considers the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi, it is the most supreme vehicle among all forms of true cultivation.
Thus, we know that "pure thought" (*śuddha-saṃkalpa*) has not yet transcended the Pure Land of the Co-residence of Ordinary Beings and Sages.

Furthermore, "emotion" (*kleśa*) is evil, while "thought" (*saṃkalpa*) is good. Rather than speaking directly of good and evil, the terms "emotion" and "thought" are used because [the latter] refers to the... of good and evil.
Karma mostly pertains to body and speech; thus, while wholesome and unwholesome karma reside in the seven [categories] of body and speech, mental karma resides only in its three [aspects].
Yet, the mind is the general [factor], whereas body and speech are the specific ones. The general can encompass the specific, but the specific may not encompass the general.

Now, when it is said that "feeling" (*qing*) includes all that is unwholesome, nothing evil is left out; when it is said that "perception" (*xiang*) encompasses all that is wholesome, nothing good is excluded.
Therefore, by summarizing the eleven types of emotional and conceptual states to clarify their relative degrees, one grasps the general principle, from which the specific details can be understood.
The "Avīci" (Uninterrupted) state of the nine emotions and one thought previously mentioned was described in reference to its lighter aspect;
whereas the present designation of "Avīci" for the Ābhāsvara Hell refers to the ultimate gravity resulting from pure emotion alone. Thus it is that—
The Avīci Hell has three grades: light, heavy, and extremely heavy. The extremely heavy grade is that which is induced by the commission of offenses such as slandering the Mahāyāna. (II.
After Birth) Ānanda, all these are what those sentient beings have experienced as the retribution for their own karma; they created ten habitual causes and received [their results].
Sixfold Mutual Retribution.

[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: The preceding section briefly clarified how emotional and conceptual thoughts trigger transformations; this section details how the faculties and their objects construct one another.

The ten habitual tendencies are rooted in the ten delusions, through which habituation forms evil karma. The sixfold mutual interaction arises from the six sense-faculties, through which they intersect.

This gives rise to evil retribution. Tianru’s supplementary note says: "As for the six mutual interactions, it is like when one creates a karmic cause through the eye while the other five serve as auxiliaries;
at the time of receiving the retribution, they likewise extend to all."

[Commentary] Changshui says: "The ten causes of habitual practice" specifically refers to evil karma. That is, by means of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), consciousness is produced at the gates of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and karma is created;
subsequently, when its retribution is received, it emerges from the six sense organs. Daolin Qinchin’s hand [of commentary] erroneously cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), stating:
"Because it can summon the eighth [consciousness] to draw forth the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), it is called 'projecting karma' (*ākṣepaka-karma*). It can summon the... [text truncated]
The six types of fully ripened *vipāka*-fruits are called "fulfilling karma" (*pūrṇa-karman*). The *Abhidharmakośa* also states: "One projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) produces one birth;
many fulfilling karmas [produce] its complete fulfillment. This is like a painting where the outline is drawn first, and subsequently the various colors are filled in.

Master Jing’s *Shiyao* explains: "That which draws one into hell is projecting karma; that which subsequently experiences the varying degrees of lightness or heaviness [of suffering] is fulfilling karma. Thus it is said.
"This is merely the habitual construction of the deluded sentiments of sentient beings. Tiantai said:

"According to the *Mohe Zhiguan*, in clarifying the correct resolve by distinguishing it from the incorrect, ten types of 'non-mind' are explained. Within each category, there is both mind and conduct.
For example, in the realm of hell, if one's mind is moment-to-moment exclusively devoted to greed, anger, and ignorance, that is 'mind'; if one gives rise to the ten grave evils, that is 'conduct'."
The present text is likewise so. The preceding section clarifies the relative abundance of emotional thoughts (*qingxiang*), which refers to the mind (*xin*).
This subsequent section clarifies the ten habitual causes (*shixi yin*), which refers to conduct (*xing*). The same applies to the six destinies (*liudao*) below.

As for the term "habitual" (*xi*) used for all ten causes, each is defined in the sense of forming a nature (*xing*) based upon habituation. If one were to remain fixed solely on this [single aspect], it would not suffice to fully elucidate the matter.
It is because their practice in this regard has become so habitual that, at the moment of death, they draw it back into themselves and are thus established in hell.

Bodhisattvas view desire as they would avoid a pit of fire.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Evil karma arises from emotional delusions, and sexual desire is the most extreme of such delusions; therefore, it is clarified at the beginning and end [of the section].
Regarding the karma of the ten habitual practices, each first describes the environment experienced as a result, followed by the specific retribution received.
Sexual desire induces the karma of fire because it is ignited by the intense friction of a deluded mind. Therefore, the [resulting]...
In the state of perception during the experience of sensation, one sees a great, fierce fire. King Shu said:

"When the habit of lust is ground away without ceasing, it naturally consumes one's essence, causing the element of fire to blaze up. Since even while alive one suffers from ailments such as parching thirst and internal heat, it is only natural that upon death one sees a great, fierce fire.
The mutual intensification of subject and object is called the 'mutual burning of the two habits. Therefore—"
The retribution of the iron bed and copper pillar corresponds to one's habitual karma. The Tathāgata, acting as a guide, designates them by name to warn [beings] of them;
the Bodhisattva, acting as a practitioner, deeply fears them to avoid them. "Designating by name" (se-mu) is synonymous with naming or labeling.

[Commentary] Changshui says: "The arousal of karma has two aspects: first, the primary arousal, which is ignorance (*avidyā*); second, the auxiliary arousal, which consists of the other afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with discrimination.
Now, among these ten causes, with the exception of the habituation to sexual desire—which is the karma that is aroused—the remaining nine are all the afflictions that act as the arousers.
Tiantai says: According to this, the karma that is aroused should fully comprise [the three types of] bodily [karma].
"Three mouths, four. Now, regarding the karma of sexual desire, it is manifest while other karmas are hidden.
Briefly, if one calculates the habitual tendencies of greed, they fully comprise sexual desire, killing, stealing, and so forth; the rest may be inferred by analogy.
Sexual karma is particularly prominent because it is the root of birth and death and the cause for its initiation. Yunjian said: "Internally, sexual desire produces the water of craving. Now, ten...

Regarding the statement that "sexual desire gives rise to fire while greed gives rise to water": sexual desire has two meanings. First, because it involves greedy attachment, it also gives rise to water.
Second, because the two organs of male and female rub against each other, they generate heat; thus, one receives the retribution of fire.

In the previous passage, the internal division took the meaning of "craving" broadly, and thus sexual desire gave rise to the water of craving. Now, in the context of the ten habitual practices, sexual desire refers specifically to the act of grinding.
This gives rise to the retribution of fire. (2. The habituation of food; 2a.

The sounds [of the hells] are like blue, red, and white lotuses, and the color of ice and frost. Wu Xing said: "Ṭa-pa-ra refers to the three—blue, red, and white;

Third, the habit-energy of pride involves mutual aggression and the arising of mutual reliance; it flows and surges without ceasing. Because of this, there are surging leaps and rushing currents, where accumulated waves form water.

All matters. (2. Censure and Abandonment by Sages and Worthies) Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the mark of arrogance as "drinking the water of delusion.

Bodhisattvas view anger as they would avoid execution.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "The mind belongs to fire, and the breath belongs to metal. One who is angry produces breath from the mind, which in turn agitates the mind.
When this is further compounded by impact and resistance, the fire of the mind becomes even more intense and the metal of the breath becomes even more rigid.
Therefore it is said: 'The heat of the mind emits fire, forging the breath into metal. Regarding punishments, *gōng* refers to castration; *shè* refers to cutting."
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Gong" (castration) was one of the five ancient punishments. Wuxing says:

"The five punishments refer to branding, mutilation of the nose, castration, cutting off the feet, and capital punishment. Branding refers to scarifying the forehead and smearing it with ink. Mutilation of the nose refers to cutting off the nose."
*Fei* (castration) refers to cutting off one's feet. *Gong* (loss of virility) refers to castrating a man; for a woman, it means confining her in seclusion.
*Dapib* (great execution) is the death penalty. *Zhan*, *zhuo*, and *cuo* (beheading, hacking, and mincing) were all methods of the new death penalty.
*Ci* (branding) was the ancient "ink-penalty" (*moxing*), while *chuiji* (beating with a mallet) was of the same category as the new penalties of caning and flogging.

Secretly harboring malice and concealing faults leads to self-harm when they are exposed; the very act of concealing sins is sufficient to oppress and crush oneself.

Because they fall [into these states], it is as if one were wearing a mountain on one's head while treading upon the sea. The ten habitual tendencies (*daśa-vāsanā*) arise from the ten delusions (*daśa-kleśa*);

they encompass both the root afflictions and the secondary ones (*upakleśa*). Among the twenty secondary afflictions, the first are anger, resentment, vexation, concealment, deception, flattery, arrogance, and harm.

Here, the habit of "fraud" corresponds to flattery; "enmity" corresponds to resentment; "injustice" corresponds to harm; and "litigation" corresponds to concealment. This is merely a brief illustration.
[Commentary] Wuxing says that the ten habitual tendencies (*daśa-vāsanā*) correspond to the root and derivative afflictions (*kleśopakleśa*). There are six root afflictions, namely:

greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, they may be categorized as five. There are twenty derivative afflictions, namely:

anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Lack of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*) are now mentioned. The habituation to sexual misconduct is the karma produced therein, fully endowed with greed (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*).

The habituation to deceit is guile (*śāṭhya*). The habituation to enmity is resentment (*upanāha*). "Views" refers to the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*). "Oppression" refers to the category of harming the virtuous through coercion;

it is also of the same class as malice (*vyāpāda*). "Litigation" refers to mutual dispute over gain and loss, preceded by resentment. This is the single nature of the dharma of affliction (*kliṣṭadharma*).

(2. Explaining the six mutual retributions; first, the general explanation: Ānanda, how do the six retributions arise? All sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses, and the evil retributions they thereby attract emerge from the six sense organs.

[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The creation of karma and the summoning of its retribution necessarily involve both the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, while consciousness is treated as the karma, the retribution is attributed to the faculties;
this is because karma generally arises from the mind, whereas retribution is mostly categorized according to form (*rūpa*).

Regarding what is called the "sixfold mutual retribution," Master Xuán says that cause and effect intersect; however, in the present case, it is not so. Rather, it refers to the six faculties at the time of fruition [interacting with their respective objects].
The retributions for evil deeds are interrelated.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: It is indeed a natural law that when all sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses, the resulting retribution for evil arises from the six sense organs.
However, in the following sections, each organ is explained individually as receiving retribution while the other five...
That the faculties experience them together is due to the influence of the six disordered delusions.
Did I not say before? "Therefore, in the world, sound exists because of movement; form exists because of sound; fragrance exists because of form;
flavor exists because of fragrance; touch exists because of flavor; and the cognition of dharmas exists because of touch. These six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma."
Thus, the twelve divisions revolve by means of this wheel. That [text] clarifies that these constitute the root of the twelve classes of birth.
Therefore it is said: "Consequently, the world of sounds, smells, tastes, and touches undergoes twelve transformations, returning as a single cycle.
Now, the sixfold mutual retribution is but one category of those *nirmāṇa*-born beings. At the time they were creating the ten causes of habitual practice, they were necessarily one...
When one faculty commits an offense, the six faculties follow along with deluded conceptualizations, racing outward and acting in concert with it.

Thus, when one faculty undergoes retribution, the other five faculties undergo it together. However, they alternate as subject and object to clarify the distinctions between the six mutual interactions.
For now, this is a general explanation; below, each will be explained individually for those who cultivate the path of *śamatha*.
To recognize these divergent paths as a water-mirror that simplifies what is erroneous and clarifies what is correct.

[II. Specifically demonstrating the two: First, the inquiry: How do evil retributions emerge from the six sense faculties? Second, the demonstration of the six [faculties]. First, the retribution of seeing: 1. The retribution of seeing invites and draws forth evil fruits. Second, the explanation [of this retribution of seeing]: First, the signs seen at the moment of death:

When this faculty of seeing and karma intersect, at the time of death one first sees fierce fires filling the worlds of the ten directions. Second, the process of rebirth through the power of karma: First, the initial signs of entering hell: The deceased’s consciousness...

first, when seeing clearly, they can see all kinds of evil things everywhere, giving rise to immeasurable fear; second, when seeing in the dark, it is silent and nothing is seen, giving rise to immeasurable dread.
(II. The interaction with the six sense organs. Thus, the fire they see burns their hearing, becoming cauldrons of boiling water and molten copper; it burns their breath, becoming black smoke.
The purple flames burn the sense objects, turning them into scorched balls of iron and gruel; they burn the sense of touch, turning it into hot ashes, stoves, and charcoal;
and they burn the mind, producing sparks that scatter and fly about, fanning and filling the entire expanse of space.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Since seeing and cognition belong to the element of fire, they evoke fierce flames. Fear regarding objects is apprehended within the mind.

As for the statement that the six modes of interaction all lead directly into the Avīci Hell, this is said with respect to the most grievous cases. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that those of extreme goodness or extreme evil have no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is why they enter directly.
Since hearing and listening belong to the element of water, the burning of hearing can serve as a cauldron.
The liver corresponds to copper. Because the nose governs the vital breath (*prāṇa*), when it is burned, its breath produces black smoke and purple flames.

The tongue governs taste; "pills" and "porridge" represent the category of tastes. The body governs touch; "ash" and "charcoal" represent the category of tactile objects. The mind properly belongs to fire;
because it flares up more intensely when burned, it scatters sparks and fans the blaze. Wuxing says: "First, this indicates the heading. 'At the time of death' below explains it."

Regarding the signs: first, seeing fierce fires and the like is the retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*); the consciousness of the deceased and so forth is the retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīyavipāka*).

The following section clarifies these two signs in relation to the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*). The subsequent section, beginning with "In this way," clarifies the mutual retribution in relation to all the faculties.

This pattern applies to all others as well. However, it is difficult to comprehend how the evil retribution of a single faculty is experienced pervasively by all five faculties; such is the principle.
When we examine this further, it must be that at the time karma is created by the six consciousnesses, their natures correspond while their functions diverge.
It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that receiving retribution according to one's karma is exactly like this. Because their natures correspond, the six types of retribution interpenetrate;

because their functions diverge, the various characteristics differ. That these are manifested solely through consciousness can be believed as being beyond doubt. [Question: Within the five types of retribution mentioned below, all...
There are signs of retribution corresponding to each specific faculty (*indriya*). Now, if the eye-faculty sees fire and subsequently experiences being burned, why is this not mentioned for the ear?

The answer is: because the experience of being burned is more easily understood through the example of seeing; furthermore, since subsequent phenomena such as black smoke, purple flames, and scattering sparks are all retributions experienced by the eye-faculty, they are not mentioned separately.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This takes the eye-faculty seeing forms and creating offenses as the host, while the other five faculties being led to create offenses together with it are the guests.

If one considers the six confused delusions created when the eye conditions form-objects, then taking the movement of the faculty to see forms as the root, there subsequently follows hearing scents because of forms, tasting flavors because of scents, and perceiving touches because of flavors.
One knows phenomena through contact, and hears sounds through phenomena. To speak briefly in terms of the commission of a single act of killing:

for instance, when one sees an animal because it has moved, one falsely imagines that the animal can be eaten; thus, one proceeds to kill, taking the movement as the cause and the visible form as the object.
Alternatively, one may kill an animal because of its odor, and as a result, there is odor within the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Or again, one may kill an animal because of its flavor, and as a result, there is flavor within the realm of fragrance (*gandha-dhātu*).

Or again, one may kill an animal because of its hot, edible nature, and as a result, there is tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) within the realm of flavor (*rasa-dhātu*). Or again, one may kill an animal because of internal mental reflection, and as a result...

There are phenomena involving contact; or again, there are phenomena that take sound as a condition, such as the sounds of roasting, broiling, and cutting, which serve as the cause for committing acts of killing.
Therefore, when one undergoes the evil retribution of hell, there are two types of experience: the primary experience and the secondary experience, which differ from one another.
Because the eye-faculty belongs to the element of fire, at the time of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions, manifesting two distinct signs.

When the primary retribution (*maulavipāka*) is experienced through the sense-faculties, the burning of hearing, smelling, and the other faculties constitutes their secondary retribution (*pārśvavipāka*).
The retribution of one faculty is thus; the retribution of the other faculties follows this same principle. As the subsequent passage states:

"Because sentient beings individually act and individually create, they enter the stage of homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) within the world, where delusive thoughts arise; these do not exist from the beginning. This is the sixth [point of] confusion."
That which is produced by deluded conceptualization does not exist from the beginning.

The commentary states that when it manifests as breath, it becomes rain and mist, for water changes according to the qi.

The commentary states that when it manifests as flavor, it becomes pus and blood, for water changes according to the flavor. The commentary states that when it manifests as touch, it becomes animals and ghosts, for water changes according to the form. When it manifests as thought...

The Avīci Hell. (II. (Second, the interaction with the six sense organs: Such perverse thoughts, when bound together, can manifest as the "direction" and the "object. When the faculty of sight is bound, it manifests as the mirror and the witness. When the faculty of hearing is bound, it manifests as... [the text continues].
It can transform stones into ice, frost, earth, or mist; when it binds the breath, it can become a great fire, a fire-chariot, a fire-boat, or a fire-cage;

The basis of the karma of thought does not transcend delusion and awakening. "Wandering in haste" refers to deluded thought; "knowing suffering" refers to awakened thought.

If one does not relinquish the human body, one will become their slave or encounter their robbery and murder.
(2. The Difficulty of Ending Retribution) Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money and goods or employs their labor to repay the debt, it will cease once the repayment is complete;
however, if in the interim one kills their life or eats their flesh, this cycle continues even through as many *paramāṇu* eons as there are grains of dust, as they continue to eat one another.
The cycle of killing is like the turning of a wheel, alternating between high and low without rest; it can only be halted through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says:
"When the retribution is fully paid, one naturally stops, and thus there is no mutual enmity. When the retribution is not fully paid, one does not stop, and thus mutual enmity persists."
It does not cease. Unless one correctly cultivates the power of right effort, there is no way to block or sever it. Wuxing said:

"Śamatha and the appearance of a Buddha in the world—these refer to cultivating meditative concentration to destroy delusions, seeing the Buddha, and attaining the Way, whereby one may finally avoid mutual harm.
Even if there is karma from past lives that has been created and is not lost, it will be requited upon reaching the fruit; yet this is like a magical illusion and is not real."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: When one has paid off a debt in full and stops, both the records of the karmic consciousness are cleared away.
It is as if there were a silent presiding authority that acts spontaneously without being sought. If it were not for this spontaneous occurrence, it would not be so.
If one kills living beings, one will be slaughtered for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; if one eats meat, one will prey upon others for a long time.

Thus, the high and the low revolve like the buckets of a well-drawing wheel. Unless one cultivates the power of *śamatha* to awaken to the Way and exert valor to emerge from the realm of dust, and unless one encounters a Buddha’s era to rely on the power of supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*) to be rescued and uplifted, [one cannot escape].
On this perilous path, by what means can birth and death be brought to rest, and by what means can karmic retribution be halted?
(2. Specific Manifestation) You should now know that those of the owl kind, once their retribution is fulfilled, will return to form in the human realm, merging with the dull-witted;
those of the omen-sign kind, once their retribution is fulfilled, will return to form in the human realm, merging with the eccentric; and those of the fox kind...
Those of the "Poisonous" class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the common folk.
Those of the "Worm" class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the lowly class.
Those of the "Eater" class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the gentle class.
Those who belong to the category of the "serving" (fu-lun) receive full recompense and are restored to form, being reborn among humans as members of the class of laborers;
those who belong to the category of the "responding" (ying-lun) receive full recompense and are restored to form, being reborn among humans as members of the literary class;

those who belong to the category of the "resting" (xiu-zheng) receive full recompense and are restored to form, being reborn among humans as members of the enlightened class; and those who follow the various categories of conduct receive full recompense and are restored to form, being reborn among humans.

The middle [category] participates in the class of those who have attained [liberation]. (Third, the summary and indication: Ānanda, all these individuals have fully repaid their past debts and returned to the human realm;
