yet, from time immemorial, they have been subject to the delusions of karmic calculation, giving rise to one another and killing one another.

Had they not encountered the Tathāgata and heard the True Dharma, they would have naturally continued to revolve within the midst of worldly toil. Such people as these are called "those worthy of compassion."
[Commentary] Tianru’s Supplement states: Because the *xiāo* (owl) feeds on clods of earth, its residual habits result in stubbornness, stupidity, and unrighteousness.
Since calamitous omens originate from licentiousness, its residual habits manifest as strange portents.

Because the fox, due to past causes of greed and delusion, encounters animals to become a *mèi* (demon), and since all *mèi* are ultimately foxes, when it is now reborn as a human, it is vulgar, base, and ignorant. [Poison.]

The *lun* (lineage/continuity) of violence is also the residue of habituation. The *hui* (parasites) attach themselves to things through decaying qi; thus they are weak and insignificant, and are not counted among the ranks of living beings.

The *shi lun* (lineage of eating) arises from voracious consumption; thus they are soft and timid, lacking courage. The *fu lun* (lineage of clothing) arises from continuous attachment [to materials];
thus labor and service never cease. The *ying lun* (lineage of response) arises from refined spirit; thus its cultural artifacts are not crude. Auspicious omens arise from...

Because they possess spiritual knowledge, they are intelligent and not dull; because they follow the social order and have experienced worldly affairs over many lifetimes, they are discerning and not ignorant.
These qualities are all not their primary karmic retribution (*vipāka*), but rather incidental to residual habits (*vāsanā*); thus, they are said to be "intermingled.
The latter three [qualities] are merely cleverness in various arts and mundane wisdom and eloquence; they do not constitute the conduct of the truly wise or the clarity of the enlightened.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: "As for the Way of humanity, in former lives one takes the five precepts and ten wholesome acts as its cause;

in this life, one takes the three fundamental relationships and the five constant virtues as its Way. Advancing along it, one may ascend to deliver the spiritual intelligence and transcend birth and death."
If one maintains this alone without losing it, then life after life they shall dwell in the Middle Kingdom, generation after generation never forfeiting their human form.

This is what constitutes the rectitude of the constant patterns (*yilun*). As for the ten categories clearly explained in the present text, know that none of them are but the fulfillment of past debts leading to a renewed human existence;
they are certainly not primary karmic retributions (*zhengbao*). Only the final three...

There are those who resemble fine jade but are actually mere agate; one must examine them closely to see whether the Three Bonds are rectified and the Five Constant Virtues are fully realized, for only then are they true reincarnations of sages.
Otherwise, as the Master of Wénlíng said, these are merely matters of clever artifice, worldly ingenuity, and sharp eloquence—not the deeds of the wise and enlightened or the clarity of civilization.
To take such things as the "eyelashes of a crane" (a triviality) is a grave error.
By this, one may verify whether those throughout the world are humans or non-humans, leaving no strategy untried. (V. The Five Classes of Immortals;

III. The Three Initial Stages; General Summary) Ānanda, furthermore, there are those among the followers who do not rely on the Right Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead separately cultivate deluded thoughts, maintaining their mental conceptions to solidify their physical forms.
They roam in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary men; these are the ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Xiān" (Immortal) means "to transcend. It refers to one whose physical form and spirit can transcend and not die.

Therefore, it is said: "Maintain visualization to solidify the form. Nevertheless, in the end, one returns to decay and ruin. Because they are inferior to Heaven yet superior to ordinary humans, they are categorized separately. Gūshān says:
*Bǎopǔzǐ* states that those who seek to become immortals must primarily rely on loyalty and filial piety, and on harmony...
Compliance with benevolence and faithfulness is the foundation. If one does not cultivate virtue but merely devotes oneself to esoteric arts, one will ultimately never attain longevity.

○ (2. Separate Manifestation) Ānanda, when those sentient beings take medicinal substances with steadfast persistence without ceasing, and their path of nourishment becomes perfected, it is called the "Accomplished Name."

The earth-walking immortal (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*) solidifies plants and trees without ceasing; when the path of medicine is perfected, one is called the flying immortal (*khecarī-ṛṣi*), who solidifies metal and stone without ceasing.
When the path of transformation is perfected, one is called the wandering immortal (*vicarī-ṛṣi*), who solidifies movement and stillness without ceasing.
When the vital essence (*ojas*) is perfected, one is called the space-walking immortal (*ākāśacarī-ṛṣi*), who solidifies the bodily fluids (*rasa*) without ceasing, thereby providing nourishment.
When virtue is perfected, it is called the Celestial-Practice Immortal (*devayāna-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in refined radiance without ceasing;

when absorbing the essence is perfected, it is called the Penetrating-Practice Immortal (*samudācāra-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in incantations and prohibitions without ceasing; when ritual methods are perfected, it is called the Path-Practice Immortal (*mārga-caryā-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in contemplation without ceasing;
and when recollection is perfected, it is called the Illuminating-Practice Immortal (*āloka-caryā-ṛṣi*), who remains firm in mutual union.
"Attaining the perfection of responsive resonance without rest is called the 'Refined Practice Immortal' (jìngxíng xiān), who possesses firm and stable transformations without ceasing.
Attaining the perfection of awakening is called the 'Transcendent Practice Immortal' (juéxíng xiān).
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Those who rely on medicinal elixirs to sustain a single lifetime's span of life, yet cannot achieve levitation, are the Earth [Immortals]."

"Xingxian" (行僊) means "practicing immortality. "Xing" (行) is pronounced with the departing tone; it refers to meritorious practice (*gōngxíng*). One who consumes yellow essence (*huángjīng*), pine, cypress, and the like, and after a long time becomes light of body, is a "flying immortal" (*fēixíng xiān*).

One who refines metallic stones and the "returning elixir" (*huándān*) to transform the bones and change the form, and who can grasp soil or touch stone to sport among humans, is a "wandering immortal" (*yóuxíng xiān*).
One who rides upon the movement and stillness of Yin and Yang to regulate... [the breath].
Those who consolidate their vital energy (*qi*), retain their essence (*jing*), and traverse the void are *xingxian* (walking immortals).

Those who stir the celestial pond (*tianchi*), swallow the essence-fluids (*jinli*), and remain as pure as ice and snow—untouched by worldly desires and indistinguishable from Heaven—are *tianxingxian* (heavenly walking immortals).

Those who inhale refined colors, consume rainbows and drink mists, and whose subtle breath penetrates in hidden ways are *tongxingxian* (penetrating walking immortals). Those who are able to transmit [these attainments] through ritual arts and methods...

The Way of spontaneity (*ziran*) is the Immortal of Way-practice (*daoxing xian*). That which clarifies and concentrates through refined contemplation, being able to respond with illumination over a long period, is the Immortal of Illumination-practice (*zhaoxing xian*).
Whether one visualizes the cranial aperture to emit the spirit, or fixes the mind on the navel wheel (*cílún*) to refine the elixir, these are all the perfect realization of recollective thought.
Internally, this involves the matching of the male of the *kan* trigram and the female of the *li* trigram as husband and wife; externally, it is the gathering of yin to provide assistance.
Those who gather and protect their vital essence so that it circulates as refined spirit are *xingxian* (transcendents by circulation).

Those who contemplate and transform through principles, whose minds follow perverse awakenings yet can achieve great transformations, and whose conduct transcends the world, are *juexingxian* (transcendents by transcendence).
[Commentary]: Those who practice the Way at the "Limit of Reality" (bhūtakoṭi) ingest cinnabar to preserve the physical form for a long duration.

Although they achieve spiritual accomplishment, their bodies cannot fly. Those who practice "flying" consume pine and cypress, remaining in a state of leisure, serenity, and profound harmony; because their essence is light and pure, they are able to levitate.
Those who practice "wandering" exhaustively investigate transformations and examine the primal nature of things, such as transmuting stone into gold.
The "Golden One" (Jinxing) relieves the poor and pities those in suffering as they wander through the human world;

practitioners of emptiness (Kongxing) employ their vital spirits (*shenqi*) and cultivate transformations as their merit, achieving perfection in virtue and attaining sovereign mastery over the void. The "Celestial Practitioner" (Tianxing) swallows elixir (*jin*) to fortify the physical substance and restrains the essence to maintain it;
thus, they do not engage with the realms of desire, remaining no different from the heavens. Yuan’s commentary states that this heaven is not among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is like Zhang Qian reaching the summit of Mount Kunlun and beholding the heavens. Those who practice this path inhale the solar energy to nourish and enhance their physical forms;
by swallowing the radiance of the dawn clouds, they shall prolong their lives beyond the mundane world. Because its Way is profound and manifest, it is called "Universal Practice" (Tongxing).
Those who practice this Way study various incantations and spells to restrain external distractions; once the power of these arts is perfected, their merit flows forth.
To benefit sentient beings, the practitioner employs their contemplation to examine the mind within its objects;
when the power of such recollection is perfected, one is able to know those objects—namely, the supernormal powers of knowing the minds of others and recollecting past lives within the mundane realm.
○ (Third, the summary indication: Ānanda, all such as these refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate right enlightenment;

instead, they separately attain a mode of existence, living for ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on great ocean islands far removed from the realm of men. This, too, is the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra;
failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.
[Commentary] Changshui says: Regarding the mention of "among humans," this is because there is no separate collective retribution (*vipāka*) for the realm of immortals (*ṛṣi*).
It refers to taking the human body’s collective retribution as the basis and adding the ten types of prior cultivation and refinement to transform it into an immortal. Wuxing says:

In the preceding text, those with little passion and much thought who achieve lightness and elevation that is not far-reaching are termed "Wind-Immortals" (*vāyu-ṛṣi*). This is based on their state at the end of life.
This is spoken in reference to birth through the power of karma. As the subsequent text states: "One minutely examines that all seven realms are merely the marks of deluded existence;
they are births through false imagination and followings of karma. To claim that there is no distinct collective retribution for the realm of immortals is incorrect.
Furthermore, how could it not be distinct when it is said that deep mountains, oceans, and islands are utterly remote from the human realm?
One should know that for those who refine the mind among humans, it does not consist merely of taking medicinal elixirs to nourish life.

It must be accompanied by precepts and wholesome deeds to be truly called "refining the mind. That one separately attains the principle of life is precisely because the karma of a human being induces a retribution in the realm of immortals.
Because the nature of that karmic seed is not lost throughout successive lifetimes, it is called the "principle of life" (*li-sheng*). Even if...
As for humans attaining the principle of longevity and far-reaching vision in the present world, how many such cases are there?

If one is born into the realm of the immortals (*siddha*), then a lifespan of thousands of millions of years is indeed possible. As the *Shanhai jing* states: "On Mount Kunlun, in the wilds of Guangdu, at the Mound of Xuanyuan, lies the Land of the Immortals;
there the vital breath is never obstructed and there is no summer heat, and all people live for several thousand years. This is so.
Furthermore, the commonality of various individuals is not without a fixed basis.

If one merely fortifies the physical form without refining the mind, yet hopes for a thousand-year lifespan, is this not like seeking a rooster at dawn upon seeing an egg? Is it not a premature calculation?
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the text on the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), the doctrine of karma is established with certainty;

thus, when the Tathāgata proclaimed it from his golden mouth, there was none who did not believe, accept, and practice it. Only the single gate of the destiny of immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*) is close to the Daoist teachings.
Since the teaching of the Dao has long vied with the two [other] traditions, and the Way of Immortals has been adopted as its primary tenet, they are not merely identical.

Furthermore, desiring to surpass them, I shall now set aside these [objections] and establish two categories to discern their underlying tenets and distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous.
This is intended to provide those entering the Buddha-way with a proper direction to follow, so that they are not deluded by the teachings of the immortals.
Regarding the clarification of its essential purport: within the text, it is fully explained that cause and effect each have their own emphases and de-emphases.
First, in clarifying the causes, among the practices for refining the mind (*liàn-xīn*), there is emphasis. In the preceding discussion on types [of practitioners], it states:

"Those who firmly consume medicinal elixirs and firmly use herbal plants" and so forth; these all refer to refining the physical form (*liàn-xíng*). Yet, when it speaks of "refining the mind," it does so because one must be firm and resolute regarding the consumption of those elixirs.
When one’s aspirations are unwavering and the mind is free from divergent thoughts, even though one refines the physical form, it is in fact the refinement of the mind.
Furthermore, since those who possess such firm and steadfast contemplation exist, there is no reason why it would be improper to speak of them as constituting the majority.

However, the reason for using the specific term "refinement" (*lian*) rather than "cultivation" (*xiu*) is precisely what the practitioners of the Way of the Immortals (*shenxianjia*) call "cultivation and refinement" (*xiulian*). It is not [merely cultivation].
"Correcting cultivation" means to restrain. Although the human mind is deluded, the Buddha’s Bodhi of correct awakening exists within it;

by cultivating it, one can become a Buddha. Yet, those people abandon correct awakening and fail to cultivate it, instead merely seeking comfort for their foul bodies and gratifying their ignorant minds, taking pride in the so-called "double cultivation of life and nature.
Therefore, they are restrained with the words: "Do not practice what is not correct."
[This section] clarifies the principle of the distinct attainment within the fruit [of enlightenment], which is the "principle of life" (shengli).

This "principle of life" refers to the principle of the continuous generation of the world, which corresponds to what the Confucian school calls "principle and qi" (liqi). As it is said: "Heaven transforms and generates the myriad things through the five elements and yin-yang;
qi forms their physical shapes, while principle is also bestowed upon them. Although this is discussed in Buddhism, [it is here applied].
It is not said that Heaven produces beings by means of *qi* (vital energy) to form their bodies; how could one possibly differ from this?

Therefore, when humans are born, the length of their lifespan—whether long or short—must necessarily follow the flourishing or decline of their underlying principle and *qi*. For instance, at the beginning of the kalpa, human hearts were simple and honest, and all practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
Because the movement of the *qi* was flourishing, there was a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years. From that time onward, day by day...

Consequently, people have gradually become corrupt and immersed in unwholesome ways. When Śākyamuni transformed the world, it was toward the end of a *kalpa* of decline, and he returned to the truth at the age of eighty.
As the ancients said, "In ancient times, it was rare for a person to reach seventy," yet the natural lifespan of human beings is limited to just that.
Now, by refining the mind among humans, one obtains the manifest retribution of a lifespan of ten million years.
Is it not the case that there is a principle by which one attains this state? Therefore, the glossators say: "Xian" (Immortal) means "to shift" (*qian*).
One may shift a short lifespan into a long life; one may shift terrestrial movement into flight; or one may shift from the human realm to a residence of jade.

Since this is the natural course of principle and not a matter of falsehood, it is said that those who live for thousands or tens of thousands of years rest in mountain forests, or [attain] greatness.
To be isolated from the human realm on a sea island is also a form of suppression within saṃsāra.
The reason one revolves in saṃsāra is that one follows the flow of deluded thoughts and fails to cultivate the samādhi of true awakening.

What was referred to in the preceding text as "separately cultivating deluded thoughts and maintaining mental images to solidify the physical form" does not go beyond internally harboring loyalty, filial piety, harmony, obedience, benevolence, and trustworthiness.

Taking the fundamental as the root and externalizing through deluded thoughts to solidify the physical form constitutes the secondary; by restraining private desires and undergoing austere hardships, one seeks retribution.
Since the mind is not permanent, how could it avoid exhaustion? Since conduct is not quiescent extinction, how could one attain the state of non-arising?

Therefore, "longevity" is a term used in contrast to a short lifespan. It is like drawing a bow to shoot at the void: when the strength is exhausted, one falls; when the retribution is spent, one returns.
They come and disperse into the various realms of existence according to the karma previously created. Second, regarding the distinction between what is correct and what is not:

if we speak precisely of the primary teachings for the human world, there are three categories: namely, the teaching of birth-and-birth (*jìng-shēng*), the teaching of longevity (*cháng-shēng*), and the teaching of non-arising (*wú-shēng*).
Within the teaching of birth-and-birth, there are the four wheels and ten [teachings] of the land of Central India.

This is correct. It is the same as the Confucianism of this land. Because it takes the uninterrupted continuity of life as its fundamental principle, it is said that among the three thousand categories of the five punishments, no crime is greater than filial impiety.
Furthermore, it is said that there are three forms of filial impiety, of which having no descendants is the greatest.
Because it takes the nourishment of life as its primary concern, it is said: "Where there is territory, there is wealth; where there is wealth," [there is ritual].
This is of practical utility. Furthermore, it is said: "Plant mulberry trees on five-mu plots; do not deprive those with a hundred-mu fields of their proper seasons.

Be diligent in the instruction of the schools and reinforce this with teachings on filial piety and fraternal duty. If the common people are neither hungry nor cold, yet there is no one who attains kingship—such a thing has never occurred.
The teaching of longevity is exemplified by the Ten Immortals; it is similar to this [Confucian] method.
It is the same as Daoism. Because it takes longevity as its foundation, it says: "Heaven is long-lasting and Earth is enduring.

That Heaven and Earth are able to be so long and enduring is because they do not live for themselves; therefore, they are able to live long. For this reason, the sage puts his own person last and thus his person is foremost;
he sets aside his own person and thus his person survives. Is it not because he is without selfishness that he is thus able [to achieve this]?
He accomplishes his private ends. Because he takes the preservation of life as his primary concern, it is said: "To go forth from birth and enter into death.
There are thirteen ways that lead to life; there are thirteen ways that lead to death; and there are thirteen ways by which people, while living, move toward the ground of death.
What is the reason? It is because they are too thick in their pursuit of life. I have heard that those who are skilled at preserving life do not [fear] traveling on land...
When encountering rhinoceroses or tigers while entering an army, one does not wear armor or weapons;

the rhinoceros has nowhere to plant its horn, the tiger has nowhere to set its claws, and the soldier has no place to apply the edge of his blade. For what reason? Because there is no ground for death.
The teaching of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is precisely our Buddha-way. Since it takes non-arising as its foundation, it is said that "all phenomena are quiescent."

The characteristic of cessation cannot be expressed in words. It is further said: "All dharmas do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both together, nor without a cause; therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. It is also said:

"The continuous succession of birth and death among all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity. This is because they take the cycle of birth and death as their master."
Therefore it is said: "The seer and the objects of sight, along with all perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and its conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi; how could there be within them 'is' or 'is not'?"
Therefore, those who nourish life must make it substantial; those who regulate life must make it sparse; and those who harmonize life must make it light.
Thus, when the three teachings are applied to the human world, they cannot do without the nourishment of life—it is only that their approaches differ in being substantial, sparse, or light.
Consequently, that which gives rise to life is destiny (*ming*); that which possesses life is nature (*xing*). It is like a physical form...
Sound cannot be far removed from its echo or shadow; when the sound is harmonious, the resonance follows suit, and when the form is straight, the shadow is upright.
Observe those in the world who practice as teachers: they seek the source-sound through turbid echoes and seek the original form through distorted shadows.
In their study of the nature and destiny (*xing-ming*), they are already far astray. As for the current discourse on the school of the Immortals (*xian-zong*)...
These individuals strive for loftiness and distance, refusing to甘心 (consent) to having their names listed among the ten immortals.
They claim that the ten immortals of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are not the celestial immortals of our own Way.

They even seek to disparage the Buddhist teachings, asserting that the followers of Śākyamuni cultivate nature (*xing*) but do not cultivate life-force (*ming*), whereas our own teaching cultivates both nature and life-force, such that body and spirit are both rendered wondrous. Alas!
To call forth the form and spirit so that both become subtle—only a Buddha can achieve this. Apart from the Buddha, who among those below him is free from change, death, and rebirth?

Furthermore, as for practitioners of immortality who wish to maintain the body born of their parents—a body composed of impure, segmented seeds—even if they were to obtain one or two elixirs of transformation to achieve levitation, longevity, and a separate mode of existence, this would certainly be [merely] a matter of faith.
They do no more than temporarily become ghosts guarding corpses, ultimately falling into the fruit of empty oblivion. To wish to traverse the Great Way while remaining thus—is it not a delusion?
Therefore, I enlightened them, saying: "There is true nature and true destiny; there is false nature and false destiny."
The stage of true nature and true life is one; the stages of delusive nature and delusive life are five. Regarding the single stage of true nature and true life, this is the Buddha.
The Buddha possesses three bodies (*kāya*). First is the *dharmakāya*. In Sanskrit, it is called Vairocana, which here means "pervading all places.
All phenomena (*dharma*) are none other than the Buddha-dharma. Exhausting the three periods of time and spanning the ten directions...
As for its location: one cannot see its head when approaching it, nor can one catch its tail when following it. This is the wondrous nature possessed equally by both sentient beings and Buddhas.
To speak specifically of true realization, only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it;
this is what is called "true nature. When speaking solely of realization and awakening, it does not depend upon cultivation or effort; this is termed the "primordial Dharmakāya Buddha."
There is the Adorned [Body]. It takes the eternally quiescent light Pure Land as its environmental retribution (*pratyaya-vaipākya*). Second is the Reward Body Tathāgata.

Having extensively practiced the six perfections and fully cultivated the myriad deeds over immeasurable kalpas, he has performed the cause of reality and accordingly received the retribution of reality.
This body is equal to the Dharma Body; the body possesses immeasurable marks, the marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics, and the secondary characteristics possess immeasurable...
The radiance of each and every mark and excellence (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) is immeasurable and boundless; this is what is called "true life" (jīva).
Although it is said that cultivation is performed in accordance with the nature (dharmatā), cultivation is itself non-cultivation.

Taking the truly retributive land of unobstructed purity as the external environment (niśraya-vipāka), matter and mind do not obstruct one another, nor do the body and the land hinder each other; this is also referred to as "life."

These are names established in accordance with worldly convention. Here, retributive wisdom (*vipākajñāna*) is designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); its coming and going, its movement and stillness, is designated as "respiration" (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*);
and its harmonious flow is designated as "warmth" (*uṣman*). This refers to what is called: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form," and so forth.
Third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). It is so called because it manifests a body in accordance with sentient beings.
Depending on whether the land is pure or defiled, the characteristics of this response body differ in size, and its lifespan varies in duration.
For example, in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the body of Amitābha’s response is sixty million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand *yojanas* in height and is endowed with the eight [marks].
He possesses fourteen thousand marks and signs of excellence and radiance, and his lifespan lasts for incalculable kalpas; therefore, he is called Amitāyus Buddha.
This is because the lifespan of those born in that land is immeasurable, and all possess the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, while Śākyamuni appears in this defiled Sahā world as one who is only six feet tall, [Amitābha appears in his own land with a body of immeasurable height].
His body was of purple-gold, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics;

yet his lifespan lasted but eighty-one years, at which point he manifested his return to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This was because, in this defiled land, the human body is coarse and inferior, and the lifespan is short.
For two reasons, he should have entered extinction: first, because the fuel of sentient beings' spiritual capacity had been exhausted, he should...
The fire shall extinguish. Second, because the physical remains are returned to the parents and the four elements are restored to their original source, it should therefore extinguish.
Now, the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya are the essence; the Nirmāṇakāya is the trace. Those who have attained realization know the essence and thus overlook the traces;
those who are deluded cling to the traces and thereby doubt the essence. They claim that although Śākyamuni attained perfect enlightenment, he likewise ended in the cessation of ashes.
To disparage the Buddha on the grounds that his nature is wondrous while his physical form is not, is how deluded one can be! There are five stages for the deluded nature and the deluded life:
first, the path of the Bodhisattva; second, the path of the Two Vehicles; third, the path of devas; fourth, the path of immortals (ṛṣis);

and fifth, the path of humans—while the three miserable realms of evil paths are excluded from these. Regarding the first, the path of the Bodhisattva, it concerns the [teachings of] the Perfect and Distinctive [Vehicles] leading to the stages of realization.
Those dwelling on the stages also realize the three bodies. They are now judged to be delusory because, although they have returned to the source, they have not yet reached wondrous enlightenment;

and although their afflictions have been severed, they have not yet exhausted ignorance. Thus, while they lack the coarse, gross birth-and-death of the segmented realm, they still possess the subtle, fine arising and ceasing of the transformational realm.
If this slight delusion is removed, all that remains is the true, which may also be called [the ultimate].
The true nature is the true life-force. Second, regarding the path of the two vehicles—namely those of the Hīnayāna, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—there are two types.
If they have not yet emerged from the triple world, although their nature realizes emptiness and stillness, their bodies remain like those of ordinary beings subject to分段 (fen-duan) birth and death;
ultimately, they return to the cessation of ashes. Even though they have not realized true emptiness, speaking of them collectively:
It may also be termed "wondrous nature. Because the body has been reduced to ashes and severed, its form is no longer wondrous.

If one has already emerged from the three realms and is born in the Dharma-nature land, receiving the Dharma-nature body, although there is no longer birth-and-death through segmentation (*pariccheda-jarā-maraṇa*), there still remains birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jarā-maraṇa*).
Since one has not yet reached the ultimate fruit, this is also judged to be a false nature and a false life-force. Although there is transformation-birth...
Death is not like the birth and extinction of the segmented [body];

rather, it is because the Dharma-nature body transforms a coarse form into a subtle essence and exchanges a short lifespan for a long one that its life span has no limit. There are three types of heavenly realms:
first, the four heavens of the Formless Realm; second, the four heavens of the Form Realm; and third, the six heavens of the Desire Realm. Each...

There are differences in the increase and decrease of their lifespans, as explained below in the section on the celestial realms. The four paths of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) refer to the ten types of immortals mentioned in this present sutra.
These individuals all refine their minds among human beings but do not cultivate perfect enlightenment; instead, they separately attain the principle of life and live for tens of millions of years.
They dwell in deep mountains or on large ocean islands, far removed from the haunts of men, like those [immortals] of the mountains and seas.
The Sūtra says: "On Mount Kunlun, in the wilds of Guangdu, at the heights of Xuanyuan, lies the Land of Immortality;
there the air is free from cold and heat, and all people live for a thousand years. Furthermore, as stated in the *Zhuangzi*:

"Upon Mount Gushu in Miao, there dwells a divine person whose skin is like ice and snow, and who is as graceful and pure as a maiden. He does not eat the five grains, but inhales the wind and drinks the dew."
[As stated] above. Furthermore, as recorded in Daoist texts, there are thirty-six *dongtian* (cave-heavens) among the human realm where immortals reside and live for thousands of millions of years.
Since such beings do not possess a separate collective retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*), they simply experience a distinct state upon the basis of their human collective retribution.
That the Sūtra says they "possess a separate principle of life" is indeed for this reason.
It is so. Among the five paths of existence, the human realm consists of four continents that differ from one another. First, to the south of Mount Sumeru lies the continent named Jambudvīpa;
this is the very place where we currently reside. The human lifespan is one hundred years, yet those who die prematurely are many.
Their height ranges from seven to eight feet, or less than five or six feet. Food, drink, clothing, and attire vary according to whether one is wealthy or poor, noble or humble. Birth and old age...
The eight sufferings, such as birth and death, cannot be avoided by anyone. To the east of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Pūrvavideha;

its inhabitants have a lifespan of two hundred years, consume the flesh of fish that die naturally rather than killing living beings, and their physical stature is equal to that of those in Jambudvīpa.
To the west of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Aparagoyānī; its inhabitants have a lifespan of three hundred years, [and their stature] is equal to that of those in Jambudvīpa.
In the continent of Jambudvīpa, people eat meat and kill living beings. To the north of Mount Sumeru lies a celestial realm named Uttarakuru.
Its land is the most excellent and blissful compared to the other three continents. There, ponds, bathing pools, flowers, and fruits flourish in abundance, and various birds sing in harmony.
It is free from ditches, pits, thorns, mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects. There is naturally growing non-glutinous rice that is endowed with every flavor.
There is a mani-jewel named Flame-Light (*jvālā-prabhā*). When placed beneath a self-arisen cauldron, its light extinguishes once the rice is cooked.
There is a tree named Bent-Bough (*namita-śākhā*); its leaves overlap one another so closely that the rain does not leak through. Men and women dwell beneath it.
When the fruits of various trees ripen, they naturally split open, yielding garments, vessels, or food. [The river...]

They board precious vessels for entertainment; when entering the central pool to bathe, they leave their clothes on the bank and, upon crossing the water by boat, put on whatever garments they encounter rather than seeking out their original clothes.
Next, they proceed to the fragrant trees, where they take up musical instruments and travel along, their voices harmonizing with the strings.
These people are free from all ailments, their complexions are uniform, and their hair is a deep blue-black color.
They stop when their foreheads meet. When a person’s desire arises, they gaze intently at a woman, and she follows them to a grove.
If it is someone such as a father or mother with whom one should not engage in sexual desire, the tree does not bend to provide shade, and they each disperse.
If it is not a relative, the tree bends to provide shade, and they enjoy themselves as they please for one day up to seven days, after which they part.
Go! That woman conceived and gave birth after seven or eight days. As soon as the child was born—whether male or female—they placed it at a crossroads.
There were passersby who extended their fingers and sucked [the child]; from their fingers, sweet milk flowed forth, nourishing the child’s entire body.
After seven days had passed, the child grew up to be equal in stature to that person. The boys went among the assembly of men, and the girls went among the assembly of women. That person’s life...
They never weep for one another. Because the human lifespan is fixed at one thousand years, they do not mourn the dead.
They adorn the corpse and place it at a crossroads; a bird named Uveṇaka then carries it away to another region. That ground is soft and yields as the foot presses down;
when they void excrement or urine, the earth opens to receive it and closes again once they have finished. Before those people...
Those who have cultivated the ten virtuous actions throughout their lives are born in this continent. Their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing;
after their lives end, they are reborn in the auspicious realms of the heavens. Because the human lifespan is fixed at one thousand years, there is no weeping or mourning upon death.

Furthermore, because a Buddha does not appear here, the Dharma of the Buddha is not heard. This is why it is counted as one of the eight difficulties. In Jambudvīpa, however, the Buddha-dharma exists.
One may study [there]. Therefore, those with the faculties for the Mahāyāna are born in great numbers therein.

Because their lifespans are short and they are oppressed by manifold sufferings, they develop a sense of dread and resolve to diligently practice the path. This is why it is the most excellent among the four continents.
As cited above, from the Buddhas at the highest level down to the gods of the four dhyānas in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), although they are truly...
Those who falsely claim there are differences all focus their efforts on cultivating *xing* (nature) while neglecting *ming* (vitality).

Although they do not cultivate vitality, their various retributive lives are long in duration and their physical forms are exceptionally beautiful. This is because *xing* is like form and sound, while *ming* is like shadow and echo.
Since the form and sound of *xing* are upright and harmonious, the shadow and echo of *ming* are straight and compliant. As for those in the Desire Realm...
If one merely cultivates the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*) of the highest grade, the retribution they induce will likewise surpass that of all the *ṛṣis*.
How could this be obtained by relying on the cultivation of life-prolonging techniques? As for Uttarakuru in the north, it originally belongs to the human realm;

yet, when its rank is discussed among the various *ṛṣis*, it lies below them, while its lifespan, rewards, and superior pleasures actually exceed theirs—this is due to the cultivation of the ten wholesome actions.

Is it not also the result of cultivating longevity? Therefore, one who wishes to hope for the sublime refinement of both body and spirit finds nothing more precious than the Buddha’s true nature and true life-force.
For those who wish to realize this true nature and true life-force, nothing precedes the clarification of the mind and the seeing of its nature.
Next, nothing is greater than practicing in accordance with that nature. Furthermore, nothing is more essential than the cultivation of merit.
These three factors constitute the completion [of practice]. For one who cultivates the Buddha-way, it is not permissible to lack even one of them.

This refers to those who focus exclusively on cultivating the nature (*xing*) while neglecting to cultivate the life-force (*ming*). Although they do not cultivate the life-force, the true life-force manifests spontaneously, and its karmic fruition is never errant—just as an echo responds to a sound and a shadow follows a form.
The wise person focuses solely on ensuring that the form is upright and the sound is harmonious.

That is all. Why must one be so preoccupied with refining the essence, energy, and spirit, claiming it to be the "double cultivation of nature and life" (*xingming shuangxiu*) and the "sublime unity of form and spirit" (*xingshen ju miao*)?
Someone asked: "The essence and energy are 'life' (*ming*); the spirit is 'nature' (*xing*).
Although the Buddhists cultivate nature but do not cultivate life, they nonetheless cultivate the spirit as nature. Why then do you categorically reject all three, asserting that none are correct?"
"How much more so when it comes to what is called 'attaining Buddhahood,' where both body and spirit are wondrous. If one does not refine the spirit, how can one reach this state? He replied:

"What is said regarding attaining Buddhahood—where both nature and life are harmoniously beautiful and both form and spirit are wondrous—is merely taking the terminology of the immortals (xian) to establish a discourse of superior transcendence.
In reality, the fruit of Buddhahood cannot be named by 'nature' or 'life,' nor summoned by 'form' or 'spirit.'"
Generally speaking, all that can be spoken of regarding form and spirit, nature and destiny, exists because of the presence of essence, vital energy, and spirit (*jing*, *qi*, and *shen*).
Since the Buddha’s two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are not born from the womb of parents, they cannot be said to possess essence.

Since they are not produced from the vital energy of the womb, they do not maintain their physical form through vital energy; as they do not maintain this, they cannot be said to possess vital energy.

Now, those who maintain the vital essence and spirit do so because they possess conscious awareness. Since the Buddha has long since transformed human consciousness into the four wisdoms, he cannot be described as possessing "spirit" (shen).
As for those in the school of immortals who speak of nature and destiny (xing-ming), they take nothing more than conscious awareness as "nature" and the vital essence as "destiny.
The Buddha possesses none of these three; he speaks of nature and destiny by conforming to worldly conventions.

Furthermore, when employing worldly conventions to speak of form and spirit, how could this be a description of the *jing*, *qi*, and *shen* (essence, energy, and spirit) as understood in the secular world?

Someone else asked: "The Daoist school discusses nature (*xing*) and destiny (*ming*). Destiny is certainly composed of *jing*, *qi*, and *shen*. As for the nature they cultivate, it is the same as that of the Buddhists;
why then do you categorically dismiss it as mere consciousness (*shenshi*)? I replied: "Based on what they themselves discuss, it is merely their emotional attachments (*qing*)."
Regarding those whose nature is supremely wondrous, it is said: "Three in the east and two in the south together form five; one in the north and four in the west join them.
Wu-ji (the central earth) likewise follows the five numbers of generation. When these three houses meet, they form the Infant. This means:
the three in the east are wood, which is my nature; the four in the west are metal, which is my emotion; the two in the south are fire, which is my...
It is the spirit (*shen*). The northern [direction] is water; it is the essence of the self. Nature is the master of the mind, and the mind is the master of the spirit (and so forth).
All of these do not transcend the five elements; how could they be anything other than the cognitive spirit (*shishen*)? Again, he asked:

"According to the *Vow Text* of the Great Dhyāna Master Sengzhao of Mount Nanyue, one wishes to study the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) like an immortal (*ṛṣi*) and prolong one's life in order to propagate the Dharma in the final age."

Dharma: Master Zhiyi was a great patriarch of the Tiantai school. Having realized the stage of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*) in his present life, he was already not far from the rank of a Buddha;
yet he still desired to study the way of the immortals (*xian*). From this, we know that the status of the immortal path is equal to that of a Buddha.
Why, then, do you say instead that the immortal is inferior? He replied: "The Great Master of Nanyue had deeply entered the stages of the Perfect Teaching."
It cannot be measured. If one seeks it through its traces, two kinds of mind are fully present: first, the mind of a great man (*puruṣa*), and second, the grandmotherly mind (*lao-po-xin*).
Master Zhigong sent word to Nanyue, saying: "The Old Monk spends his entire day with his head and face covered in ash and dust;
why does he not go out into the red dust of the world to save sentient beings? Nanyue replied: "The Buddhas of the ten directions..."
"If the Buddha were swallowed by me in a single gulp, what sentient beings would there be to deliver? This is the mind of a true man.

If, however, one composes a vow-text wishing to study the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the immortals (*ṛṣi*), that is the "old woman’s heart" of Mount Nanyue—earnestly hoping to prolong one's lifespan during the final kalpa when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, so as to circulate the *Prajñāpāramitā* and cause the Buddha-dharma to...

His wisdom-life remained unextinguished as he delivered all those sentient beings who were stubborn, fierce, and mired in defilement. This was prompted by a heart of compassionate concern (*pobin*) moved by a profound sense of urgency.

At that time, various evil masters of debate, seeing that the Great Master’s virtue and morality were flourishing and that he was tirelessly propagating the *Prajñāpāramitā*, gave rise to intense jealousy.
They repeatedly attempted to take his life with various poisons, yet through the Way...
By the power [of his merit], he was restored to life after being cut down. Therefore, he resolved to create the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra in golden letters;

upon its completion, he made a great vow. This vow had both a primary intention and a secondary intention. The primary intention was to leave behind both the scripture and his own body to await Maitreya.

The secondary intention was to seek the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and prolong his lifespan. However, although he possessed such a mind, he lacked the corresponding practice. Consequently, his retribution was exhausted.
He also attained parinirvāṇa; his golden-linked skeletal remains still remain beneath the Three Lives Pagoda on Mount Nanyue, which serves as a verifiable testament.
Contemporary scholars, harboring heterodox views while professing to serve the Buddha, frequently cite this as a pretext for their own positions. Therefore, I caution them:
if one possesses the two kinds of mind found at Mount Nanyue, it is acceptable. First, there is the mind of a true man who seeks the Buddha-way from within.

This is the mind [of the Bodhisattva]. If one does not yet see even a single sentient being to be saved, then even the Buddha-way—such as that practiced on Mount Nanyue—is something not to be grasped, let alone the Way of the Immortals (*xian*).
This is the "old woman’s heart" (*lao-po-xin*), the mind that transforms sentient beings below;

if one still desires to manifest forms throughout the nine realms, avoiding nothing even within the three miserable paths, how much less would one avoid the Way of the Immortals? If either of these two minds is lacking, [the path is incomplete].
All such people are called "half-men. If you choose what is appropriate for your practice, it is better to possess the former mind than to harbor the latter intention.
For in this current age of the Dharma’s decline, it is difficult to attain the correct path of the Bodhi-mind.
To fall into even a single thought of this kind is to become a person who clings to life and fears death, falling into the net of the demons of attachment and views. Thus it is said.
"Master, I have seen such practitioners. As soon as they conceive this thought, there is nowhere they will not go.

Having failed to achieve the Way of the Immortals, they are likewise not received into the Way of the Buddhas. In the end, they fall into the net of Māra; how can they lament when their lifespan in hell lasts for kalpas?
Those who study the Way of the Buddhas must take this as a warning; they must be cautious! Someone else then asked: "What of the Immortals?"
The Master says: "Regarding essence, there is true essence, which is not the essence produced by sexual union; regarding breath, there is true breath, which is not the vital breath of blood and qi;

regarding spirit, there is true spirit, which is not the spirit of consciousness. Therefore, when these three elements meet and form the infant, it is because they transform the triad of essence, breath, and spirit into the Great Elixir.
This is what is meant by 'refining essence to transform it into breath,' and 'refining breath...'"

To transform the spirit and refine the spirit so as to return it to the void: one takes heaven and earth as the crucible and furnace, the sun and moon as water and fire, and yin and yang as the mechanism of transformation.
One causes the post-heaven *kan* (male) and *li* (female) trigrams to interact and unite, thereby returning to the pre-heaven *qian* (father) and *kun* (mother) trigrams.

This is called "the intersection of points in the *qian* palace descending into the Yellow Court. How could this be accomplished by means of essence (*jing*), energy (*qi*), and spirit (*shen*) alone?
[He] asked, "Are you speaking of this? [The other] replied, "Based on what you have said, you may discourse at will upon the profound and mysterious;

yet it is evident that you have not transcended heaven and earth, yin and yang, the creative transformations, and the five elements. You do nothing more than refine the consciousness-spirit and solidify deluded thoughts, taking these birth-and-death delusions as your cause.
How could such things possibly accord with the true and eternal nature and life? He further said, "The followers of Śākya cultivate the nature."
To cultivate only the life-force while merely refining the yin-spirit is like catching the wind or grasping a shadow; it possesses no reality.

In the tradition of the immortals, one cultivates both life and nature (*xing-ming shuang-xiu*), whereby the yang-spirit is refined and both form and spirit are wondrously harmonized. This is like the clear blue sky and the bright sun, where nothing fails to be illuminated.
Formerly, a monk and an immortal made a pact to project their spirits (*chu-shen*) together to enjoy the Jasper Flowers, each tucking [the flowers] into his sleeve.
Flowers were brought back as proof. If the monk had taken them in his sleeve, there would have been no flowers; since the flowers remained with the immortal, it was not a falsehood.
If this is taken as evidence, then the immortal clearly surpasses the Śākya [Buddha] by much; why, then, do you dismiss him as being deceptive and false? In response, he said:
"Entering meditative absorption and projecting the spirit is what the Buddhist gate denounces as the 'playful manipulation of the vital soul'—the livelihood of the ghostly household."
If this is not even accepted within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, how much less so in the Mahāyāna? If such a monk truly exists, he is a heretic within the Śākya gate;
those of noble character would regard him with contempt as they would spit, and he is not even worth mentioning.
Otherwise, it must be that practitioners of the Way have falsely made this claim to slander the Sangha. Or, it may be asked again: "Recently I have seen..."

In his writings, he sought to unify the Three Teachings into a single family. He claimed that the Golden Elixir (*jindan*) of the immortals is identical to the Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*) of the Buddhists;
why then do you so bitterly disparage one while praising the other? I replied:

"If he were truly able to synthesize the Golden Elixir into Perfect Enlightenment and take Perfect Enlightenment as his primary tenet—abandoning the Immortal Way to become a Golden Immortal—then he would indeed be my Bodhisattva."

This is the original intent of our aspiration; why, then, should we reject it? I only fear that this doctrine consists of words without substance, serving no purpose other than to invoke the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué*) as a prop for its own sake.
Though they claim to be identical [to our view], their true aim is to surpass us.

They employ the categories of superior and inferior based on physical form as their pretext, and preach that both body and spirit are wondrous. This is not merely an attempt to equate the inferior with the superior, but will likely lead to—
The superior becomes inferior; that is to say, the unsurpassed *amṛta* (the finest essence) encounters such people and is transformed instead into arsenic and lethal poison.

[Section on the Six Heavens of the Realm of Desire] First, a specific presentation of the various heavens. First, the Realm of Desire. First, the primary designation of the six [heavens]. First, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). Ānanda, the people of the world do not seek the permanent and are unable to renounce their wives, concubines, and the attachments of affection.
In matters of sexual misconduct, their minds do not flow outwardly or dissipate; they are clear, limpid, and luminous. After the end of life, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. [Commentary] Wēn-líng says:
"Being unable yet to leave desire behind, they are nonetheless able to block it so that the waters of craving do not flow; thus they are tranquil."
Because one's nature is pure and translucent, one is able to take birth in the first heaven. The six heavens are attained by practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;

here, we consider only those cases where desire is slightly increased in excellence. Love and desire are the root of saṃsāra. As previously explained, the process of sinking and falling also begins from this point;
now, it is explained that transcending and ascending likewise begins from this point. This is intended so that those at the initial stage who are not yet [capable of... may...
If one accomplishes meditative concentration and wisdom and swiftly cuts off the root, then one may emerge from saṃsāra.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The Sūtra clarifies the ranks and positions of the various devas with two intentions—the lateral and the primary.

The primary intention fully elucidates the celestial realms as a comprehensive warning against errors for practitioners of the Perfect Teaching who seek to ascend and exit the triple world. This is because birth...

Although receiving heavenly blessings is not one's original intent, because delusions have been suppressed or severed to varying degrees, the resulting retribution differs in its refinement or coarseness.
As long as one has not yet transcended the triple world, how can one avoid being reborn there? If one does not understand this, they will follow their meditative states with attachment;

midway through the process, failing to realize what is not realized, they claim realization and thus incur the fault of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Furthermore, as for the bliss of the third dhyāna, that bliss—

[The text] says: "There is no limit. [Some] believe they dwell in *nirvāṇa* and do not advance; yet if even the ultimate fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is thus lacking, what need is there to mention the actual retribution of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*)?
This is something that must be understood, and therefore it is explained in full detail here.

Furthermore, this serves as an exhortation to practitioners of the perfect path (*pūrṇayoga*), who must ensure that the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) are all fully perfected. As the *Qing Sheng Yuan Shou* already stated: "If the mind is not..."

Regarding sexual misconduct: among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, even proper sexual conduct is rare and slight; it is only upon reaching the sixth heaven that one is said to have clearly transcended it.
Is this not a matter of distinguishing between light and heavy degrees from the outset of the four pārājikas, thereby establishing a progression from the coarse to the subtle?

As for the four heavens dwelling in space, they invariably cultivate the concentration of the threshold stage (anāgamya-samādhi); how much more so for the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, which derive their names from meditative absorption.
Only by being without desire and free from defilement can one emerge from the realm of desire.

Can a practitioner who has perfected their cultivation possibly transcend the three realms without precepts and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to destroy delusions? These two points imply a meaning beyond the literal words.
To state it explicitly: "The people of the world do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditation) and thus possess no wisdom. Combining these [statements], we see that...
Is it not the case that the Threefold Training cannot be deficient in even one part?

Nowadays, those who speak of the Mahāyāna uniformly regard the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) as supreme, asserting that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) need not be cultivated and that ethical discipline (*śīla*) need not be urgent.

I ask you to consider this by examining the intent of the sutras. The text generally consists of two sections: first, a separate exposition of the various devas; second, a summary of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
[The realms] are falsely distinguished into three: first, the desire realm; second, the form realm; and third, the formless realm.
The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "Heaven (*deva*) means natural. Because they possess natural, supreme bliss, supreme bodies, and supremacy, the treatise says:

'Because they are pure, radiant, most excellent, and most honored, they are called heavens. If one does not possess the cause of supreme excellence, how could one be born in a place of supreme excellence?"

What is called the "supreme cause" refers to the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). Because one prevents transgressions through the three types of action (*trikarma*), that which accords with principle is termed the "ten wholesome actions.
Since these ten wholesome actions transport beings out of the five destinies (*pañcagati*), these ten precepts are called the "Celestial Vehicle" (*devayāna*).
If one cultivates the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions alone, one reaches two heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).

First, the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). If one cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) while also attaining the *anāgamya* concentration, one is born in the second heaven, the Yāma Heaven;
the third, the Tuṣita Heaven; the fourth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and the fifth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.
By the power of dhyāna-concentration, these four heavens all dwell in the air and do not rely upon the earth. If one cultivates the four fundamental dhyānas and is free from...

If one craves coarse and scattered [sensory objects], one is born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). If one becomes weary of the cage of form and cultivates the four formless absorptions (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), one is born in the four formless heavens, which is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Now, the first heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) serves as the primary point for ascending toward purity.
It is situated on the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth. To the east is the golden tiered city named "Supreme" (*Uttara*).
The Abode of the Worthy Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the city of Vaiḍūrya-parvata in the south, named Sudarśana, where the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka resides;
the city of Rūpya-parvata in the west, named Cūḷa, where the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa resides;
and the city of Sphaṭika-parvata in the north, named Devasaṃmata, where the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa resides. Their bodies are half a *li* in height, and they wear robes...
[Those who] weigh half a *liang* [of gold] shall live for five hundred years, with fifty human years constituting one day and night.

Now, this scripture holds that taking the observance of the precept against sexual misconduct among the ten wholesome actions—whereby the mind does not flow or stray and becomes clear, bright, and luminous—as the cause, and dwelling in proximity to the sun and moon as the fruit.
Indeed, the sun and moon are the ultimate, most perfect manifestations of light within the human world.

This is one who is full. If one lacks the clarity of the precepts, how can they even neighbor [the sages]? That Nanda was led to fall through sexual misconduct and thereby initiated the teaching has its reasons. (2.

Trāyastriṃśa Heaven) When one’s lustful attachment toward the chamber of one’s own wife is slight, yet one fails to fully savor the flavor during the time of dwelling in the Pure Abodes, at the end of life—
Later, surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon, they dwell at the summit of the human realm; such human beings are called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Trāyastriṃśa" means the Thirty-three; Śakra rules over them. Wên-lǐng says:

Because their craving is thinner than that of those before, their retribution is to dwell above them; subsequent heavens follow this pattern. "Pure Abodes" (Śuddhāvāsa) refers to those who are pure and self-...
The reason one does not yet possess the flavor of complete purity while dwelling there is that there remains a subtle attachment.
The sun and moon dwell on the waist of Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwells upon its summit; because they are clear, limpid, and increasingly luminous, they are able to transcend it.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The former was named the first heaven of the earth-dwellers; this is named the second heaven of the earth-dwellers.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) resides at the summit of Mount Sumeru, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the earth.
The Great City of Sudarśana is ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference and represents the pinnacle of worldly adornment. [The inhabitants] are one *li* in height, and their robes weigh six [ounces].
The lifespan in Zhushou is one thousand years, with one hundred human years constituting a single day and night.

This sutra states that taking the attenuation of sexual misconduct as the cause results in surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon as the fruit. Having just now matched one's neighbor, one now surpasses them.
It can be seen that the passion of lust is the root of sinking and falling, while the thought of pure precepts is the cause for ascending and being rescued. ○ (The Third:
Suyama Heaven) Upon encountering desire, one may briefly unite, yet afterwards there is no lingering thought; in the human world, movement is slight and stillness is abundant, until the end of life.
Later, they dwell serenely in the midst of empty space; the radiance of the sun and moon shines upward but cannot reach them.
These people possess their own natural light, and such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because the desire-mind does not arise, movement is slight and stillness is abundant.

Among the six heavens of the Desire Realm, the lower two are called the Earth-Dwelling Heavens (*bhūmi-vāsin*), and the upper four are called the Space-Dwelling Heavens (*antarīkṣa-vāsin*). They do not require the sun or moon for illumination, as they are perpetually bright;
they distinguish day and night by the opening and closing of lotus flowers, and are thus named the Time-Portion Heavens (*Kāmadhātu-kalpa*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This heaven is the foremost among those dwelling in space. Its inhabitants are one and a half *li* in height, their garments weigh three *zhu*, and their lifespan is two thousand years.
One hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night for them.

According to the present sutra, they take as their cause "meeting desire and briefly uniting, yet departing without thought or recollection, with little movement and much stillness. Their bodies possess radiance and do not rely on the sun.

The Moon is the fruit; this means that desire is even thinner than before. This deity further cultivates the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration), because they have not yet entered the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*).

As stated in the *Zhiguan*: "If one sits upright, restraining the body and harmonizing the breath until it becomes utterly tranquil and still, the body is like a shadow in the clouds—vast, empty, and pure—and yet one still perceives the existence of body and mind."
This characteristic is what is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).

From this point onward, one suddenly no longer perceives the body, head, clothing, bedding, or other objects within the state of the desire-realm concentration; it is like empty space, brilliantly clear and profoundly tranquil.
The body is an obstacle to the matter [of concentration]; this obstacle hinders the future. Once the obstacle is removed and the body is empty, the future [attainment] can arise.
This is called the characteristic of the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*). Based on this, it follows that the first two heavens already possess concentrations of the desire realm;

therefore, it is said of the first heaven that "clarity and purity give rise to luminosity," and of the second heaven that "at the time of dwelling in the Pure Abodes, one cannot yet attain it in its entirety."
Is it not the case that this is so because those among the laity who are fond of practicing meditation gradually stifle their desires?

As for the description of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings as having "little movement and much stillness," is this not a sign that the concentration of the desire realm has already been established and that one is about to achieve the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*)?
Regarding the Fourth Heaven, its state of being "always still" implies that it encompasses the two lower heavens as well.
Having already attained the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the concentration of "not-yet-arrived"), one also concurrently cultivates the fundamental dhyānas.
○ (Tuṣita Heaven) At all times, while remaining in stillness, even when sensory objects arise, one is unable to be disturbed by them;

after death, one ascends to the subtle and refined realm, never descending again to the levels of humans or devas, and remains beyond the reach of the three calamities that destroy the kalpa. Thus it is said.
The category is named Tuṣita Heaven. [Commentary] Wēnlíng says:

"Though one may increasingly cultivate a tranquil mind, one cannot yet avoid responding to sensory contact. This indicates that while one is able to have few desires, one has not yet attained the state of no-mind.
The Tuṣita Heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court; when the three calamities reach the third dhyāna, this [inner court] remains."
"Those who do not reach [the lower realms]" refers to those within the Inner Court. That their subtle and refined states do not intersect with the lower is entirely a matter of the Inner Court.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These are the two heavens dwelling in space. Their bodies are two *li* tall; their clothing weighs one and a half *zhu*;
their lifespan is four thousand years, with one day and night equaling four hundred human years. Now, according to this sutra, it is calculated by...
At the moment of death, there is a cause consisting in the presence of a touch that one has not yet been able to resist;

its result is the ascent to a subtle state that does not reach the lower realms. As for the mention of "inner and outer courtyards," this likely refers to those seeking rebirth in the inner courtyard.
If this is so, then anyone seeking rebirth in the inner courtyard must not rely solely on mundane virtuous deeds; they should practice [the following].
One must first attain the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) up to the "not-yet-arrived" stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*) before [the Pure Land] can be born into.

Therefore, those who seek rebirth in the Inner Court (*abhyantarapura*) with the desire to see Maitreya Bodhisattva should cultivate three dharmas: first, the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions; second, Mahayana meditative concentration;
and third, the profound aspiration for rebirth. These three dharmas are indispensable; if one seeks to go there by means of a mere fragment of goodness, it will not suffice.
To be born [there] would be like seeking a roasted osprey after seeing only its bowstring. Someone asked: "Why must one practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and make vows? He replied:
"If one lacks the power of non-attainment (*anāgamya*), there is a fear of falling short. If one falls short, one may be reborn in a lower heaven or even outside the courtyards.
If one lacks deep vows, there is a fear of overreaching and being reborn in a higher heaven."
○ (The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations): "I have no desire for the mind, yet I comply with your actions; when we lie together, the flavor is like chewing wax.
After the end of life, one is born in the realm beyond emanation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations."

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: When objects arrive spontaneously without intentional effort, it is called "laid out horizontally" (héngchén). The phrase "chewing wax" refers to the fact that the flavor is extremely thin.
All the heavens possess realms of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), yet this heaven’s pleasures are enjoyed through spontaneous transformations;
because it transcends the lower heavens, it is named "Transcending Transformations" (Yuèhuà).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These are the three heavens dwelling in space. Their bodies are two and a half *li* tall;
their clothing weighs one *zhu*; their lifespan is eight thousand years. Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for them.

According to this sutra, taking the savoring of sensual desire as being like chewing wax is the cause, while the enjoyment of self-transformed pleasant realms is the fruit. This is because of sensual desire.
Furthermore, because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is increasingly superior, both cause and effect transcend those of the lower heavens.
The horizontal arrangement of the characters was a stylistic embellishment added by the translators of the sutras, drawing from Song Yu’s *Fengfu* (Rhapsody on Satire), which says:
"With a heart of trepidation, he hastens to the bed; lying across, he presents himself by the side of the lord."
○ (6. Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven): Without a worldly mind, yet performing actions identical to those of the world, they clearly transcend the engagement with such activities;
after the end of life, they are universally able to emerge and transcend both the realms of created and uncreated transformations. This class of beings is called the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "To transcend with utter clarity" means that there is no flavor [of desire] whatsoever. "Transformation" refers to the fifth heaven; "non-transformation" refers to the heavens below it.

Since all objects of sensual pleasure do not require one's own effort to transform them, but are instead enjoyed with mastery through the transformations of others, they are called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Wǔxīng says: According to the teachings of Tiantai, these are the six heavens of the desire realm.
All karma has the ten wholesome actions as its foundation. If one additionally possesses a mind that protects the Dharma, this is the karma for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

If one additionally employs compassionate transformation of people, this is the karma for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If one additionally maintains non-affliction toward sentient beings with skillful mastery, this is the karma for the Yāma Heaven.
If one additionally cultivates meditative concentration, including both coarse abiding and subtle abiding, this is the karma for the Tuṣita Heaven. [Regarding] desire...
The *dhyāna* of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* heavens is the karma of the *nirmāṇarati* heavens; the *anāgāmya-samādhi* is the karma of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* heavens.
Now, this sutra limits its classification of the six heavens based solely on the gravity of sensual desires; there should be two reasons for this: first, because it was prompted by Ānanda’s inquiry;
second, because it concerns the fundamental basis for rebirth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These are the four heavens dwelling in space (*ākāśavāsin*). Their bodies are three *li* tall; their clothing weighs half a *zhu*;
their lifespan is sixteen thousand years. One thousand six hundred years of the human world constitutes one day and night for them.
This sutra takes the "clearly transcending the engagement in affairs through desire" as the cause, meaning that one transcends its "wax taste."
Furthermore, it takes the universal ability to transcend both the realms of transformation and non-transformation as its fruit.

In the first three heavens, practitioners all sit in the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preliminary concentration), whether deep or shallow, yet have not yet achieved perfection. Only upon reaching this heaven do they finally accomplish it. Within this heaven, there should be two types of deities:
one correct and one deviant. The correct ones achieve the *anāgamya-samādhi* and further cultivate the fundamental [dhyāna] so that it may become capable [of full realization].

When one is born into the first dhyāna of the form realm, if they are inclined toward evil, Māra Pāpīyān—whose lifespan is thirty-two thousand years—will remain attached to the objects of desire and stay there without proceeding further. When his retribution is exhausted, he returns and scatters into the various realms of existence (*gati*). Someone might ask: "Is the length of the lifespan of the various devas fixed or unfixed? Is it certain that when their retribution is exhausted, they will scatter into the various realms of existence? The answer is given in the Sūtra: [The Buddha said: "Ananda, the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas is sixteen thousand kalpas; this is their fixed measure. When their merit is exhausted, they fall back into the three evil realms. The lifespan of the Cāturmahārājika devas is five hundred years; this is their fixed measure. When their merit is exhausted, they fall back into the three evil realms. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "If a person has committed grave transgressions, even if they are reborn among the gods, their lifespan will be short. Because they have not cultivated wholesome roots, they fall back into the three evil realms. This treatise speaks for the most part regarding those who abide solely in the retribution of their fruit and do not further cultivate;

as for those who do advance in cultivation, their lifespans would have no fixed limit according to where they are reborn in higher dhyāna realms. If they are not reborn above but instead disperse into the various destinies, why should there be any doubt?
○ (2. Summary and Indication) Ānanda, although the forms of these six heavens involve outward movement, the traces of their minds are still intertwined;
from this point downward, they are called the Realm of Desire.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Although their forms involve outward movement"—this refers to the two destinies of humans and *ṛṣis*, which receive the designation of "outward movement."
"Mind and physical traces still intermingle" means that the traces of desire and the physical acts still possess the appearance of union. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says:
"The six [classes] experience desire through intercourse, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. This refers to the two classes of gods dwelling on earth who engage in physical intercourse;
those of Yāma embrace; those of Tuṣita hold hands; those of Nirmāṇarati gaze at one another while laughing; and those of Paranirmitavaśavartin...
One should understand that while those texts each explain the reception of desire according to the six heavens,
this present sutra only distinguishes the lightness and gravity of sexual matters among human beings to reveal how the retributions experienced by the six heavens differ accordingly.
[Commentary] Wuxing further states that one should analyze this by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
1. Physical union but no mental union; this corresponds to the sixth case of this sutra and also extends to the fifth. 2. Mental union but no physical union;

this corresponds to the latter two cases of the *Abhidharmakośa*. 3. Both mental and physical union; this corresponds to the first four cases of both this sutra and the *Abhidharmakośa*. 4. Neither mental nor physical union.

Their interaction is like that of those in the first dhyāna and above. Master Huān of the Dào school cites the *Lóutàn jīng* (Lokasthāna-sūtra), which states that the various devas of the desire realm possess ten characteristics:
first, they come by flying in infinite numbers; second, they depart by flying in infinite numbers;
third, their going is unimpeded; fourth, their coming is unimpeded; fifth, their celestial bodies lack skin, sinews, veins, blood, or flesh; sixth, their bodies...
1. There is no impurity of excrement or urine. 2. The body never experiences exhaustion. 3. The celestial maidens do not give birth.

4. The eyes of the heavens do not sleep. 5. The body and mind follow one’s wishes: if it is desired to be blue, it becomes blue; if yellow, it becomes yellow; and the same applies to all other colors.
