If this error persists, by what means can one depart from the house of the triple world, and by what path return to the house of nirvana?

Furthermore, even in the practice of delighting in the pure and loathing the defiled, it is not a matter of abandoning the foul to seek the pure; rather, it is through delusion itself that wisdom is realized.

Thus, as focused contemplation deepens day by day, and as long-term contemplation transforms into realization, it is said: "Suddenly, the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions are seen."
All become Buddha-lands. This demonstrates that while they appear defiled, they are in fact pure; thus, it can also be seen that they are neither defiled nor pure.

○ (9. Seeing Afar in the Night: Part One, Pointing to the Phenomenon and Tracing its Source) Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching, suddenly in the middle of the night, one sees afar the markets, streets, and alleys.

When relatives and kinsmen in the neighborhood hear such words, they say: "This name was forced upon him by his mind; it was driven to its extreme and flew out, so that he sees many things through obstructions.

This is not a sign of saintly realization. (2. On the Correctness or Deviance of Mental Application): Not conceiving the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if one takes this to be the realization of sainthood, one will immediately fall under the influence of various demons.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "By refining the mind to exhaust its depths and pressing the spirit to its limits, one leaves the body behind and emerges into the profound darkness until reaching a destination;

thus, one is able to see and hear events from afar. All of the above have not yet transcended the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); they merely rely on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to emerge beyond obstructions so that seeing and hearing reach far.
If the aggregate of form is exhausted, then the ten directions open up clearly, and there is no longer [the obstruction of form]."
In the darkness, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are exercised with such mastery that even mountain walls pass through them directly;

of this there is no doubt. [Commentary] Tiantai says: "Being able to see through many obstructions is because the essence of the nature (prakṛti) is all-pervasive. Not seeing through many obstructions is because the essence of delusion is limited.

The vision of the essence of the nature is manifested only at the stage of fruition (phalāvasthā). Now, before having ascended to the state of a sage, one suddenly claims to be able to see through many obstructions."

[The Master] said: "It is seen that it flies out because it is impelled by true cultivation; this is why it is so. Someone asked: "If the mind has no coming or going, why is it impelled to come forth?
He replied: "That which has no coming or going is its essence (tǐ); that which has coming and going is its function (yòng)."
Suppose, for instance, that the affliction of a nightmare ceases; the mind leaves the body and looks back at its own face, moving and staying with complete freedom.
Is this not the function of the mind coming and going? Yet, this is precisely the function of the essence itself; though it comes and goes, there is no coming or going.
It is like the entire ocean becoming a bubble, and the bubble returning to encompass the ocean. If one can realize it in this way, then one may be said to understand the Way.

○ (10. The Transformation of the Ten Consciousnesses, Part Two: First, Pointing to the Phenomena and Tracing the Source) Furthermore, when one investigates this mind to the ultimate degree of refinement, one may perceive the physical forms of spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) shifting and changing;

in a mere moment, they undergo various transformations without apparent cause. This is called the perverse mind harboring *chimei* (goblins and specters), or it is the work of celestial Māras entering one’s heart and belly to preach the Dharma without cause and claim mastery of subtle meanings—this is not a sign of saintly realization.
○ (2. The Perversity or Correctness of Mental Application) Do not conceive the thought of being a sage, for these are the affairs of Māra.
If one regards this cessation as a realization of the sacred, one will immediately succumb to various forms of evil.
[Commentary] Zizhong said: This person previously possessed seeds of a deviant mind; thus, they encounter external demonic realms as a consequence.
This is not a wholesome state but is purely a demonic affliction, unlike the preceding nine cases which were all termed wholesome states.

Regarding the statement, "Only when one gives rise to the thought of seeking personal realization does one become possessed by a māra," Wēn-líng says: "The 'knowledgeable person' perceived is actually a manifestation of a māra.

While the preceding nine sections clarify only the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this section alone clarifies the affairs of māras. This is because when the power of concentration has not yet been perfected, one cannot move a māra;
it is only when one's investigation reaches its ultimate refinement that the affairs of māras gradually emerge. Therefore, the following text concerns the affairs of māras.
It becomes even more severe.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Now, the heterodox path and the orthodox path are always opposites; the true mind and the deluded mind are always in mutual conflict.
Although the preceding nine objects are not directly realized, their manifestation is correct. By examining them through these objects, one may verify...
The mind must be true. As for that subsequent single object which manifests as boundless transformations—is its appearance illusory?
By examining the object, one finds the mind must be false. The Patriarch said: "How far apart are Buddha and Mara? What deficiency or surplus exists between the heterodox and the orthodox?
If you do not conceive of a 'sage-mind,' demonic affairs will subside. If you conceive of it as a 'sage-interpretation,' you will immediately be seized by the host of demons."
Whether these are demonic or genuine is determined by success or failure; the responsibility for this lies with the person. (2.

Concluding the faults and exhorting to show the way) Ānanda, these ten kinds of present states within *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner toward the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); thus these phenomena appear.
When sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, they do not reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they remain confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:
"To claim to have attained the state of a sage is a great falsehood that leads to falling into the Avīci Hell.

You all should, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma-ending period, proclaim and reveal this meaning so that no celestial Māras may find an opportunity; protect and sustain it so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."

[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The interaction of mental activities" refers to the interaction between the mind of *dhyāna* and the solid delusions of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which causes these phenomena to appear.
This principle applies analogously to the other aggregates up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Why is this?

Because each of the five delusive thoughts, within the domain of its respective aggregate, becomes the object of observation for *dhyāna*; as they are on the verge of being destroyed yet not yet destroyed, it is like...
When a lamp is about to go out, its light flares up once more; this is the result of the struggle between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and demonic power.
Thus, whether one succeeds or fails depends on whether it is the way of Mara or the Buddha;

as Mount Gu said, "A great falsehood leads to falling into the Avīci Hell," which refers here to those practicing dhyāna-concentration within the stage of the "name" (*nāman*) and those in the five grades of the stage of "contemplative practice" (*kuan-hsing*).

There is no sense of falling away for one who cannot yet practice patient endurance, because in both cases one has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression. However, the characteristics of the exhaustion of the five aggregates differ.

While within the state where the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is not yet exhausted, one remains in the stage of names and words (*nāma-pada*). One whose aggregate of form is exhausted still dwells in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

When the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, one is in the first two stages of the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), namely the first and second levels of faith (*śraddhā*). When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted...

Thus, when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is exhausted, one is at the stage of the fifth and sixth stages of faith (*śraddhā*). When the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness) is exhausted, the various faculties function interchangeably;

this occurs from the seventh stage of "conformity" (*sādṛśya*) onward, which is precisely the stage of the "purity of the six sense organs" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) where the coarse defilements have first fallen away.
Furthermore, each of the five aggregates serves as the basis for ten seeds of Māra, totaling fifty.

The ten grave offenses all occur because they are initiated during the initial stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and thus there is the possibility of falling back. If one enters the stage of "semblance" (*sādṛśya*), the meaning of "falling" does not apply.
Therefore, the Buddha sequentially and minutely distinguished their characteristics so that those at the initial stage may recognize the specific energy-moments (*vāsanā*) they have initiated.

This is, for example, like when a celestial Māra appears within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) before it has been broken through; this is precisely the energy-moment of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

This is what arises from that. Question: Since one has already entered the state of "similarity" (*sādharmya*) when the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, why do ten kinds of demonic realms (*māraviṣaya*) arise again within the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others?
Answer: If one were discussing the actual destruction of the aggregates, how could demons possibly arise?

However, the text states that these are what arise within the mind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) prior to reaching the stage of similarity. This is done so that one may know their basis; thus, they are enumerated across all five aggregates.
I shall explain this in sequence. Furthermore, it would also be reasonable for one in the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*) to give rise to such objects.
Why? If even a Māra can afflict those in the profound stages, how could he not afflict those in the shallow stage of semblance?

However, when a person in the stage of semblance gives rise to them, they ultimately do not take them to be the realization of a sage. This is also like an Arhat who turns their mind to enter the Mahāyāna.
Although their positions may appear similar, because they have entered [the path] and thereby shattered ignorance, they remain unmoved.
If those at the stages of the name and contemplative practice possess strong contemplative wisdom, they will be tranquil like space and will not regard this as a holy realization.
Those whose power of contemplation is weak, however, will be deluded by it, fall into the paths of Māra, and undergo further cycles of saṃsāra. If...
When one is in a state similar [to the final stage] or gives rise to craving for the Dharma, one is called a "Bodhisattva who falls from the Peak.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Master Gushan elucidated the characteristics of the exhaustion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the basis for fifty types of demonic hindrances (*māra-bīja*).
His exposition may indeed be called detailed. However, there are two meanings: the horizontal and the vertical. Regarding the exhaustion of the five aggregates...

If one examines their meaning according to the vertical progression, it is said that those within whom the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has not yet been exhausted are at the stage of names and words (*nāman-pada*).

Those who have exhausted the aggregate of form still abide in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). This continues until the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), which occurs from the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) onward.

If, however, one considers them according to the horizontal classification based on the manifestations of demonic seeds, they fall into the category of regression; thus it is said that they all remain within the initial mind of contemplative practice.

Because they have been aroused, there is regression and falling away. It is further said: "The Tathāgata has sequentially and minutely distinguished their characteristics so that those of initial resolve may recognize the nature of the arousal of these factors" (and so forth).
This means that the fifty layers of the *skandhas* all arise within the context of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
One must verify what kind of characteristics they possess: what constitutes the nature of the *rūpa-skandha*, and what constitutes the nature of the *vedanā-skandha*?
Even down to the constituent elements of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), one understands each clearly and distinctly without error.

It is like when about to administer a medicine, one first identifies the illness; having identified the illness and recognized the medicine, one prescribes the medicine according to the illness and then administers it.

Someone asked: "The illness has now been understood; what then shall be done regarding the medicine? He replied: "Although the objects of perception are fifty in number, speaking in general terms, they do not go beyond the 'hard' and the 'soft.
As for the hard, it is tranquil and still like space; as for the soft, it is illuminated yet ungraspable.

Once the wind of wisdom has fanned and the water of meditative concentration has become clear, the myriad demons will lose their spirits in the realm of *kūṭastha* (the non-existent), and the hundred illnesses [shall likewise vanish]."

"It shall now conceal its traces in the realm where sprouts have not yet emerged. He asked again: "The aspect of the exhaustion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is profoundly encompassed within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Yet, the aspect of the manifestation of the five aggregates is relatively shallow, residing only in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). What is the meaning of these horizontal and vertical aspects? He replied:

"For the practitioner who cultivates the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*) are cultivated within a single mind, and the three truths (*tri-satya*) are cultivated within a single [mind]."

When the objects of perception are illuminated, the three delusions are suppressed within a single thought-moment. Although they are suppressed within a single thought-moment, there is nevertheless a sequential order regarding their manifestation;
thus, the coarse delusions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya*) occupy the foremost position.

Among these, the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusion of views, together with the first six grades of the delusions of thought in the desire realm, constitute the very basis upon which Māra relies. To destroy these—

When these two delusions are thus addressed, Māra finds no opportunity. As for the five kinds of false conceptualization, which are alternative designations for the afflictions of views and mental taints (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*), they are precisely engaged in mutual combat within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
Therefore, the fifty kinds of "vital energies" (*vāyu*) are divided into the orthodox and the heterodox, the manifest and the latent;
their emergence and disappearance are not constant, and their victory or defeat is indeterminate, being decided in a single moment.
This is to achieve mastery within the present thought-moment. ○ (2. The second section on the aggregate of sensation [vedanā-skandha]:

1. First, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; 2. First, concluding the preceding primary practice. Ānanda, when that virtuous man, while practicing samādhi and śamatha, has exhausted the aggregate of form, he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested in a clear mirror.

○ (2. Second, the appearance of the subsequent arising: 2. First, showing the two aspects; 2. First, the aspect of not yet being exhausted. If there is something attained that he is as yet unable to employ...

It is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet appear perfectly intact; though their sight and hearing are not confused, their mind is possessed by an external malevolent spirit such that they cannot move.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Sensation" takes the meaning of receiving and grasping external objects. Having already shattered the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), both internally and externally, it is empty.
Therefore, I see the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a mirror. The mind of all Buddhas is precisely my own wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
To say that images appear in a mirror means it is pure, empty, and still, and is understood to be free from form and obstruction.

Although it possesses this wondrous essence, it has not yet been able to exercise its function because it is shrouded by sensation; thus, it is like a person in a nightmare whose limbs are fully present [yet paralyzed].
The six sense organs are clear and discerning, yet they cannot move; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Now, "sensation" takes "receiving and grasping" as its meaning. However, sensation does not receive by itself; it becomes sensation because of form (*rūpa*).
Yet, form also does not become form by itself; it becomes form because of sensation. These two characteristics function as a pair.
This has been so for a long time. Once the preceding aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is shattered, sensation (*vedanā*) has already lost its mate.

Nevertheless, it cannot exist without a mechanism acting alone, because the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) still remains. Therefore, when the aggregate of form is exhausted, its characteristics are illustrated by the analogy of a clear mirror manifesting an image;
it is like an ancient mirror that, having been polished again, has had one layer of coarse dust removed. One sees...

The minds of all Buddhas manifest like reflections appearing before them. Yet, because they still possess the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), it seems as though there is something to be attained, and thus they have not yet reached full functional mastery.
This is because they are obscured and hindered by the domain of the aggregate of sensation; therefore, another analogy is drawn:

it is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly intact and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is possessed by an external malevolent spirit and cannot function.
"Movement": when the hands and feet move naturally and what is seen and heard is not confused, this is used as a metaphor to explain the metaphor;
it is like an image appearing within a clear mirror. When the mind is touched by adventitious heterodoxy and cannot move, it is as if there is something attained that has yet to be put into use.
However, these two metaphors seem each to illustrate one of the aggregates (*skandha*); specifically, the metaphor of the clear mirror manifesting an image illustrates [the aggregate of form].

When form (*rūpa*) is exhausted, it is like a person whose mind is possessed by a malevolent spirit; though they are touched, they cannot be moved—this serves as a metaphor for the persistence of sensation (*vedanā*).
If taken as a general metaphor, it can all be understood as the phenomenon where, although form has departed, sensation remains.

(2) The Mark of Exhaustion: When the affliction of being haunted by nightmares ceases, and the mind detaches from the body to look back at one's own face, such that going and staying are free and there are no further obstructions, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). (2) Revealing the Source of Delusion:
One observes its origin and finds that empty luminosity and false conceptualization constitute its root.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: One whose aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted has already departed from physical obstruction; yet, because one is still haunted by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā*), one is unable to exercise this freedom.
Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation subsides, one is able to detach from the body and reflect back upon it, such that going and staying are unimpeded.
Because illusory objects of compliance and resistance give rise to false sensations of loss and gain, the aggregate of sensation lacks any substantial essence and exists only as a void.
Because it is luminous, it is called "empty-luminosity delusion.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the mind cannot go or stay at will, it is externally obstructed by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and internally detained by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Since these two aggregates have been exhausted, the mind is able to depart from the body and return.
One contemplates their faces. In the preceding passage on the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it was explained that seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching are congested and obstructed;
water, fire, wind, and earth revolve and interweave with these perceptions of cognition, falsely forming what is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

This is precisely because seeing and hearing grasp at forms, and these forms mix with seeing and hearing, such that the sentient and the insentient harmonize to produce false reception. Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted...

One is then able to transcend it. (2. The Manifestation of the Aspect of Empty Luminosity; Part 1: The Direct Explanation of the Ten Aspects; 10. Seeing Objects and Giving Rise to Compassion; 2. First: Pointing to the Aspect and Tracing the Source. Ānanda, when that good man is within this state, he attains a great radiance.

His mind becomes luminously clear, yet because his internal restraint is excessive, he suddenly gives rise to inexhaustible compassion toward those very objects. Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gadfly...
If, like an infant, a feeling of compassion arises in the mind such that one unconsciously sheds tears, this is called the "excessive suppression of the mind through effortful application.

(2. On the Correctness or Deviance of Mental Application) To realize this is not a fault, nor is it a sign of saintly realization; if one remains awakened and does not become deluded, [the phenomenon] will naturally subside after a long time.

However, if one mistakes this for a state of sainthood, then the demon of grief will enter one's heart and viscera; upon seeing others, one will weep boundlessly, thereby losing right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
"One shall fall into ruin.
[Commentary] Wénlǐng says: Since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been destroyed, there is no longer any dark obscurity; thus, one attains great radiance.

Knowing that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is a fault, one suppresses and subdues it within oneself to destroy it. However, if this suppression and subdual are excessive, one loses the quality of compassionate gentleness.
Therefore, because he possesses much compassion, the demon of sorrow (śoka-māra) has attached itself to him. Wuxing says that "the illumination of his mind" refers to what follows in the text:

"when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is eliminated, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes clear. Those who explain this by means of "mad wisdom" (unbalanced insight) are incorrect.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: Now, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness, while compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering;

these are the noble intentions by which Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings and the magnificent deeds by which the Tathāgata delivers humanity. Nevertheless, they both rely solely upon the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Therefore, there are three ways of explaining them:
namely, provisional loving-kindness, empty loving-kindness, and middle loving-kindness. If any one of these three is lacking, [the practice is incomplete].
Yet this is not permissible. Now, because one suppresses internal [distractions] to give rise to compassion, if one speaks of it in terms of its accompaniment, it belongs to the condition of birth;
if one speaks of it in terms of its exclusion, it falls into the realm of attachment and views. Compassion based on the provisional truth of the condition of birth must certainly not be absent.
However, if there is no mind of emptiness conditioned by the Dharma to restrain it, and no Middle Way beyond conditions to unify it, one will rarely fail to fall into attachment.
It is vision. Because this vision belongs to the category of afflictions associated with craving (*rāga*), the demon of compassion seizes the opportunity to enter his heart and innermost being.

(2. The Simultaneous Binding of Courage and Wisdom) Ānanda, furthermore, when those good sons within that state of concentration perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright, their excellence...

When signs manifest before one, being excessively moved by them, one suddenly gives rise within that state to infinite courage; the mind becomes fierce and sharp, and the will is equal to that of all Buddhas, thinking that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
This is called "the transgression of overstepping through forceful effort. (2) Regarding the correctness or deviance of mental application:

if one awakens to this, there is no fault, and it does not constitute a holy realization. If one remains aware and does not become deluded, [the experience] will naturally subside after a long time. If, however, one takes this to be a holy attainment, [it will lead to error].
Then a mad demon will enter his heart and viscera; whenever he sees others, he will boast with incomparable arrogance.
His mind will reach such a state that he perceives neither Buddha above nor other people below; having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), he shall surely fall into ruin.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "When form (*rūpa*) is exhausted and sensation (*vedanā*) manifests, it constitutes the superior sign of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because one achieves success through joy, one becomes stirred and moved, thinking that the fruit of Buddhahood can be equaled and that merit and practice are easily attained. This is the error of overconfidence;

thus, mad demons (*māra*) attach themselves to such a person. Nowadays, those who consider a little to be sufficient, who are arrogant and transgress their proper limits, and who look upon themselves as having no equal—all these are [like this]."
This is the fault of excessive impetuosity (*ling-shuai*). Wuxing says: "Excessive impetuosity refers to a courageous mind that is overly headstrong.
[Tiantai’s] Commentary: Previously, because of excessive internal suppression, sorrow arose; the illness lay in an excess of *śamatha* (calm abiding), leading to a fall into dullness.
Now, because of excessive emotional arousal, courage arises; the illness lies in an excess of *vipaśyanā* (insight), leading to a fall into madness.
Once one falls into the sorrow of craving and views, it becomes the seed of pride. The Great Master said:
"Though the faults of madness and folly differ in their degree, there is no distinction between them regarding the cycle of existence caused by false views.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Although the practitioners addressed in this sutra take their own lack of extensive learning and inferior wisdom as their fault and request the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama, the essence of samādhi is perfectly integrated such that cessation (*śamatha*) is itself contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). this means that having attained a mere semblance of the noble state, one considers it sufficient. Is this not the fault of having too little concentration and too much wisdom?
For the sake of practitioners, the Tathāgata pointed out this fault, saying: "One loses constant discernment and fails in knowledge and vision. Indeed, the cultivation of dhyāna is most valued for...
The efficacy of knowledge and vision lies in constant examination; this constant examination, in turn, is accumulated through extensive learning.
As the *Fuyuxing* states: "In the past, there was a Chan monk dwelling in an araṇya. Having long cultivated meditative concentration, he had not yet attained profound awakening.

When the ice melted, he thought that his realization and traces were identical to those of a Buddha and that he had already attained the Way of Buddhahood.

He waited for the time when the light of dawn appeared, expecting that Brahmā and Śakra would request him to turn the Wheel of Dharma; yet when that time arrived, there was nothing to be seen or heard.

He then reflected upon the matter and verified through these events that he had only attained the fruit of Arhatship. Thereafter, he entered the city to beg for food and encountered adverse circumstances.
When anger arises upon encountering favorable conditions, greed is stimulated. As these states revolve and manifest, one may mistakenly claim the third fruit or the second fruit.

Eventually, through the emergence of false interpretations and deviant views, one realizes that the first fruit has not been realized. Thereupon, feeling shame and remorse, one repents and resumes cultivation with vigor as before.
This is what is meant by "not losing [the path]," constant examination, not being submerged in views and knowledge, not being entered by Māra, and not following [delusions].
This is the merit of sinking and falling. (5.

The Five Kinds of Births and Endless Sorrow; Part 2: First, Pointing Out the Characteristics and Tracing the Source. Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good men see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) vanish and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "This is called 'light ease' (praśrabdhi); those who lack wisdom and merely restrain themselves" means that the method for entering the Way must rely on wisdom to achieve proper balance.
For there are states of stagnation and agitation in the maladies of meditation, while the medicinal remedies are *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

If one can thus restrain oneself through wisdom, there is no illness that will not be eliminated and no medicine that will not be effective. Nevertheless, within this process, there are also [states] that appear similar...
To mistake what is wrong for medicine is to turn the medicine itself into a disease. For instance, if one says that the mind being at ease is not the factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),

However, there arises an infinite joy; when joy is excessive, it further leads to levity.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: There are seven names for pride (*māna*). To rely on oneself and despise others is called *asmimāna* (self-pride). To be arrogant toward those of equal virtue is simply called *māna* (pride).
To contend for superiority among equals is called *adhimāna* (excessive pride). To contend for superiority over those who are superior is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
To claim one has attained what one has not attained is called the pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*). To boast of oneself despite being inferior is called the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).

Not paying homage to stupas and temples and so forth is precisely perverse pride (*mithyāmāna*). Those who are currently deluded and neither pay homage nor recite [the scriptures] are all under the influence of the demon of pride (*māna-māra*).

If one harbors such deviant views while still clinging to life, how can they ever attain the Middle Way? It is only because they fail to respect themselves that they treat the scriptures and images with contempt.
Once the wind of heterodoxy fans out, the foolish delight in following it.

"Full" does not mean being full in the way that a vessel is full by receiving objects within it. Therefore, it is said:

To consider oneself full when one is full is to treat others with arrogance; to consider oneself full when one is empty is to treat others with reverence. Thus it is said:
"The vast ocean is able to become the sovereign of the hundred valleys because it is able to humble itself. How much more so for one who has entered the Ocean of Sublime Adornment?
How much more so for one who considers themselves full while still being incomplete? How much more so for one who harbors arrogance even to the seventh degree? This is great arrogance.
It is only fitting that Māra should enter their hearts and lungs; it is no misfortune that he deludes sentient beings and causes them to fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This passage criticizes those who rely on extensive learning, suggesting that being "without learning" (wuwen) would be appropriate.
However, many who consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress become "monks without learning," misleading sentient beings and falling into the Avīci Hell;

It is simply that one does not lose their correctness. If one takes extensive learning as the primary achievement and remains fixed therein without moving forward, then there is no true achievement.
However, just as hearing the instructions allows one to contemplate the mind—leaving behind the finger to see the moon—extensive learning is an indispensable aid on the Way.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Because one attains a state of empty clarity, one erroneously clings to nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*), thereby incurring various false faults.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Within clear awakening, one attains the nature of empty clarity; empty clarity is indeed correct reception (*samādhi*).

Because they take cause and effect as their basis, they enter exclusively into emptiness and give rise to the view of annihilationism.

Therefore, by violating the Buddha’s disciplinary code and erroneously leading others into sin, they lose right reception (*samyak-samādhi*) and shall inevitably fall into ruin.

Having departed from that form like a bird escaping its cage, one is already able to achieve accomplishment. (2. The Manifestation of the Subsequent Thought-Phase; Part 1: Showing the Signs; Part 2:

The Sign of Non-exhaustion) From this ordinary body, one ascends through the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva to attain the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body), proceeding everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who, while in deep sleep, utters words in a dream;
although that person has no distinct conscious awareness, the words they speak already possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who are not sleeping to hear them.
All of them understood his words; this is what is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
[Commentary] Gushan said: From the initial three gradual stages up to the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*), there are both the worthy and the sage.

Since these are all positions traversed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they are collectively termed "sage-positions" (*ārya-vihāra*). Now that the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) has been shattered...
Because one immediately enters a stage resembling that of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is called the "body born of mind" (*manomayakāya*).

"Born of mind" is a metaphor for moving as swiftly and without obstruction as the mind; there are three types. First is the body born of mind through the bliss of entering samādhi, which refers to the mind being tranquil and unmoving;

this corresponds to the stage resembling the first to the seventh faiths, wherein one enters the position of emptiness. Second is the body born of mind through the awakening to the self-nature of phenomena...
The nature-born mind-made body (*prakṛti-manomaya-kāya*) refers to universally entering Buddha-fields with the Dharma as its intrinsic nature;

this corresponds to the stage of emerging into the provisional [world] through the eight levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Third is the category of the spontaneously born mind-made body without volitional effort (*anabhisamskāra-manomaya-kāya*), which refers to realizing the Dharma realized by the Buddhas;

this corresponds to the middle stage of cultivation during the nine and ten levels of faith. Changshui said: "Because they have not yet destroyed the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it is like..."
Deep sleep is like speaking in one's sleep (*svapna-vāda*). Because there exists the potential for the stage of sainthood (*ārya-bhūmi*), it is like the orderly sequence of phonemes and rhymes.
This causes those who are not yet awake to fully awaken to that speech; just as when one realizes they are a sage, they know that such a person possesses the potential for the stage of sainthood.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The Tathāgata knows all and sees all that these persons shall all attain the accomplishment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: For humans, there is nothing greater than consciousness (*vijñāna*) in bringing about afflictions and birth-and-death;

likewise, there is nothing greater than consciousness in obscuring bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the wondrous functions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). However, consciousness does not establish itself without activity (*saṃskāra*);

activity is not accomplished without perception (*saṃjñā*); and perception is not complete without sensation (*vedanā*). Therefore, among the three aggregates (*skandha*), sensation is taken as the primary factor.

This is the root of delusion. Therefore, within the established gates of the teachings, regarding the *dāna* (giving) it is specifically said that one "does not receive," and regarding *samādhi* it is specifically said that one enters "right reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*).

If one can truly have no receiving of dharmas and thus return to right reception, then conceptualization has no means to exert its ingenuity, conditioned activities have no power to apply their force, and consciousness likewise has no basis upon which to rest.
This is its merit. Nevertheless, sensation (*vedanā*) must depend upon the sense faculties (*indriya*), and the faculties must correspond to their respective objects (*viṣaya*).
Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) serves as the garden for the aggregate of sensation; the aggregate of sensation is the gardener of the aggregate of form.

Now, since the aggregate of form has already been destroyed beforehand, sensation likewise has nothing upon which to depend. Once sensation is subsequently forgotten, perception (*saṃjñā*) likewise has no function. Therefore, sensation...
One for whom the aggregates (*skandha*) have been exhausted has already decisively breached the barriers of birth-and-death and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Only the fundamental root within remains; before long, one will wither and dry up that very root of birth-and-death and afflictions.

Now, having undergone this breaking through, the mind is free from obstruction; thus, although the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) has not yet been attained, one can leave the physical form behind like a bird.

Having emerged from the cage, one is already able to decisively accomplish the shallow and deep stages of ascending from the mundane to the sacred, attaining the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) that moves everywhere without obstruction.

Although the preceding exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is like a person who has awakened from a nightmare—their hands and feet are perfectly functional and their seeing and hearing are unconfused—yet when the mind encounters external deviant influences, it cannot move.
This is because it serves as a metaphor for the fact that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) has not yet been shattered.
The heavy slumber of the long night of birth and death is now present as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), like a person in deep sleep who utters words in a dream;
this is taken as a metaphor for the fact that once the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has been broken, the heavy slumber of the long night of birth and death becomes light.
This, too, is one instance of the illumination provided by a simile.

○ (2. The Characteristic of Exhaustion) If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, so that the awakened, luminous mind is like a surface cleared of dust and grime, and one can perfectly illuminate the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). ○ (2.
Revealing the Source of Delusion) One contemplates its origin and finds that pervasive delusive conceptualization (*yǒngtōng wàngxiǎng*) serves as its root.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "Awakened clarity is like a mirror; floating thoughts are like dust. When thoughts are exhausted and the mind is clear, it still resides in the stage of 'semblance,' where the beginning and end are as they were from start to finish.
If one awakens to the true permanence that is without beginning or end and free from the distinction of birth and death, it is therefore called 'perfect illumination.
Wenzheng says: "Thoughts can cause transformation and change, making the mind follow the object and the object follow the mind. It is like...
The thought of a sour plum is able to penetrate through material obstructions; therefore, it is called the "delusive thought of pervasive penetration.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: When the preceding aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, the metaphor established is like a mirror. When the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is present, the metaphor established is like sleep.

Now that [the aggregate of sensation] is exhausted, it is illustrated by the analogy of sleep. When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, one grasps the image within the awakened, luminous mind, like removing dust and grime.
If one applies this dharma to the analogy, it is like an ancient mirror that, upon having its dust removed once more, again manifests a further degree of clarity and purity.

II. Correctly Explaining the Manifestation of Arising (2). A. Correctly Explaining the Ten Signs (10). 1. Craving for Skillfulness (2). A. Receiving the Samādhi in Vain and Clarifying It. Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of perception is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration becomes luminous.

B. The Manifestation of the Aggregate of Thought (3). A. Craving Due to the Mind. Within the state of samādhi, his mind comes to cherish its own perfect luminosity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and craves skillful mastery. B. Causing Demons to Attach Themselves (2). A. The Demon Arrives to Display Marvels.

At that time, a celestial demon seizes the opportunity and sends forth his essence to attach itself to a person, who then speaks the teachings of the sūtras. This person does not realize it is a demon.
Clad in their own [false] claims that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, they come to the places of those sons of good family who seek skillful means;

there they arrange seats and preach the Dharma, their forms momentarily appearing as bhikṣus so that those people may see them, or as Śakra, or as women, or as bhikṣuṇīs, or even lying in dark rooms while their bodies emit radiance. These people, deluded by folly, take them to be Bodhisattvas.
The demon believes in their teachings and agitates their minds, violating the Buddha’s precepts and secretly indulging in lustful desires.
They delight in speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and supernatural anomalies;

they may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or describe the terrors of war, causing people's wealth and property to dissipate without cause. These are called "strange ghosts," who become such as they age.

The Mara. (2) When the Mara departs, he brings calamity upon himself; he harasses this person until his mind becomes weary and satisfied, and he leaves that person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril.
(3) You should awaken first; do not enter the cycle of rebirth. If you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The exhaustion of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) is called 'empty and wondrous. Being free from the demons of feeling is called 'not encountering them.
Regarding "perfect concentration," this refers to the concentration within the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate).

"Loving perfect clarity and seeking skillful means" means that because of this empty wonder, one gives rise to attachment and contemplates the essence of perfect clarity in order to manifest the function of *upāya* (expedient means). This is the manifestation of the celestial Māra.
"Converting and teaching" refers to the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of attaching oneself to others—that is, attaching to other people.
"The person to whom one attaches" and "those people" both refer to those who practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the ten sections on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the old commentaries do not distinguish between them; however, following the current analysis of the sutra, they are divided as follows: the preceding section provides a general introduction.
It is said: "Whether it be your *skandha-māra*, or the *deva-māra*, or being possessed by ghosts and spirits, or encountering *chi* and *mei* demons. The final summary states:

"These ten kinds of *māras* either attach themselves to the human body or manifest their own forms; these 'Māra-teachers' transmit lasciviousness from one to another, and evil *piśācas* and *rākṣasas* delude the heart and viscera.
As for the raising of the ten *māras*, such as grief and so forth, within the *vedanā-skandha*, these are the *skandha-māras*."
Furthermore, when the first ten categories of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) are raised, they are precisely the celestial Māras. The text states:

"Secretly practicing lustful desires" refers to the demon-teacher who transmits the various forms of lewdness. Next, the raising of such things as "fond of speaking words [of seduction] from the mouth" refers to ghosts and spirits, *chimei* (goblins), and their simultaneous attachments;
this is what is meant by "evil essences deluding the heart and viscera. The *guǐguài* (strange ghosts) and *bàiguǐ* (drought demons) are all those previously mentioned.

As for this, Wu Xing said: "When a flying spirit (*fei-jing*) attaches itself to a person, it must attach to one who is worthy of such attachment—namely, one who practices meditative concentration and cultivates wisdom.
A disciple and a teacher are like a craftsman seeking a skilled son or a Dharma teacher seeking a disciple. The following cases are all analogous to this.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is the wondrous function of skillful *upāya*. If one can practice concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in a perfect manner, the coarse defilements of the five aggregates will first be eliminated.
Progressing further through the eight, nine, and ten stages of faith, the provisional principle will manifest before one, and the function of *upāya* will naturally be revealed.
Why, then, would one midway abandon this reliance on diligent reflection and greedily seek other virtues?

They are cunning. Unaware that as soon as a single thought of greed sprouts, the celestial Māras watch for their opportunity and eventually attach themselves to people through skillful means to delude them, causing practitioners to ultimately fall into their trap.
This continues until they encounter royal peril, enter the cycle of saṃsāra, and descend into the Avīci Hell without ceasing. Such is the way Māras harm people; thus should practitioners act.
Be careful with your thoughts! ○ (2. Greed for Experiencing; Part 1:

Receiving the Samādhi in Vain) Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s *skandha* of sensation becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous, ○ (2.

The Manifestation of the Mind of Thought; Part 3: First, Greed Arising from the Mind) within this *samādhi*, his mind loves to wander and rove, causing his refined contemplation to fly forth as he greedily seeks to experience various realms. ○ (2. Causing Demons to Attach; Part 1: The Demon Arrives and Displays Marvels) At that time, the Deva...

When Māra seizes the opportunity, he sends his essence to possess a person who speaks of the Dharma; yet that person is unaware they are possessed by Māra, and while possessed, they claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
He comes to the place of the son of good family seeking instruction, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma;
his own form remains unchanged, while those listening to the Dharma suddenly see themselves sitting upon jeweled lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed.
They become a mass of purple-gold light, and each person in the assembly attains such an unprecedented experience. These people, deluded by folly, mistake this for a bodhisattva;
their minds are licentious and they violate the Buddha’s code of discipline, secretly practicing greed and desire.

They are fond of saying with their own mouths: "A certain Buddha has appeared in the world; a certain person in such-and-such a place must be the incarnation of that Buddha come here; that person is indeed [the Buddha]."
When such beings as these *bodhisattvas* come to transform the human realm, people see them and their hearts give rise to longing;
yet, as false views secretly arise, the wisdom of the All-Knowing One (Sambhogakāya) causes them to perish. These are called *pūtana* ghosts who have grown old and become demons.

(2) When they afflict and disturb this person until they feel satiated, they depart from that person's body; both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. (3) You should be the first to awaken; do not...
Entering the cycle of saṃsāra in delusion, they do not realize they are falling into the Avīci Hell.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Is it not what we today call "travelling for study" (youfang) that involves such experiences?

In ancient times, because their insight into the Way was not yet clear, people would continue their travels even at the age of eighty. However, there is an appropriate time for both leaving home and remaining in the world. Now, regarding...
During the hundred-day sitting meditation, one should settle the mind in samādhi and prajñā. If the appointed period is reached without achieving the result, one must vow not to rise from the seat.
If one is hasty and the mind wanders in attachment or greedily seeks out experiences, the celestial māras will be able to take advantage of the interval.
If someone says, "This person is an emanation of such-and-such a Buddha who has come here," it is not a Buddha, but a māra using the hook of desire to entice them.
Experiencing this, one partakes in and receives it. (3. Seeking Accordance; Part 1:

Receiving the Clarity of Stillness in Emptiness) Furthermore, O Good Man, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) manifests its brilliance. (2. The Manifestation of the Mind’s Thoughts; Part 1:

Greed Arising from the Mind) Within this *samādhi*, the mind cherishes a continuous and lingering attachment, purifying its refined contemplation as it greedily seeks accordance with the truth. (2. Causing Demons to Adhere; Part 1: The Demon Comes to Display Marvels) At that time, the celestial Māra awaits his opportunity.
Finding an opportunity, the flying spirit enters a person’s mouth and speaks the Dharma; yet that person is truly unaware of it.

Possessed by the Māra, they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place where a seeker of the Way—a son of good family—has spread his seat to preach the Dharma.
Neither their own form nor that of the listeners undergoing the teaching undergoes any outward change, such that the minds of those listeners remain as they were before they had heard the Dharma.
From the moment they attained awakening, their thoughts shifted and changed from moment to moment:

some gained knowledge of past lives, some possessed the power of knowing others' minds, some beheld the hells, or knew all manner of human affairs, both good and evil; some spoke verses aloud, or recited sutras themselves, each rejoicing at having attained what they had never experienced before.
These people were deluded by folly, imagining themselves to be Bodhisattvas; with hearts bound by lingering attachment, they violated the Buddha's precepts and hid in secret.
Practicing greed and lust, they speak with pleasure of the Buddha’s greatness or smallness, claiming that such-and-such a Buddha was earlier and such-and-such a Buddha was later;
among them are true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas, and the same applies to Bodhisattvas.

Because people see these things, their original minds are washed away and they easily fall into heterodox enlightenment. These are called "possessing ghosts" who, when old, become demons. (2) They disturb and confuse this person, bringing calamity upon them.
When a sense of satiety arises, they depart from the person’s body; both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity. (3. Exhorting the Enlightened First):
You should be the first to awaken so as not to enter saṃsāra; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The love for the subtle and profound" refers to the desire for a secret union with the wondrous principle. Because one hopes for such a union, the Māra grants awakening.
From the phrase "self-awakening" downward, all concerns the matter of secret union. Zīzhōng says:

"When the mental mechanism is extinguished and the illumination is still, the principle naturally meets in mystery. If one hopes for and seeks a union, the very moment the mind is directed toward it, there is error. Thereupon, the celestial Māra...
To "attain its opportunity" means to find the favorable condition.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Mianmi" (綿密) means dense and subtle; "He" (合) means merging. This refers to the merging of the preceding mind's penetrating clarity.
Now, my causal awakening is profoundly still and can merge with the resultant awakening of all Buddhas; one should also seek this spontaneous functioning.
And that is all. If the mind loves softness and clarity, and through refined contemplation craves spiritual resonance, then the celestial Māras will find their opportunity.
They cause those who hear the Dharma to experience self-awakening, extending even to the knowledge of others' minds and past lives—all of which they manifest as matters of spiritual resonance.
Changshui said: "The Buddha values men and women who lead practitioners to practice desire."

Desire does not hinder the attainment of Buddhahood. While there are indeed distinctions between the partial (*piān*) and the perfect (*yuán*) according to the teachings, since the origin is the same while the ends differ, how could there truly be a difference of small and great?
Yet heterodox persons clearly speak of "small" and "great. How easily can they know the Buddha’s fundamental and manifested traces?
Heterodox persons arbitrarily judge that one came before and another came after, further indulging their own...
To distinguish between the true and the false in this way is how foolish one is! Those who seek to cleanse their fundamental mind instead eliminate right views with their own distorted views.

Initially Receiving the Clarity of Samādhi) Furthermore, O good son, when the *skandha* of reception becomes empty and subtle, and one is no longer beset by distorted thoughts, the perfect samādhi will manifest its brilliance. ○ (2. The Appearance of the Arising Mind; Part 3: Initially Due to Mental Craving) Samādhi...

At the center of the earth, they exhaustively investigate the root of craving and survey the beginning and end of the transformation of things; they refine their spirits and minds, greedily seeking analysis and discernment.

(2. The Demon Attaches Itself, Part 2: Initial Appearance of the Demon’s Manifestations of Wonder) At that time, the celestial demon waits for an opportunity and sends his refined essence to attach itself to a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma.
That person was previously unaware that the demon had possessed them, yet they also claim to have personally attained supreme Nirvana and come to those who seek the source of goodness.
When the Manzi (the Bodhisattva) sat upon the prepared seat and preached the Dharma, his body possessed such majestic spiritual power that it subdued those who sought instruction;

even though they had not yet heard the Dharma, their minds were naturally humbled as they sat beneath him. These people took the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi-dharmakāya* to be identical to the fleshly body before them;
they saw that fathers and sons, generation after generation, mutually giving birth to one another, was itself the eternal *dharmakāya*.
Abiding in uninterrupted continuity, they point directly to the present as the Buddha-land, claiming there is no separate Pure Abode or golden-hued marks.
Those people accept this with faith, losing their former resolve; they take refuge in body and life and attain what they have never had before. Such deluded fools mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas;
when their hearts are scrutinized, they are found to have violated the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practiced lustful desires, their mouths fondly speaking of the eyes.
The ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands; the male and female organs are the true abode of Bodhi and Nirvana.

Those who do not know this believe these are foul words; such people are called those possessed by *gūdu* (poisonous spirits), *yan-sheng* (hypnotizing demons), or evil ghosts, and they become demons in their old age.

(2) When these demons depart, they bring calamity upon the person. Having exhausted their power of harassing and disturbing them, they leave the person's body. Both the disciple and the master will then fall into royal punishment.
○ (Exhorting Those Already Awakened) You should be among the first to awaken; do not enter into the cycle of saṃsāra through delusion and ignorance, lest you fall into the Avīci Hell.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because attachment reaches the very root of the myriad transformations, one’s mind becomes impaired by analytical discrimination.
To equate the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* with such things as the physical body as the fruition of virtue, or to regard illusory birth as eternal, is to negate [the truth].
The claim that the retributive bodies of the Pure Land are all fundamentally identical is a false assertion of syncretism resulting from a failure to analyze the source of transformation.
To regard defiled impurity as true purity is, in intent, to lead toward licentious desire. Wuxing said: "The ocean of nature is perfectly clear and tranquil;
therein the myriad phenomena naturally manifest. If one seeks worldly principles in a biased manner, it only serves to increase the outflowing mind, violating original *dhyāna* and leading astray."
"The ghosts enter.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The beginning and end of the nature of the transformation of things is precisely what the Tathāgata elucidated in the fifth fascicle regarding worldly and world-transcending dharmas—knowing their fundamental cause and how they emerge according to conditions.
It is like knowing the number of raindrops or the pine thorns."
The curvature of the crooked and the straightness of the upright, or the whiteness of the crane and the blackness of the crow—all these are understood through their causal conditions (*pratyaya*).
Yet, this arises from the Buddha’s provisional wisdom and the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) which discern things as they ought to be; when the merit reaches its fulfillment, it arrives of itself.

Why, then, must one pre-emptively devise plans, cling to the root of craving, examine the source of transformation, or indulge in the analysis of greed? The Mara King seizes such opportunities to fulfill his own desires through the methods he employs.
Yet, by confining them within such limits, one causes people to sink into vulgarity and obscenity before they can ever come to an end. [5. Greed for Mysterious Resonance (2):

First, Receiving the Clarity of Empty Samādhi] Furthermore, O good man, when the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and one is no longer beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect samādhi will manifest its clarity. [2. The Manifestation of the Arising of Thought (3): First, Greed Arising from the Mind] Within this *samādhi*, the mind comes to love and long for a distant response;

it circulates and investigates with intense scrutiny, greedily seeking a mysterious resonance. [2. Causing Demons to Attach (2): First, the Demon Comes to Display Marvels] At that time, the celestial demon (*deva-māra*) awaits his opportunity.
Seizing an opportunity, the flying essence (*fei-jing*) enters the mouth of a person and speaks the Dharma; yet that person is fundamentally unaware that they are possessed by a *māra*.

The *māra* also claims, "I have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa," and comes to the place of a seeker of spiritual response, a son of good family, where he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma.
He causes the listeners to behold his body for a time as if for hundreds of thousands of years; their hearts give rise to attachment and lust, and they are unable to let go.
Acting as their servants, they provide the four kinds of offerings without feeling weary;

each causes those in their retinue to recognize them as former teachers or original spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), giving rise to a distinct attachment to the Dharma that is as sticky as glue or lacquer, such that they experience what they have never known before.

These people are deluded fools who falsely claim to be Bodhisattvas; though they draw near to them, their hearts violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code (*vinaya*) as they secretly practice greed and lust. Their mouths...
They often speak with longing of themselves in a previous life, saying: "In such-and-such a birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person;
at that time, they were my wife, concubine, brother, or sister. Now I come to deliver them, accompanying you back to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha.
Or they say: "There is another Great Radiant Heaven where a Buddha dwells; it is the place of rest and residence for all Tathāgatas."
Those who lack wisdom believe this to be false and deceptive, thereby losing their original mind; this is called the "leprosy-demon," who becomes a malevolent spirit in old age.

(3. The Demon departs and brings calamity. It will harass and disturb this person until it becomes satiated; having left the person's body, both the disciple and the teacher shall fall into royal punishment.

○ (Exhorting Those Already Enlightened) You should be among those first awakened; do not enter the cycle of saṃsāra, nor fall into delusion and ignorance, whereby you would descend into the Avīci Hell.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The response is suspended in the sages, while the resonance lies within oneself. This refers to seeking signs of attainment before the principle has yet been realized."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the Way of Resonance (ganying), there are two expositions. The first holds that initial awakening (shijiao) acts as the stimulus, to which fundamental awakening (benjiao) responds;
this is the practice of those who cultivate the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi. The second holds that sincere seeking acts as the stimulus, to which physical transcendence (shentong) responds;
this is the practice of those who cultivate the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (nianfo). However, these two are sequential in their practice.

Thus, while they are divided into distinct gates, their profound convergence constitutes a single essence. There has never been a case where initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) lacked efficacy, yet another Buddha could respond to it.
Now, within *samādhi*, you harbor a longing for a distant response;

since initial awakening lacks its requisite efficacy, your constant circulation and refined study—your greedy pursuit of a hidden resonance—arise from a state of mind still possessed of volition. How, then, can this possibly achieve harmonious accord?
Because there is no external object to connect with, the celestial Māras are able to seize this opportunity and manifest their responses from afar.

[6. Craving for Quiescence] (Part One: Receiving the Samādhi in Emptiness and Clarity) Furthermore, O virtuous son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect samādhi manifests its brilliance. [2. The Manifestation of the Arising Mind] (Part One: Craving through the Mind) Within this *samādhi*, the mind desires to penetrate deeply;

through diligent self-discipline, one takes pleasure in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and craves quiescence. [2. Causing Demons to Attach] (Part One: The Demon Arrives and Displays Marvels) Thereupon...
At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, sent his essence to possess a person who then spoke of the Dharma and the sutras.
That person was originally unaware they were possessed by a Mara, yet he claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He came to the place of the good man seeking the aggregates (*skandha*), spread out a seat, and preached the Dharma, causing those listening to each recognize their own past karma. Or, at that place, he might say to one person: "You..."

While he was still not yet dead, he had already been reborn as an animal; he commanded one man to step on his tail from behind, causing the man to be instantly lifted up so that he could not remain there.
