Although one contemplates the myriad forms, because there is no conceptualization, it is like the bright reflection in a mirror—unadhered to and traceless.

Receiving and responding to illumination in emptiness, with no lingering habits, there is only the singular, refined, and true clarity; thus, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) reaches its ultimate limit.

It is here that they are revealed. Since the activity [of consciousness] is the root-source of the birth and extinction of the myriad transformations, when its characteristics are revealed, the origins of the twelve classes of living beings are fully manifested.
Each has its own lineage of consciousness (*vijñāna*); they share the same basis of birth and the same course of action.
Because it agitates what is dark and hidden, it is likened to a wild horse; because it arises and perishes momentarily, it is called "flashing" (*yi yi*). It is non-existent...

Furthermore, because it is a coarse shadow, it is called "clear agitation. Since the movement and stillness of the faculties and their objects both originate from this, it is called the "ultimate pivot and aperture."孤山 (Gushan) says:

"Although not yet 'descending' means that although one has not yet been able to see those sentient beings in their particular aspects as they cultivate causes and tend toward fruits, one is already able to see those classes of beings in their general aspect as all proceeding by way of karma."
It arises; this is what is named the "common basis for co-arising" within this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It refers to wild horses, mirages, and floating dust.
"Gleaming radiance" describes the appearance of shimmering flashes. "Clear agitation" refers to the phrase from the text below: "profoundly clear and agitated movement."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the phrase "one for whom the skandha of perception is exhausted," the following first restates that perception has been exhausted, and then proceeds to explain its fulfillment.
First, it clarifies the essence of the exhaustion of perception; next, it clarifies the function of the exhaustion of perception.

To say that "this person’s ordinary dream-thoughts have been extinguished, remaining constant whether awake or asleep" means that dreams exist because of perception. Since [during the day] one has already bound these into various perceptions, although...
When one is not confused by what is seen or heard, yet at night manifests as the six types of dreams, these are inverted and disordered;

thus, the states of waking and sleeping cannot remain constant. Now, for the practitioner whose *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) has been exhausted, both ordinary dreaming and conceptual thought are extinguished.
Waking and sleeping, their minds remain constant and unified. Thus, the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment is empty and non-existent.
Objects are still and motionless, like the clear and bright void where coarse sensory objects no longer exist, being merely like the shadows of floating clouds or gentle breezes.
Next, the function of the exhaustion of conceptualization is explained: once this essence is attained, the functions of the six sense organs likewise become subtle and wondrous.
Therefore, one contemplates the great earth, mountains, rivers, and the six sensory objects of the world.
In the realm where the sense organs encounter their objects, it is like a bright mirror reflecting forms;

though objects appear as images, the arising mind is not adhered to by sensory dust and does not rush outward in flight. When objects depart and the dust vanishes, the mind does not linger upon them to gather conditions and cause internal agitation.
In its essence, it is empty of that which is received; in its function, there is nothing it does not encompass.
Illumination and response. It is precisely because of this that the six faculties function through illumination, yet there is nothing presented as habitual tendencies;

there is only the solitary, refined, true, empty, still, and luminously aware state. This concludes the description of the phase where conceptualization is exhausted. Next, within the description of the subsequent phase of activity (*saṃskāra*), the first clarifies the phase where it is not yet exhausted.
For when the aggregate of conceptualization (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ceased, the aggregate of activity (*saṃskāra-skandha*) manifests before one. Birth and cessation...

The root source is thus revealed from this point. It is like polishing a mirror: once a layer of coarse grime has been scraped away, the subtle shadows of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) appear before one.
Consequently, one perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category of their kind.

Although one has not yet penetrated the individual origins of their life-destinies, it is said that the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness) is still being dominated by the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

This is the obscuration of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. To see the basis of co-arising as shimmering and turbid like a mirage—this specifically refers to the subtle phenomena of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, which are like a mirage whose appearance is shimmering.
That is to say, the state of clarity and turbulence is like a heat-haze (*marīci*), yet it is also like a flickering light;
it seems to exist and yet seems not to exist, appearing and disappearing in rapid succession. Thus, the *saṃskāra*...
In the first three aggregates (*skandhas*), the movement of the *āyatanas* is coarse; now, within their own aggregate, their arising and ceasing are subtle.

This constitutes the ultimate pivot-hole of the ephemeral sense organs (*bhrānta-indriya*). It is precisely because the governing authority over the opening and closing of the six gates resides in this pivot-hole. While conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) certainly precedes it, it is still not equal to action (*saṃskāra*), which serves as its ultimate consummation. Thus it is said: [The original Chinese text provided is: 陰遍前三陰其動也麤。今在本陰其生滅也細。乃為浮塵根究竟樞穴。正以六門開閉所司者在于樞穴。想固當其先而猶未若行以為之究竟是為 [The English translation provided above is: In the first three aggregates (*skandhas*), the movement of the *āyatanas* is coarse; now, within their own aggregate, their arising and ceasing are subtle. This constitutes the ultimate pivot-hole of the ephemeral sense organs (*bhrānta-indriya*). It is precisely because the governing authority over the opening and closing of the six gates resides in this pivot-hole.
While conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) certainly precedes it, it is still not equal to action (*saṃskāra*), which serves as its ultimate consummation. Thus it is said:
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is its domain. The *Bùyì* (Supplement) states that according to the *Zōulǐ* (Rites of Zhou) and the *Lièzǐ* (Lì Zǐ), there are six types of dreams:

first, the "regular dream" (*zhèng-mèng*), which occurs spontaneously while in a state of composure; second, the "startled dream" (*wò-mèng*), which occurs due to being shocked or alarmed; third, the "thoughtful dream" (*sī-mèng*), which occurs as a result of constant reflection;
fourth, the "awakened dream" (*wù-mèng*), which occurs when one recounts something from the waking state; and fifth, the "joyful dream" (*xǐ-mèng*), which occurs out of delight... [and so forth].
Dreams. The sixth is the "dream of fear," wherein one dreams out of terror. The *Fahua wenju* states:
"Only a Buddha does not dream, because he has no doubt and no residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). Dreams arise from five causes. As a verse says:

"Due to a doubting mind, discrimination, learning, past experiences, and the arrival of non-human beings to speak—through these five things, dreams occur. These are the five matters; there are six periods [of dreaming].
All these are fundamentally the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 92, states:
"Sleep is of two kinds: first, sleeping with dreams; second, sleeping without dreams. An Arhat does not sleep for the sake of seeking security or attachment to pleasure;
rather, because they possess a body composed of the four great elements, they must naturally have eating, resting, sleeping, and waking. Therefore, they take a brief rest."
This is called "sleeping" but not "dreaming while asleep.

(2. The Characteristic of Exhaustion) If this turbid agitation subsides and the original nature shines forth, such that the nature enters the primordial clarity, and through this single clarity the habitual tendencies are extinguished—like waves ceasing and transforming into still water—this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. (2. Revealing the Source of Delusion) Observe its...
The source from which [the skandhas] arise is obscure and hidden; false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) constitutes its root.

[Commentary: Wēnlíng says: Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) have become one's nature, they are called "fundamental nature" (*yuánxìng*) and "fundamental habits" (*yuánxí*).

If one can extinguish these turbulent habits, one returns to the fundamental clarity of the essence, and the phenomena of flux and movement are exhausted. Thus, it is like the subsiding of waves and ripples.
It is for the purpose of clarifying the water. Because birth and death ceaselessly continue and karmic forces constantly shift, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Therefore, when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, one transcends it. Since the aggregate of formations shifts secretly without any awakening, it is termed "subtle and hidden delusive thought."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Clarity, agitation, and shimmering" refers to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Original nature" (*mūla-prakṛti*) refers to the essence (*svabhāva*) of the aggregate of formations.

This means that this clarity, agitation, and shimmering are precisely the root-source of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), capable of acting as the branching streams for the preceding three aggregates;
therefore, it is called "original nature. If the aggregate of formations is exhausted, the nature of flux and movement becomes tranquil and returns to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the *skandhas* are profoundly still and unmoving, it is called "the nature enters primordial clarity. Once one enters the stillness of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the fundamental habits of the *saṃskāra-skandha* are all empty;
hence it is said, "once clarified, the original habits are gone" (and so forth).
To speak by way of metaphor, the *saṃskāra-skandha* is as subtle and fine as the ripples on water. If this *skandha* is shattered, the ripples are extinguished and transform into clear water.
However, this stillness is not the true flow; it is not seen because it is spoken of in conjunction with movement, and for this reason it is likened to clear water.

(2. Correctly Clarifying the Manifestation of Characteristics, Part 1: Correctly Clarifying the Ten Characteristics, Section 1: The Two [Points] on the Theory of Causelessness, Subsection 1: The True Mind Excludes Demons. Ānanda, you should know that when these sons of good family attain right awareness within *śamatha*, their minds become concentrated, luminous, and upright;

thus, the ten classes of celestial Māras find no opportunity to gain advantage. (2. Thoroughly Investigating the Source of the Arising of Vision, Section 1: General Exposition. Only then are they able to investigate with refinement and exhaustively reach the root of all living beings, returning to that very source.
Among those who emerge from the category of "originating from species," those who perceive that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source of movement,
and within that perfect source give rise to speculative calculations, fall into the two theories of causelessness.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because dreams and desires have vanished and one remains constant in both waking and sleeping, it is called "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*) and *śamatha*.
It is also called "concentrated clarity" and "rectifying the mind"; these are all signs that conceptualization has been exhausted. External demons are all summoned by the mind;

therefore, when conceptualization is exhausted and concentrated clarity is attained, celestial Māras will not arrive. From this point on, there is only the cultivation of dhyāna, free from deluded understandings.
To falsely conceptualize this is precisely the demon of the aggregates (skandha-māra). Sentient beings are fundamentally identical to the basis of co-arising.

Within that fundamental category, when the primal source of life is revealed, one perceives the primordial source within the basis of co-arising. This profound, pure, and moving source is precisely the primordial source of activity.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "This is one who has attained right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Since the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, both waking thoughts and dreams are empty;

thus, whatever is known in ordinary experience is entirely correct. As it says below, "The mind is concentrated and clear, and the mind is correct. This "mind" is precisely "knowledge," which is what is meant by "attaining right knowledge.
If one gives rise to extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) regarding this, then one loses right universal knowledge (*samyak-sarvajña*). This is because...

"Right Knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*): this is a brief expression; in full, it should be "attainment of Right Universal Knowledge. This is because a person of perfect realization possesses the six universal knowledges;
thus, when it says "attainment of Right Universal Knowledge," it refers to either the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*) or the stage of contemplative practice (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*).
"Within *śamatha*" refers here to the midst of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). When the mind is stilled and luminous, internal protection is powerful, and Māra cannot [disturb] it.
Thus, the heterodox will not interfere with the orthodox, and one may finally engage in refined investigation to exhaust the root of the categories of living beings.

This means that once the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been brought under control, one can then employ the power of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to conduct a subtle and detailed study in order to exhaust the root of the categories of living beings within the aggregate of formations.
Within these fundamental categories, there are precisely the twelve classes of beings. "The source of birth being revealed" specifically refers to the object [of investigation].
This is the contemplation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

When one contemplates that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source of movement, one employs *śamatha* to observe that within the characteristics of the aggregate of formations, amidst all motion, there exists the eternally abiding true mind that is unmoving;

this is for the purpose of perfect cultivation. All of the above demonstrates the manifestation of the object and the contemplation before one. Within this perfect source, one gives rise to conceptual calculation.

When one clearly understands that the arising of non-affirming negations constitutes a mark of error, yet at the very source of the perfect circle (*pariniṣpanna*) one prematurely gives rise to attachment and considers it the fulfillment of *bodhi*, then because the vision of the Path is not true, one gives rise to conceptual constructions that result in the two types of "causeless theories" (*ahetuvāda*).

This calculation places primary weight on the character "original" (*yuan*); "original" here refers to the "cause. These two causeless theories are fundamentally based upon this. Thus the commentator establishes [the argument].
"Words" refers to exposition and debate. Once a biased view has taken root in the mind, its verbal expression must inevitably manifest in formal treatises.
All the "causeless theories" (ahetuvāda) established by the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) of the Western Regions originate from this. The same applies to all subsequent cases.

Thus, one should know that the doctrines of the outsiders are all fundamentally rooted in internal principles; it is simply because their vision of the Path is not true that they do not fail to rely upon shadows and echoes.
This is measured by what is driven by form and sound.

(2. Specifically revealing the two [aspects]; first, calculating that there is no fundamental cause; first, the direct explanation. First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?

Because this person, having attained the complete breaking open of the life-faculty (*janman-karaṇa*), rides upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, their karmic currents winding and circling.
Seeing beings die here and be born there as they circulate through their realms, yet observing nothing beyond eighty thousand kalpas—shrouded in darkness—he formed this understanding:
"These sentient beings of the ten directions throughout the world have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas, without cause."

○ (2. Concluding the Faults) By means of this conceptualization, one forgets right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and falls into the ways of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "The faculty of perception being completely shattered" — "faculty" (*jī*) is a metaphor for agitation, which is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

It is said to be "completely shattered" because it is no longer covered by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). As for the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, since these are already calculated in terms of the three periods of time and the four...
I shall now discuss this. Seeing that the beginning is without cause, one immediately mounts upon past merit; seeing that the end is without cause, one immediately mounts upon future merit.

This arises from the manifestation of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) within meditative concentration, whereby the faculty of the eye displays this functional power.

The winding and circling of karmic flows is the circulation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). As for "darkness with nothing observed," this refers to the darkness of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

This is indeed true. For the karmic conditions of good and evil are merely transformations created by consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since these persons cannot perceive even the formations (*saṃskāra*) beyond eighty thousand kalpas, how much less can they perceive consciousness itself?
Therefore, from this point onward, they give rise to the view that there is no cause.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: As for "seeing that which is fundamentally without cause," it is seen by virtue of the power of the eight hundred merits of the eye-organ (*cakṣur-indriya*).
These merits possess two kinds of distinctions: "the world penetrating the directions" and "the directions penetrating the world.
"The world penetrating the directions" takes that which horizontally pervades the five directions as its basis; this is not the intended meaning here. Now...

Regarding the causes that extend across the world vertically through the three periods of time, the discussions of these merits differ in the two contexts [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*].
The present sutra clarifies that the cause is intrinsically possessed by the mind, which is not the intended meaning here.

One should instead take the discussion of the "semblance fruit" (*pratirūpa-phala*) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, because it concerns what is accomplished through cultivation. Furthermore, if one has already seen the Truth within the stage of semblance, [the cause is already realized].

The principle of the Truths does not further admit of such a calculation. This must be a person at the stage of contemplative practice who, having fully suppressed the five abodes through the merit of the eight hundred faculties of the eye in the stage of contemplative practice, gives rise to this conceptualization upon seeing.
II. (2) The Second Calculation: That the Phenomenal World Has No Cause (Part 1: The Direct Explanation). Second, this person perceives that the phenomenal world has no cause. Why is this?

Because this person, having already seen its root in the process of birth—knowing that humans produce humans, awakening to the fact that birds produce birds, seeing that crows have been black from the start and cranes have been white from the start, and realizing that humans and devas are fundamentally upright while animals are fundamentally horizontal—they understand that whiteness was not produced by washing and blackness was not created by dyeing;
from eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further alteration or change.
Now, even as this physical form comes to its end, it is likewise so; since I have not seen bodhi from the very beginning, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi?
One should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "They erroneously cling to the roots of their birth and fail to comprehend the principle of transformation.

They take a human to be ultimately a human, and even black to be ultimately black, with no further change or movement. Consequently, they infer that since I did not see the Way in the beginning, there can be no accomplishment at the end;
this means the end has no cause. The original character in the text should have been "end" (末) rather than "text" (文). Wú-xīng says: "There is no longer..."

Regarding "transformation and shifting": this view arises because some people observe that among the various classes of sentient beings and animals, there are those whose karmic fruits have not been altered despite the passage of long periods of time;

thus they give rise to this calculation. As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) clarifies, Śāriputra observed that for eighty thousand kalpas, the pigeon’s body remained unchanged in its species from beginning to end.
Now, having seen such a phenomenon within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one clings to [the notion that] all things are... [self-existent].

Nevertheless, this is precisely because they do not know the life-origins of each of the twelve classes of beings. Now, by exhausting this present form and so forth, they clarify that there is no cause for the future;
yet they should also perceive eighty thousand kalpas, for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are identical in their views to the śrāvakas.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The preceding passage relied upon the fundamental to calculate the fundamental, asserting that the fundamental has no cause.
This present passage uses the fundamental as an analogy for the derivative, calculating that the derivative has no cause. It is not only this;

furthermore, the reason why those seen in the six realms of existence do not undergo further change is that they fundamentally have never seen Bodhi. This is truly because they harbor false interpretations within.
Because of these seeds planted in former lives, they give rise to delusions and form attachments based on erroneous interpretations.
(2. Conclusion of the error) Due to such conceptualizations, they lose right and universal knowledge, falling into the ways of external paths and becoming confused about the nature of Bodhi. (3.
Conclusion and demonstration) This is called the first type of external path, which establishes the theory of causelessness.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: Master Zhaolun stated that the non-Buddhist teacher Makkhali Gosāla claimed that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are not obtained through karma (*saṃskāra*), but are entirely spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
A previous sutra states that Makkhali and others all asserted that after the death of this body, there is total extinction.

Although the present doctrine of causelessness does not explicitly mention death and extinction, it must likewise be categorized as being of the same kind [as nihilism], even until the end of the kalpa.
One should know that all views do not transcend the four propositions: namely, annihilationism (*uccheda*), eternalism (*śāśvata*), both, and neither.

Of these, the first two—being causeless—are the view of annihilationism. The latter four—the pervasive eternalism, partial impermanence with partial eternity, and even the "neither" regarding what exists after death—constitute the final three propositions.
All other speculative reckonings originate from and flow forth from these.

○ (24. The Four Theories of Universal Permanence; Part 1: The Right Mind Excludes Demons) Ānanda, within this *samādhi*, the various good men whose minds are concentrated and upright allow no opportunity for demons to gain entry. ○ (2. Exhausting the Origin to Reveal Vision;

Part 1: General Exposition) When one exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if one gives rise to speculative calculations regarding this perfect permanence, such a person falls into the four theories of universal permanence.
[Commentary] Changshui says: Because the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) continues in succession without interruption, it is called "constant" (*nitya*).
Because the four types of calculations encompass all phenomena, it is called "round" (*parimaṇḍala*). Wēnlíng says:

The previous mention of the "round source of agitation" and this current mention of the "constant source of agitation" refer to the source of arising and ceasing, which is entirely contained within this [aggregate]. Consequently, one clings to it as being constant and gives rise to [delusion].

The "Theory of Universal Permanence" (*pūrṇa-nityavāda*). "Universal" (*pūrṇa*) means "round" (*vṛtta*). Therefore, the title here is marked as "Universal Permanence," while the concluding title is "Round Permanence.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, within the "Perfect Origin" of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), one gave rise to calculations. "Origin" (*yuan*) means "root" (*mūla*). Thus, the initial calculation was that there is no cause for the root;
furthermore, because one calculated the derivative based on the root, it was called "no cause for the derivative. Now, regarding...

Within the [false views of] "round" and "eternal," four theories of universal permanence are established due to the arising of conceptual calculations. These all refer to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) pervading the twelve bases of existence;
this is called "round. Because one fails to perceive the locus where the flow of birth and death is so rapid, it is called "eternal.
That is to say, within the midst of birth and death, one prematurely calculates that which is truly eternal. If one were actually to see the truly eternal, what calculation would there be?

○ (2. Specifically revealing the two [types of views]; first, the correct explanation of the four [views]; first, the twenty thousand eons of permanence. First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects;

finding no cause for these two locations, they cultivate the practice of knowing that all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions over twenty thousand kalpas circulate in a cycle without ever being lost, and thus reckon them to be permanent.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Because one falsely calculates the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as a perfect source of arising and ceasing, one consequently calculates the mind, objects, the four great elements, and so forth, as being permanent.

Zhēnjì says: "Although the two spheres of mind and objects are without cause, because they have continued in succession for twenty thousand kalpas without interruption, they are calculated as being permanent."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The nature of the two locations—mind and object" refers to the nature of these two locations, mind and object.
This discourse on the universal permanence of the four [elements] originates from the previous discussion on the absence of causes. Therefore, it is said that the two locations are without cause.
Previously, it was called "seeing" because of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty; now, it is called [hearing] because of the twelve hundred merits of the mind-faculty.
With this mental knowledge, one perceives vertically the subtle aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and conceives of it as permanent;
however, the supernormal power of mental penetration thus obtained is inferior to the former, and therefore one can only cultivate the ability to know events within twenty thousand kalpas.
2. Second, this person exhausts the source of the four great elements and realizes that their four natures are eternally abiding;

through cultivation, they come to know that throughout forty thousand kalpas, all the births and deaths of sentient beings in the ten directions are entirely constant in essence and never dispersed or lost, and thus they reckon them to be permanent.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Sentient beings arise and perish in dependence upon earth, water, fire, and wind; yet the four fundamental natures are eternally abiding.
Thus, all phenomena of arising and perishing are, in their essence, eternal."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, regarding the two natures of mind and objects, the conceptualization of his views was still broad, encompassing both form and mind.
Now, having exhausted the four great elements as being fundamentally the four natures eternally abiding, his view is narrow, limited merely to the form of the four great elements.
Herein, because the merit of this mental faculty (*manas*) is twice that of the former, it is said to be "forty thousand. This refers to cultivation.
One who is able to know through practice must first contemplate the manifestation of the breaking of formations; only after further cultivation can they truly know it.
(380,000 characters) Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties and investigates the fundamental source within the *manas*, the grasping, and the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Because the nature of the locus is eternal and constant, through cultivation one is able to know that within eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings circulate without losing their original, eternally abiding nature;
thus, failing to realize this, they reckon it to be permanent.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The six sense organs and the manas that grasp and maintain [the body] are the eight consciousnesses.

Within mind, thought, and consciousness, the fundamental source is the nature of consciousness itself. This means its original nature is eternally constant; sentient beings rely upon it to circulate and abide, never losing it.
This is to recognize the spirit of consciousness and falsely calculate [its nature]. Zhēnjì says: "Regarding the statement of the six sense organs..."

This refers to citing the supporting faculty (*indriya*) to reveal the supported consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since it states "within mind, thought, and consciousness," we know that one is observing the eight consciousnesses.
Wuxing said: "According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the ālayavijñāna cannot be known by anyone except Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage;
all other followers of the two vehicles and practitioners of external paths are unable to know it. Judging from this, [it is clear].
Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted, how could one reckon this state as permanent?

One should know that "mind-consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) here refers collectively to the eight consciousnesses, while the "original source" (*mūla-yuan*) specifically points to the aggregate of formations.

This is because the Śūraṅgama Samādhi suddenly exhausts the eight consciousnesses and perfectly subdues the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*); yet, at the point where the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, one does not yet fully comprehend the aggregate of formations.
One falsely perceives subtle arising and ceasing as being permanent; this does not mean that one has already perceived the eighth consciousness within meditative concentration.
Master Kuò said, "If one understands the eight consciousnesses, how could one harbor such divergent views? These words are excellent. Tianru’s Supplemental Notes state:

"The *Abhidharmakośa* says that 'accumulation' is called mind (*citta*), 'deliberation' is called thought (*manas*), and 'discernment' is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). The *Bǎifǎ shū* states: "The eight consciousnesses..."

The mind (citta) is named the seven consciousnesses, the intellect (manas) is named the [seventh] consciousness, and the six consciousnesses are named cognitions (vijñāna). Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the mind is simply the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
It is like fire, which is called a flame, a blaze, and also that which burns wood; it is but a single mind with three distinct designations.

Regarding the various interpretations herein, one should adopt Master Yue’s view—which broadly cites the eight consciousnesses while specifically pointing to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations)—as being closer to the truth.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the preceding second case, permanence was reckoned based on the four great elements; now, it is reckoned based on internal form.

One reckons the four aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as permanent. The mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the basis for the two consciousnesses grasped by the *manas*.
By mentioning the agent, the object is revealed; however, it is not necessarily the case that non-Buddhists are able to perceive the eight consciousnesses.

Within this context, because the merit of the mental faculty is twice as vast as the aforementioned [six thousand], it is said to be eighty thousand. The rest is as explained in the traditional commentaries.

○ (4. Permanence as Non-arising and Non-ceasing) Fourth, since this person has exhausted the source of ideation (*saṃjñā*), their fundamental nature no longer undergoes the movement of flowing, ceasing, or revolving;

thus, the mind of arising and ceasing is now eternally extinguished. Within this principle, there naturally arises a state of non-arising and non-ceasing, which the calculating mind takes to be permanence.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The 'element of perception' (*saṃjñā-skandha*) refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The 'aggregate of formations' (*saṃskāra-skandha*) refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

To falsely claim that the flow, transformation, birth, and extinction all belong to the mind of perception—now that these have been eternally extinguished—it follows naturally that the principle of non-birth and non-extinction belongs to formations.

One fails to realize that the aggregate of formations is itself the very source of birth and extinction. Chángshuī says: "This is to calculate non-birth and non-extinction within birth and extinction."
Therefore, they grasp it as being permanent. Wuxing says: "The previous [view] took the original source as permanent;
this was to calculate non-arising-and-non-ceasing within arising-and-ceasing, like seeing a thin stream and calling it still water.

Now, taking that which is within the principle as permanent is to calculate non-arising-and-non-ceasing within non-arising-and-non-ceasing, like seeing empty space and calling it eternally abiding. This, too, is delusion."
They merely take the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to be the principle.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, it was based on the four aggregates as the foundation for the calculation of birth; now, however, one abandons the broad for the narrow, giving rise to calculations solely regarding the aggregate of formations.
One should know that non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the principle, relying upon false principles to form their calculations.
In principle, who would not say that the five aggregates are all empty, that one has already transcended suffering and calamity,
and that one has already realized the true reality? Yet the Tathāgata, using his correct wisdom, examines their underlying basis and exposes their calculations to point out their errors,
so that those of future generations who observe these failings may return to the correct path and, it is hoped, not be swayed by erroneous interpretations.

(2. Concluding the Faults) Because of this adherence to permanence, they lose right and universal knowledge, falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. (3.
Concluding the Demonstration) This is called the second type of external path, which establishes the doctrine of the perfect and eternal.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: These four stages represent the realms of ultimate exhaustion, arranged in sequence from the broad to the narrow.

The first encompasses all five aggregates (*skandha*); the second is restricted to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the third concerns only the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and the fourth pertains solely to the principle of the non-arising and non-ceasing of formations.

If one says that the third stage involves the calculation of the eight consciousnesses, while the fourth again involves the calculation of the aggregate of formations, its meaning is already [established].
To lose one's place is likewise not correct.

○ (34. Part One: The Theory of Permanence; 2. Initial: The Right Mind Excludes Demons) Furthermore, within samādhi, when sons of good family firmly concentrate their right minds, demons find no opportunity. ○ (2. Exhausting the Origin to Develop Vision; 3. Initial:

General Description) One who exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, and gives rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others—this person is...
They fall into the view of the four inversions, the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This is not a calculation arising from a distinction between self and others;
rather, it is the construction of self and other within the *saṃskāra-skandha* itself—such as (2) regarding the country, (3) regarding the mind, and (4) regarding the self.
In all instances of mental activity, one is said to engage in conceptual construction regarding self and other. To illustrate this with the first case:

when all sentient beings arise and die within my own mind, these twelve classes of beings—though they are merely the manifestations of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) belonging solely to myself—are taken as "others.
Thus, within a state where neither self nor other truly exists, one falsely constructs the notions of self and other.
Furthermore:

(2) Specifically revealing the two [views]. First, the correct explanation of the four [types of views]. (1) First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate *ātman*.
From this, they calculate that the self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving, such that all sentient beings exist within their own mind.
If one dies and is reborn within this [state] spontaneously, then my mind-nature is called "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: From "observing the subtle" (*guān miào*) downward, he again raises the topic of contemplative practice (*guānxíng*). From "serene and still" (*zhànrán*) downward, he correctly clarifies the arising of conceptual attachments. Furthermore...

Because they do not understand the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they falsely claim that the nature of the mind in this state is tranquil and take it to be a "divine self" (*ātman*).
What is called the "divine self" is the term used by non-Buddhists for the "Lord Truth" (*īśvara-tattva*);
they assert that all phenomena are "mine," and that this divine self is their master.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Although the "wondrously luminous mind" (*miaomingsin*) is a matter of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), it refers to the mind at which thought has ceased and practice manifests as the wondrously luminous mind.
This is because for a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) path, delusion is observed as being identical to awakening;

they take the very source of the five false thoughts as the objective realm of observation to establish their contemplation of principle (*liguan*). If one observes with thorough discernment, the aggregates (*skandha*) are shattered.
The "Origin" (yuan) is used to manifest the true permanence. If one does not recognize it with clarity, one clings to the origin of thought as being wondrously luminous.

Now, within the midst of the exhaustion of thought and the manifestation of activity, one observes that profoundly pure and eternally agitated origin, calculating it to be wondrous, luminous, pervasive, and profound, and taking it to be the ultimate *ātman*. Thus, that which is profoundly pure and eternal is taken to be permanent.
The twelve types of disturbances consist of [the views that] birth and cessation are non-existent, or that because they are eternal, there is a partial non-eternality and a partial eternality;
thus, regarding what is eternal as being self and what is non-eternal as being other.
Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead universally observes the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate them as the nature of ultimate impermanence; seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate them as ultimate permanence.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: Those from the third dhyāna downward are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities and are thus called the "nature of impermanence.
Those from the fourth dhyāna upward cannot be destroyed by calamities and are thus called "ultimate permanence."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Not observing the mind, but universally observing the lands" refers to the *xing-yin* (consciousness aggregate) observing all external forms beyond the preceding *se-yin* (form aggregate).

Nevertheless, this also means that by means of one's own progression through successive stages—from the lower levels ascending to the heights of the third and fourth *dhyānas*—one realizes which of the three calamities (*san-zai*) are destructible and which are indestructible.
Regarding the state of permanence or impermanence, if it were permanent, it would be the state of *nirvāṇa* realized by oneself;
if it were impermanent, it would be the state of birth and death belonging to others.

Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely dense, like a minute particle that circulates through the ten directions without its nature ever changing.

This [mind] can cause the body to arise and perish in an instant; its indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self," while all deaths and births that flow forth from it are called the "impermanent nature."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) pervading internal form (*rūpa*) to give rise to conceptualization.
Generally, that which governs the human body as it pursues birth and death is the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

That which is subject to its transformations—discussed from the perspective of abandoning the external and following the internal—is the *rūpa-skandha*. Thus, one falsely calculates that the nature [of form] is not destroyed by the *saṃskāras*.
The nature of the self is eternally the self. The arising and ceasing of form flows forth from this self; thus, that which is impermanent in nature is termed "other.

(Four are eternal, the rest are impermanent. Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended and perceives the circulation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); because the aggregate of formations flows on continuously, they reckon it to be eternal.
The nature of form, sensation, perception, and so forth has now already ceased and perished; this is called impermanence. (2. Concluding the fault:

Because of this speculative reckoning that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. (3. Concluding the demonstration:
This is what is called the third heterodox doctrine of the "partially eternal."

[Commentary] Wuxing said: Previously, although I observed that my mind, though circulating through the ten directions, was in its nature unchanging, I did not realize that this "I" was the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), whose essence is in constant flux.
Now, although I see this flow, I have still not perceived the characteristics of the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).
Therefore, one contemplates whether form, sensation, perception, and so forth are permanent or impermanent. These are the four inversions.

First, one contemplates the self and all sentient beings, which refers to the primary retribution (*zhengbao*). Next, one contemplates the land and the kalpas, which refers to the environmental retribution (*yibao*).
These two [categories] clarify permanence and impermanence in relation to others. The third contemplates one's own mind and body; the fourth calculates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
These two clarify permanence and impermanence with respect to one's own form and mind, proceeding from the broad to the narrow.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This view arises from the notion that while formations (*saṃskāra*) persist after perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased. The intention is that since formations persist, they already belong to the truly permanent and thus can no longer be extinguished;
whereas form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) have already been extinguished, and therefore that which is extinguishable must be of a truly impermanent nature.
Thus, they take that which is subject to extinction as "other" and that which is not subject to extinction as "self.

(44. Discourse on Having Limits; Part 2: Correcting the Mind to Exorcise Demons. Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that demons find no opportunity. (2. Exhausting the Origin and Developing Vision; Part 3: General Exposition.

One who exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, yet still engages in conceptual calculations regarding its various states—such a person is...
This falls into the fallacious theory of the four limits of existence.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: There are four stages, namely: the stage of the three temporal limits, the stage of seeing and hearing, the stage of self and other, and the stage of arising and ceasing.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: These four types of stages do not go beyond time and place.
For instance, the first and fourth are explained in terms of time, while the second and third are explained in terms of place.
Furthermore, it is also consistent to take time as the "division" (*fen*) and place as the "stage" (*wei*), such that the combination of time and place constitutes these four types of stages.

(2) Specifically revealing the two [aspects]. First, the correct explanation of the four [points], beginning with the three times: First, because people’s minds calculate the origin of birth and reckon that its flowing function never ceases, reckoning the past and future is called "having limits," while reckoning the continuous mind is called "being limitless."

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The 'origin of life' flowing and functioning is the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because of this shifting flow, one calculates across the three periods of time.
Since that which has passed has already ceased and that which is yet to come is not yet seen, it is called 'having a limit. Because the present continues in succession, it is called 'limitless.'"
One does not know that the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is fundamentally neither finite nor infinite.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Here, the three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception that have already been destroyed are taken as the past;
the aggregate of consciousness that has not yet come into one's experience is taken as the future. Since the past is already past and the future is yet to come, they are so named.
It is finite. Because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) corresponds precisely to the mind’s conceptualization of the source of birth, its functioning flows on without ceasing;
because there is a sense of continuity, it is called infinite.
(2. Sentient Beings) Second, when this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas, they see that before those eighty thousand kalpas, all was silent and nothing was heard.
To see [the realm] where there is no hearing is called "boundless"; to have sentient beings where there is hearing is called "bounded.
[Commentary: Wuxing says: "The subsequent eighty thousand kalpas should also be as before; I now fear that this is an abbreviation for the sake of brevity.
Wenling says: "Previously, 'not seeing' was taken as 'bounded'; here, 'not hearing' is taken as 'boundless. This is a case of inverted and reversed calculation."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The meaning is that because [the realm] is boundless, it prevents me from seeing or hearing it; whereas because it has boundaries, it can be seen and heard.
One does not realize that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is limited, yet falsely calculates it to be either boundless or bounded.
Third, as for those people who reckon that their self possesses the nature of universal knowledge and attains boundlessness: since all those people are manifest within the scope of my own knowing,
and I have never known the nature of their knowing, they are said not to attain a mind of boundlessness, but rather to possess a mind with limits.
[Commentary] Gushan said: "I previously stated that one merely perceives that person appearing within the scope of one's own cognition, yet cannot know that the person's nature is all-pervasive;
therefore, one reckons that nature as having limits."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The nature of the Perfectly All-Knowing One is equal for both self and others. It is like a thousand lamps in a single room;

though their individual functions differ, how can one, knowing that one's own light is pervasive, yet failing to realize that the light of others is likewise pervasive, falsely calculate that one’s own self is great and boundless while reckoning others as small and finite?
(4. Extinction of the Four Births) Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Based on what they perceive through the pathways of the mind, they calculate that within the single body of every sentient being, there is a half-birth and a half-extinction;

they thus clarify that everything in the world is such that one half has limits and one half is limitless. (2. Conclusion of the Fault) Because of these calculations regarding having limits and being limitless, they fall into error.
The non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. (Third, the summary of the three points. This is called the fourth type of non-Buddhist who establishes the doctrine of finite existence.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because they exhaustively investigate the practice of emptiness—where what existed before is now gone—they conclude that one of the five aggregates undergoes half-birth and half-extinction, and that this applies to all internal faculties and external environments alike;
thus, they take birth as finite existence and extinction as non-existence.

Regarding "limits" (*anta*): Wu Xing says that among these four [views] concerning limits, the first refers solely to oneself; the second refers exclusively to others; the third encompasses both self and others;

and the fourth is a double calculation regarding all things, both the primary (the person) and the secondary (the environment). Thus, the preceding is narrow and the succeeding is broad, thereby forming their sequence.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Exhausting the emptiness of the aggregate of formations" clarifies the function [of contemplation].

"Half-arising and half-ceasing" refers to the objective realm of the aggregate of formations being contemplated. Within a single body, "half-arising and half-ceasing" is calculated based on the pervasive internal matter of the aggregate of formations.
That "the world has limits or is limitless" is calculated based on the external matter upon which one relies.
Also. ○ (5.

The Five Types of Evasive and Confused Discourse; 2. First, Rectifying the Mind to Cut Off Demons) Furthermore, when those good sons among the assembly of *samādhi* have stabilized and concentrated their correct minds, demons find no opportunity. ○ (2. Investigating Birth to Develop Insight; 3.

First, General Exposition) One who exhaustively investigates the root of all classes of living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, yet within their knowledge and views gives rise to conceptual calculations—this person is...
They fall into the four kinds of inverted, immortal, evasive, and pervasive false discourses.
[Commentary] Zizhong says: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the heterodox schools' calculation that the heavens are eternally abiding is called "immortal."

One calculates that by not answering in a confused manner, one will be reborn in that heaven. If one were to answer impulsively when actually ignorant, one fears it would constitute evasive equivocation (*vibhāṣā*).
Therefore, when questioned, one says, "This is cryptic terminology; it should not be explained in full," or one answers indeterminately.
The Buddha’s Dharma rebukes this, calling it true equivocation; thus it is named "the Immortal Equivocation and Empty Discourse. Wénlǐng says:
"Because of perverse inversion, one harbors wild and indecisive interpretations regarding knowledge and views, and consequently equivocates their speech.
Many of the heterodox people today who falsely claim to have attained the Way and thereby delude others with a lack of internal rectitude are of this same kind.
Regarding these four:
[The Commentary] Tiantai says: "Within knowledge and vision" means that one takes that profound, pure, yet constantly agitated source as the essence of the Way known and seen.
Because one does not clearly perceive the Way, truth and falsehood are not distinguished, and thus false conceptualizations arise.
They attain the deathless through the confused and incoherent discourse of vain arguments.
(2. Specifically revealing the two [aspects]; first, the direct explanation of the four [views]; first, the general calculation: First, this person contemplates the source of transformation;

seeing the place of shifting flux, they name it "change"; seeing the place of continuity, they name it "permanence"; seeing the place of what is seen, they name it "birth"; not seeing the place of the seer, they name it...
The state where the causal nature of the continuity of cessation is not severed is called "increase. The state within the midst of correct continuity that is free from [extremes] is called "decrease.
Each respective place of arising is called "existence," while the mutual absence of one another is called "non-existence.

Contemplating this through principle as a whole, yet seeing it differently according to the application of the mind, when seekers of the Dharma come to ask about its meaning, I answer them thus: [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya* or a similar treatise concerning the nature of existence, non-existence, increase, and decrease.]
Now, by asserting that things both arise and cease, both exist and do not exist, and both increase and decrease—
at all times they confuse their speech so that the person before them loses the chapters and sentences.
[Commentary] Changshui says: Within the single life-span of the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is divided into eight distinct meanings for observation, namely:
transformation, constant arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, existence and non-existence. In the answer, six of these meanings are briefly cited;
because he cannot definitively establish their underlying principles but answers by holding to both sides, he says "both arising and ceasing," and so forth.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Taking only the mark of the continuous flow and succession of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the fundamental basis, one forms eight views to give rise to eight reckonings.
First, within this fundamental basis, one reckons the place where there is flow and change as being "changeable";
since it changes, it is not constant. One also reckons the place where there is continuity as being "constant"; since it is constant, [it is eternal].
It is unchanging. From this, he expands his vision and makes calculations based on the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
He regards the place where seeing perceives as the two phases of arising and abiding, naming them "arising.

He regards the place where seeing does not perceive as the two phases of changing and ceasing, naming them "ceasing. These four phases follow one another without interruption, each succeeding the last.
Arising in a higher state is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*). Once the four characteristics have arisen in succession, they abide; having abided, they change; and having changed, they cease.
Within this continuous process, the removal of each preceding stage as one passes through the intervening points is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Because arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing each arise in their respective locations, they are called "existence" (*bhava*). Within arising, there is no abiding, and so forth.
Within cessation there is no difference; their mutual absence is what is called "non-existence. According to principle, one contemplates all eight characteristics as a whole;
yet when applying the mind, one perceives each of the eight characteristics individually.

When one perceives them individually, because one perceives arising (*jāti*), if someone comes and asks about its meaning, one answers according to what is seen, saying, "I am now also arising. This is the case when one perceives cessation (*nirodha*) individually.

He replied to him, saying, "It also ceases," and so forth. Having just seen [the Buddha] speak of arising and answered regarding that arising, he suddenly saw [the Buddha] speak of cessation and answered regarding that cessation.
Thus, the responses to the questions posed by the same person were inconsistent; for this reason, he caused the former person to lose the sequence of the verses.
(2. Calculating Non-existence) Second, this person observes their mind with discernment and finds that it has no mutual location; because there is nothing to be found, they realize non-existence.
When someone comes to question them, they answer with only a single word, saying merely "non-existent," and beyond this non-existence, they have nothing further to say.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Mutually non-existent" refers to the characteristic of moment-to-moment extinction (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*). One who attains realization awakens to the fact that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent.
[Sub-commentary] Tiāntái says: "Mutually non-existent" means that within arising there is no extinction, and so forth; furthermore, arising itself is able to be mutually non-existent with it.

The cessation of cessation can mutually lack its arising; this is also called mutual non-existence (*itaretara-asat*). In the former case, it refers to the branches among the eight [consciousnesses], whereas now it is determined within non-existence itself.

○ (3. Calculating Existence) Third, this person contemplates their mind with discernment, seeing that each has its own location; because existence exists, they attain realization and conclude that there is a person who comes.
The questioner asked, and the Master answered with a single word, merely saying "Yes" (*shi*). Beyond this, he had nothing further to say.
[Commentary] Wénlíng says: "Each and every one" refers to the characteristic of arising in every thought-moment (*nien-nian*). To speak of "no" or "yes" is both an unclear response.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Each has its own arising within arising, and its own abiding within abiding," and so forth.

This simply means that because arising, abiding, change, and cessation circulate without loss, it is said that "each has its own. The phrase "there is someone who waits for verification" means that there is proof that this is not false.
When it is merely stated that "it is so," it implies that there must be someone who comes to inquire about the arising of all phenomena.
When asked "Is it so?", he replied, "It is. When asked "Does it abide?", he replied, "It is. When asked about difference and cessation, he replied "It is" to both. (4.
The Dualistic View) Fourth, this person holds the view that both existence and non-existence are true; because they see their object as bifurcated, their mind is likewise distracted.
If someone comes and asks them, they answer, "It exists and is also non-existent," or "Within non-existence there is not 'also existence'"; all such responses are merely pretenses.

This confused evasion cannot be further scrutinized. (2. Conclusion of the fault) Because of such speculative calculations, deceptive evasion, and nihilism, one falls into the ranks of external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
(3. Conclusion and indication) This is called the fifth type of external path: the fourfold nature of perversion, the "immortal" evasive confusion, and the pervasive false theorizing.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: From the second to the fourth [positions], there is a distinction between existence and non-existence within the previous eight.
The second and third are calculated individually; the fourth is both. Existence is precisely non-existence, just as ice is water; non-existence is not existence, just as water is not ice.
Within these four positions, only three are involved, and the "neither-nor" (double negation) has not yet been seen. This is their calculation.
[This is] still coarse.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Because the cause is established based on the object, once that object is fragmented, the mind also becomes distracted.
"That which exists is also non-existent" means that the arising of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) ultimately returns to extinction. Within this non-existence...
As for this "existence," that which has ceased cannot be made to arise again. Now, existence and non-existence are both affirmed when they are affirmed, and both denied when they are denied.
It is never the case that existence is already identical to non-existence while non-existence is not identical to existence;
since your current calculation differs from this, it constitutes a confused and contradictory position.

○ (66. Discourse on the Existence of Characteristics, Part 2: Initially, the Right Mind Excludes Demons) Furthermore, within *samādhi*, those sons of good family who firmly concentrate their right minds cannot be taken advantage of by demons. ○ (2. Investigating the Origin of the Arising of Views, Part 1:

General Exposition) One who investigates the root of all living beings and observes that profound, pure essence which is the source of constant agitation, yet engages in conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow—such a person falls into the delusion of perceiving characteristics after death and develops inverted views.
○ (2. Specific Manifestation, Part 1: Direct Explanation, Part 1: Original Calculations) Or, they may cling to their own bodies, saying, "Form is the self," or...
Seeing me as perfectly encompassing all lands, one says, "I have form"; or, seeing the preceding objects of perception revolving according to me, one says, "Form belongs to me";
or again, seeing me as persisting within the continuity of formations, one says, "I am in form.
Such conceptual reckonings regarding existence after death involve sixteen such modes that circulate in this manner.

[Commentary] Zizhong said: "The inexhaustible flow" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because one perceives it as inexhaustible, one speaks of the existence of signs after death. Wunling said:
"Alternatively, due to the inverted views of those with inferior capacities, they stubbornly cling to the physical body, asserting that 'form is the self.
Furthermore, they claim that because the essence of the self is pervasive and all-encompassing, form belongs to the self. The 'prior conditions' refer to the forms currently before one's eyes."

The characteristic of the continuity of formations (*saṃskāra*) is also form (*rūpa*). By applying these four reckonings to form, and likewise to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations, sixteen characteristics are established.
All of these reckon that after death there is further existence. Xielì says:

"The 'consciousness-aggregate' (*vijñāna-skandha*) is not mentioned because the self being reckoned is precisely the consciousness-aggregate. Wŭxīng says: "Not so; [this refers to] the six dharmas of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."

Subsequently, there is the inversion of the mind that gives rise to the markless. When cause and effect vanish and cease, these are combined in discourse to form eight characteristics. (2.

"No. Because one calculates both the four aggregates and their negation, eight "neither" positions are formed. Wuxing says:

(a) The primary explanation: Within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives existence and non-existence; within the flux of formations (*saṃskāra*), one internally contemplates neither existence nor non-existence. Exhaustively investigating the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*), one encounters eight types of views regarding non-existence; each, according to its respective condition, asserts that after death there is both existence and non-existence.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: This calculation represents the "both-and" view (*ubhayatobhāgīya*). To perceive existence as non-existence means to claim that form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) do not exist.

To observe that there is nothing which is not non-existent is to say that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) exists. In this manner, through such circular reasoning and analogies, the "both-and" position is established:

namely, that the non-existence of the other three aggregates is like the existence of the aggregate of formations, and the existence of the aggregate of formations is like the non-existence of the three aggregates.

Because each of the four aggregates possesses these two aspects, they are called the "eight characteristics of neither-one-nor-the-other. The term "neither-one-nor-the-other" (ubhayām-ubhaya) is used in contrast to the preceding partial reckonings of existence and non-existence.
This is how it is named. The meaning of the text lies simply in the dual reckoning of existence and non-existence. Therefore, it concludes by saying "with marks" and "without marks.
Wēnlíng says: "To encounter any single condition" means that regarding any of the four aggregates (skandhas), one gives rise to conceptual attachment as soon as they are mentioned.
