○ (2. Concluding the Faults and Exhorting to Instruction) Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded understandings regarding the *dhyāna* of the *saṃskāra-skandha* all arise because the mind’s application within the *saṃskāra-skandha* is in mutual conflict; thus, these realizations manifest.
When sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves, they encounter these manifestations and mistake their confusion for understanding.
Claiming to have attained the state of a sage, they commit a great falsehood and fall into the Avīci Hell. You all must take the words of the Tathāgata as...
After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.
Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamities; maintain and protect them, quelling false views and instructing their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning.
In the unsurpassed path, do not encounter divergent branches; do not allow the mind to pray for little and consider it sufficient. Become great awakened kings and purify [the world].
Jingbiao points this out.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: Previously it was stated that when *dhyāna* manifests objective realms, it is the celestial Māra who seizes the opportunity;

here it is stated that when *dhyāna* produces deluded understanding, it is the mental Māra that gives rise to deep calamity. Generally, when the realization of the Way is not true, many divergent paths lead to false views.
All such calculations are merely deluded interpretations; this is what is called the "demon of the mind," which one must guard against most deeply.

You who are charged with propagating [the Dharma] below should take the Tathāgata’s words and universally preserve and protect all sentient beings, ensuring that demons do not invade, afflictions do not arise, they do not fall onto deviant paths, and they do not settle for minor realizations, but instead ascend directly to the stage of enlightenment. This is called performing the Great [Work].

This is the pointing finger of the King of Awakening. Wuxing says: "This refers to the 'demon of the mind' (*citta-māra*); later, in the section on the *vijñāna-skandha*, it is called the 'demon of views' (*dṛṣṭi-māra*).
Mind and view do not go beyond the two delusions of 'views' and 'craving,' which are precisely the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*)."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Master Wenling stated that those who do not truly realize the Way of Seeing (darśanamārga) engage in manifold false conceptualizations;
these words deeply strike at the vital point of the malady afflicting students. For most practitioners in the world fall into two kinds of errors:

first, they follow their own minds and establish their own positions without a lineage of transmission, merely admiring the lofty character of ancient worthies and entering deep into forest hermitages (āranyaka).
A desperate state. Through perverse speculations and deluded fabrications, their minds suddenly become empty; like a fish caught between ice, they mistake this for the True Way.
Consequently, they give rise to biased views and fall into heterodox sects.

They establish their own schools and cite the teachings of the Patriarchs as proof, comparing brass to gold and using jade-like quartz to confuse the white jade. Thus, they bring ruin upon themselves and others, ultimately falling into the ranks of Māra. One.
Having not yet mastered the essence of the teachings after a short period of study, they are fond of acting as teachers for others and establishing their own rules.
Unwilling to place themselves below others in terms of rank or status, they further seek to draw the multitude toward themselves.

Their shoulders of Chan are held ever higher, and the head of their school becomes increasingly aloof. Since they have never tasted the medicinal ingredients themselves, how could they possibly prepare decoctions with the same skill as Shen Nong?

Zhang Zhongjing [stated]: "If the medicine does not correspond to the disease and the prescription does not fit the ailment, to indiscriminately administer it at random is to regard the people as mere grass.
While there may be slight benefit at first, it will later lead to great harm. One enters the thicket of false views and falls into the net of Pāpīyān."
I have offered counsel and established arguments to serve as a model for future generations. Yet, our Master lost his footing and entered the fiery pit without realizing it;

we disciples were blindly led into perilous paths without awakening. This is entirely because we sought to cultivate the Way prematurely without first seeing the Way, relying on heterodox paths and erroneously claiming to have realized the fruit.

○ (The first part of the two sections on the fifth aggregate of consciousness: 1. Connecting the preceding to the succeeding; 2. Connecting the preceding to the exhaustion of the practice. The first part: Describing the signs of the exhaustion of practice.

Ānanda, when that virtuous man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, pure, and turbulent commonality of all worldly natures and the generative impulses of living beings suddenly collapse and fracture. The deep channels through which *pudgalas* repay their karma and the resonance between cause and effect are suspended and severed.

○ (The second part: Describing the essence and function of the exhaustion of practice. At the threshold of the heaven of nirvāṇa, he is about to attain great enlightenment, like a rooster crowing at the break of dawn.

Looking toward the east, there was already a refined radiance; the six sense-faculties were empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipating. Internally and externally, all was limpid clarity, entering that which has nowhere to enter.

(2. The Characteristics of Consciousness After Birth, Part 1: Showing the Two Characteristics, Part 1: The Characteristic of Non-exhaustion) He profoundly penetrated the twelve types of beings throughout the ten directions and the fundamental source from which they receive their life-force. Observing the source of grasping, he saw that none of these classes could summon him;
within the realms of the ten directions, he had already attained sameness. This refined radiance did not sink away, but manifested in profound obscurity.
To conceal this is called the realm of the *vijñāna-skandha*.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This generally describes how the cessation of *saṃskāra* leads to the manifestation of *vijñāna*.

*Saṃskāra* is the essential nature of the flux of the mundane world, the pivotal mechanism for the arousal of the life-force, and the deep pulse through which the *pudgala* repays its karma; it is capable of obscuring the true nature.
The heavens gallop away and the six sense-faculties are turbid and agitated within; they serve as the ultimate pivot and cavity for the floating roots and sensory objects.

Therefore, when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the tethers and cords of the life-force suddenly break apart, and the deep channels of the *pudgala* become suspended and severed from all response.
Yet, when the sky of one's nature is about to be greatly awakened, the six sense faculties no longer wander or stray.
Because they do not wander or stray, both internally and externally there is profound clarity. Because there is no pivot-hole [of sensory engagement], one enters that which has nothing to enter.

By reversing movement and returning to stillness, becoming deeper and yet deeper, it is called "internal and external. The sky of the nature of *nirvāṇa* is shrouded by the five aggregates, obscured as if by a long night.

The exhaustion of the first three skandhas is like the first crowing of a rooster; although it is a sign of dawn, it is still submerged within the two remaining skandhas, and their essential colors have not yet been distinguished.
This exhaustion of the saṃskāra-skandha is like the rooster’s subsequent crowing; because only one skandha remains, one is about to awaken to the Great Illumination.

The primary source of receiving life is the vijñāna-skandha. Because the extinction of saṃskāra reveals vijñāna, one deeply penetrates it; since there is no pivot-hole [of obstruction], one attains liberation.
It can be observed. Because it does not undergo transition or flux, it can be grasped; because it lacks the impulse of arising, it cannot be summoned.
Thus, one realizes that the ten directions—both the environment and its inhabitants—are all transformations of consciousness, and thereby attains identity with them.

Although the pure radiance of the celestial nature has not yet become clear and penetrating, its profound and mysterious aspects have already begun to manifest; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Wuxing said: "Receiving the mandate."

Regarding the "original source": life is formed by the combination of consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*). At the moment of taking birth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is primary.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The text describing the aggregate of consciousness consists of three parts: first, the description of the signs of the exhaustion of the life-process; second, the description of the process... [text continues].

This concludes the threefold exposition on the characteristics of the manifestation of consciousness through its essence and function. Within this section on the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, there are three analogies combined with the preceding material.

The first analogy compares the opening and closing of the six gates, wherein the *saṃskāra* acts as the pivot. The second analogy compares the web-like network of sentient beings, wherein the *saṃskāra* acts as the binding thread of the net.
The third analogy compares the resonance between karma and retribution, wherein the *saṃskāra* acts as the deep-seated channels. When the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, the pivot is removed.
The cessation of the web-like cords and the snapping of the deep veins—these are all signs that the formations (*saṃskāra*) have reached their end.

Second, in describing the essence and function of the exhaustion of formations, the long night and the fifth watch are used as metaphors for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of birth and death; the clear dawn and the first sunlight are used as metaphors for the sky of the nature of *nirvāṇa*.

Since one watch corresponds to one aggregate, their numerical correspondence is exact. Thus, when the aggregate of formations is exhausted, it is like the crowing of a rooster at the end of the night.

Looking up and turning back toward the east, there was already a subtle radiance. What remained unfinished was merely one *kṣaṇa* of the *āśraya-ābhāsvara* (the luminous substrate). These are all metaphors for the essence.
When the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are empty and still, they function as the full manifestation of clarity.

As for "the six sense-faculties being empty and still": if the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has not yet been exhausted, the faculties still possess objective entities. If entities persist, then [the faculties are not empty].
One attains non-distraction. Thus, when practice reaches its consummation, all is void and without substance; it is still and not chaotic. Internally and externally, all is limpid clarity.

Since the objects of the senses are no longer conditioned, the faculties have nothing with which to pair; there is no further wandering or fleeing, and one enters that which has no entry. Third, this describes the manifestation of consciousness.
It is only through the consummation of practice that one can reach the source from which beings are categorized and receive their life-force. Once consciousness—
When [the truth] is manifest before one, then by virtue of being observable, all categories that could originally be grasped are no longer summoned.

Because the celestial nature (*dharmatā*) is about to become luminous, the refined radiance does not sink; because the refined radiance does not sink, the Tathāgatagarbha mind—which has been consistently hidden within the various aggregates (*skandhas*)—is fully revealed.
However, this is merely the revelation of what was hidden; if one were to shatter and eliminate consciousness (*vijñāna*), [the result would be different].
In its hidden state, it is like the rising of the clear sun into the heavens, such that there is no darkness it does not illuminate and no secret it does not reveal. Therefore, it is said:
"This is what is called the realm of the aggregate of consciousness.

(3. The Characteristic of Exhaustion) If, among the various summonings, one has already attained identity within the midst [of phenomena], and the six gates have been dissolved and integrated, achieving the perfection of seeing and hearing, they become mutually pervasive.

When one’s surroundings, the ten directions, the world, and one’s own body and mind are mutually pure and as transparent as *vaiḍūrya* glass, with nothing obstructed internally or externally, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life. (2. Revealing the Source of Delusion) If one examines its origin, it is found that a phantom-like, vacuous, and inverted false imagination constitutes its root.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The 'multitudes summoned together within' refers to the *vijñāna-skandha*, the life-essence consciousness of the twelve classes of beings.

If, within this state, one uses the power of samādhi and prajñā to dissolve the six gates, so that the sense organs merge without division and their boundaries open without obstruction, then seeing and hearing will become perfectly penetrating and the six faculties will function interchangeably. From this, as for the external world and the internal..."

The body and mind are again subject to obstruction; this is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted. By nature, the essence is fundamentally one true reality, yet it is separated by sensory objects.
Between the essence and its function, the standards for identity and difference are lost, which is termed the turbidity of life (*jīva-kaṣāya*).

Therefore, when consciousness is exhausted, one transcends it. Consciousness is but a shadow of deluded awareness; its luminosity is originally without self-substance. Because it arises from inversion, it is called "delusive" (*wang*).
"Elephant-like emptiness refers to inverted, deluded conceptualization. Wuxing said: "The six faculties are not separated from one another; they all interpenetrate.

This is precisely what is clarified in the *Lotus Sūtra* as the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*). Gushan said: "'Wangxiang' (entailing the image) and 'fǎngxiàng' (imitating the image) both describe that which is unreal."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "If, among the various summonings, one has already attained 'sameness and centrality,' this correctly refers to the manifestation of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).
'Exhausting the six gates' correctly refers to the characteristics of the contemplation of objects. 'Exhausting' means to fully digest the efficacy of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*)."
The essence and consciousness are themselves True Suchness (*tathatā*); like ice melting when heated by hot water, they transform in their very substance into unsurpassed Bodhi.

"Grinding" refers to the power of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*); by destroying delusions to form wisdom, it is like stone polishing jade until the entire substance is perfected as the vast Nirvana.
The following text combines and opens [the gates], achieving the mutual use of seeing and hearing, which are pure and pervasive.

This is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom and abandonment. Although a *srotāpanna* has attained the six extinctions (*kṣaya*), they have not yet eliminated one name; thus, because it is combined, it is not yet perfected.
Furthermore, for all sentient beings, the six functions are separated and distinct, and they constantly undergo defilement; this is called "open" and unperfected.
Moreover, all sentient beings cannot [exercise] the six at all times, nor can they exercise each of the six individually at every single moment. This is collectively [the state of non-perfection].
If one speaks of their combination, they cannot achieve completion; yet now, when the six gates are dissolved and merged into one, the six functions remain vividly distinct.

When opened into six, the single mind is sovereign. Thus, although the six gates of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing differ, they harmonize as a single household and share a single master, flowing freely through all four directions and eight openings. Or, it may be considered as "seeing."
It is not a hindrance to see forms while hearing sounds and smelling fragrances; it is to see forms while seeing sounds and seeing fragrances.
Because it is thus, one sees forms without being stuck by them, and form cannot stick to the vision.
This is the purity of the mutual functioning of the six sense organs. This is a general statement regarding the purity of the five aggregates as the primary retribution. Below—
It is said that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) refers to the purity of the environmental retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*), hence the mention of the worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, the phrase "as well as body and mind" cites the environment while including the primary [subject] to manifest their perfect interpenetration. Indeed, the three realms are but mind and all phenomena are but consciousness;

yet, due to delusion regarding the awakening of one's nature, [consciousness] becomes the functioning of cognition, volitional action, perception, sensation, and form. Now, as for this consciousness...
Because their nature is restored to its source, the five kinds of delusive thoughts are entirely transformed into supreme awareness.

Thus, the internal body and external environment become as clear and translucent as vaidūrya crystal. Only when one reaches this state can it be called the sign of the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).

○ (2. Correctly explaining the manifestation of the signs; 2. First, the direct demonstration of the ten signs; 10. First, attachment to causes and what is caused by them; 2. First, returning to the source through the emptiness of all formations. Ānanda, you should know that this good man, having exhausted the emptiness of all formations and returned to the source within consciousness, has already extinguished arising and ceasing.

○ (2. From consciousness, the objective realm manifests; 2. First, the direct explanation of the manifestation of the signs. Yet, because his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected, he can cause his own body’s sense organs to either remain separated or merge together.

He can also cause himself to commune with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions, such that their awareness and his awareness become one, and he can enter into the perfect source. If he establishes a notion of "true" regarding that which he has returned to...

Regarding those who constantly give rise to superior understanding based on causes: (2. Arising Attachment and Forming Error; Part 1: Direct Demonstration) such persons fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons, becoming companions of Śivaka who take refuge in the obscure principle (*tattva*).

They become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. (Part 2: Conclusion and Manifestation) This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks attainment and forming a fruit that serves as a place of refuge;
it is far removed from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving birth to the seeds of external paths.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Since consciousness flows from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), when volitional formations are emptied, one returns to the source.

Because the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) has been emptied, birth and death have already ceased. Yet, because one still relies on the source of consciousness, quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.

Nevertheless, as one can gradually shatter the aggregate of consciousness and dissolve the six sense-gates, the six faculties of cognition become fused and unimpeded, and the various modes of awakened nature are harmoniously integrated.

Because it is non-dual, one is able to enter the perfect source (*yuan-yuan*). This "perfect source" is precisely the fundamental consciousness that fuses the barriers of the sense organs and penetrates all categories of beings.
If one takes this as the true ground of return and establishes it as the true cause, one falls into the attachment to a cause and its causal basis.
For a true cause is not something possessed; everything that is possessed is false. Thus, the *Sāṃkhya* heretics identify the *ālayavijñāna* [as their principle].
That which is the primordial state before form arises, the dark and silent initial mark, is that to which one returns as the true cause; it is precisely like this.
Because the mind has something to acquire and the fruit has something to return to, both cause and fruit fall into delusion.

This is why they oppose perfect penetration and turn their backs on Nirvana. Wuxing said: "To demonstrate the contemplation that allows awareness and cognition to universally penetrate and enter the perfect and primal source—"

This is a sign that arises within [meditative] practice. Such a state is merely a temporary attainment through the power of cultivation; it is not called a "virtuous realm" because one has failed to give rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Due to the arising of false attachments, one falls into the category of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

[Commentary] Tiantai says: There are two fundamental sources of consciousness (*vijñāna*). The first is the true source, which is the *āmalaka* (amala-vijñāna); the second is the deluded source, which is the *ādāna* (appropriating consciousness).
What is here called "returning to the source" refers to the eight consciousnesses. That which is "quiescent, extinguished, subtle, and wondrous" is the truly eternal, pure consciousness.

As long as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not been exhausted, consciousness has not yet returned to its source. Once birth-and-death has been extinguished, one is correctly practicing the Way.

The sense-faculties (*āyatana*) have already been exhausted, yet regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, they are not yet perfected. Although one may speak of returning, the source of delusion has not yet returned to its true origin.

While one can cause the separations and unions of one’s own faculties to open and close, though this speech is not yet truly attaining the pure mutual functioning of the six faculties, once the general characteristic of the faculty-gates has returned to the source, then union and opening are fully accomplished.
The signs of this have already sprouted. By means of them, one is able to enter the perfect and primordial source of true permanence.
The above summarizes the virtue of the cessation of consciousness and the manifestation of awareness. What follows below cites its faults;

that is, if one establishes the cause of true permanence within the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) to which one has returned—this is what the subsequent text refers to as "producing a realization of fulfillment where fulfillment does not yet exist."
The rest is as explained previously. However, regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and the five kinds of deluded thoughts:

although they differ in subtlety and coarseness based on their arising and cessation, in the daily activities of sentient beings, there is truly no moment when they do not pervade all the sense-gates (*indriya-dvāra*).

As stated in the first fascicle: "The single essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous and can give rise to all conditions," which means that the five aggregates are already fully present. Thus, now...
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is called "returning to the source" and "that to which one returns.

Within the gateways of the practitioner’s sense organs, those various conditions that have not yet arisen are termed the *ādāna-vijñāna*, the subtle consciousness. It is from this that the cavern of birth and death first takes its beginning;
it is also from this that the *tattva* of the non-Buddhists first takes its beginning. If one can truly perceive, see, hear, smell, and taste within this, [one realizes the truth].

To awaken to awakening and to know through knowing is like cutting down a tree by reaching its root or treating an ailment by finding its source; then, though there be a thousand branches and a hundred maladies, they will naturally wither away.

This is what is meant by not observing form and yet form being spontaneously destroyed. It may truly be called an excellent prescription for shedding the skeletal remains and a wondrous elixir for restoring life.

○ (2. Grasping at the Capable and the Incapable; Part 1: Returning to the Source through the Emptiness of Conditioned Phenomena) Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man has thoroughly investigated the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has extinguished arising and ceasing, ○ (2. The Arising of Objects from Consciousness; Part 1:

Correctly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) yet his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected—if he regards that which he returns to as his own self-nature, and perceives that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space arise from a single stream within his own body, and thus forms a superior conviction (*adhimukti*), ○ (2.
Giving Rise to Attachment and Forming Deviance; Part 1: Direct Demonstration) this person then...

Falling into the attachment to the "capable" and the "incapable," they see Mahesvara manifesting boundless bodies and take him as their companion; thus they become deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lose their true knowledge and vision.
(2. Concluding Summary) This is called the second [type]: establishing the "capable" as the mind, thereby accomplishing the fruit of capable activity;
it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of the great arrogant devas whose "I" is all-pervasive and complete.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "One clings to the source of consciousness (*vijñāna-mūla*) as one's own self, and claims that all sentient beings flow forth from it.
Consequently, one clings to the notion 'I can produce them,' yet in reality, this is impossible; therefore, it is said: 'This is not the grasping subject.
Maheśvara is the Māra-king of the Peak of Form (*rūpa-kṛtsnāyatana*). He falsely calculates that 'I can manifest boundless sentient beings. Furthermore—

"Capable" and "incapable" refer to categories. To conceive of oneself as capable of performing mental functions and producing results is to reckon that one is the support for those [functions] and can accomplish those tasks.
The "Greatly Arrogant Deva" refers to Maheśvara; because he claims capability where there is incapability, he is called "Greatly Arrogant.
"Pervasive and Complete" refers to reckoning that one's own essence is perfectly pervasive throughout the realm of space.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Although the preceding aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) serves as the common basis for the birth of the twelve classes of beings, this basis of birth is itself fundamentally rooted in consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Thus, it is indeed true that the twelve classes of beings flow forth from the aggregate of consciousness.
Yet, one alone does not know that there are twelve classes of beings of self-nature (*svabhāva*) and twelve classes of beings of other-nature (*parabhāva*).
It is similar. If one says that the twelve classes of beings arise from the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate), that may be so;
but to say that all sentient beings within the entire realm of empty space are but a single class flowing forth from within my own *vijñāna-skandha* body—how could this possibly be acceptable?
This would not only mean viewing the *vijñāna-skandha* as one's own self...
They take the delusory to be the real, and furthermore, they do not understand the principle that one’s own and others’ births and buddhahoods are both shared and unshared.

Those who discuss the inherent nature (xingju) today generally fall into this error. Since they have not yet mastered the tenets of our own school, what is there to be surprised about in their speaking thus?

○ (3. Grasping at Permanence and Impermanence; Part 1: Returning to the Source through the Emptiness of Conditioned Phenomena) Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you have already extinguished arising and ceasing. ○ (2. How Consciousness Gives Rise to Objects; Part 1: Correctly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) Yet, regarding that which is quiescent, subtle, and wondrous, it is not yet perfected.

If, within that which is the ultimate refuge, there is something upon which to rely, and you yourself suspect that your body and mind flow forth from that [refuge], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it—then, regarding that ground from which everything flows forth, you will conceive of it as a truly permanent body, free from birth.

Their understanding of cessation exists within the midst of arising and ceasing; they prematurely calculate that there is permanence, yet they are deluded regarding non-arising and confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell in this deep-seated attachment and establish their superior understanding [in this way]: (2. Establishing Attachment and Forming Deviance—Part One: Direct Demonstration) Such persons fall into the dualistic grasping of permanence and impermanence;

they take the Lord of the Self (Īśvara) as their companion, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. (2. Concluding and Manifesting) This is called the third [stage]: establishing causes based on the mind.
This results in a false conceptualization of the fruit, which is far removed from perfect penetration; it turns its back on the city of Nirvana and gives rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because one takes the source of consciousness as that upon which one relies, one suspects it to be that which can produce both oneself and all dharmas.
Consequently, one conceptualizes the place of origination and outflow as being the true, eternal, and non-arising essence. This is...

Within the process of arising and ceasing, one falsely conceives of permanence. Thus, one is both deluded regarding the true nature of non-arising and confused about the presently manifesting phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Because one takes the impermanent to be permanent, this is called the "clinging to permanence in the impermanent.

Since one conceives of that [source] as being able to produce the self, it is identical to conceiving of Maheśvara as being able to produce all things. This arises from relying on the source of consciousness to falsely conceive of permanence.

Because it abides, it is called the "established cause" (*pratītya-hetu*); based on the mind, it produces deluded conceptualizations as its fruit. The former [delusion] conceptualizes the self as producing the external world;
this [delusion] conceptualizes that external world as producing the self. Therefore, it is called the "inversion of the external world. Wuxing said:
"That which flows forth from 'that' refers to the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness) as the source to which one returns; it does not refer to another person."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, one took the aggregate of consciousness as oneself and regarded the various classes of beings throughout the ten directions as flowing forth from this "self.
Now, one takes the aggregate of consciousness as "other" or "that," and suspects that one's own body and mind flow forth from "that."
The empty space of the ten directions all arise from it; based on this, one forms the understanding that the true, eternal body is without birth or extinction.
Not only do they prematurely calculate the true and eternal within the midst of birth and extinction, but they also give rise to delusions and inversions regarding the perfect seed-nature.

○ (4. Knowing the Non-existence of Knowledge; Part 2: First, Returning to the Source through Emptiness of Formations) Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all formations (*saṃskāra*), you have already extinguished arising and ceasing. ○ (2. The Arising of Objects from Consciousness; Part 1: Correctly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.

If, among what is known, one’s knowledge is universally pervasive, then because of this knowledge one establishes a view such that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all called sentient beings and are no different from humans;
when these grasses and trees become humans, upon death they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions without distinction.

Regarding those who give rise to resolute conviction through universal knowledge: they fall into the dualistic attachments of "knowing" and "not knowing," becoming companions to the Pāṭha and Śākya adherents who claim that all-encompassing awareness constitutes awakening.
They lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth error:

calculating that a universally cognizing mind results in a false fruit; it is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted knowledge.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "That which is known" refers to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) that is being observed. This means that consciousness possesses the faculty of knowing, and all phenomena arise through this knowing.

Because one reckons that the essence of knowing is pervasive throughout all phenomena, a divergent interpretation is established: namely, that even insentient things are everywhere endowed with knowing.
Because there is no discernment [of such a claim], it is called "indiscriminate universal knowing. This is based on a lack of true knowledge.
Because they claim to know, they are called those who hold the attachment to "knowing while being ignorant. Bāṭa and Śākya are two non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas).
Their attachment to "all-encompassing awakening" means they cling to the notion that everything possesses cognition. This erroneous calculation takes perfect knowledge as the cause;

yet, since the mind is the cause, the result will ultimately be empty and false. To take what is without cognition as cognition is inverted knowledge. Guishan asked regarding what was previously stated:
"What difference is there between this text and the views that insentient things possess nature and that insentient things can become Buddhas? Is this not a dogmatic attachment? Answer: It is not so.

The eternally abiding true mind is of one essence and non-dual. It is through the functioning of various deluded thoughts that the distinction between the primary (the sentient) and the secondary (the insentient) arises.
Therefore, sentient beings, grasses, and trees are all like flowers in the sky. One should know that grasses, trees, mountains, and rivers are all produced by the own-mind of sentient beings.
Because they transform, it is said that when sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, grasses and trees likewise possess nature;

and when sentient beings attain Buddhahood, grasses and trees likewise attain Buddhahood. This is because there are no objects external to the mind, no space external to the flower, and waves do not exist apart from water.
Because their deluded attachments prevent them from understanding this, they claim that each individual blade of grass and tree possesses its own consciousness, and thus they speak [in such a way].
"When wood dies it becomes a person; when a person dies it becomes wood. This fails to clarify the single essence, resulting in erroneous calculations regarding pervasive perfection.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This person is returning to the source within consciousness and is about to realize the realm of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).

Seeing that the consciousness which is the object of knowledge is pervasively perfect, they perceive that every blade of grass and every tree is a manifestation of consciousness-only; yet they do not understand this.
Consciousness creates grasses and trees, and grasses and trees are themselves consciousness.

It is an error to claim that each individual blade of grass and tree possesses its own knowledge and awareness, asserting that they are all sentient beings no different from humans. There is no distinction between the animate and the inanimate;

if grasses and trees already possess knowledge and awareness, they must inevitably become human beings, and though humans possess consciousness, they too must inevitably return to being grasses and trees. This is called "no discrimination."

Because they have attained universal knowledge, they fall into the attachment that there is both knowledge and ignorance, giving rise to seeds of inverted cognition. This is also a profound state of delusion and confusion. (5. Grasping at Birth and Non-birth; Part 1:

Returning to the Source through the Practice of Emptiness) Furthermore, O son of good family, having thoroughly investigated the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you have extinguished birth and death. (2. How the Object Arises from Consciousness; Part 1: Correctly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected.

If, within the mutual functioning of the sense organs in their perfect fusion, you have already attained adaptability, then you will be able to respond to all transformations within the perfect permeation.

Giving rise to the desire for the light of fire, the joy of water, and the pervasive wind of craving, they contemplate the accomplishment of various sensory objects and each perform their respective venerated rites.

Taking these manifold objects as the fundamental cause of manifestation, they establish a doctrine of eternal permanence. (2. Arising of Attachment and Formation of Deviance; Part 1: Direct Demonstration) These people fall into the attachment to birth and non-birth.
All the Kāśyapas and Brahmins diligently exert their minds and bodies, serving fire and venerating water in their quest for [liberation].

Born into birth and death, they become its companions; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. (2. Conclusion and Manifestation) This is called the fifth [delusion]:
clinging to and venerating external objects, whereby the deluded mind follows after things to establish false causes for seeking and false hopes for results.
Thus, one strays far from perfect penetration, turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of perverted transformations.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The exhaustion of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) means the dissolution [of barriers] so that the various faculties of the six gates function interchangeably.

At present, because this has not yet been exhausted, one merely attains compliance [with the truth]. Because of this compliance with the perfect interfunctioning, one then calculates that all phenomena are capable of perfect transformation and can produce superior fruits;
for instance, claiming that fire can manifest radiance, and even that dust can achieve [such results]."
Regarding the realm of material phenomena (*bhājana-loka*), they consequently engage in perverse seeking and perverse contemplation, diligently honoring and serving them with a zealous mind.

They cling to these as being able to produce superior fruits, yet in reality they cannot; therefore, this is called "clinging to the non-arising of arising. These are the likes of the three Kāśyapa followers and other such heterodox practitioners.
Since they are deluded regarding the true mind and seek hope from external objects, both cause and effect are illusory, resulting in a perverted transformation.

The principle is called "transformative seeds. Wuxing says that "perfect transformation" refers to the realm of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) characterized by perfect fusion and transformation as perceived within contemplation.
"The arising of all things" refers to the characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The accomplishment of these objects is specifically termed the earth element; thus, these various objects collectively indicate the four great elements. Since one perceives that all these [arise] from...
The "Perfect Transformation" (yuanhua) refers to calculating that the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits do not transcend the radiance of fire and the purity of water;
hence it is said: "To manifest the original cause is to establish the understanding of permanence. Kāśyapa was also a distinct clan name among the Brahmins.
The "combined" [passages] below collectively subsume their respective categories.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: This also concerns the state of conforming to the realm of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) within the context of the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused sense organs.
Seeing fire as being consciousness-only yet possessing luminosity is to seek it through its phenomenal aspect; seeing water as being [consciousness-only... is likewise.
The water of consciousness has a pure master whom one delights in; the wind is the wind of mere-consciousness which can circulate throughout the source and which one loves;
the dust is the dust of mere-consciousness which can accomplish the sublime and which one contemplates.

Taking these various dusts as the fundamental causes for the manifestation of radiance, purity, and so forth, one establishes a view of permanence, unaware that deluded consciousness is entirely exhausted.
The luminosity of the fundamental essence manifests spontaneously; as arising and ceasing are extinguished, the purity of its nature is naturally revealed.
Obstructions dissolve and the essence flows through all things; when the dust of delusion vanishes, realization is achieved in this very place.
Thus, that which is incapable of arising serves as the basis for the perpetual arising of phenomena—this is the deluded seed of clinging to birth within non-birth.

○ (6. Taking that which has no refuge as a refuge; Part 2: First, practicing emptiness to return to the source) Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to their emptiness, you have already extinguished arising and ceasing. ○ (2. How consciousness gives rise to objects; Part 2: First, correctly clarifying the manner of their arising) Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*), it is not yet perfected. If, within this perfect luminosity, you reckon the voidness within clarity to be the cessation of all transformations, and take this eternal extinction as your ultimate refuge, thereby giving rise to a superior resolve—○ (2. Śūnyatā becomes their companion; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their knowledge and vision. (2. Conclusion and Manifestation) This is called the sixth fruit:

the result of a void and non-existent state produced by a mind that is utterly empty and non-existent. It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of nihilism.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: Because one does not clearly perceive the principle, one erroneously falls into nihilism. Thus, within the nature of perfect luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), one calculates everything to be void and non-existent.
Consequently, one annihilates all manifestations and returns to eternal extinction, unaware that this is a delusion;

it is called "returning to non-return" and is an attachment to external emptiness. *Śūnyatā* (舜若多) means "emptiness. To speak of "non-conceptual *śūnyatā*" is precisely to cling to the emptiness of annihilation.

This is the Way [of the heretics]. Because they cling to nihilistic emptiness (uccheda-śūnyatā), they take a void and non-existent state as their causal mind, thereby producing the fruit of annihilationist emptiness.
This eternal extinction of the basis is the nirvāṇa of the external paths (tīrthika). Wuxing says: "Non-extinction" does not mean that the manifold transformations are not destroyed;
"non" here is like "to break. The "manifold transformations" refer to the four great elements and so forth.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Perfect clarity" refers to the perfect clarity of returning to the source within consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Although there is still the subtle arising and ceasing of the consciousness aggregate, the coarse and heavy arising and ceasing of the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has already ceased.

Taking this absence of arising and ceasing as perfect clarity, one reckons that which is empty within the luminosity. From this, one destroys the myriad transformations and takes eternal extinction as the place of ultimate return.

Regarding this basis, there are two divergent paths. If one destroys the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and reckons that the voidness within illumination is not the cessation of the manifold transformations, thereby seeking to extinguish the body and annihilate wisdom for the sake of eternal extinction—this belongs to the ninth category as a refuge for those śrāvakas who are born into the seeds of entanglement in emptiness.
Now, as for the non-Buddhist practitioners of the "Non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*), they reckon that the nature of consciousness is profound, subtle, and continuous.
Cotton represents eternal cessation; by relying upon it, one destroys coarse perceptions, yet this is not the extinction of the manifold transformations.

Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), you have already extinguished arising and ceasing. However, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent cessation, it has not yet reached perfection.

If, within that perfect permanence, you firmly maintain the body as eternally abiding—identical to the subtle and perfect—it will long remain without decaying or passing away, giving rise to a superior state.
As for the explanation: [This] person falls into the attachment to what is not greed, becoming a companion to those Āsuras who seek long life;
they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh:

clinging to the source of life, establishing a cause of solid delusion, pursuing the fruit of prolonged toil, straying far from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of false extension.
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "The clarity and brilliance of the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha), in its state of profound stillness and immovability, is called 'permanence.

Now, seeing this permanence, one clings to the physical body as being identical to this subtle, perfect essence. Yet the body is fundamentally impermanent; it truly cannot be craved as something enduring.
Because one now stubbornly craves and adheres to it, it is called 'craving what is not to be craved' and 'clinging. Wēnlíng says: "Asita..."
This "Incomparable One" (Abhaya) is none other than the Long-lived Seer (Āyuṣmat Ṛṣi). Although his life was prolonged, it ultimately ended in destruction.
Now, if one seeks to make this delusory body solid in order to attain permanence, it is merely a fruitless exertion and a vain prolongation of existence. Changshui remarked:
"Regarding 'fruitless exertion' (cháng láo), 'láo' should actually be pronounced as 'láo'; it is an error for the character 'láo' (firm)."

[Tiantai’s Commentary] This is also a mistaken view regarding Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). [The practitioner] assumes that the physical body is identical to consciousness—pervading the body, pervading the mind, pervading the support, and pervading the supported—and thus is perfectly eternal.

Within this perfect eternity, they desire to make their physical body permanently endure, identical to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), eternally refined, full, and never declining or passing away.
They do not realize that the seeds of the impure body will ultimately undergo transformation.
It is ruined. Although it is truly not something to be craved, because one now stubbornly craves it, one falls into the attachment of craving rather than non-craving.

Even the disciples of our own inner teachings nowadays imitate this by practicing the dual cultivation of nature and life, calling it the "joint school of Immortals and Buddhas"; all such cases are of this kind.

○ (8. True Non-attachment to the True; Part 2: Returning to the Source through the Emptiness of Phenomena) Furthermore, O son of good family, having thoroughly investigated the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you have extinguished birth and death. ○ (2. Arising of Objects from Consciousness; Part 2:

Properly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction that has not yet reached full perfection, you perceive that life-force and consciousness are mutually pervasive.

Fearing that the defilements (*kleśa*) might be entirely exhausted, you remain within them at this juncture, sitting in a Lotus Palace, extensively manifesting the seven treasures and increasing the number of precious women, indulging your mind as you please. For those who give rise to such superior resolve: ○ (2. Giving Rise to Attachment and Forming Deviance; Part 2: Proper Demonstration) This is...

Such a person falls into the false attachment that there is no truth in truth; they become companions of Ṭakkirāja, deluding themselves regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and losing their true knowledge and vision.

(2. Conclusion and Manifestation) This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thought and establishing the fruit of blazing dust, which is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives birth to the seed of celestial Māras.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Because they take the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the source of their life-force, it interpenetrates the three periods of time.

If the consciousness-aggregate were to end, their life-force would also end; who then could realize the true permanence? Therefore, within meditative concentration, they transform various objects of desire to maintain their defilements and prevent them from being extinguished.
Relying on such perverse thoughts, they wish to realize true permanence, yet they do not know it is wrong."
This is called the "attachment to the non-existent as real. Ṭakkirāja can transform objects of desire to amuse himself;

he belongs to the class of the *Kāmeśvara* (Lord of Desire) gods. Because of his perverse thoughts, he is reborn as a celestial demon (*devaputra*). Indulging solely in worldly desires, he is named the "Fruit of Blazing Dust.
Uṣā is a beautiful woman.
[Commentary] Tiantai said: "In contemplating the mutual interpenetration of the three periods of time, one fears that [the seeds of the māra] will be exhausted.
This interpretation applies to the Hīnayāna: if one wishes to transform others, one must retain afflictions to nourish rebirth; if one seeks nirvāṇa, one must extinguish the body to terminate wisdom.
However, the species of the present māras are different from this; they instead manifest the seven treasures and increase their precious concubines, indulging in unrestrained excess."
Yet their minds remain attached to worldly toil; this is why they belong to the lineage of the celestial Māras.

They do not realize that while the body of birth and death is finite, the dharmas inherent in its nature are infinite. As the Prajñāpāramitā states: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form;
the same applies to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. By relinquishing the body of birth and death, one attains the true and eternal.
To cast aside the body that experiences the joy of nirvāṇa and instead pursue the body that possesses the marks and signs of a subtle dust-atom,
and to abandon the joy that is fully endowed with pure and wondrous retribution— to practice the teachings of Ḍākinī-kalpa while being deluded by them is truly extreme folly.

"Furthermore, O son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you have brought to an end birth and death. Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), it is not yet perfected.

Within the clarity of life, you distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and resolve upon the true and the false; cause and effect respond to one another as you seek only for spiritual resonance, turning your back on the path of purity.
This is what is called 'seeing suffering, abandoning accumulation, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path,' wherein you rest once cessation has been attained."

Furthermore, those who do not advance further but give rise to a fixed resolve will fall into the category of the "determined-nature Śrāvakas" and become companions to the arrogant monks who have heard nothing.

They will be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage: when the perfectly refined essence corresponds to the mind, it results in the fruit of seeking quiescence;
it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.

[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The 'clarification of destiny' refers to the thorough investigation of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) to clearly understand the fundamental source from which sentient beings receive their destiny.
Since birth and death arise from the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*), while coarseness and subtlety arise from karma, one relies on the Four Noble Truths for analytical discernment.

One regards suffering and its origin as coarse and false, and cessation and the path as subtle and true. Thereupon, one focuses exclusively on cultivating the causes of the Path to seek the resulting realization."
The fruit of cessation. Because they are content with a mere fraction [of realization], they abide in cessation and immediately cease their efforts;

these are specifically those among the śrāvakas of fixed nature who are characterized by overweening pride. This, then, is the subtle fruit of seeking quiescence, achieved through the causal mind of perfect application.

"Perfect application" refers to the definitive discernment of coarse karma, wherein one seeks only the application of perfection to realize the partial truth, becoming entangled in emptiness and pursuing quiescence.

Guishan said: "Regarding 'turning one's back on the path of purity,' since one has already given rise to a limited understanding [of the Lesser Vehicle], one turns away from the path of perfect fusion—permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Here, among these four virtues, only one is briefly cited."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Now, as for distinguishing the refined from the coarse and resolving the true from the false, cause and effect respond to one another;

one seeks only through resonance and response to perceive suffering, sever the origin of suffering, realize cessation, and cultivate the path. This serves as the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-way and the essential road for ascending to the site of Bodhi.
It is likewise a matter of seeking out how refined or coarse, and true or false these are. Indeed, there are three [aspects].

The suffering and its accumulation within the realms are as follows: they consist of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*), and the birth-and-death of limited segments (*paricchinna-bhava*).

The suffering and its accumulation beyond the realms are as follows: they consist of the dust-like and infinite ignorance-afflictions (*avidyā-kleśa*), and the transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*).

There is the Way and its cessation that transcend the realms: they consist of the Path Truth of arising-extinction and non-arising, which eliminates the active afflictions and completely eradicates their habitual tendencies, resulting in the partial-true Nirvana (*pratisaṃvid-nirvāṇa*).

There is a path that transcends the boundaries of the world, wherein cessation occurs. This is the true emptiness of Nirvana, where the three delusions are exhausted through the immeasurable and unconditioned Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
It is here that the Lesser Vehicle and the Greater Vehicle are distinguished; it is here that the gradual, the sudden, the partial, and the perfect are established.

Now, within the clarity of life during the stage of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), one discriminates between the subtle and coarse, and the refined and crude, of the Truths of Origination and the Path.
One must resolve the authenticity of the extinction of suffering by taking the two types of causal paths—those involving birth-and-death and those being birthless—as the means of response.
One hopes for the fruit of partial truth (*pratyekabuddha-nirvāṇa*) as the corresponding reward.

This does not exceed the vision of the suffering of the triple world, the severing of the accumulation of views and afflictions, the realization of the extinction of partial truth, and the cultivation of the path of the three trainings; once abiding in extinction, one rests.
They do not advance further; this is what is called turning one's back on the path of purity and falling into the fixed nature of a śrāvaka, etc.

(10. The Fixed Nature of the Pratyekabuddha: Part Two, Initial Practice of Emptiness and Returning to the Source) Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as empty, they have already extinguished arising and ceasing. (2. From Consciousness Arising the Object: Part One, Correctly Clarifying the Manner of Arising) Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), it is not yet perfected.
If, within the perfectly interfused, pure, and luminous awareness, they develop an investigation into the profound and subtle, they establish a nirvāṇa that is not [the ultimate].

As for those who advance by generating resolute conviction: they fall into the company of those of fixed nature among the *pratyekabuddhas*—those solitary practitioners of various conditions who do not resolve their minds [to seek the Mahāyāna].
Thus they become their peers, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth stage:

the "Ocean-like Mind" (*yongxin*) which achieves the fruit of profound clarity, yet which violates and distances itself from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to a sense of awakened perfection and brightness.
"Not transforming the perfect seed.

[Commentary: Wēnlíng says that the fusion of pure enlightened clarity is precisely the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Although it is free from delusive habits and is perfectly fused and pure, because it has not yet transcended consciousness, it is called "enlightened clarity" (*jue-ming*).
If one were to take this as profound and subtle and establish it as the fruition (*phala*), [it would be a mistake].

If one realizes [this], it is merely the fixed-nature pratyekabuddha or solitary buddha. This is simply the result of stagnation in profound clarity, achieved by taking the "oceanic" (yǒng-hù) nature of perfect enlightenment as the causal mind.
When the oceanic nature of enlightenment is like the mind, the penetration of that oceanic nature of enlightenment is the penetration of the oceanic nature of enlightened awareness.

This means that one merely penetrates the universal penetration of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) without advancing further. "Profound clarity" (*zhanming*) refers to the perfectly integrated enlightened clarity.

Because what is perceived is limited to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-śukti*) within the perfect luminosity, and its fundamental nature does not turn back, it is called the "perfectly clear enlightenment of the unchanging perfect seed."
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The perfectly interfused, pure, awakened clarity" refers to the destruction of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

The principle of the partial truth of *nirvāṇa* realized therein is the same as that realized by the *śrāvakas* mentioned previously; however, it differs slightly from theirs in that it erodes the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) and develops a profound and subtle penetration.

Nevertheless, there are two distinct types—*pratyekabuddhas* (solitary realizers) and *bodhisattvas* (or *pratyekabuddhas* who rely on conditions)—and it is the former who are referred to here as having "accomplished."
Their companions are not necessarily those of the same two types due to identical conduct.

What was previously called "entanglement in emptiness" and what is now called "non-transformation" both refer to those of fixed nature who are unable to redirect their resolve; this is also a clear textual authority from the present sutra for refuting śrāvakas of fixed nature.

○ (2. Concluding by refuting the heterodox and extolling the orthodox. 2a. Refuting the heterodox. 2aa. Revealing the faults. Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* result in madness midway through their practice because they rely on delusion;
within what is not yet sufficient, they produce the realization of sufficiency. This occurs because the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) functions in mutual conflict, leading to this state.
When sentient beings encounter this manifestation, being stubborn and deluded, they fail to reflect upon themselves; each rests content with their own cherished habitual delusions.
If you claim that this cessation shall be the ultimate ground of rest and that you have already attained the fulfillment of unsurpassed Bodhi, you commit a great falsehood;
you will be influenced by external paths and demonic spirits, and when your karma is exhausted, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. You will fail to advance as Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

(2. Exhortation and Praise, Part One: The Exhortation) "You all must maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, so that after my parinirvāṇa, you may transmit and reveal this Dharma-gate."
In the final age, may you cause all sentient beings to universally awaken to and understand this meaning, so that they do not encounter demons or bring about their own ruin;

may you protect and comfort them with compassion, quelling perverse conditions and causing their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby they shall achieve fulfillment and never again encounter divergent paths.

[Commentary] Wuxing says that "great false speech" specifically refers to the preceding eight [categories]. The preceding eight are collectively termed externalists (*bāhyaka*) and demonic influences (*mārakarma*).
Alternatively, one may specifically designate seven as externalists and the eighth as demonic influence. Since neither has severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said they "fall into hell.
The Two Vehicles differ from this, hence it is said they "do not advance. Regarding the phrase "seeing demons," "seeing" here implies a violation of principle.
Regarding the names: the first eight [afflictions] contradict the True [Nature], while the middle two give rise to false views within the realm;
the latter two contradict the Middle Way principle and give rise to false views outside the realm. This is because the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is itself ignorance.

Furthermore, among the first eight, seven are purely views, while the eighth possesses both views and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because it retains the dust and toil (*rajas*) to produce superior resolve (*adhimukti*). Wēnlíng says: "The preceding..."
"Guarding against the demons of the mind and guarding against the demons of views exhausts the essentials for assisting the Way.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: In the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the ten realms (*daśa-vastūni*) are fully elucidated. Only the realm of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) is that which is observed through the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the beginner.
The remaining nine realms are observed only when they manifest; if they do not manifest, they are not observed. Now it is said:
The consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) wherein the mind and its objects interact is precisely the object of contemplation for the beginner.
Each person’s own cherished habitual delusions of the mind constitute the objects manifested through the application of calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).

To command them to preserve and protect themselves, to compassionately rescue them, and to eliminate false conditions so that their body and mind may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is to contemplate while awaiting their manifestation. This is because...
Since beginningless time, as sentient beings have transmigrated through the six realms, what kind of seeds have not existed? What habits have not been cultivated?
Without the conditions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, these seeds and habits do not manifest.

If one does not anticipate this principle in advance, then upon encountering an object that triggers them, one will be dragged away by it—becoming either a follower of external paths, a malevolent spirit, a *śrāvaka*, or a *pratyekabuddha*.

Awakening. At first, one uses penetration to break through obstruction; yet in the end, that very penetration comes to hinder penetration. Encountering a forked path midway, one loses the home of the precious jewel.

Therefore, out of great compassion, the Tathāgata spoke this spontaneously without being asked, so as to cause all sentient beings to awaken to and understand this meaning, hoping that none will allow demons and the like to create deep calamities for themselves. Now, regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*):
Regarding the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*), Master Wuxing’s analysis concerning non-Buddhists, demonic influences, and those of the two vehicles is already detailed.

As for the first eight types, since they have fallen into heterodoxy and externality, their afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) remain entirely intact; he merely indicates the portions of vital energy (*vāyu-bhāga*) manifested within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
If this is so, then as for the latter two types, there should be a distinction between the exhaustion and non-exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness. If...

Those who have not yet exhausted [the afflictions] give rise to entanglements within emptiness and fail to undergo transformation; this is the division of the qi of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).

If they have already exhausted them, then the coarse defilements of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava*) fall away together, and they realize the principle of true emptiness. To give rise to attachment to the dharmas of birth is for a Bodhisattva to fall from the "summit" (*mūrdhan*);
this is what the Master of Wuxing meant by "contravening the Middle Way and giving rise to heterodox views outside the realms."

This accords with Tiantai’s clarification that those of sharp faculties in the Perfect Teaching may, in a single lifetime, transcend and ascend to the ten stages.
From "Perfect Clarity" down to "Jewel Moon," the realization of this final mind is demonstrated; it possesses both the Dharma and its metaphor, as well as its essence and its function. Vajra Dry...
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) of sublime awakening. Upon transitioning into the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is itself sublime awakening;
hence it is said that one "enters into the Tathāgata. The ocean of sublime adornment is the culmination of merit (*puṇya*). The perfection of *bodhi* is the culmination of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Returning to non-attainment is the culmination of principle (*tattva*). Merit is liberation (*vimukti*); wisdom is *prajñā*; and principle is... [the ultimate].
This is the Dharma-body. The secret treasury of the three virtues, neither vertical nor horizontal, is fully manifested herein.
To investigate its cause from afar, it truly results from the power of the three types of cessation—*śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*—cultivated by the initial mind.
Wénlǐng says: "The Ocean of Sublime Adornment" unifies all virtues and harmonizes diverse streams; it is adorned without being adorned, and realized without being realized.

This is the fruition-ocean of realization. What was previously called the "wondrous path of adornment" consisting of the ten thousand practices of Śūraṅgama is nothing other than tending toward this very state.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present sense organs will function interchangeably. This clarifies—

In this sutra, it is taught that within the stage of "semblance" during the seventh faith of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) are exhausted, and the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) is realized.

however, Master Yuechuan refuted this as not necessarily being the case. He argued that, for instance, in the case of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the four aggregates (*catvāraḥ skandhāḥ*) have already been exhausted, yet they remain deluded.
