powerful spirits lose heart and flee; and *chi* and *mei* demons no longer arise. Until reaching Bodhi, one shall lack nothing; those of inferior capacity will advance, and their minds will not be confused regarding Great Nirvana.
(2) For those of dull faculties who rely on secret mantras: If there are ignorant and dull-witted sentient beings in the final age who do not yet recognize the stages of dhyāna and samādhi...
Knowing that you delight in preaching the Dharma and practicing samādhi, yet fearing you might fall into heterodoxy, I wholeheartedly urge you to uphold this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī Mantra.
If you are unable to recite it, write it down and place it in your meditation hall, or carry it upon your person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to disturb you.
(3. Commanding Veneration) You should reverently honor this final instruction left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions as they reached the ultimate stage of cultivation and advancement.
[Commentary] Wēn-líng says: This concludes the intent of the five aggregates to discern the māras, so that one may know how to guard against them deeply.
"Vipaśyanā within śamatha" refers to the wisdom of meditative concentration. "Analyzing with awakened clarity" means to analyze this awakened clarity;
such is the syntactic force of the Western [Sanskrit] text. "Tǐ" (褫) means to lose or to be stripped away.

[Commentary] Tiantai said: Someone may raise this objection: "If deluded and dull sentient beings have not yet recognized *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), they do not know how to preach the Dharma.
Yet it is further stated that they 'delight in practicing *samādhi*. Is there a *samādhi* distinct from *dhyāna*? In response, I say:
To recognize *dhyāna*, one must know the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) of this sutra; thus, regarding all phenomena...
His entry into the gates is like the cook Ding’s dissection of an ox; there is nowhere he cannot go.
Toward all demonic realms, he is like the vajra-king’s precious mallet; there is nothing he encounters that he does not shatter.
Those who now delight in practicing samādhi are merely beginners who receive oral instructions from their teachers regarding the twenty-five gates; having heard one dharma—be it emptiness or...

Since provisional phenomena are identical to reality, yet one must diligently cultivate the Buddha’s contemplation lest it become identical to heterodox views, he exhorted him to recite divine mantras.

[Section Two: Further Resolving Remaining Doubts] [Part One: The Question] [Subsection One: The Sūtra Narrator’s Account] Ānanda immediately rose from his seat; having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in reverent reception, memorizing it without loss.

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more. [Subsection Two: The Formal Petition] [Part One: Stating the Doubt] "As the Buddha has said, within the characteristics of the five aggregates, there are five kinds of delusion."
"Regarding our original thought-mind, we have not previously received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed instruction.
Furthermore, as for these five aggregates, are they to be eliminated simultaneously or exhausted sequentially? Within these five layers, what constitutes their respective boundaries?
[Second Request] "We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion to clarify the minds and eyes of this assembly, and for the sake of all beings in the future age."

"Be born to become the eye for the future. [Part Two: The Answer and Explanation (divided into two sections)] [A. Direct Answer to the Question (divided into three sections)] [1. Answering the Delusive Conceptions of the Five Aggregates (divided into two sections)] [a. Direct Answer (divided into three sections)] [i. Clarifying that the Five Aggregates Share the Same Characteristic (divided into three sections)] [aa. Clarifying that Original Enlightenment is Free from Delusion] The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The subtle, true, wondrously bright, and originally enlightened nature is perfectly pure; it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements of the sensory world. [ii. Clarifying that Delusion Gives Rise to Manifestation] "Even up to empty space, all are produced by the arising of delusive thoughts. [iii.

Clarifying the Joint Arising of the True and the Delusive] "This is fundamentally because the wondrous brightness and subtle truth of original enlightenment give rise to delusion, thereby producing the various vessel-worlds, just as in the case of the one named Yan-ratuo (Śaśaviṣāṇa)."
"Confused about one's head, one recognizes its reflection.

[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Essential truth" (*jīngzhēn*) is the Middle Way. "Wondrous brightness" (*miàomíng*) is quiescent illumination. Because it is quiescent, it is provisional; because it is illuminating, it is empty.
The three truths are interpenetrating and fundamentally free from defilement; this is collectively termed original enlightenment (*běnjué*) and perfect purity. This is the single [aspect].
This section discusses the true nature (*tathatā*). It continues by discussing, in isolation, how all phenomena arise from deluded thought (*vikalpa*).

This is fundamentally intended to clarify, in combination, how the world arises from the interaction of the true and the deluded. The reason for this is that without the preceding discussion in isolation, one would not understand the meaning of "separation" (*li*);
without the subsequent clarification through combination, one would not understand the meaning of "identity" (*ji*). Wénlǐng says: "Birth-and-death is the karma of delusion; it is dust and grime."
Regarding delusive conditions: since nothing remains within the truly pure nature, all arises due to delusion, just like being confused about one's own head.
Thus, it can be known that among the characteristics of the five aggregates, the five delusions constitute the root.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: The Tathāgata’s revelation of the five kinds of false conceptualization first clarifies the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and subsequently clarifies the differentiated characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Within the common characteristic, he first clarifies that true awakening is devoid of falsity;
this is the section beginning with "The refined truth is wondrously luminous. Next, he clarifies how falsity arises; this is the section beginning with "down to empty space. Furthermore, next...
This clarifies that birth exists through the conjunction of the real and the false; this refers to the section beginning with "This is originally the fundamental awakening.
Without the first two sections, it would be insufficient to manifest their separation; without the final section, it would be insufficient to manifest their identity.
As for separation, the real and the false proceed together without harming one another; as for identity, the essence of the real and the false is fused without obstructing one another. They do not...
If there is harm, the false can be eliminated and the true can be restored. If they do not obstruct one another, then the false has no form and its essence is empty stillness;
the metaphor of the flower is best for careful investigation, while the analogy of waves and water is still worthy of being taken as a model.

[II. Explaining that [the two views] are not yet identical with the Fivefold [Teaching]. First, explaining that they arise from the primary cause and conditions. Delusion originally has no cause; yet within deluded thought, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. [Second, explaining the attachment to spontaneity.

Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*). [Third, explaining that both are false. That nature of empty space is like a real illusion arising; thus, both causes and conditions and spontaneity are all conceptual constructions of the deluded mind of sentient beings.

[Fourth, explaining that even the medicine should be forgotten. Ānanda, you know where delusion arises; you speak of the causes and conditions of delusion. If delusion were fundamentally non-existent, what would there be to speak of as the delusion?
Causes and conditions are fundamentally non-existent. How much more so for those who do not understand that they are naturally so? Thus, the three fetters are all delusions;
for this reason, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false imagination.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: This clarifies that delusion has no cause and cannot be subject to conceptual calculation. One may speak of causes and conditions when one knows the origin of delusion;
however, since its origin is unknown, how could there be any causes or conditions? Furthermore, would not inferring it to be "spontaneous" (zìrán) merely constitute another false calculation?
[Commentary] Tiantai says: Previously, the identity of the root was clarified; now, the identity of the branches and their extremities is clarified.
Since only the branches and extremities arise from the root, it is said that delusion fundamentally has no cause, yet within deluded thought, the nature of causes and conditions is established.
This statement that the five aggregates arise from direct causes and conditions refers precisely to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions designate them as "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*), which refers to the proponents of non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*) who calculate things to be spontaneous.

Dependent origination is the medicine for the new physician to destroy the non-Buddhists' doctrine of spontaneity. Once the illness has been removed, the medicine should be forgotten; if one continues to cling to the medicine, [it becomes a hindrance].

Medicine, conversely, becomes an illness; therefore, both medicine and illness are refuted. It is said that the nature of empty space is likewise real yet produced by illusion, and that causes, conditions, spontaneity, and nature are all merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.
The subsequent section beginning with "Ānanda" further clarifies why both medicine and illness are to be dispensed with.
This is because the establishment of causes and conditions is intended to clarify the arising of deluded causes and conditions.
The fruits of delusion may have causes and conditions that can be explained; however, if the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty, what causes and conditions could there be?
This clarifies that even the medicine should be forgotten. If the medicine itself should be forgotten, how much more so the illness?

Therefore it is said: "How much more so for those who do not know to infer the natural. One must understand that once the establishment of causes and conditions is termed "delusive," then what [further cause or condition could there be]?

Because they exist through the spontaneity of causes and conditions, it is said: "Therefore, the Tathāgata has clarified for you that the fundamental causes of the five aggregates are likewise nothing but false conceptualization.
Thus ends the explanation of the common characteristics of the five aggregates.

[II. Explaining the Distinct Characteristics of the Five Aggregates (5): First, explaining the delusion of solidity. Your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents; if your mind were not characterized by thought, it could not have come here to transmit life within these thoughts.
As I previously stated: when you think of the taste of vinegar, saliva arises in your mouth; when you think of climbing a high peak, a tingling sensation arises in your feet.
Even if the precipice does not exist and the vinegar has not arrived, your body certainly possesses the same sensory faculties as others, and your saliva is no different.
For what reason do you speak of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that this manifested physical body of yours is called the first delusive thought of solidity.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Thought" refers to the illusory image of desire and love, which is a deep-seated channel; it is the self-love of the abandoned physical form.

Because it flows forth, it is said that the body arises from the perception of parents. Because the mental aggregate (*skandha*) rides upon the darkness of craving for perceptions, it is said that the mind transmits life within perceptions.
The analogy of the sour plum and so forth is used to verify that the body arises from false perceptions;
thus, it corresponds to the principle of falsity. If it were not of the same category as falsity, falsity could not induce it. The body arises from perception, and the mind [arises] from...

Recollection arises; life is transmitted through recollection. Because various recollections intersect and solidify to form the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is called "solidifying deluded thought" (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: From here below, the specific characteristics are clarified. This is precisely because the common characteristic depends upon deluded thought. This is...

Therefore, the specific characteristics do not depart from their fundamental basis. Now, first we shall clarify the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). When it says "your substance," this refers to the essential nature and characteristics of the aggregate of form;
that is, the original seed. Both the red and white drops exist because of the parents' lustful thoughts, and they have birth because of the seeds of your own mind's desire-thoughts.
A single mind and a single form bind together with firm solidity, arising from...
From birth until old age, they have never been separated, being like a form and its shadow, never diverging from one another. When one imagines the taste of vinegar, saliva flows;
when one thinks of ascending a height, the feet ache. Such mental conceptions cause the physical senses to become sour and numb.
That false imaginings pervade all categories of existence is proven by this very evidence.
II. (Explaining the Delusive Perception of Luminosity) This aforementioned perception of luminosity at a height can cause your physical form to truly experience a stinging sensation.

Because this sensation arises from a causal condition, it can move the substance of your form. What you now experience before you—the agitation caused by the alternation of the favorable and the injurious—is called the second delusive perception, that of "empty luminosity."
[Commentary] Wuxing said: "To be born by reason of causes" means that one is born because of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

That which can move the substance of form (*rūpa*) is precisely the experience of bitterness and astringency within the physical form. One should know that the three aggregates (*skandha*) of form, sensation (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) arise through mutual dependence upon false conceptualization and are necessarily inseparable.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Your body was previously produced from the conceptualization of your parents," and the subsequent text says: [as follows].
The various mental constructions that arise as grasping at forms—such as the perception of shapes—are all like the mental images of a precipice or sour objects.

By this it is clarified that these three types of false conceptualization are coarse and manifest in their substance; they do not function like the subtle and difficult-to-perceive *samprayukta-vijñāna*.
For this reason, the celestial Māras produced within the first three *skandhas* also have coarse characteristics, whereas the mind produced within the latter two *skandhas* [is otherwise].
Seeing the two māras, their characteristics are likewise subtle. "You now appear before me" is the direct indication of the characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*).

That which is favorable and beneficial is pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*); that which is adverse and harmful is painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*). There is also that which is neither adverse nor favorable, namely neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), but this is merely omitted from the text.
Wēnlíng says: "Facing the void, one's false conceptions give rise to a truly bitter and astringent [feeling]. This refers to the adverse [sensation].

Since all that follows is false, and the appearance of gain and loss is in constant flux, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substance; it is merely a void clarity that appears to exist, and is therefore called "false imagination of void clarity.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: According to conventional discourse, sensation arises from the colors of the sense organs and their objects. Now, we rely on the perspective of delusion...
Taking "perception" (*saṃjñā*) as the basis for this treatise, it is because of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) that feeling (*vedanā*) arises. Therefore, it is said:
"This aforementioned mind of high-flying perception can cause your body to truly experience bitterness and astringency. However, feeling does not arise solely because of perception;
furthermore, form (*rūpa*) arises because of feeling. Thus, it is said: "By reason of the arising of feeling, the substance of form is moved. This, then, is feeling.
Because sensation arises from thought, it causes the perception of form; yet sensation does not perceive itself. That which is clearly manifested is thus empty, and this can be known. (Third:

The Interpenetration of Delusive Thought) It is because of your mental deliberations that they drive your physical body. The body is not of the same category as thought; for what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
It takes on various forms, and the mind gives rise to shapes that correspond to those thoughts. When awake, these are the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, they become the various [dream-images].
"In dreams, the movement of your thoughts and deluded sentiments is called the third false imagination, 'fusion.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: 'Thoughts' refer to empty sentiments; 'the physical body' refers to substantial reality.

That the dissimilar—emptiness and substance—can influence one another is due to the fusion of thought. The mind generates empty thoughts, while the form grasps substantial objects; thus, mind and form..."
That diverse functions can correspond to one another is due to the pervasive nature of perception (*saṃjñā*).

As for the fluctuations and transformations between waking and sleeping—which cause the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind—all of these are the interpenetration of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: The five kinds of false conceptualization explained here consist of the two dharmas of form and mind, which are never separated from one another.

This is because they initially take up name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their seed. Once they have become firm and mutually bound, if the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) do not exist, then the four aggregates (*catvāraḥ skandhāḥ*) do not exist;

and if the four aggregates do not exist, then the six sense faculties do not exist either. Form and sensation (*vedanā*) have already been discussed as above. As for the following, perception (*saṃjñā*)...
The same applies to the three aggregates of formations, consciousness, and feeling. Now, it is said that the mind arises and takes on form in correspondence with thought;

the meaning of their mutual integration is thus clearly understood. That awakening is perception and the sleeping mind constitutes various dreams also expresses the principle of the integration of form and mind.
This is what Liezi meant when he said: "In awakening, the form opens up; in sleep, the form merges."

It is so. (The Subtle and Hidden Delusions of the Four Ming Mountains): The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves secretly and incessantly. The fingernails grow, the hair turns white, the vital energy wanes, and the face becomes wrinkled.

Day and night they replace one another, yet there is never any awakening to this. Ānanda, if this were not you, how could the body undergo such change? If it must be truly you, [then why do you fail to perceive this?]
"How is it that when there is no cognition, your various formations (*saṃskāra*) do not cease for even a single moment, yet this is called the fourth subtle and hidden delusion?
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "If this were not you" refers to the fact that the principle of transformation does not abide, and so forth.

"How is it that the substance shifts? is an inquiry into such things as the growth of nails and hair. As for the phrase "if necessarily," it means: if one claims that the shifting of the substance is indeed you.

Why is it that one does not perceive this characteristic as being replaced by another? Because it is not perceived, the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is termed "obscure and hidden.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The principle of transformation" refers to the principle of cosmic creation. Regarding the passage of time, it consists of days passing and months...
As the spring and autumn seasons alternate, for all things there is growth, development, ripening, and harvest;

for the human body, the nails grow, the hair turns white, the vital energy wanes, and the face becomes wrinkled. This is precisely what the current text discusses in detail regarding the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Those of the world who explain this principle attribute its efficacy solely to the power of cosmic transformation (*zhìhuà*), failing to realize that [it is actually... the work of the mind.
The principle of transformation is entirely rooted in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the aggregate of formations, in turn, is rooted in the human mind.
The statement that "the three realms are but mind; all is but consciousness" can be verified by this.
Because it undergoes change while receiving its own essence, yet remains utterly without awakening, it is therefore called "hidden delusion."

○ (5. Explaining the False Conception of the Phantom-like; Part 1: Correctly Discerning its Characteristics) Furthermore, that which you call "constant," being a state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness, does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body.
If it were truly a refined reality, it could not admit the delusions of habitual practice;

for what reason, then, did you all once in years past behold a strange object, and though many years passed, there was neither memory nor forgetting of it, until later, upon suddenly beholding that former anomaly again, the memory was vividly restored?
Yet, since it has never been lost or forgotten, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, there is no calculation as to how many moments of thought have been perfumed.

[Commentary] Zhenji said: "This aggregate (skandha) encompasses all eight consciousnesses; its function is active while its essence is constant. Its seeing and hearing are clear and brilliant, identical [to the nature of mind]."
First, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Master Jie of Wuxing said: "The intention of [the Master] is that seeing and hearing constitute its function, thus it is active;

its clarity and precision constitute its essence, thus it is constant. Yet he does not realize that the present text takes seeing and hearing themselves as the clarity and precision, and regards activity and function as the constant essence.
Why is this? Because consciousness has no fixed location and is omnipresent throughout all the sense organs (*indriya*). When an organ encounters an object, although it involves...

When functioning, it operates within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state before the arising of good or evil. This indeterminate state is designated as "the place of clarity, brilliance, and profound stillness.
To clarify its boundaries: the five sensory consciousnesses, the five mental consciousnesses, and the sixth mind-king (*manas*) all constitute this locus.
Fearing that sentient beings might reckon this to be permanent, the Buddha entrusted [this teaching] to Ānanda to first establish its definition.

Regarding the phrase "called 'eternal'": if it were truly pure and real, it could not admit the habitual influence of delusion; this refutes its eternity. "Pure" refers to spiritual clarity, and "real" refers to constancy.

The passage beginning with "By what cause... demonstrates the characteristics of delusional habituation. That which is "moment by moment perfumed" means that in the past, upon seeing extraordinary things, one took up their seeds within consciousness.
If it were not perfumed, even if one later encountered those same strange objects, there would necessarily be no recognition of them.
Regarding the characteristic of memory: since it is never lost, one knows that throughout the interval, ignorance constantly perfumes the mind-moments.
Since this perfuming is delusory, what essence of true reality could there be?

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Furthermore, regarding "the place where your clarity and brilliance are tranquil and unshaken," this sets aside the primordial luminosity (*mūla-prakāśa*) to discuss the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-sāra*) alone—namely, the essence of seeing, the essence of hearing, and so forth.

As in the first two fascicles on the ten meanings of the nature of seeing, and the sixth fascicle on the three virtues of the nature of hearing, these are all demonstrated by focusing specifically upon the consciousness-essence within the six sense organs. Therefore, it says: "Within the body..."

It does not emerge from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. This essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is precisely the "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, which has not yet been liberated from the essence of seeing and properly belongs to ignorance (*avidyā*).
To grasp it as permanent would be a profound error. Therefore, it is said: "If it were truly an essential reality, it could not admit the habituation of delusion.
However, if there were only the essence of seeing, it could not habituate itself; it must depend upon consciousness.
The essence can give rise to various conditions; that is, the six types of consciousness arise through the union of mother and son, resulting in habit-energies (*vāsanā*).

These habit-energies reside within the six [consciousnesses], yet they accumulate within the eighth. Now, we shall refute [the notion of] that which accumulates these habit-energies. Consider how one perceives something extraordinary in the past and now recollects it:
if this were not due to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) with respect to sensory objects (*viṣaya*), how could such a thing be possible? — Wu-xing.
This teaching is also a case of knowing how to speak. ○ (II.

Repeatedly Revealing the Subtlety) Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the True Suchness. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance; because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it is not that there is no flow at all.
If it were not the source of thought, how could it receive the habitual tendencies of delusion? It is not the same as the mutual functioning of your six sense-faculties.
Because this deluded thought cannot be extinguished at any time, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, you have become habituated to a certain degree of clarity;
yet, internally, there is a vague, empty, and non-existent fifth inverted state of subtle, refined ideation.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "Profound stillness is not truly profound; it is merely a state of hidden depth that one fails to perceive.

Therefore, it is likened to a torrential stream flowing in deep concealment, such that its course cannot be measured or known. This is the very source of true recollection and the substance of delusive thoughts.
One must simply dissolve the six sense-gates so that delusive habits have no place to lodge; only then can they be extinguished. (Strung together constantly)
It is habituation (*vāsanā*). "Near" (*jī*) refers to the subtle and minute. That which seems non-existent is called *wang*; that which seems existent is called *xiang*.

Because its substance is refined and subtle, it is named *wangxiang* (phantasmal image), *xuwu* (voidness), and *dian dao jing xiang* (inverted refined ideation). Wuxing says: "The mutual functioning of the six sense organs and so forth first breaks through view-delusion and thought-delusion;

therefore, when deluded thoughts are extinguished, the coarse defilements fall away first. Question: In the preceding passage, the reception of perfuming was discussed in relation to ignorance (*avidyā*).

[Question: It was said [previously]: "Now, when deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) are extinguished, why would they stop at merely the cessation of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation)?

[Answer: Because that which is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*) also contains the seeds of *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*. Therefore, what was previously pointed out—that objects are remembered or forgotten—is precisely the coarse aspect (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*). Now, although the seeds and their manifestations (*bīja-vyakti*) are exhausted, the fundamental [ignorance] still remains.
This does not mean that the six sense organs have attained true mutual functioning (*anyonya-viniyoga*). [Question: Does this essence of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi lack...?
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), there is nothing that is not ultimate. As for the power and function of destroying the aggregates (skandhas), how could they be short? Answer:

It is not that the power and function do not accord with the essence and principle of the teaching. This is because, among the fifty levels of demonic states discussed in the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, all arise from the deluded thoughts of the five aggregates of the segmented realm (*bhavāgra*).

Now, since we are discussing the cessation of these [delusions] up to this point, we have reached the stage where the six sense organs function interdependently (*ṣaḍindriya-saṃprayoga*). If it were as previously stated...

When the flow is reversed and the one is made whole, the six functions cease to operate; this immediately destroys fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is distinct from the deluded conceptualizations within this state.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: This stillness is not True Suchness (*tathatā*), like a rapid current... namely, the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).

"The subtle consciousness and its habitual tendencies form a torrential stream; fearing that [disciples] might be deluded regarding what is real and what is unreal, I have never openly expounded this.
This is precisely because habitual tendencies accumulate within consciousness: if one were to say they exist, the current is so swift that they cannot be seen;

if one were to say they do not exist, seeds ripen and suddenly arise. Because they lie in the interval between "as if existing" and "as if non-existent," they are called "phantom-like, void, and illusory."

Regarding this "perception" (*saṃjñā*): Wu-xing took this consciousness to refer precisely to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the mundane realm (*dhātu*).
Yet Yue-chuan, being unacquainted with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), refuted this as incorrect; his error was even more egregious.

(2. Conclusion of the answer) Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of false conceptualization. (2. Answer to the question regarding the boundaries) If you now wish to know the depth of their causal boundaries:
only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form; only contact and separation constitute the limit of sensation; only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception;
only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into stillness that merges with stillness constitutes the limit of consciousness.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are also called the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādāna-khandha*).

Because of a single moment of delusive ignorance, one undergoes and grasps these [aggregates] to conceal and hide oneself. Regarding the statement "due to the realms" (*dhātu*): fundamentally there are no realms;
they arise due to delusive appearances. Thus, form is not form in itself; it exists because of emptiness, and thus the limit of form is established. This applies even up to cessation.

Because the arising of existence from its own extinguished causes is thus extinguished, one reaches the limit of formations (*saṃskāra*). Consciousness is called "profoundly lucid," yet this profundity does not lucidify itself.
Because formations do not flow outward, the nature enters the primordial clarity and merges with profound lucidity, thereby reaching the limit of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "Only form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitute the limit of form. Form is the fundamental aggregate (*skandha*), whereas emptiness is not an aggregate.
However, form does not manifest itself; it is manifested by means of emptiness. Therefore, emptiness serves as the boundary of form.
"Only contact (*sparśa*) and separation (*viveka*) constitute the limit of sensation (*vedanā*). Contact is the fundamental aggregate, whereas separation is not...
The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is merely contact; it does not contact itself. Because it manifests through separation, it takes separation as its sphere (*dhātu*).
As for "recollection" and "forgetting," these are the limits of perception (*saṃjñā*): recollection is the fundamental aggregate, while forgetting is not an aggregate.
Memory itself does not remember; it is manifested through forgetting. Thus, forgetting constitutes the boundary of memory.
Only cessation and arising are the limits of formations (*saṃskāra*). Arising is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), whereas cessation is not an aggregate.
However, arising does not arise of itself; it exists because of cessation. Thus, cessation constitutes the boundary of formations.

"Deeply entering the profound stillness and returning to the limit of consciousness" means that the profound stillness of the six faculties is their fundamental *ālayavijñāna* (the true, eternal, and wondrous stillness), not the [defiled] *skandhas*.
However, this stillness does not exist in itself; it is because of the wondrous stillness that the delusive stillness is revealed.
Therefore, the wondrous stillness constitutes the boundary of consciousness. This precisely describes how delusion arises from the truth, as if from...

It originates as a source and flows forth as a stream. It begins with the wondrous stillness (*miao-zhan*) which becomes consciousness (*shi*); from the stillness of consciousness it becomes the surging current of formations (*xing-lan*);
and from the surging current of formations it becomes the waves of perception (*xiang-bo*). Feeling (*shou*) and form (*se*) are like the surface of the waves and the skin of the ripples.

○ (Third: The Answer Explaining the Sequence; First, Clarifying the Sequence by Way of Arising and Ceasing) These five aggregates originally arise in a layered succession: their arising has consciousness as its cause, and their ceasing begins with the elimination of form.
[Commentary] Gushan says: In terms of arising, one proceeds from the internal to the external and from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on clothes.

Thus, when deluded regarding the principle, there is consciousness and even form. In terms of cessation, one proceeds from the external to the internal and from the coarse to the subtle, like taking off clothes.
Thus, when awakening to the principle, form is exhausted and even consciousness is exhausted.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: "These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession" summarizes the characteristics of the aggregates, wherein there are these five stages.
Regarding "arising occurs because of consciousness and ceasing begins with the removal of form":

the characteristic of the fivefold arising has the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as its beginning, while the characteristic of their cessation has the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as its starting point.

"○ (2. Clarifying the Sequential and Non-sequential in Terms of Principle and Phenomena): In terms of principle, there is sudden enlightenment; with enlightenment, [delusions] are simultaneously extinguished. In terms of phenomena, they are not suddenly eliminated;

they are exhausted through gradual stages. [Commentary: Wēnlíng says: "Sudden enlightenment and simultaneous extinction are like knowing that the cloth fundamentally has no knots, and thus neither [the knots nor the cloth] exist."

[Commentary] Tiantai says: "The principle is suddenly realized," and so forth. If one relies on the text itself as the Tathāgata explains it, the meaning of the "Heavenly Turban" (the *tian-jin*) is fully exhausted.

However, should this still not be clear, it is permissible to further cite the passage from the preceding section on the five aggregates being fundamentally the *Tathāgatagarbha* to facilitate understanding for others.
This refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) being like flowers in the sky, and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)...

The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is like the perception of touch in empty space; the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is like saliva produced upon smelling vinegar; the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is like a torrential stream;

the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is like lifting the void for a thousand li. To understand it thus is to realize that fundamentally nothing exists, and one should contemplate its emptiness and fusion.
The wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is then majestically and alone revealed. As stated in the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (Yuánjué jīng): "To know illusion is itself liberation."

To depart from non-action through skillful means and to depart from illusion through awakening—this is precisely what is meant by "there being no gradual sequence. As for the statement, "Matter is not suddenly eliminated;

it is exhausted through a sequence," this is because the signs of the arising of the true cause possess an orderly progression; therefore, the signs of its cessation likewise possess an orderly progression.
If one can use principle to harmonize with phenomena and use phenomena as a ladder to ascend to principle, then the sudden and the gradual are one.
From gradual to sudden: once the sudden and the gradual proceed in tandem, both the sudden and the gradual are simultaneously extinguished.
One who can understand in this way may be said to know the Way.

(Third, regarding the previous demonstration of the sequence and non-sequence: "I have already shown you the knots on the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth; what is it that you do not understand that you must inquire about once again?"

[Commentary] Wuxing said: The preceding explanation also possesses two meanings—sudden and gradual. The substance of the cloth is one, which serves as a metaphor for true nature; awakening to this constitutes the sudden.
The knots on the cloth differ from one another, which serves as a metaphor for deluded thoughts; their removal constitutes the gradual.
To trace it back, the celestial cloth was knotted through a sequence and must likewise be unraveled through a sequence. This is what is illustrated by the six...
Regarding the arising and ceasing of the sense organs (*indriya*) and the five aggregates (*skandha*), at first glance they appear similar, yet upon further investigation, they differ.
Why? Because the meaning of the six sense organs is horizontal, whereas the meaning of the five aggregates is vertical.

For instance, when the six sense organs delude the truth and give rise to falsehood, and through that falsehood form the sense organs, there is certainly no sequence such as "eye first" and "ear second. This remains the case even when returning from falsehood to the truth.
Is the principle of proceeding from the coarse to the subtle not, by its very nature, a lateral progression?

When I previously used the sequence of untangling knots as a metaphor, I was merely referring to the distinctions between the six sense organs and the selection of the Perfect Penetration—that is what I meant by "sequence. Now, I clarify that the five aggregates likewise arise from delusion regarding the Truth;

they originate from false imagination and, through that falsehood, constitute the aggregates. Since it is said that their arising cause lies in consciousness while their cessation proceeds from form...

Is it not the case that "removing" (*chu*) signifies "erecting" (*shù*) the meaning? If one employs the metaphors of "binding" and "untying" to illustrate this, then the sequence of the two stages possesses a clear and orderly progression.
One should understand that the metaphors presented in the preceding passage cannot be used to challenge the nature of the dharmas;

likewise, the examples cited here cannot be used to challenge the aggregates (*skandha*) by means of the sense bases (*āyatana*). These timely explanations require an understanding of their general framework.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Wuxing stated that the principle of the arising of the six sense organs previously discussed is horizontal (*tieng*), whereas the principle of the arising of the five aggregates (*skandha*) now discussed is vertical (*shu*).
One must not use the previous metaphors to challenge the present Dharma; one must not use the examples cited here to challenge the sense organs.
These are teachings suited to the occasion, and one must understand their general framework. Although the meaning is correct, however—
Furthermore, there is a principle here of the horizontal being vertical and the vertical being horizontal, which has not been discussed by the various masters of past and present;

let me attempt to explain it. What is meant by "the horizontal being vertical"? For example, the nature of the six sense organs is fundamentally horizontal, yet the Tathāgata defines them according to the vertical principle, saying:
"When the six are liberated, the one perishes; it is likewise so. This is because of you...
The mind-nature, beginningless and deluded, gives rise to false perceptions; as this delusion does not cease, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to the dust of the world.

"The mind-nature, deluded" refers to the false manifestation of what is called "luminous awareness. "The wearying faculty of sight gives rise to the dust" means that from this, the weariness of worldly toil and afflictions are induced.
The intermediate points may be understood by themselves. This meaning of arising is both horizontal and vertical. Furthermore:
The statement, "This root is first understood as initially attaining the emptiness of persons," refers to the meaning of extinction (*nirodha*), which is horizontal while being vertical.

What is meant by "vertical while being horizontal"? As clarified in the current text, the five kinds of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are all explained without departing from the substance of the six sense organs and their objects;
this is the meaning of origination (*utpāda*), which is vertical while being horizontal. Furthermore, it says: "Principle..."
Thus, sudden enlightenment involves the simultaneous dissolution of both [delusion and its objects]; this sense of extinction is precisely what is meant by "vertical" and "horizontal.
If this is so, then in the preceding passage where metaphors were cited, each knotting of the rope possessed a sequential order from beginning to end.
However, when citing any single knot to correspond to the Dharma, how can one use the metaphor to challenge the Dharma? The example cited here is vertical.
Among these, there are horizontal correlations that extend to the six sense organs; by this analogy, how can one use the sense organs to challenge the [classification of] the aggregates (*skandhas*)?
At present, the general outline lies precisely here. Furthermore, the subtle and profound characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) must also be understood.
Thus, the meaning of the previous passage’s statement regarding "the mind-nature becoming deranged" already encompasses the five aggregates. In the present passage, the five kinds of delusion...
The meaning of "conception" (saṃjñā) likewise encompasses both the three subtleties and the six coarsenesses.

It consists of the five aggregates summoned by the delusions of the four abodes (catur-vāsa-bhūmi), as well as the five aggregates summoned by fundamental ignorance (avidyā). These are the delusions that produce karma within the four and five abodes.
These two types of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the fruits of suffering summoned by delusion and karma. Yet Master Gakuen was unaware of this;

he generalized that the five abodes of affliction (*pañca-vāsa-bhūmi*) are summoned solely by the one type of five aggregates belonging to the internal realm (*dhātu*) and the four abodes of attachment (*catur-āsaya-bhūmi*).
Having fundamentally erred on this point, he gave rise to numerous fallacious arguments to criticize the Wuxing commentary—this was a mistake.
This is an error.

(2. Concluding Exhortation and Transmission) You should take this root-source of deluded thought and achieve a thorough understanding of it, transmitting it to future practitioners during the age of the Dharma’s decay (*mofa*), so that they may recognize its falsity, develop a deep revulsion for it, realize the existence of *nirvāṇa* within themselves, and no longer cling to the three realms.

The Realm. [Commentary] Wēn-líng says: "Now, by means of this principle, one awakens oneself and awakens others, forever severing the source of delusion and collectively returning to the ultimate fruit.
The preceding section on the "Aids to the Path" is concluded. The main body of the text ends here. What follows below is the "Flowing... [section].
This refers to the general classification.

[The Commentary] Tiantai says: There are three meanings of *nirvāṇa*: *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (intrinsic purity), *pariniṣpanna-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (perfect purity), and *upāya-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (purity through skillful means).
Taken together, these are simply the secret treasury realized by the Tathāgata. Regarding its nature...
Purity corresponds to the Dharmakāya; perfect purity (*pariśuddhi*) corresponds to Prajñā; and skillful means purity (*upāya-śuddhi*) corresponds to Liberation.

Separating these according to persons: essential purity (*prakṛti-śuddhi*) belongs to the Buddha; skillful means purity belongs to the Bodhisattvas; and perfect purity belongs to the Three Vehicles. Separating these according to stages:
perfect purity belongs to the Perfect [Vehicle] at the stage of the Seven Faiths; skillful means purity belongs to the Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Faiths; and essential purity belongs to...
From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-garbha*), these are all explained by enumerating them individually.

If one speaks in terms of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), then to mention one is to include the three, and to mention the three is to include the one. The present text, for the time being, speaks from a general perspective regarding those who shatter the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the realm of birth and death;
this pertains to the *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa* (perfectly pure nirvana). If one truly knows that the quiescence and extinction of nirvana is something to be rejoiced in...
Then one will no longer cling to the defilements of the triple world.

○ (Part Three: The Distribution [of the Sūtra], in two sections: First, the Tathāgata’s Exhortation to Circulate the Sūtra; Second, the Extinction of the Evil Causes of Avīci Hell to Reveal the Power and Function of the Sūtra. First, the Comparative Measurement of Merit from Giving. First, the Questioning of the Magnitude.

Ānanda, suppose there were someone who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven precious gems, and offered them to serve and make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, with a mind that never failed in its devotion—what do you think? Is this...?
"Would a person obtain much merit through the causal conditions of such a gift to the Buddha? [The second answer: Superior] Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless.
In the past, there were sentient beings who gave the Buddha seven coins; by relinquishing their bodies, they still obtained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

How much more so for one who, before the Buddha's very eyes, gives precious jewels throughout the entirety of space, filling all Buddha-lands, even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa."
Even this cannot equal such merit; how could there be any limit to it? (2. Encouraging Circulation: Part One, How Even Grave Evils Can Be Eliminated) The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not false. If there is another person who has committed the four grave offenses or the ten *pārājika* transgressions, they will pass through the Avīci Hell of this world and other worlds in a mere instant, and until the end of the ten directions, there is no place of uninterrupted suffering (*avīci*) that they shall not experience."

If one can, throughout their life, take this Dharma-door and reveal it to those who have not yet studied it during the final kalpa, that person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very thought;
the causes for suffering in the hells they were to undergo will be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss. (2.

Merit Surpassing Previous Giving) The merit obtained shall surpass that of the previous givers by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million, a billionfold, and so on, even to the extent of incalculable numbers.
"Beyond the reach of analogies.
[Commentary] Changshui says: There are many reasons why one obtains supreme merit. First, the sutra being propagated is the Buddha’s ultimate discourse;
its teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are all inconceivable. Second, in the final age there are many obstacles, yet one is able to [propagate] this...

This is because circulating this sutra is truly rare and extraordinary. While the merit of the three types of giving yields only the retribution of saṃsāra and thus benefits only oneself, propagating this sutra benefits others and leads them to the fruit of the outflow-free state (anāsrava). For this reason, a single thought [of propagating the sutra] surpasses the aforementioned forms of giving.
Wénlǐng remarked: "By using the Dharma to instruct people, one can eliminate severe retributions and transform suffering into joy."
As for those who excel: by means of this, they cause the mind to become luminous and realize its true nature (*xinxing*), detach from sensory clinging and restore profound stillness;

they resolve the six consciousnesses, eliminate the single [root], shatter the *skandhas*, and strip away demons, thereby attaining the fruit of the Treasure King (*ratnarāja*) without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Since that is so, then the elimination of severe retribution is merely a shallow and mundane description; in truth, one shall realize the same as them.

[Commentary] Tiantai says: Regarding the comparison of the merit of propagating this sutra, while the explanations of Changshui and Wenling are broad, the most precise [teaching] is that the essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous;
"the seeing of seeing is not seeing" and "the hearing of hearing is not hearing.

This is the essential gateway for clarifying the mind and perceiving the nature, and the swift path for shedding attachments and returning to stillness. It is the method for resolving the six and losing the one...

The wondrous finger is the adamantine mallet that shatters the aggregates and strips away demons; by looking directly downward, one suddenly attains the Dharma-body, and in this very life, one may ascend to the precious fruit.
May people hear this Great Dharma, contemplate this Great Meaning, cultivate this Great Practice, and realize this Great Fruit.
May they dissolve karmic retributions in a single instant and be born in the Land of Bliss with a mere snap of the fingers, so that the merit of their transformation returns to themselves.
The same applies to its merit. The Buddha’s own lips have weighed and measured this; it is true and not false.
Having heard of these benefits, how could one not admire them and circulate them to benefit both oneself and others?

○ (2. Manifesting the Power and Function of the Sūtra through the Good Fruit of Generating Bodhicitta) Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sūtra and uphold this dhāraṇī as I have extensively explained—exhausting kalpas without end—and who act according to my instructions and practice the path as taught, they will directly attain bodhi, and demonic activities shall no longer exist for them.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "The preceding [section] exhorted the circulation [of the text]; this exhorts its recitation and upholding. Wǔxīng says: "The former [benefits] others and gains merit;
this [benefits] oneself and achieves the Way. Alternatively, one may explain the preceding passage based on this meaning:

that the merit gained by revealing and teaching those who have not yet studied is superior, because sentient beings derive benefit from the teaching, the recitation and upholding, and even the attainment of the Way.
[It is] because it is great.

○ (2. The Sūtra Master’s Conclusion on the Circulation) After the Buddha had spoken this sūtra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, all the worldlings—including devas, humans, asuras—and the bodhisattvas from other directions, the noble ones of the two vehicles, the ṛṣis, youths, and so forth... [all were present].
The spirits and deities of great power who had resolved their minds were all filled with joy; they paid homage and departed.
[Commentary] Wēnlíng says: "All" refers to the assembly of listeners present at the gathering. "Sages, seers, and youths" refers to the class of celestial seers (*deva-ṛṣi*).
The powerful spirits, ghosts, and various protectors of the Dharma all attain the joy of the Dharma according to their respective levels of realization. Wuxing says:

"Those who have first resolved their minds" refers to those at the stage of ordinary beings outside or within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). "All experience great joy" means this universally encompasses both ordinary beings and sages.
[Commentary] Tiantai says: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three meanings for "joyful" (*pramudita*):
first, the purity of the person who preaches; second, the purity of the Dharma preached; and third, the purity of attaining the fruit by relying on that Dharma.

Since the sutra records that the Buddha was greatly joyful after preaching this sutra, it refers specifically to the purity of the Dharma preached. However, this wondrous Dharma cannot be [realized] unless one possesses the appropriate capacity (*yogyatā*).

If one were to object that this should not be explained, it must be said that because the subject and object mutually establish one another and the response and stimulus are manifested together, these three meanings are fully present.
Thus, all sutras without exception possess this meaning; yet, whether Mahayana or Hinayana, partial or perfect, they are both the same and different.

If one were to fully explain the characteristics described in this sutra, then there would be nothing—be it teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stages, cause, or fruit—that is not [present].

Because it is ultimately pure, it is titled *The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas and the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa*.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas and the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa*.
Fascicle Ten (End). Preface to the Encouragement to Maintain:
Revealing the Path of Śamatha through the Cultivation of the Samādhi of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*), which is the King of Śūraṅgama and is fully endowed with the ten thousand practices.

The wondrous essence of sentient beings lies in transcending through a single gate. Because Ānanda regretted that his extensive learning had not yet perfected the power of the Way, Kāśyapa (Kāśyapa-Matanga) used false perceptions as a means to point directly to the human mind.
By questioning him at the seven locations, he polished the dust from the precious mirror so that its original clarity naturally appeared;

by distinguishing the eight returns, he scraped away the film with a golden lancet so that illusory reflections were simultaneously eliminated. Thus, he rejected all攀緣 (*pán yuán*, objective clinging).

The mind is not the mind. To reveal true awakening, even seeing is already transcended by seeing. Having manifested the true to shatter the false, he nevertheless uses the false to discourse upon the true.

He exhaustively investigates the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), arranging them into four categories; both "caused by conditions" and "spontaneous" are cast aside.

He synthesizes earth, water, fire, and wind, collectively naming them the seven elements (*mahābhūta*). Thus, the three truths—the conventional, the ultimate, and the middle path—are perfectly interfused.
The fundamental Tathāgatagarbha contains and exhales the ten voids; it manifests various signs in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.

Thus, even the one and the many are mutually identical, and the small and the great are mutually accommodated. It manifests jeweled lands upon the tip of a hair and turns the wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust.

For those who have attained freedom from obstruction, inverted perceptions are dissolved over the course of billions of kalpas; for those who do not follow discursive thought, the wild mind ceases and is itself Bodhi.
Those with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching have already deciphered the secret cause; those of middling or inferior vessels must now set forth the wondrous practices.

Thus, the path for the long-traveling guest to return home is opened, and the gate to the house bestowed by the Heavenly King is pointed out. One must interrogate the fundamental cause of all sages and rely upon the realization of the proof.
Wu spoke of the initial expedient means. In accordance with the teaching-body of this region, he selected hearing as the foremost perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).

Next, for the purpose of gathering the mind, he again administered the precepts. Relying on the pure and clear instructions proclaimed by the World-Honored One of former times, the manifested *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha expounded secret gāthās.
When the three studies are fully perfected, that which is realized is not partial; all delusions are消 (dissolved).

If one has passed away without attaining the truth, what can be expected? How much more so for those who have meticulously investigated the seven realms of rebirth and how beings are born according to their karma;

who have understood through painful analogies the six modes of sensory interaction and how retribution is summoned by habitual tendencies; who have been shown the fifty stages of *dhyāna* to deeply guard against the demons of craving and false views;

and who possess the eighty thousand types of capacities for liberation to counteract worldly toil and afflictions—such as these, you must maintain and protect them, and entrust them with the exhortation to propagate [this teaching].

From beginning to end, there is nothing that is not the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization. Whether refuting or establishing [doctrines], one does not depart from the eternally abiding true mind.
When the lute, the harp, and the *konghou* encounter skillful fingers, the forests, trees, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the sound of the Dharma.

This causes even those of the icchantika class to destroy their Mleccha ways and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) through samādhi; or, by discerning the truth within themselves, they establish themselves as sages.

Whether one proceeds from the mutual application [of the stages] and transcends to the final mind, sitting at the Great Site of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*) and ascending to Unsurpassed Awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), all matters are ultimately firm and solid.
One extensively opens the many gates of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) for Bodhisattvas;

throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one moves freely and spontaneously, entering together into the Tathāgata’s wondrous sea of adornment (*vyūha-sāgara*). How ultimate is this teaching! How magnificent is its merit! I am ashamed of my own errors.
Yet, I have ventured to provide a tentative synthesis and harmonization of these teachings. Out of a deep love for the Dharma, I offer this earnest encouragement and exhortation.
I trust that scholars from all quarters will deign to examine and peruse it.

Written by Weize of Sīhalavana, this "Synthesized Commentary" (Huìjiě), along with the preceding and following prefaces and introductions, is compiled together with the root scripture in ten fascicles. It was completed yesterday, in the year Jiǎshēn.
In the past, this was once carved into palm-leaf format (Sanskrit *vajra-patra*) and widely circulated.

Some have remarked that while the palm-leaf version is indeed excellent, those scholars from all quarters who travel to study under Chan and lecture masters still lament its inconvenience for inclusion within their satchels.

Thereupon, Zhang Ziming of Wu Commandery led his fellow practitioners to carve it again into booklets (*fangce*). This was simply to accommodate the convenience of each individual. Thus it is recorded.
The one who [provided] the woodblocks was Luo Yuan of the same commandery. The one who provided the wooden boards was Wang Wenyong.
Those who proofread, collated, solicited donations, and managed the project were Si Ju of Yichun, Shixun of Huating, Shan Yu of Gaochang, and Zheng Yin.
Carving began in the late spring of the Renchen year of the Zhi Zheng era and was completed in the eleventh month.
It is hoped that those who provide the offerings, those who transcribe the text, and those who exert their strength to assist in its completion;

those who hear it, see it, read and recite it, and uphold it—may the karmic conditions for their registers of merit arise, and may the causes for the Way be manifested through these words. May every character emit light, manifesting auspicious signs to eternally support the sacred transformation.
As the Dharma-seal is proclaimed and transmitted, may every person awaken to the truth and return to the source, attaining the fruit of Buddhahood without passing through the kalpas of a *saṃgha*.
Completed. Respectfully inscribed again by Linchuan Keli.
